items.title: New Zealand's World-Beating Sovereign Wealth Fund Returns 14.2%
body: The New Zealand Superannuation Fund, one of the world’s top-performing sovereign wealth funds, returned 14.2% in the year through June, powered by a rally in global equity markets despite being underweight in outperforming tech stocks.

About half of the portfolio is invested in equities while being underweight US stocks, Jo Townsend, chief executive of Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation that oversees the fund, said Wednesday in an interview.

“For us, it’s about the valuations,” Townsend said, adding that US stocks look expensive. Instead, she said the fund has “found other investment opportunities that we believe will add diversification and return benefits to the portfolio over the longer term.”

NZ Super takes a total portfolio approach, a strategy that involves collaboration across the portfolio management team to optimize the whole portfolio rather than individual asset classes. Around 40% is in private markets investments such as property, timberland and private equity, she said. The fund has also been buying bonds while they are cheaper, although it doesn’t amount to a significant asset allocation change, she said.

Townsend was speaking after NZ Super posted its pre-tax return after costs in the latest financial year, with funds under management rising NZ$9.3 billion ($5.4 billion) to NZ$94.4 billion. The fund is still on track to double in size every 10 years, Townsend said, adding that as it gets bigger, investing become a “more challenging” task.

“That’s occupying our mind,” she said. “How do we use AI to improve capability and manage risk in the organization?” She cited “getting ready to manage scale and manage risk in an increasingly volatile environment,” as a key challenge.

The fund, which began investing in 2003, was created by the then-center-left government to help finance the rising cost of the state pension. As a result, there will not be meaningful withdrawals for another 30 years, Townsend said.

Over the 10 years from 2015, the fund’s average annual pre-tax return after costs is 10.3%, making it one of the top-ranked funds tracked by consulting firm Global SWF. Over the past 20 years, it has achieved an annual average return of 9.7%, compared with the reference portfolio’s annual average return of 8.2%.
Read more: A $600 Billion Experiment Kicks Off at Biggest US Pension Fund

items.title: Shrinking Chinese Fuel Inventories Raise Chance of Export Curbs
body: China’s gasoline and diesel inventories are plunging as refiners grapple with a tightening domestic market, raising the chance the government may move to limit fuel exports again.
Gasoline stockpiles at Chinese state-owned fuel suppliers dropped 2.9% last week to the lowest since 2022, according to JLC International. Diesel holdings declined 2.4% to a 15-month low.

Beijing moved quickly to curb oil product exports in the early weeks of the US-Iran war, depriving Asian buyers of much-needed fuel but also helping to keep a lid on global crude prices. Authorities subsequently eased the restrictions, and shipments of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, known as clean products, had recovered to a combined 2.55 million tons in July, according to the latest Chinese customs data.

“With the domestic market tightening, we see an increasing risk that Beijing could restrict monthly clean product exports to around 1.2 million tons in the fourth quarter,” said Jianan Sun, an analyst at Energy Aspects Ltd. in London.

China’s government strictly controls the amount of fuel refiners can export, and they were only allowed to resume and increase shipments on the condition that they keep inventories at elevated levels.

With some oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz, volumes are still well below pre-war levels. And the recent closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline and Houthi territorial gains in Yemen are threatening shipments via the Red Sea. Chinese independent refiners, meanwhile, have lost access to their favored Iranian crude due to the US blockade.

That’s pushing up premiums for oil from Africa and Latin America, as Chinese buyers scramble to source alternative barrels. The situation is becoming so dire for the independents, or teapots, that they may have to cut run rates in the coming weeks.
JLC, a Chinese industry consultant, collects data directly from oil majors’ provincial marketing companies across the nation. The government doesn’t release official inventory figures.

Xinjiang’s rail expansion will triple outbound coal capacity to almost 300 million tons by 2027, shifting China’s marginal thermal coal pricing toward cheaper inland supply and away from seaborne imports, said Bloomberg Intelligence.

The US and China are discussing slashing tariffs on certain goods, including on American energy and agricultural shipments — a potential sign the leaders’ summit next week will lead to an extension of the one-year trade truce.
China’s top iron and steel industry body has called on domestic mills to rein in production and reduce inventories as oversupply and weak demand weigh on the market.
(All times Beijing)

items.title: Meta's Zuckerberg Favors Evaluators Over Slowdown for AI
body: Meta Platforms Inc. Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg said artificial intelligence labs should rely on independent evaluators and advisers to ensure that models are safe.

“Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice,” Zuckerberg wrote Tuesday in a post on X, joining a growing chorus of technology executives weighing in on a global debate over the best way to prevent AI systems from harming humanity.

Some company officials have voiced support for decelerating the pace of AI development and advocated working together to achieve consensus. Meta decided on its own to slow work on the Muse AI tool, rather than ask peers to also check their own progress first, Zuckerberg wrote.

“Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security,” he wrote. “We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us.”

A turbulent debate over AI’s economic and safety risks accelerated over the weekend with a 3,800-word essay from Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei, who urged a slowdown in the pace of development of the most advanced systems so researchers can better understand potential threats. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk — whose companies are bitter rivals to Anthropic — endorsed Amodei’s missive, and an OpenAI executive said the company was working with Anthropic and Alphabet Inc.’s Google on AI safety.

Zuckerberg’s post marked the CEO’s first public foray into the latest round of discussions about how to address the escalating concerns, adding to comments from executives from across the AI industry and lawmakers worldwide. Earlier Tuesday, Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang made similar remarks, saying safety should be a regular part of the development process, and companies can decide not to release things that are harmful.
“Safety is paramount,” Huang said during a Salesforce Inc. event. “In a lot of ways, it’s job one. However, safety is an engineering problem.”

If we reach a point when “the company is out of control and the product’s not going to be safe, take a pause and make sure you get it right,” he said. Huang also dismissed the need for new AI security regulations, arguing that market forces will help companies safely innovate.
“We don’t need new laws — we don’t need new regulations,” Huang said. The CEO added that there’s a “false choice” about AI development being either safe or fast.

“You can definitely have both at the same time,” Huang said during a conversation with Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff. “You pace yourself until you’re confident you’re releasing something that the market would appreciate. The market forces are already there.”
Read More: Anthropic, OpenAI Safety Push Risks ‘Regulatory Wall’ for Rivals
At the same Salesforce conference, OpenAI’s Altman likewise struck a calmer note, saying he thinks AI companies can develop the technology safely, without causing significant harm to people.
“I am very confident in our company’s ability — our industry’s ability — to do this safely,” Altman said.
While OpenAI is working with Anthropic and Google’s DeepMind lab to address safety issues, Altman said AI companies should be able to safely improve AI models on their own.
“I’m disappointed by how it’s been framed,” he said.

items.title: Gold Steadies Below $4,300 as Markets Await Fed Rate Decision
body: Gold was steady after a two-day drop as high oil prices continued to fuel inflation concerns and keep interest-rate hike bets a near-certainty ahead of the Federal Reserve’s policy decision later Wednesday.

Bullion was trading around $4,290 an ounce. Elevated energy prices pushed bond yields higher, and traders are now pricing in a 92% chance of the Fed hiking rates. Higher borrowing costs are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest.

The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest level in almost two decades, the latest milestone in a bruising global bond selloff driven by booming capital investment and soaring energy prices that are exacerbating inflation. The yield, which serves as a benchmark for borrowing costs across the globe, rose as much as five basis points to 5.04% on Tuesday, the highest since 2007.

That’s adding to investor expectations that the central bank will raise interest rates for the first time since 2023. If it doesn’t, or if Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is noncommittal about additional increases, traders may demand even higher yields on long-term bonds to safeguard their investments against the risk of inflation remaining elevated.
Read More: US 10-Year Yield Rises to Highest Since 2007 as Fed Looms

“With markets already pricing a high chance of a Fed hike this week, the main uncertainty is less about the hike itself, and more about what comes after,” said Christopher Wong, a strategist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. “If the Fed keeps the door open to further tightening, gold may be more vulnerable,” and move lower toward $4,000 an ounce if key support at $4,250 is broken, he added.

Oil steadied after a two-day gain, as the duration of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline shutdown after attacks last week remains unclear. The route had allowed millions of barrels a day to avoid passing through the Strait of Hormuz, and Saudi Aramco is now delaying deliveries to some European customers.

Gold is down more than 3% in September, after trading above $4,700 an ounce in late August, as traders repeatedly recalibrate the outlook for Fed policy. Still, many investors are betting that bullion will regain momentum once it rediscovers its traditional value as a portfolio hedge.

Spot gold was 0.2% lower at $4,284.99 an ounce at 8:45 a.m. in Singapore. Silver was little changed at $63.68 an ounce. Platinum dipped 0.2% and palladium was up 0.1%. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was 0.1% higher after gaining 0.6% in the past two sessions.

items.title: Apollo Gives $585 Million of Financing to The Executive Centre
body: Apollo Global Management has provided $585 million of financing to flexible workspace provider The Executive Centre, according to a statement, in the global asset manager’s largest Asian hybrid deal combining debt and equity.

The Executive Centre, acquired by a KKR & Co. and a Tiga Investments Pte.-led consortium in 2021, operates in 38 cities in 15 markets across the Asia Pacific and the Middle East. Proceeds of the funding will be mainly used to refinance existing debt, according to the statement.

Apollo, like other major global alternative asset managers, is increasing its presence in Asia and the TEC funding follows deals with companies including international school chain Global Schools Group and Charles Monat Associates, an insurance brokerage firm for wealthy clients. The current deal involved a competitive process, and is an example of how the US firm is taking share in the region’s loan market, where many deals are still controlled by banks.
Apollo recently invested $1.5 billion in a fund of Singapore asset manager Keppel Ltd. The fund will hold a portfolio of offshore energy assets.
The US asset manager had over $1 trillion of assets under management at the end of June, according to its website.

items.title: Japan's Export Growth Stays Solid as Shipments of Chips Jump
body: Japan’s export growth slowed a tad in August while remaining at an elevated pace, with shipments of semiconductors and chip manufacturing equipment surging.

The value of exports rose 19.3% from a year earlier, slowing from a 23.2% gain in July, the Finance Ministry reported Wednesday. The result, the 12th straight month of increases, compared with economists’ median forecast of an 18.4% increase.

Imports rose 28%, compared with economists’ estimate of a 26.3% increase. The trade deficit widened to ¥1.1 trillion on an unadjusted basis from a revised ¥638.3 billion ($4.1 billion) deficit in July, marking a fourth straight month in the red.

Wednesday’s report highlighted the impact on the balance of trade stemming from market movements. Oil prices remained relatively high in August, with Brent averaging around $88 per barrel, while the yen continued to trade at levels near 160 per dollar. Japan’s imports of oil rose about 59% by value, while edging 3.6% higher in terms of volume.

“High crude oil prices are driving up import costs, leading to a widening trade deficit,” said Atsushi Takeda, chief economist at Itochu Research Institute. “With crude oil prices now exceeding $100 per barrel, I believe this will continue to increase the trade deficit going forward, making it increasingly difficult to return to a surplus.”

Brent oil rose above $100 a barrel last week amid an uptick in attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, with the US and Iran positioning for the war to drag on. The yen has strengthened more than 3% versus the dollar so far in September, making it Asia’s best-performing currency in the period.
By destination, shipments to the US increased 24.9%, while those to China and Europe climbed 20.6% and 11%, respectively.

Exports of electronic components such as semiconductors drove the overall gains, rising 52%. Shipments of those products to China more than doubled, while exports of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to the US and EU also rose more than 100%. Cars also advanced, albeit at a slower pace than in previous months.

The value of Japan’s crude oil imports from the US rose more than 1,000% to ¥400 billion. Shipments from the Middle East gained just 3.7% by value, as volumes from that region slumped by about 31%. Japan has been reducing its dependence on oil from the region amid ongoing disruptions to shipping resulting from the war, turning to the US in order to procure a stable supply.
One of President Donald Trump’s top energy chiefs sought to push back against speculation the US might ban fuel exports ahead of midterm elections in a bid to lower domestic prices.
“We would consider an export ban if we thought that it might actually lower prices, but that’s not the case,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said earlier this week.

The yen traded at 160.64 against the dollar on average in August, 8.7% weaker than a year ago, according to the ministry. A weaker yen makes it more expensive to import materials while it gives exporters a competitive advantage overseas.
Although the yen has since strengthened, it remains well below its 10-year average. Wednesday morning in Tokyo the yen was trading around 155.18 per dollar, compared with a 10-year average of 126.55.
Economists said the outlook for trade remains bright thanks largely to continuing demand for cutting-edge technology.
“I believe demand for AI-related products will remain strong, so I expect exports to be supported by that,” Takeda said.

items.title: Nvidia CEO Set to Attend Trump Dinner With Chinese President
body: Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang is slated to attend President Donald Trump’s state dinner with Chinese leader Xi Jinping next week, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The tech executive is expected to be a guest at the event as part of a trip to Washington, said the person, who asked not to be identified because the invitation list hasn’t yet been made public. A representative for Nvidia declined to comment, while the White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Huang and Trump have built an increasingly close relationship in recent months. Just this week, the CEO took a call from the president while on stage during a conference to discuss artificial intelligence.
The two men have both pushed back on the need to slow down AI and data center development, with the president calling concerns about the technology “a hoax.”
Read More: Nvidia CEO Puts Trump on Phone While Downplaying AI Risks

Trump also helped lift export restrictions on some Nvidia chips, which had been barred from sale in China over national security concerns. Still, a relatively small amount of the semiconductors have made their way into the country — and only older-generation processors are permitted.
Read More: Nvidia Steps Back Into China Market With First H200 Chip Sales

As they approach the summit, Trump and Xi are facing escalating tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and the Middle East. Trump said earlier this week that he maintains a “great relationship” with Xi.
CNBC previously reported on Huang’s plans for the dinner.

items.title: Crypto's Push Into Wall Street Suffers Setback After Bill Fails
body: Crypto’s long march into mainstream finance took a step backward Tuesday when the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, denying the industry a chance to turn its newfound influence in Washington into fresh rules that could outlast the current administration.

Crypto exchange Coinbase Global Inc. closed 10% lower, while stablecoin issuer Circle Internet Group Inc. declined more than 11%. Bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency, dropped as much as 5.3% to below $75,000 after the bill failed in a procedural vote.

Odds for the bill passing had plunged in recent months as key Democrats lined up against it, but its defeat hardly explains crypto’s broader malaise. The euphoria around artificial intelligence has drawn away retail attention, while tighter liquidity and weaker appetite for risk have prolonged the bear market. Clarity offered something different: its passage would have given market participants a clearer understanding of the legal parameters governing the industry and a well-defined pathway for companies deciding whether to invest, expand or strike deals in the US.

Now much of that work falls to the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Under the Trump administration, the SEC and CFTC have moved to ease restrictions on digital assets. Their rules, however, could prove easier for a future administration to change.

“The failure puts the ball in the hands of the regulators,” said Austin Campbell, a crypto expert and former banker who is now an adjunct professor at the NYU Stern School of Business. “And while they can make rules, those are less stable and permanent than legislation.”

Crypto had been on a winning streak in Washington. The industry spent heavily to build political clout, and Republicans made extensive changes to Clarity in a last attempt to pick up Democratic votes. Among them were tougher ethics provisions covering elected officials’ crypto holdings. The issue had become particularly contentious given President Donald Trump’s and his family’s financial ties to the industry.
It still wasn’t enough. With the midterms approaching, Democrats were being asked to vote for a bill strongly backed by an industry that has added substantially to Trump’s wealth.
For Wall Street firms already deep in crypto, little changes immediately.
“This doesn’t affect our current plans or our strategy,” said Robbie Mitchnick, head of digital assets at BlackRock, whose IBIT is the largest US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund.
The industry uncertainty is greater for investments that haven’t been made yet, from acquisitions to new businesses and US expansion.

“What happens if the Democrats take the House and the Senate” in the midterm elections, said Larry Tabb, global head of financial sector research at Bloomberg Intelligence. “That opens up a lot of risk for people that really want to make a substantial investment, it could conceivably be taken away with the stroke of a pen.”
Here’s what the setback could mean:
Clarity’s failure to advance removes one potential boost for a market already struggling through an extended slump.

“If Clarity had passed, crypto would have been the consensus smart money trade in Q4,” said Matthew Hougan, chief investment officer at Bitwise Asset Management. “It would have been a rip-roaring bull market. With Clarity failing it’s a more challenging market. I am still bullish we’d end the year higher, but it would be a bit slower. I don’t think it delays the bull market, it’s more of a speed bump than a road stop. It would have been better for crypto if it passed.”

The agencies can keep writing rules without Clarity. The industry has been through a change in Washington before. Coinbase and other major crypto firms were fighting SEC lawsuits only a few years ago; regulators under the current administration later dismissed them. Clarity would have resolved some of the legal questions behind those fights, including which digital assets are securities or commodities and which agency oversees them. Without the bill, regulators and the courts will have more influence.

“The longer this takes, the more the question shifts from whether capital moves to how much of it the US keeps,” said Javier Martinez, chief executive at sFOX, a digital-asset dealer and trading platform.
The uncertainty could also delay acquisitions of crypto exchanges, custodians and asset managers by traditional financial companies.

Brian Dixon, chief executive of Off the Chain Capital, a fund that invests in crypto companies, said prospective buyers want greater regulatory certainty before committing to large acquisitions. The SEC and CFTC could eventually provide much of that clarity themselves, but agency rule-making takes time and could face court challenges or reversal under a future administration.
“Regardless, we are going to get regulatory clarity, it’s just the timeline,” Dixon said.

Banks themselves complicate that picture. They fought parts of Clarity, particularly provisions involving stablecoin rewards that they argued could draw deposits away from traditional lenders. Some traditional financial firms are also prospective buyers of the crypto businesses whose future the legislation was meant to clarify.

“Next Congress — if they took this up, and if political makeup of Congress changes — then you will not have the bill the way it’s written now,” said Chris Hayes, a partner at Thorn Run Partners, a lobbying firm. “You might not have a bill, and it might be less favorable to what the industry would like under Democratic control of House or Senate. It exposes them to risk in the future in the longer term.”

items.title: How the AI Boom Is Minting Billionaires, Rewarding 'Picks and Shovels' Sellers
body: King Slide Works Co. started out in the 1980s making furniture handles and drawer slides.
Today, it’s making a fortune from artificial intelligence, one of a growing number of unlikely manufacturers riding the boom — and minting a new class of billionaires.

By any standards, the company’s rise has been meteoric. Lin Tsung-chi, King Slide’s octogenarian founder, is now one of the world’s wealthiest according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, with a $19.4 billion fortune as of late August. Earlier this year, he briefly surpassed Quanta Computer Inc.’s Barry Lam as Taiwan’s richest person. The firm’s market capitalization grew more than 3,000% to $43 billion in just under four years after ChatGPT’s debut in November 2022 triggered a massive boom in AI investment.

“It’s like gold bars raining from the sky,” Jane Lin, Tsung-chi’s daughter and King Slide’s president, said in an interview at the firm’s headquarters in Kaohsiung, an industrial port city about five hours drive south of Taipei.

It’s an example of how the AI boom is creating wealth far beyond the companies building the models and designing the chips. It’s enriching the “picks and shovels” sellers, or firms that make often overlooked industrial products or the obscure hardware, materials and equipment needed to build the infrastructure. For investors, that’s creating a second layer of AI winners — companies that may have little to do with the technology but are selling the tools needed to make it possible.

King Slide, founded in 1986, pivoted from making furniture hardware to server rail kits in the early 2000s. Today, every time an AI server, which weigh hundreds of pounds, needs to be installed or pulled from a rack for maintenance, there is likely to be a piece of their hardware doing an unglamorous job behind the scenes: a slide rail.

In China, Guangdong Dtech Technology Co. offers an even less obvious example of the AI wealth effect. The company makes micro drill bits used to make tiny holes in the printed circuit boards inside AI servers. As servers become more powerful and their circuit boards more complex, demand for high-precision tools is rising. Guangdong Dtech has emerged as the world’s largest PCB drill-bit maker by sales volume, according to estimates.
Dtech’s rise has created substantial wealth for its founder Wang Xin, worth $12 billion as of Aug. 27.

Others range from Swiss vacuum-valve maker VAT Group AG and advanced ceramics producer Chaozhou Three-Circle Group Co. to AI-chip cooling specialist Jentech Precision Industrial Co., cybersecurity firm Fortinet Inc. and server connector maker Lotes Co. Many were founded decades ago by entrepreneurs with engineering or technical backgrounds who spent years mastering obscure components long before the AI boom happened.

Lotes, for example, was founded four decades ago by two brothers trained in machinery and mold-making. It’s grown to be the world’s top supplier of CPU sockets, a critical piece of hardware that carries power and data signals.

The rapid pace of AI development is becoming a challenge for suppliers across the industry, as customers demand even faster product cycles and suppliers must develop new technologies to keep up with the speed of change.
King Slide’s Jane Lin said those gold bars from AI may be raining from the sky, but they are falling at “incredible speed.”
“If you aren’t fast enough, you won’t be able to catch them,” she said.

The firm’s ability to do just that was cultivated long before the current boom. The critical moment came about a quarter-century earlier, when it was forced to pivot from furniture hardware to the server supply chain after a major US customer demanded a 30% price cut during the rise of Chinese manufacturing. Rather than accept the lower prices, King Slide walked away, a decision that led to the loss of nearly half of its workforce. It later secured orders from companies including Compaq Computer Corp. and International Business Machines Corp., and laid the foundations to become a key supplier to the tech industry.

Since the crisis in 2000, the company accumulated over 3,800 patents that serves as a competitive moat, according to its executive vice president JC Wang, with their engineering team growing from seven to more than 500 currently. It can also deliver prototypes to customers within weeks of request, a capability built over four decades of engineering and through several crises.
“We spent years honing our craft,” Wang, Tsung-chi’s son-in-law, said. “When the AI wave arrived, we were ready.”

King Slide is estimated to command more than 70% of the high-end AI server rail market, underscoring its dominant position in a market with high technical and IP barriers. What’s less clear is how long the AI wave can continue on its current trajectory. The dispute over the pace of development has triggered a selloff across technology stocks and brought into question the resilience of a global data center boom.

One lesson King Slide learned long ago was the risk of relying too heavily on the furniture industry with a handful of customers. Today, it has diversified across servers, communication and internet applications, while expanding its manufacturing footprint in Taiwan and the US. The company expects to start trial production in Houston this September, along with new plants planned in Taiwan for next year.

“My biggest concern is that we might not be able to develop the next-generation product,” said Lin. “Every day, I’m both happy and worried. I’m happy when we bring something we’ve been working on to life, but then I start worrying: now that we’ve made this one, what’s next?”

Bloomberg News identified at least seven firms, located from China to Switzerland, that have moved from niches such as vacuum components and ceramic products to dominate quiet corners of the AI supply chain. Together they have collectively created over $62 billion of additional wealth for their major shareholders.

items.title: ANZ CEO Matos Warns on AI, Data Centers, Treasury Yields: Australia Briefing
body: ANZ CEO Nuno Matos has joined a slew of business leaders like Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman in raising caution about the dangers of rapid artificial intelligence development in recent days.

The bank chief’s warnings about the technology coincide with a new push by top AI firms to coordinate with one another on safeguards. Anthropic’s Amodei on Saturday called for leading model makers to “voluntarily work together to set standards” for AI and slow the technology’s progress to mitigate the potential for catastrophic harms. At the same time, the public opposition to AI has received pushback from some finance executives. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink said delays in the AI buildout will make the technology the “domain of large firms”  and limit access. — Jackie Edwards, Sydney editor
ANZ’s Matos warned about the rising, unpredictable risks linked to artificial intelligence and failed to rule out large-scale job cuts at the bank as it adopts the quickly emerging technology.

His comments come as the global debate over AI safety is intensifying, as US President Donald Trump dismisses industry calls for a slowdown and China brands fresh warnings about the tech “fearmongering.” Toby Walsh, Scientia Professor of AI at the University of New South Wales, joins Bloomberg: The Asia Trade to discuss the outlook for AI regulation in Australia.

Meantime, Australia’s data-center boom could drive as much as A$225 billion in spending as the buildout of server farms spurs new renewable energy supply, according to Westpac’s Pat Bustamante. The data center pipeline is worth about A$175 billion, with around A$110 billion likely to occur in the next three years, he said.

Brookfield is bringing in Australian Retirement Trust, Mercer Super and other investors for a recapitalization of Center Parcs that values the British holiday park operator at about $6 billion, people familiar with the matter said.
Nickel Industries halted the ramp-up of one of its Indonesian processing plants due to water shortages, a sign of how an El-Niño linked drought is hurting output in the world’s top producer.

The 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest since 2007 before retreating as rising oil prices kept global bonds under pressure. items.title: RBNZ Assistant Governor Karen Silk to Step Down in December
body: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Assistant Governor Karen Silk will leave at the end of the year, triggering a refresh of the central bank’s senior leadership.

Silk will depart in December after the final monetary policy decision of the year, the RBNZ said Wednesday in Wellington. She joined the bank in 2022 after a lengthy banking career with Westpac, and most recently was assistant governor money, responsible for a range of functions including financial markets operations and economics.

“After a long and varied career in banking and public service, this feels like the right time to begin a new chapter,” she said in a statement. “I am looking forward to spending more time with family and pursuing personal interests, while continuing to contribute to New Zealand’s business and investment community.”

Governor Anna Breman, who joined the RBNZ at the end of last year, said Silk will continue to lead her portfolio through December, and there are plans in place to ensure an orderly handover and continuity of decision-making. Silk sits on the Monetary Policy Committee, which makes interest rate decisions.

The departure allows Breman the opportunity to reshape her leadership team after she inherited a slimmed down group. The RBNZ will establish two assistant governor roles — assistant governor monetary policy and assistant governor payments and cash — to strengthen leadership capacity, clarify accountabilities and support closer coordination across the RBNZ’s core responsibilities, she said.

After ructions in 2025 that saw former governor Adrian Orr abruptly quit in March and his deputy Christian Hawkesby step aside after he missed out on the permanent role, Silk’s commitment to stay until the end of the year also delivers stability as Breman — formerly deputy governor at the Riksbank in Sweden — continues to familiarize herself with a new role.
The new assistant governor monetary policy is expected to join the MPC, subject to approval by the finance minister, the RBNZ said.
The MPC currently has three internal members and three external members. The bank is also working through arrangements for a short-term appointment of a new internal member of the MPC, it said.

items.title: BlackRock's Fink, Blackstone's Gray Back Carney's Canada Investment Push
body: Welcome back to Canada Daily, the newsletter on business, economics and politics from Vancouver to Montreal and beyond. If this was forwarded to you, sign up.
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s inaugural Canada Investment Summit dropped a package of tax breaks, privatization moves and project-approval reforms, all designed to lure more capital to the country.
Now, he’s asking investors to deliver.

It was Canada’s ambassador to the US, Mark Wiseman, who laid out the challenge. As he wrapped up a panel discussion with BlackRock’s Larry Fink and Blackstone’s Jon Gray, Wiseman set a “key performance indicator”. The metric? Come back next year with more invested in Canada than you have today.

Carney’s summit — a high-profile effort to channel foreign dollars into Canadian projects — delivered what his government badly wanted: Visible enthusiasm from the world’s biggest money managers. Many of them were already in Carney’s phone contacts, which helped. But the public pledges mattered.

Fink told the crowd at Toronto’s Four Seasons hotel that BlackRock currently has C$500 billion ($359 billion) invested by Canadians abroad — about the same as the firm has invested in Canada itself. With Ottawa’s new measures, that balance is poised to change, he said: “If the opportunity is there, if the projects are there, I do believe international capital will seek out these opportunities.”

The government arrived with a pitchbook of 167 projects — data centers, ports, wind turbines, critical minerals — and layered on new incentives. Carney outlined a major tax break for long-term investors and a plan to open Canada’s four largest airports to private capital.

The tax measures will allow companies to write off a large share of project costs upfront, garnering applause from industry groups. The airport policy change will let private investors take on long-term contracts to operate hubs in Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal and Calgary. Carney argues that will unlock billions for upgrades and expansion.

Carney also touted his forthcoming Build Canada Strong Act, legislation designed to slash permitting timelines that have stretched for years. “Our standard will be simple: One project. One review. One year,” Carney said.
Gray called Canada a “sleeping giant” held back by a decade of cumulative regulatory drag. “The potential growth rates are much higher than most people would expect.”
Carney, for his part, framed the day as a turning point for Canada, calling it “a country unleashing its enormous potential. We are just getting started.”
After some bullish talk from the prime minister and from investors, now comes the test: Whether they all really mean it.

Also in this newsletter: Brookfield and CPPIB put up C$50 billion for the invest-in-Canada effort. The country’s largest-ever venture fund debuts. And OpenAI sees data center potential in Canada’s abundant land and energy.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

Brookfield Asset Management and CPP Investment Board are launching a new C$50 billion initiative to invest in Canada over the next five years, according to a person familiar with the matter. The global asset manager and Canada’s largest pension fund will each allocate as much as C$25 billion over the period. The so-called Maple Fund will invest in strategic sectors, including infrastructure, the person said.

Stephen Harper, who led a Conservative government in Canada from 2006 to 2015, backed the decision by Prime Minister Mark Carney to walk away from US trade talks last month. Harper said that rejecting President Donald Trump’s proposed terms was necessary and worth it — despite the economic damage caused by the escalation of the tariff war between the two countries. “It is clear that the current US administration views our level of economic integration as incompatible with our separate sovereignty,” he told the investment summit.

Toronto-headquartered Radical Ventures unveiled a new late-stage growth fund with more than $1 billion of capital after an initial close, making it the largest-ever venture fund in Canada. It’s backed by three of Canada’s largest pension managers — PSP Investments, CPPIB and the fund for Ontario’s healthcare employees, known as HOOPP. Radical Co-Founder and Managing Partner Jordan Jacobs said he aims for it to eventually be a multibillion-dollar investment vehicle.

OpenAI is taking a close look at Canada under Carney, said one of its top executives, who previously hired the Canadian to lead the Bank of England. George Osborne, who was chancellor of the UK from 2010 to 2016 and is now head of OpenAI for countries, told Bloomberg News that there is potential for data center partnerships in Canada. What’s more, he said, “Mark Carney has articulated one of the clearer plans for AI adoption of a western government.”

Ardian is considering setting up a buyout fund that invests in Canada’s middle- to lower-market companies, as the private-asset manager pushes deeper into the country. “There’s a real case to be made for the small- and medium-sized businesses in Canada and to invest directly in them,” Co-Chief Executive Officer Mark Benedetti said in an interview. The Paris-based firm is in talks with Canadian pension plans that would anchor the fund, he said, adding that he expects it to debut in less than two years.

Delays in the build-out of artificial intelligence because of public opposition will make the technology the “domain of large firms,” limiting access, BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned. “The faster we can build out more capacity, the more we can democratize and make it available for everyone,” Fink said during a panel discussion at the Summit.
Read our full coverage of the summit on our live blog.

items.title: NZ's Dominant Grocer to be Broken Up Under National Party Plan
body: New Zealand’s center-right National Party will break up one of the nation’s two dominant grocery chains if it returns to power after the November election, as it attempts to win over financially squeezed voters.

National will pursue the structural separation of Foodstuffs into two competing nationwide supermarket chains, Finance Spokesperson Nicola Willis said Wednesday in Wellington. The change will be subject to an independent assessment by the Commerce Commission to ensure it can be implemented in a way that delivers net benefits for shoppers, she said.
National proposes splitting Foodstuffs in two — creating existing brands New World and Four Square as one nationwide chain and PAK’nSAVE as another.

The move is designed to appeal to voters who have been buffeted by soaring fuel prices and other living costs, including more expensive essential items such as groceries. New Zealand’s supermarket sector is dominated by Foodstuffs, a nationwide cooperative, and Australian-based retailer Woolworths Group Ltd., which together have been accused of making excessive profits and shutting out smaller rivals.
Pak’nSave and New World have a combined 47% share of the market, while Woolworths has 27%, according to the Commerce Commission.
A spokesman for Foodstuffs said they were reviewing the announcement and would respond once they had considered the details.

The proposal would be one of the most aggressive attempts to shake up a concentrated supermarket sector in the region, where governments and regulators have come under pressure to rein in grocery prices as households struggle with higher living costs.

“Our initial view is that New World and PAK’nSAVE would compete harder on prices, specials and service if they were genuinely independent of each other,” Willis said. “Separation would create three major nationwide grocery chains and put more pressure on supermarkets to win and keep customers.”

The push echoes concerns across the Tasman, where Australia has also intensified scrutiny of its highly concentrated supermarket sector as Woolworths and rival Coles Group Ltd. account for roughly two-thirds of grocery sales nationwide. Their market power is increasingly fueling political and public scrutiny of grocery prices, discounting policies and treatment of suppliers as households grapple with surging living costs.
Read More: Australia’s Cost Squeeze Is Turning Shoppers Into Value Hunters

The National Party will amend the Grocery Industry Competition Act within 100 days of forming the next government to empower the Commerce Commission to develop and assess a detailed implementation plan, and determine whether the separation can be delivered in a way that leaves consumers better off, she said. The regulator will have to provide its recommendation in six months, and if it recommends separation, the government will legislate to implement it.

Willis cited independent analysis that the restructuring would deliver consumer benefits of NZ$12.6 billion ($7.3 billion) over 20 years. Grocery prices are projected to be around 3.5% lower than they otherwise would be one year after separation, and around 5% lower after six years, she said.

“New Zealanders are paying more than they should for groceries because supermarket competition is still too weak,” Willis added. “Families deserve more choice, better prices and supermarkets that have to fight harder for their dollars.”

items.title: Asian Stocks Steady in Runup to Fed, Oil Declines: Markets Wrap
body: Asian stocks steadied after four days of losses as investors held back ahead of the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision, with markets expecting its first hike since 2023. Oil declined, supporting gains in regional bonds.

MSCI’s Asian equities index edged up 0.2%, with winners and losers evenly matched in the gauge. Contracts for Wall Street gauges nudged 0.1% higher as OpenAI weighed a new funding round at a $1.2 trillion valuation.

Helping sentiment, Brent dropped 0.8% to just under $108 a barrel after gaining almost 20% this month. Treasury futures consolidated before Wednesday’s Fed announcement, while government bonds opened higher in Australia and New Zealand. The rally in energy prices and growing bets on a Fed rate hike had fueled a bond selloff, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield as high as 5.04% Tuesday — the highest in almost two decades.
The yield dropped edged lower to 4.99% in early Asian trading.
Elsewhere, Bitcoin extended its slide to trade around $75,700 as the US Senate blocked a landmark crypto market structure bill.

The Fed’s decision Wednesday is in focus after hotter-than-expected core inflation last week and concerns over government budgets bolstered expectations for tighter monetary policy. Markets are pricing in a more-than-90% chance of a hike. Higher rates would come as surging energy prices threaten to keep inflation elevated, while rising bond yields increase financing costs and add another headwind for equities.

“If the Fed follows the futures market and hikes rates, our sense is that stocks are likely to see downward pressure over the near-term,” said Chris Senyek at Wolfe Research. “However, we’ve found that over a longer time horizon — six to 12 months after the first rate hike — stocks typically recover and push into positive territory.”
Read: Fed Seen Hiking Rates in Defiance of Trump: Decision-Day Guide

In other corners of the market, gold fell for a third consecutive day to trade around $4,280 an ounce. Higher interest rates typically diminish the appeal of the non-yielding metal. A Bloomberg gauge of the dollar edged up for a third day.
Central bank decisions remain the main focus this week, with the Fed followed by policy announcements in the UK and Japan that could reshape the monetary-policy outlook for the rest of 2026.

A decision to hold rates — or a hike without clear guidance on further increases — may push investors to demand higher long-term yields as protection against inflation, while shorter-dated yields track the Fed’s policy path more closely.

Officials have held their benchmark rate steady in a range of 3.5%-3.75% since December as a majority of policymakers argued that progress in lowering inflation was being stalled by temporary factors.

Elsewhere, Brent slipped in early Wednesday trading after settling almost 3% higher Tuesday as outages at a key Saudi pipeline and Libyan oil fields added to supply risks in a market already hit by disruptions from the Iran war.

Traders were watching for signs of how long Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline will remain closed after drone attacks halted operations last week. Saudi Aramco is delaying oil supplies to some European customers this month, people familiar with the matter said.

“The combination of higher interest rates and elevated oil prices is like asking equities to run a marathon with ankle weights strapped on,” said Darrell Cronk at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. “Higher rates increase the discount rate investors apply to future earnings, while higher energy costs drain purchasing power from consumers and pressure profit margins.”

items.title: Trump Advisers Lutnick, Michael Meet With Anthropic Executive Over AI Safety
body: Senior Trump administration officials met Tuesday with Anthropic PBC’s top Washington executive to discuss artificial intelligence safety risks.

Anthropic’s chief compute officer Tom Brown, who has become the face of the company in Washington, spoke virtually with Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, according to people familiar with the matter.
Anthropic declined to comment. In a statement, a Department of Defense official said it “maintains contact with frontier AI companies. Although the department’s stance on Anthropic has not changed.”

Tensions between Anthropic and the administration were reignited by a 3,800-word essay posted Saturday by the company’s Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei, who called for government regulation and urged pacing development of the most advanced AI systems so researchers can better understand potential threats.

Amodei’s missive, which was quickly embraced by rivals OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk, prompted a vehement reaction from President Donald Trump. He dismissed fears about AI risks as “a hoax” and rejected the idea of new rules.

Still, leading AI developers have begun discussing AI safety concerns among themselves. OpenAI’s global policy chief Chris Lehane said his company has been engaging with Anthropic and Google DeepMind for several weeks on the issue. “It’s better to try to work together to prioritize safety,” Lehane said at a Tuesday briefing in Washington.

Mounting concerns about the risks of cutting-edge AI models took center stage in forums across the US on Tuesday. At Salesforce Inc.’s annual Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, Amodei, Altman and Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang all weighed in on the topic, while an AI gathering in Washington saw progressive Senator Bernie Sanders and ex-Trump adviser Steve Bannon share rare common ground as both warned that AI companies are jeopardizing human interests.
At Dreamforce, both Altman and Huang acknowledged concerns but argued AI companies would safely pace their technology, without needing regulations.

Worries about the potential dangers of advanced AI went mainstream over the past week after the high-profile departure of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who accused AI companies of “gambling with our lives” in a resignation post he shared on social media.

Michael, who has led Pentagon efforts to accelerate AI adoption across the military, has publicly rejected Coxon’s claim that AI could kill all humans, while Lutnick is eager to push back on negative messaging about the technology ahead of the midterms in November, according to people familiar with the matter.

Relations between Anthropic and the US government have been strained following a disagreement earlier this year with the Commerce Department over the security of its advanced Mythos and Fable AI models and a tiff with the Pentagon over the use of its tech in military operations.

Michael helped lead negotiations with the company over the military’s use of its tech, but those talks broke down when the Pentagon rejected Anthropic’s terms, calling them an infringement on the military’s authority. It then blacklisted the firm, declaring it a threat to the US supply chain. Anthropic is still engaged in an active lawsuit against the Pentagon in a Washington court over the blacklisting.

Brown emerged on the Washington scene earlier this summer, as he led high-stakes negotiations with US officials to lift export controls that were placed on Anthropic’s most advanced AI models. He succeeded in that task, and spoke publicly alongside Lutnick at a tech-focused G20 summit earlier this month, making a point to praise Trump’s support for data centers.

In a Bloomberg Television interview from the sidelines, Lutnick said the company had “gotten religion” and patched its relationship with the government, though the Pentagon later said that its own blacklisting of the company remained in place.
Read More: AI Bosses Clash With Trump on Their Calls to Slow AI Development
Brown is now likely to face yet another fraught challenge: easing tension with US officials over AI safety at a time when the president is rejecting such concerns.

Trump said in a post to his Truth Social network Monday that his presidency is the only safety guardrail needed for AI. He added that slowing down AI is a bad idea that would only serve US adversaries like China.

items.title: Blackstone Seeks $8 Billion for Green Infrastructure Credit Fund
body: Blackstone Inc. is seeking to raise at least $8 billion for its private credit fund focused on renewables and digital infrastructure investments, according to people familiar with the matter.

The new fund will provide loans to companies in the energy transition marketplace, including energy security, power and utilities, data centers and chip financing, said the people, who asked to not be identified discussing confidential information. It is the fourth iteration of the fund.
Blackstone declined to comment.
The prior version closed with $7.1 billion in 2023 and generated a net internal rate of return of 15% as of June 30, the people said.

Blackstone, the largest alternative asset manager, has emerged as one of the biggest backers of artificial intelligence. Those AI bets continue to drive Blackstone’s performance, with nine out of the top 10 appreciating investments tied to data centers, energy, power and large language models.
Read More: Blackstone Profits Jump, Boosted by Exits and Bets on AI

The firm’s latest fundraising effort comes as the gap between large asset managers and their smaller counterparts widens. Blackstone hauled in over $260 billion in the past 12 months, up 24% from the prior period, according to Chief Financial Officer Michael Chae.
Demand for private credit from institutions remained strong even as retail demand softened, Chae said at a Barclays Plc conference on Tuesday.

items.title: Three Big Central Bank Decisions Loom: Evening Briefing Americas
body: Three major central bank decisions — starting with the US Federal Reserve on Wednesday and followed on successive days by peers in the UK and Japan — may recast the monetary policy landscape for the rest of 2026.

The US will be most closely watched in the wake of rising inflation that has investors betting Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and his colleagues will raise the benchmark rate for the first time in three years. Bond traders are pricing in an interest-rate hike with a level of conviction that has proven right for decades.

Interest-rate swaps tied to Fed meeting dates show traders see more than a 90% chance that Warsh, despite his mixed messaging over the summer, will raise the rate by a quarter point from the current 3.5%-3.75% range.
Whenever expectations of a hike have been that high, the Fed has invariably delivered it, according to Bloomberg-compiled data going back to 2008.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is expanding the scope of a major investment tax write-off, adding oil and gas pipelines, mining property and more to the list of assets eligible for accelerated deductions. Carney announced the tax measure Tuesday at an investment summit where dozens of firms have gathered to discuss possible stakes in Canadian projects in natural resources, manufacturing and other sectors.

Under the new rules, a number of those projects will now qualify for immediate expensing of some of their capital spending. It’s one of the most significant changes in decades to the tax treatment of business investments in Canada, and is poised to ease the income tax burden for many companies.

The Iran war has reached a crisis point for American ally Saudi Arabia. The kingdom was spared the worst of the Islamic Republic’s retaliation for the US-Israel bombing campaign, but that all changed when Iran-aligned Houthis started firing at Saudi Arabia on a near-daily basis this month.

The hostilities had already pushed Saudi oil production to the lowest level in decades. Now they threaten to complicate the kingdom’s multitrillion-dollar plans to diversify the economy, and come just weeks before a flagship investment conference in Riyadh set to feature JPMorgan Chief Executive Officer Jamie Dimon and Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon.

Trump’s decision to join Israel in going to war with Iran in February has reportedly resulted in almost 8,000 deaths across Iran and Lebanon, and scores more elsewhere in the Middle East. It has also cost US taxpayers more than $38 billion and will push inflation up about 0.5 percentage points by early next year, a new congressional study finds.

In addition, the war has depleted stockpiles of munitions that could take five years or longer to rebuild, reducing the military’s capacity to respond to another major conflict, according to the report. That echoes a study from the Pentagon’s inspector general, who said Monday that the American industrial base can’t keep up with the munitions shortfalls.

items.title: OpenAI's Sam Altman 'Confident' Industry Can Police AI Safety
body: OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman said he believes artificial intelligence companies can develop the technology safely without significant harm to people at large.

“I am very confident in our company’s ability — our industry’s ability — to do this safely,” Altman said Tuesday during a discussion with Salesforce Inc. CEO Marc Benioff at the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco.

Altman comments about the pace of AI advances came as policymakers and others in the industry debated whether government regulation is needed to keep AI from slipping beyond human control. Dario Amodei, CEO of OpenAI rival Anthropic PBC, set off the latest debate after authoring an essay Saturday that raised the potential risks of the technology and suggested development needed to be slowed.
While OpenAI is working with Anthropic and Alphabet Inc.’s AI lab Google DeepMind to address safety issues, Altman said AI companies should be able to safely improve AI models on their own.
“I’m disappointed by how it’s been framed,” he said.

items.title: Sheinbaum Tax Change Eyes New Revenue But Businesses Fear Impact
body: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum is proposing sweeping changes to corporate income tax rules to raise as much as 140 billion pesos ($8.2 billion) next year, part of an effort to narrow the budget deficit but one that risks squeezing low-margin businesses.

The proposal, part of Sheinbaum’s 2027 budget blueprint, marks the leftist leader’s largest revenue-raising push to date. It would restrict deductions businesses can claim against income taxes owed in order to curb tax evasion. Finance officials argue that the vast majority of companies have used the deductions to sidestep taxes by claiming they made no profit. If approved by lawmakers, the reform would require firms to pay up to 3% of their revenue in taxes, even if they didn’t turn a profit.
“Nine out of ten companies do not pay taxes or have very low effective tax rates,” according to a finance ministry assessment of the proposal.

But business groups warn that broad limits on deductions could increase the tax burden on companies that legitimately operate with thin margins, potentially tipping some into insolvency while deterring investment. Two years into her term, Sheinbaum has increasingly sought more private capital to revive growth while also boosting government revenue to balance growing social spending she favors.

“If no changes are made, it will hurt investment,” said José Medina Mora, head of Mexico’s top business lobby, known as CCE. Wholesalers in sectors including groceries, pharmaceuticals and technology operate on high volumes and thin margins, he said, leaving many of them exposed.
Despite the criticism, the measure stands a good chance of passage as Sheinbaum’s ruling coalition commands large congressional majorities, though it may be amended.
Read More: Sheinbaum Budget Sees Smaller Deficit, More Public Works
The president has repeatedly argued that a broad tax reform isn’t needed, and that public finances can be strengthened by improving collections.

Like her populist predecessor, she’s generally opposed raising taxes, though some levies have been hiked in previous budgets. Specifically, she’s supported targeted so-called “sin” taxes and new tariffs, while proposing tougher limits on how companies calculate taxable income. Each step has been justified as health policy, industrial protection or a crackdown on evasion, even as households and businesses pay more.
The cumulative effect of Sheinbaum’s policies increasingly resemble a tax overhaul in all but name.

“There are minor fiscal reforms every year, but I think the latest are among the most significant changes we’ve seen in recent years,” said Gabriela Siller, head of economic analysis at Banco Base. “They aren’t calling it a ‘reform’ because of the political cost.”
The careful branding of the proposal comes as concerns mount over Mexico’s public finances from credit rating agencies.

The first wave of tax changes took effect at the start of this year as taxes on sugary drinks nearly doubled, while new or higher levies on cigarettes and gambling were also enacted. On the trade front, lawmakers approved Sheinbaum-backed tariffs on more than 1,400 product categories, including vehicles, auto parts and steel. The import duties of up to 50% were applied to goods from countries that lack a free-trade deal with Mexico, mainly China.
Those measures have lifted collections, but income tax revenue fell 6% in real terms though July, coming in well below the government’s original forecast.

“Such a sharp drop in income tax revenue hasn’t been seen since 2009, when Mexico was in a recession. There’s no recession now,” Siller said. She pointed out that the falling collections track with lower company profits due to higher labor costs.
Sheinbaum’s proposed budget package estimates 3.29 trillion pesos in income tax revenue for next year, or about 7% more than lawmakers approved for 2026.

Still, the push to cap income tax deductions may not be ambitious enough to avoid a sovereign credit downgrade even if fully implemented, according to Rafael Ch, a senior analyst at Signum Global Advisors. He argues that Sheinbaum will likely wait until next summer to consider further revenue-enhancing measures due to other constraints, including high-stakes trade negotiations with the US.

Iván Arias, head of economic studies at Banamex, sees the government’s push for more revenue by reducing tax evasion as positive. But he thinks the proposal falls short as Sheinbaum pushes for higher spending elsewhere while still running a large deficit.
“These measures don’t foster greater confidence,” he said. “At best, they’ll maintain the status quo.”

items.title: Treasury Yields Stay Elevated as Stocks Fall Before Fed
body: Good morning. Treasury yields stay high and stocks slip ahead of the Fed’s rate decision. Elon Musk teases a SpaceX-Tesla merger again. And monks are turning to the market as their finances get squeezed by inflation. Listen to the day’s top stories.

The 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest since 2007 before retreating as rising oil prices kept global bonds under pressure. US stocks fell in the countdown to a rate decision where the Federal Reserve is expected to lift borrowing costs. Brent crude held steady while US diesel futures surged to a record high, leading Senate Majority Leader John Thune to say he’s “open to exploring” an export ban on the fuel.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US only deployed a “nominal” amount to support the yen compared with Japan’s record $96.4 billion and defended the operation as in the American interest. Bessent plans to meet his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, this weekend ahead of the Donald Trump-Xi Jinping summit, with Iran-related sanctions on the agenda.

Glencore accused Radiant World and associated companies of sending falsified invoices to lenders — just as a senior executive at the group of traders said they had filed a $2 billion lawsuit against Glencore. The claims mark the explosive end of a yearslong, extremely close business relationship.

Meta Platforms plans to deploy a new in-house artificial intelligence chip in data centers during the first half of next year. Elsewhere in the sector, OpenAI has been working with Anthropic and Google DeepMind for several weeks on AI safety measures. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang meanwhile dismissed the need for new AI security regulations.

Trump or his money managers have made nearly 28,700 trades since he returned to office, more than all of Congress combined, even as he seeks to pass a stock-purchasing ban for lawmakers that would exclude him.
Elon Musk once again teased the idea of his AI and rocket firm SpaceX combining with electric-car maker Tesla, noting the extensive cooperation between the two companies he leads.

France’s Shein fee is a bad fit for China Inc., writes Juliana Liu. While there are legitimate reasons to curb the environmental costs of throwaway clothing, a measure crafted so narrowly that it effectively singles out Chinese companies is neither effective nor intellectually honest.

items.title: Leon Black Contempt Resolution Advanced by House Epstein Panel
body: The House committee investigating disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein voted to recommend holding billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress Tuesday after he defied subpoenas for testimony and documents related to women in Epstein’s orbit.

The matter now goes to the full House for a vote to refer the Apollo Global Management co-founder to the Justice Department for review by a grand jury and possible prosecution. Contempt is punishable by a fine of up to $100,000 and imprisonment that can last from one month to a year, though the Justice Department does not pursue every contempt citation referred by Congress.

The 41-0 House Oversight Committee vote comes after Black didn’t show up for a Sept. 3 deposition with the panel. Instead, he filed a federal lawsuit seeking to block the subpoenas, arguing the committee exceeded its authority in issuing them. Black has denied any wrongdoing.
House Oversight Chairman James Comer said Black has “refused to comply” with subpoenas and is “not above the law.”
“We have no choice but to hold him in contempt,” Comer, a Kentucky Republican, said just before the panel vote.
In a statement Tuesday, Black’s attorneys, Susan Estrich and Aaron Cutler, called the contempt resolution a “complete abomination” and an abuse of power.

The attorneys said they filed a confidential complaint to the Office of Congressional Conduct requesting an investigation into Comer. They also blasted Robert Garcia, the panel’s top Democrat, over his previous statements about Black, which the lawyers said were false.

Black was issued two subpoenas by a congressional committee and walked out early from voluntary testimony in June regarding his relationship to Epstein. Black left the June interview after refusing to answer questions about nondisclosure agreements he made with women in Epstein’s orbit, the committee said.

“He voluntarily appeared before the Committee, provided a detailed opening statement about his relationship with Epstein, and offered to answer questions about his legitimate payments for tax and estate planning services,” Black’s attorney said in their statement. “Chairman Comer did not ask one question and sat silently as the transcript reflects from that day.”
The committee also issued a subpoena for copies of the NDAs.
At that time, Black said in an opening statement to the panel that he never abused women and wasn’t blackmailed by Epstein, his longtime friend and adviser.
Black has acknowledged paying Epstein $158 million over the years, which he said was for advice on estate and tax planning.
Read More: Epstein’s Mysterious $158 Million ‘Work of Art’ for Leon Black

“Mr. Black has repeatedly said that he feels terrible for Epstein’s victims and that he regrets ever doing business with Epstein,” his lawyers said in their statement Tuesday. “Mr. Black had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s heinous conduct.”

Epstein died in a New York jail cell in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges. The House Oversight Committee is investigating Epstein’s networks, as well as potential lapses in federal law enforcement’s response.

items.title: Which Is Worse: AI Groupthink or Extinction?
body: This is Bloomberg Opinion Today, the independent evaluators of Bloomberg Opinion’s opinions. Sign up here.

I was blissfully enjoying some peace and quiet on vacation in Europe when I got the news that there’s a 10% chance AI will wipe out humanity in the next decade. I took it in stride because, well, I was pretty sure the pool of brown butter on top of the taleggio-studded polenta I inhaled in the Italian Alps was going to kill me first:
I don’t want to guess how many calories were in the thing, but it was worth it. As my Italian grandpa used to say, “This stuff’ll kill ya, but what a way to go!”

I’m not sure everyone feels the same way about AI, though. Fortunately, 10% is not 100%, although a lot of the headlines might have you thinking it is. So instead of resigning yourself to being decimated by the same technology that has forever ruined restaurant menus, I encourage you to consider the flip side: What about the 90% chance we have of surviving?

Even if the AI race continues, as Parmy Olson suspects it will, the US and China could theoretically come together to create a pact on AI. “It can be tempting to frame any talks as fruitless. How could two countries, intensely distrustful of each other, reach a credible agreement to slow development or play on a more transparent AI field?” asks Dave Lee. “But trust need not be a prerequisite,” he explains. “While it may not be possible to point a satellite at a data center and assess AI progress in the same way a nation might count nuclear warheads, China observers say that Xi [Jinping] is sincerely willing to open up Chinese AI to independent evaluators if the US sector were subject to the same.”

Catherine Thorbecke says China views the AI situation differently. “In a recent essay about AI’s biggest dangers, a Chinese official didn’t mention human extinction once. Instead, the top concern is that deepfakes and influence operations could ruin social stability,” she says. “In China’s eyes, humanity — and not itself — is the real threat.”

So, let’s say that humans do stave off AI armageddon. What does life look like then? A lot like The Matrix, according to Matt Levine, who recently learned about dopamine sites that allow users to shop online without actually buying anything. “One of them is called Food Never Arrives. You order food, which doesn’t come, and you don’t pay for it. When you’re in a vat of goo being harvested to power Claude, that’ll be perfect,” he writes. Right now, such sites are free, but Matt says the category is ripe for disruption: “In principle, there’s no reason you couldn’t charge people $12.99 to not deliver them a sandwich.” Personally, I can’t imagine many people would be willing to pay a company to make them hangry. (Then again, stranger things have occurred in this economy.)

As AI animosity grows, Stephen Mihm says data centers are actually helping mend America’s longstanding political divisions. “It seems impossible to think that such a thing could happen. Research and commentary dedicated to analyzing today’s fragmented media ecosystem have, at times, made it seem like we’ve reached the point of no return,” he writes. But the rise of AI seems to have changed that. Stephen says LLMs “are quietly — if unintentionally — promoting consensus in both how and what the public learns about the world.”

Still, Stephen warns of the “zero-click” future, in which users will blindly accept AI summaries that have a built-in bias toward conventional wisdom. This could lead to “a new kind of groupthink that is no less dangerous for democracy than the polarization it replaces.” That’s definitely a bummer. But not nearly as big a bummer as human extinction.
Bonus AI Reading: Chipmaker stocks will weather any AI slowdown. — Dave Lee

One of my favorite food influencers at the moment is a young gentleman named Harrison Wallace. Not only are his recipes excellent, he really has a way with words. Consider how he describes his “chicken spaghetti,” a dish from his youth he’s carried into adulthood: “This smells like Obama is president. I’m watching the Good Eats x Unwrapped double feature on Food Network at night before Full House/Fresh Prince of Bel Air. My homework is done. And tomorrow is Friday.” Pure poetry.

If a nostalgic casserole made out of RO-TEL, shredded cheese and Campbell’s Cream of Chicken soup1 isn’t your thing, there’s always another way to feel like you’re living in Obama’s America: Move to Ohio. I’m ... not kidding?? Erika D. Smith says the Buckeye State’s status as a reliably red bastion is in question as we approach midterm elections.“Republicans should be worried about Ohio — and not just because of the Senate race,” she writes, referring to GOP candidate Jon Husted, whose campaign has been blemished by a now-fired aide who went wild with Nazi imagery online. Representative Max Miller also faces an uphill battle to reelection amid allegations of familial abuse. And Vivek Ramaswamy, who hopes to succeed Governor Mike DeWine, is polling neck and neck with his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

“This is saying something,” Erika writes. The last time Ohio had a Democratic governor was during (surprise!) Obama’s first term. Although Erika notes Ohio’s gubernatorial race isn’t about to change the trajectory of American politics, she says “losing the governorship in a supposedly red state, which the sitting vice president and likely MAGA heir JD Vance calls home, would be a psychological blow for Republicans.”

Fresh off my vacation in Portugal and Italy, I can tell you this: Chinese cars really are everywhere. I saw Tesla clones at Lake Como. BYD Dolphins in Porto. Xpengs in Lisbon. Writing from his perch in Germany, Chris Bryant says market shares of Chinese vehicles have exploded in Europe. “Previous attempts by Brussels to stem these imports haven’t worked,” he writes. “Unless Beijing curtails its massive trade imbalances, governments here will have to offer domestic automakers more protection. And they need to get on with it — while this continent still has a car industry to save.”

On Tuesday, the US confirmed for the first time that it’s deployed weapons in space. I’m not sure that’s such a wise idea considering we’re running rather low on them here on Earth. As the Bloomberg Editorial Board writes: “The Department of Defense has burned through a shocking number of its most sophisticated missiles in the war with Iran. The US not only needs to accelerate efforts to replenish those weapons — it ought to rethink their centrality to its warfighting strategy, too.”

And so does Ed Sheeran.
