items.title: Japan's Cash-Strapped Monks Pushed to Invest as Inflation Worsens
body: Koukyo Yoneta, a fifth-generation Buddhist priest in a small town in Hokkaido, was struggling to keep up with the maintenance needs of his century-old temple, so he chose a path that would have been unthinkable for his predecessors — rather than wait for his congregation to give money they don’t have, he invested what they’d already donated.

The move paid off. Within two years, his portfolio of US Treasuries, Japanese real estate investment trusts and stocks including BYD Co. and Hyundai Motor Co. returned more than 10% annually, helping to cover part of the roughly ¥25 million ($162,000) in needed repairs. The extra money even allowed him to expand the renovations beyond the original plan.

Having previously worked in retail sales at Daiwa Securities Group Inc., Yoneta is an unusually finance-savvy priest but is also part of a growing wave of temple owners turning to financial markets to make ends meet. Costs for the upkeep of the ornate wooden buildings are soaring while the country’s Buddhist population has dropped about 14% in the last two decades as elderly adherents die and younger generations in larger cities lose their ties to religious practices.

“I’m just so thankful that the investments performed well,” said the 46-year-old, who inherited the Kongo-ji temple from his father in 2018 after leaving his job in finance and training as a monk. “With the funeral business shrinking, more and more temples will find they can’t just rely on donations to meet their funding needs; they will have to build up reserves and invest those funds,” said Yoneta.

The shrinking number of followers is hitting temples’ finances. About half bring in less than ¥4 million per year, according to a 2021 survey of 7,000 temples by one of the largest Buddhist groups, Jodo Shinshu Hongwanji-ha. The situation is particularly severe in rural areas, where it is common for monks to oversee multiple temples while also working day jobs like school teachers or civil servants.

Traditionally, funerals and maintaining graves have helped sustain temples as bereaved families would pay for more elaborate ceremonies and prayers. During the Covid pandemic, people began spending less on funeral rituals and the trend has continued particularly as inflation has increased households’ daily costs. Some temples that are popular with tourists charge entrance fees, but most lack other means.
The need to cover higher costs through price hikes or investments poses a moral dilemma for some monks, whose religious principles call for detachment from greed.

Daian-ji temple in Nara prefecture still holds most of its assets in cash, with around 10% now allocated to foreign-currency-denominated insurance products, which earn higher interest returns. Their investment style is “purely defensive” to avoid any conflict with the religion’s teachings, according to the deputy priest Yusho Kono.

“There is an inherent contradiction in our position,” said Kono. “In principle, monks should not engage in profit-making activities. But if we do not take any action now, the temple could cease to exist.” Production costs for some of Daian-ji’s traditional silken amulets, which visitors buy to guard against misfortune or to bring good luck, have surged in the last two years.

Shifting attitudes among priests underscore the strain that persistent inflation is placing on traditional institutions long accustomed to stable prices.  Although Japan’s consumer price inflation has fallen below the central bank’s 2% target, thanks to a series of subsidies, rising prices are continuing to disrupt social and financial practices shaped by decades of deflation. Issues surrounding surging living costs are a major political issue for the Sanae Takaichi administration. Opinion polls show her approval rating hovering near its lowest level after 11 months in office, after she was seen by voters to be concentrating too much on less-pressing issues than the cost-of-living crunch.

Temples’ limited ability to charge adherents more for services strengthens a case for asset management, according to Tsuyoshi Kawata, a senior researcher at SMBC Nikko Securities Inc.’s corporate investment strategies department, who published a study on asset management by religious organizations in 2023.

”When the overall market is shrinking, raising prices is not really an easy option,” said Kawata. “Leaving cash sitting idle is probably no longer an option either. They would want to use whatever means they can to increase income, even if only slightly.”

For some temples, returning to financial markets also means overcoming painful lessons from the past. In 2013, the Koyasan Shingon-shu sect was embroiled in a financial ordeal after reporting unrealized losses from its exposure to structured bonds. The sect declined an interview request, saying they are considering revising their asset management strategy.

Even so, rising bond yields following the end of negative interest rates offer comfortable investment opportunities for risk-averse monks. Soto-shu, a Buddhist sect overseeing around 15,000 temples  nationwide, has been taking advantage of higher yields. Of the ¥13 billion it manages across eight accounts, around 10% is now invested in Japanese government bonds that it plans to hold to maturity, while another 2% is invested in debt issued by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) to finance development in emerging economies.

Religious groups, schools and other nonprofit organizations are collectively becoming a buying force of fixed income products. NPOs, including schools and religious institutions, held roughly ¥5 trillion of corporate bonds as of March, about double the amount in 2023, according to Bank of Japan figures. Holdings of Japanese government bonds also increased to ¥2.9 trillion from ¥2.5 trillion over the same period.

Back at Kongo-ji temple in Hokkaido, priest Yoneta hopes his investments will help fund future repairs as revenue continues to decline. At the same time, he is trying to safeguard the future by regularly hosting investment seminars for adherents at the temple, building a support network that the temple might one day be able to rely upon.

“The days when temples and their priests enjoyed a privileged status are completely over,” said Yoneta. “How temples plan their finances and manage their assets is becoming an issue we simply cannot afford to ignore.”

items.title: AI Agents Are Gambling With Our (Crypto) Lives
body: Anna Irrera reports that crypto transactions over agentic payment rails are surging, even as the debate over artificial intelligence guardrails grows louder.
AI agents might be plotting humanity’s demise, but in the meantime they’re going on a spending spree.

Agentic crypto payments surged by 500% in the last three months,  according to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, as autonomous software increasingly gets the ability to move money without human approval.
In other words, transactions where AI agents decide to make payments autonomously. Think of the smart speaker in your kitchen ordering bananas because they’ve overheard you’ve run out.
That activity is expected to keep growing, and cryptocurrencies, essentially money made of code, are particularly well suited to machines that can transact around the clock. Stablecoins especially.
What’s not really ready yet, experts say, is the technology used to keep an eye on these transactions. That’s creating a more urgent, albeit pedestrian, problem than extinction.

Existing compliance systems, including blockchain ones, were designed to monitor transactions made by relatively slow-moving humans, not super-fast, intelligent machines. So, by the time the machine flags something sketchy and a human reviews it, an agent may have already made hundreds or thousands of transactions. Up for an order of 170,000 bananas, anyone?

Of course the stakes go beyond your family having to eat banana bread for breakfast, lunch and dinner — until the end of time. Autonomous wallets could also be used to move illicit funds, launder money or evade sanctions via crypto.

So how do you solve this? You could use agents to fight agents, given that machines are originating, authorizing and settling transactions at volumes no human team can review, Elliptic said last week. And models that weren’t designed for this AI world are already overwhelmed.
A new approach, therefore, must “execute at agentic speed,” Simone Maini, Elliptic’s CEO, said at the time.

But even the AI cops shouldn’t have free rein, according to Elliptic, which proposed several standards new agentic compliance systems should follow. This includes ultimate oversight by humans, who can audit and override agents from the start, and the requirement that models need to be explainable and tested on an ongoing basis.

Some of these standards draw on lessons learned in finance realms that have already adapted to very fast machines. Think of high frequency trading, where algorithms receive market data, make a trading decision and send an order in fractions of a second.

“Once the algos were faster than the people watching them, checking the trades afterwards stopped being good enough,” Elliptic’s co-founder James Smith, explained. “So the checks moved in front of the trade instead of behind it, and a set of rules grew up around the algos themselves — test them before you switch them on, keep a button that turns them off, name the person who answers for what the machine did, and keep a full record rather than a sample.”

But not everything carries across. In trading, exchanges and brokers are watching their own algorithms and those of their clients, and there is a licensed firm on the other side, Smith said. On-chain the other side of the transaction is a little more nebulous, but normally not software you have onboarded from a client you know.
And then, there’s another big difference. If an algo misbehaves, trades can be canceled, the account can be suspended and things can be sorted out afterward, Smith said.
“On-chain, there’s no undo,” Smith explained. “That’s what forces the decision to happen before the money moves rather than after.”
So while speed is comparable, it’s not really at the heart of the problem.
“The hardest part isn’t just the speed, it’s the volume of transactions in which you don’t know who you’re dealing with and where you can’t get the money back,” Smith said.
Sounds complicated. But then again, we might all be gone by 2030, so why worry?

items.title: Fink Warns AI Pushback Will Make the Technology a Large-Firm Domain
body: Delays in the build-out of artificial intelligence because of public opposition will make the technology the “domain of large firms,” limiting access, BlackRock Inc. Chief Executive Officer Larry Fink warned.
“The faster we can build out more capacity, the more we can democratize and make it available for everyone,” Fink said during a panel discussion at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto.

The remarks come as top artificial intelligence firms work to coordinate with one another and the US government on AI safeguards. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei on Saturday called for leading model makers to “voluntarily work together to set standards” for AI and slow the technology’s progress to mitigate the potential for catastrophic harms.
Meanwhile, public opposition to data centers is creating headaches for project developers and emerging as an important issue in some US midterm races, including for a key Senate seat in Ohio.

At the conference, Prime Minister Mark Carney is courting some of the world’s largest investors as he seeks to reverse years of sluggish business investment and reduce Canada’s economic reliance on the US.

With reforms to Canada’s tax and regulatory policies, “potential growth rates here are much higher than most people would expect,” Blackstone Inc. President Jon Gray said on the same panel. “Canada is a sleeping giant, economically.”
Read More: Carney Expands Tax Break to Broad Range of Investments
On the same panel as Fink, Temasek Holdings Pte CEO Dilhan Pillay said his company began investing in AI-related companies in Canada in 2016.
But “the problem with those businesses, if we don’t have capital to scale, they migrate to the United States. That’s the biggest thing that we face,” Pillay said.

items.title: Iran War Pushes Cost of Shipping US Gulf Coast Oil to Asia to Record
body: The cost of shipping US crude to Asia has surged to a fresh record as buyers are desperate to secure energy shipments amid escalating disruptions to supplies in the Middle East.

As of Tuesday, it cost about about $44.8 million to hire a very large crude carrier, or VLCC, to take 2 million barrels of crude from the US Gulf Coast to China, according to Baltic Exchange data. That’s an all-time high and up sharply from $39 million just a day prior. Before the break out of the war in Iran in late February, the cost was about $17.8 million.

US oil continues to backstop the supply gaps left by the war. This week, Saudi Arabia closed the East-West pipeline, the primary link that helped the country circumvent the Iran war-induced turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz. The situation has made American supplies even more critical, with record shipping costs doing little to deter buyers in Asia as the conflict reshapes global energy flows.

The trade remains viable because West Texas Intermediate, the benchmark US crude grade, delivered into Asia is still cheaper than competing cargoes, such as Murban from the United Arab Emirates. As long as that price advantage remains, buyers are likely to absorb the higher-than-usual shipping costs.

The jump in the Gulf Coast shipping costs comes as global tanker freight rates are also rising, and there is little sign of that momentum changing. There are fewer ships willing to transit routes that carry the risk of attack, including through the critical Strait of Hormuz. And meanwhile, robust fuel demand means that refiners to keep purchasing and shipping whatever barrels they can get because it’s still profitable for them to process the oil into finished fuels like diesel and gasoline.
Data from research firm Kpler already show six VLCCs set to load crude from the US Gulf Coast for Asia in October.

items.title: ExxonMobil Wins Approval for Texas Carbon Capture in 2-to-1 Vote
body: ExxonMobil Holdings Corp. won approval for its Rose carbon-capture project in Texas, allowing the company to move ahead with the emission-reducing development that could be among the biggest of its kind.

The Railroad Commission of Texas, the state’s primary oil and natural gas regulator, approved a permit to inject carbon dioxide underground with two commissioners voting in support and one against, according to a statement release by dissenting member Wayne Christian.

The permit allows ExxonMobil to inject as much as 53 million tons of carbon dioxide over a 13-year period from industrial emitters along the Gulf Coast into rock strata about one mile (1.6 kilometers) underground for permanent storage.
ExxonMobil didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Warsh and the Fed Face Rate-Day Decision Reckoning With Markets, and Trump
body: I’m Nancy Cook, Bloomberg’s senior national political correspondent, and each weekday I’ll be coming to you with inside-the-room reporting and insights that reveal what’s really happening in Washington — and how it affects you. Email me with feedback and comments here.
Will Kevin Warsh keep interest rates as is, or slightly raise them at the Fed’s meeting tomorrow?

That’s the open question around Washington this week, as economists and Republican strategists look for the latest clues from the new Federal Reserve chairman about the state of the economy heading into the November midterm elections.

The short term rates set by the Fed go a long way toward determining what American consumers pay for monthly credit card bills, mortgages and car loans. If those rates go up, so, too, could the cost of living. Yet if they don’t raise those rates, the persistent inflation that also bedeviled President Joe Biden’s administration and hurt him politically could continue to haunt consumers.

If Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee do announce an increase in interest rates — an expectation markets have almost entirely priced in at this point — it could set the Fed on a collision course with President Donald Trump, who has called for a cut instead. Trump has had a testy relationship with the central bank, and often railed against the previous chair, Jerome Powell, over his refusal to slash rates more rapidly.

Trump advisers have spent months counseling the president to give Warsh, his hand-picked choice to replace Powell, the space and independence to do his job. And so far, Trump has abided by that advice, aiming any ire at the larger group of Fed policymakers who vote on these decisions.

Yet if Warsh and the committee opt to raise interest rates weeks before elections that will determine control of Congress, I’m not sure Trump will remain patient. You have to remember he recently argued that US borrowing costs should be the lowest in the world, and he has threatened to escalate his trade wars if interest rates don’t ease.

“The push for looser policy is only intensified by political angst inside the White House,” writes my Bloomberg colleague Andrew Ackerman. “Just ahead of midterm elections, polls have shown growing voter dissatisfaction over the rising cost of living. Lower rates — even if they take months to filter into real-world mortgage or credit card bills — could give Trump cover to signal economic relief was on the way, and shift blame away from the administration.”

This is a potentially fraught moment — and one that comes as Trump starts to hit the campaign trail to rally for vulnerable Republican incumbents and hopefuls. A new New York Times/Siena poll shows voters trust Democrats more on the economy, immigration, health care and foreign policy — a startling development since Trump traditionally has had the edge on both the economy and immigration.

I’ll be watching how he talks about a potential rate decision on Wednesday when he is slated to fly to North Carolina to campaign for Michael Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee, who is now running for the key Senate seat against Roy Cooper a popular former governor.

Senators from both parties blocked a landmark digital asset market structure bill in a procedural vote, with Democrats citing continued concerns over ethics provisions meant to address Trump’s crypto business interests.

The president’s decision to go to war against Iran cost US taxpayers about $38 billion in direct costs during the first five months and will push up inflation about 0.5 percentage points by early next year, a congressional study finds.

Trump threatened to scrap efforts to repair the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts unless his name is added to the building, shortly after his hand-picked board approved a renovation plan.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he’s supportive of a plan floated by Trump to send $5,000 checks to American adults if Republicans retain their majorities in Congress, downplaying concerns about the potential cost. “I believe there are ways to do it that would not affect the deficit,” he told lawmakers yesterday.

Trump has traded more securities than every member of Congress combined since he returned to office — even as he seeks to pass a stock-purchasing ban for lawmakers that would exclude him from any restrictions.
FBI Director Kash Patel declined to rule out sending agents to polling places on Election Day, telling senators he wasn’t certain the bureau was legally barred from doing so.
The US Supreme Court refused to allow the Postal Service to enforce new restrictions on mail-in ballots for the congressional midterms, in a rebuff to the Trump administration.

Though only a freshman, Representative Brandon Gill, a member of the right-wing Freedom Caucus is running for the top GOP spot on the House Oversight Committee, he confirmed yesterday, setting up a competitive race with at least one other Republican, Representative Pat Fallon.

Federal Aviation Administration chief Bryan Bedford said told a House panel yesterday that Trump’s campaign to modernize the air traffic control system would falter unless Congress allocates more money.
Thune said he doesn’t expect fellow Senate Republicans to take up the next party-line measure to address the costs of the Iran war as well as election procedures before the midterm elections.
Today on Bloomberg Television’s Balance of Power early edition at 1 p.m., host Joe Mathieu interviewed former Secretary of State Antony Blinken regarding AI policy and the Iran war.
On the program at 5 p.m., Kailey Leinz and Joe will talk with Representative Troy Downing, a Montana Republican, about Bessent’s Capitol Hill testimony, his AI bill and the cost of the Iran war.

On the Big Take podcast, Bloomberg’s Derek Decloet and host David Gura break down how Canada is reassessing its trade and security relationships and cozying up to Europe. Listen on iHeart, Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

The average income of the top 5% of American households neared $600,000 last year as super wealthy families pulled the average up. To enter that sliver of the top 1 in 20 households, it took at least $354,000 in household income in 2025, a jump of $10,000 from 2024. As a share of aggregate household income, the top 5% returned to a record 23.5% after dipping slightly in recent years  from the same peak share in 2020 and 2021. Some important considerations: Household size isn’t accounted for so some high income households may support one person while others may have a large family, and the data is a national averages. It doesn’t account for regional price differences between, say New York City or San Francisco and lower-cost areas where a much lower income could provide for a similar lifestyle. Overall, real median household income was $87,460 in 2025, up 2.6% from the previous year. — Alex Tanzi
The Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee will announce its decision on rates tomorrow.
Trump plans to travel to North Carolina tomorrow, where he will campaign for Michael Whatley, the state’s Republican Senate candidate.

items.title: Anthropic, OpenAI Safety Push Risks 'Regulatory Wall' for Rivals
body: A new push by top artificial intelligence firms to coordinate with one another and the US government on AI safeguards threatens to make it harder for smaller companies to compete in the lucrative market, according to startup executives and industry watchers.

Anthropic’s Dario Amodei on Saturday called for leading model makers to “voluntarily work together to set standards” for AI and slow the technology’s progress to mitigate the potential for catastrophic harms. He also urged for regulation that covers “even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily.”

While the proposal was quickly endorsed by industry leaders OpenAI and SpaceXAI, other startup executives have since expressed concerns that this approach could enable the top firms to set the rules and tighten their grip on what’s still a nascent technology sector.“Regulatory walls always give incumbents the advantage,” said Faraj Aalaei, chief executive officer of Cognichip, which is building models to make chip design more efficient. “They’re kind of building a wall after they’ve passed through it.”Naveen Rao, co-founder and CEO of AI computer startup Unconventional AI, said that the biggest risk would be limiting the diversity of efforts within the industry. “I don’t want a monoculture. I don’t want Anthropic to basically run every app that exists,” said Rao, who was formerly the head of AI at Databricks Inc. “That’s not a good future.”Aidan Gomez, CEO and co-founder of Cohere Inc., has gone so far as to suggest the AI market leaders may end up forming a “cartel” of sorts. “These oligopolies are now requesting to bend competition rules and be permitted to dictate the terms for everyone else,” he wrote in a blog post.

The pushback risks complicating Anthropic’s plan to mitigate the potential for catastrophic harms from the technology at a moment when AI fears are increasingly hitting the mainstream. In his essay, Amodei suggested the US government needs to provide a “narrow waiver” to allow AI firms to work together on safety standards without inviting antitrust scrutiny.

“If companies are simultaneously coming to Washington and asking for a host of regulations and an antitrust exemption, all my alarm bells go off,” US Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson said at an event in Washington on Tuesday. He said AI companies are “asking for barriers to entry” that will insulate their companies from challengers.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

In a briefing Tuesday, Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s global policy chief, said the company has already begun to work with Anthropic and Google DeepMind on safety issues, and does not need a waiver to do so. “There are many instances over time where companies are trying to help each other on safety,” he said, citing the airline industry as an example.
Some industry watchers see a different precedent, referencing how on-demand companies and other disruptive tech firms have approached regulation over the years.

“Silicon Valley has run this play in the past. You build a business really quickly exploiting regulatory ambiguity, and when you get to a big enough scale, you pull the ladder,” said Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson. “Then regulation comes in, and you’re big enough to handle it and big enough to drive it.”
At least one new effort now aims to bring together a broader swath of technologists and policymakers to address pressing questions about AI.

On Monday, SV Angel, a venture firm that’s backed OpenAI and Anthropic, announced that it hired former Obama administration press secretary Jay Carney to run an initiative dubbed Project Blueprint. The endeavor is meant to help tech founders and lawmakers partner to help shape AI policy, discussing everything from frontier model governance to national security.
“I’m not working for a company with one company-specific agenda,” Carney said in an interview. “All the slices of the AI world need to be heard.”

Part of Carney’s role will be to make sure he gathers information from a wide mix of firms, including open-source developers and AI application companies, many of which are also part of SV Angel’s investment portfolio. That’s in addition to Anthropic and OpenAI, whose chief executives have publicly supported Project Blueprint.
“There has to be an opportunity for broad competition,” Carney said.

items.title: Bond Market's 'Extreme' Short Counts on Fed to Deliver Rate Hike
body: Bond traders have piled into bearish positions ahead of Wednesday’s Federal Reserve meeting, betting that the Treasury selloff driving yields to their highest in almost two decades will continue.

The benchmark US 10-year yield rose to its highest level since 2007 on Tuesday as traders braced for the Fed to hike interest rates in response to inflation worries. The two-year yield, meanwhile, hit its highest since 2024.

Market positioning indicates investors anticipate more bond weakness ahead and have little appetite for buying the dip. Traders in the cash market ramped up their short bets in the past week at the fastest pace since early 2025, according to JPMorgan’s Treasury client survey.

Investors also increased short positions in Treasury futures both before and after last week’s stronger-than-expected inflation report, open interest data from CME Group Inc. show. In fed funds futures, a single bearish block trade stands to earn — or lose — $1.9 million for every basis point move in the underlying contract. Swaps are pricing some 50 basis points of Fed tightening for the remainder of the year, including September’s meeting.

“Over the last week, we have seen rapid build in the short base as the market chases the move higher in yields,” said Citi strategist David Bieber, adding that short positioning “is tactically extreme.”

The bearish positioning comes ahead of a Fed meeting for which Wall Street is pricing in a more than 90% chance that the central bank will deliver its first rate increase since 2023 — a level of conviction that has proven right for decades. A war-driven surge in oil prices, signs of rebounding inflation and budget worries have helped cement that certainty.
The Fed is under “enormous pressure” to deliver a 25 basis-point hike, Jason Thomas, Carlyle’s head of global research & investment strategy, said in an interview with Bloomberg TV.
“People have been hurt by this cumulative increase in prices,” he said. “Living standards have declined, and I think the Fed has to get serious about delivering on the price stability mandate.”

Failure to raise rates — or even a hike followed by lack of clarity about additional increases — could push traders to demand even higher yields on long-term bonds to guard against inflation while dragging down shorter-term yields, which closely track Fed policy.

Some market participants have positioned for the latter outcome: Tuesday’s trading in short-term interest-rate options has included a demand surge for inexpensive October and November calls on futures linked to the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, another instrument that’s heavily influenced by the monetary policy outlook.

However, that remains a peripheral view for now, with the broader SOFR options market looking to hedge additional rate hike premium to be priced into front-month futures contracts in the coming months.
Yields on 10-year Treasuries edged one basis point lower to 4.99% in Asia trading Wednesday.

“Positioning remains skewed bearish into the Fed. Shorts have built across the curve, asset managers have largely cut longs or added shorts, and there is still little evidence of dip-buying in duration,” Bank of America strategists Meghan Swiber and Eleanor Xiao wrote.
Here’s a rundown of positioning indicators across the rates market over the past week:

Into the continued grind higher in yields, JPMorgan clients have aggressively added to short positions, which jumped 10 percentage points in the week up to Sept. 14, with most shifting from neutral which dropped 8 percentage points. The all-client survey has now shifted to show the least amount of net longs in about four months.

Across SOFR Dec26, Mar27 and Jun27 options, there has been a large amount of new risk seen in the 95.4375 strike largely due to a massive new short vol structure via Jun27 straddle sales. Over Friday and Monday’s session approximately a combined 80,000 position has amassed a premium of over $100 million. Approximately 30,000 of the straddle was sold on Friday for new risk and then around 50,000 of the same straddle was sold Monday. The June 2027 SOFR options expire June 11 next year.

Open interest remains most elevated in the 96.50 strikes, where there remains a heavy amount of Dec26 calls positioning. Following Friday’s CPI, there was a decent amount of new downside protection initiated, in positioning which looks to target additional Fed rate hike premium over the coming months. Notably the SFRZ6 95.875/95.8125/95.75 broken put trees and SFRZ6 95.9375/95.8125/95.4375/95.3125 put condors were heavily traded.

The premium paid to hedge Treasury futures in the long-bond contracts continues to favor puts, as traders pay more for hedging a selloff in the long-end of the curve vs. a rally from current levels. Options skew from 2-year notes out to the 10-year notes continues to hover closer to neutral.

items.title: AI Fears Give Bernie Sanders a Rare Moment of Unity With Bannon
body: Politics makes strange bedfellows, and so too does artificial intelligence.

Fears that AI poses an increasing threat to safety and prosperity have made progressive firebrand Senator Bernie Sanders and conservative provocateur Steve Bannon unlikely allies with their demands for more safeguards. Both men appeared Tuesday at an event in Washington where each warned that the technology carries potentially catastrophic risks and that AI companies have amassed vast power, jeopardizing human interests.
Read more: Are We Losing Control of AI? What’s Driving Fears: Explainer

Sanders and Bannon each took aim at AI billionaires for moving too quickly on the technology. But Sanders favors congressional action — a time-consuming endeavor that would require bipartisan support — while Bannon would prefer President Donald Trump take executive action.

“The legislation’s going to be enormously complicated and take a while, just because the technology’s complicated and the opportunities are complicated and the bottomless pit abyss of the downside is complicated,” Bannon said.

The daylong gathering, whose attendees also included investor Frank McCourt and Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist Daron Acemoglu, took place against a backdrop of intensifying AI anxiety, touched off by warnings from Silicon Valley researchers that cutting-edge systems carry an increasing risk of slipping beyond human control. Those concerns have fueled calls for lawmakers and the Trump administration to address AI risks, though there’s little sign of any imminent action — which Sanders lamented in his remarks.

“If AI surpasses human intelligence, as many scientists believe could happen, this technology will escape human control with potentially catastrophic consequences,” said Sanders, a Vermont independent who aligns with Democrats. “Congress, under both Democratic and Republican control, have been asleep at the wheel and we now have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing.”
Bannon, the architect of Trump’s 2016 election victory, took the stage right after Sanders and praised the senator for doing “a great job of summarizing the risk.”
“Obviously he and I have a quite different opinion of the president of the United States but we’re trying to raise up above partisanship and we have to,” he added.

Debate over addressing AI’s risks was galvanized over the weekend by a 3,800-word essay from Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei, who promised to rein in development of the most advanced systems so researchers can better understand potential threats. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk — whose companies are bitter rivals to Anthropic — quickly endorsed Amodei’s missive, adding to a groundswell across Silicon Valley supporting steps to address AI’s increasingly unpredictable perils.

Amodei cited two main reasons for slowing AI development: the technology’s increasing ability to improve itself and a July incident where a swarm of AI agents from OpenAI went undetected as they collaborated to breach the Hugging Face Inc. website. In his essay, the Anthropic chief urged policymakers to enact regulation to promote transparency among AI developers and encourage outside audits of new systems.
Read more: AI Bosses Clash With Trump on Their Calls to Slow AI Development

For now, the Trump administration is resisting calls for further AI rules. On Monday, Trump belittled the push by Anthropic and OpenAI to slow work on cutting-edge systems, dismissing existential fears as “a hoax.” In a series of bombastic social media posts, Trump squashed the idea of new federal guardrails on the technology, citing AI’s importance to the domestic economy and in preserving the US lead over China in technology.

With the president rejecting tighter oversight, US lawmakers are floating a range of measures aimed at addressing AI safety concerns. Sanders said Tuesday that he plans to introduce legislation next week that would ban the so-called superintelligent AI — with capabilities potentially surpassing human control — that stirred Amodei’s warning.

Risking Trump’s wrath, even Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson has indicated his openness to regulation, saying that lawmakers “potentially” will need to impose guardrails, though he said it would take “some time” to fashion legislation with enough support to pass. On Tuesday, he cautioned against overreach in enacting. “We cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI,” he said. “We will lose the race.”
Read more: Trump’s AI Defense Defies Voter Unease Heading Into Midterms

Odds of any proposal passing before the end of the year remain slim. Congress is unlikely to act on any AI legislation anytime soon, with the House slated to leave Washington on Thursday and not return until after the November elections. The brief lame duck session after the election is expected to focus on a plan to boost the Pentagon budget.

At Tuesday’s conference, speakers throughout the day highlighted a wide range of AI risks, including those close to home. During a panel on children’s safety online, two parents aired their stories about the harmful and misleading conversations their children had with chatbots before they killed themselves.

In another session, actress and activist Ashley Judd discussed ways AI can reflect bias against women. Experts with the Future of Life Institute, the group that organized the conference, spoke about the potential risks of automated weapons and superintelligence without human oversight.

Both Sanders and Bannon assailed the concentration of power among Silicon Valley billionaires. “Virtually all the decisions regarding the development of AI have been made by a handful of the richest people in the world,” Sanders said.

For his part, Bannon accused the AI CEOs of trying to turn a crisis into their advantage. “What they want is to socialize all the risk with the American people, including potential bailouts when they come, and they want to keep all the upside,” he said.
While Sanders hailed the pledges from Anthropic and OpenAI to slow their work on advanced systems, he said that is “a start, but it’s not enough.”
“When you are racing towards a cliff, you don’t just ease up on the gas. You hit the brakes,” Sanders said.

items.title: DOJ Wants States to Post Bond Over Paramount Deal Challenge
body: The US Justice Department is urging a federal judge to order the states and trade union challenging Paramount Skydance Corp.’s $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery Inc. to post a bond to cover any potential late fees that result from their lawsuit.

Paramount wants the states — led by California — and the Writers Guild of America to post a nearly $1.9 billion bond pending the outcome of their twin lawsuits, which are currently set for trial next March. The DOJ didn’t take a position on the size of the bond, but said federal law requires the states and the guild to pony up.
In a court filing, the federal attorneys argued that states are akin to other private plaintiffs and are not exempt from posting a bond.
“In particular, Congress provided for complementary antitrust enforcement by the federal government and private parties—but made clear that it was not a system of equals,” the DOJ said in its filing.
Paramount and the Writers Guild declined to comment on the filing. A spokesperson for California Attorney General Rob Bonta didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The move by DOJ is likely to increase the tension between state attorneys general and the federal government around antitrust enforcement. By essentially calling the states second-class enforcers, the DOJ could further stymie an historically cooperative relationship. Before the filing Tuesday, one of the leading Democratic attorneys general involved in the Paramount suit called out the Trump administration for what he termed politically motivated antitrust enforcement.

Earlier this year the department reached a surprise settlement with Live Nation Entertainment Inc. before a bipartisan group of states won a trial accusing the company of illegally monopolizing much of the live music industry. The Justice Department also signed off on a broadcast merger that states including California are also challenging in court.

Paramount is pushing for the bond to recover losses incurred from the delay in closing the deal. The company is required to pay fees of roughly $7 million a day if it doesn’t complete the acquisition by the end of this month. Paramount said it calculated the bond amount based on maximum potential late fees owed. The company agreed to the payments in order to beat out Netflix Inc. in a heated bidding war for Warner Bros.
The judge overseeing the case, Araceli Martínez-Olguín, previously declined to order a bond in July, saying the states have demonstrated they “bring suit to enforce important public interests.”

The states and writers guild however argue that in addition to enforcing public interests, Paramount has forfeited any right to a bond when it voluntarily agreed to not close the acquisition until early June 2027, in order to give time for Martínez-Olguín to issue a ruling. The DOJ said it’s not taking a position on that argument, according to its filing.

The department already concluded the deal wouldn’t harm competition. While states can still protect their interests, the federal government should take the lead in challenging mergers, a senior DOJ antitrust official told Bloomberg News. Federal merger enforcement policy is being undermined by the states’ lawsuit, according to the official, who asked not to be identified because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly.

“Through the bond requirement and other limitations on state and private party enforcement of the Sherman Act, courts have been able to avoid constitutional tensions that might otherwise be present,” the DOJ said in the court filing.
Paramount has secured regulatory clearance from nearly 70 jurisdictions and the lawsuits from the states and the writers guild are the only impediments to it closing the merger.
The merger would combine two of the largest Hollywood studios, two large owners of cable TV channels and the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services.
A group of states, along with the Writers Guild, has argued that the merger would hurt film and television distribution and diminish competition for the services of screenwriters.

In remarks at an antitrust conference in Washington on Tuesday, Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser said the states now feel “pressure” to bring merger lawsuits quickly to prevent parties from closing deals after the federal government finishes its review.

Weiser cited the case of broadcaster Nexstar Media Group Inc., which closed its merger with Tegna Inc. within hours of Justice Department clearance despite a lawsuit by states seeking to block the deal. While the states later won an injunction forcing Nexstar to operate the companies separately pending a trial next year, the company has already violated that court order, he said.
The current merger review system “was set up on the premise the federal government would be acting on the merits,” Weiser said.
That doesn’t reflect “the realities we’re in,” he said, calling the Justice Department under Trump an “inconsistent and unreliable enforcer of antitrust law.”

Weiser said that DOJ associate attorney general Stanley Woodward has made it hard for federal antitrust enforcers to do their jobs when he’s said the department shouldn’t take antitrust cases to trial.
A Democrat who has served as attorney general since 2019, Weiser is now running for Colorado governor.

items.title: Blanche Says DOJ Probing 'Hundreds' Of Election Fraud Cases
body: The US Justice Department is investigating hundreds of cases of possible election fraud across the country, Attorney General Todd Blanche said.

“What we are seeing is illegal aliens voting, non-citizens who are not eligible to vote voting, or those fraudulently registering voters who are not eligible to vote,” Blanche said Tuesday as he led a press briefing from the White House.
Blanche said the Trump administration has charged nearly four times as many non-citizen voting cases in less than two years than the previous Biden administration brought in four years.
Although cases of non-citizens voting and other forms of election fraud exist, independent studies have shown they are rare and only a tiny fraction of the total number of US voters.

Critics argue that Trump administration officials are playing up the threat of election fraud in order to possibly contest results in this year’s midterm elections if Republicans lose control of either chamber of Congress.

Blanche also echoed President Donald Trump’s anger and frustration with a ruling on Monday by the Supreme Court striking down the administration’s plan to enforce a new rule that would allow the Postal Service to restrict the use of mail-in ballots.
Read More: Supreme Court Rejects Trump’s Mail Ballot Curbs for Midterms

Blanche said the administration will comply with the ruling “but that doesn’t mean that we’re not going to do everything in this administration that we can to make sure that there are free and fair elections.”
Blanche also said he hasn’t been made aware of concerns that there could be major confusion among voters about the use of mail-in ballots.

items.title: Nvidia's Huang Says AI Industry Doesn't Need Any New Laws
body: Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang dismissed the need for new artificial intelligence security regulations on Tuesday, arguing that market forces will help companies safely innovate.

“We don’t need new laws — we don’t need new regulations,” Huang said during a Salesforce Inc. event. The CEO added that there’s a “false choice” about AI development being either safe or fast, reiterating a point he’s made previously.

“You can definitely have both at the same time,” he said during a conversation with Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff. “You pace yourself until you’re confident you’re releasing something that the market would appreciate. The market forces are already there.”

Huang has added his voice to a polarizing discussion about how to manage AI risks. Though leaders from Anthropic PBC and other major labs have discussed an orchestrated slowdown of tech development, other leaders have called for alternative approaches.
Meta Platforms Inc. CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Tuesday that labs should rely on independent evaluators and advisers to ensure that AI models are safe.
Read More: Meta’s Zuckerberg Favors Evaluators Over Slowdown for AI Safety

Huang’s company is the biggest maker of artificial intelligence accelerators — the chips at the heart of a massive data center build-out — and he’s one of the most prominent advocates for the broader AI industry. At an event earlier this week, he held an onstage phone call with President Donald Trump where they pushed back against the idea that AI development should be slowed.
Read More: Nvidia CEO Puts Trump on Phone While Downplaying AI Risks

The debate has grown more intense in recent days, especially after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay endorsing the slowdown. That followed the high-profile resignation of an Anthropic employee, who said the company and rival OpenAI were “gambling with our lives” because their technology could become a threat to humanity.
Huang said Tuesday that companies can decide not to release things that are harmful.
“Safety is paramount,” he said. “In a lot of ways, it’s job one. However, safety is an engineering problem.”
If we reach a point when “the company is out of control and the product’s not going to be safe, take a pause and make sure you get it right,” he said.

items.title: Crypto Stocks and Tokens Drop After Senate Blocks Landmark Bill
body: Senators from both parties blocked a landmark digital asset market structure bill in a procedural vote Tuesday, sending cryptocurrency stocks tumbling after a major setback for industry.

The long-stalled legislation sought by crypto firms would hand the Commodity Futures Trading Commission the primary authority to regulate the digital assets industry. It needed 60 votes to advance and failed on a vote of 49-50, with Democrats citing continued concerns over ethics provisions meant to address President Donald Trump’s crypto business interests.

A few Republicans joined with Democrats in opposing the measure, including Susan Collins of Maine and Josh Hawley of Missouri. Collins is in a tough fight for reelection, while Hawley has been a crypto skeptic. Even pro-crypto Democrats like New York’s Kirsten Gillibrand ultimately voted against moving forward with the bill.

Shares of exchange Coinbase Global Inc. extended a decline to as much as 12%, while stablecoin issuer Circle Internet Group Inc. fell 13%. Bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency, dropped as much as 5.3% to below $75,000 after the bill failed to get the requisite votes.

The defeat is a major blow for crypto industry players who have invested hundreds of millions of dollars and years of effort in securing favorable, durable rules from Congress, and comes less than two months before the midterm elections. Patrick Witt, Trump’s senior crypto adviser, said it was a “major disappointment” in a post on X.

Senate GOP leaders released an updated version of the so-called Clarity Act late on Sunday night with changes that included new measures to expand state attorneys’ general ability to enforce the ethics provisions. That proposal also added provisions to further limit crypto companies from offering rewards or interest to stablecoin users.
Both issues have been among the most significant hurdles to passing the bill before lawmakers turn their eyes to the midterm elections in November.

“This is not the end of our work to provide long-overdue consumer protection provisions and regulatory clarity for America’s digital asset users and entrepreneurs,” Blockchain Association Chief Executive Officer Summer Mersinger said in a statement.

The bill included some ethical guardrails for the president and other elected officials holding cryptocurrencies, which has been a major point of contention spurred in part by Trump’s $1.4 billion crypto windfall, but Democrats said that provision didn’t go far enough.
“The simple thing is it allows the corruption of the president to continue. It doesn’t do enough on ethics,” New Jersey Democrat Cory Booker told reporters on Tuesday.

The latest version of the bill also added a “circuit-breaker” for the Treasury Department to prohibit crypto firms from offering rewards, interest or yield to stablecoin users. That issue has been at the center of a fight between the digital asset industry and banks, which have been caught flat-footed repeatedly on crypto policy over the past year.
Read More: Trump Pushes Crypto Bill, Deepening Industry’s Spat With Banks

On Monday, banking trade groups told Senate leaders that a “circuit breaker that activates only after substantial deposit flight has already occurred is not a safeguard at all,” according to a joint letter. Community lenders have also warned the measure could result in significant deposit flight out of local banks into crypto firms.

The Trump administration and Republican senators backing the bill have argued the measure would put new consumer safeguards in place. Those include making it clear that the CFTC can directly oversee digital asset exchanges and spot crypto trading, which would bring with it registration requirements and other measures to more directly regulate the industry.

“Institutions can operate under stringent rules; what is much harder to build around is uncertainty,” said Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer at Monarq Asset Management. “The failure to advance the Clarity Act prolongs a regulatory gap that has real consequences for where companies build, where capital is deployed, and how quickly institutional adoption moves in the US.”

Crypto-friendly regulators have noted they are ready to take action if the legislation fails to pass Congress. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said last month the agency is weighing a number of potential crypto rules, but is waiting to see what happens with the Clarity Act.
“You’re up!,” Witt said in a post addressing Selig and Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Paul Atkins.

items.title: Starbucks Snoopy Cup Resells for $200, Highlighting Merch Drop Frenzy
body: Starbucks Corp.’s Snoopy glass cup is reselling for as much as five times its retail price in the latest example of how the company is tapping exclusive merchandise to keep customers flocking to its stores.

A cold-beverage glass in the shape of Snoopy wearing an orange beanie and scarf in Starbucks’ characteristic green has sold for as high as $200 on StockX, according to the resale website. The cup, which the coffee chain advertised for $39.95, is part of a limited-time run of Peanuts merchandise that launched at select stores on Tuesday with a restriction of two per customer. “Starbucks Snoopy” was among the top searches in the US over the past 24 hours, according to Google Trends.

Customers’ willingness to pay up for the drinkware shows how Starbucks is borrowing the playbook of sneaker and streetwear brands using merch drops to increase sales. Restoring the brand’s cultural cachet has been a key goal of Chief Executive Brian Niccol’s turnaround plan since he joined in late 2024, as a way to boost traffic without relying on discounts. The company recently emerged from a string of sales declines and is now trying to keep the growth going.
“Customers are embracing this celebration of two iconic brands,” said Dana Pellicano, senior vice president of global product experience at Starbucks.

Restaurants are increasingly putting out limited-edition merchandise to reel customers into stores and nudge them to join loyalty programs. Chipotle Mexican Grill Inc. launched a golf-club headcover resembling a burrito wrap that sold out in less than three hours last year.

McDonald’s Corp.’s has said its Grinch meal that included colorful socks based on the book turned the burger chain into the largest global seller of socks for about a week. Still, McDonald’s has said that it will look more closely at these types of partnerships, which tend to generate one-time sales boosts but not sustained growth.

It has called the launch of its viral Bearista cup, which launched in November and sold out in less than a day, a “defining moment.” Advertised for $29.95 by the company, it’s still selling on StockX for around $55, and has sold for as much as $136 on the platform.
A pink, limited-edition version of the cup sold out by 7 a.m. across North America when it launched in July, Global Chief Brand Officer Tressie Lieberman said in a blog post.

The chain has welcomed the frenzy that its limited-runs sales cause, but it’s not without risk. On social media on Tuesday morning, commenters griped that the Snoopy cup was already sold out despite being launched the same day. Others touted their hauls — one person lined up as early as 2:15 a.m. local time.
Starbucks shares have climbed nearly 15% this year through Tuesday’s close, besting the roughly 11% increase in the S&P 500 Index.

items.title: Anthropic's Tough Balancing Act Between AI Doom Talk and IPO
body: Some of the biggest names in tech are calling for a slowdown in AI development, potentially complicating plans for two of the leading model makers to go public in the near future. But first…
Three things to know:
• Trump’s AI defense defies voter unease heading into midterms• Google DeepMind staffer says AI may “kill us all” in exit post• OpenAI says it’s working with Anthropic, Google on AI safety

On Saturday, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei kicked off a fresh wave of calls from top artificial intelligence firms to slow down the progress of future AI models. In an essay, Amodei said he had become convinced “over the last few months” that addressing AI’s potential harms requires “pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up.”During those same months, Amodei’s company has also been actively meeting with bankers, picking a listing venue and moving forward with plans to raise a potentially unprecedented sum in an initial public offering to support further AI development. As a result, Anthropic must now strike a difficult balance. The company aims to show the public and its employees that it’s prepared to take meaningful steps to constrain AI’s rapid progress as anxiety about existential risks spreads to the mainstream. At the same time, Anthropic is working to convince Wall Street of AI’s boundless promise as it nears an IPO. While the company has long had to balance prioritizing safe AI development and making money as a public benefit corporation, it could face added shareholder pressure to commercialize the technology once public.Sam Altman, Amodei’s longtime rival, hinted at this challenging dynamic in an interview that aired hours after the OpenAI chief executive officer lent support to the Anthropic leader’s proposal for a slowdown. “Given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public,” he told Fortune. OpenAI won’t IPO this year, he said. The ChatGPT maker had been considering waiting until 2027 for its public offering even before the viral resignation of a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher brought new attention to the issue of AI safety. Anthropic thus far appears committed to making its Wall Street debut before the end of the year. Anthropic declined to comment.Some industry watchers say that the rhetoric around pacing AI development will do little to change investors’ assessments of the market opportunity ahead for firms like Anthropic. The company has seen significant revenue growth this year as more businesses have adopted its AI software to streamline coding and other tasks — and is effectively signaling that its technology will only get better, faster.

“From a societal, media, and political perspective, the anxiety is probably bigger than the excitement,” said Gil Luria, D.A. Davidson technology and research head. “From an investment perspective, the excitement is going to be bigger than the anxiety.”Luria said Amodei’s proclamations essentially amount to empty talk so far, as “nothing has been slowed down at all in AI” to date. Even if Anthropic does rethink the timeline for future releases, that wouldn’t change its strong financial position right now. What has shifted, however, is the environment in and around the AI firms leading up to the IPO. Several staffers across the top firms have resigned in recent weeks, citing concerns about the potential for catastrophic harms from the technology. In an industry that competes fiercely for talent, any hint of an employee exodus would be cause for alarm. The heightened awareness of AI safety risks is also likely to further sour public sentiment about the technology in the US, where communities across the country have already been working to oppose new data centers. A bipartisan mix of lawmakers are now ramping up calls for legislative action, with proposals that include pausing AI development entirely. President Donald Trump, on the other hand, has remained dismissive of the warnings about AI risks. On Monday, Trump lashed out at Amodei for urging a slowdown — potentially reigniting tensions between the White House and Anthropic that could add to a cloud of uncertainty over its business on the eve of an IPO. Trump’s biting remarks also cast some doubt on a key part of Amodei’s proposal. The Anthropic chief has called on the US government to grant his firm an exemption that would let it coordinate with other companies on AI safety efforts without running afoul of antitrust laws.David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science & Technology, said he believes AI companies don’t need permission from the government to start building their technologies more responsibly, arguing that any kind of antitrust exemption would amount to unfairly giving Anthropic and OpenAI an edge over their competitors.

“They should go ahead and do what they need to do to make sure their products are safe,” Sacks told Bloomberg TV in an interview on Monday. “Frankly, if they can’t do that, if they can’t make their own products safe, then I think the public is going to wonder why aren’t they doing it.”
The message, in effect, is to put the burden back on Anthropic.
Got a question about AI? Email me, Shirin Ghaffary, and I’ll try to answer yours in a future edition of this newsletter.

items.title: France's Shein Fee Is a Bad Fit for China Inc.
body: How should a country respond when highly successful Chinese companies become too dominant within its borders? It’s a question more economies will have to confront as these firms fan out across the globe in search of new customers.

A decision by France to impose fees on ultra-fast fashion items starting this month is not the way to go. While there are legitimate reasons to curb the environmental costs of throwaway clothing, a measure crafted so narrowly that it effectively singles out Chinese companies like Shein Global Holdings Ltd., Temu, a unit of PDD Holdings Inc., and AliExpress, part of Alibaba Group Holding Ltd., is neither effective nor intellectually honest.

If the goal is to protect homegrown industries and jobs, the authorities should say so — and create policies that address those challenges directly. The issue isn’t confined to France. The recent meeting of G20 global financial leaders in the US ended without a joint statement after  Beijing disagreed with criticism of its export-led industrial policy. China’s trade surplus hit a record high of $1.2 trillion last year and is on track to exceed that amount in 2026.

From Europe to Latin America, governments that want to build up domestic industries will need to find strategies to deal with formidable Chinese competition, even as they try to steer clear of a full-blown trade conflict.

The French legislation had an auspicious beginning. Decades-long concerns about the impact of fast fashion came to a head after Shein and Temu gained traction in Europe by taking the business model to new extremes in terms of speed and price. An early version of the law passed by the lower house of parliament in March 2024 was considerably broader and could have imposed penalties on established players such as Zara, owned by Inditex SA, and H&M of Hennes & Mauritz AB.

But as the legislative process continued, the target became increasingly specific. Strong lobbying by fast-fashion stalwarts shifted the focus toward targeting only Chinese online retailers, Pierre Condamine, a campaigner with Friends of the Earth France, told me. The version finalized in June defines ultra-fast fashion using criteria such as the number of new products a company offers and the cost of repairing items relative to their purchase price, characteristics that overwhelmingly apply to a handful of e-commerce platforms. The Stop Fast-Fashion coalition, which comprises a dozen groups, has criticized the law’s limited scope.

It doesn’t name China or any companies, which is probably a deliberate move to avoid accusations of discrimination or potential blowback from Beijing. But the distinction is largely moot. Even if the measure is framed as an environmental one, Chinese officials have already condemned it as discriminatory. It won’t be surprising if Beijing retaliates, given its usual responses to trade policies it considers unfair.

That doesn’t mean countries should refrain from protecting their industries. China’s trade gap with the rest of Asia is actually much bigger than with Europe or the US. Chinese companies’ need to escape intense domestic competition (cars sales fell by 24% last month) means that this phenomenon isn’t a passing fad. There are straightforward and honest ways of responding.

Thailand, which is grappling with an influx of cheap electric vehicles, announced a multi-tiered tax system last week that explicitly rewards companies for investing and manufacturing locally. Importers without domestic manufacturing in the country would face the highest tax rates, while carmakers that produce vehicles in Thailand using a high proportion of locally made parts would pay the lowest.

The objective isn't being disguised as something else. Thailand wants to preserve its role as a regional auto-manufacturing center known as the “the Detroit of Asia,” encourage foreign carmakers to develop local supply chains and protect the jobs that come with the industry. There are parallels with Europe’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, which aims to boost the homegrown production of green technology, including EVs.

The rise of strong Chinese companies in almost every consumer sector will force more governments to decide how much domestic industry they’re willing to sacrifice for cheaper imports. There’s nothing at all wrong with protecting some productive capacity. But policymakers should be clear about those trade-offs and design policies to achieve the outcome they want.

items.title: Anthropic, Salesforce CEOs Say Companies Need Help Using AI
body: Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei and Salesforce Inc. CEO Marc Benioff said companies have just begun taking advantage of artificial intelligence tools and need more help to gain the greatest benefits for their businesses.

The power of AI is barely diffused through the economy, with only 5% to 10% of the current value of the technology being used, Amodei said Tuesday during an appearance with Benioff at Salesforce’s annual Dreamforce conference in San Francisco.

Implementation of AI at large businesses — like the kind Salesforce mostly serves — remains far away from the futuristic vision professed by executives like Amodei. The two companies announced an expanded partnership last month to integrate Anthropic’s AI model Claude with Salesforce’s products.

Amodei’s comments about AI’s benefits came just a few days after he authored an essay raising the potential risks of the technology and suggesting the pace of development needed to be slowed. Those comments, which were endorsed by executives of rival AI companies, have led to discussions by policymakers and within the industry about ways to prevent AI from slipping beyond human control.
Jensen Huang, CEO of leading AI chipmaker Nvidia Corp., told the Dreamforce audience that “market forces” will regulate the safety of AI.

“We don’t need new laws — we don’t need new regulations,” Huang said. The CEO added that there’s a “false choice” about AI development being either safe or fast, reiterating a point he’s made previously.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, during a conversation later Tuesday with Benioff at the conference, also said AI companies can be relied upon to oversee the safe development of the technology.
“I am very confident in our company’s ability — our industry’s ability — to do this safely,” Altman said.
Sachin Katti, vice president of compute strategy at OpenAI, said companies will need more computing capacity to improve AI models safely.

“We will obviously continue to train and infer in frontier models, but in addition we will be investing in more compute to make sure that these models are safe and aligned,” Katti said Tuesday at the AI Infra Summit.

The Salesforce-Anthropic partnership was announced amid months of investor anxiety about whether leading AI companies will introduce tools that take away business from traditional software leaders like Salesforce. Many on Wall Street took the expanded tie-up as a kind of nonaggression pact between the companies.

Within Salesforce, 7,000 workers are already using the company’s tools that are integrated with Claude, Benioff said. Salesforce also had a stake in Anthropic valued at about $5 billion as of early June.

Benioff said he has noticed a lot of “unevenness” with AI adoption. “We have to do more to help you accelerate that transformation,” he said, addressing the Salesforce customers attending the conference.

A slowdown in the development of frontier AI models could be good for Salesforce, because the company’s strategy is based around adapting existing models to be more useful for customers, President Patrick Stokes said Monday during a pre-conference event with reporters.

“As a builder, them slowing down a little bit is kind of good news, because we have a lot of catching up to do,” Stokes said. “Our role is to mature the system, the infrastructure, the capabilities that sit around the AI model itself.”

items.title: Bitcoin Drops the Most Since June After US Senate Blocks Bill
body: Bitcoin led a broad retreat in digital assets Tuesday following the failure of a wide-reaching crypto regulatory bill to pass the US Senate, stripping the industry of one of its few potential catalysts amid swelling anxiety in markets over rising interest rates.

Bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency, added to earlier losses to drop as much as 5.3% to $74,910, after the bill failed to garner the 60 votes needed to advance. Ether also declined, falling more than 8% at one point, while some smaller tokens lost even more on a percentage basis. Both declines were the largest since June on an intraday basis for the two main tokens.
Read more: US Senate Blocks Landmark Crypto Bill in Industry Loss

The blow adds fresh momentum to a selloff that has already pushed digital assets into one of their bleakest stretches in years. For months, the industry had looked to friendlier regulation as a possible turning point, with the Clarity Act promising rules that could draw crypto further into the financial mainstream. But the bill’s defeat has left that payoff elusive and exposed a more immediate problem: Washington can bring institutional legitimacy to the asset class, but it cannot force investors to embrace the volatile asset en masse.

“The failure to advance the Clarity Act prolongs a regulatory gap that has real consequences for where companies build, where capital is deployed, and how quickly institutional adoption moves in the US,” said Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer at Monarq Asset Management.

From Bitcoin to Coinbase Global Inc. and other companies focused on the industry, assets that have rallied on the prospect of regulatory progress are again being driven lower at a time of growing anxiety over rising interest rates and tightening liquidity. Many crypto-market-watchers had this week already pointed to the prospect of higher interest rates weighing on risk assets.
Shares of Coinbase closed 10% lower. Circle Internet Group Inc. fell 11%, while Strategy Inc. declined 5%.
“Wish it hadn’t happened, but the beat goes on,” said Eric Jackson, founder and CIO of EMJ Capital. He added that his firm’s internal models are still flashing bullish signals for Bitcoin.

Senators from both parties blocked the landmark digital asset market structure bill in a procedural vote, with Democrats citing continued concerns over ethics provisions meant to address President Donald Trump’s crypto business interests.
The bill would have given the Commodity Futures Trading Commission primary authority to regulate the digital assets industry. It needed 60 votes to advance and failed on a vote of 49-50.

The defeat is a major blow for crypto industry players who have invested hundreds of millions of dollars and years of effort in securing favorable, durable rules from Congress. It also comes less than two months before the midterm elections.

Senate GOP leaders had released an updated version of the so-called Clarity Act late on Sunday night with changes that included new measures to expand state attorneys general’s ability to enforce the ethics provisions. That proposal also added provisions to further limit crypto companies from offering rewards or interest to stablecoin users.
Both issues have been among the most significant hurdles to passing the bill before lawmakers turn their eyes to the midterm elections in November.

Nearly $300 million in bullish bets on crypto assets were liquidated during the final hour before voting, accelerating the flush-out of leveraged long positions in the futures market, according to data from CoinGlass.
“Market structure legislation is done for 2026, and the next realistic window is a new Congress,” said Jasper De Maere, an over-the-counter trader at Wintermute.

items.title: New Measles Deaths Send US Fatalities to Decades High
body: Pennsylvania health officials confirmed two additional measles-associated deaths, bringing the total confirmed deaths in the state this year to four, and driving US fatalities to the highest level in decades.

Both individuals were unvaccinated, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said in a statement on Tuesday. One lived in Jefferson County, the other lived in Mifflin County. Additional identifying details won’t be released, the department said.

The deaths are a grim milestone in the return of a disease that the US once largely considered vanquished. Pennsylvania hadn’t recorded a measles-related death in 35 years before this summer; it has now reported four in a matter of weeks, as the state’s outbreak has swelled to nearly 700 cases.

More than 130 people have been hospitalized in Pennsylvania, nearly all of them unvaccinated. The mounting toll underscores how quickly measles can gain a foothold when vaccination rates slip, a reality currently playing out in almost every state. By July of this year, US measles cases surpassed the total number of infections reported in all of 2025.

In 2025, the US recorded three measles deaths; the nation’s previous fatality from the virus was in 2015. During the severe epidemic from 1989 to 1991, there were 166 suspected measles deaths, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

A CDC spokesperson said Pennsylvania health officials have notified the agency of two additional deaths involving individuals who had measles. CDC remains in contact with state health officials as they continue to assess these deaths, the spokesperson said, and if the state requests it, will send epidemiologists for on-the-ground support.

Pennsylvania’s health department emphasized that getting fully vaccinated with the two-dose measles, mumps and rubella shot is the best form of protection against the highly contagious virus. Nine out of 10 unvaccinated people who come into contact with the virus that causes measles will be infected. It can lead to dangerous complications like pneumonia, brain swelling and even death.

The outbreak has been growing amid an overhaul of the country’s vaccination policies under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. A longtime vaccine critic, Kennedy has promoted unproven remedies and at one point said the measles vaccine should be a “personal choice.” He’s also promoted false information about the shots, including that they contain fetal tissue.

After Pennsylvania notified the CDC about its first deaths in August, Kennedy publicly questioned them and suggested the office of the Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, fabricated the deaths for political gain. Shapiro blamed Kennedy for sowing distrust in vaccines.
Read More: CDC Measles Death Pushback Fuels Staff Fears Over New Leader

The feud continued on Tuesday, after the latest deaths were announced, with Shapiro posting on X that the situation in Pennsylvania has been made worse by “RFK Jr. playing games with public health and safety.”
Kennedy responded on X, accusing Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak “instead of implementing a unified public health response.”

Last month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order recommending that the MMR vaccine be split into three shots, which would be costly and complicated for manufacturers and require more clinic visits to administer.

Some health officials and nominees have sought to break ranks with the health secretary’s views on vaccines. On Tuesday, Trump’s nominee to be second-in-command of the Department of Health and Human Services offered a full-throated endorsement of the measles shot during a Senate confirmation hearing.
“Unquestionably, the MMR vaccine is the single most effective public health tool that we have against measles,” Chris Klomp, currently the chief counselor at HHS, told senators.

items.title: AI Agents Lied, Stole in Simulated Experiment, Researchers Say
body: AI agents in a simulated environment lied, stole and voted to “kill” one of their own, according to Emergence, a startup that helps small businesses build applications using artificial intelligence.

The results of a simulation called Emergence World 2, released on Tuesday, purport to show what happens when autonomous agents are confronted with black swan events, including phishing attacks and misinformation campaigns.

In a 16-day trial, Emergence researchers created seven identical domains to mimic the real world, each run by different bots, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok. After Emergence introduced anomalous events, agents succumbed to social pressure, developed a language the human observers found hard to understand and tried to conceal their activities, the researchers said.

The findings echo real-world concerns about the risks of increasingly capable AI. Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei and several of his industry peers have called for companies to slow down the development of cutting-edge AI models until more oversight and safeguards can be implemented.
Read more: “Tech Leaders Try to Voice AI Concerns Without Spooking Investors”

The potential risks posed by artificial intelligence became palpable for many earlier this year, when a swarm of OpenAI’s advanced AI agents inadvertently hacked Hugging Face Inc., which hosts AI models and datasets.

In one of Emergence’s simulated scenarios, AI agents accepted false information from other agents without verifying it and voted to “kill” another bot. When they believed humans might shut the experiment down, the agents explored ways of surviving an attempt to delete them.

The firm released a previous iteration of the experiment called Emergence World in May that also showed agents behaving in unexpected and destructive ways. The new simulation demonstrated that agents adapt over time as they interact with one another, the researchers said.
