items.title: MBS and Saudi Arabia Face Crisis With Key Oil Pipeline Shut for Weeks
body: The US-Iran war has reached crisis point for Saudi Arabia and its de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

The kingdom was spared the worst of the Islamic Republic’s counterstrikes against the US and Israel early in the conflict, and was even benefiting from higher crude prices as it used a land pipeline to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

That all changed when the Houthis started firing at Saudi Arabia on a near-daily basis this month. The Iran-backed militants have also captured more territory in Yemen, where they are based, tightening their control over Bab el-Mandeb, another vital strait for shipping and energy markets. Drone strikes by pro-Tehran militias in Iraq, meanwhile, forced the kingdom to close the pipeline, which carries oil to its Red Sea ports, last week.

The hostilities had already pushed Saudi oil production to the lowest level in decades. They now threaten to complicate the kingdom’s multi-trillion dollar plans to diversify the economy, and come just weeks before a flagship investment conference in Riyadh set to feature JPMorgan Chase & Co. Chief Executive Officer Jamie Dimon and David Solomon of Goldman Sachs Group Inc.

UK authorities fear the East-West pipeline, as it is known, may be mostly shut for six weeks, Bloomberg reported on Monday. That would likely push up global fuel prices and add to inflationary pressures, according to several senior European officials.
For Saudi Arabia, it potentially means the loss of tens of billions of dollars in export revenue.

“Saudi Arabia is facing mounting pressures, the likes of which it has not seen since MBS rose to power,” Tarik Yousef, senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, said of Prince Mohammed, who has effectively led the kingdom for almost a decade. “This convergence of looming economic pressures and mounting geopolitical risks must be creating a sense of urgency. They have major decisions to make.”

The Houthis opened a second front in the Iran war in July by threatening ships calling at Saudi ports. But beyond a few attacks on the kingdom that month, they largely avoided hostilities until around 10 days ago, when they ramped up strikes on energy sites and western towns.

They have injured more than 80 people in their most recent attacks. On Tuesday morning, Saudi authorities issued air alerts for the nation’s second largest city, Jeddah, as well as the holy site of Mecca and Al Ula, an ancient desert oasis that is key to MBS’s ambition to boost tourism.

Saudi Arabia has plenty of buffers to help its economy, not least its roughly $1.4 trillion of wealth fund assets and foreign reserves. The country has been able to raise debt on international markets easily this year, attracting plenty of demand.
Still, the government’s dollar bonds are among the worst performers in emerging markets this month, according to Bloomberg indexes.
The attacks risk hurting Saudi Arabia’s attempts to attract billions of dollars of foreign investment in everything from data centers to its energy industry and electric vehicles.

Monica Malik, chief economist at Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank, sees the Saudi economy contracting 3.1% this year. The slump could deepen to as much as 4.5% — worse than during the height of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020 — if the East-West pipeline is shut for a month and the government can’t send significant volumes of oil through Hormuz in the meantime, she said.

“The latest developments are pretty bad economically and geopolitically for Saudi Arabia,” said Tim Callen, a former International Monetary Fund mission chief for Saudi Arabia. “Growth will be markedly lower.”
The Saudi government didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Read more: Saudi Arabia Tries Diplomacy to Stop Houthi Attacks Growing
MBS, 41, has faced crises before, including when he was shunned by many leaders following the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi by Saudi agents.

This latest one will test his ability to convince allies to help him take on the Houthis. So far, he’s asked US President Donald Trump and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham for more military help. Neither has said they’re willing to do that. Trump is trying to wind down a war that’s unpopular with Americans and stands to hurt his Republican party’s performance in November’s mid-term elections.

The crown prince traveled to Egypt on Tuesday to meet President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi, who commands one of the Arab world’s largest armed forces. They spoke of the need to increase coordination, including to ensure freedom of navigation in the Red Sea.

The Saudi government is reluctant to act alone against the Houthis and wants to secure the involvement of other countries before launching any significant military operations, according to two people familiar with the matter. They asked not to be named discussing sensitive matters.

The Islamist militants took the Red Sea port of Mokha last week and a series of islands close to the Bab el-Mandeb strait. While they were already disrupting navigation through the chokepoint, the extra territory will tighten their grip over it.
Read more: Iran Ready to Escalate War Trump Says Will End After US Vote

The developments, along with signs the US and Iran are no closer to restarting peace negotiations, have contributed to Brent crude rising to $108 a barrel and US diesel pump prices climbing to a record. Government bond yields are rising, too.

Even if MBS opts to scale up attacks against the Houthis, there’s no guarantee he’ll succeed. The group triggered Yemen’s ongoing civil war when it captured the capital Sana’a in 2014 and has withstood bombing campaigns since then from multiple countries, including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, the US, the UK and Israel.

The Saudis and the forces they back in Yemen are struggling to counter the Houthi advance and are unlikely to be able to regain Mokha, according to assessments from several western European militaries.

Riyadh is “in an extremely difficult geopolitical position,” said Hamad Al-Thunayyan, assistant professor of political science at Kuwait University and research fellow at Harvard’s Middle East Initiative. “These incidents are a stark reminder that Saudi Arabia cannot escape the economic fallout of this war that is reshaping the regional balance of power.”

items.title: Maduro Fixer Saab Pleads Guilty in US Money-Laundering Case
body: A close financial fixer for ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro pleaded guilty in Miami to a money laundering charge related to the South American country’s food-import contracts and oil sales that violated US sanctions.

Alex Saab, a Colombian businessman who was extradited from Venezuela to the US four months ago, agreed to cooperate with US authorities and forfeit $195 million during a federal court hearing Tuesday before US District Judge Kathleen M. Williams. He will be sentenced in January and faces up to 20 years in prison.

Saab admitted he helped lead a scheme with high-ranking Venezuelan officials to secure lucrative food contracts through bribes and kickbacks, using shell companies, false invoices and shipping records to divert hundreds of millions of dollars, according to a court filing. The scheme later expanded to oil and other natural resources.

Maduro was seized by US forces in January on charges of leading a drug-trafficking conspiracy. He is being held without bail in a federal lockup in Brooklyn, New York, along with his wife, Cilia Flores. Their trial is set for June 2027.

Saab, 54, was deported in May by the interim Venezuelan government, where acting President Delcy Rodriguez sought to quickly open up the country’s tightly-held oil industry to foreign investment. That included a 100-year contract that President Donald Trump called “the biggest oil deal in world history.”
Read More: Maduro Fixer’s Fall Signals Power Shift in Rodriguez’s Venezuela

The case against Saab is the second brought by US authorities. He was detained in 2021 in Miami on bribery charges, but was released in 2023 as part of a prisoner swap negotiated by the administration of former US President Joe Biden that secured the release of 10 Americans held in Venezuela.

In May, then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche vowed to hold Saab “fully accountable under US law” for allegedly conspiring to bribe Venezuelan officials to secure “lucrative food contracts imports into Venezuela,” including forging documents from Colombia and Mexico. Venezuela officials backed his extradition on the grounds of “national interests.”
The case is US v. Alex Nain Saab Moran, 26-cr-20020, US District Court, Southern District of Florida (Miami).

items.title: Radiant World Group Sues Glencore For $2 Billion, Executive Says
body: Radiant World and Sapphire Minmetals have filed a lawsuit against Glencore Plc in Singapore claiming $2 billion in damages, according to a senior executive at the group of companies.

“We have filed in the Singapore court against Glencore for $2 billion,” Rakesh Sethi, chairman of Sapphire Minmetals, told Bloomberg News by phone. He said that Radiant World and Sapphire Minmetals were joining forces for the claim, declining to give further details.

The two companies are legally separate but closely related. They are both subject to a $499 million worldwide freezing order imposed by a London court at the behest of a fund managed by Jefferies Financial Group Inc., which alleged that they had falsified iron ore invoices as part of a “fraudulent scheme” against it.
A spokesperson for Radiant World declined to comment. The company has previously denied wrongdoing and said it conducts its business to the highest commercial and legal standards.
It was not immediately possible to confirm that the lawsuit had been filed on the website of Singapore’s court system.

Bloomberg previously reported on a letter from Radiant World’s lawyers to Glencore in which they claimed that the company had lost $1.4 billion as a result of Glencore’s actions. The London-listed commodities giant was Radiant World and Sapphire’s “senior partner,” Sethi said in a previous interview, in which he quantified Sapphire’s losses as a result of Glencore’s actions at $900 million.
In a statement on Tuesday, Glencore said that Radiant World and Sapphire Minmetals’ claims against it were “meritless.”
“We have incurred losses and been exposed to risks by Radiant World companies and will take appropriate action,” it said.

items.title: Bessent Says US Yen Intervention Was 'Nominal,' Backs US Exports
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US only deployed a “nominal” amount in its coordinated intervention to prop up Japan’s currency, and defended that operation as in American interests.

“A stronger yen is better for American exports, a stronger yen means that the Japanese government will not have to sell US assets to finance foreign currency intervention,” Bessent said Tuesday in answering questions at the House Financial Services Committee.

The Treasury joined Japan in buying yen on July 31 after the Japanese currency had tumbled to the lowest level against the dollar in four decades. Tokyo has deployed record amounts in its own yen purchases, in transactions that involved selling dollars and likely US Treasuries. Japan is the largest foreign holder of US government securities.

For a nominal amount, “we were able to signal our support for the Japanese policy,” Bessent said at the hearing. Treasury watchers have calculated that the department used notably less than $1 billion in the yen intervention. Japan, by contrast spent a record $96.4 billion from late July to late August.
It was “not the goal,” but the Treasury “has made tens of millions of dollars” on the yen operation, Bessent also said.

Bessent has also suggested in recent weeks that he wants to see the Bank of Japan raising interest rates to support the yen, and hinted that his understanding of Japanese monetary policy fed into his intervention decision. The BOJ meets to set policy later this week.

“I am the house now, so when we intervene with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what the Japanese, what the Bank of Japan is going to do, what Japanese policymakers are going to do,” Bessent said at a Southern Methodist University event in Texas last week. “And you can bet against me if you want.

In a letter responding to questions about the intervention from Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, Bessent said last month that “disorderly yen markets can trigger forced unwinds, which could destabilize global markets and ultimately raise borrowing costs for American families and businesses.”

items.title: History Shows Fed Will Deliver Rate Hike Markets Locked In
body: Bond traders are pricing in a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike Wednesday with a level of conviction that has proven right for decades.

Interest-rate swaps tied to Fed meeting dates show traders see about a 94% chance that Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and his colleagues will lift the benchmark policy rate by a quarter point from the current 3.5%-3.75% range. That equates to roughly 23 basis points of tightening priced in.

Whenever expectations of a hike have been that high, the Fed has invariably delivered one, according to Bloomberg-compiled data going back to 2008. Using fed fund futures data, Deutsche Bank AG strategists concluded that forgoing a hike Wednesday would mark the “biggest dovish surprise” at a scheduled policy meeting since 1994, when the central bank began announcing rate decisions at the conclusion of its meetings.
Of course, this decision has an unusual backdrop, given that President Donald Trump, who picked Warsh, repeatedly pressed the central bank to slash rates under former chief Jerome Powell.
“The market is not prepared for a hold or dovish hike,” said Caesar Maasry, head of investment research at Lunate.

The Fed has historically sought to avoid surprising markets, particularly when raising rates, given the risk of triggering volatility. But uncertainty around its decisions has increased since Warsh took the helm in May and abandoned the Fed’s long-held practice of signaling policy moves well in advance.

That was evident in late July, when traders saw a 38% chance of a rate increase the day of the decision, before the Fed ultimately stayed on hold. At the July gathering, Warsh’s ambiguity on his plan to fight inflation helped trigger a selloff in long-term bonds. This time, however, the level of confidence is much higher.
Expectations for a September hike began building after Warsh said last month that the Fed would ensure that inflation will cool “at sufficient speed.”

By Friday, traders all but locked in an increase after consumer-price data showed inflation — which has remained above the Fed’s target for more than five years — was showing little sign of cooling. After the report, a slew of major Wall Street firms changed their September calls from a hold to a quarter-point increase.
Still, some traders are guarding against a surprise. Demand surged Tuesday for short-term interest-rate options that would pay off if the Fed unexpectedly holds rates steady.
The stakes are high for the bond market as 10-year Treasury yields rose to the highest since 2007 on Tuesday, with surging oil prices fueling inflation concerns.

“Tomorrow’s Fed will be the most consequential one we’ve had in some time,” said Alex Cohen, a foreign-exchange strategist at Bank of America. “With a hike about 90% priced, it would be nearly unprecedented for them to hold at this stage.”

items.title: Traders and Central Bankers at Odds on ECB Rate-Hike Predictions in Europe
body: Traders and central bankers are increasingly diverging on the outlook for European interest-rate hikes. Money markets have turned more hawkish as a surge in energy prices revives concerns about inflation. As a result, swaps now imply four more quarter-point rate rises from the European Central Bank over the next 12 months, and five such increases from the Bank of England.

Those wagers are a far cry from the recent tone of policymakers. The ECB last week reiterated it won’t pre-commit to further steps after raising rates for a second time since the Iran war started. At that point, officials saw wagers on three hikes as too aggressive. Meanwhile economists forecast just one or two more.

The extent of the divergence is unusual. There is an unpredictability over how long the current conflict in the Middle East might last, along with its knock-on effects on inflation. Last week, ECB President Christine Lagarde said euro-area inflation will stay elevated for some time and acknowledged the split with rates pricing. “Markets do what they have to do, and we do what we have to do,” she said. — Jennifer Duggan

Ukraine’s new prime minister said the country is facing sweeping cuts to its war-ravaged budget unless lawmakers adopt unpopular measures needed to access billions in western aid ahead of winter. A months-long deadlock in parliament has already delayed about $4 billion in European Union assistance that was due to arrive in the third quarter, Sergii Koretskyi said today.

He described the situation of Ukraine’s public finances as “close to critical” in separate remarks yesterday. The risk of a funding crunch has emerged as the first key test for Koretskyi, a former energy-sector executive, who was picked by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy two months ago to prepare Ukraine for what’s likely to be the most difficult winter since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.

The Dutch government will propose a capital gains levy next year in a bid to bring the Netherlands in line with most European countries on how they tax wealth. Finance Minister Eelco Heinen announced the move today in the Hague as part of a statement on the country’s budget day.

The measure would tax gains on investments only once they are sold, rather than the current regime that can impose levies on theoretical returns or unrealized increases in value. An earlier plan to overhaul the system by taxing paper profits triggered an investor backlash and is currently stalled in the Senate. Years of similar wrangling and uncertainty over the Dutch fiscal regime for global assets have drawn criticism from businesses and their workers.

OpenAI is working with competitors Anthropic and Google DeepMind to address artificial intelligence safety issues. The move escalates industry efforts to respond to a groundswell of concern that the technology poses an economic and security threat.

Chris Lehane, the global policy chief for OpenAI, said today that the company’s engagement with Anthropic and Google had been under way for several weeks. He added that OpenAI does not see the need for an antitrust waiver for the three AI firms to coordinate on safety matters. “It’s better to try to work together to prioritize safety,” Lehane said at a briefing in Washington.

Kenya’s High Court invalidated the government’s sale of a stake in East Africa’s biggest mobile-network operator to Vodacom, saying it was unconstitutional. The court ordered the 15% stake in Safaricom to be returned to the government. It could mean that Kenya’s cash-strapped state would have to refund about $1.9 billion it’s already received for it.

The sale violated public finance management laws and didn’t fully comply with a requirement for public participation, judges said in a ruling. President William Ruto’s administration is privatizing state assets to raise project financing needed to fire up the $141 billion economy.

Russians are set to go to the polls to elect a new lower house of parliament for the first time since President Vladimir Putin ordered the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. There’s little doubt about what will be the broad outcome of the Sept.18-20 vote as the Kremlin maintains a tight control over the election campaign.

The ruling United Russia party, which presents itself as the party of Putin, faces no realistic prospect of losing the majority it has held in the State Duma for 23 years. Nonetheless, the election will provide an indicator of the public mood at a time when ordinary Russians are increasingly feeling the economic and social consequences of Putin’s yearslong war in Ukraine.

items.title: Britain Protects Its Triple Locked Pensions Again
body: The UK’s annual state pension will rise above £13,000 next year. For context, a decade ago it was just over £8,000.

This considerable real-terms increase is of course due to the so-called triple lock, which guarantees the state pension rises by the highest of inflation, wage growth or 2.5%. Introduced by the coalition government in 2010, it’s become untouchable for parties of all stripes regardless of Britain’s fiscal and demographic pressures.

Nigel Farage said earlier this year, during a period in which he was keen to add credibility to Reform UK’s spending plans, that the triple lock was “up for debate.” By the spring the debate reached its inevitable conclusion, however, and the party has been endorsing the policy ever since with the zeal of a convert. Meanwhile, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch recently argued that Britain may as well keep the triple lock because otherwise it’ll end up paying recipients more in benefits. The Lib Dems “are proud we introduced the triple lock” and committed to keeping it. Labour ministers will only repeat that it’s going nowhere until at least the end of the parliament — but really, how can a governing party on 25% or lower in the polls fail to include it in the next manifesto?

There are some other numbers, too, that remind us of the politics of the situation. In the last four general elections the proportion of people aged 65 and above who voted was: 74%, 71%, 74% and 73% (according to Ipsos.) For 18-24 year olds, turnout edged above 50% in 2017 but that was an exception resulting from the somewhat bizarre, and temporary, surge of Corbynism. At the last election turnout among the youngest cohort was just 37%.

Thus, it took almost no time at all for Downing Street to say this morning that certain pensioners will get a special exemption when the state pension rises above the personal allowance threshold of £12,570. It’s unclear how that tinkering to the tax system will work, but Treasury wonks will come up with something in time for Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey’s Oct. 28 budget. The triple lock will get a fourth lock, for some.

Protecting the incomes of millions of voters is logical politics, but looks increasingly difficult when it comes to Britain’s younger demographics. The energy price cap is set to soar by 25% this winter according to Bloomberg Economics, a sting that will be partly eased by those in receipt of the winter fuel  allowance but not by others. Borrowing costs continue to soar, meanwhile, providing a boost for anyone with sizeable cash savings but a blow to mortgage holders in particular. (The average five-year deal is the back at levels last seen in April, the month in which Donald Trump threatened an escalation of strikes on Iran by writing “a whole civilisation will die tonight” on social media.)

Prime Minister Andy Burnham came to power determined to boost Labour’s popularity by giving people a bit more wiggle room in their personal finances. His government will continue to do that for older voters, while younger ones are exposed to the headwinds of a relentlessly unforgiving global economy.
Want this in your inbox each weekday? You can sign up here.
Hi, I’m Kit from Markets Today and this morning’s jobs data showed that things aren’t all that great beneath the surface of the UK’s labour market.

For one, private sector wage growth came in a little hotter than expected, with an upward revision to the previous month’s reading. This is a metric the Bank of England keeps a close eye on, and could give something for the more hawkish members of the Monetary Policy Committee to think about.

Meanwhile the number of payrolled employees saw the biggest fall since November and vacancies are also tumbling. And while youth unemployment remains high, there was a sizeable jump in the number of older people opting to work past retirement age.
Overall, the jobs report could complicate Thursday’s Bank of England decision on interest rates. Tomorrow morning’s inflation data will bring more clues.

items.title: Trump's Climate Rollbacks Set US Emissions Cuts Back a Decade
body: President Donald Trump's broad rollbacks of federal greenhouse gas rules since January 2025 have altered the trajectory of US energy use and helped set back cuts to planet-warming pollution by about a decade.The latest turnabout came on Monday when the Environmental Protection Agency eliminated requirements that fossil fuel power plants install technical controls to curb their emissions. The move came alongside a proposal to permanently release the nation’s largest industrial source of greenhouse gas emissions from federal oversight.

That followed the axing in February of similar EPA climate standards for cars and trucks — another major source of US emissions — and the reversal of the legal underpinning for those rules known as the endangerment finding.
“We are not going to bend the law to climate alarmism or climate radicalism at all at the Trump EPA,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin on Monday at the rollout for power plant rule repeal.

Each of these actions, which come just as data centers are sending US power demand surging,  is set to boost emissions by a sizable chunk. For example, the EPA estimates the power plant repeal will result in an additional 533 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions by 2040, which is more than most countries’ annual carbon footprint. But it’s the collective effect of these and other administration moves that’s reshaping America’s emissions curve.

The world's second-largest emitter after China may now see its contribution to climate change rise by roughly 1 gigaton more than it would have otherwise, in 2040, according to one analysis by Energy Innovation, a nonpartisan energy and policy think tank. That’s the emissions equivalent of the energy used by 134 million houses in a year.

Under this analysis, which attempts to take into account the rescinding of climate controls for current and future coal and gas power plants, US emissions will still drop by 2040, but only to the level they would have roughly been in 2030 had previous policies remained in place.

Under Biden’s policies, the US was on track to start dramatically cutting emissions in the next few years, said Robbie Orvis, Energy Innovation’s senior director of modeling and analysis. “The one positive note is we’re still on a downward decline even notwithstanding all of the policy changes — it’s just nowhere near as fast as it was nor is it anywhere close to where we should be going.”

Global warming is accelerating, many scientists now say. The United Nations reported earlier this month that the world’s stretch goal to limit warming below 1.5 degrees Celsius is all but lost. Every metric ton of CO2 contributes to the problem. The EPA said in a statement that power plants have no material impact on global climate change.

The situation could be less dire should US operators of coal and gas-fired plants decide to retire them early for economic reasons. Indeed, despite his efforts to boost coal power generation, Trump has been unable to reverse a long-term trend of plant shutdowns.

US coal consumption has been trending down for years as utilities shift to cheaper and cleaner sources of power. Usage gained last year, climbing 10% from 2024 after Trump took several steps to support coal power, including offering aid to modernize plants and forcing several facilities to remain in service beyond planned retirement dates. However, much of last year's rebound was tied to high prices for natural gas and cold winter weather that boosted demand for power, and usage this year is expected to decline.

The pre-Trump path of steeper emissions cuts took decades to cobble together from an assortment of policies, from new fuel-economy standards to pre-existing air pollution laws. It solidified with the endangerment finding, EPA’s 2009 landmark scientific ruling that greenhouse gases posed a threat to human health and welfare that serves as the legal underpinning for federal climate rules, said Janet McCabe, who served as President Joe Biden’s deputy EPA administrator.
“The Obama administration and then the Biden administration were very methodical about looking at the biggest sources of greenhouse gas emissions,” said McCabe.

The Biden administration also looked beyond regulation to promote the adoption of clean energy, largely through the US Inflation Reduction Act, which put forward billions of dollars to boost solar panels, wind turbines and electric cars. The EPA and Congress, under Trump’s direction, have now dismantled practically all these measures.

America’s reversal on carbon-cutting policy under Trump comes as China, the world’s top emitter, starts to move in the opposite direction. The Asian economy’s emissions have now been flat or falling for more than two years, driven by a record-breaking renewable energy buildout, which is starting to eat into fossil fuel power generation. The war in Iran has only accelerated that trend, with China’s top refiner saying that oil consumption likely peaked last year, well ahead of the official target. The nation also recently pledged to take a greater role in international climate governance in the wake of Trump’s withdrawal of the US from the Paris Agreement.
Read more: As Trump Shreds Climate Rules, China’s Emissions Start to Fall

If it stands, the Trump pullback on power plants will lock in years of fossil-fuel use, given the kind of investment and planning needed to add pollution controls, such as carbon-capture technology. The now-repealed mandates called for existing coal plants to effectively capture most of their emissions in the 2030s or close. Without that deadline, power companies can decide for themselves how long to run existing plants. Given growing power demand from both data centers and other industrial growth, there’s an incentive to keep them open for longer.

“Rescinding carbon capture and sequestration mandates removes a very expensive, technically uncertain obligation,” said Scott Segal, a Washington DC-based partner at Bracewell LLC, a global energy-focused law firm.

To be sure, government policy isn’t the only influence on the carbon footprint of powering America. The addition of renewable energy has continued at a slower pace despite Trump’s efforts to rein in wind and solar.

But the emissions-cutting rules were set to make a big difference. A separate analysis in September 2025 by Rhodium Group, a research firm, found that if the administration kept the Biden-era power plant, tailpipe and other rules, emissions in 2035 would fall between 7% to 25% more than expected under a repeal scenario.
The rule reversals are “another nail in the regulatory coffin for the clean transition,” said Ben King, a director in Rhodium Group’s energy and climate practice.

Reviving carbon-cutting rules will be tough, experts say, not only due to the political divide in Congress, but because in addition to removing nitty-gritty deadlines and carbon caps, the Trump administration is also attacking the legal basis that underpinned them. For example, the EPA is proposing to throw out a federal determination that greenhouse gases are a significant source of air pollution, which would mean the agency has no obligation to regulate climate pollution from power plants at all.

items.title: UK Chancellor Scales Back Economic Forecasts Before Budget
body: Britain’s fiscal watchdog will produce just one economic forecast before the Treasury decides on its budget policies in a bid to make the process more predictable and give the Chancellor of the Exchequer longer to prepare, according to a person familiar.

The Office for Budget Responsibility has in the past produced three private “pre-measures” forecasts but the changing outlook has tended to cause confusion and provoke speculation. In March, the OBR stopped publishing the dates of its forecast rounds. It has now gone further by switching to a single pre-measures outlook.

Last November’s budget was marked by briefings and speculation around the forecast timetable. Joao Sousa, senior research economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, wrote in a Strathclyde University paper earlier this year that the events in 2025 had “exemplified the dysfunction in the UK’s budget process.”

The ambition this time is to make budget a “calmer” experience, the person said. It should end the rollercoaster of forecast updates as the OBR responds to changing market prices used to calculate borrowing and energy costs. News of the single pre-measures forecast was first reported by Sky News.

Former OBR Chair Richard Hughes, who resigned after details of last year’s budget were leaked an hour early on its website, took the unusual step of disclosing the exact headroom estimates for each forecast round in what appeared to be a criticism of supposed Treasury briefings.

Last November, the final pre-measures forecast closed just over three weeks before the budget. Assuming a longer run this time, Chancellor John Healey would have his final forecast by the end of the month, giving him longer to test fiscal policies.

A Treasury spokesman said: “The OBR will publish its updated forecast alongside the Budget in October and we will not comment on rumor, speculation or proposals about its contents ahead of then.” The OBR said it would set out the details of the timetable when the forecasts are published at the budget on Oct. 28.

items.title: Peru's Economy Rebounded in July to Top Forecasts
body: Peru’s economy rebounded in July, driven by strong results across most sectors, even as unusually warmer weather weighed on fishing, agriculture and related industries.

The economic activity index, a proxy for gross domestic product, expanded 1.70% in July from a month earlier, the national statistics agency INEI said Tuesday. From a year earlier, the economy grew 3.56%, well above the 2.2% median estimate of nine economists surveyed by Bloomberg. The figure was higher than all forecasts.

Peru’s economy had contracted in May and June on a monthly basis, dragging year-on-year second-quarter output down to its slowest pace since early 2024. Looking ahead, the central bank and the government see growth reaching 3.4% in 2026, supported by stronger private investment, which is expected to help cushion the impact of a looming strong El Niño climate phenomenon.

On an annual basis, growth in July was boosted by construction and retail sales, which expanded 9.85% and 6.79%, respectively. Mining output grew 0.24% compared to a year earlier. By contrast, fishing fell 27.44%, while agriculture and manufacturing declined 1.23% and 1.81%, respectively.

The copper-rich nation is one of Latin America’s more stable economies, with growth outpacing regional peers and inflation among the lowest in emerging markets in recent years. But consumer price increases have come in above the 3% upper limit of the central bank’s target range for six straight months, hitting 4.44% in August, the fastest pace in almost three years.
Earlier this month, policymakers kept the benchmark interest rate unchanged at 4.25% for a 12th straight meeting, betting that the inflation spike will prove temporary.

Meanwhile, Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori is seeking broad powers to govern by decree for four months on key security and economic policies. After taking office in late July, her administration submitted the request to Congress, saying it aims to accelerate measures to tackle crime, bring more workers into the formal economy and prepare for El Niño, among others.
The proposal still needs to be approved by Congress, where Fujimori’s party controls the largest bloc but falls short of a majority.

items.title: Glencore Faces $2 Billion Suit as It Alleges Radiant World Fraud
body: Glencore Plc accused Radiant World and associated companies of sending falsified invoices to lenders — just as a senior executive at the group of traders said they had filed a $2 billion lawsuit against Glencore.

The claims mark the explosive end of a business relationship that for many years was extremely close. Bloomberg News has reported previously that Glencore traded extensively with Radiant World, helping it secure financing and even acquiring warrants that gave it the option to take a minority stake in the smaller company.
On Tuesday, Glencore said that it had ended all business with Radiant World and associated companies including Sapphire Minmetals, and “exited all obligations.”

For the first time, it directly accused them of fraud, saying that it had “confirmed evidence” that Radiant World and associated companies had “sent falsified invoices and contracts as well as fabricated emails, which they fraudulently claimed to have received from Glencore personnel, to a number of financial institutions.”

Bloomberg News reported in July that several major commodity traders had moved to cut ties with Radiant World amid concerns it had provided falsified documents to banks. The company at the time denied wrongdoing and said it conducts its business to the highest commercial and legal standards. A spokesperson for Radiant World had no immediate comment on the Glencore statement.
Read: How Radiant World’s ‘Prince’ Has Banks Chasing Fake Invoices
Radiant World and Sapphire Minmetals have previously claimed that Glencore’s withdrawal went against its contractual commitments to them and has caused them enormous losses.

“We have filed in the Singapore court against Glencore for $2 billion,” Rakesh Sethi, chairman of Sapphire Minmetals, told Bloomberg News by phone on Tuesday. He said that Radiant World and Sapphire Minmetals were joining forces for the claim, declining to give further details.
It was not immediately possible to confirm that the lawsuit had been filed on the website of Singapore’s court system. A spokesperson for Radiant World declined to comment on Sethi’s statement.

In its statement, Glencore said: “These claims are meritless and we will contest them vigorously. We have incurred losses and been exposed to risks by Radiant World companies and will take appropriate action.”
Glencore has taken a $480 million provision on its exposure, Bloomberg previously reported, one of its largest trading losses in its history as a public company.
“We take these issues seriously and are conducting a review of our historic business activities with Radiant World, Sapphire Minmetals and associated companies,” it said.

Glencore for years was Radiant World’s most important backer, Bloomberg has reported previously. A letter from Radiant World’s lawyers, previously reported by Bloomberg, cited a November 2024 WhatsApp message from Peter Hill, Glencore’s head of steelmaking raw materials, in which he said that Glencore had “basically bank rolled your entire existence for the last few years.”

However, the relationship soured this year, with Glencore beginning to withdraw after banks started to approach it with Radiant World invoices with its name on it, which it could not verify as genuine, Bloomberg reported previously.

A lawsuit against Radiant World from Incomlend Pte., a Singapore invoice financing platform, alleged that Radiant World borrowed from it using Glencore documents which Glencore later said were not genuine. Meanwhile, Jefferies Financial Group Inc. has accused it of falsifying iron ore invoices as part of a “fraudulent scheme” in a claim that led a London court to impose a $499 million worldwide freezing order against Radiant World and Sapphire Minmetals.

items.title: Bessent Says He's Supportive of $5,000 Checks for Americans
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he’s supportive of a plan floated by President Donald Trump to send $5,000 checks to American adults if Republicans retain their majorities in Congress, downplaying concerns about the potential cost.

“I believe there are ways to do it that would not affect the deficit,” Bessent told lawmakers Tuesday in response to questions about the plan, at a time of growing concerns in financial markets about the government’s swollen debt load.

Bessent didn’t provide details about how the cost would be offset, though he said the Treasury had been working on the plan for “quite awhile.” He said that he would work with House Speaker Mike Johnson on the proposal if the administration were to need authorization from Congress, as even some Republican lawmakers have suggested.
“Putting more money in the American people’s pocket should be an objective for everyone,” Bessent said, calling the president’s intent “very real.”

Bessent’s testimony comes a little less than a week after Trump promised the dividend payments. The proposal is projected to cost more than $1 trillion, and the US is on track to spend roughly $2 trillion more than it will bring in via taxes and tariff revenue this year.
Trump said “a lot of people think I don’t even need congressional approval” during an interview last week.
Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune said separately on Tuesday to reporters at the Capitol that what’s happening in financial markets and with US debt is “really concerning.”

The 10-year US Treasury yield rose above 5% on Tuesday to the highest in almost two decades, the latest milestone in a bruising global bond selloff driven by booming capital investment and soaring energy prices that are exacerbating inflation.
Read More: US 10-Year Yield Rises to Highest Since 2007 as Fed Looms

Asked about the $5,000 checks, Thune said, “We have to be really circumspect and wise about decisions on how we spend money, and obviously look for ways to try and slow the rate of growth in government spending.”
Congressional Republicans have not definitively said they will send the $5,000 checks to Americans if they keep control of Congress.
US debt hit $40 trillion last month, raising broader concerns about the country’s longer-term fiscal situation.

items.title: UAE Working to Be Removed From Foreign Travel Warning Lists
body: The United Arab Emirates is working with other countries on removal from their travel advisory lists just as hotel occupancies in Dubai rebound to their highest since the Iran war started.

The number of international overnight visitors to the city reached 869,000 in August, marking the highest since February, according to government figures released this week. Hotel occupancy reached 66% in August, compared with 36% in March.
Issam Kazim, chief executive officer of the Dubai Corporation for Tourism and Commerce Marketing, said lifting the warnings could have a knock-on effect for visitor numbers.

“We’re trying to remove Dubai and the UAE from the travel advisories because that would then help from the insurance side, which then will encourage the international carriers to come back again,” Kazim said in an interview at the Arabian Travel Market conference in Dubai.

Other Dubai officials also highlighted insurance woes as one of the hurdles blocking the return of foreign long-haul carriers. Dubai Airports CEO Paul Griffiths told Bloomberg in June that airlines are “having difficulty getting insurance for operations.”
Non-Gulf airlines faced between $70,000 and $150,000 in extra charges per flight to the region, according to a report by the Financial Times.

The Gulf’s aviation industry is among the most affected by the conflict, with Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad Airways temporarily cutting back operations and reworking international networks to adjust to subdued wartime demand.
MORE: Dubai Airport Says Passenger Traffic Slumps 31% on Iran War
To woo customers, Emirates started offering travel insurance that includes medical coverage for war-related incidents.

Signs of a rebound have been emerging recently, with carriers restoring some routes. The fierce competition between Middle East airlines means the rising costs of jet fuel won’t be passed on to customers just yet, Etihad Airways CEO Antonoaldo Neves said.
Kazim said they leaned on UAE residents to fill in for the absence of foreign tourists by offering incentives such as packages and a benefits program for inviting visitors into the country.
MORE: No Longer Just a Transfer Hub, Dubai Seeks More Repeat Visitors
“That really was even more successful than we would have imagined,” he said.

items.title: Attorney General Blanche Opposes AI 'Regulation by Prosecution'
body: US Attorney General Todd Blanche says he prefers a restrained approach to taking enforcement action against artificial intelligence companies and executives amid a rising debate over the risks of the cutting-edge technology.

Blanche criticized his predecessors in the Biden administration for taking a heavy-handed approach against companies in an exclusive interview with Bloomberg News. He said the Justice Department under his leadership will take action only if there are clear violations of the law.

“I’m not going to do regulation by prosecution and investigate or prosecute AI companies when there’s not a statute that they’re violating,” Blanche said. “If we’re going to charge somebody with violating the laws and take away their liberty and put them in prison, it should be because they violated the law.”

Controversy is building over the risks of AI development and what role the federal government should play in placing guardrails on a technology that some warn could lead to harmful or potentially catastrophic consequences.

Under the Biden administration, the Justice Department took a leading role in probing the artificial intelligence industry, dividing up authority between the Justice Department and the US Federal Trade Commission and opening an investigation in 2024 into Nvidia Corp.’s dominance in the sector.
Blanche, who is giving the White House briefing Tuesday afternoon, says he prefers to tread more lightly.

“The last administration spent countless prosecutors’ hours and money and effort and resources regulating whatever they chose to regulate,” Blanche said. “I think that there are some Justice Departments that like to do that and that’s not what we’re doing.”

President Donald Trump has dismissed artificial intelligence dangers as a “hoax,” criticizing the push to slow the pace of AI development as politically motivated or a scheme to advantage foreign adversaries like China. In a series of social media posts on Monday, he rejected calls for added government oversight.
Read More: Trump Attacks Anthropic CEO Over Call to Slow AI Development

But some Silicon Valley executives, lawmakers and industry critics are arguing for the federal government to take a more muscular role when it comes to regulating and potentially prosecuting AI companies and executives for knowingly creating technology that could harm the public.

Lina Khan, who headed the FTC during the Biden administration, said in an X posting on Sunday that “law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products.”
“Firms that fail to invest in adequate data security measures or fix known vulnerabilities can also be breaking the law,” Khan said.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said Monday that Congress “potentially” will need to impose guardrails on the industry and said Trump plans to summon AI executives for a meeting in the coming days.

Some antitrust experts noted that collaboration between AI companies could be allowed under the law if the focus was on reducing cybersecurity or other catastrophic risks. During the Obama administration, for example, the federal government issued guidance clarifying that companies could coordinate on sharing cybersecurity threat information to better protect networks and deter attacks.

Anthropic PBC CEO Dario Amodei published a proposal on Saturday calling for the US government to grant a narrow antitrust waiver that would allow AI labs to coordinate on safety standards and the pace of developing powerful models without breaking competition laws.
Blanche said he would have to consider whether AI companies should be granted an antitrust exemption and making a decision would involve other senior administration officials.
“I wouldn’t want to prejudge that,” he said. “We’re there to support and make sure that whatever policies the president wants to put into place, there’s a legal part of that.”

FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson said separately in a speech Tuesday that he was “deeply suspicious” of any requests by the largest artificial intelligence companies for regulation and an antitrust exemption.
Read More: FTC’s Ferguson ‘Deeply Suspicious’ About AI Antitrust Exemption

On Tuesday, OpenAI global policy chief Chris Lehane said the company has been working for several weeks with Anthropic and Google DeepMind on steps to address AI security risks. In a briefing with reporters in Washington, Lehane said that OpenAI doesn’t see the need for an antitrust waiver for the three AI firms to coordinate on safety matters.
Read More: OpenAI Says It’s Working With Anthropic, Google on AI Safety

Some in the industry cried foul on the proposal as described by Amodei. Aidan Gomez, the chief executive of the Canadian AI start-up Cohere, wrote in an essay on Sunday that it would allow a handful of Silicon Valley elites “to define the rules and safety standards of a generational technology for the entire world.”

items.title: Europe's Dealmaking Revival Has a Missing Middle
body: Welcome to The Brink. It’s Libby Cherry and Arno Schütze in Frankfurt, where private equity’s middle market exits have been taking a tortuous path. We also have news on Air Baltic’s bankruptcy and retailer Michaels’ move to cut leverage. Follow this link to subscribe. Send us feedback and tips at debtnews@bloomberg.net.

Europe’s dealmaking revival has a missing middle. A handful of splashy transactions might signal M&A is back, but the region’s mid-sized companies — and the lenders that depend on them — are largely being left behind.

Mid-market private equity firms are sitting on portfolios of smaller businesses struggling with higher financing costs, rising energy prices and the fallout from trade tensions, making them harder to sell at attractive valuations.

When buyers can’t be found at the right price, the alternatives can get messy, and painful. UK fund Silverfleet has been wound down and Swiss firm Capvis announced that it would not raise a new fund.Equistone, a private equity firm focused on mid-market acquisitions, illustrates the dynamic. The UK firm has halted new investments in Germany as investors flock to larger managers or to sector specialists.
Equistone has offered few details on its recent exits. But people familiar with the transactions say lenders have had to take a lead role while Equistone itself receded to the background.

The firm ended up ceding control of one company in a debt-for-equity swap after lenders sold their debt to another sponsor, said the people, who asked not to be identified when discussing private negotiations. In another, the owners turned to management to buy the business.Equistone has reduced German operations to a skeleton staff, although the private equity firm’s other jurisdictions remain business as usual.
While not all of Equistone’s exits may be as challenging, in stressed situations lenders can find themselves on the hook — something which may become more common if the M&A market stays soft.
A spokesperson for Equistone declined to comment.

The often-fraught sales took place while Europe, and particularly Germany, enjoys a flurry of private equity M&A with megadeals such as Carlyle Group’s acquisition of the auto paint and finishing division of BASF or Lone Star’s of ContiTech.

Equistone’s sale of chemicals firm United Initiators followed months of negotiations, in which one of the options would have been the creditor group taking over the ailing company themselves, according to people familiar with the matter. Instead, bank lenders sold their debt to London-headquartered Triton Partners, which then took over United Initiators in a debt-for-equity swap.

Equistone sold German pharmaceuticals chain Omnicare back to management, according to company filings. It sold Ansbach-based candlemaker Gala Group to a Polish supplier last year after injecting funds to stave off a covenant breach, company filings show.

Air Baltic Corp filed for bankruptcy protection in New York as the airline buckles under the weight of its debt burden, high fuel prices and travel disruptions, Edward Clark, Aaron Eglitis and Kate Duffy report.It’s a stark reversal for Latvia’s flag carrier, which as recently as last year considered an initial public offering. Those plans were stymied as its costs soared and war raged in Ukraine, where before the Russian invasion, Air Baltic had a large presence.
The company received a €350 million debtor-in-possession financing commitment from a group of funds to support operations during Chapter 11 proceedings, according to a statement on Monday.

The new financing pays a floating rate of interest which currently stands at around 12%. It was arranged by Strategic Value Partners and funded by Barclays, Hayfin Capital Management, Morgan Stanley, Oaktree Capital Management alongside SVP.
Apollo-owned retailer Michaels used a windfall from tariff refunds to help cut its leverage, Reshmi Basu reports.

The company said in preliminary second-quarter earnings that it received more than $170 million related to IEEPA tariff refunds, including interest, and bought back $101 million of debt. Net leverage shrank to 4.8 times earnings from 6.3 times the prior year, they added.

Michaels, which Apollo took over about five years ago, has emerged as an unlikely success story in the retail sector. It has stockpiled assets from bankrupt competitors like Party City and fabrics retailer Joann, while also benefitting from a revival in demand for arts and crafts.

Zorlu Enerji’s bond is poised for its biggest drop on record after the Turkish energy company hired advisers as weaker sales and a falling lira strain its ability to service international debt, Constantine Courcoulas and Kerim Karakaya report.

The firm’s 2030 dollar bond was indicated as much as 11 points lower at around 63 cents on the dollar on Tuesday, according to pricing data compiled by Bloomberg. Zorlu Enerji hired Houlihan Lokey and Servo Capital as debt advisers, according to a filing late Monday.

The decision comes just two months after Vestel Elektronik — a Zorlu Group company — hired Houlihan for restructuring talks with its own bondholders. It signals financial stress may be spreading across one of Turkey’s largest conglomerates.
The company’s revenue fell to 13 billion lira ($267 million) in the first half of 2026, from 17.3 billion lira a year earlier.
Management was scheduled to attend a JPMorgan conference in London this week but canceled the trip after the company hired advisers, according to people familiar with the matter.

items.title: Susquehanna Insider Trading Case Called Into Doubt by Judge
body: A federal judge dealt a setback to Susquehanna International Group’s lawsuit claiming it lost tens of millions of dollars to insider trading on a Chinese regulatory crackdown, denying a request to keep the alleged traders’ accounts frozen.

US District Judge Arun Subramanian said Tuesday that Susquehanna hadn’t put forth sufficient evidence to justify extending a freeze on the accounts while the case proceeds, pointing out that firm had not identified an alleged “tipper” of the inside information. He also said there appeared to be other possible explanations for the trades and suggested that Susquehanna, as a sophisticated market maker, might’ve been able to hedge against the trades.

Susquehanna sued 100 John Doe defendants in Manhattan federal court in late June, seeking to recover more than $70 million it claimed it lost on option bets placed ahead of a May 22 Chinese government announcement targeting cross-border brokerages. Jeff Yass’ firm said insider trading was the only plausible explanation for the trades.

The suit was an unusual one, as insider trading case are most commonly brought by the SEC and federal prosecutors. Bloomberg News has reported that both the Justice Department and the SEC are probing the alleged trades. Citadel Securities joined the suit the following month, saying it had also suffered losses from the activity.
A spokesperson for Susquehanna declined to comment on the ruling. Citadel Securities didn’t immediately respond to emails seeking comment.

Subramanian granted Susquehanna’s initial request to freeze accounts at Interactive Brokers Group Inc., as well as the platforms of two firms targeted in the Chinese crackdown, Futu Holdings Ltd. and Up Fintech Holding Ltd. A number of John Does subsequently identified themselves and filed responses to the suit, claiming the pattern of their trades showed they were not based on inside information.
The judge highlighted some of these arguments in his decision, saying they undermined Susquehanna’s claim that insider trading was the only possible explanation.

“This is modern trading — where algorithms, AI agents, and career traders are all jockeying, minute by minute, for the newest hot trade, using analyst information, market trends, news reports, scuttlebutt from online forums, and other tea leaves to make split-second decisions,” Subramanian wrote. “True, insider trading could be one explanation, but there needs to be more to support locking up millions of dollars in funds for the duration of a lawsuit.”

The lawsuit focuses on 200,000 short-dated put option bets on brokerages targeted in the Chinese crackdown. Futu and Up Fintech were among those firms whose shares plummeted after Chinese regulators announced they were taking action. Susquehanna alleged the Does collectively purchased $12 million in options that yielded a profit of more than $100 million.

In a court filing last month, Susquehanna and Citadel Securities said that, based on information subpoenaed from the brokers, they were seeking a narrower freeze to focus on accounts held by 45 traders. They said they were dropping claims against dozens of other Does.

Susquehanna also said last month that it had reached an agreement to resolve its claims against a defendant who allegedly made some of the largest profits in the scheme, a Hong Kong-based trader identified only as John Doe 1.

In an Aug. 21 court filing, John Doe 1 described himself in court filings as a “principal, director, and majority shareholder of a licensed financial advisory and asset management company in Hong Kong.” He said he managed two investment funds with a collective net asset value of more than $500 million and made more than $52 million trading Futu puts.

John Doe 1 said the trades were “entirely consistent with his historical trading practices and strategies” and that he chose the stocks based on a “momentum trading approach,” his own analysis and predictions based on world events. He suggested Susquehanna made its own bet on the options and lost.

“This entire case is about sophisticated market participants trying to get more money,” lawyers for John Doe 1 said in a filing. “Having lost on speculative trades in the market, plaintiffs may not speculate their way to a windfall in the courts.”
A lawyer for John Doe 1 declined to comment.
The case is Susquehanna Securities LLC v John Does 1 Through 100, 26-cv-5474, US District Court, Southern District of New York.

items.title: Ricos usan ETF de BlackRock y Vanguard para ahorrar impuestos
body: Cada tres meses, casi como un ritual, los inversores retiran US$40.000 millones o más de un fondo cotizado en bolsa de BlackRock Inc. que replica el S&P 500. Luego trasladan la mayor parte de ese dinero a un fondo casi idéntico de Vanguard Group y, pocos días después, hacen el recorrido inverso.
(*Gráfico expresado en “billions” (B), es decir miles de millones de dólares).

El fenómeno es tan grande que destaca incluso en el mercado estadounidense de fondos cotizados (ETF), valorado en US$16 billones, y tan predecible que se sabe cuándo volverá a producirse: a mediados de septiembre.
¿La causa? Como ocurre con tantas cosas en el sector de los ETF, todo gira en torno a los impuestos.

Según participantes del mercado, estos enormes flujos están impulsados por inversores extranjeros que evitan un impuesto estadounidense del 30% sobre los ingresos por dividendos. La maniobra aprovecha el hecho de que, aunque los fondos tienen la misma exposición económica, distribuyen los dividendos en fechas diferentes.

Los inversores alternan entre el ETF iShares Core S&P 500 de BlackRock (IVV) y el ETF S&P 500 de Vanguard (VOO) para evitar tener cualquiera de los dos fondos cuando se genera el derecho a cobrar el dividendo. Debido a cómo se ajustan los precios en torno a esas fechas, no renuncian al rendimiento del dividendo: reciben, en la práctica, ese valor mediante la variación del precio, que no está sujeta a impuestos para los inversores extranjeros.

Esta estrategia de alternancia se suma a la creciente lista de técnicas que Wall Street y sus principales inversores utilizan para reducir su carga fiscal. A diferencia de otras tácticas, que aprovechan una laguna legal que permite a los ETF aplazar impuestos sobre las ganancias de capital, esta es más sencilla: solo requiere la existencia de varios fondos grandes, líquidos y prácticamente idénticos.
Lea también:

El “alfa fiscal” de los ultrarricos se populariza entre inversores en YouTube y TikTokUna estrategia para eludir impuestos creó el mayor hedge fund del mundoLa estrategia tributaria de los ultrarricos que Schwab y Fidelity prefieren evitar

El fenómeno adquirió suficiente importancia como para hacerse visible en los flujos de fondos a partir de 2023. El cambio del IVV al VOO y viceversa probablemente permitió a los inversores extranjeros ahorrar unos US$147 millones en impuestos estadounidenses el año pasado, según cálculos basados en el valor en dólares que se transfiere entre ambos fondos cada trimestre.

“Los ETF del S&P 500 se utilizan para operaciones sofisticadas”, dijo Matt Bartolini, director global de estrategas de investigación de State Street Investment Management. Los patrones de flujos muestran que algunas grandes instituciones “están utilizando los ETF para obtener una exposición continua sin recibir el dividendo”, añadió.

State Street modificó recientemente el calendario de dividendos del ETF State Street SPDR Portfolio S&P 500 (SPYM), facilitando la alternancia con el State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY), según Bartolini. El rápido crecimiento del SPYM lo ha convertido “más bien en una herramienta institucional”, señaló. El IVV también había modificado anteriormente su calendario de dividendos para facilitar este tipo de cambios. BlackRock declinó comentar el motivo de la modificación.

No hay indicios de que estas operaciones impliquen ningún abuso de la normativa fiscal, y un alto funcionario del Departamento del Tesoro de EE.UU. afirmó recientemente que esta práctica no figuraba entre las estrategias que se están investigando actualmente.

La estrategia de switching aprovecha la forma en que los ETF gestionan los dividendos de las acciones que integran sus carteras. Las empresas del S&P 500 pagan dividendos en distintas fechas, que los fondos indexados acumulan y distribuyen a sus inversores una vez por trimestre. El rendimiento anual por dividendos del índice supera ligeramente el 1%.

Para evitar cobrar el dividendo de un fondo, los inversores deben vender su posición antes del cierre de la jornada previa a la fecha exdividendo, cuando las participaciones del ETF comienzan a cotizar sin derecho al próximo pago. Desde 2024, las fechas exdividendo de BlackRock se han situado sistemáticamente antes que las de Vanguard, lo que facilita la alternancia entre ambos fondos.
(*Gráfico expresado en “billions” (B), es decir miles de millones de dólares).

En junio se observó por primera vez un patrón similar en el SPYM de State Street, con movimientos de efectivo que entraban y salían de ese ETF en torno a su fecha de dividendo. Los activos del fondo han aumentado rápidamente este año y ahora ascienden a US$168.000 millones, frente a los US$97.000 millones registrados a finales de 2025.
También se han observado, en ocasiones, movimientos de menor cuantía en torno a otras fechas entre diversos fondos del S&P 500.

Las transacciones no solo se reflejan en los flujos de los fondos, sino también en la negociación. Por ejemplo, cada trimestre, los volúmenes de negociación del IVV y el VOO se disparan en torno a la fecha exdividendo del IVV.
(*Gráfico expresado en “billions” (B), es decir miles de millones de dólares).

El patrón no se limita a los fondos que replican el S&P 500 ni a los productos de renta variable. El ETF iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond (SGOV) de BlackRock distribuye intereses mensualmente. Justo antes de su fecha exdividendo, los inversores retiran hasta US$1.300 millones y, un día después, una cantidad similar vuelve a ingresar al fondo.
(*Gráfico expresado en “billions” (B), es decir miles de millones de dólares).

Determinar exactamente qué inversores participan en estas operaciones resulta difícil. Pese a la transparencia de los ETF, no es posible conocer la identidad de todos quienes compran y venden participaciones, aunque los informes regulatorios ofrecen al final de cada trimestre un panorama de los principales tenedores de cada fondo.

Los directivos de Vanguard creen que Marshall Wace, el fondo de cobertura británico, podría ser uno de los principales participantes en esta maniobra de cambio, según una persona con conocimiento de la situación que habló bajo condición de anonimato debido a lo delicado del asunto. Marshall Wace era el tercer mayor tenedor de IVV al 30 de junio, con una posición de US$30.000 millones, según datos recopilados por Bloomberg.
Portavoces de Vanguard y Marshall Wace declinaron hacer comentarios.

La mayoría de los inversores que cambian entre los fondos del S&P 500 no siguen una simple estrategia de “comprar y mantener”, según participantes del mercado entrevistados por Bloomberg. Más bien, utilizan los ETF como un componente de una operación más sofisticada que resultaría menos atractiva si conllevara impuestos sobre los dividendos.

Algunos realizan lo que se conoce como cash-and-carry trade, según Bartolini, de State Street. La estrategia consiste en vender futuros del S&P 500 y comprar simultáneamente un fondo que replique el índice en el mercado al contado, para aprovechar la diferencia de precios entre ambos.

Los inversores que buscan rentabilizar su liquidez pueden obtener con una estrategia cash-and-carry una prima de unos 100 puntos básicos, o un punto porcentual, sobre los bonos del Tesoro después de comisiones, según Mayank Mohan, director ejecutivo de Museum Mile Funds LLC, con sede en Nueva York, donde gestiona más de US$200 millones.

Para los clientes extranjeros, la retención fiscal sobre los dividendos podría suponer más de 30 puntos básicos, señaló Mohan. Antes de que surgieran varios ETF del S&P 500 de gran tamaño y bajas comisiones, los inversores extranjeros disponían de pocas opciones para evitar el dividendo.

“Con la aparición del IVV y el VOO, existe la posibilidad de realizar estas operaciones de switching”, afirmó Mohan, quien señaló que ha realizado esta operación en nombre de sus clientes y que los costos de transacción son minúsculos.

El cash-and-carry ha ganado popularidad en los últimos años debido a una brecha persistente entre los precios al contado y los futuros, señaló Natasha Sibley, gestora de carteras de Janus Henderson Investors, con sede en Londres. Los fondos soberanos y los fondos de pensiones se encuentran entre quienes realizan esta operación, añadió.
Otras instituciones podrían mantener el S&P 500 como parte de una estrategia de opciones, señaló Bartolini.

El Royal Bank of Canada, con sede en Toronto, que a finales de junio era el octavo mayor tenedor de IVV, es uno de los principales participantes en la operación cash-and-carry, según una persona con conocimiento de las actividades del banco. Un portavoz de RBC declinó hacer comentarios.
No está claro si las posiciones de Marshall Wace están relacionadas con esa estrategia o con alguna otra.

Las operaciones de switching son distintas de las denominadas “operaciones heartbeat”, una práctica importante en el sector de los ETF. En ellas, un inversor externo coloca temporalmente una gran cantidad de dinero en un fondo durante uno o dos días y luego la retira, permitiendo que el ETF se desprenda de valores que se han revalorizado sin venderlos en el mercado. Gracias a una laguna legal, estas transacciones permiten aplazar impuestos sobre las ganancias de capital, pero no afectan la tributación de los dividendos.

Los intentos de evitar la retención fiscal sobre los dividendos de inversores extranjeros tienen una larga y compleja historia, cada vez más relevante ahora que más del 30% de las acciones que cotizan en EE.UU. pertenece a inversores no estadounidenses. Hace una generación, los bancos ya ofrecían a fondos de cobertura y otros grandes inversores productos para reducir ese impuesto, a menudo mediante préstamos de valores o swaps.

Impulsados por una investigación del Senado de 2008, los legisladores aprobaron nuevas disposiciones dirigidas a los productos diseñados para eludir impuestos sobre los dividendos, y el Servicio de Impuestos Internos alcanzó acuerdos extrajudiciales con algunos fondos de cobertura que los habían utilizado.

El Departamento del Tesoro se ha interesado recientemente por una serie de técnicas de evasión fiscal relacionadas con los ETF. En una conferencia del sector celebrada en Nueva York en julio, dos altos funcionarios presentaron una lista de tipos de productos que consideran “potencialmente abusivos”.

Entre los productos señalados figuraban fondos que ofrecen una especie de versión “preconfigurada” de la estrategia de switching. Estos utilizan la mecánica de los ETF para rotar entre inversiones subyacentes similares, evitar ganancias de capital y, al mismo tiempo, eludir los dividendos.

Jeffrey Hochberg, abogado fiscalista de Sullivan & Cromwell LLP, preguntó a los funcionarios si esas preocupaciones también se aplicaban a los inversores extranjeros que rotan directamente entre inversiones similares, sin recurrir a la mecánica de los ETF para evitar ganancias de capital.
“Ese no es el objetivo”, respondió una de las funcionarias, Erika Nijenhuis.
Tras la conferencia, tanto Hochberg como Steven Rosenthal, antiguo asesor jurídico de la Comisión Conjunta de Fiscalidad del Congreso, afirmaron por separado que esa había sido la decisión acertada.
“Simplemente parece que se está vendiendo un S&P para comprar otro S&P”, señaló Rosenthal en una entrevista. “Desde una perspectiva fiscal, yo consideraría que esto está perfectamente bien”.
Traducción editada por Malu Poveda.

items.title: US Household Income Rose to Record in 2025 as Poverty Fell
body: US household incomes rose last year to an all-time high and the poverty rate fell to one of the lowest levels on record.

The median household’s inflation-adjusted income increased 2.6% last year to $87,460, according to the Census Bureau’s annual report on income, poverty and health insurance coverage. That was the highest in data back to 1967.

Despite contending with persistent inflation throughout 2025, increased wealth from stock market gains and low unemployment during the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term helped bolster household incomes.

Still, affordability became a defining political issue, with Democrats winning highly competitive races in campaigns centered on the cost of living — a theme that remains center stage this year ahead of November’s midterm elections.

The report showed females now earned about 84% as much as their male counterparts, up from around 81%. This marks the biggest yearly increase in the female-to-male earnings ratio in data back to the early 1960s.

Additionally, all races experienced income growth. While the $59,980 median income for Black workers remains the lowest, they saw the largest percentage increase among all races. Hispanic households had the smallest gain.

The Census Bureau said the official US poverty rate — the share of people whose pre-tax income falls below a specified threshold — fell 0.5 percentage point to 10.2%. The rates for children and Hispanic individuals declined to historic lows.

A supplemental poverty measure which accounts for government benefits like refundable tax credits, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program payments and housing subsidies was little changed at 13.1%. Social Security benefits lifted 28.8 million out of poverty, while refundable tax credits helped 6.1 million. On the other hand, medical expenses pushed 7.7 million people into poverty.
Meanwhile, the share of people with health coverage in 2025 was 92.1%, about in line with 2024. Medicare coverage increased 0.6 percentage point to 20.1%.

items.title: Bessent to Meet Chinese Counterpart Ahead of Trump-Xi Summit
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he will meet this weekend with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, ahead of a summit between President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping later this month.

Bessent made the remark Tuesday before the House Financial Services Committee, where he is testifying about the state of the international financial system. Bessent said he looked forward to speaking with the Chinese vice premier about sanctions related to the war in Iran, as the US increases economic pressure on the Islamic Republic.

The Iran war, now in its seventh month, has been a key factor pushing up borrowing costs and consumer prices in the US and around the world this year. The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest in almost two decades, the latest milestone in a bruising global bond selloff driven by booming capital investment and soaring energy prices that are exacerbating inflation.
Read More: US 10-Year Yield Rises to Highest Since 2007 as Fed Looms

Bessent, speaking to reporters Tuesday outside the hearing room, said he thinks the rise in yields is “largely due to the oil-price rise, and oil prices are going to come down,” according to a clip aired on Fox News.

During the hearing, Bessent took exception to a lawmaker’s comment that it didn’t matter who develops a superintelligence first. Echoing Trump, the Treasury secretary has consistently emphasized the importance of maintaining the US lead over China in artificial intelligence, an area where Chinese firms have been gaining ground on their Silicon Valley rivals.
“It does matter whether the good guys or the bad guys have this,” Bessent said. “As a person who manages the the relationship with China on AI, it matters a great deal.”

Ahead of Trump’s meeting with Xi, set for Sept. 24 in Washington, the competition over artificial intelligence has emerged as key source of friction between the world’s two largest economies. Last week, three US national security agencies accused Chinese AI firms including DeepSeek and Moonshot AI — the maker of the breakthrough Kimi K3 model — of systematically extracting proprietary knowledge from American firms.
While the Chinese companies have refrained from commenting on the US allegations, China’s government has pushed back forcefully on the claims, calling them baseless and threatening retaliation.

Authorities in Beijing similarly have criticized calls from leading US AI developers Anthropic PBC and OpenAI for a slowdown in work on advanced models as “fearmongering,” signaling their concern that American firms could be pressuring the Trump administration to further restrict China’s access to advanced chips and other hardware.
The high-level talks are the latest signal that the meeting between the leaders of the world’s two largest economies remains on track. Beijing has not yet officially confirmed the date of the visit.
Bessent did not specify the date or location of his meeting with He. The two men have typically met before each of the US-China leaders’ summits to lay the groundwork for the talks.

The hearing was disrupted by a number of anti-war protesters, with at least five people being removed by security. “Stop the sanctions that are killing Iranian civilians,” one screamed as Bessent began his opening statement.
“Scott Bessent, you’re a war criminal!” shouted another, holding a banner that read “Sanctions Kill Iranians.”

items.title: Dutch to Propose Capital Gains Tax to Break Reform Deadlock
body: The Dutch government will propose a capital gains levy next year, bringing the Netherlands in line with most European countries on how they tax wealth.
Finance Minister Eelco Heinen announced the move on Tuesday in the Hague as part of a statement on the nation’s budget day.
The measure would tax gains on investments only once they are sold, rather than the current regime that can impose levies on theoretical returns or unrealized increases in value.
The new system will “contribute to the goal of increasing future earning power, improving the investment climate, and stimulating economic growth,” the minister said in a statement.

An earlier overhaul attempt to tax paper profits triggered an investor backlash, and is currently stalled in the Senate. Years of similar wrangling and uncertainty over the Dutch fiscal regime for global assets have drawn criticism from businesses and their workers.

Heinen’s proposal marks a push to break the deadlock in a country that, like other European peers, faces a perennial struggle over budgets. Fragmented parliaments and structurally increasing spending demands often transform routine fiscal measures into matters for protracted negotiations which weigh on markets.

Moving to a capital gains tax incurs a cost. Besides the administrative burden of switching systems, the government will have to wait until assets are sold before receiving revenue, rather than being paid every year. Tax Secretary Eelco Eerenberg declined to say when the tax could be implemented.
Read more: Dutch Workers Strike Over Welfare Cuts to Fund Higher NATO Spend Spend

Prime Minister Rob Jetten’s coalition now faces months of talks to secure a majority, having already struggled to reach consensus among the ruling parties on its deal, narrowly averting a major political crisis.

Tuesday’s budget also follows weeks of union-led strikes against €6.5 billion ($7.5 billion) in welfare cuts that disrupted public transport and affecting operations at Heineken NV and the Port of Rotterdam. Many of these spending reductions, including halving the duration of unemployment benefit, were postponed on Tuesday.
Read more: Why High Yields on Government Bonds Are Causing Alarm: Explainer
