items.title: Supreme Court Rebuffs Trump's Mail Ballot Changes, Thrilling Democrats
body: I’m Jonathan Tamari, senior Washington reporter for Bloomberg Government, and each weekday I’ll be coming to you with inside-the-room reporting and insights that reveal what’s really happening in Washington—and how it impacts you. Email me with feedback and comments here. If this newsletter was forwarded to you sign up here.
Today: SCOTUS stops Trump on mail ballots, the Senate tries to take on crypto, and AI worries reach fever pitch.
The Supreme Court has decided one of the biggest lingering questions around the midterm elections in Democrats’ favor, ruling against Donald Trump’s long-running crusade against mail voting.

The justices on Monday blocked Trump’s plan to use the Postal Service to restrict mail ballots, clearing the way for a voting method used by nearly 1 in 3 voters — and around 38% of Democrats — in the last two federal elections.
Democrats are thrilled, but don’t expect this fight to end after November.
“This was one of the most important cases to protect voting rights before the Supreme Court,” said Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer.
We wrote earlier this month about how significantly Trump’s limits could affect crucial House and Senate races across the country this fall.

Opposition to the Trump effort came from Democrats, voting rights groups, and a number of Republican state election officials who warned that the changes were so big and late-breaking they would cause chaos in November.
Trump has long claimed, against the public evidence, that mail voting is rife with fraud.
The ruling appears to shut the door on the fight for November’s elections, but we know that when Trump wants something, he rarely lets go of it easily.

Conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh concurred with the decision to block the rules because, he wrote, election officials don’t have enough time. But he said “there is at least a fair prospect” that the Postal Service would eventually prove it has the legal authority to do what Trump wants.
That opens the door to continuing this fight in 2028.
Today brings a key test of whether Congress can regulate a disruptive technology that has moved fast with few guardrails.
No, not AI. Instead, we’re talking about a crypto bill that has been the subject of months of negotiations and intense lobbying.

The Senate is planning an initial vote on it today. A failure would likely signal a delay in regulation until after the midterms (at least) and would be a grim sign of lawmakers’ ability to handle the tougher and higher-stakes issue of AI.

The crypto plan’s fate was uncertain Monday as senators debated whether the proposal is a good start or not enough — illustrating the challenge for Congress keeping up with new tech, especially in the final weeks of an election.
The bill, known as the Clarity Act, has been pushed with heavy backing from the crypto industry, which hopes for the legitimacy conveyed by a federal law.
As is often the case, Trump’s presence looms largest.

Democrats have insisted that any bill address the president’s stake in his and his family’s crypto ventures, which earned him more than $1.4 billion last year — and some prominent voices say this version still falls short.
She called new ethics provisions “a weak fig leaf” that are full of loopholes and which give “his political appointees the power to turn off enforcement.”

Democrats want to force public officials and their families to fully divest their crypto holdings. The latest version of the bill stops short of that and would require Trump to put his crypto business in a blind trust.
But it will only take a handful of Democrats to move the proposal to the next step, and Democrats were sending the GOP a counter-offer, said Senator Mark Warner, per Bloomberg’s Steven T. Dennis.
Republican Senator Cynthia Lummis, meanwhile, implied that Democrats would never be satisfied.
The White House supports the bill and says it’s critical to “stay ahead of foreign competitors and lead the world in innovation” on crypto, BGOV’s Mica Soellner reports.
It’s the same argument Trump has used on AI — while opposing regulation there.

Trump’s opposition to AI guardrails puts him at odds with a growing number of lawmakers from both parties. The president dismissed AI dangers as a “hoax” after Nvidia’s Jensen Huang put him on speakerphone during a panel.
But another public warning came from an AI researcher who resigned from Google DeepMind, suggesting humanity is running out of time to prevent the tech from causing widespread harm.
Barack Obama joined the chorus calling for laws and regulations. The former president said AI could unleash “potential catastrophe” if mismanaged.
Mitch McConnell returned to the Senate Monday for the first time since a fall in mid-June. He said he is “still not quite back to 100%” but will do his best to be present for “tough votes.”
Ukraine said it hit a Russian refinery as the two nations continued attacking critical infrastructure, despite Trump’s claim of a truce around the energy sector.
Scott Bessent has insisted faster economic growth can wipe away concerns about troubling fiscal trajectories, a key theme of his recent G20 leadership. History suggests otherwise.
Meanwhile, the 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest in almost two decades, the latest milestone in a bruising global bond selloff.
Trump’s picks for the top legal job at the IRS and the vacant US Tax Court judge position face a Senate grilling today.

Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg is expected to make the case for the Pentagon’s record-breaking $1.5 trillion budget request in a briefing with House lawmakers Thursday, BGOV’s Roxana Tiron scoops.

House Democrats promise to promote clean energy, boost climate resilience, and ensure data centers pay for more electricity and water use if they regain the majority, under policy proposals being released Tuesday.
The Justice Department is seeking forfeiture of $61 million it says was generated from Iranian black-market oil sales and laundered through the cryptocurrency exchange Binance.
Canada’s housing market momentum stalled in August as trade talks with the US broke down and the countries hit each other with new tariffs.
New York Assemblyman Alex Bores is launching a $30 million project to create an AI safety agenda he hopes will influence the 2028 election.
It’s the last legislative week for the House before the election and 31 lawmakers didn’t vote on at least one of the bills that moved on the floor.
There were two recorded votes on Monday, kicking off a week with nearly 80 bills scheduled for legislators’ attention. The outcomes of more than 20 other bills were decided by voice vote.

items.title: Ukraine PM Koretskyi Warns Lawmakers: Unblock Aid or Face Cuts
body: Ukraine faces sweeping cuts to its war-ravaged budget unless lawmakers adopt unpopular measures needed to access billions in western aid ahead of winter, according to its new prime minister.

A months-long deadlock in parliament has already delayed about $4 billion in European Union assistance that was due to arrive in the third quarter, Sergii Koretskyi told Bloomberg News. He described the situation of Ukraine’s public finances as “close to critical” in separate remarks on Telegram on Monday.

The risk of a funding crunch has emerged as the first key test for Koretskyi, a former energy-sector executive, who was picked by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy two months ago to prepare Ukraine for what’s likely to be the most difficult winter since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Lawmakers’ resistance to backing reforms demanded by the EU and the International Monetary Fund, Ukraine’s two biggest donors, follows Kyiv’s admission that it was facing an additional $27 billion defense budget shortfall for this year due to rising costs of war.

“I see this as a lack of awareness of the scale of the problem,” Koretskyi, 48, said in Kyiv in his first interview with international media since taking office. “This budget is not elastic. So I want to tell you in advance: no. You need to vote. You need to move forward.”

At the same time, Koretskyi urged international partners to reduce funding uncertainty by making medium- and long-term financial commitments for Ukraine. Zelenskyy has separately called on the EU to accelerate some payments from the bloc’s €90 billion ($104 billion) loan earmarked for next year due to growing budget difficulties, prompting questions from western allies.
Read More: Ukraine Faces Mounting Cost of War as Talks With Donors Drag On

Koretskyi said that Ukraine now often has to use costly missiles to shoot down more advanced Russian Shahed drones. That’s one of the reasons why the bill for the war, currently in its fifth year, continues to climb, he said.
“If an interceptor costs tens of thousands, now it costs hundreds of thousands, perhaps as much as a million,” he said.
Kyiv’s foreign donors have demanded measures be undertaken to reduce the size of Ukraine’s shadow economy, bolster tax revenues, and align the nation’s laws with the EU.

The most contentious requirement concerns a value-added tax on cheap foreign parcels, which are currently exempt from such duties. Critics argue it would do little to boost tax revenue while increasing the burden on Ukrainians, many of whom rely on such parcels.

Koretskyi has defended the proposal, saying that the current arrangement gives foreign producers an unfair advantage. The government has resubmitted the parcel bill, urging lawmakers to pass it as soon as possible.
“What is the alternative?” he said. “Cutting spending to the bare minimum.”

Koretskyi is a political novice who spent most of his career in the private oil industry. He replaced Yuliia Svyrydenko as premier in July after leading state-run energy company JSC Ukrnafta and NJSC Naftogaz Ukrainy.

Ukraine is now bracing for what Koretskyi warns could be the worst winter since it gained independence in 1991, with air defenses becoming less effective against increasingly sophisticated Russian drones that have added a new layer of terror to daily life.
Read more: Russia’s Non-Stop Drone Barrages Upend Daily Life in Kyiv
At the same time, Ukraine is also desperately short of interceptors needed to counter ballistic missiles, and asks daily for more help from allies.

In the past week alone, Russia launched nearly 1,200 drones, most of them jet-powered and difficult to intercept, Zelenskyy said on Sunday. Among the latest targets were a passenger train locomotive and a gas station just miles from the Polish border in the Volyn region, where Koretskyi was born.
The strikes underscored a shift in Russia’s tactics, now increasingly focused on civilian and commercial targets.

“This is pure terror,” he said. “Russia cannot achieve any significant success on the battlefield, and therefore it has resorted — and continues to resort — to extreme forms of terror, striking businesses and civilian infrastructure, striking people.”

While Koretskyi said Ukraine is better prepared for the coming winter thanks to fortified physical protection and government efforts, he urged households to do their part, including by making greater use of government support programs offering relatively cheap loans.

For many Ukrainians memories are still raw of last winter, when abnormally low temperatures compounded the impact of relentless Russian airstrikes that knocked out electricity, heating and water to millions for days or weeks at a time.

Koretskyi’s government plans to significantly ramp up the number of “points of invincibility” — mobile assistance centers — and repair crews across the country. The plan also calls for bringing in foreign emergency specialists to help repair damaged infrastructure.

“Each of our partners could send specialized machinery, equipment and personnel here to help restore and restart damaged facilities as quickly as possible, or respond to these attacks,” Koretskyi said.
The winter will be a litmus test for both the rookie prime minister and his team. Asked about the government’s main objective, he replied: “To endure.”

items.title: Ten-Year Treasury Yield Rises to Highest in Nearly Two Decades
body: Good morning. Bond prices take another tumble. The Supreme Court rules against Donald Trump’s mail-voting curbs. And Matthew Rhys and Widow’s Bay are the big winners at the Emmys. Listen to the day’s top stories.
— Marcus Wright and Harry Black

Yields on 10-year US Treasuries rose to their highest level in in almost two decades, the latest milestone in a bruising global bond selloff driven by surging energy prices, mounting debt and inflation. The fears spread into equities, with stock futures prices taking another turn lower. Still, one fund manager is going against the trend, hunting for bargains in the most beaten-down corners of the bond market.

The Supreme Court rejected Donald Trump’s bid to enforce new Postal Service restrictions on mail-in ballots for the midterm elections, saying the changes came too late for states to implement without disruption. More than a dozen states are preparing to mail ballots by the middle of September. Here’s our explainer.

The debate about the threat from AI is becoming political. Trump’s attempts to downplay the issue are putting him at odds with some lawmakers and voters heading into the midterms. Barack Obama joined those criticizing Trump’s approach, calling for further regulation of AI. A researcher who recently resigned from Google DeepMind joined the chorus of developers sounding the alarm, writing that the technology has the potential to “kill us all.” And during a panel discussion, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a live phone call from Trump in which the president labeled AI fears as “a hoax.”

The US used so many munitions against Iran that it caused “strategic inventory shortfalls,” the Pentagon inspector general said, officially confirming a problem the White House has repeatedly downplayed. War-related disruptions continued to push up oil prices, with a critical Saudi Arabian pipeline still offline. And the DOJ is seeking forfeiture of $61 million it says was generated from Iranian black-market oil sales and laundered through the cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

Gavin Newsom said he wouldn’t run for president in 2028 if Kamala Harris enters the race, potentially avoiding a showdown between two of California’s most prominent Democrats. On Capitol Hill, Mitch McConnell returned to the Senate for the first time since suffering from a fall in June. That’s welcome news for Republican leaders after facing nail-biting votes in the Senate, most recently over Todd Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general.
Business schools are racing to deploy AI in their MBA programs, transforming everything from how students do their research to how they receive feedback from their teachers.

America’s favorite kitchen countertops are slowly killing the workers who make them. Silicosis lawsuits are now running into the billions but defenders in Congress are pushing to shield manufacturers from liability.
Big Take Podcast

The US’s munitions shortfall is a crisis in the making, Bloomberg’s Editors write. As well as accelerating efforts to replenish stocks of Tomahawks and other sophisticated missiles, the Pentagon needs to rethink their centrality to its warfighting strategy.

items.title: Calls to Pace AI Won't Slow Robust Data Center Demand
body: Welcome to Tech In Depth, our daily newsletter about the business of tech from Bloomberg’s journalists around the world. Today, Lynn Doan looks at the debate over whether to slow the pace of artificial intelligence development.

Presidential phone call: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was in the middle of a panel discussion Monday when he got a phone call. US President Donald Trump was on the line to talk about artificial intelligence.

Social media crackdown: The EU is planning a “Kids Act” to limit social media, AI chatbots and online gaming for kids younger than 15. The proposal would strengthen moves made by individual countries in the bloc.
Kioxia shares: The Japanese memory-storage maker is considering listing $10 billion in American depositary receipts. The company’s Tokyo-based shares have surged almost 400% this year.

Buildots, a startup that uses AI to help speed construction of big, expensive projects such as data centers and hospitals, raised $130 million in a round that valued the company near $1 billion. Its customers include chipmaker Intel Corp. and data center builder Digital Realty, along with large US construction firms STO Building Group and JE Dunn Construction Co.

On Saturday, Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei posted a piece of not-so-casual weekend reading on his personal website, calling for the industry to slow the pace of AI development before humans lose control of the technology and it wreaks havoc upon the world.

A day after Amodei’s essay, which was quickly endorsed by Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and longtime Google AI leader Demis Hassabis, technology stocks — hardware shares in particular — began to tank. Among the hardest hit as of Monday were OpenAI investor SoftBank Group, chip designer Arm Holdings, server maker Super Micro Computer and AI computing provider CoreWeave. Nvidia, the world’s top AI chipmaker, slid the most in two weeks.

On the face of it, I know it looks bad. AI development slowdown = less AI computing demand = end of the AI data center boom. But here’s what’s wrong with this equation: Increasingly, the demand for computing power isn’t coming from developing and training new, more advanced AI models. It’s coming from using the models, what’s known as inference. And that inference demand, based solely from companies around the world plugging in AI systems that have already been built and are in service, is staggering.

Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Derek Mogull told me he expects inference to account for about 85% of flash memory storage growth through 2030. In research published last week, his colleagues similarly said inference demand from businesses rapidly adopting AI is already becoming the larger share of overall computing demand, exceeding 65% by 2029.
“There’s a growing number of buyers for storage and compute,” Mogull said. “Total demand is not going to go anywhere.”

A splashy promotion for inference will be on display beginning Tuesday in San Francisco at Salesforce’s annual Dreamforce conference. The enterprise software giant takes over several blocks of the city with a series of big-name guests and presentations. Altman and Amodei are scheduled to appear — separately — alongside Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff. As part of the event, Amodei and Benioff will share their vision for bringing Anthropic’s Claude AI chatbot to Salesforce’s platform for businesses.
If there’s any event that will reinforce the dramatic uptake of enterprise AI tools, it’s this one.

That unwavering demand is what has Seth Demsey absolutely unfazed by Amodei’s call for “pacing” over the weekend. I asked Demsey, the co-CEO of the relatively new AI cloud computing company Corvex, if he called an emergency leadership meeting. Or whether it made him rethink any contracts he has signed to obtain more data center capacity.
“Nobody called anybody,” he told me. “It’s not because we’re naive. It’s because we know the shape of demand. We know the backlog of training and inference compute.”
The day’s most read story in tech and entertainment:

The debate over the pace of artificial intelligence took a turn when US President Donald Trump attacked Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for suggesting a slowdown in the development of new models. Trump said the US needs to stay ahead of China and called the idea that AI could destroy humanity a “hoax.”

items.title: Agility Robotics Unveils Humanoid Designed to Work Safely Alongside Humans
body: Agility Robotics Inc. on Tuesday unveiled a new humanoid that is designed to safely work in close proximity to people, a milestone for an industry that typically separates robots from human workers.

The latest humanoid from the Salem, Oregon-based company, the Digit 5, is designed to conduct complex work such as loading materials onto equipment, sorting parts, sequencing and inspecting items. That’s a step up from Agility’s previous humanoid, the Digit 4, which was known for its ability to stack plastic bins.

The prior Digit models were required to operate behind physical safety barriers, limiting their ability to take on tasks from humans. The Digit 5 is  engineered to work near people without those barriers as part of a broader effort to deploy the company’s autonomous robots across more facilities.

“It’s a big deal, because what you’re looking at, probably for the first time, is a robot that has been built and designed around customer needs through operational deployments,” according to Daniel Diez, Agility’s chief business officer. “You cannot put 150 robots into a warehouse where every one of them has to be surrounded by a 10-by-20 plexiglass set of walls,” he said.
Read More:  Do Humanoid Robots Really Need Legs?

The robotics firm currently operates in nine customer facilities, including those of Schaeffler AG, GXO Logistics Inc. and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada Inc., and has logged more than 65,000 hours of operation. Agility said it has about $300 million in multiyear orders for Digit and plans to expand in Europe starting early next year.

Agility is going public this year via a merger with special purpose acquisition company Churchill Capital Corp XI in a deal that values the robotics company at $2.5 billion. The company generated about $1.8 million in revenue in 2025 while posting a $140 million operating loss.

Chinese robotics firm Unitree went public in August on Shanghai’s stock exchange. Agility is among a crop of humanoid companies that have attracted investors in recent years. The company has raised $500 million to date.

To improve safety, the Digit 5 uses artificial intelligence algorithms and new sensors to understand when it is nearby people and take action, such as stopping or sitting, if necessary, to avoid a collision. It also uses visual and auditory cues to send alerts to others when it’s about to move. A software-based safety control mechanism powers the robot’s response in real time, the company said.
Still, humanoids with legs like the new Digit are more unpredictable and a bigger safety risk when operating near humans compared with similar devices with wheels.

The Digit 5 features a new leg design engineered to better handle repetitive lifting and up carrying capacity from about 35 pounds to 50 pounds at a time. It also has a 90-minute battery that charges in nine minutes, the company said. It has a swappable hand gripper that can handle a paddle, pincher, claw or five-fingered artificial hand.

“Everyone is obsessed with seeing these robots in the home, and what’s needed is cooperative safety — the ability for the robot to work in close proximity with people,” Diez said. He added that the company firmly believes “that the path to getting to the home is through industry.”

items.title: Corteva CEO Makes a Case for Crop Chemicals in the Age of MAHA
body: Luther C. Kissam IV paused in a glass-walled corridor at Corteva Inc.’s Indianapolis headquarters to take in one of his favorite places on the roughly 200-acre campus of the crop protection company he’s helmed since June.
“Those are all our greenhouses and R&D,” he said, gesturing at the line of buildings visible across a glistening pond and vibrant lawn. “Where the magic happens.”

Inside, employees in lab coats, safety goggles and gloves run hundreds of experiments with microbial, biological and chemical compounds. They’ll screen 100,000 strains this year to identify and test potential solutions to help manage the weeds, diseases and pests that, in some cases, are expected to plague agricultural crops in 10 years or more.

“It’s just so exciting to go and look, and you see untreated this weed is just flourishing, and treated it’s just dead as a wedge,” Kissam said, in a drawl reflecting his small-farming-community roots in South Carolina.

The 62-year-old former chief executive officer of lithium producer Albemarle Corp. is leading Corteva as it separates from its seed and genetics business, now known as Vylor Inc., during a broader shift in the industry. His remit: to make the case for agricultural chemicals amid opposition from the Make America Healthy Again movement and pressure from the Trump administration, which is investigating high prices for crop inputs like seeds and fertilizer.

Brand-name crop protection products also are facing more competition from less-expensive generics as financially squeezed farmers worldwide look for cost-savings. More than 30% of row crop farmers surveyed in North America, Europe and Latin America say they expect to shift toward generic crop protection in the next two years, according to McKinsey & Co.’s Global Farmer Insights 2026 report.

“Growers are looking to manage volatility in input costs more aggressively,” McKinsey senior partner David Fiocco said in an interview, adding that because the quality and availability of generics has improved, producers “no longer need to buy the branded for supply certainty.”
Read More: Farmers Are Embracing AI More Than Any Other Tech, McKinsey Says

Kissam — who is returning to a CEO role after a battle against cancer forced his retirement from Albemarle in 2020 — is pragmatic about the challenges and how the company will face them after Oct. 1, when Corteva is scheduled to officially split from the seed business. Both Corteva and Vylor on Tuesday were updating on their separation at individual investor days.
The divide is already physically under way inside the Indianapolis campus, where red cautionary tape and construction cones mark off the office spaces being set aside for some of Vylor’s operations.

Kissam’s office is still sparsely decorated. A gilt frame with a photo of his wife in her wedding dress adorns Kissam’s desk, while a poster of lessons from Robert Fulghum’s bestselling book, “All I Really Need to Know I Learned In Kindergarten” leans against a wall waiting to be hung.

“If you live your life by this little thing here, it makes things a whole lot easier,” Kissam said while pointing out his favorite lessons from the book, including a bit of wisdom about strong roots making healthy plants.

Corteva was formed after the 2017 merger of Dow Chemical and DuPont. The decision to separate the seeds business from the crop protection side was made to give both businesses more flexibility, especially as the pesticides side faced stiffer competition.

When the split was announced last October, Corteva’s stock initially fell, with analysts from Barclay’s saying “we see a potential breakup resulting in the deterioration of both businesses.” While shares have since rebounded — they climbed as much as 2.1% on Tuesday and are up about 25% year-to-date — some are still cautious about the prospects for the standalone crop protection company.

“There’s going to be a laser focus on the chemicals product pipeline,” said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Jason Miner, especially as investors look for Corteva to address potentially lower usage as farmers use new technology to get more precise with applications. “If you’re going to offset the volume threat with fancy new discoveries and changing your product mix, that has to show up really quickly in a much bigger pipeline.”

Meanwhile, California on Monday asked a federal court to temporarily block the spinoff, arguing the company will be left with insufficient assets to cover liabilities on so-called forever chemicals. “Our planning hasn't changed,” Vylor CEO Chuck Magro said at the investor day Tuesday. “We're going to defend ourselves against the allegation and we plan to separate."
The separation comes amid major changes throughout the industry.

Bayer AG, maker of weedkiller Roundup, put its US glyphosate business into a subsidiary in a move seen as a way to limit litigation risks.     FMC Corp., which has been under pressure as patents on key products expired, completed a review of strategic options this summer by agreeing to sell a minority equity stake to Tessenderlo Group. And Swiss agri-tech company Syngenta Group recently appointed a new chief executive after losing its former leader, Jeff Rowe, to Archer-Daniels-Midland Co.

Kissam, who most recently was a partner at Bernhard Capital Partners Management LP, said it wasn’t long after a search committee approached him about leading Corteva that he was sold on the proposition. He’d retired from the C-suite at Albemarle earlier than he wanted in order to monitor his health and maintain treatments for non-Hodgkins lymphoma, which he was diagnosed with in 2019. While he stayed active on boards, he said he eventually missed the teamwork that comes from working to try to solve large-scale problems.
“Farmers are my people,” Kissam said while explaining his decision to join Corteva. “It was the right fit, it was the right customer group — it just felt right, so I jumped in.”

He was especially drawn to the company’s pipeline, which includes Reklemel, to protect against parasitic worms known as nematodes, and Haviza, a fungicide that controls Asian soybean rust and is expected to launch in 2028.

“We’ve got the best portfolio in crop protection,” Kissam said, touting a pipeline valued at $11 billion through 2040 with 12 new products launching in the next decade. “We’re not dependent on any one area of the world, one crop or one innovation.”

Vylor, meanwhile, said it has a pipeline value of $19 billion and will launch 12 new technology platforms in the next decade. It touted its hybrid wheat technology at the investor event, with Magro saying the product “is essentially a new global crop for us.”
Kissam acknowledges the headwinds facing the crop protection industry.

The Trump administration for months has been investigating crop input suppliers for potential antitrust violations, saying consolidation in agriculture has hurt competition and led to high prices for everything from seed to fertilizer. Tariffs, geopolitical strife and inflation also have been pushing up prices and squeezing farmers.
Read More: USDA Wants Farmer Help With Fertilizer Probe as Prices Soar
Kissam said he thinks any examination of crop protection should consider not only product prices, but what kind of yields those products help farmers achieve.

“It’s no different than looking at the national debt without looking at what GDP is,” Kissam said. “The ag industry is trying to do a pretty dadgum good job of helping that farmer increase the yields off of that acre.”

When it comes to the politically-connected MAHA movement, which advocates against pesticides over worries about links to developmental disorders, Kissam is also clear: Crops would suffer without the kinds of products Corteva supplies — all of which go through lengthy regulatory reviews for safety.
“Yields would just go down because you’d have more weed pressure, you’d have more insect pressure, you’d have more disease,” he said. “You wouldn’t be able to feed or fuel the world.”
Kissam also recognized other threats to Corteva’s business, including technological advancements that help farmers more precisely apply pesticides and other chemicals, resulting in less usage.

“In the ’80s, there were big volumes that were being sprayed,” he said, recalling when he scouted cotton and soybeans in high school. “Today, it’s amazing to me the small amount of chemistry that’s actually applied over acres.”
Kissam said all of these challenges mean there’s less room for error as Corteva stands on its own as a crop protection company.

As such, he is focused on improving the company’s operational efficiency and shrinking how long it takes to move products from ideas to launch — currently a 12-year timeline. He expects artificial intelligence to play a big role, helping the company to predict weather and disease patterns that can guide its work, cull good ideas from bad earlier, and identify regulatory hang-ups before a product gets stuck in the approval process.

Kissam said he also sees big potential for growth in biologicals, a growing segment of crop protection products derived from natural materials. The company expects to launch five new biologicals in the next decade.
The CEO said his overall strategy boils down to one thing: focusing time and resources on the best products, even if that means weeding out some lower-performing offerings.
“We have to provide a solution that’s better than the alternatives,” he said. “If we can’t compete and win on the value proposition, we’re not going to be there.”

items.title: AI Is Quietly Reversing Political Polarization. But It Comes at a Cost
body: Political polarization has become so extreme that when Democrats and Republicans find common ground on a single issue — like their shared hatred of AI data centers — it becomes major news.

But those same data centers could also be mending the nation’s political divisions. The large language models people increasingly rely on to understand the world are far from benign, but they are quietly — if unintentionally — promoting consensus in both how and what the public learns about the world. For better or worse.

It seems impossible to think that such a thing could happen. Research and commentary dedicated to analyzing today’s fragmented media ecosystem have, at times, made it seem like we’ve reached the point of no return. Looking back at the roots of our extreme political polarization underscores why we may be ripe for a reversal of that trend.

An ever-shrinking overlap between the two major parties began in the 1970s, but it intensified in the 1990s and beyond. Why that happened is the subject of longstanding debate, but one particularly compelling explanation traces the shift back to evolutions in the media landscape during that same period.

The rise of radio and television broadcasting resulted in a handful of stations and networks catering to a mass audience in the 1950s and 1960s. That meant the average person got much of the same information, even if there might be slight variations between outlets.

Those of us old enough to remember that era can recall legendary anchors like Walter Cronkite, who presided over CBS Evening News, building a brand based on overt neutrality. Such was the faith in this kind of media figure that Cronkite typically closed his broadcasts with a revealing catchphrase: “And that’s the way it is” — as if there was no other version of the truth. This was problematic in that it tended to oversimplify reality, banishing dissident voices to the margins. As an antidote to polarization, though, it proved quite effective.

That carefully constructed shared reality fell apart in the late 1970s, with the rise of cable television. Then Congress effectively removed barriers to entry in 1984 with the Cable Act, which allowed the number of cable networks to explode. Instead of three or four broadcast networks, Americans could seek out channels that suited their particular political and cultural sensibilities. By 1998, the US had 174 different national cable networks — it was 82 just six years earlier — along with thousands of local cable stations.

The rise of the internet only accelerated these trends, giving everyone with access to a computer the ability to go down various rabbit holes. The resulting amplification of conspiracy theories and other fringe ideas was bad enough — then social media said, “hold my beer” and effectively obliterated any vestiges of a national common ground. Different platforms gave rise to a collection of adversarial digital tribes living in their separate realities.

Consensus and moderation prevailed when citizens relied on a highly centralized and homogenous group of media outlets. When that system was replaced by a multiplicity of outlets and sources, polarization intensified to dangerous levels.
Enter AI. Critics have predicted that the technology’s chatbots and models will sow disinformation, further fueling polarization. Yet there’s some early evidence to suggest a different outcome.

Consider how people rely on the internet for information. In the past, someone might “Google” a particular topic and then spend an inordinate amount of time clicking through links, searching for results that interested them or perhaps resonated with their own biases. Or they might turn to their own social media connections, effectively amplifying their own prejudices.

AI has upended that system. Increasingly, we’re looking at what has been described as a “zero-click” future, where someone posing a query instead accepts an AI summary rather than exploring the cacophony of the internet. Or AI is relied on more directly, as when people pose questions to chatbots, which many often trust as much as, if not more than, other humans.
These developments represent a return to the spirit, if not the reality, of broadcast networks and moderating voices. This is inevitable, given the way that AI works.

Models are trained on vast collections of information in order to generate words and phrases. As such, they’re probability machines, producing the likeliest answer based on training data. This means that chatbots and AI-generated search results tend to move to the middle, distilling an otherwise invisible consensus about any given issue. Answers come across as a reassuring, neutral and believable summary that comes across as the objective truth. Something like a digital Walter Cronkite. Little wonder that, even as Americans tell pollsters that they don’t trust the “media,” they increasingly turn to AI for information.

Some hint of where we’re going was captured in a recent report on election disinformation from the Brennan Center for Justice. It found that AI chatbots, far from amplifying fringe theories of election fraud, did the opposite, gently pushing back on these claims and banishing them. A study published in the Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication found that individuals who interact with chatbots about political issues tended to moderate their views.

That’s all well and good, but we should not forget that AI models have a built-in bias toward conventional wisdom, not minority or fringe points of view. The public has been so conditioned to associate “fringe” with bad that we might forget those views can lead to a more equitable society. Many civil rights that we now regard as necessary began as ideas far outside the mainstream.

As our reliance on AI grows, a decades-long drift toward polarization may reverse. But the resulting consensus could come at a cost: a new kind of groupthink that is no less dangerous for democracy than the polarization it replaces.

items.title: WTO and rules of global trade
body: The World Trade Organization is kicking off a public symposium in Geneva on Tuesday with a nearly 200-page report that tries to make the case for its continued relevance in a world were the rules of commerce between 166 member countries are giving way to power politics.
The three-decade-old trade body is clinging to the fact that 72% of global goods trade still happens under one of its guiding principles — non-discrimination, under most-favored nation tariff terms.
But it’s also a running simulations on the economic costs if that number declines further and imagining cross-border commerce without rules.
WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala acknowledges that the rules-based system faces its most severe disruption in 80 years.

“We have seen trade rules challenged on a scale unseen since multilateral institutions were created to underpin open, stable and predictable global trade in the wake of the Great Depression and the Second World War,” she wrote in the report.
Consider the trade news of just in the past few weeks:
In the report, WTO economists plot out three scenarios through the year 2050 and offer estimates on the costs and gains of each.
In a world fragmented along geopolitical blocs, real gross domestic product drops 5.1% and exports sink 18.6%.
In scenario two, free trade areas form where tariffs are set in non-cooperative ways. As a result, real GDP declines 6.9% and exports plunge almost 27%.
In the rosy scenario, where the WTO reigns and integration widens, real GDP increases 2.9% and exports swell 17.9%
Cost of Inaction
That’s a big gap between worst- and best-case scenarios, according to WTO Chief Economist Robert Staiger, who emphasized that these are simulations not a range of forecasts.
“If the status quo is unsustainable, as many members believe, this illustrates the potential cost of inaction on reform,” Staiger, a Dartmouth College economics professor, told reporters on Monday.

“These numbers tell a clear story,” he said. “The WTO remains an important force for shaping world trade, but the economy it governs is now far more integrated, digital, multipolar and complex than the one its rules were designed for — and the stakes of reform are high.”
—Brendan Murray in London

Bloomberg’s Tariff Tracker follows all the twists and turns of global trade wars. Click here for more of Bloomberg.com’s most-read stories about trade, supply chains and shipping. Subscribe to Fault Lines, a Bloomberg Economics newsletter about how geoeconomics is reshaping business and markets.

Two speeds | China’s consumer spending and investment languished in August even as industrial output improved more than expected, in a sign of a widening divide within the economy. Retail sales rose 0.4% in August from a year earlier, down from 0.6% in July. In contrast, industrial output climbed 5.2% in August, exceeding expectations and accelerating from July’s 4.5% gain. Double-digit growth in exports is largely behind the uplift, as hundreds of billions of dollars flow into the global buildout of data centers and drive up demand for artificial intelligence-related products such as integrated circuits.

items.title: China Stuck in Economic Slow Lane Relies on AI-Fueled Export Boom
body: I’m Malcolm Scott, international economics editor in Sydney. Today we’re looking at China’s slowdown and reliance on the AI-led export boom. Send us feedback and tips to ecodaily@bloomberg.net. And if you aren’t yet signed up to receive this newsletter, you can do so here.
China’s domestic economy remains firmly stuck in the slow lane as the ongoing property slump saps consumer spending and a drip feed of stimulus does little to revive investment.

Even still, the nation’s economic growth target for this year can’t be written off just yet as the artificial intelligence boom fuels surging exports. That was on display in data Tuesday showing August industrial output was a rare bright spot.

Against that backdrop, Anthropic and OpenAI’s calls to tap the brakes on AI — discussed in Monday’s newsletter — are not just a threat to China’s tech ambitions. They’re also a threat to it’s macro-economic outlook. Any industry-wide slowdown “would severely dampen” China’s AI-driven exports, Bloomberg Economics’s China economists Chang Shu and Eric Zhu wrote in a note after Tuesday’s downbeat data. There’s a lot at stake for America’s economic momentum too, with BE’s Anna Wong and colleagues arguing in a recent note that AI is already contributing more to US growth and productivity than official statistics capture.

For the world economy, the takeaway is significant: Neither side is likely to tap the brakes anytime soon on an AI investment bonanza that’s reshaping capital flows and propping up economic growth rates.

“The robots will not be taking over. AI will not be taking over the rest of the world,” US President Donald Trump told Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang, who was onstage at the All-In summit in Los Angeles. “We have to do things, and we have to do them prudently, but that doesn’t mean we’re going to stop an industry.”

The global economy in the next 25 years will see the ranks of middle- and upper-income consumers jump by some 1.2 billion people, with India leading the charge, according to HSBC economists Bethan Ellis and James Pomeroy.

Other takeaways from the duo in a note this month include that by 2050 Asia will have a majority of the world’s upper-income ranks. That criterion is defined as $110 of income per day, using purchasing power parity exchange rates, which account for different price levels of products across countries.

Consumer spending is seen rising roughly 2.4% a year, after inflation, with recreation as the biggest driver. Meantime, while working-age populations are set to fall in Europe, North America and Oceania (which includes Australia and New Zealand), “the movement of consumers up the income distribution means their upper-income population is nonetheless set to rise 75%,” HSBC said.

items.title: JD Sports Names North America CEO, Chief Marketing Officer
body: JD Sports Fashion Plc named new executives for marketing and North America as the sports retailer looks to reverse soft sales and an extended slump in the stock market.

The owner of the Hibbett and DLTR chains named John Mersho as chief executive officer for North America, effective immediately. Mersho, whose family founded Shoe Palace in 1993, was chief commercial officer for JD Sports North America since 2025. He replaces John Hall, who is retiring.
Mersho will look to improve the company’s product lineup as well as its e-commerce capabilities, according to a statement. He’ll also aim to boost customer awareness.
JD Sports also named company veteran Mike Grimes as chief marketing officer of the global business. He previously held the same role for North America.
The shares fell less than 1% in London trading on Tuesday.

JD Sports is looking to bounce back as weaker-than-expected sneaker sales led to a guidance reduction for the full year, and the stock has declined close to 70% from their peak in 2021. The retailer recently named former Ikea Group Chief Executive Officer Peter Agnefjäll as chair to oversee turnaround efforts.

North America is JD Sports’ largest region, accounting for 38% of sales in the latest fiscal year. This was followed by Europe, which generated 34% of revenue in the same period, and the UK, which was nearly 25%.

Late last month, JD Sports competitor Dick’s Sporting Goods fell the most on record after reporting struggles at Foot Locker, citing a rise in promotions. The company said legacy sneaker styles aren’t resonating like they once did, without naming specific brands.

items.title: GM to Offer Apple CarPlay After Shift Away From the System
body: General Motors Co. is integrating Apple Inc.’s CarPlay in its latest infotainment system, three years after upsetting some consumers by eliminating the popular interface from its electric vehicles.

The new system will allow drivers to use CarPlay or Google’s Android Auto on a split screen that also shows key vehicle gauges such as fuel, tire pressure, Super Cruise hands-free driving and towing information. In addition, the system enables the driver to use vehicle functions and phone apps with less toggling between screens.

The user interface will debut late this year in the 2027 Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks, GM said Tuesday. The vehicles will come with 60 inches of screen space, including a screen for the front-seat passenger to view video content. GM plans to roll the new system out in future models.

While GM hadn’t removed Apple’s system from its gasoline-powered vehicles, executives said they planned to phase it out. That irked some GM vehicle owners, who took to social media to decry the loss of the popular interface linking iPhone apps to the in-car screen. Some workarounds have emerged: A company called EVPlay offers a device that allows drivers to project CarPlay onto the screens of the GM EVs and vehicles made by Rivian, which do not use CarPlay.

GM has developed its own infotainment technology as part of a vehicle software system and was moving away from phone-projection connections like CarPlay. The automaker wanted a more seamless system that could also be connected to vehicle gauges and controls and give the company a crack at software service revenue.
The new CarPlay user interface was jointly developed, showing that GM and Apple are working closer together.

“We listen to our customers, what they want, and, going forward will still have have projection in our trucks,” Michael Wahlstrom, GM’s executive director of connected apps and services, said in an interview. “We worked with both Apple and Google to develop a new split screen that includes the projection experience right next to the native experience.”

Wahlstrom wouldn’t say if GM will bring CarPlay back into its electric vehicles, which started using the company’s in-house system that has some iPhone apps. Late last year, GM struck a deal to bring Apple Music into electric vehicles that could not connect to CarPlay.
GM shares rose less than 1% to $87.43 in premarket trading Tuesday in New York.

items.title: Emerging Assets Extend Four-Day Slide as Oil, 5% US Yield Bite
body: Emerging-market stocks and currencies fell for a fourth session as rising global bond yields and oil prices kept riskier assets under pressure.

An MSCI Inc. gauge for developing-nation currencies ended the day 0.3% lower Tuesday, bringing its four-day drop to almost 1%. South Korea’s won underperformed, offsetting gains in some Latin American currencies including Chile’s peso.

The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest in almost two decades as a jump in energy prices fueled inflation concerns. That’s adding to pressure on emerging-market assets ahead of the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision on Wednesday, when investors expect officials to raise borrowing costs for the first time since July 2023. Attention is likely to focus on the path for rates through year-end, with Bloomberg Economics expecting this week’s move to be the only hike in 2026.

“Markets are essentially priced for a 25 basis-point hike but there is still some uncertainty around what the path looks like after tomorrow,” said Brendan McKenna, a strategist at Societe Generale in New York. “That uncertainty might get LatAm FX moving sideways until we get some more clarity.”
In credit markets, Gabon’s bonds surged after the government announced that an audit found the OPEC member’s debt stock stood at $16.7 billion, almost a fifth below an initial estimate.
The Dominican Republic is offering to buy back some of its bonds coming due next year and said it’s seeking to sell new dollar-denominated notes.

The sale of government bonds has remained slow so far in September as mounting inflation concerns pushed US yields higher. Morgan Stanley expects some sovereigns to downsize issuance and to continue a shift away from dollar-denominated debt, strategists including Simon Waever wrote in a note Monday.

Emerging-market equities fell to a three-week low. BlackRock Inc. strategists returned to an overweight recommendation on the asset class, betting that access to the scarce resources needed for the artificial-intelligence boom and strong earnings will drive outperformance.

items.title: From Frier to Flyer: Used Cooking Oil Fuels Luxury Antarctic Tours
body: Sasol Ltd. has begun selling sustainable aviation fuel to a company that organizes luxury trips to Antarctica, tapping into a new market that may help reduce its environmental footprint.

The Johannesburg-based firm, which is the world’s biggest producer of fuel and chemicals from coal and ranks as one of South Africa’s biggest greenhouse-gas emitters, is making the sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, from used cooking oil at its Natref refinery.

Tour operator White Desert, whose offerings range from one-day trips from Cape Town that cost $16,500 and features attractions such as rappelling down a glacier and a champagne toast in an ice bar, to a seven-day itinerary that includes a visit to Antarctica’s Blue Rivers for up to $120,000, has been signed up as a first customer. It began using SAF in 2021, according to its website.

SAF is a low-carbon fuel alternative made from non-petroleum feedstocks that help cut air pollution from air travel. Aviation accounts for 2% of all carbon dioxide emissions and 12% of the gas from transportation, according to the US Department of Energy.
Production of SAF is a spoke in Sasol’s strategy to eventually move away from fossil fuels, though its near-term focus has been on increasing output at the Secunda manufacturing hub.

Finding an offtaker for the product demonstrates Sasol’s capability to make the fuel in South Africa, Danie Cronje, senior vice president for business building, strategy and technology. “This we see as a very first practical commercial step.”

The market for SAF is currently tiny, accounting for about 0.6% of jet fuel demand last year. Producers and consumers of SAF globally expect prices of the fuel to increase as blending mandates ramp up in Europe and new policies come into effect in other regions, BloombergNEF analysts said in a July report.

Sasol can produce as much as 2 million liters of SAF annually at Natref, with the capability to increase to 100 million liters a year by 2030, according to Cronje. That could double after certification is achieved at the Secunda plant, which uses a different manufacturing process.

For now, supplying White Desert is “a bit seasonal” and even though SAF prices can be two to three times higher than conventional aviation fuel, Sasol has seen interest from other potential customers and is finalizing commercial terms with them, Cronje said.

items.title: Zorlu Enerji Bond Plunges as Energy Firm Taps Debt Advisers
body: Zorlu Enerji’s bond is set for its biggest drop on record after the Turkish energy company hired advisers as weaker sales and a falling lira strain its ability to service international debt.

The firm’s 2030 dollar bond was indicated around 63 cents on the dollar on Tuesday, down as much as 11 points, according to pricing data compiled by Bloomberg. Zorlu Enerji hired Houlihan Lokey and Servo Capital as debt advisers, according to a filing late Monday.

The decision comes just two months after Vestel Elektronik — a Zorlu Group company — hired Houlihan for restructuring talks with its own bondholders. It signals financial stress may be spreading across one of Turkey’s largest conglomerates.
JPMorgan Chase & Co. analysts led by Lorenzo Parisi said they were surprised by the timing of the announcement and downgraded the bond to neutral.
“We would not recommend investors to add while discussions are ongoing, given the uncertainty around the potential outcome of this process,” they added.
Zorlu Enerji sold its debut $1 billion international bond in 2024 but the note has since come under significant pressure.

The company’s revenue fell to 13 billion lira ($267 million) in the first half of 2026, from 17.3 billion lira a year earlier. Meanwhile, the lira has weakened roughly 15% against the greenback over the past 12 months. This makes dollar-denominated debt much more costly to repay from lira earnings.
Zorlu Enerji’s net debt stood at $1.25 billion at the end of of the first half, according to an August company presentation.

Management was scheduled to attend a JP Morgan Chase & Co. conference in London this week but canceled the trip after the company hired advisers, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.
A spokesperson for the company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The company is part of the broader Zorlu Group, a Turkish conglomerate controlled by the Zorlu family with interests spanning energy, electronics, and real estate.

items.title: Romania Farmers' Protest Turns Violent Amid Provocation Claims
body: A farmers’ protest in the Romanian capital erupted in violence on Tuesday when demonstrators spurred on by alleged agitators clashed with riot police, in the worst civil unrest the country has seen in years.

The protest against a temporary export ban on livestock escalated after some people threw objects at law enforcement, who fired tear gas. More than 25 people needed medical assistance or were injured, including eight policemen, according to the riot police.

Authorities said that outside agitators seeking to stir trouble infiltrated what was initially a peaceful rally of several thousand farmers. Some of the most violent protesters were detained and taken in for questioning, while several cars were damaged.

The rare outbreak of street violence in the Black Sea nation comes as interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan is steering Romania through a protracted political crisis. The country has been left without a stable governing majority, the economy is in stagnation and the government needs to deliver painful spending cuts to avoid a credit rating downgrade to junk status.
“The violence we are witnessing today is extremely serious,” said President Nicusor Dan. “I strongly condemn any attempt to turn a legitimate protest into street fighting.”
The president went on to criticize “the attempt by irresponsible politicians to artificially escalate social tensions.” He didn’t name names.

The focus of the farmers’ and shepherds’ anger was an export ban on the country’s livestock imposed by the European Union following outbreaks of sheep and goat pox. Bolojan said his government had already met some of protestors’ demands and was seeking funds to compensate them for losses caused by the preventive culling of sheep.

The prime minister lost some of his powers after losing a no-confidence motion in May. Sorin Grindeanu, whose Social Democratic Party quit the ruling coalition in April, blamed “extremist forces” for trying to take advantage of the protest and “generate chaos.”
Read More: Romanian Social Democrats Gain in Poll Still Led by Far Right

“We respect the right of the people to peacefully protest, but what happened today breaches this,” Bolojan said, calling for calm and saying that none of the country’s largest agricultural businesses were present in the protest.

Romania’s far-right leader George Simion, whose Alliance for the Unity of Romanians is leading in the polls and emerged as the main beneficiary of the political bickering, showed his support for the farmers. He has tapped into deep discontent on a range of social and economic issues in a deeply divided nation.
Simion’s party issued a statement urging repercussions for those who engaged in violence, but also claimed that the conduct of the riot police inflamed the situation.
“Romania needs a leadership that protects its citizens and knows how to work for them,” Simion said earlier on Tuesday.

items.title: Magnum Says Ben & Jerry's Chair Fostered Toxic Culture
body: Ben & Jerry’s former independent chair Anuradha Mittal was “abusive, discriminatory and unprofessional” and fostered a toxic culture before she stepped down from the board earlier this year, according to a legal filing by Magnum Ice Cream Company.

In one instance, Mittal said she did not need “white bi----- on the board” and also called a former director a “white bi---,” the owner of Ben & Jerry’s said in the document filed with a New York court on Sept. 4.

These counterclaims accompany Magnum’s legal defense against allegations that it wrongfully removed Ben & Jerry’s independent board directors from their roles, and failed to honor an agreement resolving the dispute over the sale of Ben & Jerry’s intellectual property rights in Israel.
Under the terms of Unilever’s 2000 acquisition of Ben & Jerry’s, the ice cream brand retained an independent board in charge of its social mission.

The relationship between the company and the board has become fractious since 2021 when a disagreement over sales of Ben & Jerry’s ice cream in the West Bank sparked a wider confrontation over the brand’s social direction. The dispute upset some US investors including Nelson Peltz, whose Trian Fund Management holds a stake of about 3.7% in Magnum.

Earlier this year, six of eight board members including Mittal stepped down after Magnum introduced retroactive term limits and a new code of conduct. Ben & Jerry’s co-founders Jerry Greenfield and Ben Cohen have backed the independent members and also criticized Magnum, which was spun out of Unilever Plc last year and listed in Amsterdam. Greenfield resigned in protest after 47 years last September and Cohen has accused Magnum of destroying the brand.
Read More: Ben & Jerry’s Co-Founder Says Brand Being ‘Destroyed’ by Magnum

In August, a federal judge dismissed large parts of the independent board members’ complaint, including claims that Magnum tried to censor Ben & Jerry’s stance on progressive issues and silence Mittal. Through its counterclaim, Magnum is now seeking to show that Mittal breached her fiduciary duties to Ben & Jerry’s and Magnum.
In response, a legal representative for Mittal accused Magnum of resorting to strong-arm tactics.

“After ousting Ben & Jerry’s CEO (a thirty-plus year employee who began as a tour guide), causing one co-founder Jerry Greenfield to resign, galvanizing another co-founder Ben Cohen to start a campaign to ‘free’ the company, and attempting to remove each of the independent directors from the company’s board, Magnum has now intensified its pressure tactics against Ben & Jerry’s Chairwoman Mittal, including regurgitating allegations that Unilever executives had previously denounced as nothing more than extreme personal slander,” her counsel said in a written statement.

“Magnum’s campaign to intimidate, threaten, and character assassinate Chair Mittal due to her advocacy for Palestinian human rights  — to the great displeasure of Nelson Peltz — is outlined in her active defamation lawsuit,” the statement added.
Peltz’s Trian declined to comment.

Magnum says Mittal not only created a toxic “us versus them” sentiment at Ben & Jerry’s but also accused her of inappropriately benefiting from her role. It says she appointed friends to the board over independent candidates and channeled around $350,000 from the Ben & Jerry’s foundation, funded by Unilever and later Magnum, to The Oakland Institute, a nonprofit organization she founded.

items.title: Republicans Are Right to Be Worried About Ohio
body: How badly are things going for Republicans in what for more than a decade has been the reliably red state of Ohio? Just ask Jon Husted.

The party’s nominee for the US Senate spent part of last week at the “Trump-a-palooza” convention in Dallas, desperately trying to cast President Donald Trump’s tax cuts for the wealthy as a fix for the affordability crisis. Then, Husted spent the weekend distancing himself from his now-former political director after it was revealed that he had promoted both Nazi imagery and songs tied to White supremacy online.

“His social media activity displays a complete lack of judgement and disregard for its impact on others,” a campaign spokeswoman told the Washington Post. “Senator Husted demands better of those who represent him.”

Even before this, Cook Political Report had rated the race between Husted, the incumbent, and Democrat Sherrod Brown as a “toss-up.” Recent polls show a Brown victory looking increasingly likely, which could help flip control of Congress.
Republicans should be worried about Ohio — and not just because of the Senate race.

In a state that Trump won three times and where Republicans have long controlled almost every statewide office, in addition to having a supermajority in the state legislature, there’s a widening enthusiasm gap ahead of the midterms. Democrats are far more eager to vote than Republicans, echoing the national anti-Trump mood. But in Ohio, problematic GOP candidates also dot the ballot, creating more headwinds for the party.

In addition to Husted, there’s Representative Max Miller, for example. Allegations that he abused his daughter and ex-wife, Emily Moreno — the daughter of US Senator Bernie Moreno — continue to hang over the race against Democrat Brian Poindexter.

Miller, whose district covers a swath of suburbs and rural towns in northeast Ohio, has strenuously denied any wrongdoing. Still, Cook Political Report changed its rating on the race from “likely Republican” to “toss-up” last month, after Miller refused to drop out to allow another, less damaged candidate to replace him on the ballot. Now Republicans are stuck.
As House Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain recently told Face the Nation: “I support anybody with an R behind their name. … At the end of the day, he’s our nominee.”

Then there’s the race to succeed Ohio’s termed-out Republican Governor Mike DeWine. Polling shows Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, a billionaire entrepreneur and Trump ally who was tapped to lead DOGE with Elon Musk, is running neck-and-neck with his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

This is saying something. The last time a Democrat was governor of Ohio, Barack Obama was serving his first term as president. Though not crucial to the balance of political power nationally, losing the governorship in a supposedly red state, which the sitting vice president and likely MAGA heir JD Vance calls home, would be a psychological blow for Republicans.
Yet the race between Ramaswamy and Acton has essentially been stuck in a statistical tie for months. Cook Political Report has rated it a “toss-up.”

This is despite Ramaswamy and his allies spending some $82 million on advertising so far — more than six times what Acton and her backers have spent — and Musk and a handful of billionaires donating close to $40 million to a pro-Ramaswamy super PAC. It’s already one of the most expensive races in Ohio’s history, and it’s only September.
Why the lack of bang for those millions of bucks?

Some of it comes back to Ramaswamy. He’s an Indian American billionaire and proud Hindu who is trying to lead a state dominated by White, Christian, working-class, populist voters, far too many of whom have bought into the nativist politics of MAGA.

But, early on, Ramaswamy’s campaign also made the questionable decision to base much of its strategy on attacking Acton for her stint as Ohio’s public health director during the earliest days of the Covid pandemic. What has followed has been a barrage of fear-mongering and MAGA-esque conspiracy theories, all aimed at ginning up support from Republican voters.

“You know Amy Acton as the Covid lockdown doctor,” one of Ramaswamy’s ads begins. In another, a Republican activist blames Acton for isolating her mother in a nursing home before her death. Never mind that the nursing home was in Kentucky, not Ohio.
At his campaign events, Ramaswamy also often accuses Acton of trying to take away Ohioans’ personal freedom and spreading "Covid ideology," usually eliciting boos.

Just this month, Acton found herself staring down an armed and “aggressive” man at a county fair. The widely reported fracas, which led to misdemeanor assault charges for the gun-toting man, left Acton looking like a hero doctor, with photos of her attending to two people who had suffered minor injuries going viral.

To be fair, Acton was criticized heavily during the pandemic. She rose to prominence appearing alongside DeWine for daily public health briefings, trying to explain why increasingly contentious decisions to close schools and businesses — and even call off the state’s presidential primary at the last minute — were necessary. Lawsuits were filed. Republican state lawmakers tried to strip Acton’s authority to issue sweeping emergency public health orders. Protesters became a regular presence outside her home. Acton certainly had her fans. But she still resigned, chastened, in June 2020.

Yet none of this history has seemed to matter much in her race against Ramaswamy. Acton could be benefiting from the political cover that DeWine has provided, repeatedly owning public health decisions that were made during Covid. It also could be that pandemic-related attacks on Democrats are finally starting to lose their potency.

More likely, though, Ramaswamy’s attacks on Acton have fallen flat because Ohio voters are simply less concerned about what happened six years ago than what Trump’s Republican Party is doing to the economy right now.

A recent Fox News poll found that 40% of Ohio voters said inflation is their top concern ahead of the midterms. In 2020, 28% of voters had described their family’s financial situation as “falling behind.” Now, 38% say so — and this from a poll conducted before Trump doubled down on his trade war with Canada and his real war with Iran.

At the “Trump-a-palooza” midterm convention, the president made it clear that he is banking on his reputation — and a blitz of campaign spending — to motivate his most loyal supporters to vote in November. “I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” he said repeatedly from the stage, sounding as desperate as Husted had. “I’m on the ballot. Just one more time.”
In Ohio, that could take Republican Party politics from bad to worse.

items.title: NY Democrat Bores Launches $30 Million AI Safety Group for 2028
body: New York Assemblyman Alex Bores and his former chief of staff are launching a $30 million effort to craft an artificial intelligence safety agenda for the 2028 presidential election.

The group, Who Decides, will work in battleground states alongside traditional Democratic groups — such as labor unions, civil rights and consumer organizations — to develop a unified AI agenda for the party’s candidates to run on in two years.

Bores, 35, who gained national attention this year for his AI-focused congressional campaign in New York’s 12th district, said Who Decides will be focused on building consensus to make AI safety a central issue in the presidential race.

“It’s about much how we can tilt the ground for the 2028 presidential election and hopefully shape the politics in a way that all the candidates are going to want to run on a platform of AI safety,” said Bores, who represents Manhattan’s Upper East Side in Albany.

The group’s founding comes as the country is fixated on concerns around potential harms and risks from AI. Prompted by the high-profile resignation of an Anthropic PBC employee, AI firms including Anthropic and OpenAI last weekend called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development, a proposal that triggered a quick selloff across technology stocks.

A 3,800-word missive Saturday by Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei — which was endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — said development of the most advanced systems must be slowed in order to prevent AI slipping beyond human control and inflicting catastrophic harm. Politicians on both sides of the aisle have argued AI regulation is needed immediately, though quick action from Congress appears unlikely.
Read More: Amodei, Altman, Musk Call for Slowing AI Model Development

Bores’ initiative seeks to harness that growing energy to “ensure that the next Democratic president will take office and be ready to move on this AI agenda in the first hundred days,” Who Decides said Tuesday in a statement. A spokesperson for the group declined to share the group’s donors, but said it doesn’t include any AI companies, CEOs or C-suite executives.

Bores and Anna Myers, his former chief of staff, previously helped to pass one of the country’s first AI safety bills, the RAISE Act, in New York in 2025. Bores partially ran on the issue this year, prompting a super PAC backed by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman to spend more than $8 million opposing him in the Democratic primary.
Though Bores lost his race, he helped to mobilize AI safety advocates across the country and ultimately received more than $15 million in support from super PACs aligned with his agenda.

Who Decides will build a network of organizers to work with national and local groups in 11 states including South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, Virginia, Wisconsin and others. They’ll stake out positions on the most advanced AI models as well as the technology’s impact on jobs, kids and safety, according to the statement.

items.title: KKR Private High-Grade Debt Deals Surge to $80 Billion This Year
body: KKR & Co. doubled the amount of private investment-grade financing it structured this year, reflecting growing demand from companies seeking flexible borrowing options.

The firm structured or syndicated more than $80 billion of deals in the first half of the year, according to a presentation seen by Bloomberg. As of Sept. 1, KKR doubled the amount it originated in all of 2025.
Chris Sheldon, KKR’s co-head of credit and markets, said insurance capital anchored many of those transactions.

“We’re seeing a big trend of financing assets off balance sheet,” he said, referring to companies’ desire to move certain assets into special vehicles that can be used to raise cash for other purposes while preserving their credit ratings.
The firm structured deals for borrowers including Kuwait Petroleum Corp., Enbridge Inc. and Samsung Electronics Co., according to the presentation.
Read More: Apollo Muscles In on Wall Street Turf With $300 Billion of Loans
KKR raised $15 billion so far this year for credit from third parties, up 29% from the same period in 2025, according to the presentation.

The estimated $7.6 trillion of capital spending on artificial-intelligence infrastructure over the next five years will drive demand for private credit as spending might outpace available capital, Sheldon said.

While KKR sees some pockets of froth in AI, there’s no evidence of a bubble, Sheldon said. The firm is relying on its expertise in infrastructure and real estate when underwriting AI deals to ensure it’s evaluating the risk appropriately.

Private credit has come under scrutiny amid concerns about the risk from AI to software companies, a key borrower for direct lenders in recent years. KKR’s non-traded credit fund experienced heightened withdrawals that later subsided. It also injected capital to support its publicly traded retail credit fund.

The firm was among alternative asset managers that struck a $500 billion agreement last month with Nvidia Corp. to finance AI chips, and it’s a big backer of data centers and related digital infrastructure.
KKR has $293 billion of credit assets under management, including $139 billion in private credit, according to the presentation.
