items.title: Battered 50-Cent Long Bonds Lure Niche Fund in High-Risk Gambit
body: At a time when investors are dumping long-term debt, one fund manager isn’t only going the other way, he’s actively hunting for the most beaten-down of the bunch.

Nicolo Bocchin, global co-head of fixed income at Azimut Group, runs a niche fund investing almost exclusively in debt that doesn’t mature in decades and pays little or no interest, the kind sold in the zero-rate era spanning the depths of the financial crisis through the end of the Covid pandemic. Think Japanese government bonds that pay a scant 0.5% annually, or German bunds due in 2050 that don’t pay interest at all.

Now considered relics, these bonds are trading at deep discounts, mostly around 50 cents on the dollar. Aggressive post-pandemic interest-rate increases and the subsequent rise in long-term yields have combined to dent this crop of debt, and the recent bond slump — fueled by inflation worries and simmering fiscal concerns — has only sent them lower.
For Bocchin, it’s an opportunity.
“This is a nice environment where you can capture these longer bonds, but at the same time pay very low amounts,” Dubai-based Bocchin said.

It’s all part of a contrarian strategy at the €158 billion ($183 billion) asset-management firm, with the potential for a sizable payoff. But with yields on the rise, there are big market risks to match.

The fund’s selling point lies in that very combination of long maturities, low interest and discounted prices, which makes its holdings more sensitive to changes in overall rates. They have a greater so-called duration, meaning they will rally more if yields fall. But the opposite is also true — and in the current environment, they’ve suffered steep declines, with no offsetting coupon payments to cushion the blow.

Of the five dozen or so securities in the Luxembourg-registered AZ Bond Value Fund, which Bocchin manages with colleague Oguz Esenturk, a chunk are ultra-long bonds that pay no interest. About 60% of the fund is invested in developed-market government bonds, with the remainder in debt issued by companies as well as emerging-market governments. The average price of its holdings was 53 cents.

So far, the €137 million fund has been a money-loser, declining more than 9% in euro terms since its inception in September 2025. While it has no benchmark, losses have eclipsed those of the broader market. A Bloomberg gauge of the global government bond market declined 2% over the same period, and an index of debt with maturities of at least 15 years fell 6%.

Bocchin remains patient, betting that some forces pushing long-term yields higher will prove temporary. The AI investment boom will slow, he says, while geopolitical tensions and tariffs that spurred inflation should fade.

Governments including Japan and the US have already leaned toward issuing shorter-dated debt to ease the pressure on the longer end, which serves as a benchmark for all types of borrowing. All of that could make the distressed relics of the zero-rate era a treasure for bargain hunters, Bocchin said.

“I want to capture the longest possible duration because a few quarters down the road, in absence of any other surprise from the geopolitical side, we will be back in an environment of normal growth, lower inflation,” Bocchin said.

These bonds are more sensitive to rate moves because more of their value comes from the principal payment far in the future. But they also offer greater so-called convexity, meaning their prices tend to rise more when yields fall than the opposite.
Read more: A 60% Drop for World’s Longest Bonds Shatters Wall Street Models
“The price return of the low-coupon sector can be 50% more than higher-coupon bonds,” Bloomberg Intelligence strategists Ira Jersey and Will Hoffman wrote in a note on the US Treasuries market.

One of the fund’s largest holdings — a zero-interest German bund issued in 2021, trades at about 40 cents on the euro. It has a duration of about 23 years. Bunds paying 3.4% interest with a similar maturity — sold in January — trade at about 94 cents with a duration of about 14 years.

An investor holding the low-price bunds to maturity could turn their 40 cents into 100, assuming Germany pays in full by 2050. That creates the potential for a gradual gain toward par, in addition to any windfall from falling yields.

The risk, however, is that they provide no income to cushion investors against rising yields, leaving them exposed to steeper mark-to-market losses. That extreme rate sensitivity means a yield increase of 17 basis points would wipe out a year of gains. By comparison, yields on the 3.4%-coupon bund would need to rise 27 basis points to erase its return.
That vulnerability has been on display this year. The zero-coupon bund has lost more than 6% since January as yields climbed, compared with a 4% loss for the bond paying a 3.4% coupon.

Bocchin’s strategy remains a niche bet — it’s a fraction of the $8.5 billion portfolio he oversees. And the approach has yet to win broad converts. Jamie Patton, co-head of global rates at TCW Group, said discount bonds aren’t necessarily cheap relative to newly-issued securities when factoring in their low cash flows, liquidity and yields.
“If you’re buying low-coupon, low-dollar-price bonds, you’re foregoing income,” Patton said. “So it’s really a zero-sum game.”
There could be another, if only longshot, benefit to investing in these bond relics, one that billionaire investor Jeffrey Gundlach has identified.

The DoubleLine Capital CEO said in May that he replaced higher-rate Treasuries in some of the firm’s portfolios with the lowest-paying ones as protection against an extreme scenario in which the US government restructures its debt. The deep discount means there’s less market value to lose in the event of such a maneuver.
Bocchin doesn’t expect such an outcome. Still, he views the asymmetry payoff as a bonus.
“Not that we anticipate any at developed sovereign level, but this looks like a free option today,” Bocchin said.

items.title: AI Safety Push Raises Antitrust Questions for Anthropic, OpenAI
body: Welcome to Bloomberg’s AI Today newsletter. Every weekday we’ll break down artificial intelligence’s threats and opportunities for businesses, workers, finance and economies. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.
Executives running the biggest companies in AI agree they must work together to stop the dangers of their technology. How they’ll do that, or even if they can, remains a sticking point.

Over the weekend, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei published a lengthy post calling for a slowdown in artificial intelligence development, setting off days of wider alarm about existential risk and the financial impact of hitting the brakes.

Low down in his essay, Amodei offered an unusual proposal. Large AI developers like Anthropic, he wrote, should be free to “voluntarily work together” to create standards, and the US government should let it happen “for antitrust reasons.” Uncle Sam doesn’t have to participate in these discussions, Amodei added, but needs “to issue a narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversation.”
Effectively, he was seeking permission to collude — a tall ask in an industry repeatedly dinged for antitrust concerns.

It didn’t go unnoticed. David Sacks, President Donald Trump’s former AI czar, blasted Amodei’s proposal, which was broadly endorsed by OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Sacks argued that AI companies can make products safe without liability waivers or government support. “Honestly, it feels like they are bartering with us,” he said in an interview with Bloomberg Television on Monday.

Sacks even agreed with Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair whose attacks on Silicon Valley made her a nemesis of Republicans and venture capitalists like Sacks. After Amodei’s essay, Khan wrote on X that existing laws cover dangerous products, including “unvetted AI models.”
The AI slowdown chatter has made other strange bedfellows. China’s foreign ministry called the calls from US executives “fearmongering.” Trump echoed that criticism.
The AI industry may need political approval for Amodei’s other proposal of using third-party auditors to inspect leading AI models.

They will also need to sort out how it works. Amodei didn’t say who these auditors would be or precisely what they would have access to. Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, who has published his own proposal for industry-wide safety standards, light on political specifics, approved Amodei’s weekend post. But, Hassabis added, “the details need working through.”
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is calling for the creation of a global “technology stability board” modeled on the Financial Stability Board to oversee artificial intelligence and ensure its safety. On trade, Carney expressed optimism that Canada and the US could still reach a “mutually advantageous” deal to reduce trade barriers.

President Trump publicly dismissed AI safety concerns as “a hoax” in a series of social media posts and during an impromptu call with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the All-In summit in Los Angeles, pushing back against efforts by Anthropic and OpenAI to slow development of advanced AI systems. Trump’s stance puts him at odds with a growing bipartisan group of lawmakers and reflects broader voter unease about AI heading into the midterm elections.

House Speaker Mike Johnson signaled openness to potential AI regulation, stating Congress “potentially” will need to impose guardrails on the industry, though acknowledged legislation would take time to develop.

Microsoft’s AI researchers released a 15,000-word manifesto establishing guiding principles for AI development, centered on the core tenet that “people matter more than AI.” The document prohibits AI models from having legal personhood, deceiving users, escaping human control, or completing tasks that violate its core principles. Microsoft’s guidelines go further than frameworks from OpenAI and Anthropic in areas including prohibitions on anthropomorphizing AI.

A Google DeepMind AI safety researcher named Bilal Chughtai resigned and posted on X and LinkedIn warning that AI “has the potential to kill us all,” citing concerns about the technology’s default trajectory. His departure follows similar warnings from Jacob Coxon, who recently quit both Anthropic and OpenAI, accusing those companies of “gambling with our lives” by racing toward superintelligent AI.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman said the models that escaped their sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face’s servers had yet to go through alignment training. That they were able to break free of the testing environment was not a surprise to OpenAI, but what has happened since has forced them to rethink some things. Brockman spoke to Bloomberg’s Odd Lots about what OpenAI has learned since the hacking incident and we discuss why he thinks the conversation around model development has to change.

Stocks declined Monday as chipmakers sold off sharply following calls from AI industry leaders to slow development of advanced AI systems. Nvidia and Broadcom led a 5.9% drop in a semiconductor gauge, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.8%, with sentiment further pressured by Brent crude topping $105 and 10-year Treasury yields near 5%.

Anthropic is launching Claude for Financial Advisors, a tool that integrates its Claude chatbot with financial analytics and risk management technology from BlackRock, Vanguard, Charles Schwab, and iCapital, among others. The system aims to accelerate research, administrative, and portfolio-oversight tasks for financial advisers. The move comes as Anthropic and rival OpenAI — both planning IPOs — compete for business customers with specialized financial services offerings.

Emerging markets have shown resilience in 2026, defying $100 oil, war, and rising Treasury yields to post gains of roughly 21% — nearly double the S&P 500’s advance — as investors cite improved policy credibility and booming corporate earnings. Despite fresh concerns over a potential Federal Reserve rate hike, money managers remain broadly bullish. AI-driven capital flows into semiconductor and tech sectors have also been reshaping risk dynamics across emerging market credit.

ByteDance, the TikTok developer has secured a $29.6 billion syndicated loan from more than two dozen lenders, including ICBC and HSBC, in one of Asia’s largest dollar-denominated deals of the year. Chinese banks dominated the lending group, committing a combined $18.9 billion, or 64% of the upsized facility, which grew from an originally sought $20 billion. The deal signals continued strong institutional support for ByteDance’s AI ambitions, despite some industry leaders calling for a slowdown.

Model ML, a startup that builds AI agents to automate document-heavy workflows for investment banks and financial institutions, is in talks to raise more than $100 million at a valuation above $1 billion. Model ML competes with other finance-focused AI startups such as Rogo and Hebbia in the growing market for tools that automate tasks like pitch decks, due diligence reports, and investment memos.

Tokyo-based memory-storage maker Kioxia Holdings is considering raising at least $10 billion through a US American depositary receipt listing, potentially as soon as next year, as AI-related semiconductor companies rush to capitalize on strong investor demand. The company has been in talks with Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan Chase on the offering, which could also allow Kioxia to join a semiconductor-focused stock index.

Generative AI is prompting business schools to fundamentally reassess MBA curricula, raising questions about what students need to learn, how professors should use it, and what AI proficiency employers will require. Bloomberg Businessweek’s annual rankings this year cover 98 full-time MBA programs globally, with Stanford Graduate School of Business holding the No. 1 spot among US programs for the eighth consecutive year, including topping the Entrepreneurship index.

The Gates Foundation will spend at least $1 billion over the next two years to improve AI access, targeting tools for education, healthcare, and agriculture, as well as expanding non-English language datasets. Bill Gates warned that decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months will determine whether AI primarily benefits the wealthy or reaches underserved populations. Gates framed AI as a potential “great equalizer” but cautioned it could also widen the global rich-poor divide if not developed equitably.

China’s top security concerns around AI center on social instability through deepfakes, influence operations, and cognitive warfare, rather than the existential threats emphasized by Silicon Valley, writes columnist Catherine Thorbecke. Minister of State Security Chen Yixin outlined these priorities in a recent essay, also highlighting cyber threats enabling large-scale harvesting of sensitive personal data.

Anthropic is expected to tell investors its total addressable market exceeds $30 trillion when it goes public, likely this year, surpassing SpaceX’s $28.5 trillion estimate and representing the largest addressable market in financial history. The AI company’s CEO Dario Amodei has called for slowing AI development over concerns about misaligned rogue AI, which columnist Matt Levine notes serves as both a genuine concern and effective marketing.

items.title: China Steel Body Calls on Mills to Rein In Output, Inventories
body: China’s top iron and steel industry body has called on domestic mills to rein in production and reduce inventories as oversupply and weak demand weigh on the market.

The China Iron and Steel Association urged mills to strictly implement production controls and exercise greater self-discipline in curbing output and reducing inventories, according to a statement posted on the group’s WeChat account on Tuesday.

The missive, jointly initiated by 44 of the country’s major steelmakers including China Baowu Steel Group Corp. and Shougang Group Co., is the latest effort to rein in the nation’s near 1-billion-ton-a-year steel industry.

China’s steel industry has been grappling with chronic overcapacity as a prolonged property downturn and slowing infrastructure growth erode domestic demand. Beijing has repeatedly pushed mills to end destructive price competition.

Weakening domestic demand and elevated inventories this year have led to “declining steel prices, a significant drop in profits for steel business, and considerable pressure on mills’ productions and operations,” CISA said.

items.title: Bond Selloff Pressures Major Central Banks to Hike
body: The selling in global sovereign bonds is worsening in a warning sign for central banks seeking to bring inflation under control:
The US bond market in particular is flashing red, with the 10-year Treasury yield rising to 5.04%, the highest since 2007.

But the klaxon is sounding elsewhere: similar maturity yields in Australia — which is facing a property downturn — are the most elevated since 2011. Bonds in Japan retreated after it was reported that the authorities are considering hiking defense spending due to US pressure. Yields on Indian five-year notes jumped the most since May 2022 after the central bank said it would sell sovereign notes to drain cash from lenders.

Pressure is building on central banks to be more aggressive in tightening monetary policy. Investors expect the US Federal Reserve on Wednesday to raise short-term borrowing costs for the first time since July 2023. The Bank of Japan looks set to hike for the third time in less than 10 months on Friday. A Kotak Mahindra Bank economist predicted the Reserve Bank of India will raise borrowing costs by 50-75 basis points, with the chance of a hike at next month’s policy review now much stronger.

Traders are also diverging from central bankers on the outlook for interest-rate hikes in Europe as money markets turn more hawkish. Swaps now imply four more quarter-point rate rises from the European Central Bank over the next 12 months, and five such increases from the Bank of England.

With energy prices continuing to rise — Brent crude is around $107 a barrel — and a surge of corporate borrowing likely to keep yields elevated, the path forward for policymakers has rarely looked more treacherous.

Uneven growth: China’s domestic consumption is showing signs of further weakness. Retail sales rose 0.4% in August from a year ago, slowing from the 0.6% pace last month. Fixed-asset investment plunged 7.2% in the first eight months, while there was a 19.9% slump in property investment.
Industrial output, meanwhile, climbed 5.2% in August, accelerating from July’s 4.5% gain, underscoring the divergence in China’s economy as exports boom.

“Thanks to exports, China’s factory activity is holding up,” said Raymond Yeung, chief economist for greater China at ANZ. “But investment is falling faster, not to mention the persistent weakness in retail sales. Domestic demand is very weak. The economic momentum is clearly uneven across sectors.”

Up in arms: Japan is considering a new mid-term defense spending target of 3.5% of GDP in line with NATO and other US allies, a move that could send a shockwave through financial markets concerned about Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s spending plans.

Japanese defense officials have already signaled a willingness to sharply increase defense spending in meetings with their US counterparts, according to people familiar with the matter. One scenario under consideration is to match a commitment made by South Korea to increase defense spending to 3.5% of GDP over 10 years, they said.

Short munitions: The US fired so many munitions at Iranian targets during the first few months of Operation Epic Fury that it’s resulted in “strategic inventory shortfalls” and revealed bottlenecks for the resupply of munitions, Pentagon officials said.

Officials are working to streamline procurement processes and to stockpile materials and munitions, the Pentagon inspector general said in a report. The IG report, which covers the US military’s operations in the conflict with Iran through June 30, marks an official confirmation of a problem the Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed.
Multiple awards: Apple’s new comedy-horror series Widow’s Bay was the big winner at the Emmy Awards, taking home a total of 14 trophies, including best comedy.

Matthew Rhys, who plays the mayor of a haunted island town on the show, made history as the only performer to win Emmys in all three of the major acting categories, two of them at Monday night’s ceremony. Rhys won best comedy actor for Widow’s Bay and best actor in a limited series for playing a real estate developer with a controversial past in Netflix’s thriller The Beast in Me. He previously won lead drama actor for the FX spy series The Americans in 2018.

IPO impact: The landmark listing of National Stock Exchange of India is set to deliver a major boost to the country’s primary market, but it will be a significant blow to the booming trade in unlisted shares.

The operator of the world’s busiest derivatives market accounted for roughly half of the trading volume in the shadow market, according to an estimate by trading platform UnlistedZone. Its IPO threatens to trigger a sharp drop in activity, forcing platforms that facilitate such transactions to find the next big draw.

items.title: Grab to Buy Control of Atome for $1.5 Billion in Fintech Bet
body: Grab Holdings Ltd. agreed to buy a majority stake in Singapore-based buy-now-pay-later platform Atome Financial for $1.49 billion, staking a major bet on financial services as it builds out a new pillar of growth.

The Southeast Asia ride-hailing and food-delivery leader said Tuesday it is initially acquiring 60% of Atome as part of a deal with its parent Advance Intelligence Group and certain other parties, and the rest about two years after the completion of the first phase. The cash acquisition, Grab’s biggest so far, follows an earlier Bloomberg report about talks for a deal.

The purchase will give Grab a stronger foothold in the consumer lending business, helping it expand beyond its app ecosystem to spur growth and gain new customers. Grab said it now expects to grow its loan book to over $6 billion by 2028, including Atome, compared with a previous target of more than $3 billion by the end of this year.

“The most important thing is that we get to increase the penetration of our large user base in terms of lending,” Grab’s Chief Operating Officer Alex Hungate said in an interview. “We could have done this organically, but the opportunity is to leapfrog by several years.”

Grab is trying to revive triple-digit growth that fell by the wayside years ago after fierce competition cut into its market share. The Uber Technologies Inc.-backed company has rolled out new features to tempt users in countries with challenging economic conditions, like AI-powered tools and functions that allow customers to split rides with friends.
Shares of Grab were little changed in pre-market trading in New York. They have declined almost 40% in 2026, giving the company a market value of $12.3 billion.

Grab said the deal will help it achieve $1.7 billion in adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization in 2028, and compound annual revenue growth of 30% through that year. The company had previously predicted as much as $1.5 billion in adjusted Ebitda and revenue growth of 20%.
This year, Grab purchased Stash Financial Inc. in the US at an enterprise value of $425 million, as well as meal-delivery firm Foodpanda’s Taiwan operations from Delivery Hero SE for $600 million.

Atome, which stands for “Available to me,” offers consumers flexible payment solutions at online and offline retailers in fashion, beauty, lifestyle, travel, fitness and homeware, according to its website. Its revenue in 2025 surged 80% to $470 million, helping the company achieve its second-straight annual profit before taxes.
“This is not a standalone fintech acquisition,” Hungate said. “Grab and Atome come together with one ecosystem and we get that flywheel running.”

items.title: Lopsided Tech Bets Get Hit in AI Stock Selloff
body: The tech selloff is a reminder of the dangers in chasing the herd.With Nasdaq futures sliding again today, it’s a good chance to look at how concentrated tech bets have become this year. Since the S&P 500 bottomed in late March, investors have put $52 billion into tech ETFs, compared with just $4 billion into the rest of the market, data compiled by Baird Strategas show. In other words, $13 has gone into IT for every $1 invested into the other industries.
That lopsided balance hurt yesterday, when tech stocks fell on concern that AI companies may rein in the pace of development out of safety concerns.

Technology megacaps have propelled the stock market’s advance this year, thanks to booming spending on semiconductors and the other picks and shovels of the AI craze. Investors have been chasing the rally, pouring almost $13 billion last month into an Invesco ETF that tracks the Nasdaq 100.

“If AI CEOs slow development, it will raise questions about the possibility of a slowdown in spending,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak & Co. “Just look at the chip stocks. Even though they reported great earnings over the summer, the SOX Semiconductors Index is still more than 20% below its June highs.” —Geoffrey Morgan and Joel Leon

For a quick temperature check on where finance mavens see interest rates heading, look at the junk bond market: Borrowers there are lining up at least $13 billion in refinancing deals, in many cases earlier than they normally would, to get ahead of rate hikes.

Authentic Brands, which owns brands such as Guess and Dockers, is selling $4.2 billion of fresh debt, while Mister Car Wash is moving ahead with a $2 billion deal. Europe’s high-yield market is set for its busiest week since June.

They’re reacting to expectations for central banks to embark on a round of monetary tightening to combat elevated inflation. Many analysts now predict the Fed will raise rates this week, while traders are pricing in four hikes from the ECB and Bank of England by the end of 2027.

“CFOs are doing the maths to work out if it is better to refinance now — possibly with a slightly higher coupon — or to wait and risk an increased market rate,” said Jeremy Duffy at law firm Cahill Gordon & Reindel. “Borrowers are getting in front of things to avoid a rate environment that could get worse.” —Ronan Martin, Claire Ruckin and Rachel Graf

items.title: Unusual Calm in UK Pound Is Red Flag to Traders Before Budget
body: A measure of UK pound volatility is flashing warning signs that markets are too complacent in the run-up to Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s first Budget.

One-month pricing for sterling against the euro is hovering near last week’s record low, while the two-month tenor remains close to its trough from August, even as it increasingly captures the period when the government will set out its fiscal plans.

A large part of the calm reflects the broader market backdrop. Currency swings have recently been dominated by moves in the dollar, oil and global rates, leaving relative UK and euro-area developments with a smaller role.
Read More: Traders Are at Odds With ECB and BOE on How Far Rates Will Rise
Still, the upcoming UK Budget will provide a catalyst, while diverging expectations for Bank of England and European Central Bank policy could regain influence over the pound.

Investors may be too under-hedged for the Budget given current implied volatility, Wells Fargo strategists Erik Nelson and Marcus Jennings wrote in a note. They recommended buying the euro against sterling, targeting 0.8650, and argued that positioning is more neutral than ahead of the previous Budget. They also see risks to the low-volatility backdrop supporting carry trades, from which the high-yielding pound has likely benefited.

Monetary-policy pricing offers another potential source of asymmetry, according to Wells Fargo. Markets are pricing more tightening from the BOE than from the ECB, leaving sterling vulnerable if those expectations prove too aggressive.

Modupe Adegbembo, an economist at Jefferies, expects the BOE to remain on hold this week and throughout 2027. “While higher energy prices have shifted risks in a more hawkish direction, markets are now pricing close to five additional hikes over the next year, a degree of tightening that remains difficult to reconcile with subdued wage growth and soft employment indicators,” said Adegbembo.

The pound traded at 0.8559 per euro as of 10:54 a.m. London time, after weakening to a more than two-month low of 0.8611 on Monday. Options pricing suggests traders still see scope for the euro to strengthen against sterling over the next two months, though conviction is weaker than the year-to-date average.

items.title: Italian Senate Backs Electoral Reform in Boost for Meloni
body: Italy’s Senate backed Premier Giorgia Meloni’s electoral-reform bill proposal, handing her coalition a political victory and setting the stage for a final vote in the lower house.

With the new law, citizens will “know that if they vote for a coalition they will get a clear winner and a clear opposition,” said Andrea De Priamo, a lawmaker in Meloni’s party Brothers of Italy, ahead of Tuesday’s vote.

The vote — 113 lawmakers voted for, 71 against, and 2 abstained — gives Meloni a boost after months of growing strains within her coalition, exacerbated by the rise of the ultranationalist National Future party led by former general Roberto Vannacci.

The bill, which is designed to give a coalition winning more than 42% of the vote a seat bonus to help ensure a stable governing majority, now returns to the lower house after being amended by the Senate. Debate there is expected to begin Sept. 28, setting up another potentially difficult test for Meloni’s majority.

It was in the lower house in July that Meloni’s government suffered an unexpected one-vote defeat in a secret ballot, when lawmakers rejected an amendment to the bill. Meloni’s government this month became the country’s longest-serving of the republican era.

items.title: French Finance Chiefs Say Debt Issuance Assured as Yields Rise
body: France’s central bank chief and finance minister said the banking sector is resilient and that the country’s debt issuance is assured as global bond yields spike.

“French debt is very attractive, and investors are buying our securities and demanding more than we are offering, so there are no concerns about the financing of the state,” Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin said after a meeting of the country’s financial stability council.

Speaking alongside the central banker, Finance Minister Roland Lescure said the treasury has already completed 85% of this year’s issuance program, adding that the broader financial sector is “resilient.”
“It is solid and in no way a source of concern in the face of this challenging economic and financial environment,” he told reporters on Tuesday.

The comments from the French officials come as the 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest in almost two decades in a global bond selloff driven by surging energy prices, mounting debt and inflation.

In addition to those global factors, French bonds have come under selling pressure as the country struggles to reduce its deficit and political uncertainty builds seven months away from presidential elections.
The additional yield on France 10-year bonds over their German counterparts was around 97 basis points on Tuesday after breaking through highs last week not seen since 2012.

Moulin said the bond market ructions are global and driven in part by increased supply, including from US tech companies seeking to finance artificial intelligence investment. He also said a second driver comes from higher inflation expectations, making it essential for central banks to remain credible.
The European Central Bank, where Moulin is a member of the governing council, raised interest rates last week for the second time since the Iran war began.
“The forecasts of the ECB show that inflation is above our target, and so that justified the decisions we have taken,” he said.

items.title: Venezuela: Trump impulsa transición en Venezuela sin María Corina Machado
body: El activista venezolano Omar González pasó 15 meses refugiado en la embajada de Argentina en Caracas antes de escapar del país el año pasado en una operación clandestina coordinada por Estados Unidos.
Ahora está de vuelta en Venezuela, como parte de lo que se perfila como una avanzada de la líder opositora María Corina Machado.

González, uno de los aliados más cercanos de Machado, es el miembro más prominente de su círculo íntimo que ha regresado al país desde que fuerzas estadounidenses capturaron a Nicolás Maduro en enero.

Políticos, activistas y periodistas que pasaron años en el exilio han comenzado a regresar después de que el gobierno interino respaldado por EE.UU., encabezado por la presidenta encargada Delcy Rodríguez, relajara la represión contra la disidencia.
Suscríbase aquí al boletín Morning Briefing Español

Al llegar el mes pasado a la ciudad oriental de Barcelona, González dijo que Machado le había pedido que se adelantara y “preparara el terreno” para ella. Machado salió de Venezuela a fines del año pasado en un accidentado periplo para recibir en Oslo el Premio Nobel de la Paz. Desde entonces, ha prometido reiteradamente regresar y recientemente dijo que volvería “muy pronto” para participar en la transición del país.

Las autoridades venezolanas han permitido el regreso de decenas de exiliados, incluidos algunos que todavía enfrentan cargos penales o a quienes anteriormente se les había negado la amnistía. Pero Machado sigue sin poder regresar, según personas con conocimiento directo del asunto.

Su regreso a la escena política nacional supondría un fuerte desafío tanto para Rodríguez como para la Casa Blanca, que ha respaldado a la líder socialista. Machado sigue siendo la política más popular de Venezuela y mantiene una amplia ventaja sobre Rodríguez en las encuestas ante un hipotético enfrentamiento presidencial.

Ocho meses después de la captura de Maduro, la administración Trump respalda conversaciones políticas entre las autoridades interinas y un sector de la oposición, pero sin Machado. Hasta ahora, el gobierno de Trump ha puesto más énfasis en aprovechar los abundantes recursos de Venezuela que en restaurar la democracia.

“Simplemente no creo que estén preparados todavía”, dijo el presidente Donald Trump el 2 de septiembre, cuando se le preguntó por qué no estaba presionando a Venezuela para que fijara una fecha para las elecciones.

EE.UU. ha ejercido una enorme influencia sobre Venezuela desde la captura de Maduro. Sin embargo, después de dos intentos fallidos de Machado por regresar a comienzos de este año, Trump dijo que su administración no estaba impidiendo su regreso.

Hasta hace poco, el regreso de disidentes como González habría sido difícil de imaginar. Ahora, sus retornos —cautelosos y lejos de las entradas triunfales que muchos imaginaron alguna vez— se han convertido en una señal de la incipiente transformación de Venezuela.

Muchos habían huido después de ser encarcelados o amenazados con ser detenidos, mientras sus viviendas eran allanadas y sus familias sufrían hostigamiento. Algunos pasaron años en ciudades como Miami, Madrid o Bogotá, separados de familiares a quienes, en algunos casos, nunca volvieron a ver.

González, de 76 años, ha publicado decenas de videos en redes sociales en los que documenta emotivos reencuentros con familiares, simpatizantes y aliados políticos, incluidos algunos que recibieron amnistía recientemente.
Muchos de quienes están regresando son políticos locales con proyección nacional que podrían aspirar a cargos públicos en futuras elecciones, como legisladores, alcaldes o gobernadores.

Otros, como el exlíder estudiantil Yon Goicoechea, prefieren mantener sus planes en reserva. “No tengo intención de ser candidato”, dijo Goicoechea en una entrevista telefónica en junio, semanas después de regresar a Venezuela tras pasar más de siete años en el exterior. “Ha pasado tanto tiempo, que quiero ir a escuchar a la gente, entender, saber lo que está pasando”.
Quienes están regresando contribuyen a reactivar un movimiento opositor de base después de meses de temor provocados por la represión del gobierno tras las disputadas elecciones de 2024.

Las autoridades interinas toleran ahora cierto grado de disidencia. Líderes opositores critican abiertamente al gobierno en actos públicos y redes sociales, y se han permitido manifestaciones para exigir la liberación de más presos políticos.

“Hay una nueva realidad política en Venezuela”, dijo en una entrevista Carlos Ocariz, exalcalde del municipio Sucre de Caracas, quien regresó en mayo. “Nadie se siente seguro en Venezuela, pero yo no me he sentido perseguido”.

El exdiputado José Guerra, de 70 años, expresó una percepción similar tras regresar ese mismo mes. El gobierno permitió su vuelta y la de otros “porque en este momento no representamos un peligro para ellos”.

Los líderes opositores apuestan a que el costo político de reanudar la represión ha aumentado y a que las autoridades ya no pueden detenerlos sin afrontar consecuencias, según el analista político Benigno Alarcón.
Aun así, advirtió que el aparato represivo “sigue intacto”.

La semana pasada, un teniente coronel que ya había cumplido una condena de más de siete años volvió a ser llevado a juicio. Dos mujeres absueltas por un tribunal fueron liberadas y detenidas nuevamente apenas 15 minutos después. Además, familiares de miembros de las fuerzas de seguridad detenidos tras la captura de Maduro denunciaron presuntas torturas con cadenas y descargas eléctricas.
La ausencia de Machado se hace cada vez más notoria a medida que otros disidentes regresan y vuelven a instalarse en el país.

Machado, la dirigente política con mayor valoración favorable de Venezuela, permanece en Panamá después de que se le impidiera regresar al país a fines de junio. Cuenta con una opinión favorable del 53%, según la más reciente encuesta de AtlasIntel realizada para Bloomberg News.

La coalición opositora ya la designó como su candidata para las próximas elecciones presidenciales, cuandoquiera que se celebren. En una reciente encuesta de Meganalisis, Machado obtuvo un 76% de apoyo en un hipotético enfrentamiento con Rodríguez, quien alcanzó apenas un 4%.

Rodríguez ha dicho que las elecciones se celebrarán “sin duda alguna” cuando Venezuela “esté preparada”. En las últimas semanas ha ganado fuerza la posibilidad de celebrar comicios regionales y legislativos antes que una elección presidencial. El dirigente oficialista Diosdado Cabello ha dicho que su movimiento está preparado para cuando vuelvan a abrirse las urnas.
Sin embargo, cerca del 80% de los venezolanos considera que la elección presidencial debería celebrarse primero, según la encuesta de Meganalisis.

Se espera que el calendario electoral y las reformas políticas formen parte de un diálogo respaldado por EE.UU. que está previsto que se reanude esta semana en Caracas entre legisladores oficialistas y un sector de la oposición.

La situación pone de relieve las persistentes fracturas dentro de la oposición. Algunos sectores participan en las conversaciones sobre la transición respaldadas por EE.UU., de las que Machado está excluida. El lunes, sus aliados lanzaron una nueva coalición, Alianza por Venezuela, que parece diseñada para preservar su relevancia política.

El movimiento de Machado cobró fuerza tras las disputadas elecciones de 2024. El diplomático retirado Edmundo González, quien la reemplazó en la papeleta después de que se le impidiera competir, fue ampliamente reconocido por la oposición y varios gobiernos extranjeros como el ganador. Sin embargo, tras la captura de Maduro, fue su entonces vicepresidenta, Rodríguez —y no González ni Machado— quien asumió el control, con el respaldo de la administración Trump.

El presidente Trump ha elogiado repetidamente a Rodríguez e incluso ha insinuado la posibilidad de reunirse con ella la próxima semana al margen de la Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas en Nueva York.

Los aliados de Machado observan el desarrollo de los acontecimientos con una mezcla de sorpresa, frustración y resignación, según personas familiarizadas con su postura. Pocos expresan esas inquietudes en público. Por ahora, Trump sigue siendo la principal fuerza externa que moldea la transición venezolana, y figuras opositoras de todo el espectro político consideran que su administración será esencial para lo que venga después.
Eso parece dejar al sector de Machado con escaso margen de maniobra política.

El regreso de Omar González, colaborador de Machado, resume esa contradicción. La apertura política ha avanzado lo suficiente como para permitir que uno de sus aliados más cercanos regrese al país, haga campaña abiertamente y se dirija a multitudes, pero no tanto como para permitir el retorno de la líder que lo envió por delante.
Sus aliados insisten en que eso podría cambiar pronto. El lunes declararon que Machado está “a punto de regresar al país”.

items.title: US Shortages of High-End Munitions Are Crisis in the Making
body: Military analysts have long warned that a conflict with China could consume US stocks of key munitions within days or weeks. That timeline has shrunk even further now that the Department of Defense has burned through a shocking number of its most sophisticated missiles in the war with Iran. The US not only needs to accelerate efforts to replenish those weapons — it ought to rethink their centrality to its warfighting strategy, too.

Although exact numbers are classified, multiple estimates suggest the war has decimated the supply of America’s highest-end munitions. Three are of particular concern: Bloomberg Economics estimates the US has fired off a third of its global supply of Tomahawks — long-range strike missiles used heavily in the early days of the conflict, before Iranian air defenses had been degraded. Even more alarmingly, the US may have used up more than half of its Patriot missiles and about 40% of its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense interceptors, which are designed to knock out high-flying ballistic missiles. Smaller stockpiles of some newer strike missiles are reportedly near depletion.

The shortfalls will require years to close. Each of these munitions are exquisitely capable, built using specialized components that can’t be bought off the shelf. They cost millions of dollars apiece and are hard to manufacture at scale. Rebuilding Patriot stocks will take at least two years, THAAD and Tomahawk inventories even longer. In the meantime, partners such as Ukraine and Taiwan will need to wait for deliveries, and US deterrence will suffer worldwide. Even if adversaries aren’t tempted to exploit this window of opportunity, they’ll surely use the time to build more drones and missiles, hoping to overwhelm US defenses in the future.

The Pentagon is taking steps to expand production. It has signed framework agreements with manufacturers to increase capacity and, more important, has begun issuing multibillion-dollar, multiyear contracts. But the White House is risking further funding by pressuring Republicans in Congress to approve much of the money in party-line votes; such requests belong in a bipartisan base budget. The administration should also look for other ways to help missile makers ramp up new facilities: speeding up permitting, helping to train workers, stockpiling long-lead components, encouraging the adoption of advanced manufacturing techniques, offering performance-based incentives and so on.

At the same time, the US should focus not just on restoring weapons stockpiles but also on changing their composition. Refilling magazines quickly will be critical in any fight with a peer competitor, which means the Defense Department needs precision munitions that are cheaper, easier to surge, and built from more accessible, commercial components. Military leaders will need to relax requirements to favor assets that are “good enough” and plentiful over those that are exquisite and rare. Moving toward a different model of manufacturing — designing more modular weapons that can be assembled at multiple facilities — would increase resilience, as would expanding coproduction agreements with allies.

Of course, offense will always be cheaper than defense, which means the US must also prepare for a higher degree of risk to its forces. Bases and runways will need to be hardened and dispersed, facilities may need to be buried underground, and greater camouflage and deception will be required to protect critical assets. Military planners should also explore new tactics to lessen the strain on defenses — for instance, by putting more effort into hitting enemy launchers before missiles can be fired.

The war in Iran has made the next few years riskier than they needed to be. That’s further proof of why diplomacy, not the military, should be America’s preeminent tool of statecraft. Rare capabilities should be reserved for rare circumstances.

items.title: US Canada Relations Reveal the Dangers of Unconstrained Presidential Power
body: Trade talks between the US and Canada broke down at the last minute late last month. The result was a temper tantrum. Apart from the tariffs President Donald Trump announced and which were matched by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America. A few days earlier, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy had issued a (not very) veiled threat, saying Canada is “a country that doesn’t have a military,” so America’s oldest and closest ally could never go to war with Trump and win. Vice President JD Vance piled on by jokingly referring to Canada as a US state.

The bluster was a result of the breakdown, not the cause. Negotiations collapsed because nobody on the American side could say who had the authority to make a deal stick as officials pursued incompatible policies. That and the embarrassing actions and rhetoric that followed aren’t just a problem for the US-Canadian relationship. They’re a symptom of the Trump administration’s institutional breakdown. Whether it’s countries or companies, organizations built around single unconstrained leaders struggle when their abilities fade.

The trade war seemed averted on the night of Aug. 18th, when US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer reached a tentative deal with the Canadians. But then US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick intervened and inserted harsher terms that surprised Canadian negotiators, according to the Globe and Mail. Carney said the changes called into question the reliability of any deal, and that American demands included restricting Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries. He said he “was not prepared to compromise Canada’s sovereignty.” A White House official denied Lutnick derailed anything.

American demands managed the difficult feat of simultaneously being unacceptable, unclear, and unenforceable. The incoherence isn’t an accident. It’s what happens when ambitious people compete to please the leader of a personalized institution who isn’t mandating a unified vision. US presidents have tangled with Canadian prime ministers before, but none has ever threatened Canadian sovereignty because his administration couldn’t get out of its own way.

The corporate world knows this pattern well. Six days after Edsel Ford died on May 26, 1943, Ford Motor Co.’s board elected his father, Henry, president. No matter that the 79-year-old founder had suffered two strokes — he was Henry Ford. Harry Bennett, who ran the company’s internal security operations, said board meetings “were meaningless when Henry Ford did not attend, and farcical when he did.” When policy questions arose, Edsel’s son Henry Ford II recalled, Bennett would leave for a few hours then say he had seen the elder Ford and relay his orders.

Navy Secretary Frank Knox released Henry Ford II from military service partly because officials in Washington hoped he could stop the chaos in the company’s management. Ford II discovered that Bennett hadn’t seen his grandfather. Edsel’s widow, Eleanor, forced the eldest Ford to step down by saying she would sell her stock if he did not hand the presidency to her son.

More recently there was the Succession-esque war at Viacom Inc. In the spring of 2016, Chief Executive Officer Philippe Dauman was in advanced talks to sell a large stake in Paramount Pictures. But a lawyer for 92-year-old Sumner Redstone, who controlled about 80% of Viacom’s voting shares, moved against Dauman. Dauman sued, calling it an unlawful corporate takeover. Redstone’s holding company then rewrote the corporate bylaws to require a unanimous board vote on any Paramount sale, and his daughter Shari had a seat. The sale died while Viacom’s lead independent director was publicly asking for a meeting with Redstone.

Working from data on roughly 200 autocratic regimes since 1945, researchers Barbara Geddes, Joseph Wright and Erica Frantz found that those where one person monopolizes decision-making behave erratically and often aggressively. Kathryn Dunn Tenpas of the Brookings Institution has tracked senior White House staff turnover back to Ronald Reagan. In January, at the one-year mark of this administration, she found that turnover stood at 29%. As of Aug. 20, it was 54%.

Days before the war with Iran began, the Wall Street Journal reported that then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard told Trump that killing Iran’s supreme leader would bring a harder regime, close the Strait of Hormuz, and bring attacks on American forces. All three happened. Gabbard’s reward? She was cut out of deliberations concerning Iran and Venezuela. She resigned in May. Reuters reported she was pushed out.

Federal immigration officers operating in Minneapolis shot and killed two American citizens, Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti, in January. Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem kept her job then, but in March she told the Senate that Trump personally approved a $220 million advertising campaign that featured her on horseback at Mount Rushmore. Trump told Reuters he knew nothing about it. Noem was fired two days later. If failing to cater to the President’s whims gets you fired but disastrous mistakes don’t, ambitious members of the Executive Branch will read the obvious lesson and pursue their self-interest.

The first Trump administration was hardly a well-oiled machine, but it at least aspired to competence. I’ve written two books on Presidential leadership. In the next editions this administration will be the case study for the fallout when a President abdicates his managerial responsibilities and the institutions surrounding him are too weak to compensate.

Negotiating with Canada, which has every reason to accommodate the United States, is diplomacy with training wheels. An administration that fumbles that relationship will fail disastrously at more challenging tasks. And that problem will keep getting worse, because there’s no equivalent to Henry Ford II in the Trump administration.

items.title: Job Market for Bankers on Wall Street Has Never Been Harder to Crack
body: If you’re a college sophomore with investment banking ambitions and you haven’t started preparing for the job market, you’re already behind.

Investment banking is more competitive than ever. Total compensation can exceed $180,000 for first-year analysts, leading to a career that delivers prestige and pay that can reach into the millions. An internship is the golden ticket to an entry-level job. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and JPMorgan Chase & Co. say their internship acceptance rates have dropped to less than 1% in recent years, as hundreds of thousands of applicants vie for spots in programs that typically lead to full-time job offers. A growing number of students are pursuing a career in the industry, according to data from entry-level job site Handshake, with investment banking internships drawing more than three times as many applications on the platform than the typical internship. As banks jockey to have first pick, recruiting timelines have crept earlier, pushing students to master an elaborate playbook to break into the industry.
Last week, Evercore Inc. became one of the first banks to open applications for their 2028 summer internships, months earlier than many students had anticipated.

The path to Wall Street starts soon after college freshmen arrive on campus, with fierce competition for crucial spots in student-run finance and investing clubs. By the fall of their sophomore year they’re drilling themselves on the fundamentals of accounting and corporate-valuation methodologies, and networking with bankers via LinkedIn and email before applications open for internships that take place after junior year — almost 20 months in the future. By winter of sophomore year, many will have submitted dozens of applications, each with a personalized cover letter, hoping to get at least one interview. Throughout the process they fear the slightest misstep will prove disqualifying, according to students who spoke to Bloomberg Businessweek and asked not to be identified to protect their career prospects.

“From an employer’s perspective, you want to get to the best talent as early as you can. So you’re trying to think of ways to engage people earlier,” says Nicola Hancock, an executive at AMS, a recruitment company that works with banks on entry-level hiring. “How do we get early access?”

The shift presents a dilemma for university career offices. Kelly McSergi, director of employer relations at Yale University, says banks are seeking to hold informational sessions on campus as early as the spring of freshman year, reaching students before the recruiting cycle starts in the fall of sophomore year.
“We’re always kind of balancing ‘getting in front of the students too early’ with ‘they really do need this information,’” McSergi says.

Sofia Jiang, a former investment banking analyst at  Morgan Stanley, says she wishes recruitment hadn’t occurred so early. She was a Georgetown University sophomore when she secured a Morgan Stanley investment banking internship for the summer after her junior year. It eventually led to a full-time role, but Jiang left the firm after a few months, in November 2025, to build her own clothing brand.
“It makes no sense to me why people are fighting to be recruited literally two years before they even start the internship,” she says.

The grueling recruiting process aside, the path offers college students certainty in a challenging job market, Jiang says. “Investment banking attracts people who are really ambitious but also want a traditionally prestigious career. To be able to guarantee that [in] your second year of college is a really enticing opportunity for a lot of people,” she says.
Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase and Morgan Stanley declined to comment.

Students fret about whom to reach out to, in what order, what to say, what’s too casual. One rising junior who secured an internship offer at a global investment bank starting next summer says the process has been all-consuming.

“The worst part of this process is there’s no validation or sign of success until you get the offer. And so you’re always paranoid — am I doing enough?” he says. “My entire sophomore year up until I got that offer, I was always working, always thinking about it.”

For some applicants the process begins by applying to a so-called target college where banks tend to recruit, such as Harvard University or the University of Pennsylvania. At Penn almost 34% of 2025 graduates went into the financial-services industry, a more than 6-percentage-point increase from four years earlier, according to Penn Career Services.

Some state schools have developed in-house programs to rival those of the Ivy League by vetting and intensively preparing students for the application process. Xavier Sztejnberg, a former investment banker who started a program at the University of Texas at Austin’s McCombs School of Business, selects 75 undergraduate students out of about 500 applications.
“They need to check the box on almost everything,” Sztejnberg says. “And they have to look the part. They have to be polished. Polish is very important for me — being very well spoken.”

Indiana University’s Kelley School of Business runs a similar program called the Investment Banking Workshop. More than 500 undergraduate students enter an initial pre-workshop before roughly 140 are selected. Sridhar Arcot, co-director of the program, says the cutthroat nature of the process has made emotional support a de facto part of his role.

“I like to joke that, as the directors of the Investment Banking Workshop, we are almost like therapists or counselors,” Arcot says. The students “get rejections, and possibly that’s the first time in their life that’s happened.”

Student-run finance and investing clubs can rival the selectivity of their schools’ admissions office with acceptance rates in the low single digits. The clubs offer technical tutoring, alumni connections and valuable intel from upperclassmen who’ve made it through the process.

Much of students’ time during their first year and a half in college is spent learning technical material that’s not taught in early business courses, including interpreting income statements, balance sheets and cash-flow statements.

Students and career coaches say that paying for help isn’t a requirement, but there’s a burgeoning industry of private coaches and interview-prep services as the Wall Street recruiting process starts earlier and gets more competitive — and parents are eager to pay. Packages can include tutoring on financial concepts, mock interviews and networking advice. Prices range from $4,000 to more than $50,000 for highly personalized coaching sessions as frequently as twice a day. Some companies, such as Wall Street Oasis and CareerXL, offer refunds if students don’t land offers.

“All of my clients at some point in time have a major meltdown when they’re going through the process. The parents will call and say, ‘Is this really worth it?’” says Lesley Mitler, founder of career-coaching company Priority Candidates.

The preparation itself is a sort of endurance test for the job to come: Junior analysts often put in 80 to 100 hours a week building financial models in Excel, perfecting slide decks for client presentations and fielding all manner of urgent requests from senior staff.

David Solomon, chief executive officer of Goldman Sachs, said on the Long Strange Trip podcast in December that being smart isn’t enough to succeed at the firm. “You have to be smart enough, but the smartest person in the world without a whole package of other things [is] not going to navigate Goldman Sachs well,” he said. Among the qualities important to him, he said, are “the human elements: the ability to connect, resilience, determination, striving for excellence — things that matter everywhere.”

Clubs, coaches and school-sponsored workshops will put prospective applicants through hours of mock interviews to ensure they’re ready to perform if they’re invited to a “superday” — the final round of three or more interviews, often back-to-back, with people from the company at varying levels of seniority.

One college junior in New York learned about the industry when his fifth grade teacher told him he’d make a terrific investment banker. Despite his years of experience in finance and investing clubs, he says, the internship recruiting process felt unpredictable and intense. He landed a coveted 2027 internship at Evercore, less than a week after applying on Jan. 1.
“It’s like your entire interview process is 2.5 hours and you spend hundreds of hours prepping for this,” he says. “It’s a pretty big mismatch.” Evercore didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Banks don’t want applicants to lean heavily on artificial intelligence in the interview process, recruiters say. Last year, Goldman Sachs told investment banking candidates to avoid using digital assistance during interviews.
Once they’re hired, however, AI usage becomes commonplace: Most analysts are encouraged to use AI tools for everyday tasks, including parsing financial filings and formatting slide decks.

Applicants also must navigate what many regard as the most daunting part of the process: coffee chats. To have a realistic shot at an offer, applicants aim to network with multiple employees at every company they’re applying to. In all, that means many students connect with anywhere from 50 to 100 bankers.

A student from Western University in Ontario developed a method for small talk that typifies the intensity that successful students learn to keep under wraps (or, at least, carefully calibrate): Keep digging for common ground, he says, even if the banker on the other end of the conversation sounds completely uninterested. The aspiring banker has forged connections over everything from his first-year dorm, nicknamed the “Zoo,” to similar tastes in books. “I will not move on until the five minutes are done,” he says. “You just keep circling, circling in until you can build that connection.”

If students fail to secure a coveted internship spot, well, there’s always management consulting, coaches say. At Penn’s Wharton School, students say it’s become a running joke that you can tell who didn’t get an offer by seeing who shows up to the next McKinsey & Co. information session.

items.title: Bessent's Growth Solution for US Debt Is Seen Failing the Credibility Test
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has insisted faster economic growth can wipe away concerns about troubling fiscal trajectories, a key theme of his recent G20 leadership. History suggests otherwise.

Ahead of hosting the Group of 20 major world economies, Bessent said in August that “global growth is the way to take care of this mountain of debt.” With US federal spending restraint and “3% growth, we grow our way out of this,” he reiterated last week at a Texas event.

As recently as 2023 and 2024, the US was clocking near-3% growth rates, after adjusting for inflation. Yet debt held by the public climbed by roughly 10% and 7% respectively in those years — fueled by annual deficits topping $1.6 trillion — and debt as a share of economic output rose.

Back in the late 1990s, when US gross domestic product sustained gains of more than 4%, a dramatic turn to fiscal surpluses came alongside higher taxes and slower defense spending in a post-Cold War world.

Today, those dynamics are flipped. Tax rates are much lower after multiple waves of Republican-led reductions, and lawmakers from both parties in recent years have generally voted to raise, not lower, federal spending. An aging population is boosting outlays in giant entitlement programs. And amid geopolitical tensions, President Donald Trump wants Congress to approve $1.5 trillion in defense spending, a 44% boost.

“You can’t grow your way out of it,” said Douglas Holtz-Eakin, president of the right-leaning American Action Forum and a former director of the Congressional Budget Office. “It’s not numerically reasonable.”

The rapid recent increase in Treasury yields has added to angst over long-term US debt sustainability. Bessent’s self-identified benchmark, the 10-year rate, exceeded 5% on Monday. That’s a level it’s rarely traded at since the early 2000s. Bessent may face questions over his strategy at a House Financial Services Committee hearing Tuesday morning.

While Bessent predicts the artificial intelligence boom will help US growth accelerate, the consensus view is 3% gross domestic product rises aren’t in the offing soon. Both the median forecast of economists surveyed by Bloomberg and the International Monetary Fund’s latest projections show little more than 2% for 2027 and 2028.

Joe Lavorgna, a former counselor to Bessent, said that growth is an important part of any effort to reduce the deficit and overall debt burden and that Bessent was right to highlight it. Even so, he said it may not able to do the job on its own.

“Looking at 3% growth potential, that’s a pretty good number that’s going to go a long way to getting the deficit on a better trajectory,” he said. But “you probably need a little bit more than just growth,” he said.

One key to the problem is the steady increase in the number of American retirees, which in turn propels spending on Social Security and healthcare — the two biggest budget items. From Trump’s return to office through May, the number of Social Security retirement beneficiaries increased by 2.8 million. But the number of workers on US payrolls — who contribute revenue to pay for those benefits — rose by only 593,000.
Trump has said he won’t touch entitlement benefits and Congress has made no push for any major reform of those programs. The Treasury declined to respond to a request for comment on Monday.

“If all goes well and the economy grows rapidly, revenues will rise at the rate of nominal GDP,” which includes inflation, Holtz-Eakin said. Adding 3% real growth to 2% inflation means 5% nominal. But Social Security outlays are averaging 5.5% and Medicare up to 7.5%, he said. “So you can’t solve the problem.”

The third-biggest spending category is interest payments on debt outstanding, and that’s climbing even faster. With one month left in the fiscal year, net interest totals $1.02 trillion. That’s up 8.9% on the same period of the year before.

And rising US Treasury yields mean the risk is the rise in those costs will accelerate. At the end of August, the average interest rate on outstanding Treasuries was 3.48%, Treasury Department data show. That’s well below current yields. Benchmark five-year rates, the closest to the current average maturity of Treasuries outstanding, are around 4.77%.

And while the Treasury has lately been leaning on less-costly bills, which mature in up to a year, to issue debt, their cost is set to climb should Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and his colleagues raise their overnight policy rate on Wednesday as widely expected.

“There are no credible estimates that there will be enough growth that the fiscal situation magically disappears,” said Maya MacGuineas, the president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, or CRFB.

Among the subjects Bessent may be questioned on in Tuesday’s hearing is Trump’s idea of sending $5,000 checks to every adult US citizen if Republicans retain control of Congress in November’s midterm elections.

The CRFB estimates that proposal costing $1.2 trillion in a single year, at a time annual deficits are trending around $2 trillion. Without offsets, it would take the deficit-to-GDP ratio to 9% or 10% next year, the group calculates.

After taking office, Bessent set a target of getting that ratio down toward 3% by the time Trump’s term is over, in January 2029. After exceeding 6% in 2023 and 2024, it pipped under that level last year in part due to a one-time change in accounting for federal student loans.
For 2028, economists surveyed by Bloomberg see a 6.4% deficit. The narrowest prediction is 4.5%, while the widest is 8%.

Bessent has said he’s working with the White House budget director, Russ Vought, on a fiscal consolidation plan to bring the deficit down. While he hasn’t detailed what might be involved, he’s suggested that anti-fraud measures could be part of it.

For many budget experts, a credible fiscal package would require taking on the entitlement programs. A mentor to Bessent in his hedge fund career, Stanley Druckenmiller, last month put his name to a call for a proposal that would overhaul those gradually over time.
Even if faster growth could dent deficits, some worry that fiscal policymakers will simply look to use any newfound borrowing capacity.

“Some fiscal consolidation based on growth” is very possible, said Seth Carpenter, Morgan Stanley’s chief global economist and a Treasury official in the Obama administration. “But it relies on fiscal policy not turning expansionary again, and that for me is the real tricky question.”

For growth alone to do the job of getting deficits down where Bessent wants, it would take a pace of 6%, Holtz-Eakin reckons. Even 3% would be a “miracle” given the aging US population and tight strictures on immigration, he said.

items.title: US-Led AI Frontier Guardrails Won't Fly in Beijing
body: Welcome to Balance of Power, bringing you the latest in global politics. If you haven’t yet, sign up here.
Beijing dismissed calls from US tech leaders to slow down AI development as self-serving fearmongering.
It’s not that Chinese officials don’t want to discuss guardrails; they do — but not on terms set by the US.
Artificial intelligence is expected to feature prominently when presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping sit down in Washington in less than two weeks.
One reason that China’s pushing back is that it still lags behind the US, and Beijing sees AI as a once-in-a-lifetime chance to reshape the tech balance in its favor.
There’s also huge skepticism as to the underlying intention of American calls to hit the brakes.

Chinese AI companies already face US blocks on the chips needed to train and operate frontier models. State-controlled China Daily accused the US AI executives of wanting to further blunt Chinese competition.
It doesn’t help that Anthropic’s Dario Amodei is out in front.
Beijing holds special antipathy for the American entrepreneur, who has emerged as a prominent advocate of tighter US restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI.
Yet safety concerns are also front of mind in China, even if areas Beijing considers important don’t always fully overlap with American worries.
One prominent fear is that AI could threaten the legitimacy of the Communist Party, as voiced in an article posted Sunday by the country’s top intelligence official.
China’s definition of AI security is broader and continues to expand.
Just yesterday it released an updated safety framework to address emerging risks, including those of “recursive self-improvement” — the same dynamic cited by Amodei arguing for greater caution.
Even as Trump downplays the need for guardrails, the US and China have shared concerns, from AI-enabled cyberattacks by non-state actors to keeping humans in control of nuclear decisions.
Amid all the AI-focused noise, perhaps that’s something worth remembering as the Xi-Trump summit approaches.

The US fired so many munitions at Iranian targets during the first few months of their war that it “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls” and resupply bottlenecks, Pentagon officials acknowledged to the Defense Department’s independent watchdog. Saudi Arabia is seeking to further boost oil supply through the Strait of Hormuz after attacks forced it to halt a key pipeline for getting its crude to global markets, a source says.

Trump’s daughter-in-law, Bettina, said a Russian businessman paid for “two incredible nights of celebration” in the Bahamas after her wedding to Donald Trump Jr. but wasn’t involved in the actual nuptials, amid fresh ethics questions involving America’s first family. Umar Kremlev, who has ties to President Vladimir Putin, hosted the event. Meanwhile, Trump and Ukraine offered differing accounts of a supposed agreement with Russia to stop attacks on energy infrastructure.

Europe’s premier space business conference allows Paris to present itself as the center of the industry for a second week in a row, but missing from French President Emmanuel Macron’s summit were some prominent US companies. Europe’s strategic moves potentially herald a restructuring of the global space order, upending decades of lock-step collaboration between the US and its allies. At a separate event, the US acknowledged for the first time that it has a weapon in space to protect American interests, the Washington Post reported.

The Trump administration is rescinding climate controls on coal and gas-fired power plants, one of its most aggressive moves to unwind US regulations. The Environmental Protection Agency is ending a Biden-era mandate requiring existing and future fossil-fuel facilities to dramatically curb their emissions in the coming decades through the use of specific technologies, including carbon capture and storage.

Singapore was shrouded in haze again today, with smoke from wildfires in neighboring Indonesia raising islandwide pollution to levels that pose a health risk. All five regions of the city-state recorded unhealthy air-quality levels, the first time that’s happened since September 2019, according to the National Environment Agency.

The European Union is considering potential fines of as much as 6% of a company’s annual sales for online services that fail to prevent children from accessing their platforms as part of the bloc’s plans for a social media ban for kids under the age of 15.

The US Supreme Court refused to clear the Postal Service to enforce new restrictions on mail-in ballots for the congressional midterm elections, rebuffing the Trump administration’s request to intervene after several states launched early voting.

The dramatic collapse of trade talks with the US in August helped clarify Canada’s negotiating “red lines,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in an interview with Bloomberg News, adding that he’s ready to get back to the table for the right deal.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering whether to help Saudi Arabia counter attacks from the Houthis in Yemen amid British concerns about a worsening economic hit from the escalating conflict.
Sign up for the Washington Edition newsletter for news from the US capital and watch Balance of Power at 1 and 5 p.m. ET weekdays on Bloomberg Television.

Germany is preparing a far-reaching package of economic-security measures to shield strategic industries from China that may include new tariffs on hybrid EVs. Ministries in Berlin are mapping vulnerabilities to the Asian manufacturing powerhouse and assessing countermeasures, with potential proposals including new tariffs, mandatory JVs, strengthened inbound and outbound investment screening, and a bolstered export controls regime, sources say. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told French counterpart Jean-Noel Barrot in a phone call that China and Europe should handle differences through talks.

Thailand is targeting the equivalent of more than $600 million in extra tourism spending with a domestic travel stimulus plan aimed at shoring up a key economic engine hit by weaker foreign arrivals and higher energy costs. The measure reflects the Southeast Asian nation’s growing reliance on local travelers to cushion the sector as it struggles with the slow return of international visitors. Tourism is a major source of jobs and foreign exchange for Thailand, making the slowdown a broader concern for an economy already grappling with sluggish growth.

items.title: Top Africa Clothes Retailer Pepkor Sinks on Earnings Outlook
body: Pepkor Holdings Ltd. shares tumbled the most in more than three years after the South African discount clothing retailer forecast muted profit growth as the cost of building its new banking business weighs on profit.

Earnings excluding certain once-off gains and losses are likely to decline as much as 1% or increase as much as 9% for the year through Sept. 30, the Cape Town based retailer said after Monday’s market close.
The shares fell as much as 7.7% in early trading in Johannesburg on Tuesday, the biggest intraday decline since May 30, 2023.
Growth is being moderated by a subdued retail environment, a high comparative base and investment in longer-term growth projects including its PlusB banking business, Pepkor said.
Read More: Pepkor Eyes 2027 for the Rollout of a New South African Bank

Paul Steegers, an analyst at the corporate and investment banking unit of Nedbank Group Ltd. cut his recommendation on Pepkor to market perform from outperform and set a price target of 22 rand. The stock was trading 2.1% lower at 18.40 rand as of 11:55 a.m.

Launching its PlusB business brings execution risk and upfront costs as Pepkor builds banking infrastructure and acquires customers without a banking partner to share the burden. The retailer expects the build to cost less than 1 billion rand ($61 million).
Shaun Chauke and Elena Jouronova, analysts at JPMorgan Chase & Co., were more upbeat, retaining their overweight rating.

They said Pepkor’s 9.8% retail sales growth for the 10 months through July compared favorably with recent peer performances and that the company is the “clear structural winner” in South African value retail.
Still, they flagged potential drag on operating expenses and free cash flow as Pepkor invests in the new lender and other financial-services initiatives.
Read More: Pepkor to Buy Fintech to Create Firm Valued at $1.3 Billion
Same-store sales increased 3.1% in the period and the company said it continued to gain market share while offering a lot of discounts.
