items.title: UK Labour Market Downturn Accelerates Ahead of BOE Decision, Burnham's Budget
body: Morning, I’m Louise Moon from Bloomberg UK’s breaking news team, bringing you up to speed on today’s top business stories.
Employers cut jobs at the fastest rate in nine months in August, underscoring the weakness of the UK labour market just two days before the Bank of England’s latest rate decision.

The number of workers on payrolls fell by 26,000 last month, according to the Office for National Statistics, while demand remained tepid, with vacancies dropping to a fresh five-year low. Older workers, however, are having a somewhat more positive experience, as my colleague Kit details below.

The latest figures suggest that a two-year downturn in the labour market is dragging on, with the outlook clouded by uncertainty over the Iran war and ahead of PM Andy Burnham’s first budget in late October.

For the BOE, the weak jobs market has so far offered some reassurance: softer demand and wage pressures reduce the risk of inflation becoming entrenched. But rising oil prices are complicating that picture. Traders have responded by sharply increasing their bets on rate hikes, pricing in as many as five by the end of next year.What’s your take? Ping me on X, LinkedIn or drop me an email at lmoon13@bloomberg.net. Oh, and do subscribe to Bloomberg.com for unlimited access to trusted business journalism on the UK, and beyond.

GSK is buying an experimental blood cancer medicine from a Chinese biotech for up to $750 million. It builds on an earlier acquisition from the same company, as GSK pushes into cancer therapies to try and prove it can succeed in the competitive oncology space it previously abandoned.

Britain could raise an additional £15 billion in tax revenue from oil and gas production during the next decade if the government replaced the windfall tax with a permanent price-triggered mechanism next year, rather than 2030 as planned. That’s according to an industry lobby group.
The Bank of England could soon stop selling long-dated bonds it amassed after the financial crisis and Covid, reported The Telegraph. It said plans have been drafted, but no final decision taken.

The UK government will work with other countries on the safety of artificial intelligence after warnings that development of the technology must be slowed to prevent it from inflicting catastrophic harm. Britain will “heed the warnings” of AI developers, First Secretary of State Louise Haigh said.

Plus, Andy Burnham is weighing up helping Saudi Arabia counter attacks from the Houthis in Yemen, after receiving requests for a range of diplomatic and military support (which also extended to the US). For Britain, an escalating conflict raises concerns about a worsening economic hit.
Here’s your daily snap analysis from Bloomberg UK’s Markets Today blog:
One thing that stands out in the latest jobs figures is the significant increase in the number of people working beyond retirement age.
The number of payrolled employees aged 65 and over rose by 62,000 in August, the biggest monthly increase in a year. By contrast, the number of payrolled employees under 25 fell by 15,000.

This chimes with recent signs that older workers are choosing to remain in employment for longer. Cost-of-living pressures and concerns about having enough to fund retirement could be playing a role, particularly when set against a backdrop of higher energy costs and interest rates.

But the figures also point to a wider problem in a stagnant labour market, where workers are staying in their jobs for longer and opportunities to move between roles are becoming scarcer. That’s making it harder for younger people trying to get their foot in the door, further adding to the UK’s youth unemployment problem.

Taken together, the figures suggest that the pressures facing the labour market are increasingly being felt at opposite ends of the age spectrum. Older workers may be delaying retirement because they cannot afford to stop working, while younger workers are struggling to get started.

Rather than simply reflecting changing attitudes to work and retirement, this could be a sign of a labour market where economic insecurity is shaping people’s choices at every stage of their working lives.
— Kit Rees
Check Bloomberg UK’s Markets Today blog for updates all day.

August inflation data is due early doors tomorrow. Bloomberg Intelligence expects an acceleration to 3% year on year, driven by rising fuel costs. The recent hike in energy prices supports its forecast that inflation will stay close to 3% through the year.
Plus, updates from Barratt Redrow, the UK’s largest homebuilder, and greeting card retailer Moonpig.
Moody’s City of London head office, 10 Gresham Street, is up for sale for about £330 million. Who bought it in 2012 for £200 million?
[Yesterday’s answer: The flat tax for foreign earners in Greece, debuted in late 2019, is €100,000.]

items.title: Crispin Odey's Lifetime Ban Blocks Routes Back to City of London
body: Crispin Odey was one of the Square Mile’s best-known investors, and his eponymous firm was naturally courted by the biggest banks in London. But he also had a reputation that led some in the industry to take precautions.

Long before the hedge fund mogul’s conduct made headlines, female members of staff in Goldman Sachs Group Inc.’s prime brokerage unit had, on occasion, been accompanied by chaperones when attending Odey Asset Management’s events, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.
A Goldman Sachs representative declined to comment.

A report commissioned in 2021 by Odey Asset Management’s executive committee and conducted by the law firm Simmons and Simmons found at least 46 alleged incidents of inappropriate conduct, including accusations of sexual assault by Odey, over a 17-year period.

Last year, the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority banned him from financial services for life and fined him £1.8 million ($2.3 million), after finding that his attempts to frustrate disciplinary proceedings against him showed  he was not “a fit and proper person” to work in the industry. On Monday, Odey’s attempt to overturn that ruling in tribunal failed, as a panel of judges upheld the ban.
Odey abandoned a £79 million libel suit against the FT in April, and in May, he settled a personal injury suit brought by a number of women who claimed they had been sexually assaulted by him.

The judgment, despite cutting his fine somewhat to £1.5 million, almost certainly ends Odey’s career as a money manager in the UK, and demonstrates that the regulator, the FCA, has the ability to prosecute powerful individuals in the financial sector beyond its traditional remit of policing financial misconduct.

“He felt the rules shouldn’t apply to him and acted to save his own skin.” Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement at the FCA said. “That arrogant entitlement and the resulting complete disregard for proper governance means Mr Odey is unfit to work in financial services.”
A lawyer that acted for Odey in the case did not reply to an email requesting comment.

Odey loomed large over London’s hedge fund scene for years. A blue-blooded, establishment figure, he was educated at the prestigious Harrow School north of London, an institution that has produced seven Prime Ministers, including Winston Churchill. His grandfather, George Odey, was a Conservative MP. His first marriage was to the daughter of Rupert Murdoch, his second to Barclays heiress and fund management executive Nichola Pease.

Odey founded Odey Asset Management in 1991. It was one of the first British hedge funds, seeded with capital from George Soros, and in keeping with the fashion at the time his name went on the door. Like many hard-charging money managers of the era, the firm was understood as an extension of the personality of its owner.

The funds that Odey himself ran had a bearish bent, making large contrarian bets, some of which brought him to the attention of the general public, including shorting the stock of  British building society Bradford & Bingley ahead of the 2008 crash. The company collapsed under the weight of its subprime exposure and had to be nationalized.

He also routinely opined on politics, often donating money to the Conservative Party and backing Boris Johnson’s bid to become leader of the party. He donated thousands of pounds to Nigel Farage’s Reform party, and to the cause of Britain leaving the European Union. The day after the UK voted to leave the EU in 2016, Odey told an interviewer “the morning has gold in its mouth.”
Behind the scenes, complaints about Odey’s conduct were mounting.

Later testimony contained in the Simmons and Simmons’ report included an allegation that Odey had groped a woman’s breasts, then sent her a text message apologizing — but saying that his actions didn’t make him unfit to manage money. One of the women interviewed as part of the report said that in the mid-2000s, sexual harassment was “part of the deal” at OAM, and that accusations of misconduct were “swept under the carpet.”

Allegations against Odey finally came to light in 2020, when he was charged with an alleged 1998 indecent assault of a woman who worked at an investment bank that had his fund as a client. That prosecution was dismissed, in part due to inconsistencies in the accuser’s account. Judge Nicholas Rimmer said in his ruling in 2021. “You will leave this courthouse with your good character intact.”

More allegations soon emerged. In 2021, Bloomberg News reported that a woman had accused Odey of touching her inappropriately. The same year, a woman told the Sunday Times that Odey had groped her at a London restaurant in 2008.

Then, in 2023, an investigation by the Financial Times uncovered multiple allegations of sexual harassment and assault leveled against Odey, spanning a quarter of a century, and his backers began to abandon him. Assets under management — which at one point had reached £13 billion — plummeted as investors withdrew their business. Key service providers, including Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase & Co, cut ties.

Odey fought back against attempts to hold him accountable. In November 2021, the executive committee of his firm scheduled a disciplinary hearing to consider whether Odey had breached a final written warning regarding his behavior. On Christmas eve, Odey used his status as majority shareholder to sack everyone on the board and appoint himself as the sole member. He appointed a new executive committee in January 2022, but also removed all of them a couple of months later, losing his temper with one of the men he appointed to run the firm.
“I have never seen rage like I saw that day,” Oliver Kelton, a fund manager that was on the second executive committee that Odey dismissed, said in court earlier this year. “It was intimidating.”

It was Odey’s refusal to adhere to the governance process that led the FCA to ban him in 2025. His decision to challenge the ruling created space for the allegations of sexual misconduct to be aired in open court.

At the tribunal, Odey tried to portray himself as a victim. “I never thought I sexually harassed anyone except one person,” Odey said during cross-examination. He admitted that he’d “said things to people that were inappropriate” but added that he’d “apologized for that.”

But the court also heard details from the lawyers’ reports into his alleged behavior, and testimony from OAM’s former chief executive officer, Tim Pearey, who called Odey a “sociopath” and a “sex pest.”

Lawyers said that the case has potential ramifications beyond Odey’s future. This month the FCA brought in rules that expand its attempts to punish bad behavior in financial services to include a wider group of brokers and investment firms. Odey is the second high profile victory against powerful men in finance who have been accused of misconduct, and who have appealed. Last year, the same tribunal dismissed an appeal against ex-Barclays Plc chief Jes Staley, who was banned for life after allegedly misrepresenting the extent of his ties to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The FCA “have had two very high profile wins and they will take satisfaction from that,” Chloe-Jane Belton, legal director at Howard Kennedy, said. “The FCA would say that it is not their job to regulate private morality, but ultimately if you have got someone in a senior position in financial services they should be trusted to comply with the rules.”
The ruling leaves little room for Odey to return to a career in the City. Barring a remarkable decision by the Court of Appeal, his career as a City money manager is almost certainly over.
In delivering its judgement, the tribunal said that Odey had demonstrated no remorse.

“He sees nothing wrong with his approach, and indeed he wrongly sees himself as the victim of both OAM’s actions and the Authority’s,” the judgement reads. “Mr Odey displayed no contrition or understanding of his power at work, his position of authority and physical size, and his abuse of power in his sexualized and inappropriate behavior.”

items.title: UK Says It'll Heed Warnings on AI Amid Criticism of Inaction
body: The UK said it will work with other countries on the safety of artificial intelligence, amid criticism that Andy Burnham’s government has been slow to respond to warnings that the technology could inflict catastrophic harm.

Britain will “heed the warnings of those who are at the forefront of developing this technology” and “be ready to work with international partners” to prioritize public safety and national security, First Secretary of State Louise Haigh, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s de facto deputy, said in a statement on Tuesday.

“AI has enormous potential to transform our public services, make our businesses stronger and deliver new scientific breakthroughs,” Haigh said. She was speaking for Burnham after the premier canceled engagements following the death of his father.

The British government has said little about AI since Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei’s call for a slowdown on Saturday, which was endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. The UK is seen as one of the global leaders on the technology after the US and China.

Britain’s AI minister Kanishka Narayan made a brief reference to the intervention in a post on X on Sunday in which he said the government would be “robust” in acting against AI risks. He urged AI labs to work with the UK’s AI Security Institute to “help you play a responsible role.”

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told Times Radio on Tuesday that Britain’s AI Safety Institute needed to continue to have access to frontier models, after Anthropic withheld its latest model from the testing agency.
“The fundamental thing to keep people safe, to keep the UK safe, is to continue to have access to those models,” Reynolds said.

Some UK officials told Bloomberg they were concerned the new Burnham administration has not prioritized AI policy, especially in light of the recent concerns which they said they share. There is a lack of interest and knowledge on AI in Downing Street and among ministers and political advisers, one of the people said. Another said they hoped government ministers would play more of a role in the face of the rising risks.

Burnham controversially abolished the UK government’s science and technology department when he became premier, folding it into other departments, though he also elevated the seniority of the AI minister to cabinet-level. A government AI taskforce is reporting to Cabinet Secretary Antonia Romeo, who is seen as becoming more personally involved in a wide remit of policies across government departments.
Still, in an unusual development, King Charles III is convening AI leaders on Thursday to discuss the technology, rather than a senior minister.

While Britain is eyeing discussions with international allies, US President Donald Trump set out his opposition to AI guardrails in a series of social media posts on Monday. He belittled the push by AI bosses to slow work on frontier systems as “a hoax.” Later, in a call to Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, he said “AI will not be taking over the rest of the world.”

Nonetheless, also on Monday, an AI researcher who recently resigned from Google DeepMind warned humanity is running out of time to prevent artificial intelligence from causing widespread harm, the latest staffer to voice concerns about the direction of the technology.

“At Google, I witnessed AI development first hand,” Bilal Chughtai wrote Monday on both X and LinkedIn “I too am extremely concerned by the default trajectory of this technology. I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all.”

items.title: UK Energy Bills Forecast to Jump 25%, Bloomberg Analysis Finds
body: UK household energy bills are poised to jump by about 25% in January amid sharpened tensions in the Middle East, according to a Bloomberg Economics forecast that threatens to upend Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s drive to bear down on the cost of living.

The regulator Ofgem will use energy futures prices observed mid-August to mid-November to reset a price cap on domestic energy bills in January, a period that so far includes a run-up in wholesale gas prices, Bloomberg Economics said Tuesday in a note. That means the cap is expected to rise by £427 ($575) to about £2,150 a year for a typical household, economists Matt Bunny and Dan Hanson said in the analysis. The quarterly adjustment means bills are already set to rise by 4% on Oct. 1.

Rising energy prices threaten to stoke inflation in the wider economy with the economic hit to ordinary Britons dwarfing the benefits of early moves by Burnham to ease living costs since he took power in July. On his second day as premier, he scrapped value added tax from household electricity bills from Oct. 1, a move the government said would save families on average £45 a year.

European energy prices have jumped since the Iran war began in late February, disrupting oil and gas supplies from the Persian Gulf. UK month-ahead gas futures have risen by 150% since the conflict started, while the equivalent power contract has more than doubled.

Bloomberg Economics said the latest increase in energy costs could push wider inflation above 4% in 2027, double the Bank of England’s target. That outlook could lead the central Bank to raise interest rates later this year, the analysts said.

Burnham and Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey now face a tricky run-up to the administration’s first budget on Oct. 28. The £23.6 billion headroom Healey inherited against the government’s fiscal targets has already been cut in half by a surge in borrowing costs fueled by the US-Iran conflict. That leaves little room to maneuver as they try to deliver the “breathing space,” for families pledged by Burnham on his first day in office.

The government is now considering further measures, including extending the £150 Warm Home Discount to people who do not currently qualify, potentially including some disabled people, carers and pensioners. Such steps could be announced in the budget, before taking effect over the winter.
Read More: Britain Faces Winter With High Gas Prices and Thin Reserves

A forecast from EDF, one of the UK’s biggest energy suppliers, show a similar price increase to Bloomberg Economics, saying their prediction is up by about £119 compared to a week earlier. Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight’s last forecast in August showed a smaller increase but wholesale prices have surged since then.

The rise in power and gas costs forecast by Bloomberg Economics would push household bills closer to the £2,500 cap brought in by the government following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. At the time, market prices were much higher, but the government subsidized the difference so that a typical household only paid the cap. The support cost the government about £21 billion.

items.title: Volvo Pivots to Long-Range Hybrids as Full EVs Take More Time
body: Volvo Car AB is rolling out new long-range plug-in hybrids in Europe and the US, betting demand for the dual technology will persist well into the next decade.

The Swedish manufacturer controlled by China’s Geely said Tuesday it’s launching its first long-range hybrids for the European and American markets as versions of the bestselling XC60 and XC90. The SUVs have more powerful batteries and a range as far as 200 kilometers (124 miles) and 160 kilometers respectively on a single charge.

Initially seen as a stepping stone to battery-only vehicles, plug-in hybrids are being given a much longer lease of life as drivers demand more electric power to help offset surging fuel prices. Charging networks also remain insufficient in many countries, slowing the transition to pure EVs.

“Five years ago, perhaps people thought electrification was a linear story: it would take four years, everything would look like Norway and then we’d be done by 2030,” Volvo Car Chief Commercial Officer Erik Severinson said in an interview.

The transition has proved less straightforward, prompting Volvo to take a more flexible approach, he added. “We have a pragmatic solution. A bridge that will probably take us several years into the next decade.”
Read More: Hybrid Cars Are Hot Again Worldwide While EV Sales Slow Sharply
Plug-in hybrids depend on two powertrains — an internal combustion engine and an electric motor — which increases their cost, complexity and weight.

Chinese manufacturers including BYD, Geely and Chery have helped reshape the segment with a new generation of the vehicles. They’re equipped with more efficient batteries, allowing them to travel much farther on electric power alone.

Mercedes-Benz Group AG, BMW AG and Volkswagen AG continue to offer a broad mix of powertrains as the shift to fully electric vehicles proceeds unevenly across markets. Hybrid offerings from the three German manufacturers, as well as from the likes of Toyota Motor Corp.’s Lexus and Jaguar Land Rover Automotive Plc’s Range Rover, will likely compete with the new XC60 and XC90 in the US and Europe.

Higher fuel prices stoked by the US-Israeli war on Iran have also had an impact. The fallout from the conflict prompted more US drivers to opt for hybrids made by Japanese and South Korean automakers this spring, leaving US automakers largely on the sidelines.
Read More: Toyota, Hyundai Sales Rise on Hybrid Demand While GM Sits Out

Robust hybrid demand is also an unexpected boon for Horse Powertrain, a joint venture created by Renault SA and Geely in 2023 with 18 manufacturing sites across three continents employing around 19,000 workers.

Horse supplies Volvo with engines from its factory in Skövde northeast of Gothenburg, continuing a tradition that began almost 100 years ago when the plant belonged to the Swedish manufacturer. It was later spun off into Aurobay Sweden AB before becoming part of Horse.

Volvo formally scaled back its electrification ambitions two years ago, abandoning a goal of selling only full EVs by 2030. It still intends to eventually become a fully electric carmaker, but no longer has a specific deadline.

“We can’t be dogmatic and say it has to happen in a certain way when that’s not what the market looks like,” Severinson said. “There could be a need well into the next decade for products with combustion engines.”
Last year, Volvo launched the XC70 extended-range plug-in hybrid in China, where such vehicles have become increasingly popular. It’s currently Volvo’s best-selling car there.

“If we hadn’t had it, the situation would probably have been even more difficult,” Severinson said. Volvo has said its exploring potential additional markets for the XC70 at a later stage, not including Europe.

items.title: AI Chip Darling Biren Said to Mull $1 Billion Share Sale
body: Shanghai Biren Technology Co. is weighing another share sale to help finance its artificial intelligence ambitions, according to people familiar with the situation.

The company, one of a group of graphics processing unit developers championed by Beijing, is considering raising about $1 billion, the people said. Banks are in the early stages of sounding out interest from potential investors, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.

Biren already raised about $900 million in a July share sale. It agreed at the time not to sell any further stock for 90 days, a period that runs out in early October. Depending on market conditions, Biren could proceed with a fresh stock offering shortly after that lockup expires, the people said.

Chinese AI firms are on a fundraising spree as they try to compete with the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI, even as concerns build about the development of advanced models and risks they might pose. On Sunday, Z.AI Co., or Zhipu, announced a $5 billion stock and convertible bond sale to follow a $4 billion deal in July. Zhipu’s shares have fallen 16% in Hong Kong this week.
Biren’s deliberations are ongoing and details such as the size and structure of a placement haven’t been finalized, the people said. The company may also decide not to do a deal.
A representative for Biren didn’t respond to requests for comment.
Biren erased an 8.2% gain in Hong Kong trading following the Bloomberg News report on the potential share sale. The stock was down 1% as of 3:08 p.m. local time.

Shanghai-based Biren listed in Hong Kong at the start of this year, climbing more than 70% on its first day in a sizzling debut. After reaching a closing high of HK$68 in June, the stock has retreated to around half of that level, giving the company a market capitalization of about HK$86 billion ($11 billion).

Hong Kong’s biggest-ever follow-on offering came last month, with Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. raising HK$80 billion, which it intends to spend on advancements in AI as well. Its shares also fell the next day, by the most in more than a year. Concerns about dilution and oversupply are reflected in the stock market: the Hang Seng Tech Index is down 22% this year.
Another Chinese tech company that issued shares in July, MiniMax Group Inc., is down 13% this week.

items.title: BOE May End Long-Dated Bond Sales as Officials Draft Plans, Report Says
body: The Bank of England could soon stop selling long-dated bonds that it amassed after the financial crisis and pandemic, according to a report by the Daily Telegraph, in a move that would be likely to save the Treasury billions of pounds.

The newspaper said officials at the UK central bank, Treasury and Debt Management Office have drafted the plans, without saying where it got the information. The BOE and the Treasury declined to comment.

The report said a final decision was still to be made by the BOE. Policymakers are due to vote on the quantitative tightening on Wednesday afternoon alongside their interest rate decision, both of which will be published Thursday.

Market participants expect the BOE to reduce the pace of its balance sheet run-off to £50 billion ($67 billion) a year in the 12 months from October. That would imply active sales remain at around £20 billion.

However, long-dated debt only accounts for 20% of the BOE’s current sales, meaning that if it maintained the same pace and skew, it would imply just £4 billion worth being sold from that part of its portfolio.

The UK central bank is facing heavy losses on its 20 and 30-year bonds after a slump in their value. Long-dated bonds are trading at as much as half their face value while shorter dated ones have a smaller discount.

Should the BOE press ahead with £50 billion of asset sales but switch from longer-dated to shorter-dated debt, it could save the Treasury around £800 million a year according to Barclays. Should it simply cancel the longer dated program the Treasury savings could be around double that.

Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is facing a difficult budget on Oct. 28 as rising borrowing costs and inflation are expected to wipe out as much as half of the £23.6 billion buffer against his fiscal rules. He is expected to find savings to repair some of that headroom.

Think tanks including the left-wing Institute for Public Policy Research and New Economics Foundation have urged the Treasury claw back some of the anticipated losses from the QT program to protect the public finances, while on the right of the spectrum Nigel Farage’s Reform UK party has called for QT to be halted.
The BOE has been adamant that QT remains a monetary policy tool that is controlled by the nine independent members of the Monetary Policy Committee.

Long-maturity gilt yields were five basis points higher at 5.94% on Tuesday morning, broadly in line with their shorter-dated peers and mostly steady against swap counterparts, suggesting investors were not surprised by the report.
While the BOE has faced calls from investors and politicians to end active sales, stopping the long-dated disposals would mark a departure from the BOE’s recent messaging and strategy.
It believes the QT program is only having a modest impact on UK bond yields. In July, it estimated that the total increase in 10-year gilts yields from QT to date was around 20 to 30 basis points.
The BOE has argued that QT auctions have little impact on market functioning and noted a number of other factors pushing up long-term borrowing costs.

A permanent shift away from selling long-dated debt would also leave the BOE with these bonds sitting on its balance sheet for decades to come. Governor Andrew Bailey has said he wants to get rid of the bonds to remove interest-rate risk from its balance sheet, as holding the debt is creating losses.

“Reserves are moving toward the upper end of their preferred range,” said Evelyne Gomez-Liechti, a multi-asset strategist at Mizuho International Plc. “One of the reasons why the BoE may not scrap active QT selling altogether is the risk that the market may see that as a lack of independence from the Treasury.”

Gilts have weakened since renewed fighting between the US and Iran lifted energy prices and inflation expectations. UK 30-year yields are within a handful of basis points of reaching 6% for the first time since 1998, and money markets have boosted wagers on Bank of England lifting interest rates close to 5% by the middle of next year.

items.title: Asian PE Firms Circle €1 Billion Racing Brand Alpinestars
body: Alpinestars, the Italian maker of protection gear used by motorcycle racers, is attracting takeover interest from Asian private equity firms including FountainVest and HSG, people familiar with the matter said.

They are among suitors that have separately been considering bids for the closely held company, the people said, asking not to be identified because the deliberations are private. Alpinestars has been working with a financial adviser on a potential sale that could value the business at about €1 billion ($1.2 billion), the people said.
Other potential buyers have also been pursuing Alpinestars, the people said. Talks are ongoing and no final decisions have been made, according to the people.

“Alpinestars regularly receives investment proposals and evaluates them in the context of its long-term strategic objectives and growth plans,” the Italian company said in a statement. “The company is focused on executing its long-term growth strategy, investing in product innovation, advancing motorcycling and cycling safety, and expanding its global presence.”
A representative for FountainVest didn’t respond to requests for comment, while HSG declined to comment.

Asian private equity firms have been eyeing deals in Europe as they seek to diversify and invest in global brands they can further expand in faster-growing emerging markets. HSG has acquired Italian sneaker brand Golden Goose, as well as a majority stake in audio equipment maker Marshall. FountainVest has also been looking at buying various assets in Europe.
Motorcycling has become popular in China after local manufacturer ZXMoto recently won some races at the 2026 WorldSSP championship. HSG is an investor in ZXMoto.

Alpinestars, founded in 1963, is owned by the Mazzarolo family. It makes protective gear including boots, helmets, jackets and gloves often used in Liberty Media Corp.’s MotoGP motorcycling and Formula One racing competitions. Other products include airbag safety systems as well as sportswear.

items.title: Rail Sabotage, Road Fires Disrupt Transport Across Netherlands
body: Railway section failures at multiple locations in the Netherlands appear to have been caused by sabotage, according to ProRail, the Dutch government agency responsible for rail infrastructure.
At the same time, fires broke out alongside several motorways across the country, threatening to disrupt road traffic.

Materials were found at multiple locations in the track that were deliberately placed there, ProRail said in a statement Tuesday, after large parts of the country’s railway system came to a standstill during the morning rush hour.
“Sabotage appears to be involved,” ProRail said. The perpetrator and the motive are still unknown, the agency said.
The disruptions come as the government of Prime Minister Rob Jetten prepares to present its first budget Tuesday afternoon.

A spokesperson for ProRail identified the materials as piping. Its employees are working to clear them and the national police unit is investigating the incidents. Over 30 disruptions have been reported and in some cases, malfunctions occurred again in locations where material had previously been removed.
“The fact that this appears to be intentional is very concerning,” Dutch State Secretary for Infrastructure Annet Bertram said in a statement, adding that an investigation is underway.

Railway services in the center and north of the country have been severely disrupted since early Tuesday morning. Train operator NS said in a statement that train traffic around locations including Zwolle, Deventer and Amersfoort is disrupted.
ProRail warned travelers to expect delays and canceled trains. At one location, Steenwijk, a train struck the material, but this had no consequences for the train, the agency said.

There are malfunctions in signals and switches at a large number of locations, NS said. Several level crossings are also malfunctioning, which could impact road traffic, according to ProRail. During a section failure, computer systems identify part of the track as “occupied” even when there is no train present.

Meanwhile, Rijkswaterstaat, the Dutch government agency responsible for managing the country’s primary road networks, warned that some lanes or entire highways could face closure on Tuesday due to several fires along the roads in the Netherlands.

items.title: Trump Dismisses AI Risks as Safety Warnings Mount
body: Good morning. Donald Trump dismisses AI fears even as warnings mount. US 10-year Treasury yields hit their highest since 2007. Check out our rankings of the best business schools. Listen to the day’s top stories.

Donald Trump opposed guardrails on AI, dismissing existential fear as a “hoax” even as a growing chorus of executives and scientists raised concerns. He made an impromptu call to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who was onstage at a tech conference and put their conversation on speakerphone. An ex-Google DeepMind researcher warned humanity is running out of time to prevent AI from causing widespread harm. Barack Obama voiced support for regulation, saying that the technology could unleash “potential catastrophe” if not properly managed. Read our explainer on what’s sparked the current panic.

The US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to the highest level in almost two decades, the latest milestone in a bruising global bond selloff driven by surging energy prices, mounting debt and inflation. Elsewhere, European Central Bank Vice President Boris Vujcic warned that soaring market valuations driven primarily by AI leave equities vulnerable to a correction.

Oil pushed higher as traders weighed disruptions to Middle East supplies, with a critical Saudi Arabian pipeline still offline. The East-West pipeline — a workaround for Strait of Hormuz flows — was shut last week after attacks, with Saudi Aramco yet to say when it may restart. Riyadh is trying to raise shipments through the waterway further to compensate, a person familiar said.German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will discuss closer cooperation in talks with his US counterpart Pete Hegseth in Washington today as Europe looks to fill its low stocks of air defense missiles and deep-strike weapons. Meanwhile, the US fired so many munitions at Iranian targets during the first few months of Operation Epic Fury that it resulted in “strategic inventory shortfalls,” Pentagon officials acknowledged.

The UK could raise an additional £15 billion in tax revenue from oil and gas production over the next decade if Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government brought forward its new fiscal regime to next year, according to an industry lobby group. Check out our Markets Today live blog for all the latest news and analysis relevant to UK assets.More Top Stories
For the second week in a row, Paris is presenting itself as the center of the space industry.

Markets blinked after the 10-year Treasury yield breached 5%, suggesting investors still see a guaranteed 5% return from a safe asset as a good deal, John Authers writes. But once the Federal Reserve embarks on tightening, it generally continues for a while and yields keep rising, with history suggesting the 10-year could reach 6% before the cycle is over. items.title: France Lobbies EU to Lift Sanctions on Russian Tycoon Usmanov
body: France is pushing European Union member states to lift sanctions on Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov as part of a prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan, according to people familiar with the matter.

The French demand has stalled EU efforts to renew sanctions for more than 2,500 individuals and companies over Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the people said, asking not to be identified because the matter is sensitive.
EU envoys agreed on Monday to temporarily extend the measures for a week to allow more time for negotiations.

Usmanov, 73, owns 49% of USM, a Russia-based investment group that controls Metalloinvest, the country’s largest iron ore producer, and holds a stake in telecommunications company MegaFon. He is Russia’s seventh richest person, with a net worth of $16.6 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Usmanov holds Russian citizenship and is an honorary citizen of Uzbekistan, where he was born. Last year, Azerbaijan joined Uzbekistan and the four other Central Asian nations in their regional cooperation group.

Spokespeople for the French government didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Usmanov’s press service declined to comment and the press office of Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry didn’t immediately respond to request for comment.
French diplomats had previously described the issue as relating to a specific national security concern.

The EU sanctions require the backing of all of the bloc’s member states. That has meant that measures are often watered down or entire packages and their renewal held up by the demands of individual countries for particular exclusions, often linked to their national interests.

Usmanov isn’t regarded as being among Russian President Vladimir Putin’s closest associates. Still, decades in Russian business have given him extensive connections in the country’s political and business establishment, including in the Kremlin.

The tycoon is better known internationally through his investment in London’s Arsenal Football Club, which he exited in 2018. He has also served for decades as president of the International Fencing Federation and a major financial supporter of the sport. His links to France are less obvious.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the prospect of easing sanctions on Usmanov. “This is definitely not the time to lift sanctions, to rescue Russian oligarchs from them,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.

items.title: Europe Hinges on Fall IPOs to Beat Last Year's $17 Billion Haul
body: European stock exchanges must raise a further $5 billion from initial public offerings before the year is out to surpass last year’s haul, a challenge in a market where deals have been prone to delays.

The transactions slated for the autumn have the potential to deliver the milestone, but there’s little room for error and only a handful of billion-dollar offerings still in the pipeline. European IPOs in 2025 raised $16.7 billion combined, higher than the previous year but still below historical levels, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Together, IPOs of mobile payments firm Airtel Money, tankmaker KNDS NV and property investor Hotel Investment Partners SA could combine with the year-to-date total of $11.6 billion to help tip the region past 2025. All three firms are considering the listing window that normally runs from September into November, according to people familiar with the matter and previous Bloomberg News reporting.

To be sure, not all of these companies may decide to go ahead with an offering. European stocks are off their highs and volatility has crept back in, driven by the wars in the Middle-East and Ukraine, as well as concerns about the AI trade and the surge in energy prices and bond yields.

Dealmakers went into 2026 with hopes that the year would bring about a flurry of listings supported by higher stock prices. Market volatility from the conflicts and concerns around the impact of AI prompted some candidates to delay their IPO plans, while others may need more time to prepare.

“The autumn window is probably not going to be as busy as we would’ve hoped earlier this year,” Egor Marisin, a partner in the corporate and equity capital markets team at law firm Freshfields, said. “But I wouldn’t be surprised if a select handful of European IPO candidates were to have a go at testing the markets.”

The relatively light pipeline for Europe stands in contrast with the US and Asia, both of which have been busy with offerings driven by artificial intelligence-related spending, a flurry of activity that means the continent’s more traditional firms are competing for global investor attention. The US has already blown past last year’s total for funds raised from IPOs, even excluding SpaceX’s blockbuster offering, data show.

US midterm elections in November further raise the stakes for this fall IPO season, with investors typically more cautious in the lead up to the polls. That means the opportunity for large offerings in the autumn could end sooner than last year.

“It would be nice to have a positive story of things being up and running again before the end of the year,” Marisin said, adding that a lower total than last year shouldn’t “sway hearts and minds that much” given events like the midterms or the UK budget in the period.

Airtel Money, part of telecom group Airtel Africa Plc, and wealth manager Oaktree-backed Utmost Group Plc are among the firms aiming for a London IPO as soon as the coming months, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing confidential matters. Airtel Money may be valued at $10 billion, in what could be the City’s largest such offering since 2021, Bloomberg reported previously.

Meanwhile, KNDS NV is considering launching a new IPO attempt later this month if investor feedback is constructive, Bloomberg News has reported. The Franco-German group, which called off plans to list earlier in the year citing defense stock turmoil, has resumed preparations, encouraged by a recovery in European defense stocks over the summer.

In Spain, Blackstone Inc. is gearing up for a potential listing of Hotel Investment Partners that could raise around €800 million ($922 million), while Vortex Energy-backed Ignis is also planning an IPO to raise as much as €600 million, the people said. Spanish newspaper Expansion first reported Ignis’ deal size.

In Scandinavia, Nordic Capital-backed dermatology specialist Leo Pharma AS is working on a Copenhagen IPO, and Swedish infrastructure group Eleda is plotting an offering in Stockholm, said the people.

No final decisions have been made on any of the IPOs and the details, including the timing, could change, the people said. Representatives for Bain Capital, HIP, Blackstone, Ignis, Leo Pharma, Nordic Capital, Utmost and Oaktree declined to comment. Eleda and Vortex Energy did not reply to requests for comment.

items.title: UK Payrolls Drop More Than Expected in Weak Jobs Market
body: Britain’s employers shed workers at the fastest rate in nine months, according to figures that emphasized the weak state of the jobs market ahead of the Bank of England’s latest interest rates decision on Thursday.

The number of employees on company payrolls slipped 26,000 in August after a downwardly revised 19,000 fall the previous month, the Office for National Statistics said on Tuesday. It was worse than the 5,000 drop that economists expected, though the provisional estimates are often revised.

Demand for workers remained tepid with job vacancies falling 8,000 to a fresh five-year low of 702,000. Unemployment held steady at 4.9% in the three months through July, though the ONS has cautioned that the estimate is still affected by a quality issue with the collection of that data.
The pound extended losses after the data, falling as much as 0.2% to $1.3472.

The figures suggest that a two-year downturn in the labor market is dragging on with employers facing heightened uncertainty from the US-Iran conflict and the first budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, set for Oct. 28.

Firms are increasingly laying off workers. The redundancy rate rose to 3.9 per 1,000 employees in the three months to July, the highest since the start of the year and the first increase since the three months to February.

A lackluster labor market has so far eased nerves among most BOE rate-setters, as it reduces the chance of second-round inflation effects seeping into the UK economy. However, concerns over the outlook for prices are mounting after oil prices climbed above $109 per barrel on Monday. Traders increased their bets on rate hikes, pricing in as many as five by the end of next year.

UK government bonds fell at the open, with yields on 30-year notes up four basis points to 5.93%, already the highest since 1998. The move was in line with European bonds, which extended losses as oil prices continued to rise.

The UK’s youth unemployment crisis, a top priority for the Labour government, has deepened over the summer. The jobless rate among 16- to 24-year-olds rose to 16.4% in the three months to July, the highest since 2014, reversing a slight dip in the previous period.

items.title: BYD's $34,000 Chinese SUVs Are Stirring Up German Automaker Angst
body: These are bleak times for European auto workers. Job loss announcements are coming thick and fast, with Volkswagen AG cutting 100,000 employees and Jaguar Land Rover Automotive Plc axing roughly 10% of its staff. Life is also tough for suppliers.

The industry’s difficulties are wide-ranging: excessive costs, uncompetitive products, declining demand in China and Donald Trump’s trade war are all denting profitability. But one can’t ignore the elephant in Europe’s car market: Sales by Chinese brands are accelerating fast, which will force incumbents to slash prices or lose market share.

Previous attempts by Brussels to stem these imports haven’t worked. Unless Beijing curtails its massive trade imbalances, governments here will have to offer domestic automakers more protection. And they need to get on with it — while this continent still has a car industry to save.

To be clear, I’m no fan of protectionism. In the past I’ve spoken up for consumer choice and the benefits of competition. Chinese vehicles are typically of high quality and provide value for money; advanced features tend to be included in the standard price rather than costly extras. And while tariffs can protect domestic sales, they do nothing to address a lack of overseas competitiveness.

European automakers are now working harder on reducing costs and launching their own lower-priced electric vehicles. Mercedes-Benz Group Co. is even calling for a longer working week — tantamount to heresy in labor-friendly Germany.

Yet I worry these efforts, while necessary, won’t be enough because China’s production costs are so much lower. Workers there earn less, and their employers profit from economies of scale and components being made in-house. The nation’s automotive sector has also benefited from government subsidies and an undervalued currency.

Weak demand among Chinese consumers has turned the world’s biggest car market into a competitive bloodbath beset by overcapacity. With their domestic sales under pressure, BYD Co., Chery Automobile Co. and others have expanded overseas — BYD’s international revenue now exceeds what it makes at home.

I’m not alone in having a change of heart about the so-called China Shock 2.0: German companies, once fierce free-trade advocates due to their reliance on exports, appear to be edging toward a more critical view of Chinese trade practices. The German government is currently preparing a comprehensive package of measures to safeguard strategic industries, possibly including tariffs on imported Chinese hybrid vehicles, Bloomberg News reported this week. Berlin is working with Paris to build support for a common position within the European Union, ahead of talks with Beijing in October.
Even the VDA German car industry lobby is reviewing its previously accommodating stance. Perhaps that’s because German automakers now have less to lose if China retaliates, as this chart indicates.

In July, VW boss Oliver Blume called for a “level playing field” vis-à-vis China, highlighting plug-in hybrid imports and “made in Europe” incentives as areas Brussels should focus on. Meanwhile, Italian lobbyists are calling for import quotas, with much higher tariffs imposed on Chinese shipments above those limits.

The concern is understandable. Chinese brands are expanding at an astonishing speed. They accounted for 10.7% of western European auto sales in the second quarter, up from just 3.4% in the same period two years earlier, according to Schmidt Automotive Research. Left unchecked, their EU share might reach 30% by 2035, according to Harald Hendrikse, an analyst at Citigroup Inc. However, protective legislation could help limit their advance and make the continent’s automakers “investable” again in the eyes of big money managers, he argues.Schmidt Automotive Research is less pessimistic, forecasting Chinese automakers market share will peak at 14% in 2029 in western Europe, thanks partly to more competitive vehicles from incumbents.

I agree — and for an indication of what might happen otherwise, look at the UK. Lower trade barriers and weak consumer loyalty to European brands have meant one in every six vehicles sold in Britain is now made by a Chinese company.British car buyers are likely more open-minded because there are fewer domestically-owned mass-market car brands and thus fewer "patriotic" purchases.

For now, manufacturers including VW, Stellantis NV and Renault SA that are focused on the cheaper end of the market have the most to lose, along with Japanese and South Korean brands. But I think it’s only a matter of time before premium automakers such as BMW AG and Mercedes get squeezed, too. Xiaomi Corp., whose designs echo those of Porsche AG and Ferrari NV but cost much less, is expected to begin selling in Europe next year, including in Germany.

So far, the EU has pursued a comparatively lenient approach towards Chinese car imports, when you consider how the US has effectively barred them via a combination of tariffs and technology regulations. Although Brussels targeted Chinese EVs in 2024, the maximum additional 35% levy was far less punitive than Washington’s 100%. (Back then, Germany opposed penalizing the Chinese.) And Chinese manufacturers found a workaround: They started shipping a lot more hybrid vehicles, as these are only subject to the bloc’s standard 10% import duty.

Beijing seems to recognize its automakers need to cool things down: It published new guidelines earlier this month urging them to avoid overly aggressive pricing overseas. But Chinese brands don’t need to offer dumping prices to undercut the local competition.

BYD’s Seal U DM-i SUV can be purchased for as little as €29,500 ($34,000) once the manufacturer’s discounts and German government sales incentives are included, well below its list price of around €45,000.Until recently the BYD list price was closer to €40,000. The discounted price is based on a cash purchases including the maximum government subsidy. Germany’s subsidies are targeted at lower-income households. The government offers up to €6,000 for EV purchases and €4,500 for plug-in hybrids, with the amounts depending on the number of children and household income.A VW Tiguan with an equivalent powertrain can cost thousands more. No wonder this BYD model is the top-selling plug-in hybrid across Europe and in Germany.

It feels self-defeating for Berlin to subsidize Chinese imports. But we’ll probably see fewer inconsistencies once European governments adopt a plan known as the “Industrial Accelerator Act.” Although the details are still being finalized, the legislation would require car manufactures to use local assembly and components before benefiting from public procurement, purchase subsidies and other financial support. Company fleets account for roughly 60% of Europe’s new vehicle sales, so the IAA is potentially quite an effective tool.

If the upshot is Chinese automakers build more vehicles in Europe, including via joint ventures with local peers, that seems like a decent compromise. BYD and Chery are already setting up factories in Hungary and Spain, respectively.

Obviously Europe still needs to tread carefully. China has ample scope to retaliate given its dominance in batteries and rare earths. But if Europe allows its industrial capabilities to be hollowed out, it won’t get them back. Even Germany is starting to recognize the status quo isn’t tenable.

items.title: What's at Stake for Putin in Russia's Duma Election?
body: Russians are set to go to the polls to elect a new lower house of parliament for the first time since President Vladimir Putin ordered the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

There’s little doubt about what will be the broad outcome of the Sept. 18-20 vote as the Kremlin maintains a tight control over the election campaign. The ruling United Russia party, which presents itself as the party of Putin, faces no realistic prospect of losing the majority it has held in the State Duma for 23 years.

Nonetheless, the election will provide an indicator of the public mood at a time when ordinary Russians are increasingly feeling the economic and social consequences of Putin’s yearslong war in Ukraine.

As Russia’s elections are stage-managed by the Kremlin, the upcoming vote is less a political contest for Putin and more about whether the result can be harnessed to demonstrate his regime’s resilience and cement a narrative of stability.

None of the parties running in the election are in opposition to Putin, even as some criticize the government or accuse United Russia of inaction on key issues. Parties often tailor their campaign messages to tap voter discontent on particular issues without ever assigning blame to the president. The Kremlin also scrutinizes candidates ahead of the election to ensure only acceptable contenders make it into parliament.

The main challenge for the Kremlin is to ensure a high turnout as voter apathy would be viewed as a signal of popular discontent. Turnout in the 2021 election was around 52%, according to the Central Election Commission. Government and local officials typically resort to what’s called the “administrative resource,” pressuring state sector workers and employees of major companies to go to the polls to avoid punishment.

The Kremlin will also be looking for a high level of support for United Russia to use as a vote of confidence in Putin’s leadership. Putin isn’t officially a member of a political party but he has aligned himself more directly with United Russia than in recent years. He attended the party’s conference last month, while United Russia has branded itself as “the party of the president” and its campaign slogans include “being for Putin is the basic minimum.”

There are signs that Russians are increasingly weary of a war that is now in its fifth year and that they’re concerned about the economic consequences. The economy is under pressure from massive government spending on the military, persistent inflation, high interest rates and low growth. In August, Russia’s central bank cut its forecast for GDP growth in 2026 to 0%-1%.

The war is becoming a more visible part of everyday life as Ukrainian drone attacks target Russia’s oil refineries, factories and e-commerce warehouses, as well as ports and ships in the Black Sea. The refinery strikes have pushed up gasoline prices and triggered widespread fuel shortages and rationing, meaning Russians in many areas are lining up for hours to fill their vehicles.

Putin has acknowledged that Ukraine’s strikes “inflict economic damage” but has insisted that Russia’s offensive will continue. There are limited options for Russians to voice any desire for change. With independent media shut down and prominent opposition figures mostly imprisoned, in exile or barred from running for office, there’s no organized political force inside Russia campaigning for an immediate halt to the war. Harsh repression of even mild criticism of the regime and its war effort means there’s little incentive to show anything but unwavering support.

There’s no public debate over whether Putin was mistaken to start the war or of the massive casualties and economic damage that Russia has incurred. Nor are candidates advocating for a halt to the fighting in Europe’s worst conflict since World War II on any other terms but Russia’s victory.

Instead, the parties running have made promises to raise living standards, maintain social spending and curb price increases for essential goods. They’re also competing to present themselves as the most patriotic and supportive of veterans, focusing on issues such as social and medical benefits for soldiers who have fought in Ukraine. Some parties have included veterans high on their list of candidates, seeking to capture support from millions of families whose relatives have fought in the military.

Russia plans to organize voting in the territories it occupies in eastern and southern Ukraine, including parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, as well as Crimea. Voting in these places will be tightly controlled by Russia’s security services.

The Kremlin is using this election to try to reinforce Russia’s territorial claims as it continues to wage a campaign to erase Ukraine’s presence in these regions. Putin annexed Crimea in 2014. He’s also laid claim to the entirety of the other four Ukrainian regions, even as his forces have never managed to fully occupy them.

The Duma possesses formal constitutional powers that include initiating and passing legislation, approving the state budget and confirming the appointment of the prime minister and members of the government. In practice, the chamber is firmly under the Kremlin’s direction, approving bills that are often handed down by officials and ministers with little or no detailed scrutiny.

Still, members of the Duma, known as deputies, do occasionally give a voice to public anger on issues such as the cost of living and rising prices, tightening internet restrictions and poor standards of social services.

United Russia currently holds a constitutional majority with 310 of the Duma’s 450 seats. That means it’s been able to pass any constitutional amendment or key legislation without support from anyone else.

Russians are electing deputies to the Duma for its next five-year term. The new Duma will be sitting when the next presidential election is due to take place in 2030, when Putin could seek a sixth term in office.

The Communist Party is the second-biggest faction in the Duma and has 56 seats right now. Its campaign declares pride in the legacy of former Soviet Union leader Joseph Stalin and backs the war in Ukraine, as well as a return to Communist-era health and education services.

Three other parties currently hold seats: the nationalist Liberal Democratic Party, the left-leaning Fair Russia Party and the New People party, which presents itself as pragmatic and business-friendly.

These four groups are collectively known as the “systemic opposition” because they’re permitted by the Kremlin to offer limited criticism, even as they very often vote with United Russia on key issues. They effectively serve as a “safety valve” for the public to vent discontent, without challenging United Russia’s dominance.

One prominent opposition party outside parliament, Yabloko, declared it would run an anti-war election campaign and its “for peace and freedom” slogan even called for an end to the conflict. The Kremlin initially appeared willing to allow Yabloko on the ballot, figuring it would have a poor showing and that this would bolster the claim that Russians remain fully behind Putin’s war.

But that calculus changed and in August the Supreme Court kicked Yabloko off the ballot in response to an application from a pro-Putin nationalist party that alleged violations of election law. One of Yabloko’s leaders was also sentenced to 11 years in prison.
The election campaign has otherwise been so lacking in drama that live televised debates in some regions were canceled because none of the candidates showed up.

items.title: Eastern Europe Is Outshining West in Region's New Bond Order
body: Investors are increasingly looking east as they seek out the best opportunities in Europe’s sovereign bond markets.

Bulgaria, Hungary and Lithuania are among the top picks thanks to an improving economic and fiscal backdrop, as well as the yields on offer, a combination that’s harder to find among their western neighbors. Political regime change and growing adoption of the euro, which comes with stringent economic requirements set by Brussels, further boost the investment case.

The increasing appeal of central and Eastern European countries is part of a historic shift in Europe’s debt market that’s been playing out over the past decade, where the distinction between once-troubled economies such as Spain and Portugal and supposedly safer nations like France and Germany has gradually been eroded.

“The only European debt I hold is Eastern European debt,” said Dickie Hodges, manager of the $2.5 billion Nomura Global Dynamic Bond Fund. Government bonds from Eastern Europe account for 15% of the fund, the highest in his career, he said.

The hunt for attractive sovereign debt is all the more important right now because government bonds around the globe are slumping, weighed down by stubbornly high inflation, a flood of new corporate offerings that are competing for investor cash and concerns over budget deficits.

Hodges singles out Bulgaria, which he argues should yield less than Triple-A rated German bunds — historically regarded as the region’s safest asset. “From a debt perspective, it’s in a much stronger position than most of core Europe,” Hodges said of Bulgaria, which adopted the euro this year.

A Bulgarian 10-year bond rated BBB+ by Fitch yields 4.40%, almost 90 basis points higher than the equivalent German security. The country has a debt-to-GDP ratio of about 30%, less than half the European Union average, and steady growth.

It’s not just Bulgaria that’s won over bond managers who have the flexibility to invest anywhere in the world. James Ringer at Schroders Plc says Hungary is his top pick out of all sovereign markets globally. At MFS Investment Management, Annalisa Piazza holds Lithuanian debt to help anchor her portfolio during bouts of volatility.

“We’ve had some overweight in some smaller euro countries, like Lithuania for example,” Piazza said. “It has been a very good trade. You get some spread. For these markets, the fundamental picture is relatively robust. They suffer much less when the markets are volatile.”
Latvia and Lithuania are the best-performing euro-denominated bonds this year, based on a Bloomberg index tracking sovereign debt. France and Belgium bring up the rear, with losses around 3%.

Southern nations such as Italy and Portugal were once market pariahs, having nearly collapsed under the burden of their debt in 2011. But investors piled into those bond markets as years of painful austerity paid off, alleviating debt burdens and triggering a cascade of credit rating upgrades.

That’s whittled away the value on those bonds, leaving investors casting a wider net in the hunt for attractive yields. In Spain, for example, the 10-year yield premium over Germany has plunged from 640 basis points in 2012 to just 45 basis points now.

“We still think there are parts of Europe you can have continued convergence; Greece is a very obvious one,” said Schroders’ Ringer. “But certainly Hungary for us provides much better opportunities than a lot of European government bond spreads.”

Hungary exemplifies some of the main attractions of Eastern European debt. An April election ended 16 years of nationalist rule under Viktor Orban, ushering in a new administration that is seeking to meet criteria for euro adoption by 2030. As part of that process, it’s aiming to cut the budget gap to 3% of gross domestic product by 2030, from an expected 7.5% now, and the central bank is taking a harder stance on inflation.
The amount of Hungarian bonds and bills held by foreign investors reached a record high in July, according to data from the debt agency compiled by Bloomberg.

“We have seen that demand has been really invigorated, foreigners are constantly looking for Hungarian debt securities,” said Janos Samu, deputy chief executive officer of Budapest-based brokerage Concorde Securities Ltd.

The region as a whole is growing in importance to the EU, emerging as a growth engine and key pillar in NATO’s defense against a hostile Russia. “The Europe we knew when the single currency was formed in the 1990s bears very little resemblance to today,” said Nomura AM’s Hodges.

The trajectory of Eastern Europe contrasts sharply with the decline of some of the region’s biggest economies in the eyes of bond investors. They’ve soured in particular on core EU nations like France and Belgium, where the outlook is worsening after successive governments failed to rein in public spending or generate growth.

French 10-year bond yields now exceed Germany by 96 basis points, the most since the euro area’s sovereign debt crisis in 2012. Political divisions have prevented the government from cutting spending and reining in the deficit, with the gridlock likely to endure beyond next year’s fraught presidential election. Further declines in its credit score are likely.

To be sure, investing in Eastern Europe comes with challenges, from local currency fluctuations to shallower bond liquidity. Landlocked countries like Hungary are also especially exposed to the energy shocks buffeting European debt more broadly. In many parts of the region, debt levels and deficits remain high.

There’s plenty of idiosyncratic risk, too. Romania, mired by surging debt and political paralysis, is years off the euro adoption it seeks. That hasn’t deterred Franklin Templeton’s head of European fixed income, David Zahn, who holds Romanian bonds alongside notes from Bulgaria and Poland.

“There are some issues, but the advantage I see of this area of Europe is you get paid for taking some of the risk,” Zahn said. “The markets can be a little bit more volatile, but I think that as long as you are focused on it and size your position right, it is a great diversifier.”

items.title: NATO Shoots Down Drone That Entered Lithuanian Airspace
body: NATO jets shot down an unidentified drone that flew into Lithuanian airspace from neighboring Belarus, the latest incursion on the alliance’s eastern flank amid rising concerns of Russia’s war on Ukraine spilling over into Europe.

“Even though the war seems to be taking place a thousand kilometers away from Lithuania, its scale is still large and extensive,” Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas told national broadcaster LRT Tuesday. “Russia’s unwillingness to come to peace negotiations affects the security of the Baltic region.”

The drone was intercepted five kilometers from a hydroelectric power plant near Pratkunai in central Lithuania, state energy company Ignitis Group said. Air alerts sounded over the capital Vilnius and the country’s second-largest city Kaunas before the drone was brought down. The Lithuanian military later found and neutralized explosives at the site, Kaunas said on social media.

“Once we have traced the drone’s flight path, we will be able to determine clearly whether this was a Russian drone — potentially a provocation — or a defensive drone belonging to another country,” Kaunas said after a meeting with his Italian counterpart at Siauliai airbase, where the Italian jets that intercepted the drone are stationed.

Tuesday’s downing was the first time NATO intercepted a drone over the territory of Lithuania and followed similar incidents in Latvia and Estonia in recent months. Intensifying exchanges of air attacks between Ukraine and Russia are turning into a growing issue for NATO members as drones are jammed or veer off course.

NATO jets downed a drone over Latvia in August after it entered the country’s airspace as a result of Russian electronic warfare. A Romanian F-16 shot down a suspected Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May.

Tuesday’s incident was also the second drone sighting over the Baltic nation in three days. On Sunday, an unidentified object authorities suspected of being a drone entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus before crossing into Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad.
It came after Warsaw said Monday that the Polish military retrieved a Russian military drone from the Baltic Sea near the town of Rusinowo.

The flurry of aerial incidents coincided with a US diplomatic mission to Minsk. A delegation led by Special Envoy John Coale traveled from Vilnius to Minsk for talks with President Alexander Lukashenko on Tuesday, state-run news service Belta said. Coale visited Belarus several times since 2025, brokering the release of hundreds of political prisoners while Belarus gained some relief from US sanctions.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys told reporters on Tuesday that his ministry would summon the Belarusian ambassador over the incident.

European officials have warned Russia may escalate sabotage and covert attacks against the continent as Moscow struggles to make progress in its war against Ukraine that’s now in its fifth year. Earlier this month, Germany attributed an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport to Russian intelligence.
The Danish military said on Monday that a Russian warship fired flares toward a Danish helicopter as it was carrying out the “routine” task of taking photographs.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the incident serious but not surprising, describing it as a “pattern we’re seeing across Europe with an increasingly aggressive and assertive Russia that’s intensified its hybrid war against Europe and is testing and challenging NATO.”
Read More: Europe Struggles to Counter Russian Attacks Falling Short of War

Meanwhile, Dutch railway infrastructure agency ProRail said Tuesday that materials were found deliberately placed on tracks at multiple locations across the Netherlands, severely disrupting some train services that morning.
“Sabotage appears to be involved,” ProRail said.

items.title: Japan Eyes Defense Spending at 3.5% of GDP After US Pressure
body: Japan is considering a new mid-term defense spending target of 3.5% of GDP in line with NATO and other US allies, a move that could send a shockwave through financial markets concerned about Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s spending plans.
Japanese defense officials have already signaled a willingness to sharply increase defense spending in meetings with their US counterparts, according to people familiar with the matter.

One scenario under consideration is to match a commitment made by South Korea to increase defense spending to 3.5% of gross domestic product over 10 years, according to the people. A lower target, such as 3%, is also possible, according to one of the people.
Responding to the news, Japanese Defense Ministry Press Secretary Kimihito Aguin denied that Japan had expressed an intention to the US to sharply raise spending to 3.5% of GDP.

“Japan’s defense buildup is something we undertake based on our own independent judgment, under the fundamental principle that we must defend our own country ourselves,” Aguin said at a press conference Tuesday. “It is also not a matter of starting with a predetermined spending figure. What matters is the substance of our defense capabilities.”

Like other US allies, Tokyo has been under pressure from the Trump administration to boost its defensive strength and reduce its reliance on the American military. Takaichi has already accelerated defense spending to almost 2% of gross domestic product in the financial year ended in March this year, two years ahead of schedule.

Until 2022, Japan had an informal cap on defense spending around 1% of GDP, an indication of how quickly thinking on defense has changed in recent years. A new five-year defense spending plan is expected at the end of this year. Committing to 3.5% could unsettle market players wary of large debt issuance, even though Takaichi has pledged to follow a “responsible, proactive fiscal policy.”

Japanese defense shares IHI Corp and Kawasaki Heavy Industries Ltd closed 1.8% and 0.9% higher in Tokyo, reversing earlier losses of more than 2%, after the report came out. Japanese government bonds extended their fall, with the benchmark 10-year yield rising to its highest level since 1996. The yen weakened as far as 155.24 to the dollar.

“There are fiscal concerns, as shown in the bond market reaction, so it’s difficult for investors to take news like this positively,” said Daisuke Aiba, an analyst at Iwai Cosmo Securities Co. “Plus, there are questions about whether Japan actually has the ability to expand its defense capabilities beyond their current limited scope.”

Borrowing costs for the Japanese government were already elevated, with bond yields hovering near three-decade highs. The benchmark 10-year note’s yield hit 3% earlier this month for the first time since 1996, driven by concerns over inflation and fiscal spending as well as expectations the Bank of Japan may need to raise interest rates more quickly. The yield was half that level around this time last year.
US defense officials have largely avoided public pressure on Japan to commit to a 3.5% defense spending goal, but they have made clear that they expect significantly more investment.
“We are anxiously looking for Japan to step up,” US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby said last month of Tokyo’s defense spending.

In June, Takaichi’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party noted that 3.5% had become a global standard for defense spending, but didn’t provide recommendations on how Japan could pay for such a level of outlays.

“We’ll review both spending and revenue across the board,” Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said Tuesday. “While keeping a close eye on tax revenue, we’ll determine a level of fiscal spending — including, of course, defense spending — that is consistent with steadily bringing down the debt-to-GDP ratio.”

In meetings between defense officials from both nations, Japan has indicated it will most likely align with other US allies but it has avoided discussing details, according to the people, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.

Some Japanese officials have said they aren’t ready to make a formal pledge and would deny the existence of such a goal if it was made public, according to these people. In public, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has also said spending will be determined by military needs rather than monetary targets.

Behind Japan’s caution over specifying a goal is concern over the amount of funding needed to reach 3.5%. When Japan set its 2% goal in 2022 it said it would continue to measure spending in comparison to GDP that year. Koizumi said in April that defense spending and related expenditures for this fiscal year of ¥10.6 trillion ($68.8 billion) were equivalent to 1.9% of nominal GDP in 2022.

Measured against the Cabinet Office’s nominal GDP forecast for this fiscal year, spending would come to 1.5%, he said. A budget of 3.5% using that forecast would amount to ¥24 trillion, more than double the current amount.
Spending 3.5% of GDP on defense has become a global benchmark for US allies since North Atlantic Treaty Organization members pledged last June to reach that level by 2035.
As a national security hawk and strong advocate of the US-Japan alliance, Takaichi has made clear she wants to further boost the military.
“Japan needs to proactively pursue a fundamental strengthening of its defense capabilities,” she said in parliament this year.

But she also has ambitious plans for the economy. This year Takaichi announced a growth plan targeting more than ¥370 trillion in combined public and private investment by 2040, a program that may strain the nation’s finances. Ramping up defense spending at the same time may test investors’ confidence in Japan’s ability to keep a lid on its debt.

After lifting its informal cap on defense spending in 2022, Japan has made significant investments in long-range strike capabilities such as land and ship-launched Tomahawk missiles. In its budget request for the fiscal year starting next April, the Defense Ministry requested a record ¥8.9 trillion for the next fiscal year, up 0.9% from the current year.

But many items in the budget request haven’t been given a projected cost, meaning the final budget is likely to be much higher. Yen weakness has also eroded Japan’s spending power for weapons from overseas.
Read more: Japan Seeks Record Defense Budget as Takaichi Plans Buildup

Even if Japan commits to 3.5%, it would lag behind NATO countries. For NATO, the target is for so-called “core” defense spending, such as weapons and troop salaries. Members have also pledged an additional 1.5% of GDP for defense-related spending, such as protecting critical infrastructure.

Japan bundles core and non-core spending in its defense budget, meaning that it would be spending less on its military as a percentage of GDP than NATO countries even if it raised defense outlays to 3.5% of GDP.

Robert Ward, Japan Chair at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said the groundwork had been laid among policymakers and bureaucrats in Japan for a big jump in defense spending. It’s now mostly a matter of timing of when Japan goes to 3.5%, he said.
“Whether it’s over five years or 10 years, I don’t see any alternative given how important the US alliance is,” Ward said.
