items.title: US 10-Year Yield Rises to Highest Since 2007 as Fed Looms
body: The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest in almost two decades, the latest milestone in a bruising global bond selloff driven by booming capital investment and soaring energy prices that are exacerbating inflation.

The yield, which serves as a benchmark for borrowing costs across the globe, rose as much as five basis points to 5.04% on Tuesday, the highest since 2007, before wrapping up the New York session at 5.00%. The jump came after oil prices jumped anew on concern that crude supplies could be further choked off as the war in the Middle East widens.

The bond slump raises the stakes ahead of the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision on Wednesday, when investors expect officials to raise short-term borrowing costs for the first time since 2023. If they don’t hike, or if Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is noncommittal about additional increases, traders may demand even higher yields on long-term bonds to safeguard their investments against the risk that inflation will remain elevated.

“It would be very difficult for the Fed to leave rates unchanged this week without eroding its inflation-fighting credibility,” said Vail Hartman, a strategist at BMO Capital Markets. “The market is vulnerable to not only an unexpected hold, but also a dovish hike that entails a more patient takeaway from the dot-plot or press conference.”

Bond yields have been rising globally since the US and Israel launched an assault on Iran in late February, disrupting the supply of Middle Eastern oil and gas. That’s on top of other factors such as massive corporate borrowing to fund artificial intelligence spending, which is both flooding markets with debt and pumping stimulus into an already resilient US economy.

It also comes as the amount of debt governments issue continues to rise, both to refinance maturing bonds and to fund deficit spending. Central banks are no longer hoovering up government bonds as part of their quantitative easing programs, and demand from other traditional buyers is cooling — resulting in a greater reliance on more price-sensitive investors.

“The scope for long-end yields to fall is somewhat limited given that we don’t see signs of weakness in the real economy and supply/dynamics in the Treasury market are very different relative to 2007,” Phoebe White, head of US rates strategy at UBS Group AG, said via email. “Structural demand for US Treasuries, particularly among foreign official investors, is materially weaker.”

A Bloomberg gauge of returns on Treasuries has declined around 1% since the start of the month, and is down 1.6% this year. Around a third of fund managers surveyed by Bank of America Corp. identified a disorderly rise in bond yields as the biggest “tail risk” to the market, ahead of an AI bubble or second wave of inflation.

The drop in US government bonds is part of a broader global move that’s seen Germany’s 10-year yield rise to the highest since 2009, while Australia’s equivalent rate touched a 15-year high. Bonds in Japan also retreated Tuesday.
An auction of 20-year Treasury bonds at 1 p.m. New York time drew the highest yield in data going back to 2020, when the US reintroduced it. Demand fell short of expectations despite the lofty yield.

In the US, the rise in the 10-year rate is particularly important because it serves as a baseline to price other loans such as mortgages. That makes its rise a headache for President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent having previously said that lowering 10-year yields was a key goal of the administration.

Tuesday’s selloff is the latest assault by bond bears on the 5% level, a closely watched threshold. Such round numbers are often seized on as key pivot points that can catalyze decisions by investors and policymakers.
Some speculate that investors in other asset classes will be tempted to lock in roughly 5% annualized returns for the next decade, potentially diverting cash away from the stock market.
“Through 5%, it starts to get worrisome for risk assets,” said Jesse Marre, a senior portfolio manager at Hilbert Group.

The worry for bondholders is that there aren’t enough dip buyers to quell the jump in rates, perhaps because energy prices keep rising or should the Fed disappoint. In that scenario, the cost of borrowing for the US government — and by extension anyone seeking US dollars — could enter a trading range not seen in a generation.

“Could things get even more sinister? Yes, where a break above 5% on the 10-year yield does nothing more than bring 6% into focus,” said Padhraic Garvey, head of research for the Americas at ING Groep NV. “Such a journey from 5% to 6% would be a far tougher one for the wider market to stomach.”

items.title: Rapid Rise of AI Is Changing How Business School Students Are Learning
body: For all the year-to-year movement — or lack of movement — in our annual business school rankings, one development sweeping through MBA programs could ultimately prove quite consequential: the rapid rise of generative AI.

What began as a curiosity just a few years ago has quickly become an imperative, raising fundamental questions for deans and faculty: What do MBA students need to learn about artificial intelligence? Should professors use it in the classroom? What rules should govern it? What kind of and how much AI proficiency will employers expect?
It’s worth considering what this year’s rankings tell us about business schools more broadly first.

A quick scan of the results — 98 full-time MBA programs around the globe qualified this year — might suggest that little has changed since last September. For the eighth consecutive year, Stanford Graduate School of Business holds the top spot among the 66 US programs. And notably, Stanford again ranks No. 1 in Entrepreneurship — one of the four indexes in our survey along with Compensation, Networking and Learning — also extending that streak to eight years.

Comments from recent graduates and alumni help explain the appeal. Many point to the school’s proximity to the technology and startup ecosystem as a draw. One graduate noted that several in their cohort founded their own companies and that “relatively few classmates are pursuing consulting, banking or private equity.” That entrepreneurial pull is present across the MBA universe. Launching and leading a business (or buying one) is increasingly seen by graduates as the path that allows for more self-determination and even more stability in a volatile job market.

Compensation remains the most heavily weighted of the four indexes. On that measure the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania comes in first, for the second consecutive year. Wharton graduates reported a median base salary of $185,000 across industries, along with a median signing/starting bonus of $30,000. Two-thirds of the graduates of the Class of 2025 for whom Wharton reported employment data went into finance or consulting — the two industries that continue to offer the highest pay. As appealing as starting a business is to MBAs today, most grads still pursue jobs in these and other critical industries, such as tech and healthcare.

Among the notable moves in this year’s rankings: Texas A&M’s Mays Business School jumped 19 places, to No. 22. The school posted significant gains in both its Learning and Networking index scores, with higher survey scores from recent graduates and alumni. Reactions from Mays’ 2026 grads explain the improved Learning score: One described the faculty and learning environment as “genuinely top-notch,” adding that many classes “went far beyond just academics and really changed how I think.” Another wrote: “I enjoyed the diverse group of people I worked with every day. From the cohort to the professors, the MBA was by far the best year of my life. I was learning and growing constantly while making connections that will genuinely last for life.”

Those results and comments point to something that can be easy to overlook when focusing on rankings: Students value not only what they learn but also how they learn it — and from whom they learn it. This will be even more crucial as AI becomes embedded in the MBA experience.

Lee Newman, dean of Madrid’s IE Business School, says he believes AI will lead to a radical rethinking and redesign of graduate business education. “We need to make bets now on what jobs and sets of skills will decline, what ones will grow and what new ones will emerge,” says Newman, a professor of behavioral science and leadership. “Those bets dictate directly what critical changes we need to make to curricula to prepare students for jobs that are changing at lightning speed.”

Despite the apparent urgency, many of the highest-ranked schools — including Wharton and Kellogg — don’t make AI a required part of their core curriculum. Some schools are getting students acclimated to the technology early. At Wharton and Duke University’s Fuqua School of Business, for example, short, mandatory intro-to-AI sessions are now part of the schools’ preterm or orientation sessions.

No matter what’s happening officially, in class and on campus, students say they’re relying on AI more and more in their coursework. In a typical week this academic term, 53% of recent graduates we surveyed for this year’s rankings said they used some form of generative AI (ChatGPT, CoPilot, Claude, etc.) for their schoolwork at least five days a week.

If AI can provide information, generate analysis, evaluate cases and perform some of the work that helps students develop business judgment, what parts of the MBA experience will become even more important? If the responses from recent graduates to our survey question “What did you like best about your program?” are any indication, the clear answer is the human component. Comments naturally mention the highly regarded faculty, networking events and access to certain special programs. But the real standouts are the comments about community, camaraderie, close and supportive cohorts, and engaged faculty … things that, so far, no AI bot can replicate.

items.title: Denmark Says Russian Warship Fired Flares at Helicopter
body: Denmark’s military said a warship from Russia fired flares toward a Danish helicopter, the latest sign of worsening tensions between the two countries.

The incident took place Monday in international waters in the Baltic Sea south of Denmark, the Danish Armed Forces said in a statement. One of the two flares passed the helicopter at close range, the military said.
Denmark’s Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen called the incident “completely unacceptable,” saying it could have put lives at risk. He has summoned Russia’s ambassador for talks over the matter.
“Russia is gradually pushing the boundaries of what it considers acceptable behavior,” Rasmussen said in an emailed comment, adding that Denmark will not tolerate that.
The episode comes amid intensifying tensions between the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and Russia, with the latter seen carrying out more and more hybrid attacks on European soil and waters.

Russia’s ambassador in Copenhagen, Vladimir Barbin, said the country will “thoroughly investigate all the circumstances of the incident” but accused Denmark of carrying out “dangerous maneuvers” near Russian warships and blamed Danish forces for communication failures. He said Copenhagen had repeatedly rejected Russian proposals for an agreement aimed at preventing incidents at sea.
“Regrettably, the Danish side has no interest – nor has it ever had any – to prevent the situation at sea from escalating and to implement confidence-building measures,” Barbin said by email.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the incident was “very serious” but “unfortunately, it is not surprising.”

“It is part of the pattern we are seeing across Europe, with an increasingly aggressive and assertive Russia that has intensified its hybrid war against Europe and is testing and challenging NATO,” she said. “Russia wants to intimidate and sow division.”

Denmark, one of Ukraine’s biggest financial and military donors, has repeatedly warned about a growing risk of hybrid attacks and pointed to Russia as Europe’s biggest security threat. Earlier this month, Denmark’s security agency said it had uncovered evidence that Russia was planning acts of sabotage against Danish defense companies.
Read More: Denmark Warns Russia Plotted Sabotage, Berlingske Says
The Danish Air Force helicopter had approached the Russian frigate to carry out a “routine” task of taking photographs, the military said in the statement.

items.title: Moody's to Buy Minority Stake in Philippine Credit Rating Agency
body: Moody’s Corp. has agreed to acquire a minority stake in Philippine Rating Services Corp. as the global credit ratings firm looks to tap the growth of debt markets in the Philippines and across Southeast Asia.

Terms of the transaction weren’t disclosed. Moody’s said Manila-based PhilRatings’ local market expertise and credit ratings complement its global credit views for investors in the Philippines, according to a statement.

Moody’s highlighted the growth potential of the region’s debt markets. Domestic corporate bonds outstanding across the Asean region are more than twice the size of cross-border holdings, while the Philippines has more than $100 billion of planned infrastructure investment over the next three years, it said.
Moody’s said it will be the first global credit rating agency to invest in a domestic ratings firm in the Philippines.
Following Moody’s investment, PhilRatings will continue to operate independently with its own management, governance and credit rating processes, according to the statement.

items.title: Why Food Prices Are Rising in India, From Onions to Cooking Oil
body: For a snapshot of India’s rising food costs, look no further than the traditional thali, the ubiquitous set meal that puts many of the country’s everyday staples on a single plate.

Those ingredients are taking a bigger bite out of household budgets. Food accounts for almost half of monthly spending for some rural families and   nearly 40% in cities. Onions, a foundation of countless savory dishes, have risen almost 50% from a year earlier. Vegetable oil used for frying street snacks is also rising, and the ginger vital for flavor has surged more than 70%, the latest consumer price index for August shows.

Several factors are at play: The annual monsoon has been weaker than usual, leaving farms thirsty. A push to increase biofuel production for energy security diverting grain. Plus, wars in both Iran and Ukraine are boosting crop and fuel prices globally.That’s made food — which comprises more than a third of the retail inflation basket — emerge as a key driver of the country’s inflation, with the broader rate in August nearing the top of the central bank’s target range. It could also offer a signal of what’s to come elsewhere, as many nations cope with the fallout of conflicts and extreme weather, exacerbated this year by   El Niño.
“In a connected world, supply is not an issue, but there will be issues with prices,” said Madan Sabnavis, chief economist at Bank of Baroda.

The monsoon rains, which end this month, are one of the obvious signs of the issue. Precipitation since they started in June is running 15% below normal, and the weather office has forecast rains to remain subpar in September. The shortfall is linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, which is known for spurring drier years in the country.

That could further dim the harvest outlook for crops from rice to soybeans, corn and sugar cane. Rice and corn plantings are running more than 3% behind last season, with little time left, and domestic sugar prices jolted higher in August on worries of a shortfall. That forced the government to allow a tranche of duty-free sugar imports, an unusual step in a country that ranks as the world’s second-largest producer. During years of deficient monsoons, every percentage point shortfall in rainfall versus normal equates to a roughly 25 basis point increase in food inflation, according to Yuvika Singhal, an economist at QuantEco.

Meanwhile, onion crops in key grower Maharashtra were damaged by unseasonable rains in March, reducing yields, according to Jaydatta Sitaram Holkar, a member of one of the state-run wholesale markets for farm commodities in the state.

Wholesale prices should start softening when the new crop arrives next month, but rising transport costs are also keeping retail rates high, Holkar said. Ginger supplies have also tightened ahead of the next harvest, although fresh supplies are expected in December and January, said V. Srinivasan, head of crop production and post-harvest technology at ICAR-Indian Institute of Spices Research.

Biofuel policy is playing a role, as well. The country pushed forward a 20% ethanol-blending target originally slated for 2030 to 2025, driving a nationwide expansion across thousands of fuel stations. The policy has increased demand for corn and rice as feedstocks alongside sugar cane.
That could further tighten domestic supplies for food and feed, with farmers likely to sell crops to ethanol makers first if it fetches them a higher price, Sabnavis said.

For Ajaz Azam Qureshi, a chicken and egg seller in Mumbai’s suburbs, feed prices for the live birds he buys daily have doubled in the last month. He has raised prices to 260 rupees ($2.74) a kilogram, from 240 rupees, even as the holy month of Shravan subdued demand for meat. But the rally could increase as the sacred period has just ended in Maharashtra, with Qureshi planning to raise prices to 300 rupees ($3.20).

“I have to protect my margin, but the price rise forces customers to cut consumption and there will be a slump in business,” Qureshi said. “If the feed prices do not come down, however, we will not be able to lower chicken prices.”

Key dairy items like paneer — a soft cheese — and milk are more expensive, too, Central Statistics Office data show.Preparing food has also grown costlier. India faced shortages of liquefied petroleum gas relied on for cooking earlier this year due to conflict in the Middle East. Shivam Fauzdar, who runs a small restaurant in the New Delhi suburb of Noida, said he raised prices after the initial surge in LPG, but with ingredient costs now climbing, he’s struggling to raise menu prices further. The business competes with half a dozen nearby food carts that offer flatbreads with a serving of vegetables or lentils at lower prices.
“We can’t raise our rates because customers will stop coming,” he said.

The situation will be particularly in focus as India’s festive season gets underway around this time, culminating in Diwali — the Hindu festival of light — in November. The period is known for an uptick in food consumption, with sugar and cooking oil demand peaking as people consume more traditional sweets, fried food and other treats.

Food inflation has accelerated each month this year, and the rise will have ramifications for interest rates as the country’s central bank targets headline consumer price inflation, according to Sabnavis. Broader inflation accelerated in August to the highest since December 2024, exceeding the Reserve Bank of India’s 4% medium-term target for a third straight month.

The central bank, which has flagged El Niño as a key risk to food prices, has kept rates unchanged since the start of the year. Economists increasingly see a greater chance of an interest-rate hike as early as October.
Inflation "is not so benign” anymore, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said in a recent interview with CNBC TV18.

“We also need to be watchful as the risks of higher food, fuel and other input prices translating into a broad-based increase in inflation and de-anchoring of expectations persist,” he said in the minutes of the RBI’s August meeting. “Any evidence of these risks materializing may need policy tightening.”

items.title: How AI Is Changing the Skills MBA Students Need to Learn
body: On Nov. 30, 2022, OpenAI introduced the world to ChatGPT, the latest version of its generative artificial intelligence software. In Philadelphia,  Ethan Mollick, the professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School who’s become something of an evangelist for AI in the classroom and beyond (his latest book, Co-Existence: The Next Phase of AI, comes out in October), was waiting. The program’s precursors, Mollick says, “wrote really good middle school essays, but they weren’t very good for anything beyond that.” But GPT-3.5, packaged as a chatbot speaking natural language, promised to be different.

He showed it to the undergraduates in his Entrepreneurship class at Wharton four days later. By that point, the students were deep into their startup projects for the course; one was building a tool that mimicked the talking paintings in the wizarding world of Harry Potter. He quickly left Mollick’s demo behind. “He told me that he stopped paying attention about halfway through, and at the end of the class showed me that he had completed the project.” It was the same in Mollick’s MBA class: “Everybody stopped what they were doing.” Weeks later he famously published a syllabus for the upcoming semester that required students to use AI for some projects.

Mollick may have been the first to embrace AI, but business schools large and small, public and private, prestigious and not, have raced to deploy it wherever and however they can — to accelerate and expand the analyses done in class, to assist in research and field questions outside of class, to provide feedback to students and teachers alike—even as more people elsewhere call for an AI slowdown. According to a recent report by the AI integration consulting firm Inspire Higher Ed, working with the Association to Advance Collegiate Schools of Business, UCLA’s Anderson School of Management now operates “roughly 25 to 30 production agents,” comprising “class tutors, classroom simulations, career-coaching agents, and a master capstone assistant that calls out to at least a dozen subagents.” All of which, the report says, puts Anderson “among the most advanced” in AI deployment of the 84 schools it surveyed.

Business schools understand, of course, that AI is on the cusp of transforming how their students will work after graduation. A study published in July found that the latest AI software already does a decent job at solving case studies across a broad range of business disciplines — though performance has lately leveled off. “This is a work in progress for all business schools and all educators, says co-author  Karim Lakhani, of Harvard Business School. “Just as math instruction learned how to adapt to the calculator, we all now need to think through how widespread availability of these AI models impact all aspects of what we teach — and how we teach it.”

And that’s just the work they do now. AI opens up a world of data analysis at a scale that would have been unfathomable just a few years ago, says Tiago Torrent, a linguistics professor at the Federal University of Juiz de Fora in Brazil. “There are tasks that humans could not do without AI — AI can find patterns that it would take us a lifetime to,” he says. “And when we’re talking about that, then teaching gains a whole new shape.”

Yet the work is fraught. To those who study how people learn, the more students let artificial intelligence do the thinking, the less thinking they’ll do for themselves — an intuitive principle that psychologists call cognitive offloading. At the same time, AI makes it harder to tell if students are actually learning anything at all — ChatGPT and its cohort can render obsolete many of the sorts of assessments professors have relied on for decades. “No one asked for this to happen,” Mollick says. “But this is kind of where we are, and there’s some very good things and very bad things about AI in education, but most of the good things require us to take action to implement. And that’s really the challenge.”

Perhaps just as important as the question of what business schools should teach about AI is what you might call its obverse: What current teaching does AI render obsolete? Do students still need to know how to determine the size of a market? Project discounted cash flow? Develop a strategic plan? Do a regression analysis?

Businesses and B-schools alike assume machines will eventually do much of that work, even if they don’t yet in the real world, where the data is often imperfect and in disharmony. For MBA graduates, “once they leave here, most of their time won’t be spent on production, it will be spent on specification and verification of models produced by AI or someone else,” says  Michael Roberts, vice dean of Wharton’s MBA program.

The problem for businesses, and businesses schools, is that AI remains deeply fallible. Large language models are probability machines, predicting what words are most likely to appear next, based on patterns detected in the massive amount of text they’ve ingested. That includes all of the misjudgments that people are prone to make in their language, and the models have no way to judge what’s logical from illogical, what’s apt from inapt, or what’s proper from improper, says Torrent, who is developing models that incorporate linguistic theories to better understand meaning. The latest models, as Mollick notes, no longer routinely hallucinate, making up scenarios out of whole cloth, but they still often leap to ungrounded conclusions, and as currently configured, Torrent says, always will.

“Effective verification requires enough domain knowledge to identify faulty assumptions, omitted stakeholders, weak causal claims, numerical errors, and incomplete recommendations,” conclude the authors of the paper on business case studies. Schools try to inculcate curiosity and skepticism in AI work. Under their professors’ guidance, students repeatedly pick apart AI results, comparing them against both traditional analyses and the work of other models. At Carnegie Mellon’s Tepper School of Business and Madrid’s IE Business School, students are tested on process as much as substance. “You can ask them, ‘Where did you get the resources, why did you choose those and no others, and why do you think that reasoning is right or wrong?’” says Cristina Fernández Tesoro, IE University’s executive director on strategic partnerships. “The process is built in the skills. It’s not only the result. It’s not only ‘Give me the answer’ but ‘Tell me, how did you get to that answer?’”

But how do you become expert enough to supervise the work of others if you don’t do the work yourself? “People who are less proficient at performing a specific task are more likely to rely on AI help,” says Tiago, “but they are precisely the ones for whom it’s going to be harder to spot AI slop.” For business schools, the authors of the case study paper say, “the instructional burden may therefore increase rather than decrease because students must learn both how to perform core analytical work and how to supervise AI-generated work.”

Experts in learning suggest a formulation for using AI tools in the classroom based on the learning objective. “Foundational” lessons, they say, should be largely free of AI, so students can master basic concepts. Successful learning requires “productive struggle.” But when those concepts become secondary to some other lesson, bringing in the machine makes more sense. It’s the difference, says Michelle Darnell, a business ethics professor at the Penn State Smeal College of Business, between “the building blocks that everybody needs and how we effectively, efficiently apply them.”

Schools, though, are loath to tell teachers how to teach. For this story, Bloomberg Businessweek interviewed eight professors who are setting or guiding AI policy at seven schools. (Most also serve in their school’s leadership.) The furthest AI policy goes at most of those institutions is requiring professors to clearly disclose how AI can be used for each assignment, following schoolwide categories. Darnell supports faculty freedom to set their own expectations in the classroom. Still, she says, “faculty benefit when there is an overarching culture that they can rely upon to support their convictions about responsible AI, and it is more likely that students will develop good habits if there are clear, baseline expectations managed at the college level.”

There are exceptions. In Spain, IE does set AI guidelines based on these learning objectives. HBS takes a blunter approach, having long banned most technology in class (except, of course, when technology is the subject). And several top schools seem to have embraced this principle in practice, if not formal policy. Few professors at the Duke University Fuqua School of Business are using AI in core courses, according to  Scott Dyreng, senior associate dean for innovation. Wharton’s Roberts says students in his finance class do the same number of “reps” — problems and cases — in the traditional manner as they did before AI, “supplemented with AI reps.”

But other schools take a very different approach. The University of Notre Dame Mendoza College of Business has woven AI into a broad swath of the MBA curriculum, including basic concepts, says  Nicholas Berente, senior associate dean for academic programs. “I think people are making much ado about nothing,” says Berente, who spent decades in IT and now studies it. Cognitive offloading, he points out, has happened throughout human history as new technologies solved old problems. To demonstrate this, Berente pulls from his shelf a chrome-plated sextant, a once-ubiquitous tool used by sailors to help them navigate by the stars. Sextants were eventually replaced by radio and satellite systems. (In fact, sailors in the US Navy and Merchant Marine, among others, still learn to navigate by stars, in case modern equipment fails them.) Already some software developers are offering programs that incorporate AI and deliver trustworthy, verifiable results, Berente says, and that trend will continue.

It’s more important, Berente says, that students learn the principle underlying an analytic technique than any particular process. “These AI tools are going to be part of their lives going forward. So it’s our obligation to incorporate those in whatever you call primary and secondary lessons. It’s incorporated in both. It’s incorporated in everything.”

Of course, schools have no control over what students do on their own time—and many professors privately assume their students are spending that time feeding their homework to a bot. Often enough, schools encourage this. At Harvard, where the business case study originated, “AI is enabling students to be more prepared to go into class, for sure,” says Mitchell Weiss, faculty chair for technology and transformation. Lately, Weiss has begun experimenting with distributing case studies in formats designed to make that off-hours AI use “more Socratic.”

Lakhani, co-founder and chair of Harvard’s AI Institute, says that, early on, he discovered ChatGPT could correctly infer what kinds of questions he’d likely ask about a case. “The case discussion gets better, deeper, faster because the obvious stuff has been covered already, and the students know this,” he says. “So our job as faculty is to really crank up the rigor in the conversation.” (Weiss, too, has turned to ChatGPT to stoke “much richer, deeper” case discussions.) Columbia Business School has developed a voice-prompted “discussion agent” to pose questions about case studies and other topics in advance of class that’s now used in courses at 25 other B-schools, including those at the University of Virginia and at the  University of California at Berkeley; in Madrid, IE is using a similar tool.

On the other hand, Weiss says, it’s easy to imagine the alternate scenario, in which students turn to AI to spit out “quick answers to the likely questions” — or worse, to simply do the work for them. In a recent survey, more than 40% of students at American University’s Kogod School of Business, which bills itself as an “AI-first” institution, admitted to using AI as “a shortcut or substitute” for their own work, but the real share, of course, is almost certainly higher. (Only 10% of the students thought AI use raised concerns about “academic integrity and loss of originality.”)

“Nothing is personally more frustrating than having to read and grade a pile of papers that I know are largely AI-generated,” says J. Cameron Verhaal, an associate professor at Tulane University’s Freeman School of Business who’s overseeing the school’s AI rollout. Beyond that frustration, instructors are finding it much harder to assess what students actually know about the technology. Verhaal says that for in-class presentations he puts a premium on “a deep understanding of a smaller range of material as opposed to broad coverage of a large one. I find that students who overuse AI in presentation design and generation tend to try and cover too much ground, because AI is so good at neatly packaging large amounts of information, and it becomes readily apparent they are unfamiliar with the content.”

Many of the professors interviewed say some of their colleagues are returning to handwritten essays in blue books — though Lakhani notes, in a wry voice that belies his seriousness, “that won’t last for long, because once you have embedded sensors …” before trailing off. Duke recently piloted a digital proctor for oral exams in its online program: an AI solution to an AI problem.

Schools don’t seem to have any solutions to what cognitive psychologists say could be a more far-reaching, even insidious, effect of AI shortcutting: the abandonment of writing. “Writing is the most important tool we have for thinking critically,” says  David Rettinger, who teaches cognitive psychology at the University of Tulsa. “Critical thinking is a set of skills that allows people to evaluate evidence in order to draw conclusions. Writing is really helpful for that, since it requires the author to organize evidence in a way that is convincing to a reader.”

Almost every professor interviewed acknowledged that students are writing and reading less, a trend many say began well before AI, and that this is compromising learning. It’s an alarm raised across higher education, but an especially bitter irony here, since that’s one thing all B-schools say they’re aiming to develop—and crucial for working with AI. But among these schools, only IE is developing strategies to preserve, or even strengthen, the role of writing, albeit often with an AI assist. As for the other, all American, schools, none have a plan to preserve this skill, apart from enforcing their codes of conduct—sometimes with detection software that many say will soon be outgunned. “We’ve communicated, not just in classes but outside of classes, ­throughout our preterm with MBA students, that a blind reliance on AI is just not going to work once you leave here,” says Wharton’s Roberts. “It’s not going to work in getting a job, it’s not going to work in keeping a job, it’s not going to work in excelling at a job.”

Rettinger says he hopes—though isn’t completely confident—that humans will find an alternative incubator for reasoning if the species offloads the task of writing to the machines. “There will be learning loss until we figure out how to deal with it.” He says schools like Tepper and IE, which are developing routines where students are obliged to articulate and defend all their choices in their AI interactions, and are assessed on them, are taking the right approach. “This is absolutely the cutting edge of AI inflected pedagogy,” he says. But, “it requires a huge investment of resources to develop those activities and assessments and to evaluate both the student and the assessment itself. I’m not sure that any non-elite institutions will be able to afford it at scale.”

When is AI most helpful for learning? Cognitive psychologists say it’s when it encourages thinking without doing the thinking. “That’s the best use of AI,” says  Beth Schwartz, senior director of teaching and learning for the American Psychological Association. “It’s great for helping you generate study questions if you have a test the next day.” Or prepare for a case study discussion.

Increasingly at business schools across the country, AI tutors are answering students’ questions about course material whenever they arise, day or night. Some schools, including Northwestern University’s  Kellogg School of Management, Tepper, and IE, are deploying AI-powered case studies. Students at Tulane’s Freeman practice negotiation and take feedback from an AI-powered simulation.

AI can be particularly potent as a coach. Last Christmas, Fuqua’s Dyreng hatched a plan to have the student teams in his spring taxation class record their out-of-class meetings and submit the transcripts for analysis. Immediately he saw class participation shoot up — more likely because students were forced to meet and debate class topics than because of the feedback. Still, the software made some surprising observations. In one project, for example, after two groups drew opposite conclusions from the same information, “what the team meetings revealed was that both teams anchored on the preference of the person who had developed the spreadsheet to do the analysis.” (AI, Dyreng notes, isn’t the only software with biased antecedents.) “Nobody asked, ‘What were the assumptions underlying your calculation on the spreadsheet?’ The AI team-evaluation tool was nuanced enough to pick that up and give them the feedback.”

Dyreng knew that more students were participating in class because of a separate program that records the class discussion and analyzes not just how much each student speaks but also the quality of their contribution. “The hard part of all of that is how does one actually figure out who said what in a classroom of 75 people,” says Dyreng. “That’s a technology we developed.”

This fall, about a dozen courses will adopt his team-meeting program. Additionally, Fuqua separately sorts entering MBA students into small leadership teams that work together across all their core courses, and it requires all the teams to record their initial meeting, where they develop a charter. Then, Dyreng says, the school sends everyone AI-generated feedback: “Here are the things that you should be thinking about with your charter. Here’s how well you did in talking about those things. Here are some suggestions for what you might want to do moving forward if you want to have a successful team experience.”
But these are the easy wins. The hard work will lie in designing an AI-infused curriculum that can resist the irresistible inclination toward finding shortcuts.

Mollick, at the Wharton School, says that’s his obligation as a professor. “In an assignment where I’m specifically asking people to interact with AI to do something, it’s my job to architect that interaction so that people get things out of it. I actually am less worried about the assignments where I require AI use, because I’ve been thoughtful about how AI is going to be used, and how to make sure it’s being used the right way, and how to have the right scaffolding around it to learn.

“I know what pedagogical techniques I’m applying in each case, and I can make the AI at least square with those things,” he says. “That doesn’t mean they can’t still cheat if they really want to cheat.”

For Dyreng, finding the right balance between easy answers and intellectual rigor is a work in progress. “Last year I thought, ‘I’m the dean of innovation. I’ve got to give these guys access to AI.’” So students in his taxation class got “full access to AI for everything.” Students could ask the chatbot of their choice to teach them everything it knows about, say, individual retirement accounts and apply it to a hypothetical situation. “Then we’re going to come to class and talk about, ‘Why did group No. 1 come up with this recommendation and group No. 2 come up with this different recommendation?’ And that’s what we did, basically every class.”

But this year, he says, “I’m going to pull back about 50% on that. What I found is they just typed in the things I told them to, and they read it, and they were done.” Instead, Dyreng plans to “give them some traditional assignments, mix in some AI, and then help them dig deeper than they otherwise would.
“That’s all I’m really trying to do. In the end, I’m trying to help them get curious and dig deep.”

items.title: China's PBOC Strengthens Yuan Fix Ahead of Trump-Xi Summit
body: China’s central bank strengthened the yuan’s reference rate for a fifth straight day, aiming to offset the dollar’s recent gains ahead of President Xi Jinping’s summit with US counterpart Donald Trump later this month.

The People’s Bank of China set the reference rate at 6.7670 per dollar on Tuesday, marking its longest strengthening streak since December 2025. The rate was 602 pips weaker than the average forecast in a Bloomberg survey. The onshore yuan is only allowed to rise or fall by a maximum 2% from the fixing rate.

The streak highlights Beijing’s effort to cushion the yuan against a rebounding dollar. By guiding the currency gradually higher, policymakers are displaying their intention to limit volatility ahead of the Xi-Trump summit on Sept. 24.

“There may be a mild policy-signaling element ahead of the anticipated Trump-Xi meeting,” said Christopher Wong, FX strategist at OCBC. “A broadly stable, or mildly appreciating, yuan would probably be preferable to policymakers at this juncture, particularly as it avoids adding the currency to the list of potential bilateral tensions.”
The yuan was little changed on Tuesday in both onshore and offshore trading. Bloomberg’s gauge of the dollar rose 0.1%, a day after posting its biggest jump in nearly three months.

“The lower USD/CNY fixing today confirms that the PBOC wants a stable and gradually appreciating yuan going into the summit,” said Dariusz Kowalczyk, head of cross-asset strategy for Asia at BBVA. “I expect the very slow appreciation of yuan at PBOC fixings to continue until the summit.”

items.title: Singapore Home Sales Fall as 'Hungry Ghost' Keeps Buyers Away
body: Singapore new home sales fell in August as developers delayed launches during a period seen to be inauspicious for property purchases.

Developers sold 153 new private units last month, the fewest since February 2024, according to figures released Tuesday by the Urban Redevelopment Authority. That compares with 731 homes sold in July and 2,142 a year earlier.

The drop was widely expected because it was during the Hungry Ghost festival in the seventh month of the lunar calendar. Developers routinely push launches into the weeks before or after the period, which this year began in mid-August and ran through Sept. 10.
The seasonal factor is unlikely to derail Singapore’s buoyant residential market. New home sales in the city-state hinge in part on how many projects developers choose to release.
Prices of private homes climbed 0.5% in the second quarter, slowing from 0.9% in the previous three months.

items.title: AI-Driven Asset Rally Prone to Correction, ECB's Vujcic Warns
body: Soaring market valuations driven primarily by artificial intelligence leave equities vulnerable to a correction, European Central Bank Vice President Boris Vujcic said.

“This is something which we have also not seen, or have not seen for a long time, this kind of price earnings, price to forward earnings ratios,” the Croatian official said in the ECB podcast Euro Matters published Tuesday. “They might in the end, end up being justified, but they might not.”

He warned that “the exposure is large and increasing,” adding that “we have to be very careful, monitor that because with such large exposure, so many investments going there, it creates definitely a risk for the repricing of the equity markets.”

The remarks add to a growing chorus of central bankers, supervisors and investors arguing that leading AI firms might be overvalued and a sudden drop in these values could trigger a broader global market correction. On Monday, ECB President Christine Lagarde also said that asset valuations in the AI sector are very high and a correction is “entirely possible.”

The comments also come at a time when AI developers including Anthropic PBC and OpenAI are clashing with US President Donald Trump’s administration over their calls for an industrywide slowdown in AI development, a proposal that’s already triggered a selloff across technology stocks and has brought into question the resilience of a global data center boom.

In the ECB podcast, Vujcic also listed geopolitical risks, which “can rapidly change the prices, the market attitudes,” and fiscal policy as potential dangers to the financial system as some countries have an “unsustainable fiscal positions in the long run.”
“And we have learned in the past when something is unsustainable, it’s unsustainable,” Vujcic said, adding that it’s better to address these problems sooner rather than later.
“This is something that we have to also monitor very closely because it’s also possible to see the repricing in those markets, which can be relatively rapid,” Vujcic said.

items.title: FTSE Russell Clients Are Asking About Big-Tech ESG Index Changes
body: FTSE Russell, the index arm of the London Stock Exchange Group, has been contacted by clients asking whether they’ll need to cut their exposure to technology investments due to the ethical and environmental implications of the sector’s AI ambitions.

At FTSE Russell, clients are asking whether the emissions of hyperscalers will automatically result in lower weightings in sustainable indexes, according to Lee Clements, head of applied sustainable investment research at FTSE Russell. Some $330 billion in passive investments track FTSE Russell’s sustainable indexes, though the total value of assets benchmarked against such gauges is likely to be much higher.

For now, FTSE Russell says it’s looking at individual technology companies’ exposure to sustainability risks on a case-by-case basis. Where relevant, the index provider “will increasingly change the weighting of one tech company versus another” to reflect such risks, Clements said. FTSE didn’t single out individual companies by name.

“There’s some concern” among clients tracking these indexes, Clements said in an interview. He also says investors worry that reducing their exposure will come at a financial cost after long relying on tech stocks to generate solid returns.
Tech has been on “a pedestal,” and now “is coming off,” he said.
Read More: Amazon AI Build-Out Risks Net-Zero Path, Fund Status on Gas Bet

For the $3.7 trillion sustainable fund market, Big Tech has long been a go-to sector. Unlike companies involved in fossil fuels, weapons or tobacco, tech stocks were treated as a low-carbon and ethically less controversial bet.

But the rapid build-out of AI infrastructure is challenging that notion. AI’s environmental impact, along with its potential to destroy jobs and even go rogue in ways that may harm human interests, have raised questions about the ethical implications of investing in the technology.

Ophelie Mortier, chief sustainable investment officer at Degroof Petercam Asset Management, says regulations are unlikely “to capture the full range of risks associated with AI deployment.” So when analzying companies, DPAM makes what it calls “ethical AI” a “core component” of assessments.
“Unfortunately, many companies developing AI still do not demonstrate these safeguards with sufficient consistency or transparency,” Mortier said in an email.
Read More: Amodei, Altman, Musk Call for Slowing AI Model Development

Sophie Flak, managing partner for sustainability at asset management firm Eurazeo SE, says she finds it “very surprising” that investors haven’t paid more attention to environmental, social and governance risks associated with AI.
“You can’t drink data, you can’t eat data,” Flak said. “You can’t jeopardize your basic needs to have a data center. So I believe it’s a flaw” to ignore the risks of AI, she said.

At Morningstar Sustainalytics, whose scores feed into Morningstar indexes, clients have been asking how the sector’s environmental footprint might affect weightings, said Clark Barr, global head of ESG methodology.

Technology companies “that were previously very focused on renewables” now instead need “to rely on natural gas” to power the AI infrastructure they’re building, Barr said. And that’s “obviously” affecting their greenhouse-gas emissions, with water seen as “another significant issue,” he said.

Investors tracking indexes that claim to comply with European Union requirements are particularly concerned, Clements at FTSE Russell said. Such indexes — which describe themselves as being Paris-aligned or climate-transition-aligned — set strict emissions metrics.
Institutional investors say they’re watching the development closely.

Shipra Gupta, head of responsible investment at Scottish Widows, which manages about $380 billon, says the environmental impacts from technology are “becoming increasingly material” for the fund. “Particularly the energy and water demands of AI infrastructure,” she said.

Scottish Widows is monitoring “whether companies are capturing AI’s productivity and innovation benefits while managing the associated operational, reputational, legal, regulatory and human-capital risks,” Gupta said by email.

Royal London Asset Management, which has £212 billion in assets, says Big Tech companies in its portfolio must show “measurable progress” in cutting emissions. PGGM, which manages $314 billion in Dutch pension assets, said last year that AI’s environmental impact will be routinely reviewed in its ESG analysis and stewardship work.

items.title: Markets Blinked at 5% Yields. They'll Be Back
body: To get John Authers’ newsletter delivered directly to your inbox, sign up here.

For weeks, there have been fears that a 5% yield on Treasuries, the most important number in global finance, could be a “tipping point.” Once the psychological level was breached, the worry was that selling would take hold and yields would surge higher.

The tipping point, made famous by a book by Malcolm Gladwell, is an infuriating concept, because it’s impossible to know in advance what point will cause a market to tip. But in this case, it looks like another Gladwell tome might be more relevant: Blink. Traders went through 5%, saw what they had done, and in the blink of an eye took it back down again. The subtitle of Blink is The Power of Thinking Without Thinking, which seems about right; in this case, we witnessed trading without thinking. At least until we hear from the Federal Reserve on Wednesday, there isn’t the appetite to take the cost of long-term money above 5%:

We’ve established that a preponderance of people still think a guaranteed 5% yield from a very safe investment is a good deal. There’s room for argument about why yields have risen as far as they have, but it’s plain that shifting expectations are more important than anything else. That turnabout has happened steadily, and it’s easy to lose sight of it.Twelve months ago when the Fed, still under Jerome Powell’s chairmanship, cut the federal funds rate down to 4%, the assumption was priced that it would drop to 3% or below by the summer of 2027. Since then, the rate itself has reduced to 3.5% — but futures now imply a return to 4.5% by next summer:

The war in Iran is of course the single biggest driver of this. A major energy shock automatically made it harder to cut rates, while the surprising intensification of the conflict in recent days has brought crude prices back above $100 per barrel. But there’s more to it than that, and new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s speech at Jackson Hole managed to push up the expected terminal rate for federal funds by a full half-percentage point. Exclude energy, plainly driven by forces beyond the Fed’s control, and inflation was 2.5% last month, as low as it’s been since early in 2021.

Briefly, once the Fed embarks on tightening, it generally continues for a while, and yields continue to rise, generally by more than a percentage point. Judging by history, as surveyed by Deutsche Bank AG’s resident financial historian Jim Reid, we should brace for the 10-year yield to reach 6% before the Fed is done:

If this is a real tightening cycle, as markets believe, Monday’s bounce from 5% will be thoroughly overcome in the fullness of time. As Reid shows, there’s plenty of historical precedent for yields to rise this much, and this selloff does not seem to be driven by worries about Uncle Sam’s ability to pay. Growth in nominal gross domestic product (it’s more usually cited in real terms, taking out inflation) is a strong driver of 10-year yields, as this chart from Michael Howell of Global Liquidity Indexes shows:
Although it doesn’t feel like it, nominal gross domestic product is growing about as fast as it ever has since the 1980s, once the extreme distortions caused by the pandemic shutdowns are excluded:

So we had better assume that this is the start of a tightening cycle, and not just the removal of one of last year’s “insurance” cuts when the labor market briefly seemed to be drifting into trouble. What should we then expect of stocks?

The answer is less negative than might be thought, because most tightening cycles happen when nominal GDP is rising — good conditions for share prices. But rate hikes would clearly imply that the US stock market should be flat at best for the rest of this year.

This chart from LPL Financial looks at S&P 500 performance after the start of the last six Fed hiking cycles. The March 1997 round, in yellow, is an outlier as on that occasion the Fed, in the wake of Alan Greenspan’s “irrational exuberance” speech, decided to hike only once — the sole time that’s happened since the fed funds rate was adopted as the main policy instrument in the early 1990s. If Warsh were to announce that this week’s hike will also be “one and done,” that would imply big stock returns ahead (as well as major ructions for bonds), but it’s probably wiser to look to the other cycles:

The overall message is reassuring. A year into a hiking cycle, the stock market is almost invariably up, with 2022 — when the Fed started a long way behind the curve — the only exception. The reason is that a central bank generally doesn’t hike unless it needs to. It’s during rate-cutting, usually as the economy is tipping into a recession, when the market damage can be done.

That said, there’s always the risk of a policy error. And the levels of government indebtedness, after more than a decade of being able to borrow at rock-bottom rates, are higher than in previous incidents. A rise in short order to 6% — which is quite plausible — would put that under strain, while also forcing traders to confront yields that hadn’t been seen this century:
This won’t be the last test of 5%. There’s nothing inherently unhealthy in yields going considerably higher while growth is strong, but markets will need to see that to be convinced.

Demands for guardrails around artificial intelligence aren’t new. Within a year of ChatGPT’s debut, major tech chief executives warned of the need for greater regulation. Events since that meeting with US Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer only reinforce the case, even as money pours into AI.

That incident was dismissed as an abundance of caution. But the market can no longer brush aside CEOs’ concerns about the potentially apocalyptic effects of frontier large language models (LLMs). In recent months, Anthropic PBC and OpenAI have both reported that AI models they’re training have broken free from controlled test environments and gone rogue. The latest global selloff in chipmakers suggests that investors are at last taking notice:

But this increasingly looks like an ideological or cultural battle. President Donald Trump responded to the calls for a slowdown by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei by belittling such concerns as “a SICK conspiracy.” With the S&P 500 down 2.4% from its all-time high a month ago, however, investors appear to be taking this seriously — even if there is no great market alarm.

There would be winners. Monday’s 3.2% rally for the S&P 1500 software index showed that some investors believe a slowdown in AI development could be a lifeline for companies most threatened by it. Fears that AI would upend software business models have given rise to the SaaSpocalypse phenomenon:

Beyond Trump’s pushback, the broader question is whether these companies can reach a consensus on their own. Makers of frontier models appear to be caught in a prisoner’s dilemma, the famous game-theory thought experiment showing that two rational actors may fail to cooperate even when doing so would be in their mutual interest. None wants to slow down if the others keep going; all prefer to decelerate, if someone can ensure that there are no free-riders.

Then there are geopolitics, on which Trump prefers to focus. Any pause that does not involve China would risk ceding America’s advantage, giving AI skeptics a high bar to clear. Noah Smith, who writes the Noahpinion newsletter, argues that coordinated restraint could also hurt the incumbents’ bottom lines by giving upstarts a chance to catch up. Bank of America’s Justin Post notes that such concerns have so far damaged sentiment about AI, notably for the hyperscalers.

Much of the more than $200 billion revenue backlog at Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. is tied to spending by the leading AI labs, which are themselves burning cash they don’t yet have. A slower pace of training for the models could delay revenues even further. Post further notes that slower development of proprietary models could allow open models — mostly from China — to narrow the gap. That would put even more pressure on hyperscalers’ margins and infrastructure spending.

Thus a slowdown could easily undermine the technology’s lofty promise even before it’s had a chance to mature, which makes it all the more significant that the major players plainly want it. To quote Smith, “The fact that they’re still calling for a slowdown, in defiance of their own financial interests, is a clear sign that their worry about human extinction is sincere.”

A deceleration in AI can have devastating consequences elsewhere. BNY’s Geoffrey Yu notes that for many economies, AI is one of the few investments to make a genuine contribution to growth. Any sudden slowdown, without obvious substitutes, could be felt well beyond the sector.

If there’s a silver lining, it concerns inflation pressures — which will likely prod the Fed into hiking this week. The AI complex adds to supply constraints and inflation pressures, while its borrowing adds to the upward push on Treasury yields. For these concerns, an AI deceleration might ultimately prove welcome. But Yu cautions that engineering a fall in inflation without triggering a hard landing will be difficult adjustment. The apocalypse may not be at hand, but it’s a difficult situation.
—Richard Abbey

Amy Winehouse would have turned 43 today, if she had not died at 27. Her story is heart-rending, but the music she left behind before the addictions took over is enduring. Personal favorites include: Rehab, Valerie, Back to Black, and Tears Dry on Their Own. Just to zoom in on her vocal talent, listen to her covering Don’t Go to Strangers, I Heard It Through the Grapevine, All My Loving, and Will You Still Love Me Tomorrow.

items.title: Petredec to Hire Gas Traders in Europe as It Expands Beyond LPG
body: Petredec Ltd., the Singapore-based energy and shipping firm, plans to build a team of liquefied natural gas traders in Europe as it expands beyond its core liquefied petroleum gas business.

The company is looking to hire as many as four people across London and Monaco, including traders, originators and shipping specialists, as well as about two additional staff in Singapore over the next 12 to 18 months, Chief Commercial Officer Jonathan Fancher said in an interview.

Petredec’s new LNG entity, Endeavour LNG, was added to the European Union’s ACER register of wholesale energy market participants in August, paving the way for the company to trade in European wholesale energy markets.

Europe’s shift away from Russian pipeline gas after the invasion of Ukraine has increased the region’s reliance on LNG, requiring more of the fuel to be shipped over longer distances and creating opportunities for trading and shipping firms. Greater price volatility and a more liquid spot market have also attracted new players seeking to profit from buying, selling and transporting the fuel.

Petredec is a major trader and shipowner in LPG, a fuel widely used as cooking gas, with about 30 vessels and a large distribution business in Africa and India. LNG requires specialized vessels because it is transported at extremely low temperatures.

As it expands into the market, Petredec plans to control physical LNG supplies and initially use chartered ships to transport the fuel, with the potential to eventually own LNG vessels, replicating the model it has developed in LPG.
“As the business grows, we would look to move into owning LNG shipping assets, similar to what we have done in LPG and ethane,” Fancher said.
Vineet Aggarwal joined Petredec at the start of 2026 as managing director of LNG to lead the development of the new business.

items.title: Tata Sons' Listed Shareholders Rally After RBI Renews IPO Push
body: Tata Group companies with minority ownership of Tata Sons Pvt. jumped, bucking a broader market decline, following Indian banking regulator’s refusal to exempt the conglomerate’s holding entity from a rule that requires it to go for a public listing.

Tata Chemicals Ltd. led the gains, rising as much as 20%, the most since 2009. Tata Investment Corp. jumped 10.4%, while Tata Motors Passenger Vehicle Ltd. rose as much as 6.3% before paring gains. Tata Capital Ltd.’s dollar bonds extended losses as credit investors focus on potential changes to the group structure.

The Reserve Bank of India has rejected Tata Sons’ plea to surrender its status as a shadow lender, according to people familiar with the matter, signaling it expects the the company to comply with rules for such entities, including an initial public offering.

While investors in the past too have cheered developments that appear to bring Tata Sons closer to an IPO, a listing is far from assured. The closely-held company has resisted going public and could continue to pursue options to avoid that outcome, potentially setting up a yearslong tussle with the central bank.

Shapoorji Pallonji Group firms Afcons Infrastructure Ltd. and Forbes & Co. also rallied as much as 20% each intraday. The SP Group owns an estimated 18.37% of Tata Sons and has been exploring ways to monetize about 7% of its holding.

A potential listing would “unlock significant dead capital long carried at nominal book value across listed Tata entities,” said Deven Choksey, managing director at DRChoksey FinServ. He estimates Tata Sons could be valued at about 12.5 trillion rupees ($131 billion).

Seven listed Tata Group companies together own about 11.94% of Tata Sons, a stake worth roughly 1.49 trillion rupees at that valuation, according to Choksey’s calculations. Investors have previously viewed a potential listing of the company as an opportunity to unlock the value of those investments.

Meanwhile, Tata Capital’s recently issued $400 million dollar notes, due January 2030, fell for an eighth straight session to a record low of 98.79 in Singapore, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

The moves reflect “increased hawkishness around the US rates outlook, coupled with uncertainty over the implications of a potential Tata Sons listing,” said Hemant Mishr, chief investment officer at S CUBE Capital. “Investors are reassessing the extent of implicit sponsor support and potential event-related risks, including any restructuring that could have credit implications.”

Tata Sons falls within the RBI’s so-called upper-layer non-bank lender category. Complying with the rules would mean that it will have to seek an IPO. The company has long resisted a public listing, citing the additional compliance and disclosure requirements it would entail.

items.title: China Media Dismisses Amodei's 'Self-Serving' AI Safety Call
body: Chinese state media accused leading US AI executives of using calls for slower development of frontier models to blunt competition from China, describing the push as a “self-serving” effort to preserve American dominance.

An editorial published Monday by state-owned China Daily said recent remarks from AI leaders in the US show how restrictions aimed at limiting China’s AI development are shifting to software after curbs on chips and equipment had failed to stop companies in the Asian nation from building competitive models.
It said calls by Anthropic PBC’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk to moderate frontier AI development amounted to a “coordinated play” intended to preserve US dominance.

“The proposed coordination among the three companies sounds rather like a club whose membership rules have been drafted before the guest list is announced,” China Daily said. “A global AI-safety framework that excludes China is not quite global.”

Over the weekend, Amodei called for easing the pace of AI development while urging tighter curbs on China’s model makers to maintain the US lead, citing concerns that a Chinese advantage in the technology could “pose grave danger” to the world. Both Altman and Musk backed his slowdown proposal.
Read More: China Rejects AI ‘Fearmongering’ After Amodei Urges Slowdown

In response, the country’s Foreign Ministry criticized the tech executives’ calls. “Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve the interests of no one,” said Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun.
The China Daily article added to criticism from Chinese state media of warnings sounded by US AI executives, even as Beijing highlighted some similar technological risks.

China on Monday released an updated AI safety governance framework to address emerging risks as the technology evolves. The document, authored by an official cybersecurity standards-setting body, said AI was showing a tendency toward “recursive self-improvement” — the same dynamic cited by Amodei in his 3,800-word essay in arguing for greater caution.

“Whether the speed and direction of technological evolution may exceed human anticipation and control demands attention and vigilance,” according to the report by the Standardization Administration of China, which was drafted under the guidance of the Cyberspace Administration of China.

Gabriel Wagner, a researcher at Concordia AI, a Beijing-based social enterprise focused on AI safety, said what stands out in the latest framework is the increased focus on autonomous AI agents, which now get a whole dedicated section.
“Much of China’s early AI regulation in 2023 focused on what AI says. With the rise of autonomous agents, the concern has expanded to what AI does,” he said.
Chinese cybersecurity stocks extended their rally Tuesday morning. Shenzhen Sinovatio Technology Co jumped as much as 10% on a fourth day of gains, while Topsec Technologies Inc. rose 8%.
The dispute over frontier technology is intensifying days before officials from the US and China are expected to hold AI discussions ahead of Donald Trump’s summit with Xi Jinping on Sept. 24.

“China and the US should cooperate where neither can manage the consequences alone,” the China Daily editorial said. “The planned AI-safety dialogue between the two sides and future high-level exchanges offer opportunities for practical engagement.”

items.title: Japan Bonds Fall on Defense Spending Report Despite Solid Sale
body: Japanese government bonds fell after the government was said to be considering a new mid-term defense spending target equivalent to 3.5% of gross domestic product, adding to fiscal concerns and outweighing support from a solid 20-year auction.

Defense officials have signaled a willingness to sharply increase defense spending in meetings with their US counterparts, according to people familiar with the matter. Bond futures extended losses after the report, while the benchmark 10-year yield rose 4.5 basis points to 3.03%, its highest level since 1996.

The proposal would be a “strong selling factor” for bonds, with no funding source indicated for the additional annual spending, said Katsutoshi Inadome, senior strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset Management. It also shows the Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s expansionary fiscal stance remains unchanged, he added.

Fiscal concerns were already weighing on the bond market. Japan’s ministries have requested a record amount of spending for the next fiscal year, intensifying scrutiny over how the plans will be financed and whether additional bond issuance will be required.

The domestic pressures are being compounded by a global debt selloff. Escalating Middle East tensions pushed oil prices higher, fueling inflation concerns and driving up borrowing costs globally. The 10-year Treasury yield breached 5% on mounting inflationary pressures as well as rising expectations of Federal Reserve tightening at its meeting this week.

The Bank of Japan is also widely expected to raise rates this week, with traders looking to Governor Kazuo Ueda’s post-decision press conference for signals on the pace and scope of further tightening.

The selloff came despite a smoothly received 20-year bond auction. The bid-to-cover ratio was 4.01, compared with 3.98 at the previous sale, and a 12-month average of 3.73. In another sign of robust investor interest, the tail, or gap between average and lowest-accepted prices, was 0.15, compared with 0.17 last month.

While the outcome of the 20-year sale was not as severe as feared, “vigilance remains necessary” given rising oil prices and the spillover of upward pressure on long-term government bond yields in the US and Europe, said Ryutaro Kimura, senior bond strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management. “Consequently, it remains difficult to expect a sustained decline in super-long JGB yields.”

items.title: India Short-End Bonds Fall Most in Four Years on Cash Drain Plan
body: Indian bonds slumped after the central bank said it would sell sovereign notes to drain cash from lenders, adding to the supply of debt in a year when the market is already under pressure from record government borrowing.

Yields on five-year notes jumped as much as 22 basis points, the sharpest rise since May 2022, outpacing an 8-basis-point increase in benchmark 10-year yields on Tuesday as domestic bonds joined a global selloff. The rupee also weakened, with the central bank stepping in to support the currency as higher oil prices strained the country’s public finances. Indian markets were closed on Monday for a public holiday.

The Reserve Bank of India late Friday said it would drain 1 trillion rupees ($10.5 billion) from lenders through bond sales, its strongest effort yet to soak up surplus cash in the banking system that poses inflationary risks. The additional supply is worsening the bond-market outlook just as high oil prices stoke inflation risks and raise the chances of an RBI interest-rate hike next month. Federal borrowing of close to 8 trillion rupees is lined up over the next six months, when bond sales by provinces are typically heavy.
The selloff in shorter debt was more pronounced as the additional supply through the RBI’s sales is largely of notes maturing in three-to-six years.

“The decision is the most stringent action the RBI has taken so far and the logical casualty has been the five-year segment, which was richly valued,” said VRC Reddy, head of treasury at Karur Vysya Bank Ltd. “I expect the yield curve to flatten further as short-end yields climb.” The gap between the five- and 10-year yield may stabilize around 20-30 basis points, he said.

The RBI has a large stock of government bonds it can sell as it was a large buyer of sovereign notes over the past couple of years. Its holdings climbed more than 40% last fiscal year to about 23 trillion rupees, or about 18% of outstanding central government securities, according to Citigroup Inc. That is significantly higher than usual, the bank said.

Worsening the outlook for bonds, India’s inflation climbed in August, moving closer to the top of the central bank’s 2%-6% target range. With price pressures rising, Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. economist Upasna Bhardwaj said she expects the RBI to raise borrowing costs by 50-75 basis points, with the chance of a hike at next month’s policy review now much stronger.

items.title: Weaker Baht Boosts Thai Export, Tourism Prospects, Official Says
body: The Thai baht’s recent decline is set to bolster the Southeast Asian nation’s exports and tourism — two key drivers of the economy, according to Vice Finance Minister Santitarn Sathirathai.

The baht has weakened about 8% since climbing to a five-year high in January amid broader dollar strength. The decline also came in the wake of Thai authorities clamping down on speculative trading in gold and the relaxation of capital outflow rules.

“The baht has weakened, but it hasn’t weakened as much as other currencies,” Santitarn said in an interview on Monday. “I do welcome some of the weakening that we have seen so far. It would help exporters as well as tourism.”

A weaker baht adds to Thailand’s appeal as a tourism hotspot, while helping its exporters remain competitive in the global market. The Thai currency ranks behind the Philippine peso, the Indian rupee and the Indonesian rupiah in a list of Asia’s worst performers this year.

Thai policymakers don’t target a specific exchange-rate level, and haven’t been forced to respond to the baht’s moves through interest-rate adjustments, said Santitarn, who served on the Bank of Thailand’s rate-setting committee from 2023 until early 2026. He added that the approach has helped the central bank preserve room to act if needed.

Santitarn said the recent steepening of the Thai bond yield curve is driven more by the short end than by rising longer-term yields. Short-term bond yields remain anchored by the Bank of Thailand’s policy rate, which was held at 1% for a third consecutive meeting in August, as well as expectations that the central bank is unlikely to raise borrowing costs even if the Federal Reserve hikes rates, he said.

The spread between two-year and 10-year bond yields has spiked to 106 basis points Monday, up from 93 basis points a month ago, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The yield on benchmark 10-year bonds has risen 67 basis points this year, compared with a gain of about 80 basis points in the US 10-year yield, which hit its highest level since 2023 on Monday.

Thailand’s long-term government bond yields have risen in line with the global market but much less than those in many other countries, Santitarn said. The relative resilience reflects the nation’s macroeconomic stability and its attractiveness to investors, he said.
