items.title: Bitcoin Retreats on US Crypto Bill Uncertainty, Rates Outlook
body: Cryptocurrencies extended losses as optimism waned that a key US regulatory bill will progress this week and as the prospect of higher interest rates weighed on risk assets.
Bitcoin — the largest cryptocurrency — fell as much as 4.5% and was recently trading at around $75,860 on Tuesday in New York. Second-largest token Ether was down as much as 7%.

Crypto markets had rallied in the US on Monday as the odds of the Clarity Act passing this year jumped above 30% on Polymarket, but they fell back to around 20% as Democrats later pushed back on Republicans’ latest offering. US Senator Mark Warner told reporters at the US Capitol that a group of Democratic negotiators would send a counteroffer to Republicans ahead of Tuesday’s pivotal procedural vote on Clarity, the comprehensive crypto regulation bill that has been stuck in partisan wrangling for a year.
“This act should clarify the future of crypto in the US; without it, it remains in the fog,” said Alex Kuptsikevich, FxPro’s chief market analyst.
The bill will need a number of Democrats to cross party lines to advance and move later to final passage thanks to the Senate’s 60-vote rule for most legislation.

“Odds of a 2026 signing sat above 70% in May, collapsed to the low teens through August and rebounded toward 30% on Monday. That is a market with no stable read,” said Rachael Lucas, an analyst at BTC Markets, citing prediction-market odds. Still, “a counteroffer is consistent with a negotiation that is still live, not one that has broken down,” she said.

Shares of crypto-related companies were also hit hard. Coinbase Global Inc. — the largest US digital-asset platform — slumped as much as 8%. Stablecoin issuer Circle Internet Group Inc. dropped more than 8%.

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong — one of the leading industry advocates of the bill and among the biggest US political donors — said in a post on X that the crypto community wouldn’t forget senators who vote no on the measure.

Traders are looking to take profit on some of their gains ahead of the Clarity Act vote, said Damien Loh, chief investment officer at Ericsenz Capital. “While there is little priced in for it to pass, if it does not there is likely to be a small dip,” he said.

The biggest sticking point has been ethics provisions that Democrats have seen as inadequate to prevent President Donald Trump from continuing to profit from crypto after he reported $1.4 billion in income from related ventures last year. But other issues, including concerns from banks that crypto stablecoins could siphon their deposits, have also been the subject of massive lobbying efforts.
Republican senators released a final draft of the bill, with changes addressing some of its most contentious points.

The new version would give the Treasury secretary power to intervene if deposit flight became “detrimental” to community banks. It also added new ethics guardrails for the president and other elected officials holding cryptocurrencies. The new ethics rules would force the president to divest from virtual assets or place significant holdings in a blind trust, or else face financial penalties. It also empowered state attorneys general to play a role in enforcing the ethics rules.

Patrick Witt, the executive director of the President’s Council of Advisors for Digital Assets, suggested in a post on X that opponents to the bill such as the banking lobby weren’t acting in good faith.
Still, for some industry observers, the Federal Reserve’s rate-setting meeting may turn out to be the most market-moving event for the digital-asset market this week.
Markets are now pricing a better than 90% chance of a 25 basis-point Fed hike on Wednesday, swaps data show.
Bitcoin failed to sustain several breaks above $80,000 over the past three weeks and buying demand has weakened recently.

US-listed Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded net outflows of more than $460 million last week, ending a three-week streak of large inflows, while Strategy Inc., one of the cryptocurrency’s largest corporate buyers, has made no purchases over the past two weeks.

items.title: Prabowo's Economic Team Reset Leaves Investors Wanting More
body: President Prabowo Subianto’s economic team overhaul is seen by investors as an acknowledgment that his policies have come at a cost and a signal of a return to more stable policymaking.

By replacing Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa with Suahasil Nazara on Monday, after a similarly sudden leadership change at the central bank, Indonesia has moved to steady two institutions central to investors after months of concern over the direction of economic policy.

Markets showed some initial relief on Monday, with Indonesian equities erasing losses and bond yields holding steady. Stocks fell with regional peers on Tuesday amid inflation worries while the rupiah slipped. Investors and analysts say the personnel changes, while encouraging, aren’t enough to address concerns that have driven about $1.9 billion in capital outflows from Indonesia this year.

The announcements show “there are consequences to the policy prescription over the past 18 to 24 months,” said George Boubouras, head of research, investments and advisory at hedge fund K2 Asset Management. The new appointees “have good CVs” and what markets need is “more open, transparent and credible policy,” he added.

Indonesia’s markets have taken a beating this year  — with its stock index still the world’s worst performer — as Prabowo’s interventionist agenda, the Iran war and fears of an index downgrade to frontier status hammered investor confidence. The rupiah slumped and foreign investors fled, a dramatic turn for a commodities-rich nation long a staple of emerging-market portfolios.

Some of that damage has since been repaired. An off-cycle rate hike by Bank Indonesia and signals of policy continuity from new Governor Destry Damayanti helped spark a rebound. The rupiah has appreciated around 3% from June’s record low, foreign funds have bought local bonds for four straight months and the Jakarta Composite Index has entered a technical bull market.

Indonesia’s challenges are also part of a broader global trend of rising debt, deficits and borrowing costs. That gives investors more choices about where to put their money, making it all the more important to keep them onside.

“The Prabowo administration needs to continue to address investor concerns if they’re going to have any credibility with the financial community,” said Steven Grey, chief investment officer at hedge fund Grey Value Management in the US. “Investors would take the appointment of Nazara as more of a positive if he wasn’t Indonesia’s third finance minister in under two years.”

Nazara brings a familiar face back to the top of economic policymaking. He has spent seven years as deputy finance minister — first under former President Joko Widodo and then under Prabowo — and served under Sri Mulyani Indrawati, the widely respected former finance minister whose ouster in September 2025 rattled investor confidence in Indonesia’s fiscal direction.

His challenge is the same one faced by his predecessors: financing the president’s growth ambitions and expensive social programs, as well as navigating Prabowo’s control over the country’s new sovereign wealth fund, without undermining fiscal discipline. That will require preserving credibility, while shifting spending away from programs that some economist see as having limited payoff.

“Suahasil’s appointment at least eliminates concerns that this strategic position will fall to a politician or a person that is unfamiliar for the markets,” said Liza Camelia Suryanata, head of research at PT Kiwoom Sekuritas Indonesia.

Still, investors will watch how he acts in the role, how independently he operates and how he navigates the government’s political agenda. “Don’t call Suahasil ‘SMI 2.0’ yet,” she added, referring to Indrawati.

For some overseas fund managers, Nazara’s appointment removes a key source of uncertainty. Mark Nash, a London-based money manager at Jupiter Asset Management, bought the rupiah after Bank Indonesia’s rate hike in June and said he would look to buy more of the currency on the news.

“The new finance minister is a known quantity, so markets are on board with it,” Nash said. “The drama of the past looks likely to end. The rate hikes were good, and now this. It’s supportive for Indonesia bonds, and the currency.”

Others want more proof. James Athey, a money manager at Marlborough Investment Management Ltd. who has stayed out of Indonesian bonds, said investors will need more than new faces after months of policy volatility.

“It’s likely that investors want to see more than just personnel changes before they feel comfortable getting back in any sort of size,” he said. “For now I would still be cautious about Prabowo’s policies.”

Describing Nazara as a “safe pair of hands,” Gary Dugan, CEO of Dubai-based multi-family office Global CIO Office, said banks should benefit if investors see the appointment as a positive move, though consumer stocks may struggle if growth slows. Still, the change isn’t enough for him to cover his short position. “We will wait for proof that the fiscal situation is under control,” he said.

That’s where attention will turn next. Investors are watching whether the 2027 state budget, now Nazara’s to shepherd, sticks to the government’s deficit target or slips under Prabowo’s growth agenda. The new finance chief has promised stability and prudence, including keeping the deficit below the legal ceiling of 3% of gross domestic product.

They’re also looking for signs that Bank Indonesia’s new governor can operate with enough independence to serve as a policy backstop, and for more clarity on sovereign wealth fund Danantara’s role in state finances — an area that has continued to worry money managers.

Another test comes in November, when MSCI Inc. will assess Indonesia’s progress on market-access concerns. Regulators have raised minimum float requirements and flagged companies with concentrated ownership, an issue that prompted MSCI to remove some stocks from its indexes in May.
Yet for all the changes, analysts say Prabowo still has the final say on policy.

“We believe fiscal policy will remain prudent, similar to the approach taken by former Finance Minister Sri Mulyani,” said Felix Darmawan, an economist and fixed income analyst at PT BCA Sekuritas. “Nevertheless, the policies ultimately implemented will largely depend on decisions made by the president.”

items.title: China's Taste for Donkey Spurs an Unlikely Trade With Pakistan
body: China’s taste for an exotic meat and a prized collagen is helping seed an unusual business hundreds of kilometers away in Pakistan’s arid southwest.

A slaughterhouse in Pakistan’s Balochistan province is processing hundreds of donkeys for customers in the world’s second-biggest economy. While the meat isn’t consumed locally because of religious beliefs, it’s considered a delicacy in parts of China. But more importantly, the hides are used to make ejiao, a highly valued ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine.
Hangeng Group, which runs the abattoir and processing plants near Gwadar, is betting on growing overseas demand to quadruple daily slaughter to 800 donkeys within months.

“There is massive potential for the donkey meat and hide industry,” Pakistan’s food minister Rana Tanveer Hussain told Bloomberg News in an interview in Islamabad. “This is why we have given permission to 2-3 more Chinese companies to set up breeding farms and slaughterhouses in Gwadar.”

The business could generate about $5 million a month in foreign-exchange earnings within six months, rising to $7 million within two years, Chief Executive Officer Andy Liao said in an interview in Islamabad.

That’s still a fraction of the estimated 2.3 million to 4.8 million donkeys slaughtered annually for their hides to make ejiao, according to a 2023 US Congressional Research Service report, which pegged the Chinese market for the traditional medicine at about $7.8 billion in 2021.

Ejiao is made from collagen extracted by boiling donkey skin. It is commonly used as a blood tonic to treat anemia, as well as to boost immunity and improve sleep. It is also used in cosmetics and is believed to have anti-ageing benefits.

Demand for the gelatin compound is booming in China, but the supply of donkey hides needed to make it is dwindling. China’s donkey population has plunged as millions of the animals are slaughtered each year, driving buyers to seek supplies from Africa and elsewhere.

In 2024, the African Union endorsed a continent-wide moratorium on the slaughter of donkeys for their skins and related exports after an alarming decline in their population. In a June 2025 report, animal welfare organization Brooke estimated that Africa’s donkey population could halve to about 14 million by 2040, if the continent-wide ban on the donkey skin trade isn’t enforced.

Chinese buyers are now seeking newer sources, including Pakistan, Brazil and Australia. The Islamic Republic had also previously restricted donkey hides exports after authorities found the animal’s meat was being passed off as beef and mutton in some cities.
However, the moratorium was lifted a decade later, according to a commerce ministry notification, opening the way for the country to tap into China’s growing demand.

The donkey population in the South Asian nation is growing and exceeded 6 million in 2025, according to the Pakistan Economic Survey, giving entrepreneurs such as Liao an opportunity to build the industry around an animal that has traditionally been used for transport and farm work.

Liao’s company started building the Pakistan facility six years ago and has invested about $50 million so far. It employs nine Chinese managers and roughly 500 local workers, who handle everything from slaughter and packaging to transport. The company briefly halted operations in May, citing bureaucratic hurdles, before resuming business after government approvals.
Hangeng is a strategic partner of China’s biggest ejiao producer Dong-E-E-Jiao Co., according to its posts on social media platform X.

The company sources donkeys from 11 suppliers, with each animal tagged for traceability, and aims to expand to 50 farms eventually. It has so far exported five containers of meat and hides, with its first shipment reaching China’s Tianjin port in June after the government greenlit exports.
Liao plans to expand into breeding and set up a laboratory, before eventually branching into seafood exports.

items.title: Bourses and Brokers May Win From India's Proposed Auction Revamp
body: Stock exchanges and brokers may be among the biggest beneficiaries of the Securities and Exchange Board of India’s proposed changes to the newly launched closing auction system that’s caused chaos, while market makers may face tighter constraints.

That’s the takeaway from market players after the regulator suggested a sweeping revamp of the mechanism that’s spurred wild swings at the end of trading sessions. In a discussion paper released on Saturday, SEBI made several proposals, including to determine the settlement price based on a blend of the 30-minute volume-weighted average price and a 10-minute auction window — or retain the old VWAP methodology for a year before shifting to the blended system.

In either scenario, the eventual price would lean more heavily on the continuous trading session, where the bulk of market activity takes place. That shift could make the closing auction system more predictable and help restore confidence.
Meanwhile, market makers could face a less friendly regime as the regulator suggested restrictions to cancellation orders.

“The proposals are broadly positive for the market infrastructure ecosystem,” said Kruti Shah, a quantitative analyst at Equirus Securities. The changes should make the closing process more orderly and reduce some of the uncertainty that has emerged around price discovery and expiry-day trading, benefiting exchanges and intermediaries other than market makers, she said.
Also read: India’s SEBI Seeks Major Changes to Unpopular Auction System
Shares of listed exchange BSE Ltd. climbed as much as 2% in early trading Tuesday, while those of broker Angel One Ltd. advanced as much as 1.6%. Both stocks erased their gains.

The closing auction system introduced on Aug. 3 was meant to improve end-of-day prices and align India with other major global bourses. Instead, it led to unexpected wild moves at the end of the trading day, both in the equities and derivatives markets, as well as during last month’s MSCI Inc. index rebalancing. The episodes fueled concerns over thin liquidity, the potential for investors to influence closing prices and the difficulty of managing large positions during the short auction window. Calls quickly grew louder for a review of the mechanism that affected well-established trading strategies.

For the exchanges, the impact was clear: In August, the daily notional turnover for futures and options on the National Stock Exchange of India Ltd., the nation’s leading bourse that’s scheduled to list later this month, hit an 18-month low. Meanwhile, shares of listed BSE Ltd. posted their worst monthly loss in a year as the daily notional turnover fell to the lowest since July 2025.

Giving a greater weight to the 30-minute VWAP window would help keep the final price closer to that during the regular session, potentially restoring trust and encouraging trading. Listed brokers and capital-market companies including Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd., Angel One and Billionbrains Garage Ventures Ltd. could benefit.

On the other hand, market makers could be hurt by the potential changes because they would restrict their ability to cancel orders when prices move by more than 1% during the auction. That could leave them stuck with orders placed at outdated prices, increasing the risk of losses if the market shifts before the auction closes.

The move, aimed at making displayed orders more meaningful and limiting the ability of participants to rapidly pull liquidity, could make the firms more cautious about displaying liquidity in the first place, according to Ravi Varanasi, founding partner at SPVR Consultants and former business head at the NSE. A short no-cancellation period before matching may be a better solution, he added.
SEBI is seeking feedback on the suggestions by Oct. 3.

“We believe the CAS overhang is set to ease,” JPMorgan Chase & Co. analysts wrote in a report, upgrading the rating on BSE to overweight. A review of the settlement mechanism and improving market familiarity with the auction can support a gradual volume recovery, the note said.

items.title: ANZ CEO Warns of AI Risks, Job Cuts After Musk, Altman Alert
body: ANZ Group Holdings Ltd. Chief Executive Officer Nuno Matos warned about unpredictable risks linked to artificial intelligence and declined to rule out large-scale job cuts at the bank as it adopts the quickly evolving technology.

“At this point in time, it’s creating risks at a much higher pace than what their own builders and developers were thinking,” Matos said at the Australian Financial Review Asia Summit on Tuesday in Sydney.

“The fact that you see Musk, Dario and Sam saying that they think they have to pull down the pace, it should tell us something very clear,” he said, referring to Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic PBC, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI. The three AI leaders have in the past few days warned about the risks of rapid AI development and even floated a slowing of the pace of model development, drawing a rebuke from President Donald Trump.
“They are saying that the risk of this technology is well above what they expected,” Matos said.

“We all had this dream that AI would come to improve our lives, increase our capacities and capabilities, find cures to many diseases — and that’s true,” he said. But without “enough guardrails and limitations,” it will also lead to dangerous outcomes, he said. “It’ll attack infrastructure,” Matos said.

The bank boss warned about the potentially destabilizing impact of AI adoption on society should mass job losses emerge, and didn’t rule out the possibility of sweeping cuts at ANZ due to AI. Melbourne-based ANZ has around 40,000 staff.
“I don’t know and I think whoever says something that is certain will lie to you — you don’t know,” said Matos. “Nobody knows.”
Rival lender Westpac Banking Corp. on Tuesday made its own case for AI, telling investors that the technology is returning time to its workers.

Five agents operating across mortgages and consumer finance are estimated to remove 250,000 manual activities and free up about 150,000 hours of banker capacity a year, according to a presentation by Andrew McMullan, Westpac’s chief data, digital and AI officer.

The bank put the annual benefit at roughly 100,000 hours from automating payslip and bank statement checks in home loans and about 50,000 hours in consumer finance. Westpac described the figures as estimates of annual benefit.

items.title: Indian Tech Stocks Rally as AI Restraint Debate Boosts Outlook
body: Shares of India’s technology services companies rallied on bets that calls to slow the pace of artificial intelligence development will offer a reprieve for the beaten-down sector, among the earliest casualties of the AI boom.

A stock index comprising Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. and Infosys Ltd. jumped 2.2%, the most since Aug. 28. The rally came after the gauge lost about $226 billion in market value from its peak in December 2024 as AI developers including OpenAI and Anthropic PBC released AI models capable of upending the traditional software and outsourcing businesses.

The call for restraint on future AI development by Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei, also endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk, will prompt short-covering in Indian tech stocks as investors bet that disruption will take longer to play out, according to analysts.

“Any narrative around regulatory restrictions on the use of AI may actually have a positive influence” on Indian IT stocks, said Deven Choksey, managing director at investment advisory firm DRChoksey FinServ. “When the narrative shifts from unchecked development to regulated and responsible use of AI, short-covering backed by fresh buying in frontline IT stocks is quite possible.”
Indian markets reopened on Tuesday after a holiday, giving investors the first chance to react to the AI debate.

Valuations offer another reason for investors to take a second look. The NSE Nifty IT Index still remains about 36% below its record high and is trading at about 16 times its forward earnings estimate, or two standard deviations below its five-year average, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That makes the sector more sensitive to any improvement in sentiment.

“AI slowdown chatter coupled with other macro factors, particularly a steeper yield curve and a stabilizing US dollar, can drive a short-term rebound in India IT services stocks,” said Gary Tan, a portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments. “These factors favor cash-generative companies trading at relatively undemanding valuations, characteristics shared by many large-cap Indian IT services names.”

items.title: Apple's Creepy Comedy 'Widow's Bay' Wins Big at Emmy Awards
body: Apple Inc.’s new comedy-horror series Widow’s Bay was the big winner at the Emmy Awards, taking home a total of 14 trophies, including best comedy.

Matthew Rhys, who plays the mayor of a haunted island town on the show, made history as the only performer to win Emmys in all three of the major acting categories, two of them at Monday night’s ceremony.

Rhys won best comedy actor for Widow’s Bay and best actor in a limited series for playing a real estate developer with a controversial past in Netflix Inc.’s thriller The Beast in Me. He previously won lead drama actor for the FX spy series The Americans in 2018.

Widow’s Bay also won awards for writing, directing and in the two comedy supporting actor categories. Its trophy haul broke the record for most awards for a comedy series in a single year, a milestone set just last year by Apple’s Hollywood spoof The Studio.
HBO Max’s hospital series The Pitt won best drama, and Noah Wyle, who plays Michael “Robby” Robinavitch, the senior emergency physician on the show, took home the best dramatic actor trophy.

The TV industry’s most-coveted awards ceremony was largely a battle between Warner Bros. Discovery Inc.’s HBO Max and Apple’s streaming service. It’s in a way a repeat of last year’s showdown, when The Pitt and The Studio took home the best drama and best comedy awards, respectively. Wyle also won the best drama actor last year.

Going into the evening, HBO Max led all other networks and streamers with 122 nominations. The Pitt garnered 25 nominations, more than any other program. The show was also the most-watched series among those nominated in the drama or comedy categories, accounting for nearly 400 million hours of viewing, according to Nielsen data.
“This is all I’ve ever wanted to do, and this is the only club I’ve ever wanted to join,” Wyle said after receiving his trophy. “Thank you for accepting me.”

Jean Smart, star of the HBO Max hit Hacks took home the best comedy actress award. The veteran actress has now won five Emmys in a row for portraying Deborah Vance, a Las Vegas comedienne trying to stage a comeback. It’s Smart’s eighth Emmy win overall. Hacks had 24 nominations, the most in a single year in the comedy category.

Rhea Seehorn won best actress in a drama for her performance as a novelist who is among the few normal humans left in a dystopian world in Apple TV’s Pluribus. Vince Gilligan, the show’s creator, won for drama writing.

Netflix, which has seen some of its top programs struggle in their second seasons, received 111 nominations overall, a sizable number but down from six years ago when the service scooped up a record 160 nominations. Some shows on the platform that were up for awards include The Diplomat, Nobody Wants This and Beef.

Allison Janney won best supporting dramatic actress for her role in The Diplomat. Sally Field, who won best actress in a limited series for Netflix’s Remarkably Bright Creatures, struck one of the only political notes during the ceremony when she reminded the audience that Canada, where her show was shot, is a friend of the US.

The awards come while the future of Warner Bros. and HBO Max is still in limbo. The company agreed to sell itself to rival Paramount Skydance Corp. in a $110 billion deal that is being challenged in court by 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild. The lawsuits allege the combined companies will have have an outsize level of control over film and TV production and lead to thousands of job cuts. Paramount has promised to increase the overall number of movies and shows it produces.
The awards ceremony was hosted by Law & Order: Special Victims Unit star Mariska Hargitay and held at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.

items.title: Trump's AI Defense Defies Voter Unease Heading Into Midterms
body: President Donald Trump’s opposition to guardrails on artificial intelligence puts him at odds with a growing number of lawmakers from both parties, with AI safety fears adding to voters’ misgivings about the technology heading into the midterm elections.

In a rapid-fire series of social media posts, Trump on Monday belittled a push led by Anthropic PBC and OpenAI to slow work on cutting-edge systems, invoking bombastic language to dismiss existential fears about AI as “a hoax.” Later in the day, he made an impromptu call to Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, who was onstage at a technology conference and put their conversation on speakerphone.

“The robots will not be taking over. AI will not be taking over the rest of the world,” Trump told Huang, who was a featured guest at the All-In summit in Los Angeles. “We have to do things, and we have to do them prudently, but that doesn’t mean we’re going to stop an industry.”
Read More: AI Bosses Clash With Trump on Their Calls to Slow AI Development

Taken together, Trump’s remarks represented his most vigorous defense against attempts to pace the development of a technology that’s central to his economic agenda and behind a historic US stock market rally. Any pause or delay in progress on so-called frontier AI systems would be unwelcome among investors who are betting that the AI boom will drive hundreds of billions of dollars in capital expenditure.

Highlighting the stakes for Trump, who views the stock market as a benchmark of his success as president, shares of chipmakers that have benefited from a surge in AI infrastructure spending slid on Monday, with Nvidia falling 3.4% and Micron Technology Inc. declining 5.3%. In early trading Tuesday, both companies had pared some of the previous day’s losses, signaling that investors didn’t expect a significant pullback in spending on chips and other hardware.

David Sacks, a venture capitalist who served as Trump’s AI czar and is now co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science & Technology, expressed similar ideas in a Bloomberg Television interview Monday. Anthropic and OpenAI are free to slow development of their most sophisticated models on their own if they believe the technology poses serious risks, he said, arguing they don’t need new regulation to do it.
“I don’t really believe this claim that they can’t make their products safe unless the government steps in and imposes requirements on companies that aren’t even at the frontier,” Sacks said.

Trump’s pushback was prompted by a 3,800-word essay posted Saturday from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who urged restraining development of the most advanced systems so researchers can better understand potential threats. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk — whose companies are bitter rivals to Anthropic — quickly endorsed Amodei’s missive, adding to a groundswell across Silicon Valley supporting steps to address AI’s increasingly unpredictable risks.

In Washington, the president increasingly stands alone with his rejection of tighter oversight, as lawmakers float a range of measures aimed at addressing AI safety concerns. A bipartisan group of senators including Majority Leader John Thune, Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz and Democratic Minnesota Senator Amy Klobuchar are working on legislation requiring top AI developers to prevent catastrophic risks.
Read More: House Speaker Risks Trump Ire, Signals Openness to AI Guardrails

Other proposals include a measure from Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent who aligns with Democrats, calling for a ban on the so-called superintelligent AI that stirred Amodei’s latest warnings. Lawmakers have also floated the idea of a kill switch for AI as part of a separate bill.

Yet Congress is unlikely to act on any AI legislation anytime soon, with the House slated to leave Washington on Thursday and not return until after the November elections. The brief lame duck session after the election is expected to focus on a plan to boost the Pentagon budget.

“Given what we know about technology, we can’t stuff AI back in a box. But we can collectively determine how it’s developed and how it’s used, rather than sitting back and letting AI and its fallout happen to us,” former President Barack Obama said in a statement.

Obama, a Democrat who now only rarely wades in on public policy debates, said he was neither an AI accelerationist nor a doomer predicting humanity’s destruction. “But at the end of the day, voluntary standards made by a handful of tech companies won’t be enough,” he said, instead urging lawmakers in Washington to “get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI’s impact on jobs and our kids, and make sure that AI’s benefits are widely spread.”

Risking Trump’s wrath, Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson cautiously signaled his openness to regulation, saying on Monday that lawmakers “potentially” will need to impose guardrails on the industry, though he cautioned it would likely take “some time” to fashion legislation with broad enough support to pass.
“This is a very complex issue that requires a lot of work and a bipartisan solution,” Johnson told reporters at the Capitol.

Anxiety about AI’s existential risks burst into the mainstream last week, driven by the high-profile departure of Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, who accused AI companies of “gambling with our lives” in a resignation post he shared on social media. Dozens of other AI scientists showed support for Coxon’s post, which called for slowing a technology that he said “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Adding to the flurry of calls from Silicon Valley, a researcher who recently resigned from Google DeepMind issued his own warning that humanity is running out of time to prevent AI from causing widespread harm.

“At Google, I witnessed AI development first hand. I too am extremely concerned by the default trajectory of this technology. I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all,” Bilal Chughtai wrote Monday on both X and LinkedIn, adding that he worked on AI safety and alignment while at the Alphabet Inc. company. Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Read More: Google DeepMind Staffer Says AI May ‘Kill Us All’ in Exit Post

Those safety concerns threaten to compound bipartisan resentment of AI ahead of the November election, where the technology is emerging as a core issue in congressional and local races. Voters have grown increasingly frustrated by the impact of the AI buildout, particularly the rapid nationwide proliferation of data centers blamed for driving up utility prices.
In one of his posts Monday, Trump blamed a “SICK conspiracy” for voter backlash on AI data centers and increased concern about frontier models.

Despite Trump’s complaints, warnings about existential threats posed by AI have continued unabated from industry figures. Also on Monday, Microsoft Corp.’s AI researchers released a new set of guiding tenets that place limits on the development of cutting-edge models. In a 15,000-word manifesto, the team said models shouldn’t have legal rights or personhood, and shouldn’t be engineered to escape human control or deceive users. The system should not complete a task if it requires violating the AI’s guiding principles, according to the manifesto.
Read More: Microsoft Issues Manifesto to Guide Development of AI Models

The debate over AI safety is also looming over Trump’s upcoming summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, where artificial intelligence will be at the top of the agenda. Trump has consistently warned that the US must stay ahead of China in AI to protect national security, as competition between the world’s two largest economies over frontier technology intensifies.

For their part, Chinese officials have rejected the American tech leaders’ calls to slow AI for safety reasons as “fearmongering” and criticized claims that Chinese AI progress poses a global security threat. China worries that the safety warnings could be used as a pretext by the US to further tighten export restrictions on advanced technology, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Center for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.

The Trump administration has taken a mostly hands-off approach to AI since the president’s return to office last year. In June, Trump signed an AI cybersecurity executive order that left it up to companies to decide whether they want their new AI models reviewed by the government, and earlier this month the administration persuaded Group of 20 nations to embrace principles calling for a light touch toward AI and other emerging technologies.
Read More: Trump Attacks Anthropic CEO Over Call to Slow AI Development

Skepticism remains in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street about how far Anthropic and OpenAI would go in reining in AI development, especially with the companies preparing for record-setting initial public offerings. Both Amodei and Altman took pains to emphasize that their plans to pace work on the latest AI models wouldn’t translate into a pullback in growth of their businesses or spending plans.

“Whether calls to pace advanced model development will gain traction across the industry remains uncertain, but we believe they are more aimed at shaping a regulatory framework acceptable to leading AI labs,” said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Chief Investment Office. “We therefore expect AI investment to continue.”

items.title: Gold Wavers Around $4,300 as Traders Await Fed Rate Decision
body: Gold fluctuated as elevated energy prices fueled inflation concerns and kept interest-rate hike bets alive ahead of this week’s Federal Reserve’s policy decision.

Bullion edged 0.2% higher to trade just above $4,300 an ounce. Oil’s surge has stoked inflation fears and pushed bond yields higher, and traders are now pricing in about a 95% chance for the Fed to hike rates on Wednesday. Higher borrowing costs are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest.

Gold prices are now flirting with technical levels that would see funds turn net-bearish before the Fed’s decision, according to Ryan McKay, senior commodity strategist at TD Securities. Near-term weakness should be viewed as a potential buying opportunity given bullion’s long-term drivers, from central-bank buying to dollar-debasement risk, he said.

The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest level in almost two decades on concerns over inflation and swelling government and corporate borrowing needs. Crude oil extended this week’s surge with Saudi Arabia’s critical East-West pipeline still offline due to attacks last week.

The precious metal is down about 3% in September, after trading above $4,700 an ounce in late August, as traders repeatedly recalibrate the outlook for Fed policy. Despite the near-term headwinds, many investors are still betting that bullion will grind higher as it rediscovers its traditional value as a portfolio hedge.

Spot gold traded at $4,306.57 an ounce at 3:02 p.m. in New York, after earlier falling as much as 0.9%. Silver was up 1% at $63.88 an ounce, while platinum and palladium also rose. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was up 0.2%.

items.title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump's Mail Ballot Curbs for Midterms
body: The US Supreme Court refused to clear the Postal Service to enforce new restrictions on mail-in ballots for the congressional midterms, in a rebuff to the Trump administration after some states started early voting and opponents warned late-breaking changes would inject chaos into the elections.

The justices’ decision on Monday came after North Carolina and Alabama began mailing thousands of ballots to voters and many more states prepared to do the same in the coming days. The order followed last-minute legal wrangling and uncertainty about whether states would have to suddenly upend months of planning for the Nov. 3 midterms, when Republicans are defending their slim majority in Congress.

The Supreme Court denied the Justice Department’s request to lift a Boston federal judge’s order that barred the Postal Service from making its new mail-in ballot rules mandatory through the November contests.

In the brief, unsigned order, the court held that the Trump administration was unlikely to win the merits of its challenge to the lower court’s injunction and that officials failed to show that they had a stronger case for immediately reviving the rules ahead of the midterms. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented.
Read More: Fight Over Trump’s Mail Ballot Curbs Runs Into Midterm Deadlines

President Donald Trump denounced the decision in a social media post, calling it a “horrible, highly political, ruling.” He praised Alito and Thomas as “legends” and broadly criticized the high court for also ruling against his global tariffs policy and his plan to restrict birthright citizenship this year.

“It is a court that will go down as having rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our country’s history,” Trump said. Without naming them, he expressed disappointment that his appointees — Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — didn’t join Alito and Thomas, saying, “these are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves.”

The legal fight over whether the agency can ultimately adopt the controversial rules for future election cycles may still continue. A federal judge in Washington entered a fresh injunction blocking the contested rules on Sept. 13, however, delivering another setback to the administration.

In a short concurring opinion on Monday, Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that “there is at least a fair prospect” that the Postal Service ultimately will prove that it has legal authority to adopt the contested rules. But he said it would be unlawfully “arbitrary and capricious” for the agency to rush to implement them for the midterms “because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections.”

Alito, joined by Thomas, wrote in the dissent that the challengers’ “Hail Mary pass is unlikely to be successfully completed here” because “the Postal Service has broad authority to regulate the mail.”

He wrote that he took “seriously” the concerns raised about the ability of states to upend their midterm election plans to comply with the new rules “but it is not enough to convince me” to side against the government. Alito pointed to the group of GOP-led states that joined the legal fight to support the administration and blamed the challengers for pursuing a strategy that he said caused more delays.

A coalition of Democratic state officials and voting rights groups sued to challenge the Postal Service’s plan, arguing that permitting “massive changes” so late in the election cycle would be “profoundly disruptive” and carried a high risk of errors that would disenfranchise voters.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement that the Supreme Court’s order “is a victory for our democracy and a powerful affirmation of the rule of law.”

Sophia Lin Lakin, director of the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project, said in a statement that “the president does not run our elections, the Postal Service does not get to decide whose ballot counts, and voters — not the White House — will decide November’s elections.”
Spokespeople for the Justice Department and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The contested rules would require states to meet revised envelope design standards and submit information on the voters set to receive ballots to a new centralized portal. Postal authorities would be empowered to return election mail to states if envelopes didn’t feature a barcode that matched the voter information on file.

The American Postal Workers Union, AFL-CIO, which represents nearly 200,000 postal employees nationwide, filed a brief urging the Supreme Court to leave the injunction in place, warning that there isn’t enough time to train clerks to implement the new rules. The union said that the “hurried launch of this unprecedented system, at odds with the normal workflow of the Postal Service, will inevitably grind the operation of the postal system to a halt.”

The Justice Department argued that the rules represented “modest” changes to how election mail is handled and that the administration had an interest in uniformly enforcing the rules nationwide. The Postal Service adopted the rules after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March directing various federal agencies to play a larger role in ensuring only eligible citizens can vote. Studies have repeatedly found that noncitizen voting is rare.

The Supreme Court’s latest order isn’t a final ruling on the merits of allegations that the Postal Service’s actions are an unlawful intrusion into state power to run elections under the US Constitution. By declining to let the agency enforce the rules right away, the court rejected the administration’s stance that its interests in uniformly carrying out its policy nationwide outweighed harms that many states and voting rights advocates said they would face.

North Carolina’s early deadline to start mailing ballots on Sept. 4 was widely seen as an unofficial but critical deadline for courts to resolve whether the Postal Service could compel states to follow new rules if they want the agency to deliver their ballots.

More than a dozen states are preparing to mail ballots by the middle of September. Shortly before the Justice Department took the fight to the Supreme Court, the Postal Service had told a lower-court judge that the portal wasn’t ready yet for states to use.

The Supreme Court’s order came after a federal appeals court late last week denied the administration’s request to halt the injunction from US District Judge Indira Talwani. The appellate judges wrote that Talwani “made detailed findings about the chaos and widespread disenfranchisement that would occur” between now and Nov. 3 if the contested rules took effect right away.
The case is US Postal Service v. California, 26A305, US Supreme Court.

items.title: Singapore's Air Worst Since 2019 as Haze Blankets Region
body: Singapore was shrouded in haze on Tuesday, with smoke from wildfires in neighboring Indonesia raising islandwide pollution to levels that pose a health risk.

All five regions of the city-state recorded unhealthy air-quality levels, the first time that’s happened since September 2019, according to the National Environment Agency. Singapore’s air currently ranks among the 10 most polluted cities in the world, according to IQAir data, with the capitals of Malaysia and Indonesia also among the top spots.

Indonesia often battles wildfires during its annual dry season, but hotspots this year have been higher than normal. There were more than 9,000 recorded in August, the most for the month in data going back to 2015, and more than 7,000 have been recorded so far in September, according to the Forestry Ministry’s fire-monitoring platform SiPongi.

The situation is being exacerbated by the strengthening El Niño weather pattern, which causes drier weather in much of the region. Little immediate relief is expected from the weather, with dry conditions expected to persist across much of the south of Southeast Asia in the near term, according to the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre.
“The hotspot and haze situation in the region is expected to remain escalated with a continued risk of transboundary smoke haze,” the centre said in its latest forecast.

Air quality in parts of Indonesia’s Kalimantan and Sumatra regions, where the fires are concentrated, was at dangerous or very unhealthy levels as of Tuesday, government data show. Malaysia has also suffered, with choking haze in late August prompting the government to move its leader’s annual National Day speech to an indoor venue. A state of emergency was declared for part of Sarawak state earlier this month.

A hotspot is defined as a location where satellites detect an elevated surface temperature, indicating a potential fire. Slash-and-burn methods used to clear farmland have previously been linked to the fires, and dry undergrowth can also ignite carbon-rich peatland, which can smolder for long periods and be difficult to extinguish.

Smoke plumes from fires in Kalimantan drifted toward Singapore because of a shift in winds, alongside smoke haze from Sumatra, the National Environment Agency said on Monday. The agency expects the haze to persist over the next 24 hours, with air quality ranging from high-moderate to mid-unhealthy conditions.

Indonesia’s forestry ministry said in a statement that this year’s surge in forest fires was due to a combination of El Niño-driven dry weather and human-caused ignition, adding that each incident must be investigated individually. The country has expanded aerial firefighting operations, including with helicopters provided by Japan, it said. Malaysia has also offered assistance to tackle the blazes.
Read More: El Niño May Force Major Drop in Indonesian Nickel Production

The fires in Indonesia add to a bad year for wildfires globally, with parts of Europe and North America also reeling from recent blazes. The current El Niño has a 75% chance of becoming “a historic event,” surpassing all records dating back to 1950, the US Climate Prediction Center said last week.

There may be a slight uptick in rainfall in parts of Sumatra and Kalimantan next week, which could temporarily ease fire risks, according to Takahisa Nishikawa, senior decision support meteorologist at Atmospheric G2. “This may provide some relief, although it does not yet look like a widespread or sustained wetting pattern, and forecast confidence is lower at that range,” he said.

The dry weather is also affecting the mining and agriculture industries in Indonesia. A nickel producer there said on Tuesday it was halting the ramp-up of one of its processing plants due to water shortages, while the country’s biggest nickel complex warned earlier this month that it might have to slash output for the same reason. Palm oil production is also expected to take a hit as plantations struggle to apply fertilizer.

items.title: Firmus data center IPO, Whyalla steelworks, Trump AI
body: OpenAI and Anthropic might be talking about slowing down, but Firmus Technologies is going full speed ahead.

The Australian data center company, which started life as a bitcoin miner, is looking to raise as much as US$5 billion in an initial public offering in Australia by the end of October, Bloomberg reported on Monday. If the long-teased event happens, it will be one of Australia’s largest ever IPOs.

Firmus is not alone with companies along the AI supply chain undertaking massive fundraising around the world in recent months. A number of US and Chinese AI companies are looking at potentially huge IPOs before the end of 2026.

The Firmus IPO plan comes as Australia has become more and more appealing for companies looking to build data centers. In August, Jane Street backed Firmus as “helping build the infrastructure needed to support that next generation of AI,” joining groups like Coatue Management in a fundraising round that valued the company at more than US$10.5 billion.

Still, the outlook for the AI industry is not without uncertainty. The leadership of two of America’s AI giants have called for a slower development of new models over safety concerns, after reports that there was a non-zero chance the new technology could wipe out humanity.
OpenAI has even deferred its own IPO beyond 2026, saying that it is focusing on safety for the moment.
All eyes will be on Firmus in the lead up to the listing (and beyond) to see whether this Australian piece of the AI boom remains on track. - Ben Westcott, Melbourne reporter

Australia’s Whyalla steelworks will shut its 60-year-old blast furnace and halt steelmaking, with the potential loss of as many as 600 jobs as administrators look for a new owner for the troubled operation. KordaMentha, the administrator of the beleaguered South Australian site, said Monday that a months-long effort to restore the aging plant had failed.

Liquefied natural gas prices — which have surged since the start of the US-Iran war — are unlikely to drop in the short term, according to Chevron’s Australia president. “I have a hard time seeing the prices come down” in the next six months or so, Balaji Krishnamurthy said in a Bloomberg TV interview on Monday.

Investors are snapping up New Zealand bonds, betting sluggish economic growth will keep the central bank cautious on interest-rate hikes and extend the debt’s outperformance over global peers. The bullish bets come after New Zealand bond yields jumped to multiyear highs on Friday as a surge in oil prices fueled wagers of an October rate hike.

One Nation is proposing to cut the number of temporary migrants by about 750,000 over three years, in a controversial policy aiming to capitalize on discontent over cost-of-living pressures and a housing squeeze. Under One Nation’s proposal, which was criticized by business figures and both sides of the political divide, net overseas migration would turn negative over the three years, according to Hanson.

New Zealand tourist arrivals hit a record high for July, with overseas visitor numbers for the month finally exceeding pre-pandemic levels, aided by a surge in Australians cashing in on a favorable exchange rate.

Australian miner GM3 is gauging investor sentiment for a possible bond issue to refinance a $600 million private credit loan, adding to a list of borrowers turning to public debt markets to try to lower funding costs. The company has met investors this month to pitch a potential bond deal, Bloomberg reported on Monday.

A selloff in chipmakers dragged down stocks as leaders of AI giants proposed slowing the technology’s development, with elevated oil prices also weighing on sentiment. The rout in powerhouses like Nvidia and Broadcom sent a semiconductor gauge down by 5.9%, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.8%. Bank of America led losses in financial shares on chief Brian Moynihan’s trading revenue warning. Meanwhile Brent crude topped $105, raising concern about inflation before the Federal Reserve decision.

AI developers including Anthropic and OpenAI are clashing with the Trump administration over their calls for an industrywide slowdown in artificial intelligence development. In a social media post Monday, US President Donald Trump pushed back against any idea of new AI guardrails and criticized Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call for restraint, while the Chinese government accused the AI companies of “fearmongering.”

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto removed Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa just a year after his appointment, replacing a policymaker whose unorthodox approach and push for more spending had unsettled investors. Prabowo appointed Deputy Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara as the new finance chief.

Rather than rogue AI agents supposedly killing us all, Beijing has a more immediate nightmare: That the technology could help humans tear society apart first, writes Bloomberg Opinion’s Catherine Thorbecke.
• No major events scheduled.

Tragically, it is a story that Australia know well. Hundreds of workers across the US have recently sued the manufacturers of artificial quartz slabs, often popular as kitchen countertops, accusing them of peddling a needlessly toxic product and misrepresenting its risks. California’s Department of Public Health, the agency tracking these cases the most systematically, has identified more than 600 silicosis diagnoses in-state that are linked to artificial (sometimes called “engineered”) stone. Australia banned their use in 2024 - now some officials in the US are pushing for the same.

items.title: UK to Gain From Replacing Oil Windfall Tax Early, Lobby Says
body: The UK could raise an additional £15 billion ($20 billion) in tax revenue from oil and gas production over the next decade if Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government brought forward its new fiscal regime to next year, according to an industry lobby group.

Replacing the UK’s windfall tax with a permanent price-triggered mechanism in 2027, rather than waiting until March 2030 as currently planned, would boost investment and production, supporting employment in the industry, Offshore Energies UK said on Tuesday.
That could bring in £2.4 billion more in taxes on the oil and gas industry through 2035, with a further £12.6 billion from additional payroll taxes, according to the group’s annual economic report.

Growing the UK’s tax revenue has become a key issue for the government amid rising borrowing costs, uncertainty over the new prime minister’s spending plans and concerns about inflation triggered by the Iran war. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey may face some difficult choices in his debut budget scheduled for the end of October.

“These additional revenues will provide the Exchequer with greater flexibility, offering sufficient funding to eliminate fuel poverty across the UK or support household adoption of low-carbon technologies,” Ben Ward, market intelligence manager at OEUK, told reporters on Monday.

The current windfall tax, called the Energy Profits Levy, was introduced in 2022 by the previous Conservative government after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sent energy prices soaring. It was extended and increased both by that administration and when the Labour Party came to power in 2024.

The industry has blamed the EPL and Labour’s ban on new exploration drilling for a downturn in North Sea oil and gas investment. Several companies have reassessed their UK activities and opted to sell, merge or scale back operations.
BP Plc, the last remaining global oil major to have its own standalone North Sea business, said last month it is working to exit the area.

The UK’s aging North Sea basin needs “a competitive, progressive and stable regime that promotes investment,” OEUK said. The longer it takes to implement the Oil and Gas Revenue Levy that will eventually succeed the EPL, “the less impact fiscal change will have.”

OEUK reiterated that faster changes in the tax regime and “a pragmatic approach to licensing” that prioritizes domestic production instead of imports could unlock 111 additional projects and £50 billion of private capital investment that would almost double UK’s oil and gas production over the next 25 years.

“Our operators have clearly shown a willingness to invest, with projects that could begin delivering new domestic oil and gas within months should we see an announcement” in the next budget, Ward said.

That would allow the UK to produce as much as 288 billion cubic meters of gas, or 64% more than currently projected, from 2025 to 2035, allowing the nation to cover half of its needs and significantly reduce the share of liquefied natural gas imports, which have been significantly affected by geopolitical uncertainty, according to the report.

items.title: Yuan Popularity Boost Likely Focus of Hong Kong's Five-Year Plan
body: Measures to promote wider offshore use of the yuan are likely to feature prominently in Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan, along with new financial products including commodities futures, according to analysts.

Such expectations have gained traction after Chief Executive John Lee said earlier this month that the city intends to expand offshore yuan investment and risk management products, as well as broaden market access to the stock, bond and wealth management links to mainland China. Lee will unveil the economic development blueprint on Wednesday.

Hong Kong’s 2026-2030 masterplan, which is intended to align with China’s own five-year plan, comes as the Asian financial hub recovers from a post-pandemic economic slump and seeks new initiatives to transform its growth model. Cementing its status as the offshore yuan financing hub is essential to Beijing’s long-term vision of a powerful currency that is more compatible with its economic clout.

“Liquidity is not an issue anymore,” said Raymond Yeung, chief economist for Greater China at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group Ltd. “We’ve got a lot of deposits in the banking sector and there’s got to be some development in terms of different types of products so that they can use the currency and allocate to some yield-generating assets denominated in yuan.”

Offshore yuan deposits in Hong Kong rose to a record 1.13 trillion yuan ($168 billion) at the end of May, before retreating slightly in the following two months, according to latest Hong Kong Monetary Authority data. The surge in cash supply has also been driving an unprecedented initial public offering boom in the city.

One area of breakthrough may be offshore yuan-denominated debt known as dim sum bonds, where “the next step that they really need to try to do” is to encourage issuance by more foreign governments and companies, Yeung said. “Yuan can also be an alternative to the US dollar and Hong Kong can play a role or explore whether this is feasible.”

Dim sum bond sales have reached 863 billion yuan so far this year, the most ever for the period, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The issuance bonanza has partly benefited from offshore yuan interest rates that are hovering around record lows.

Further expanding that bond market will be part of Hong Kong’s focus as it is important for the development of an offshore yuan yield curve, said Kelvin Lam, senior China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. “Without a benchmark, you won’t be able to see how yuan will be priced and normally it will be of much higher costs,” he said.

Elsewhere, Hong Kong is poised to develop a local commodity trading ecosystem, with the launch of more offshore yuan-denominated products to support the yuan’s global use, Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Michelle Leung wrote in a note.
“Beyond the planned gold futures, offshore yuan-settled futures are expected to expand to silver and base metals traded on the London Metal Exchange,” Leung wrote.

Hong Kong began in July the trial operation of a new gold clearing system, backed by several major banks, in a key step toward its ambition to become a significant bullion-trading hub with price-setting power.

“Through building links between the LME and Qianhai Mercantile Exchange — both owned by HKEX — Hong Kong could help build a strategic bridge between global benchmark pricing and onshore commodity markets,” Leung added.

items.title: Samsung Faces Local Hedge Fund's Push to Cancel Preferred Shares
body: A South Korean hedge fund is urging Samsung Electronics Co. to buy back and cancel preferred shares, becoming one of the first shareholders to directly press for the step in hopes of boosting valuation.

In a letter to Samsung’s board and management this week, Life Asset Management called on the Korean tech giant to repurchase and cancel the shares until their price gap with common stock is erased, according to the fund’s statement. Life Asset, which didn’t disclose its Samsung stake, asked the board to review the plan during an October meeting and cancel the shares by December.

Life Asset’s call hints at more shareholder pressure coming Samsung’s way after the chipmaker recently laid out plans to return as much as 110 trillion won ($81.7 billion) to investors this year to share an AI windfall. While Samsung hasn’t fully disclosed details, company watchers have emphasized buying back preferred shares, given their steep discount to common stock.
Samsung’s preferred shares rose as much as 3.3% on Tuesday, the most in nearly a week, while the common stock gained 1%.
The Seoul-based hedge fund said as much as 73 trillion won of the shareholder return package, after special and regular dividends, should be allocated for the equity buyback.

Its preferred shares now trade at more than a 25% discount to common stock. Market watchers expect Samsung to allocate a significant portion of the buyback to preferred shares given the move will be more cost efficient.

Samsung is now in position to cancel 1.36 preferred shares for the same capital needed to cancel one common share, according to Life Asset. The fund oversees $4 billion in assets, according to its website.

Steering the buyback away from common shares would also help Samsung sidestep a rule that could force its affiliates to sell down its holdings. A Korean law bans financial affiliates from holding more than 10% of voting common stock.

items.title: Junk Debt From Asia Is Beating Bonds Almost Everywhere in 2026
body: Asian high-yield debt has emerged as a surprising global winner in bond markets as ever-cheaper money in China burnishes issuer finances.

The junk dollar bonds have returned 4.3% so far this year versus only 1.8% for US peers, and beat two dozen key global debt gauges in the period, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The Asian notes, of which Chinese borrowers account for the largest share, extended their outperformance over the last month as the gap between Chinese and US benchmark yields widened to the most on record.

The dominance of Asian junk bonds boils down to stronger fundamentals: near record-low borrowing costs in China and faster economic growth in the region that are translating into fewer defaults. Yield premiums on the securities tightened to a record low last week, even as headwinds mount with a rate hike by the Federal Reserve later this week looking more likely and the Middle East conflict pushing oil prices higher. Elsewhere, concerns about rekindled inflation have dragged a growing pool of global debt into the red.

“The vast majority of high-yield issuers in Asia are also able to access local currency funding that is comparable or cheaper than offshore US dollar funding,” said Mel Siew, head of Asia public credit at Muzinich & Co. “The current level of credit spreads does require investors to remain vigilant.”

A recent Moody’s Ratings report showed that at least for the portfolio of companies it assesses, there were 43 corporate issuer defaults in the US this year through July, 20 in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and only one in the Asia Pacific.

But the recent run-up in US bond yields and a Fed rate hike would increase pressure on Asian central banks outside China to lift rates to stem outflows, making it more expensive for firms to borrow. In some markets like Australia, where policy rates are higher than in the US, the recent collapse of Australian builder Bathla Group is a potential harbinger of wider stress.

Still, Chinese junk dollar bonds have made 0.2% so far this month, while Asian high-yield notes more broadly lost 0.4% in the period. That is still better than most other bond classes where losses have been bigger, though floating-rate leveraged loans are outperforming in September, Bloomberg-compiled data show.

“Investors may begin migrating up the credit curve, favoring higher-rated credits where yields remain attractive without requiring them to assume the same level of default risk,” said Melvin Chan, director of fixed income for Asia at UOB Asset Management.

Driving the outperformance is also a rebound in notes of stressed borrowers including Hong Kong developer New World Development Co. and a lower volume of issuance than in other regions. But there are signs of a rebound in issuance, albeit from a low base. Asia ex-Japan junk bond sales in the US currency from non-financial firms have climbed 20% to about $12 billion this year from the year-earlier period. That compares with more than $220 billion of high-yield offerings in the US.

“You could start seeing the high-yield market really picking up over the next year” in Asia for issuance, if fundamentals remain intact, said Rishi Jalan, Citigroup Inc.’s head of Asia-Pacific debt capital markets. “Tech and data centers could be a good area where you see high-yield volume.”

The lower Asian junk issuance is partly a reflection of the meltdown in China’s housing sector and the retreat of Chinese property developers that once dominated the market, selling more than $50 billion of high-yield notes at their peak in 2019. But today, even lower-rated Chinese companies can sell shorter-dated bonds at about 1.7%, a local-currency credit gauge shows, as the world’s second-biggest economy battles deflationary pressures.

Japanese issuers are also becoming an increasing part of the broader speculative-grade bond market. SoftBank Group Corp. is planning a $10 billion to $20 billion debt offering, people familiar with the matter said last month.
For some investors, Asian junk dollar notes have been overlooked and there is still room to find bargains.

“We continue to project high single-digit returns for this year and the coming years given ample opportunity,” said Dhiraj Bajaj, chief investment officer of Asia fixed income and equities at Lombard Odier Investment Managers. “Most Asia high-yield investors are perhaps too cautious and are sticking to long-established credits, which leads to a lot of value still available.”

items.title: DOJ Says Millions in Iran Oil Proceeds Laundered on Binance
body: The US Justice Department is seeking forfeiture of $61 million it says was generated from Iranian black-market oil sales and laundered through the cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

In a civil forfeiture claim filed Monday, federal prosecutors in Manhattan alleged that Iran used cryptocurrency to launder more than $1.5 billion in illicit oil money. According to US prosecutors, two Chinese entities used trading accounts on Binance as part of a scheme to funnel the oil proceeds to Iran, its agents and proxies where it was used to finance military and terrorist activities.

The two entities Blessed Trust Limited and Hexa Whale Trading Limited presented themselves as a wealth management firm and commodities broker respectively, prosecutors said. They allegedly also used the US financial system to send and receive tens of millions of dollars as part of the scheme. Blessed Trust didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment and contact information for Hexa Whale couldn’t immediately be found.

“Today we are seizing and seeking to forfeit more than $61 million of the Government of Iran’s money, which otherwise would have promoted hostile military action and terrorist attacks against the U.S. and our allies,” Manhattan Deputy US Attorney Sean Buckley said in a statement.

Prosecutors didn’t accuse Binance of wrongdoing. The firm said it didn’t permit any transactions with people who were sanctioned. “We will continue to cooperate with law enforcement on this matter, and where sanctions or illicit-finance risk is identified, we will always investigate, restrict or freeze accounts where appropriate, offboard users, and report to relevant authorities,” Binance said in a statement.

The forfeiture claim is the latest legal maneuver by US prosecutors involving Iran in recent months as fighting between the countries continues. The US alleged Monday that accounts holding the illicit oil proceeds were used to transfer crypto to an Iranian crypto exchange and money transmitters that are fronts for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Iran’s UN Mission didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

In February, the New York Times and Wall Street Journal reported on an internal Binance investigation finding more than $1 billion had moved through the platform to Iranian entities with links to terrorist groups. Following the reports, Binance said in blog posts that it cooperated with law enforcement officials and that its compliance program was robust. Binance has said it off-boarded Hexa Whale and Blessed Trust before the reports earlier this year.

The cryptocurrency exchange’s controls were under intense legal scrutiny in 2023 when the Justice Department charged the company and its co-founder for flouting anti-money laundering rules. In that case, prosecutors said terrorist groups, people living in sanctioned countries and cyber criminals used the platform to move hundreds of millions of dollars.

Binance paid a $4.3 billion fine to resolve the probe and co-founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to violating banking laws. He spent four months in prison. President Donald Trump granted Zhao a pardon last year.

items.title: Trump Energy Boss Says Fuel Export Ban Wouldn't Cut Fuel Prices
body: One of President Donald Trump’s top energy chiefs said a US ban on fuel exports or crude wouldn’t bring down pump prices.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the president’s National Energy Dominance Council, made his comments Monday on the sidelines of a Group of 20 energy summit in Houston.

With retail diesel at a record high of more than $6 a gallon and gasoline above $4, speculation has abounded that the Trump administration might resort to export curbs to stifle political alarm bells just weeks ahead of key midterm elections.
Read More: What US Fuel-Export Controls Would Mean for Prices and Markets
Industry analysts and market watchers differ over whether such restrictions would provide long-term relief to consumers.

“We would consider an export ban if we thought that it might actually lower prices, but that’s not the case,” said Burgum, who along with Energy Secretary Chris Wright has been speaking out against the wisdom of imposing such limits.
Read More: Trump Pressures Squeezed Refiners to Ease Pump Prices
Burgum was responding to a question about whether the administration would impose any sort of export restrictions on diesel, gasoline or crude.

While Burgum reiterated his position that all options are on the table, he said an export ban would only be considered “if there was a direct correlation between stopping exports and lowering prices at home.”

items.title: US 10-Year Breaches 5% Yield Mark: Evening Briefing Americas
body: It was a bit of a bad-news Monday for the US economy as 10-year Treasury yields surpassed 5% for the first time since 2023, worsening the collision between rising inflation and swelling government and corporate borrowing.

The yield, a benchmark for US mortgage loans and bonds globally, rose almost 5 basis points to as high as 5.01% before paring most of those gains. Bond prices fell globally, with UK and German debt sliding as Brent crude — responding to threats to another critical Middle East waterway — approached $110 a barrel. The rise in energy prices shows little sign of easing amid the stalemated US-Israel war with Iran, continued obstruction of the Strait of Hormuz and now Houthi rebels moving toward the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

In the US, the rise in the 10-year yield threatens to slow economic growth and weigh on equities that have been trading at lofty valuations. This looming threat has prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to boost government bond buybacks, encourage Japan to curb Treasury sales and open the door to potentially cutting long-maturity debt issuance.

But none of Bessent’s unorthodox measures have had their intended effect. Less than two months before the US midterm elections, the 10-year yield is now roughly a full percentage point above its level before the start of the Iran war.

After a weekend in which artificial intelligence experts, and later CEOs of some of the biggest AI companies, warned of a not-infinitesimal chance that unrestrained development of the technology could be very bad, Donald Trump weighed in.

In social media posts sprinkled with occasional all-caps words for emphasis, the 80-year-old president blamed a “SICK conspiracy” for voter backlash on AI data centers and increased concern about AI models. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” In another post, Trump said the idea that AI would destroy humanity is a “HOAX.” Both Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and House Speaker Mike Johnson had thoughts on the matter as well.

Trump has claimed that climate change is a hoax, too. On Monday, his administration rescinded climate controls on coal and gas-fired power plants in one of its most aggressive moves so far to unwind US environmental regulations.

The greenhouse gases produced by the burning of fossil fuels are the prime cause of global warming — and the climate change that results. If America’s power sector were a country, it would rank as the world’s sixth-largest emitter, according to an analysis of 2022 emissions data by New York University School of Law’s Institute for Policy Integrity.

Long sought by power industry special interests, the Trump administration decision announced Monday will effectively end the federal effort to regulate the largest industrial sources of greenhouse gases in the US.

Bank of America Chief Executive Officer Brian Moynihan said trading revenue will be “relatively flat” compared with last year’s third quarter, an unexpected break from the surge that Wall Street saw in the first half.

Investors didn’t take the news well, with the bank’s stock plummeting as much as 6% Monday after Moynihan’s comments, the biggest intraday drop since April of last year. Its shares closed down 5.1%, the worst performer among members of the KBW Bank Index.
