items.title: Silicosis Lawsuits Mount as Workers Seek Billions in Damages
body: Silicosis is a killer that’s been at large for millennia. It’s an incurable workplace disease caused by breathing in dust with tiny, jagged particles of respirable crystalline silica, which is released by cutting or crushing objects like stone or gravel. These invaders, each less than one-tenth the width of a human hair, are difficult to keep out of your body; mucus is no match for them. As they pile up, RCS particles gradually destroy your lungs, inflaming them, scarring them, shrinking them, hardening them. Along the way, the silica dust can also cause lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, autoimmune disorders and kidney failure. “My patients with silicosis, I wish they only had lung cancer,” says University of California at Los Angeles pulmonologist Jane Fazio, who’s been studying a new surge of US cases. “Lung cancer can be cut out.”

In recent history, silicosis has typically been associated with decades of intense work around harmful dust. Doctors were used to diagnosing miners in their 60s and 70s. But the wave of patients whom Fazio and others are studying has started to look a bit more like 32-year-old Tyler Jordan. Once an athletic stonecutter, Jordan found in 2022 he could no longer take a full, deep breath, and he hasn’t since.

Jordan felt unwell for weeks before he first met with doctors, cycling through fevers and chills. His wife, Caitlin, made him go in after he collapsed from shooting pain in his back. A physician told him he was far too young to have silicosis, until results came back from a biopsy of the lung that was stuck to the wall of his chest. A specialist concluded that Jordan had contracted the disease by breathing in silica dust from slabs of trendy artificial quartz, while working for his father turning them into countertops. What followed was chemo, dialysis, depression, renal failure, a kidney transplant and a more sensitive surgery to mitigate the brutal side effects on his reproductive anatomy.

A father of three, Jordan used to mountain bike, snowboard and play hockey. These days, basic activities are exhausting or dangerous. And organ transplants tend not to last more than a decade or two, so he’s likely to need several kidney or lung transplants if he’s lucky. “Right now, it’s just focusing on my kids,” he says. “I can do frisbee with them, but I stand in one spot, and if they miss me, then they have to go get the frisbee.” His daughter Faith, the oldest, is 11.

The family of five have moved from Colorado to Missouri, for the cheaper cost of living and greater help from his in-laws. “It’s hard to be a great role model, and I can’t be a hard worker — show them hard work, like my dad,” Jordan says. He’d always wanted to inherit Jordan Marble & Granite, the countertop business owned by his parents, Jimmy and Tina. Instead, he got his father’s kidney.

Jordan is one of hundreds of workers across the US who’ve recently sued the manufacturers of artificial quartz slabs, accusing them of peddling a needlessly toxic product and misrepresenting its risks. California’s Department of Public Health, the agency tracking these cases the most systematically, has identified more than 600 silicosis diagnoses in-state that are linked to artificial (sometimes called “engineered”) stone, which contains far greater concentrations of silica than the natural marble and granite products it’s displaced. Most of those patients are Latino; almost all are men. Their median age of diagnosis is 46, and 35 of those Californians have died of the disease, at a median age of 52.

Over 6,000 workers with artificial stone silicosis have been identified worldwide, and many more could be at risk. Scientists project there will be thousands of cases a year among the fabrication workers grinding, polishing, cutting and customizing manufacturers’ slabs to create the countertops consumers want. Those slabs increasingly consist of artificial quartz, which in recent decades has surged in popularity. When Australia’s Queensland set out to test its fabricators, it found that close to 1 in 5 had silicosis. Within a few years, Australia banned the use of artificial stone slabs, effective in 2024. In the US, some officials are pushing to do the same. Others are moving to protect the manufacturers against lawsuits instead.

Artificial stone manufacturers, led by Cambria Co., have insisted that their products aren’t the problem. Cambria, which didn’t respond to detailed inquiries, has blamed afflictions like Jordan’s on small businesses like his parents’, arguing that the track records of its in-house shops show the slabs can be safely fabricated. Part of the basis for that claim, Cambria research chief Jon Grzeskowiak testified during Jordan’s trial this spring, is that sampling of the air in Cambria’s own shops shows silica levels lower than the “action level” set by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. “We have air monitoring results that confirm that all the dust levels are below the action level in our shops,” Grzeskowiak testified.

But an investigation by Bloomberg Businessweek shows that over the past decade, that has frequently not been the case. Confidential company records reviewed by Businessweek detail dozens of instances of dust levels above that threshold in Cambria shops — in some cases, far above it. Thousands more pages of company documents, court filings and transcripts complicate the company’s narrative further, as do interviews with scientists, doctors, attorneys, enforcers, fab shop owners and the workers whose lives have been upended by the dust.

Silica is the nickname for silicon dioxide, one of the most abundant materials on Earth. It’s found in sand and glass as well as all sorts of rocks, and it’s safe when it’s just sitting inert in a slab in your kitchen. The crystalline type is the one to worry about. And studies from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, the workplace-research team at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, have found that fabricating artificial quartz releases a lot more RCS than its old-school counterparts.

That’s not surprising. While marble contains 5% or less crystalline silica and granite tops out around 45%, the number for artificial quartz can be as high as 93%. The other ingredients include resin binders with toxic components and carcinogens that can make the product even more dangerous to workers, according to a staff report from California’s safety agency Cal/OSHA. The particles that artificial quartz releases are also smaller, making it easier for them to “penetrate deeply into the respiratory tract,” wrote Cal/OSHA’s standards board, deeming artificial quartz fabrication “highly toxic.” Cal/OSHA is taking steps toward banning the fabrication of such products, and NIOSH has said the safest approach for shops is to use slabs with little or no crystalline silica.

In interviews with Businessweek, more than a dozen fabrication workers with silicosis who are now suing various manufacturers say they had no idea how dangerous artificial stone was to their lungs when they started grinding it. “Our concern was more getting crushed” if a slab tipped over, says Florida fabricator Wade Hanicker. He and others say representatives from the slab manufacturers visited often to promote product lines or give out swag without voicing safety concerns. Owners of fab shops, which tend to be small, often mom-and-pop operations, say much the same. “We were misled to believe from the get-go that it was just like natural stone, to fabricate it like natural stone, treat it like natural stone,” Tina Jordan says. “Totally duped.”

Fab workers say they never would’ve gone into that line of work if they’d understood what it could cost them. Silicosis has left some living in shame, feeling helpless, useless, futureless. One says he feels like a piece of furniture. Another compares himself to an avocado that looks good on the outside but is rotten under the skin.

Some workers spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation, either from the manufacturers or President Donald Trump’s immigration authorities. Attorney Raphael Metzger, who represents many undocumented fab workers suing manufacturers, alleged in January in a California court filing that defendants were illegally intimidating his clients about their immigration status, including by pressing them for ID during depositions. He also said in an affidavit that one plaintiff, the wife of a worker with silicosis, had recently been assaulted outside her house by a masked man who addressed her by name, “told her that if she and her husband didn’t stop talking to lawyers, he would kill them,” and struck her in the head with a blunt instrument.

The defendants in these cases have denied wrongdoing. They include a slew of companies in the countertop supply chain, among them retailers such as Costco, Home Depot, Ikea and Lowe’s; distribution middlemen; as well as foreign manufacturers like Caesarstone, Cosentino and Hyundai L&C, whose products include slabs of artificial quartz. But no defendant has more at stake than Cambria, the largest domestic producer of the artificial stuff. Cambria, a family-owned firm in Minnesota, produces artificial slabs with quartz from its own mines. Chief Executive Officer Marty Davis is a prolific Trump donor who’s hosted the president at his home, visited him in the Oval Office, lent $5 million to help launch his social media site Truth Social, and encouraged his efforts to overturn the 2020 election. (Asked later about text messages in which he made comments like “I told Potus there was extensive cheating in Minnesota,” Davis said, “I gave information or input to what I thought they needed to do to investigate,” Talking Points Memo reported in 2022.)

In response to inquiries, Cosentino said that it wouldn’t comment on ongoing litigation, but that it “stands by the safety of its products and the use of appropriate safety protocols” and that “silica-based materials,” including its slabs, can endanger workers “if handled improperly.” Home Depot said in a statement that it wants everyone in its supply chain to be safe and expects fabricators “to comply with applicable laws and regulations.” Caesarstone and Ikea declined to comment, citing ongoing litigation; Costco and Lowe’s didn’t respond to inquiries, nor did Hyundai L&C (not the one that makes cars). In a Los Angeles courtroom this winter, after a back-and-forth with a judge about estimating the number of people likely to die from exposure to silica, Hyundai lawyer Rey Yang mused, “You could live life without any risk, and then where would you be?”

In a 2023 email to trade association and company leaders including Cambria’s Davis, a Home Depot senior director for government relations strategized about how to forestall a California ban of artificial stone. In the email, later viewed by Businessweek, he wrote that the retailer’s lobbying firm agreed that “the creation of a stakeholder advisory committee is a good way to slow things down a little bit and a productive alternative.”

Cambria’s chief lawyer, Rebecca Shult, has testified that those with questions are welcome to come see its facilities firsthand. Cambria declined Businessweek’s requests for a tour and for interviews with its leadership; its spokespeople, in-house and outside attorneys, and CEO didn’t respond to subsequent detailed inquiries. In court, the companies have argued they were forthright about the need to fabricate their slabs with care, and that the blame for workers’ illnesses lies with third-party fab shops that cut corners figuratively as well as literally. “The problem is the process, not the product,” Shult told lawmakers in January. Because other stone products also contain silica, she told Cal/OSHA at a March hearing, banning products like Cambria’s “may provide a dangerous false sense of security.”

While Cal/OSHA takes steps toward enacting a ban similar to Australia’s, the US Congress is cooking up a different sort of restriction. A bill that cleared committee in June would immunize manufacturers from lawsuits over their slabs, which the proposed legislation says “are not inherently dangerous.” If passed and signed into law by President Trump, the legislation would mandate dismissal of hundreds of pending cases by countertop workers, attributing fault instead to those mom-and-pop shops, where enforcers have frequently found safety violations.

Cambria has often touted its success at containing RCS levels in its own in-house fab shops, arguing that it’s proved its products can be safely fabricated when in full compliance with Occupational Safety and Health Administration standards. “We know that workers can be protected by following OSHA’s regulation and controlling silica exposure to below the permissible exposure limit,” Shult testified at a congressional hearing in January. “And in fact, at our shops, we control exposures below the action level, which is half of the PEL.”

Corporate records reviewed by Businessweek, however, paint a different picture. Since the current OSHA requirements kicked in about eight years ago, air sampling commissioned by Cambria has dozens of times found RCS exposures above the threshold that the company insists it’s staying below. Of 65 batches of air testing Cambria ordered among its own US fab facilities, 30 showed concentrations of RCS in some areas exceeded OSHA’s action level. Six documented RCS levels that were also above the permissible exposure limit.

The records, which were discovered in ongoing litigation and shared with California regulators, cover testing conducted for Cambria at in-house fab shops in California, Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio. What they show is “alarming,” says Deborah Berkowitz, who served as OSHA’s chief of staff under President Barack Obama, “and clearly contradicts their testimony at the hearing when they wanted Congress to provide them a get-out-of-jail-free card.”

The litigation poses an existential threat to the artificial stone industry, especially for Cambria, which only makes artificial quartz slabs. “The enormous resources required to defend against these lawsuits, coupled with the potential risk of nuclear verdicts, place an enormous burden on us,” Shult told lawmakers. “The legal fees for just one trial can be millions of dollars, and we are currently defending against 400 of them.” (It’s now over 600, with more in the works, according to attorney James Nevin, whose firm represents many of the plaintiffs.) Juries have ruled against Cambria in two of the three cases that have reached verdicts, including Jordan’s, in which the manufacturer owes about $7.7 million to Jordan and his wife. The company has settled several others on undisclosed terms.

Cambria has urged jurors to see its product not as a threat to workers’ safety but as a boon for the health of their children. “We all cut chicken on our countertops, and we all have kids who eat off the countertops sometimes,” company attorney Lindsay Weiss said during a 2024 trial. Because Cambria’s product is less porous, she argued, it’s more hygienic: “It’s safer for us.”

Turning natural rock into artificial stone is somewhat like turning potatoes into Pringles. Rocks get quarried from mines, then pulverized into a mash; mixed with resins, dyes and sometimes metal; poured into molds; deaerated; baked in an oven; then polished and packaged for fab shops to turn into countertops. This process, invented in Italy half a century ago, was popularized in the US in the past couple decades by the Davis family in Minnesota, who previously made a fortune from cheese and whey products. Mom-and-pops sourcing artificial stone from companies like Cambria, as well as their yuppie customers, quickly observed the product’s perks. “What they want is marble that holds up like granite,” Jimmy Jordan says. Compared with some natural stone, the artificial stuff is easier to work with (less chipping), to keep clean (less absorption) and to customize (it can be dyed whatever color you want).

Tyler Jordan started hanging around his parents’ shop, a colleague would later testify, when he was “knee high to a French fry.” By age 8, they stuck him on the payroll for some hours doing office work. He was doing part-time fab work in high school, then full-time for most of the decade after he graduated in 2012. (Two brief breaks: when Jimmy temporarily fired him for rolling in late too often, and when he temporarily quit out of frustration that Jimmy wasn’t giving him enough responsibility.) When he was 18, Jordan met Caitlin, then 21, who a friend had lured to a hangout with the false promise of guacamole. They married a few years later and had three kids by the time he was 26.

It wasn’t all  Norman Rockwell, as Cambria’s lawyers would later point out. In 2019, Jordan and Caitlin went through a brief separation, which he testified at trial may have been related to his alcohol use. A couple of years earlier, he received inpatient treatment after a mix of booze and prescription ADHD medication led to a mental-health episode. But he had a good life, anchored by the family business.

Not least, Jordan adored the shop. “He was always smiling, even when his dad was chewing his butt,” a former co-worker testified earlier this year. The work was active enough to be a good fit for his ADHD, Jordan says, “almost like a zen state.” Turning big slabs into beautiful counters while listening to Toby Keith or My Chemical Romance on his headphones was a great vibe. He felt proud seeing satisfied customers during installations and helping turn their houses into homes. And he loved working with his father, watching the business thrive. “We were, pardon the pun, rock stars,” Jimmy testified in April, recalling his early days in the industry. “Granite countertops, those were showstoppers.”

But the business was changing. Fabricating artificial stone, primarily from Cambria, would become the majority of the Jordan family’s work by the early days of the first Trump administration. Across the US, demand grew about eightfold over the course of a decade. Jordan remembers how strikingly blue the first slab was, and also how various corporate reps said to handle it: “They told us to treat it like natural stone. Nobody ever told us that it was far, far worse.” Jimmy brought him along on a trip to Minnesota to watch artificial stone being made at Cambria headquarters, with a stop at the nearby pizza shop that honors the Davis family’s dairy legacy — served at artificial stone counters that represented its future. “Family-owned, American-made, I thought was the coolest thing,” Jordan recalls.

By that time, however, Chest, the journal of the American College of Chest Physicians, had published an article now titled “Artificial Stone Silicosis: Disease Resurgence Among Artificial Stone Workers,” describing an outbreak of cases in Israel. The initial title of that 2012 article, walked back after Caesarstone threatened to sue, called it “CaesarStone Silicosis.” (According to the New York Times, the journal’s then-editor said the change was made not due to legal threats, but because the issue was broader than one manufacturer.)  Similar  studies  followed. By 2020, when the global market for artificial stone was estimated around $21 billion,  more than 500 total cases had been documented in countries including China, Canada, Italy and Spain.

In 2023, Cosentino owner and chairman Francisco Martinez reached a plea deal with Spanish authorities in which he was convicted of five counts of serious injury due to gross negligence and accepted a six-month suspended sentence. In emailed statements, Cosentino said the settlement was about five workers at one fab shop “who claimed they did not receive sufficient health warnings and experienced adverse health effects,” that in fact “Cosentino did not conceal information about risks associated with its surfaces that could endanger the health of any professional worker,” and that the matter “doesn’t set a precedent for any future cases.” The judge’s ruling in the case said Martinez for years didn’t provide fab shops with any information about his product’s risks, even though he was aware of them and some of his own employees had silicosis.

Later that year, Australian authorities approved an industrywide ban, a move the country’s worker-safety agency had deemed “the only way to ensure that another generation of Australian workers do not contract silicosis.” By then, it was clear America hadn’t been spared. A paper published by Fazio, the UCLA pulmonologist, and several colleagues reported 52 cases of silicosis associated with fabricating engineered stone in California. Ten of those 52 people had already died.

When Jordan was diagnosed with silicosis, he took his doctor’s advice and quit working, but within months, his symptoms got worse anyway. Rashes covered his legs. Vasculitis swelled his legs and feet until his shoes didn’t fit, and chemotherapy was little help. Worse, his kidney function was declining. “When Tyler got sick,” Caitlin would later testify, “I explain it as a light switch turning on and off.”

After that came the thousands of hours of dialysis, first at the hospital and an outpatient clinic, then overnights at home. His weight fluctuated by 65 pounds, leaving stretch marks. His kids watched him have a seizure during a car ride. His 2-year-old son learned to say “dialysis” and his 9-year-old daughter helped set up the machine. He thought about death. “There were days I broke down, saying there’s no way I can keep doing dialysis, it’s just too much,” he recalls. Relief came when his father was approved as his kidney donor. “I would have given him anything,” Jimmy says. “I would have told the doctors, if you see anything in me that he needs, take it.”

“Knowing that he helped me was pretty great,” says Jordan. After the transplant, he got some of his vigor back. But complications from a stent required a penile surgery that left him a mess in both the bedroom and the bathroom. “I’m not the same down there anymore,” he says. He can only use the toilet sitting down. “It sucks,” he says, citing the innocent but painful questions from his kids. “That’s pretty hard. But yeah, that’s—” He pauses. “I guess that’s life now.”

Running across the yard wipes Jordan out. While the medical bills drove the family into debt, a chat with his doctor about future jobs was a bust: “All of the ones I brought up, she was like, ‘You can’t do that.’” Welding means fumes. Carpentry means dust.

Jordan and his wife sued 20 companies, alleging negligence and deceptive business practices. They accused Cambria and other slab manufacturers of peddling defective products that were too dangerous to use, misrepresenting those products and failing to properly warn of their hazards. They also sued manufacturers of equipment used with the slabs or to protect fabricators from them, arguing they misrepresented how their products would work with silica-rich artificial quartz. Like other plaintiffs, Jordan says he’s hoping his lawsuit will help force manufacturers to abandon artificial stone. He rejects their claims that Jordan Marble & Granite is to blame for his condition. “Not at all,” he says. “My dad was quite the stickler with safety stuff.”

At a deposition last year in Jordan’s case, one of the defendants’ lawyers asked his father if he’d done “any retrospective thinking about what maybe Tyler did differently, that he would be the unfortunate one to come down with silicosis, and not others in the shop?”
“I constantly think of it,” Jimmy testified, after bursting into tears at an earlier version of the same question. “But there is nothing that he did more or differently than anybody else.”
“Is there anything you wish you would have done differently?” a company lawyer asked him. “No,” Jimmy answered. “I did everything I thought I could do. I did more than I thought we needed.”

Jimmy described the phalanx of dust fans, the 3-foot exhaust fan, the wet floors and the $500,000 cutting machinery he bought to try to keep his guys safe. When pressed, he said he might regret not getting medical exams done on his half-dozen employees and going more than a decade without doing the periodic air sampling that OSHA mandated. But he voiced no regrets about working with artificial stone, as his shop still does.
“I would not fabricate it if I didn’t think we could do it safely,” he said during the deposition. The reason to use it is simple, he would testify at trial: “Customers, that’s what they want.”

A year later, when asked by Businessweek whether he believes there’s a way to safely fabricate artificial quartz countertops, 10 seconds go by before Jimmy speaks. “The experts, they’re saying no. We’re doing everything we can to do it as safe as we can. So I don’t, I mean—” He pauses, and his wife finishes his sentence: “I mean, we still don’t know.” Both Jimmy and Tina say that after getting satisfactory results when OSHA itself tested the air in 2011, they thought further testing wasn’t needed, because they didn’t know about the greater danger of artificial stone.

In a separate interview, Tyler Jordan says it bothers him that his father testified artificial stone can be safely fabricated, but that he understands why the matter isn’t so simple for his parents. “If they stopped working with it right now, they’d go out of business.”

During the trial in April, Jordan’s lawyers presented a series of warning labels and safety guides in which the manufacturers had suggested to fabricators that their artificial stone was akin to natural rock — or was one itself. Instructions that Cambria disseminated read, in part, “Cambria is a natural stone product,” “One must treat Cambria slabs like granite,” and “Cambria is pure natural quartz.”

At trial, Cambria said much the same thing. The manufacturer’s lawyers bristled at its slabs being called anything other than natural and urged the jury to think of them like grated Parmesan cheese — still very much Parmesan. “It’s a product the company is very proud about,” Cambria attorney Claire Weglarz said in her opening statement. “The risk does not come from the presence of silica in these materials.” After one of the plaintiffs’ scientific experts testified that it was “difficult, if not impossible, to reduce the exposures to an adequately low level for engineered stone,” Weglarz said to him, “If we’re going to eliminate silica in quartz, we are eliminating basically almost all the rocks on earth?” (“No, that’s not correct,” said the expert, industrial hygienist Michael Ellenbecker.)

Cambria dismissed the phrase “artificial stone” as an “artificial term,” and behind the scenes, also tried to keep the phrase “engineered stone” out of the jury instructions. That term, attorney Ryan Hebert argued, “has become synonymous in the minds of the jury with the concept of toxicity.” He added, “We are concerned such a characterization risks eliciting a Pavlovian response from the jury, predisposing them to the conclusion that the product is inherently defective.”

In a deposition played at the trial, one of Jordan’s lawyers asked a Caesarstone product director, Yoni Atar, “Does Caesarstone USA have any responsibility for ensuring the health and safety of stone fabrication workers who are working with and around Caesarstone quartz products?” Atar, who was testifying as his company’s designated representative in the case, replied, “I’m not sure.” Asked whether Caesarstone could provide the same benefits with a product that was only 10% silica rather than around 90%, he said, “I believe so.” (Caesarstone’s lawyer said in a closing statement that Atar “gave the wrong answer.”)

Jordan opened his hours of testimony by flagging that he might need extra bathroom breaks for the diarrhea caused by his cocktail of daily meds and the copious water his new kidney demanded. He recounted having to go to urgent care for a cut on his finger, because immunosuppressants can make that a crisis, and to avoid his kids when they get colds, for the same reason. He described his diagnosed anxiety and depression about “all of the things that I can’t do.” A transplant surgeon estimated he’ll need around three kidney transplants and noted that the immunosuppression involved leads to some form of cancer for about 1 in 4 recipients.

Caitlin testified about the dread she’d been feeling in the months before Jordan’s diagnosis, when she started waking up damp with his sweat; about the ways the disease had swallowed up their family physically and emotionally; and about how they had no money saved for their kids’ college educations. Both spouses testified that Jordan’s treatment had compromised their physical intimacy.

Cambria and other defendants blamed Jordan’s illness on his parents for not running a safe enough shop and for letting him hang around there starting as a child. They noted citations that Jordan Marble & Granite had received from OSHA following its 2011 inspection, including for not monitoring the air, and pointed out that the shop had failed to do so for most of the years since. “They sped for 28 years, and unfortunately Tyler, the passenger, is the one that got injured,” said Cambria lawyer  Khaled Taqi-Eddin. Jimmy and Tina were the ones controlling Jordan’s workplace, Taqi-Eddin said: “Not to steal a line from Frank Sinatra, but they did it their way. But their way was not the right way.” The defendants repeatedly quoted a line from Jordan’s deposition about his visits to the shop as a kid: “Everything was dusty, there was — it was impossible to not play in the dust.”

Jordan testified at trial that though he sometimes skateboarded through the fabrication floor as a child, or came in to fetch his dad for lunch, or sat in the office watching movies, he wasn’t actually playing with dust. (He says he got some things wrong during his deposition while heavily medicated, brain-fogged, and drained by dialysis treatment.)

His lawyers noted that Cambria has received its own OSHA citations, for violations that, like some of the fab shop’s, the government deemed “serious.” (Cambria’s citations, issued last year, involved non-silica concerns such as insufficient emergency shutdown procedures for the manufacturer’s giant resin mixing tanks, according to documents Businessweek obtained via public records request.) They called former co-workers to the stand who described Jimmy’s business as a safe shop, and they showed the deposition of a former Caesarstone rep who said, based on his many visits, Jimmy “was one of the best fabricators in northern Colorado” and his operations “always looked clean and always in order.”

Cecile Rose, one of Jordan’s doctors, rejected the theory that childhood exposure was what got him sick. The onset of his symptoms was consistent with the “accelerated forms of silicosis” caused by artificial stone, testified Rose, a pulmonologist and the author of several peer-reviewed studies on the topic. Although exposure to natural stone dust contributed, it wouldn’t have been enough to cause his condition, she said, noting that there’s never been a documented case of silicosis from a countertop worker just fabricating natural stone. Jordan’s symptoms were all consistent, she said, with “engineered stone silicosis.” The companies’ lawyers then asked Rose if she had told Jordan to lay off the vaping (“yes”) and pushed again on whether the evidence pointed to his childhood fab shop visits as the real culprit. Rose said “No,” and “I’d be happy to explain.” The lawyers didn’t ask her to.

Instead, during cross-examination, company lawyers asked Jordan about his history with alcohol; his use of cigarettes, vapes and THC gummies; his brief separation from his wife; his wife’s relationship with his parents; and his parents’ ongoing use of artificial stone. Later, when an economist testified about the millions of dollars of damages Jordan had suffered, an attorney for defendant Pental Granite & Marble LLC suggested considering the upsides of a career pivot: “Let’s say he got into computer programming. He would make more money than he was making as a fabricator, fair?” (Pental, now known as Architectural Surfaces, didn’t respond to inquiries.)

While mocking the Jordan fab shop’s safety record, Cambria talked up the standards in its own facilities. When asked why masks aren’t worn in Cambria’s fab shops, Grzeskowiak, the company’s research chief, said such personal protective equipment wasn’t required “because our air monitoring results confirm that our wet cutting engineering controls and wet cleaning have kept our values below the action level.” (The next month, in California litigation, Grzeskowiak would file an affidavit attesting that “the air monitoring results produced by Cambria,” the ones showing the company had frequently exceeded the OSHA action level over the prior eight years, were “true and complete copies” of Cambria records.)

Grzeskowiak emphasized that zero of Cambria’s own in-house fab shop employees had reported contracting silicosis. Under cross-examination, he acknowledged he wasn’t aware of the company offering X-rays to check for the disease, or checking with current or former employees about whether they were having silica-related health issues.

In closing arguments, Cambria stressed that even Jimmy was still fabricating engineered stone. “He said he thinks they can fabricate it safely — that’s Tyler’s father,” Taqi-Eddin said. Jordan’s lawyers argued that if the defendants were allowed to stress this point, the plaintiffs should be permitted to tell the jury that such slabs are banned in Australia. The judge still didn’t let them, on the grounds that that would be prejudicial.

After a day of deliberation, the jury reached a mixed verdict. They found several companies, including Caesarstone, not liable, and rejected claims that the artificial stone slabs were defective products. But they found Cambria and Hyundai liable for misrepresenting the facts about those slabs. In the peculiar math of tort verdicts, they deemed Jordan’s parents’ business (which wasn’t a defendant in the case) to be 63% at fault for his injuries, Cambria 32%, Hyundai 3% and Jordan himself 2% to blame. The jury valued Tyler and Caitlin’s total damages at about $17.5 million, which put Cambria on the hook to pay roughly $7.7 million once interest was factored in. (Under Colorado tort law, while the nondefendants don’t pay for their portion of the verdict, it can reduce how much the liable parties owe.)

While lobbying Congress to halt such trials, Cambria has asked the judge to overturn the verdict against the company, arguing that there wasn’t enough evidence to support it and that the jury’s judgments were “irreconcilably inconsistent” with each other. “This case is just as important to us as it is to plaintiffs,” Taqi-Eddin told the jury at the end of Jordan’s trial. The manufacturer has also sent demand letters to Jordan’s parents, arguing that under an indemnification clause they accepted to work with its slabs, their business should be the one to pay for Cambria’s portion of any verdict.
US Representative Darrell Issa opened a January hearing by holding up a tile of artificial quartz and intoning to his colleagues, “I’ll be touching it, I’ll be holding it, and I will have no fear.”

The California Republican’s hearing was dubbed “Between a Rock and a Hard Place: Protecting the US Stone Slab Industry From Lawfare.” Company reps and conservative Congress members there made the case for the bill introduced by Representative Tom McClintock, which would shut down all civil actions against slab manufacturers for workers’ illness related to fabrication by “third parties.”

The cases “are very difficult to defend,” Cambria lawyer Shult testified: “These workers are very injured and very sympathetic. And so when they go to a jury, it’s a perfect case for a product liability lawyer to have the opportunity to show a very endangered worker.” She noted that Congress had previously acted to shield airlines from liability for the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Gary Talwar, the vice president of Natural Stone Resources, a family-owned slab distributor, told the lawmakers he’s facing 65 silica lawsuits. He echoed Shult’s message with a metaphorical flourish of his own: “We’re fighting for our lives,” he said.

Republicans at the hearing argued that the silicosis problem was really about California’s failure to crack down on fabrication sweatshops exploiting illegal labor, that the lawsuits were endangering US manufacturing jobs and that Cambria, in particular, was being picked on because of its owner’s support for Trump. McClintock suggested Democrats were aligning themselves with sketchy fab shop bosses out of ire at the president. “Do you get the impression that a lot of this is political, and that some of our members are missing the big picture of what this is doing to the livelihoods and safety of tens of thousands of American workers?” he asked Shult.

“I’m afraid so,” she replied. “We should prioritize worker safety over politics.” After talking up Cambria’s record of keeping its fab facilities below the OSHA action level, she said, “Workers are protected when we follow OSHA’s regulations and requirements, which we do. And our workers are safe and protected, and in fact, our CEO’s own children work on the floor of our fab shops.” Along with dozens of other times its fab shops exceeded OSHA’s action levels, the air-monitoring records Cambria released in discovery a few months later showed levels at a facility in Ohio that were quintuple OSHA’s permissible exposure limit at one point in 2020, and more than quadruple it during a test in 2023.

House Democrats’ sole witness at the hearing was David Michaels, a public-health professor at George Washington University who ran OSHA under Obama. “Australia has not banned lawsuits — after careful study, Australia banned the deadly product,” Michaels told the committee. That change forced manufacturers to switch to a safer alternative, he said: Recycled glass with virtually no crystalline silica is now fabricated into countertops by the same Australian workers who were previously handling the dangerous artificial quartz.

Like Jordan’s trial, the hearing was a metaphor derby. Michaels compared the slabs to cigarettes, dangerous when used for their intended purpose (fabrication). Issa said they’re more like cars, whose manufacturers aren’t blamed for drunk driving. As he closed the hearing, he held up the tile again and, sticking out his tongue as he lifted it to his mouth, said it was “something that I could lick, and it isn’t going to hurt me.”

One of the workers suing the companies, 56-year-old Jeff Rose, recently wrote a letter to Trump, urging him to oppose the McClintock bill. “I want my story to mean something,” he wrote. Rose is part owner of  Artistic Granite & Marble, a fab shop in Kentucky. He’s tried to limit his time on the fabrication floor since his diagnosis, but he still drags himself each day to the shop, where his son works and contracted silicosis too. The best-case scenario, he says, is that the disease shaves only a decade off each of their lives. Already, he can no longer carry his grandkids up the stairs. Pulling a Christmas tree made him lose his breath and worry he was about to die. “I was never afraid of anything, and now I’m afraid of everything,” he says.

Rose, who voted for Trump in the past three presidential elections, says signing the bill likely wouldn’t cost the president his support. “If he swayed the way of the manufacturers and decided that he wasn’t going to let them get sued or anything like that, I would probably still vote for him if he ran again.”

This spring, workers and advocates flooded into the Ronald Reagan state building in Los Angeles for hours of public testimony, the culmination of months of Cal/OSHA standards board hearings and deliberations. Some carried white carnations to honor those already dead. A drab PowerPoint from the agency’s in-house doctors and engineers presented the team’s findings: “Rising counts of artificial stone silicosis is an occupational health emergency,” with 3,000 new cases expected in the year 2030. A worker testified while hooked up to an oxygen tank, pleading for action. Doctors, including the president of the California Medical Association, joined the assembled fab workers in urging a ban; one said she wanted to stop “giving out death sentences.”

After a gusher of testimony, as the hearing neared the time at which security was obliged to close the building for the night, one of the board’s members addressed the workers present with regret: “Your society owes you an apology,” industrial hygienist Nola Kennedy told them. “We have failed you.” She and her colleagues then voted to ask the agency to start drafting an emergency regulation, a step toward banning fabrication of the product. Two weeks later, the US House Judiciary Committee voted along party lines to advance McClintock’s ban on silicosis lawsuits.

For now, the lawsuit ban’s prospects depend on whether House Speaker Mike Johnson brings it to the floor. The California ban on artificial stone fabrication would require a future standards board vote to approve and is sure to draw legal challenges if it goes forward. Either proposal could help dictate whether manufacturers ease away from, or double down on, artificial quartz.

In the meantime, Trump just delivered Cambria a different sort of victory. This summer, the president issued heavy new tariffs on foreign slabs, including less-hazardous glass as well as artificial stone, sought by manufacturers. Trump’s tariffs exceed those recommended by the members of the US International Trade Commission. Despite the pleas of the American Public Health Association, they don’t include exceptions for products less likely to cause silicosis. Asked about the tariffs’ safety impacts, the White House directed Businessweek to the president’s proclamation announcing them, which said they would “provide greater economic and social benefits than costs.”

Many workers have come to see different trade-offs from the slabs. One artificial stone countertop worker with silicosis says he’s constantly exhausted but loses sleep at night thinking about death. Another can’t put on his socks without taking a break in between, but he can’t qualify for a lung transplant because of a brain infection. A third was traumatized by a hellish transplant: Hallucinating because of his meds, he tried to tear out the tubes that were stitched into his skin to help clean his blood. The hospital tied him down and then, when that wasn’t enough, tied gloves to his hands to restrain his fingers. He tried to scream, but no sound came out because of the hole doctors had cut for a breathing tube in his neck. Like many of his counterparts, he lives with an artificial stone countertop he fabricated himself. It sits at his home under images of the Last Supper and the Virgin Mary. He says he knows it can’t hurt him anymore.

In Oregon, plaintiff Frankie Evans says a manufacturer’s lawyer implied he was to blame for his own silicosis during a deposition, then put a hand on his shoulder in the hallway afterward and told him everything was going to be OK. Evans is a 46-year-old father of six who turned his life around after a few years of prison time in his youth. He’s agonizing less over his physical pain, which can be intense, than the knowledge that he can’t support his family. “Everyone’s telling you, work hard and it’ll pay off,” he says, sitting at a Portland coffee shop. “I did that, and I didn’t get shit from it but a disease that’s going to kill me.” Eventually, he calls his girlfriend to pick him up and drive him the three blocks back to his house.

While Tyler Jordan’s parents worry about him, he worries about them. Over the summer, Jimmy, too, was diagnosed with silicosis. But they’ve got bills to pay (he and Tina are only in their 50s) and customers are still demanding artificial stone, so he’s still in the shop, fabricating it himself. “That’s just who you are,” Tina says to Jimmy during a September evening phone call with Businessweek, and he agrees. “I’ve always been in the shop,” he says. “The alternative is to quit the business, but then what do you do?”

Had they known the hazards, Jordan’s parents say, they never would’ve brought artificial stone into their shop and their family in the first place. “It’s just so dangerous,” Jimmy says. “If we can get away from it, we would get away and just do natural stone again. But it’s hard to do that.” They’re hoping a ban takes the issue out of their hands, and their customers’. “If it’s not there,” Jimmy says, “then we don’t have to worry about it.”

“And people are safe,” Tina adds. During that Issa hearing, Democrats placed in the congressional record a letter she wrote saying that her son’s ordeal shows the product is the problem. For now, she and her husband have been doing air monitoring, reminding other fab shop owners they know to be as safe as they can, and hoping customers pick natural stone.
Later in the conversation, Tina says she wishes she could get her kids’ childhood back. “I miss them little,” she says. “If we could rewrite Tyler’s—”
“Rewrite his story,” Jimmy says.

“If we had all of the knowledge regarding engineered stone, to fabricate it or not, prior to it being introduced to us, if we could have made a more informed decision,” Tina says through tears, “things could have been different for him.”

Their son says if the federal lawsuit ban goes forward, there will be many more people like him, because the companies would have no reason to switch to safer products. “Nobody would care anymore,” Jordan says. Does he wish his family had never gotten into the stone business in the first place? “I mean, in a way I do,” he says. “But I just more so wish that the products were safe.”Read next: What Trump Delivered for Amazon

items.title: Minebea Mitsumi Pauses M&A to Chase AI, Nvidia Demand for Components
body: Minebea Mitsumi Inc., one of Japan’s biggest corporate dealmakers, is hitting pause on acquisitions to focus on its output of ball bearings, motors and actuators for AI hardware to chase lucrative returns from the emerging technology.

The key supplier to Nintendo Co. is eyeing climbing market forecasts for data centers and humanoid robots and sees “unlimited” upside ahead, according to Chairman Yoshihisa Kainuma, who said the company has no current plans for deals.
“We are so busy,” he said in an interview. “It’s more important for us to focus on the volume of work in front of us, rather than on M&A and pouring managerial resources into a new arena.”

The Tokyo-based company, which supplies parts such as haptic devices used in Nintendo consoles, is among a plethora of hardware makers such as Fujikura Ltd. whose businesses have been transformed by AI’s hunger for all kinds of formerly mundane mechanical components.

Minebea Mitsumi is now fielding ballooning orders for its ball bearings, used inside AI server fans and humanoid joints. Nvidia Corp.’s next-generation Vera Rubin platform, which relies on direct liquid cooling, is expected to spur demand for a wider range of Minebea Mitsumi components: The list includes stepping motors once used to feed paper in fax machines that can now help control the exact flow of liquid in AI servers’ cooling systems.
Read more: AI Boom Is Lifting Makers of Fiber-Optic Cables, Ball Bearings

Soaring orders are supporting Minebea Mitsumi’s newfound preference for organic growth. “We will need a staggering number of bearings if what people are predicting today about robots and AI servers is to come true,” Kainuma said. “Even if it turns out to be only half that, our capacity would be nowhere near enough to meet demand.”

In June, the company’s shares rose close to 70% since the start of the year, but they’ve since given up almost all those gains amid growing sector-wide fears about an overcapacity of computing power and rising debts, coupled with calls by AI leaders to slow the pace of development.

Minebea Mitsumi’s capital expenditure plans remain modest, despite some investors’ calls to boost spending. The company plans to invest ¥58 billion ($377 million) to bring up ball bearing manufacturing capacity to 500 million units a month by 2030, up from a little over 400 million units now, a spokesperson said separately.

Kainuma said he prefers to be cautious, adding that the company can lift production capacity significantly in under a year, if necessary. “We never know whether what we’re talking about today will actually materialize, and we shouldn’t take on all of that risk today,” he said.

Since taking the helm in 2009, 70-year-old Kainuma has relied heavily on acquisitions for growth, overseeing 30 deals. Last year, he waged an unsuccessful takeover battle against Taiwan’s Yageo Corp. for Japan’s Shibaura Mechatoronics Corp. whose high-precision thermistors are key for monitoring the temperatures of devices inside data centers to keep them from overheating.

The buyout spree stemmed from Kainuma’s prior concern that demand for mechanical components in his portfolio would wane as the world shifted toward semiconductors, sensors and capacitors. But now, dealmaking is no longer on the agenda, he said, although he wouldn’t rule out the possibility of an acquisition.

“Back then, we couldn’t see what lay ahead and we were struggling to figure out how we could keep growing,” Kainuma said.  “Now, that fog has lifted, and we can see what will become major growth areas over the next 10 to 15 years.”

items.title: Japan's Economic Comeback Faces Hardest BOJ Test in a Generation
body: Sign up for the Next Japan newsletter, for an inside view of the forces reshaping Japan, and what’s next for its businesses, markets and consumers.

Japan’s transformation from sleeping economic giant to magnet for growth and investment is set to face its fastest sequence of interest rate hikes since the bursting of Tokyo’s asset bubble more than a generation ago.

Amid a wave of pressure from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, chronic weakness in the yen and prices that keep going up, the Bank of Japan looks set to raise benchmark borrowing costs for the third time in less than 10 months at its meeting on Friday. That would mark the fastest pace of interest rate hikes since 1990, when Japan was still seen as a rival to US global economic dominance.

Four outsized rate increases in less than a year back then brought the Tokyo stock market to its knees and marked the beginning of the nation’s descent from overheated growth into economic stagnation. This time around Japan is on a more modest growth path and the most obvious dangers lie in the currency and bond markets.

One potential fault line runs from the yen into the US Treasury market, and from there into higher loan repayments for American businesses and consumers. Another threat comes from any sharp rise in yields for Japanese government debt. This would reverberate globally and also make it harder for Japan to fund Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s $2.4 trillion investment package to get the country back in the economic fast lane.

Yet if the BOJ can deliver a rate hike while managing market expectations for further increases, it may preserve a nascent recovery in the yen, nudge inflation closer to target and ensure an orderly rise in bond yields.

“The September meeting has become crucial,” said James Athey, a London-based fund manager at Marlborough Investment Management Ltd. with over 20 years of industry experience. His fund is still betting on the yen to strengthen, but sees some in the market needing little encouragement to sell the currency.
“The BOJ needs to hike and deliver a more forceful message lest they undo all the work done so far,” Athey said.

Much will depend on Governor Kazuo Ueda’s performance at the post-decision press conference, which comes late in the afternoon in Tokyo at a critical point in the day as the center of gravity in currency trading shifts from Asia to Europe.

The yen, which remains significantly weaker than its average over the past decade, has advanced close to 6% since late July, when Tokyo started its latest round of intervention to bolster the currency. The US also weighed in, helping Japan prop up the yen for the first time in 28 years, and upping the stakes for speculators.

Failure to deliver a hike now would put the BOJ at odds with Bessent, and jolt markets that are primed for further increases in coming months. The transactional nature of President Donald Trump’s administration, and the forcefulness of comments from his Treasury secretary, have even led to suggestions that the US and Japan struck a deal that included a near-term rate hike.
Read more: Bessent Dares Traders to Bet Against Yen

“I am the house now, so when we intervene with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what the Japanese, what the Bank of Japan is going to do, what Japanese policymakers are going to do,” Bessent said last week. “And you can bet against me if you want.”

Japan spent a monthly record of ¥15.4 trillion ($100 billion) on the intervention and appears to have funded a portion of this by selling Treasuries. Another turn downward in the currency that forced Japan to sell Treasuries again would add to upward pressure on US yields and could prove painful for Republican politicians heading into November’s midterm elections.

A sixth rate increase by the BOJ under Ueda — the most by any governor in at least half a century — is almost fully priced into the market for overnight index swaps. They point to the policy rate rising by a quarter point to 1.25% on Friday and peg the probability of another increase by late December at more than 80%.
Beyond the market positioning, this also reflects deepening perceptions that Japan is relinquishing its decades-long role as an outlier in monetary policy that anchored low global yields.
“The BOJ is ending its gradual normalization,” said Chotaro Morita, chief strategist at All Nippon Asset Management. “This has major implications for the future rate path.”
Board member Kazuyuki Masu reiterated the central bank’s upward trajectory Thursday.

“The Bank will continue to raise the policy interest rate” given that financial conditions remain very easy, Masu said in a speech to business leaders. “What is most vital from now on is to ensure that the underlying inflation rate does not significantly exceed 2%.”

While Japan’s core inflation rate of 1.8% hardly seems to call out for faster rate hikes, it has been held down by the Takaichi government’s energy subsidies. Economists warn that long lasting weakness in the yen and high oil prices from conflict in the Middle East are fueling inflationary pressure that may push the gauge toward 3% later this year.

“Bessent may be talking too much about the BOJ, but he has a point: The BOJ is falling behind the curve,” said Seisaku Kameda, a former BOJ chief economist. Kameda, now executive economist at Sompo Institute Plus, sees a good chance of a follow-up hike in December after this week’s expected move.

The perception of BOJ slowness hasn’t been helped by Takaichi herself. Her government appears ready to go along with a September hike, but it remains unclear how receptive the Prime Minister will be to further moves. While Takaichi’s thinking has softened since she characterized rate hikes as “stupid” before she became leader, she is still very focused on stoking economic growth and avoiding any swoon in stocks.
The Nikkei 225 measure of blue-chip Japanese stocks is around double the level of summer of 2024, but the valuation of equities is nowhere near the extremely stretched levels seen in 1989.

Japanese stocks traded at 70 times earnings during that extraordinary boom, which some analysts described as “the biggest bubble in human history.” The Nikkei currently trades at about 21 times earnings and the broader Topix index is around 17 times.
“Compared with 1989, Japanese stocks are trading at reasonable valuations from a global investor’s perspective today,” said Tomochika Kitaoka, chief equity strategist at Nomura Securities.

“The market crashed when long-term interest rates rose above 6%,” he said, contrasting the circumstances with much lower rates now. “About half of Japanese companies are net cash, so the negative impact from higher interest rates won’t be that significant. Companies should be able to cope with a moderate rise in interest rates.”
Read more: How the Nikkei Found Its Mojo in World-Beating Stocks Rally

Takaichi’s vision for Japan rests on the economy staying on a growth path, underpinned by new budget dynamics that mimic the US. She wants to focus on controlling the ratio of debt to the size of the economy, instead of simply balancing the books.
This involves inflation helping to push up the size of gross domestic product in nominal terms and boosting tax receipts to create more room for spending.

“The economy is likely to keep recovering moderately even if the BOJ raises rates this week,” said Yoshiki Shinke, senior executive economist at Daiichi Life Research Institute. While business spending is sensitive to borrowing costs it’s unlikely overall capital spending will drop when companies need to invest in labor saving technology and AI, he said.
“Still, Japan’s economy hasn’t had this kind of steady rate hike cycle for a long time, so we really need to watch carefully to see at what point the weight of rate hikes hits the economy,” he said.

The rub from this inflation is higher bond yields that translate into bigger debt-servicing burden. These costs account for a quarter of Japan’s annual budget and the Finance Ministry projects they will increase by almost a third to ¥41.3 trillion in 2029.

The implication of higher yields in Japan also affects international money flows. For many years, the nation’s biggest investors have built enormous portfolios of global stocks and bonds. Meanwhile, foreign funds have dived into carry trade strategies that involve borrowing cheaply in yen and putting the proceeds to work around the world.
Read more: Japan’s Rising Yields Stir Debate Over Growing Repatriation Risk

“If domestic yields continue to rise, Japan may gradually retain more capital at home,” said Ales Koutny, head of international rates at Vanguard Asset Management Ltd.’s active funds. “That matters not only for the yen and JGBs, but also for Treasury markets, European bond markets and broader global funding conditions.”
This might not result in a wholesale shift of overseas investments back to Japan, but it may limit the amount of money flowing abroad, and help support the yen.

Marlborough’s Athey said “the big underestimation” is how quickly the yen could appreciate if and when conditions align for Japanese life insurers, pension funds and banks to reevaluate the case for stashing money overseas.
Vanguard’s Koutny goes further.

“The story is not really about whether the BOJ hikes once more or twice more,” Koutny said. “The more important question is whether Japan is transitioning from being a supplier of global liquidity to a stronger competitor for global capital.”

items.title: In Japan, Bars and Hotels Go 1970s Retro With Showa Era Style
body: When Japan shut its borders during the Covid pandemic, expats and longtime friends Hillary Hewins and Blake Piper started spending their weekends in Atami, a small seaside city just a 40-minute bullet train ride from their adopted home of Tokyo.

Known during the 17th and 18th centuries for its soothing hot springs, Atami steadily surged in popularity during the four decades after World War II as a destination for Japanese holidaymakers. Sprawling concrete resorts opened, and the city center filled with lively bars, cabaret shows and other nightlife venues, all lit up by flashy neon signs.

When Japan’s bubble burst in the early 1990s, Atami’s prosperity collapsed as well. In five short years, hotel revenue dropped by around 25% and dozens of properties were abandoned. By 2011 visitation numbers had plummeted by 55% from their peak. The local population shrunk accordingly, from 50,000 residents to about 30,000 today.

Hewins and Piper fell in love with Atami’s faded glamour. They began investing in akiya — Japan’s famously inexpensive abandoned houses — in the area, renovating them into home rentals. Last year, they bought a pair of run-down buildings in city’s downtown for almost 37.8 million yen (about $245,000) that they plan to open as a boutique hotel in 2027. They hope to restore the two brashly designed structures to their former glory.

They’re not alone. Hewins and Piper are part of a new guard of entrepreneurs eschewing the contemporary form-follows-function Japanese aesthetic and resurrecting the maximalism of what’s called “Showa retro.” It references a period during Emperor Hirohito’s long reign, largely from the 1960s to the ’80s, when mid-century modernism was embellished with warm colors, touchable fabrics and bright signage. (The word showa originated in ancient Chinese texts; meaning “radiant peace,” it was chosen as an auspicious name to mark Hirohito’s rule when he ascended the throne in 1926.)

This decorative revival doesn’t merely reflect a nostalgic yearning for brighter times amid a weak yen and other economic doldrums. It marks a return to a more analog format of human connection during an epidemic of loneliness. In 2025, kodokushi — individuals found deceased alone in their home — accounted for one in every three deaths in Japan.

The extreme flavor of design is also a reaction against a perceived sameness of so-called third-space decor, the corporatization of casual hangouts like coffee shops around the globe, and signals a renewed focus on preservation in a culture that has long preferred to knock down old, obsolete structures rather than restore them.

“When people think of Japan they picture washitsu,” a traditional-looking room featuring paper screens and tatami floors, says Takuji Kitagawa, a marketing strategy specialist based in Tokyo. “Showa retro is something else entirely — it has its own visual language that’s genuinely distinctive on a global scale.”

It’s an aesthetic of excess — every opportunity for a design flourish is taken to stress uniqueness in the face of temperance and conformity. In 2025, Kitagawa opened Showa Club in Tokyo’s Kanda neighborhood, a modernized version of a sunakku, a type of small drinking establishment that developed during the postwar boom, which emphasizes intimacy and sociability, purveyed by the host-owner behind the bar.

“War, growth, the bubble and its collapse — in my many ways, Showa was the most eventful and alive stretch of Japan’s modern history,” Kitagawa says. He was born in 1981 and grew up in what he and many others call the Lost Thirty Years — three decades of economic stagnation that followed the burst in the early 1990s. Opening his speakeasy, with its bright red walls and sociable bar top, was a chance “to experience Showa’s energy firsthand,” Kitagawa says.

Like Kitagawa, Tokyo-based music producer Jung Kyung-ho, who goes by Night Tempo, is a child of the ’80s seeking to recapture his analog youth. Though originally from South Korea, he’s best known for his Showa Groove remixes of “city pop,” a genre of Western-influenced music that originated in 1970s Japan. To his delight, it’s gained new momentum, as “young people have longing in their imagination for cultural experiences of decades past” he says.

The most recognizable relic from Showa times may be the kissaten, literally meaning “tea-drinking shop,” though it’s more broadly a cafe where patrons can read, chat with friends or work. The kissaten is characterized by a baroque aesthetic that often verges on clutter and is highly individualized, based on the owner’s personal taste. Expect large collections of stuffed animals or antique clocks or keepsakes from around the world, all displayed among thickly upholstered seating and plenty of dark wood accents.

“The kissaten boom is unmistakable,” Kitagawa says. On Instagram, the hashtag #junkissa (another derivation of “coffee shop”) in Japanese has recently reached almost a million posts. He adds that these spaces are a balm to the automation and urban sprawl that’s perpetuated extreme amounts of isolation in a country plagued with an aging population and low birthrate. With an average of just over 4 square meters per person, Tokyo has an extreme lack of public space when compared with London (27 square meters) or New York (30 square meters.)

Keita Amano, an associate professor at Osaka Metropolitan University, asserts that the upswing in Showa retro interest has to do with what he calls “light exoticism.” He describes the phenomenon as a human curiosity about our adjacencies. We wonder how people in other places are living, and how others lived in the recent past, before the advent of certain technologies. These facets have sparked a surge in interest in sunakku, kissaten and other Showa relics by domestic travelers: throwback shotengai (covered shopping arcades), sento (bath houses with elaborate tile mosaics) and dagashiya (bodega-like candy shops).

Kitagawa says the record-breaking onslaught of inbound tourists may be playing a large part as well. In 2025 international arrivals reached 42.7 million. That’s the first time in the nation’s history that travel numbers surpassed 40 million, and up more than 16% from the 36.9 million visitors the previous year. According to the World Travel Index, Japan is the highest-ranked destination for global tourism.

“Thanks to social media, everyday scenes that Japanese people have taken for granted for decades suddenly look soulful and evocative to the foreign eye,” he notes. “Then young Japanese who never gave these places a second look start paying attention too.”

Piper adds, “I hate to minimize it, but I think a lot of the interest from the young people is because it looks good on social media.” Piper notes the word baeru in Japanese, which is the verb form of Insta-bae, which means “to look good on Instagram.” “This term gets thrown around a lot when young Japanese talk about Atami and the whole Showa retro interest, and they come to town to get a coffee at a throwback cafe for the photo opportunity,” he says.
In 2025, Atami surpassed 3 million overnight visitors, up from 2.8 million the year before. Other leisure destinations within Tokyo’s orbit are also seeing an analogous rise in nostalgic interest.

Take Chichibu in Saitama prefecture, 80 minutes from central Tokyo by train, where Odekake Watcher, which tracks GPS movements from users’ smartphones, clocked a 37% increase in female visitors in their 20s between August 2025 and this August. Like Atami, Chichibu flourished in the 1960s with the expansion of modern railways, filling up with of-the-era businesses that catered to domestic tourists interested in exploring the nearby national park. A representative from the prefectural tourism board attributes renewed interest to tourists’ desire to capture the “emoi” — the slang Japanese equivalent of “emo” — aesthetic of the area’s homes, cafes and bars for their social media feeds.

As Hewins spends more time in Atami, she’s noticing that the relic resorts are having a renaissance as well, even the ones that haven’t been renovated. “Three years ago, I was one of few guests at Hatoya Hotel, just outside of Atami. During a recent stay, there were at least 150 others at breakfast.” These were all domestic visitors, she notes.

International guests may still be wrapped up in exploring ancient temples and modern towers: A 2025 analysis by the Japan National Tourism Organization found that 70% of the country’s visitors only visit five specific destinations: Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, plus Hokkaido for skiing and Okinawa for beaches. “But as foreigners begin visiting for the third or fourth time,” Hewins adds, “the Showa retro aesthetic will soon be of great interest to them too.”

One publicly traded Japanese enterprise is doubling down on the potential growth. Komeda’s Coffee, a Showa retro cafe chain from Nagoya with over 1,000 locations nationwide, is on a hungry expansion plan to franchise globally over the next five years, with established locations in East Asia, and forthcoming growth in Thailand and elsewhere. Beyond the throwback decor (think red velvet booths, warm wooden interiors and bubble lettering on the signage), Komeda is also holding on to hospitality tenets like table service, sensing that customers crave a human touch in the face of automation and AI.

“Showa, and the bubble especially, represents the last time Japan felt like it was decisively winning,” Kitagawa says. “For younger Japanese who never lived it, that maximalist confidence is aspirational rather than remembered. For tourists, it’s an authentic, photogenic Japan that isn’t the polished minimalism they expected.”

items.title: Trump EPA Axes Carbon Pollution Standards for Coal, Gas Plants
body: The Trump administration is rescinding climate controls on coal and gas-fired power plants, one of its most aggressive moves so far to unwind US environmental regulations.

Under the final rule announced Monday afternoon at the G20 summit for energy ministers in Houston, the Environmental Protection Agency is ending a Biden-era mandate requiring existing and future fossil-fuel-fired power plants to dramatically curb their emissions in the coming decades through the use of specific technologies, including carbon capture and storage.

“It is plain and simple: The reality is that America produces energy better and cleaner than anywhere else in the world and power plants should not be unfairly targeted,” said the EPA’s top air regulator Aaron Szabo in a press call on Monday.
The agency estimates the final rule will save $310 billion, making it the “largest power sector deregulatory action ever,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin in Houston.

The decision will effectively end the federal effort to regulate the largest industrial sources of greenhouse gases in the US. If America’s power sector were a country, it would rank as the world’s sixth-largest emitter, according to an analysis of 2022 emissions data by New York University School of Law’s Institute for Policy Integrity.

“This is very unusual,” said Meredith Hankins, the federal climate legal director at the Natural Resources Defense Council, an environmental nonprofit. “They are just fully repealing standards with no intent to replace them.”

The move comes after the EPA already delayed restrictions on super pollutants used in refrigeration and air conditioning, axed greenhouse gas standards for automobiles and struck down the endangerment finding, a key scientific determination that climate change poses a threat to human health and welfare.
There are multiple pending lawsuits against these other climate rollbacks, and environmental experts anticipate the new power plant rule will likely be challenged immediately in court, too.

Agency officials on Monday also proposed a new rule repealing the federal finding that greenhouse gases from power plants specifically are a significant source of air pollution, effectively a separate endangerment finding for power plants under the Clean Air Act.

In its new proposal, the EPA takes the position that regulating climate emissions from power plants is beyond its authority under the Clean Air Act, according to Szabo. “If finalized, it would prevent a future EPA from being able to regulate greenhouse gas emissions for global climate change for power plants,” he said.

Under the Obama administration, the EPA created new standards — the Clean Power Plan — that required existing and future fossil-fuel-fired plants to cut their climate pollution. Industry groups for the power sector and some states sued over the rule and the courts put it on hold before it took effect. Ultimately, the Supreme Court struck it down in 2022.

President Joe Biden’s EPA then finalized rules in 2024 that essentially forced the nation’s current fleet of coal plants to capture most carbon emissions by 2039 or close. They also put strict emissions limits on current and future gas plants. These are the mandates now being repealed.

Various members of the power sector lobbied for the change, claiming the Biden-era standards were unrealistic. The elimination of the mandates comes as the Trump administration is taking unprecedented steps to keep coal-fired power plants online, including ordering some plants not to retire as planned, in response to growing electricity demand from data centers and domestic manufacturing.
Industry groups celebrated the rollback.

“Overturning these examples of EPA overreach will help preserve and strengthen the US coal fleet, protect grid reliability and shield electricity consumers from higher costs,” said Michelle Bloodworth, president and CEO of the coal industry group America’s Power, in a statement. The Edison Electric Institute, which represents all US investor-owned electric companies, “welcomes EPA’s repeal of carbon capture and storage-based standards,” said the trade group’s chief legal officer Rachael Marsh.

Meanwhile, former EPA officials and environmentalists have criticized the repeal and warned that its economic and environmental fallout could be significant, given that the effects of climate change are increasingly playing out across the globe in the form of deadly heat waves, record-setting wildfires and collapsing glaciers.

“The Clean Air Act is clear: EPA has a statutory obligation to regulate significant sources of pollution that threaten public health,” said former EPA Administrator Gina McCarthy, who now chairs the climate group America Is All In. “Everyone will be affected by their actions, but the most vulnerable among us, our kids and grandkids, will suffer the most.”

items.title: Sysco Seeks to Raise $1 Billion in Share Sale for Jetro Deal
body: Sysco Corp. is seeking to raise $1 billion in a share sale to partially fund the food service firm’s $29.1 billion acquisition of Jetro Restaurant Depot LLC.
The Houston-based firm’s share sale is being led by Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Toronto-Dominion Bank, according to a statement Monday.
The shares are being offered for $80.20 to $81.90 each, according to people familiar with the matter. The range represents a discount of as much as 4% discount to Monday’s closing price of $83.54.
Sysco supplies food to restaurants, hospitals and schools across the US. Its shares traded flat after-hours, giving it a market value of nearly $40 billion.
Read More: Cash-and-Carry King Caps Second Act With $29 Billion Sale
The deal is oversubscribed following an earlier confidential marketing effort, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is private.
The offering is expected to price later Monday, the people said. A representative for Sysco didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Bank of America Corp., JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Wells Fargo & Co. are also working on the share offering, the statement shows.
