items.title: Oil Tankers Earn $1 Million a Day as War Leaves Ship Shortage
body: The cost of hiring an oil tanker on the industry’s benchmark trade route topped $1 million a day for the first time, as the Iran war leaves too few ships willing to cross the Strait of Hormuz to collect cargoes.

Vessels hauling oil from inside the Persian Gulf to China were being hired at $1.035 million a day, according to data from the Baltic Exchange in London on Monday. The benchmark route has become less relevant during the war because the main means of exporting Persian Gulf oil has shifted to shuttling barrels through Hormuz for collection just outside by tankers that don’t want to navigate the strait.

Even so, transporting crude to China from the Gulf of Oman, which doesn’t require transit through the chokepoint, costs the equivalent of about $644,000 a day. In bad markets in the past, the same ships sometimes barely covered their running costs.
Shipping costs have been propelled higher by a combination of factors, many of which center around the Iran war and a giant bet by a secretive Korean tycoon.

The supersized earnings also partly reflect oil-refining margins that have spiraled out of control because wars in Iran and Ukraine mean world isn’t making enough fuel to meet demand. That’s spurring refiners to keep purchasing and shipping whatever barrels they can get because it’s still profitable for them to process the oil into finished fuels like diesel and gasoline.

At the same time, the number of vessels shuttling cargoes out of the Hormuz is adding time to each tanker journey, sucking up vessel supply. That comes alongside disruptions to Saudi oil flows from Yemen’s Houthi rebels, which has forced some ships to sail a voyage that’s 30 days longer around Africa.

items.title: Ebola Patient's Journey in Congo Shows Challenge of Tracing Virus
body: Ebola continues to spread in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where almost half the confirmed cases in the outbreak have been fatal. Today, Jason Gale, who covers global health for Bloomberg News, writes about one man who shows how difficult it can be to stop the virus. Plus: Southern and Western Sun Belt states are dealing with slow growth (free link) amid the immigration crackdown, and the new B-school dean at the University of Virginia confronts AI.

Four months after authorities identified an Ebola outbreak in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, the epidemic has largely disappeared from international headlines. The virus hasn’t been nearly so accommodating.

The latest reminder came last week from Gwaka, a small community in northwestern Congo. According to a local official, a 23-year-old man died there early last week after developing a fever and vomiting blood. Samples taken after his death tested positive for Bundibugyo, the rare form of Ebola driving this epidemic. The diagnosis was the first in South-Ubangi, making it the seventh Congolese province reached by the outbreak — and the first in the country’s northwest.

What happened before he arrived is even more concerning. The man left Kamanyola, a village in South Kivu province, two months earlier, traveling through neighboring Rwanda and Uganda before reentering Congo.His journey covered roughly 2,500-kilometers (1,550 miles) through scores of cities and towns. Part of that distance he traveled via the Congo River, which would likely have meant several days in close quarters with dozens of others. Ebola has an incubation period of 2 to 21 days, but people generally don’t transmit the virus until symptoms appear. The man became ill on Aug. 27 while traveling by boat.

Health authorities are now confronted with the painstaking job of finding people he may have encountered while sick. In neighboring North-Ubangi, 53 passengers from a boat the man used were reportedly quarantined. Two who slipped away and traveled by motorcycle to Gbadolite were later found with symptoms and are being investigated as suspected cases.

It’s an extreme example of the problem that has dogged the response from the beginning: Ebola is moving through an extraordinarily mobile population faster than health workers can find it. “I call on traditional leaders, religious leaders, healthcare workers, the media, youth organizations, and women’s groups: spread accurate information,” Jean-Jacques Mbungani, a former Congolese health minister and lawmaker from the area, wrote on X. “You are on the front lines. Every hour counts in preventing an imported case from leading to local transmission.”

Congo had recorded 7,022 confirmed infections and 3,398 deaths as of Thursday. Cases have also been reported in Uganda and France, but the only country where active transmission is known to be happening is Congo. The World Health Organization described it last week as a “large and geographically expanding epidemic” with an increasing risk of further international spread.

There is some good news. In parts of Ituri province, where the epidemic began, along the border with Uganda, transmission appears to be falling. People with symptoms are being identified much faster than they were early in the outbreak, and contact tracing has improved markedly.
But Ebola is shifting elsewhere. North Kivu reported 43 new infections on Thursday, 13 more than Ituri. Treatment centers there had 311 patients in facilities with only 220 beds.

That pattern helps explain why the epidemic has proved so difficult to contain. By the time responders strengthen surveillance, treatment and community engagement in one hot spot, another can emerge somewhere else.

Experimental vaccines and treatments are being tested, there are thousands of responders on the ground, and laboratories are vastly better equipped than they were during the catastrophic West African Ebola epidemic a dozen years ago. But controlling Ebola still depends on decidedly low-tech work: finding sick people quickly, tracing everyone they encountered, isolating infections and persuading communities to cooperate.
The man who died in Gwaka illustrates what happens when that chain breaks. One infection can leave health officials retracing a weekslong journey across borders, cities, roads and rivers.

The Houston neighborhood of Gulfton has for decades been a bustling haven for immigrants in a city whose economy was built on oil, space exploration and people from somewhere else. It’s where new arrivals start their American journey. Their first homes are often cheap apartments in squat complexes with names like Le Chateau or Pelican Pointe, surrounded by strip malls filled with restaurants serving Mexican tacos, Salvadoran pupusas, Vietnamese pho or Ethiopian curries.

These days, though, Gulfton is confronting a shock poised to rival the 1980s bust that cleared out the oil boom chasers for whom those apartments were built. As the Trump administration stems the flow of immigrants into the country and tries to chase out millions more, Sun Belt cities like Houston that have relied on relentless population growth to power their economies are seeing that expansion stall.

As Shawn Donnan and Catarina Saraiva write, Trump’s anti-immigration push, combined with falling birth rates and an aging population, means the US faces the possibility of the first population decline in its recorded history sooner than demographers anticipated. What does that mean for the Sun Belt?

Yael Grushka-Cockayne became dean at the University of Virginia’s Darden School of Business on Aug. 1. The school’s 10th dean and the first woman in its 71-year history, she didn’t need to spend time getting to know staff or the campus, as she’s been a professor and academic leader at Darden for 17 years. It’s Grushka-Cockayne’s knowledge about artificial intelligence, though, that may prove to be her biggest advantage. Business schools around the world are scrambling to devise strategies to teach and use the transformative technology. Grushka-Cockayne has been working on AI at Darden for several years now, including as co-academic director of the LaCross Institute for Ethical Artificial Intelligence in Business.
Carol Hymowitz interviewed Grushka-Cockayne for Bloomberg Businessweek. Here’s a sample of their conversation.
What in your early life led you in the direction of technology and its applications in business?

I was a very math-oriented child, and later I was drawn to industrial engineering and operations research because I loved quants. In the late 1990s, information systems were both new and exciting, and there was a lot on the hook. The year 2000 was looming, the internet was starting to bloom, and companies realized they could think about the flow of information more efficiently. I focused on what I identified as a need, which was making sure senior leaders recognized the importance of efficiency, of things like the use of resources, project planning and management, and decision-making. Today AI is at the heart of these issues.

items.title: DOJ Covid Loan-Fraud Crackdown Finds $245 Million in Losses
body: The US Justice Department said a federal crackdown by prosecutors this summer uncovered hundreds of millions of dollars in fraud tied to Covid-relief programs, resulting in criminal charges against dozens of defendants.

Working with US Attorneys Offices and state agencies from June to September, DOJ brought charges against almost 80 people while securing guilty pleas from dozens more, the department said in a statement Monday. The cases involved about $245 million in intended losses to taxpayers, DOJ said.

The alleged fraud included cases tied to Paycheck Protection Program claims for employees who didn’t exist and business owners seeking Economic Injury Disaster Loans for damage that did not occur, the department said.

“Pandemic loan relief was meant to keep American small businesses alive during government lockdowns — not line the pockets of fraudsters,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said. “The defendants charged during our summer surge allegedly fabricated businesses, submitted false payroll and revenue claims, stole identities, and concealed foreign ties on their applications — but they will now be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

At the end of President Donald Trump’s first term, Congress passed legislation in 2020 creating more than $2 trillion in economic relief for workers, families, small businesses and some industries as the global pandemic led to widespread lockdowns and job cuts. Under President Joe Biden, another $1.9 trillion of economic stimulus was passed.

While those programs provided aide for many Americans, they also created “immense challenges” for the Treasury Department to combat fraud, the Office of the Inspector General has said. In Trump’s second term, the White House created the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, led by Vice President JD Vance.

“Unfortunately, we’ve seen this with so much of our anti-fraud efforts and hard work over the past couple of years,” Vance said Monday at a press conference in Kansas City, Missouri. “This should have been done earlier. It’s kind of ridiculous that some of the fraud that we saw with the PPP program wasn’t actually enforced. So what we’ve done here is say that no fraud is too small.”
The surge in enforcement was orchestrated by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division.

items.title: UK Mulls Supporting Saudis Amid Fears of Houthi Economic Hit
body: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering whether to help Saudi Arabia counter attacks from the Houthis in Yemen amid British concerns about a worsening economic hit from the escalating conflict.

The premier has received requests from Saudi Arabia for a range of diplomatic and military support, according to people familiar with the matter. Those requests include operational support for the Saudi military to repel the Iran-supported group’s push south along Yemen’s Red Sea coast toward the Bab el-Mandeb strait, as well as help to defend against strikes on its territory oil infrastructure, they said.

It’s unclear whether Burnham is willing to approve the requests, which haven’t been disclosed by the UK government. A spokesperson said Britain would work with partners to support regional stability, declining to be drawn on specifics. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment.
The Saudis have also asked the US for more help, though Washington — keen not to see the Iran war escalate — has not said if it will provide extra assistance.

Saudi Arabia has suffered from several Houthi missile and drones attacks this month, with the militant group targeting southern towns and Red Sea ports. On Tuesday morning, Saudi authorities issued air alerts for cities including Jeddah, Yanbu, Jazan and Al Ula, a medieval site that’s key to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s attempts to boost tourism. While the government said the danger soon passed, dozens of people have been injured by strikes over the past week or so.

The Houthis, who control land holding most of Yemen’s population, have also made gains inside their country and last week captured the port of Mokha and some islands near the Bab el-Mandeb strait. While they were already disrupting shipping through the chokepoint, the extra territory tightens their grip over it.
Read more: Houthi Gains Leave MBS With Few Good Options in Yemen

The fighting presents Burnham with one of his first major foreign policy and economic dilemmas since he became prime minister in July. The UK is determined not to get drawn into another Middle East conflict, not least because it didn’t support US President Donald Trump’s war on Iran. Yet the crisis is posing serious challenges for UK economic policy ahead of his administration’s first budget next month.

The advance by Houthi militants in recent days, and Saudi Arabia halting its East-West oil pipeline following attacks, has helped push up energy prices even more. The pipeline has been the main outlet for Saudi crude exports since the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude rose 1.5% to $107.25 a barrel on Tuesday, extending its gain this month to almost 20%.

Gilts extended a drop Monday as money markets added to bets on Bank of England interest rate rises off the back of inflation fears. Traders now fully price five quarter-point BoE hikes by the end of 2027, an outcome that would badly complicate the new premier’s key pledge to reduce the cost of living.

Burnham has been advised by his officials that if the Houthis take control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait it would have a “catastrophic” impact on international shipping and provide another hit to the global economy through a further spike in the oil price and inflation, according to the people, who requested anonymity talking about behind-closed-doors discussions.

British officials fear it could be as long as six weeks before a return to service for the East-West pipeline. It’s a bleaker assessment than that of US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who on Monday said he expects the conduit to be up and running “very soon.”
Read more: Saudis Seek to Boost Hormuz Oil Exports as Key Pipeline Attacked

The UK Treasury is additionally worried that the recent escalation is taking place as the Office for Budget Responsibility prepares its economic and fiscal forecasts for the Oct. 28 budget. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey had been hoping to see inflation concerns which are weighing on government borrowing costs ease during the assessment window. Instead, market moves are going further in the wrong direction and potentially leaving Healey with even less headroom against his budgetary rules.

Burnham has agreed to send British military advisers to Saudi Arabia to support its efforts, the people said. The UK premier is not alone in receiving requests from the Saudis for support. The crown prince, known as MBS and the kingdom’s de facto ruler, called Trump last week and urged him to strike the Houthis, Axios reported, though so far Washington has stayed out of the fight other than sending military advisers.

On Saturday, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband spoke by phone to Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan to discuss the Houthi attacks. “The UK stands firmly with Saudi Arabia and the internationally-recognized Government of Yemen,” Miliband said.
The Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, triggering a civil war that still divides the country. The Saudis back the internationally-recognized government.
Read more: How the Houthis Are Upping the Stakes in the Iran War: Explainer

In 2024, under Conservative former premier Rishi Sunak, Britain’s military struck Houthi targets in Yemen in response to the group launching attacks in the Red Sea. Labour’s then opposition leader Keir Starmer supported the strikes. As premier, Starmer later deployed military assets to Saudi Arabia, and in March, Britain’s Sky Sabre air defense system was integrated into the country, including radars, a control node and missile launchers.

items.title: Puig Agrees to Take Control of Isdin in €1.2 Billion Deal
body: Puig Brands SA agreed to buy the 50% of Isdin SA it didn’t already own for €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion), giving it full control of the skincare brand. Shares fell.

The Barcelona-based fragrance company will pay €900 million to Corporación Químico-Farmacéutica Esteve SA when the deal closes, followed by another €300 million in the first quarter of 2029, according to a regulatory filing on Monday.
Isdin, which sells sun creams, lotions and skin treatments, was founded in 1975 as a joint venture between the Puig and Esteve families.
Puig dropped 3.3% to €16.92 per share at 9:24 a.m. in Madrid. The stock is up 14% this year.

Isdin gives Puig, which listed on the Spanish stock exchange in 2024, a bigger presence in skincare. Isdin’s flagship brand is Uriage, and it also owns smaller names including Apivita, Kama Ayurveda, Loto del Sur and Dr. Barbara Sturm. Puig’s beauty brand, Charlotte Tilbury, also has a skincare line.

Skincare has been the smallest part of Puig’s business, accounting for just 11% of the group’s €5.2 billion of revenue in 2025. Fragrances and fashion are by far Puig’s biggest source of revenue, with nearly three quarters of sales.
Last year, Isdin posted slightly higher revenues of around €648 million, while Ebitda fell 27% due to higher costs. The company aims for €1 billion in sales by 2030.

“Full ownership of higher-margin Isdin will likely add scale to Puig’s Skincare segment and could create synergies that lift profitability across brands,” Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Andrea Ferdinando Leggieri and Deborah Aitken said in a note.

Puig’s stock has slumped nearly 30% since the company’s listing two years ago as demand for perfumes waned following a pandemic-era boom. The shares have rebounded some this year, however, as first-half results beat market expectations. The company is set to present a new strategy in October.

Earlier this year, Puig was in talks with Estée Lauder Cos. for a deal that would have created one of the world’s largest fragrance and skincare companies. The conversations fell through in May, sending Puig’s stock down the most on record.

items.title: AI Era Coincides With Weak Pay and Employment for College Graduates
body: The rise of artificial intelligence has coincided with a significant decline in both initial earnings and employment among graduates with the most-exposed college majors, a worrisome trend that could shape career outcomes for years afterward, according to a new study.

Economists at the US Census Bureau examined data covering roughly 29% of US bachelor’s degrees issued between 2016 and 2024, finding notable effects on new graduates after ChatGPT’s debut in November 2022.

Grouping college majors into deciles by exposure to AI, the economists found that the most-affected decile saw their likelihood of initial employment drop by 5 percentage points after ChatGPT’s introduction. Earnings slipped by 13% initially, partly because many new graduates took entry-level jobs in lower-paying fields including retail and restaurants, the study found.

“This earnings decline is comparable in magnitude to the earnings losses associated with graduating into a large recession,” the authors said in the study. Computer science, information systems and other software-related fields dominated the most-exposed decile.
Read More: BLS Expands List of Jobs Threatened by AI to 45 Roles

AI’s role in displacing young people is just one of myriad worries emanating from the booming sector. Recent security-related incidents prompted industry leaders, including Dario Amodei of Anthropic PBC and Sam Altman of ChatGPT parent OpenAI, to suggest the industry slow development on the most advanced AI models. President Donald Trump, in response, suggested doing so would provide a leg up to China’s rival AI program.

The study adds to evidence that young people are struggling to break into the labor market, despite a fairly modest 4.1% unemployment rate for workers of all ages. Data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York show the unemployment rate for recent college graduates was 5.7% as of June, almost double the 2.9% jobless rate for all college graduates.

Before ChatGPT’s debut, young workers surged into computer fields now most exposed to AI, and for a time, employment kept pace with their numbers, the Census economists noted. Now that AI appears to be reversing things, a question is whether exposed graduates will catch up to their peers who graduated before large language models became prevalent, they said in the study.

“These findings suggest that the rise of AI could have long-term consequences for early career workers, especially recent college graduates who have made costly human capital investments in AI-exposed fields,” the authors wrote.

items.title: Goldman's Dan Dees on AI's Broad 'Blast Radius'
body: Hi, it’s Ryan Gould in New York, bringing you the highlights of a recent chat I had with senior Goldman Sachs executive Dan Dees. Elsewhere, bankers who once chased Gulf IPOs are having to look elsewhere as deals slump.
Today’s top stories

Goldman Sachs has just wrapped up its Communacopia + Technology Conference in San Francisco. In the run-up to the event, I spoke with Dan Dees, the firm’s co-head of global banking and markets, to get his thoughts on the trends driving tech dealmaking this year and further into the cycle. Here are some edited highlights from our chat. —Ryan Gould

What’s changed since Goldman held this conference last year?The scale of everyone’s ambitions has lifted, and part of that is because of what we’re seeing play out in technology and in the macro. But another part of it is, in our industry, activity begets activity... When you see that other people may act on the asset that you want to act on, the urgency to move is higher. When you see that financing markets are open and available in meaningful size, or that your competitors are accessing those markets in meaningful size, it impels you towards action.

So is it all AI, AI, AI?What we’re seeing is a capex boom around a disruptive technology. And that technology drives the need for scale, the need for change, the need for new ways to access your customer, the emergence of new competitors. And that is quite a powerful cocktail for M&A activity and financing activity.

What about PE firms? They’re not really adding to that cocktail yet, right?A lot of those deals that we would expect to happen involve sponsor-backed companies, and those have been slower to transact. While activity in that patch is up year over year, it’s up much less than the broader market.

When might they get more involved?When I look out and say, “what could take us higher than even these elevated levels of activity?” one of the places I get excited about is if the financial sponsor community kicks in the same way strategics have done. I do see that happening. I see a lot of those dialogues, a lot of activity. Financing markets are still pretty wide open. And with every month that goes by, every quarter that goes by, there will be more pressure on sponsors to transact.

Can you speak about circular financing versus M&A in tech right now?In a world where the rise of this disruptive technology is what is catalyzing a lot of activity, and where it’s enormously capital intensive and requires the build-out of significant amounts of infrastructure and significant capital to fund all of that, it’s hard to separate the financing from the strategic moves. They’re interlinked. It’s all part of a continuum.
What’s the scope of this current cycle?The blast radius of the AI activity is so broad because it’s an infrastructure build that is leading to activity in every sector.

And what do you see as the biggest risk to it?We sit in a world where any of the following macro issues would have been the highlight of our conversation a year ago: oil at $100, with a chance it could go to $120 or back down to $80; the Fed raising or cutting rates and by how much; or the Bank of Japan going through a historic shift in its posture. Those are fascinating macro drivers of activity and context for deals and yet none of them are rising to the top of the discussion, partly because they’re being overshadowed by this enormous capex cycle that is really driving all this activity. So if I were to tell you the thing that would make you concerned that all this could slow down, it would be some hiccup in that AI story.
Michael Dell’s family office and Sequence Holdings teamed up to acquire Baldwin Insurance Group in an all-cash deal valued at $7.7 billion. Baldwin colleagues will retain a minority stake.

Apollo Global Management is in talks to acquire Johnson & Johnson’s DePuy Synthes in a deal that could value the orthopedics unit at $20 billion. If talks are successful, it would be Apollo’s biggest bet yet on healthcare.

Monte Paschi has pledged to keep pursuing its twin offers for Banco BPM and Banca Generali even if it gets bought by Intesa Sanpaolo. The bids are “irrevocable” and not subject to Intesa’s takeover, Monte Paschi said.

French automotive supplier Forvia is considering selling its Japanese unit Clarion Electronics as it looks to cut debt and streamline. Clarion could attract interest from local players and Asian strategic buyers.
Private equity firm GTCR is in talks to acquire supply-chain software maker SPS Commerce. A deal could be announced in the coming weeks. SPS has a market value of almost $3 billion.
Kioxia Holdings is considering raising at least $10 billion by listing American depositary receipts, potentially joining other AI-related companies seeking to tap strong investor demand.
Aliko Dangote has long been Africa’s richest man. He’s now poised to make a $23 billion leap up the list of the world’s wealthiest as he opens an IPO — the continent’s biggest yet — for his refinery.

Anthropic has picked Nasdaq as its listing venue ahead of a potential record-setting IPO. The Claude chatbot maker is seeking to raise as much as or more than SpaceX in an IPO that could take place as soon as October.Meanwhile, rival OpenAi has pushed back an IPO to 2027, according to CEO Sam Altman, who said the firm is focusing on addressing safety-related concerns around the technology before a listing.

Firmus Technologies is looking to raise as much as $5 billion in an IPO in Australia. The data center provider is targeting a listing at the end of October and the deal is shaping up to be as one of the largest-ever IPOs in Australia.

Just three years ago, global bankers would fly into the Gulf to corner a slice of the world’s hottest market for new share sales. Now, even local advisers are being forced to hunt for business outside the region as deals dwindle. Listing volumes in the Gulf began tapering off last year and have fallen to under $1.1 billion so far in 2026, due in part to the monthslong regional conflict.

Robinhood Markets made it easier and cheaper for armchair investors to trade all kinds of financial markets and now it wants to open doors to IPOs, too. The online broker will get a chance to show what it can do with its first underwriting role, on the $3 billion listing of smart-ring maker Oura. Don’t expect a revolution, though, writes Paul J. Davies.

PSG Equity has raised more than €4.4 billion for a new fund targeting European software and technology companies, a vote of confidence from investors in a sector that suffered a heavy selloff earlier this year.

Gulf fintech firm Tabby said it was valued at $6.5 billion in an investment round led by Blue Pool Capital, the Hong Kong investment firm that manages the assets of Alibaba’s Chairman Joseph Tsai. The latest number tops New York-listed peer Klarna.
Hugo Boss said Chairman Stephan Sturm will step down, as largest shareholder Frasers Group seeks to beef up its board representation alongside its takeover bid for the German fashion house.

Sullivan & Cromwell is opening its first Middle East office in Abu Dhabi, becoming the latest US law firm to try and tap into accelerating dealmaking activity across the region. Ahmed T. el-Gaili will lead the new practice

items.title: This Is A Different Kind of AI Selloff
body: Hello and welcome to the newsletter, a grab bag of daily content from the Odd Lots universe. Sometimes it’s us, Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway, bringing you our thoughts on the most recent developments in markets, finance and the economy. And sometimes it’s contributions from our network of expert guests and sources. Whatever it is, we promise it will always be interesting.
If you like chatting with us, check out the Odd Lots Discord, where you can hang out and talk with us and with other listeners 24/7.
Good morning from Los Angeles! The two of us are in Southern California today to participate in the Future Proof conference, as well as our own LIVE show at the Vermont theater in Hollywood.
We’ve got an amazing lineup of guests, and you should buy your tickets here.

Basically from the day ChatGPT was revealed in 2022, the market has been in the grips of the so-called AI Trade. Sometimes it’s been straightforward, like buying shares of Nvidia. Something it’s been exotic and desperate, with weird bankshot ways in, or people buying anything with AI in the name. Anyone else remember the market’s brief love affair with C3.ai? Remember when people were obsessed with the publicly traded Bitcoin miners on the premise that their pre-existing connections to the power grid would be more valuable in the hands of AI datacenters?

Earlier this year, the hot move was to short traditional software companies on the premise that the big model makers would eat their respective lunches. The trade has been expressed in other ways too, from buying shares of Caterpillar and GE Vernova (makers of natural gas turbines) to the entire Korean stock market. But yeah, it’s been all over the map.

And while in some sense, the line has gone straight up, there have certainly been speedbumps. I remember early on there was a mini-freakout because of some sell-side research which said that Microsoft was slowing down its datacenter expansion. There was the famous DeepSeek selloff in early 2025, which was the moment everyone started talking about Jevons Paradox.

The bulls have consistently pointed to a straight line up in demand, while the bears question whether American frontier companies will be able to cover their huge future capital outlays or whether end users would even get a sufficient ROI for all of their token spending.
But the one thing that’s almost never really been discussed by market participants is the idea that at some point the politics would really shift against AI itself.

It’s very weird that within AI there’s been almost two completely separate conversations running in parallel. You have one group (a lot of VCs and the podcasts they go on) who almost exclusively talk about capabilities, exploding token consumption, and all the Gigawatts of power needed to satisfy this demand. And then you have this whole other, separate conversation (which includes a lot of lab employees) who talk about things like rogue AI, alignment, mechanistic interpretability, “loss of control”-incidents, and so forth. And somehow, the two conversations almost never intersect.
In my opinion, this began to change a little over two weeks ago. Here’s what I wrote on August 27th, just after the organization METR came out with its report on the OpenAI/Hugging Face attack:

Basically, just investigating the incident was so overwhelming — so much volume of data and text — that the researchers had to depend on models to sift through all of the information and put together a cogent story about what happened. This is a costly process, and so the dynamic is this: Capability continues to expand rapidly (arguably exponentially) while our ability to monitor AI behavior expands much more slowly.

And so it was easy to foresee that this would mark a turning point where everyone involved in the frontier, either literally or figuratively, would have to spend more resources on monitoring and relatively fewer resources on capability-maximizing.

Since the Hugging Face report, there’s been a cascade in this direction. Some politicians have woken up to the issue, moving beyond data center politics to the politics of model development itself. First it was Bernie Sanders. Now more recently, it’s Senator John Ossoff. And then just in the last few days, we’ve had the leaders of the major AI companies (including Elon!) talking about the importance of slowing down capability gains and establishing a permanent role for third-party monitors, with direct line-of-sight into the day-to-day goings on of the company.

When it comes to regulating AI, there are a number of analogies that people reach for. Finance is a common one, and so people talk about auditors of the operations, third party ratings agencies putting a letter grade on debt, FINRA, and so forth.

In the Odd Lots episode out today, we spoke with OpenAI President Greg Brockman, and I brought up the analogy of restaurant health inspectors, who come in from time to time to make sure that the dishwasher works, that the gas lines are installed correctly, and making sure that everyone in the kitchen is washing their hands and not letting their hair fall into the food.

Greg was circumspect and didn’t want to endorse anything without specific details, but just in the time between when the episode was recorded and when it came out this morning, it’s clear that the industry is moving in this direction, with Sam Altman joining arch rival Dario Amodel in calling for these third parties to be given employee-like access.

And now today, we see the AI-linked names sliding. They’re not crashing, but the moves are notable. ADRs of Softbank (which has an equity stakes in OpenAI) is down 14% as of the time I’m typing this. SMH, a popular semiconductor ETF, is down 4%. Nvidia is down about 3%. GE Vernova is down 8%.

Of course, you have to put all these moves into context. These have been high flyers, with high vol. And I think the whole world expects AI activity to be bigger next year and the year after that and the year after that and so forth. But in the markets, everything is at the margins. And so any shift from development and sales to safety and oversight is going to ripple outwards in its effect, and change people’s thinking about growth trajectories.

Bear arguments are nothing new. Selloffs in AI are nothing new. But the timing and texture of this one looks a little different. And it’s the first time in this entire cycle that market participants (who mostly talk about lines that are going straight up and to the right) and the discussions that they’re having are actually crossing streams with the discussions about technology danger and risk.

As mentioned, in today’s episode we speak with OpenAI President Greg Brockman about doing business in the wake of the Hugging Face attack. We talk about the challenges of alignment, pacing the frontier, the role of third party auditors, and more.

Watch: Bloomberg / YouTube

items.title: Trump Jr.'s Wife Says Russian Paid For Parties But Not Wedding
body: President Donald Trump’s daughter-in-law said a Russian oligarch paid for “two incredible nights of celebration” in the Bahamas after her wedding to Donald Trump Jr. but was not involved in the actual nuptials, amid fresh ethics questions involving the first family.

The couple had a private marriage ceremony on a Friday in May, Bettina Trump wrote in an Instagram post, and then a celebration the following weekend in the Bahamas. That second event, which had been planned before the wedding date was finalized, was hosted by Umar Kremlev, Bettina Trump said. Kremlev is a Russian oligarch with ties to President Vladimir Putin.

“Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” the post states.

ProPublica reported Monday morning that Kremlev bankrolled the Bahamas celebration, shelling out hundreds of thousands of dollars to rent a private island and put on a fireworks show, among other expenses.

While Kremlev may not have been involved directly in the wedding, paying for the two-day party with the president’s eldest son and his associates only deepens questions about conflicts of interest with the Trump family.
Kremlev is the head of the International Boxing Association, which receives financing from Russian energy giant Gazprom, a company that is currently subject to extensive US financial sanctions.

He has been personally sanctioned by Ukraine over his ties to Putin; he accompanied the Russian president on a recent state visit to China. Kyiv has also penalized an organization linked to his family over allegations it played a role in a program involving the abduction of Ukrainian children, ProPublica reported.

The president and his sons have been scrutinized over the Trump Organization’s decision to continue pursuing overseas business deals during Trump’s second term, as well as the activities of crypto company World Liberty Financial, in which Trump Jr. and other family members hold large stakes. The president said in his latest annual financial disclosure that he earned at least $1.4 billion from crypto and memecoin-related businesses.
Read more: Trump Reports at Least $1.4 Billion in 2025 Crypto Earnings
In the Instagram post, Bettina Trump said that the Bahamas getaway had “actually been planned well in advance as a fun weekend with friends.”

“It was never intended to be our wedding weekend. When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds,” she wrote. She added that there was “no conspiracy” and “no mystery,” and that “friendship doesn’t require a political motive.”
Kremlev’s press office told ProPublica he and Donald Trump Jr. met a couple of years ago and “have a friendly relationship.”
The White House declined to comment, pointing to Bettina Trump’s Instagram post.

items.title: Saudis Seek to Boost Hormuz Oil Exports as Key Pipeline Attacked
body: Saudi Arabia is seeking to further boost oil supply through the Strait of Hormuz after attacks forced it to halt a key pipeline that’s been the main means of getting its crude to global markets during the Iran war, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The kingdom had been raising shipments through the contested Hormuz waterway in the first 10 days on this month from August levels, and is now trying to increase supplies further, the person said, asking not to be identified because the plans are confidential.

Saudi Arabia closed the East-West pipeline, the primary link that helped the country circumvent the Iran war-induced turmoil in Hormuz, after at least two points along the route were targeted last week. The halt puts at risk millions of barrels a day that were moving through the pipeline at a time when markets are clamoring for supply, with crude near $110 in London in recent days.
Saudi Aramco declined to comment and the energy ministry said it had nothing to add to its statement on Friday.

The pipeline will be out of service for several weeks, the Associated Press reported Monday, citing two regional officials. Meanwhile, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said he expects the conduit to be up and running “very soon.”

A pumping station along the pipeline was also targeted in April as part of a wave of attacks on production, refining and petrochemical facilities. The link had suffered only limited damage and flows had continued, people familiar with the matter said at the time. Supplies returned to normal levels within days.

Even prior to last week’s attacks, loading rates were gradually ramping up, while an armada of more than a dozen Saudi ships had begun to wait just outside the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks. Satellite images indicate an uptick in tankers loading at a major Saudi export terminal in the Persian Gulf over the last few days.

Still, any effort to put more barrels through the waterway would also have to confront a dramatic shortage of ships that has sent freight costs to the highest on record. Saudi Arabia operates a vast tanker fleet, but sometimes hires extra vessels to support its operations. The cost of hauling oil from its ports inside the Persian Gulf to China neared $1 million a day on Friday for the first time ever.

It’s not immediately clear how much and how quickly Saudi Aramco can increase Hormuz shipments to offset the pipeline’s shutdown. The company had been raising its total exports closer to 4 million barrels a day in early September, with about 1 million a day going out through Hormuz and the remainder via the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, where the East-West pipeline terminates, the person familiar said.
Total shipments had dropped to about 3 million a day in August, the lowest in at least nine years, according to tanker-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg, Vortexa and Kpler.
Also read: Asian Refiners Seek Saudi Updates After Oil Pipeline Closure

The slide followed increasing risk from the Yemen-based Houthi militants, who said in July that they would blockade Saudi shipping in response to a siege on the Yemeni capital. The group has since hit vessels, including a supertanker, and various energy sites inside the kingdom.

At the same time, the usual export route that Saudi Arabia and other major producers in the Gulf use through the Strait of Hormuz has been fraught with risk since the war started more than six months ago. While some like the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Kuwait have been getting tankers out through the waterway at the risk of attacks, Riyadh has tended to send fewer through, likely because it had supplies flowing through the East-West pipeline.
Also read: Saudi Arabia Taps Key Pipeline the World Didn’t Know It Needed

The 1,200-kilometer link that runs across the Arabian peninsula has turned out to be a lifeline for oil markets after Saudi Arabia activated the link within days of the Iran war. It shifted flows away from the virtually shut Strait of Hormuz toward the Red Sea and quickly reached the link’s full capacity of 7 million barrels a day, with about 5 million earmarked for exports and the remainder used at refineries along the coast.

items.title: BofA, Tallbacken Lift S&P 500 Views, Differ on Rate Risks
body: Market watchers might not agree with how interest rates will impact the S&P 500 Index, but they’re still more optimistic about where stocks are headed than they were before.

Bank of America Corp.’s Savita Subramanian, among the top equity bears, raised her Street-low target for the benchmark, while flagging that it is still prone to interest-rate risks. With the S&P 500 more than 11% higher this year, Michael Purves, CEO and founder of Tallbacken Capital Advisors, does not see higher interest rates breaking the rally.

Subramanian, who is BofA’s head of US equity and quantitative strategy, upped her year-end forecast to 7,400 from 7,100, implying a 2.9% drop from where the S&P 500 closed on Monday. Her forecast remains one of the most bearish on Wall Street, based on a Bloomberg survey of more than 20 strategists. She expects the S&P 500 to hit 7,800 in the next 12 months, a mere 2.4% jump from the latest close.

Tallbacken’s Purves increased his year-end target to 8,500 from 7,400, reflecting “exceptional” earnings growth. The new target eclipses the current Street-high forecast held by Yardeni Research’s president and chief investment strategist Ed Yardeni, and predicts the S&P 500 will climb about 12% from Monday’s close.
Read More: BofA’s Subramanian Takes ‘Flak’ for Street-Low S&P 500 Call

US stocks declined on Monday as leaders of major artificial-intelligence companies called for development to be slowed down, clashing with the Trump administration and Wall Street. Treasury 10-year yields briefly jumped above 5% for the first time since 2023 on concerns about elevated oil prices, inflation and consequently higher borrowing costs hitting the US economy.
Investors are now awaiting the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision on Wednesday, with swap traders largely pricing in a quarter-point hike.
Subramanian remains cautious on inflation risk and interest-rate hikes from the Fed, noting that any catalyst pushing financing costs higher from tight levels could “hasten pain.”
She also says stocks are “overdue for a pullback.”

That’s because there has only been one 5% pullback in 2026, which happened in March, whereas there are typically three per year, Subramanian said, adding that 50% of the strategist’s bear-market signposts have been triggered.
For Purves, the equity rally has “strong legs.” He also pushes back on the fear that interest-rate changes will bring earnings down, saying there’s minimal correlation between the two.

Ultimately, earnings growth is “exceptional, durable and broad-based,” Purves said. “Combined with moderate price-to-earnings expansion, the S&P 500 can easily trade to the 8,500 region, perhaps higher.”

Subramanian is similarly optimistic about earnings growth. In addition to touting productivity as the long-term bull case for the S&P 500, she says that earnings are “not the problem.” She sees earnings per share growth of 33% in 2026 and 12% in 2027, “with growth outpacing what macroeconomic forecasts would suggest, supported by AI capital expenditure, manufacturing and productivity.”

She is also less concerned about a potential blue sweep in the midterm elections this year challenging artificial-intelligence spending, noting the buildout is more driven by state governments in red states.

The tweaks to the targets follow forecast hikes by others on Wall Street. JPMorgan Chase & Co. strategists led by Dubravko Lakos-Bujas raised their view on the S&P 500 to 8,000 points in August, while Yardeni raised his to 8,400 soon after.
items.title_zh: 美银和Tallbacken上调标普500预期，对利率风险看法不一

items.title: Can the King Help Persuade Tech Leaders to Slowdown AI?
body: AI safety continues to be the biggest story right now with Westminster waking up to it over the weekend – parliament’s joint committee on human rights is today calling for an urgent new regulatory framework. This afternoon, Microsoft added its voice to the AI Slowdown Movement. With executives from some of the largest AI firms in the world flying in to attend King Charles’s summit this week, that meeting is now taking place at a very dramatic moment.

Bloomberg is lucky enough to be home to a world expert on these tech firms and today Parmy Olson calls the 3,831 word Amodei essay published on Saturday “vague”. If Amodei was as worried as he insists he is, Parmy writes, he would halt his firm’s most cutting-edge research.

These ideas may seem of the moment at the King’s summit, but the trouble is that once President Trump came out to say he opposed the slowdown, there was a limit to what this country can do. Sam Altman wrote in a post on X yesterday that firms like his and Anthropic will need the help of our government for “international cooperation” but, in a similar vein to Parmy, this piece here also has voices suggesting that if Altman and Amodei really believed it, they could go right ahead and jam the pause button.

Another cohort that has been hurt by AI is the UK’s recent graduates and today there is further detail on why young people have not managed to make the same inroads into the jobs market as previous generations. Our Irina Anghel has been writing the most interesting analysis on the labour market for young people for a while now. She has trawled the latest Office for National Security figures to find that whereas back in the early 2000s there were as many as 10 young workers for every one over-65... now there are just two, as more mature workers cling on to their jobs in Britain’s “low hire, low fire” workforce. Longer life expectancy and better health are delaying retirement.

The Bank of England meets this week - Bloomberg’s survey has most economists expecting them to hold rates the same but if oil continues to rise on the back of events in the Middle East, it will be hard for Andrew Bailey to rule out rate rises before the end of the year.
Want this in your inbox each weekday? You can sign up here.
Hi, I’m Sam from Markets Today and once again there is carnage in global bond markets.

Another jump in oil prices has filtered through into more bets that central banks will have to raise interest rates. In the UK, the change has been striking. Investors now see five BOE rate hikes by the end of 2027. At the end of August, they weren’t even pricing three. Not good news for potential homebuyers or remortgagers.

The outcome for the country is the same as it ever is. The UK’s borrowing costs are soaring and yields are hitting various multi-year highs. Absent a sustainable, credible plan to end the war in Iran and get oil flowing, there’s no real sign that this is going to slow down. Very tough times to be a chancellor.

And all this is happening while the world is grappling with a sharp bout of AI-related existential crises and warnings that if development doesn’t slow down, then the post-apocalyptic world of Terminator 2 might become reality. What a September it has already been.

items.title: US Takes $450 Million Stake in Tungsten Firm to Counter China
body: The Pentagon will take a near-20% stake in a US producer of tungsten — a metal used in military hardware — in a move that expands the Trump administration’s push to secure critical minerals supplies outside China.

The $450 million investment in the Elmet Group Co. will be used to increase tungsten manufacturing in the US, while boosting the company’s long-term access to feedstock for its plants, Elmet said on Monday. Its shares jumped as much as 55%.

President Donald Trump has led a US effort to ease China’s stranglehold on supplies across a range of strategic commodities, especially those that are critical for the defense industry. Prices for tungsten — a super-dense material used in armor-piercing weaponry — have risen more than eightfold since China tightened controls on exports in early 2025.

“Tungsten is essential to the systems that protect American warfighters and sustain deterrence, and this investment helps secure a domestic processing capability the United States cannot afford to leave exposed,” George K. Kollitides II, director of the economic defense unit at the Department of Defense, said in a statement.

The Elmet agreement adds to a string of White House deals with American miners or refiners, kickstarted last year by a landmark $400 million investment by the Pentagon in rare earths champion MP Materials Corp. Other targets include USA Rare Earth Inc., Canada’s Lithium Americas Corp. and mine developer Trilogy Metals Inc.

The investment in Elmet will be made through a redeemable preferred-equity structure and will give the Defense Department a 19.9% stake, the company said. The Pentagon will have the right to appoint an independent director to Elmet’s board of directors.

Tighter supplies of tungsten materials have sparked a global scramble to secure alternative sources for both the long and short term. On Monday, American miner Almonty Industries Inc. unveiled a partnership with Rwanda to source tungsten from the African nation, a deal that the US government helped structure but won’t directly fund.
Price gains for tungsten accelerated earlier this year as buyers exhausted stockpiles, and the Middle East conflict sharpened focus on military needs. The market has stabilized in recent months.
Read More: Munitions Metal Tungsten Eclipses Gold, Copper in 557% Rally

The investment in Elmet is supposed to help finance the company’s operations in Maine, Michigan and Ohio, where it manufactures and processes tungsten, molybdenum and other materials, according to the company. The funding will also support the firm’s investments in mining and processing operations in the US, Australia and Spain, it said.
Advisors on the deal include Cantor Fitzgerald & Co. and Goldman Sachs & Co.

items.title: Africa's Richest Aliko Dangote Eyes $23 Billion Boost from Refinery IPO
body: Africa’s wealthiest man is about to get a lot richer. Aliko Dangote is poised to make a $23 billion leap up the list of the world’s wealthiest as he opens an initial public offering — the continent’s biggest yet — for his petroleum refinery. Demand for the IPO was so high that some Nigerian investing apps crashed after the share sales started today.

The 69-year-old tycoon’s net worth is projected to reach as much as $58.2 billion with the IPO of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals, according to Bloomberg calculations. That would catapult him past US hedge fund tycoon Ken Griffin and technology billionaire Eric Schmidt.

The IPO is part of plans for an Africa-wide empire that will double capacity of his Nigerian refinery to create one of the world’s biggest and build a processing plant in Kenya to extend his reach from the Atlantic to Indian Oceans.

The timing couldn’t be better, with the global focus on limited refining capacity that’s sent diesel prices to a record, driven by the fallout from wars in Iran as well as in Russia-Ukraine. — Zoltan Simon

Oil surged on a report that Saudi Arabia may take weeks to reopen a pipeline that’s been key to bypassing the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Iran war. Brent rose about 5% toward $110 a barrel, before paring gains slightly. The kingdom’s East-West pipeline, which was halted after it was struck by militants, will be out of service for several weeks, the Associated Press reported, citing two regional officials.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on lawmakers to immediately dismiss the country’s chief prosecutor who recently clashed with anti-corruption agencies. Ruslan Kravchenko submitted his resignation as chief prosecutor last week after a senior official in his office was detained and accused of taking part in an alleged protection racket involving scam call centers.

Kravchenko remains in his role until Ukraine’s parliament holds a vote to remove him. A vote could be held as early as tomorrow. The prosecutor general has denied any involvement in the alleged corruption scheme.

Germany is preparing a set of economic-security measures to shield strategic industries from China. The steps may include new tariffs on hybrid electric vehicles, mandatory joint ventures, strengthened inbound and outbound investment screening and a bolstered export controls regime, according to people familiar with the plans. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is said to target cabinet approval on Oct. 14 before seeking broader European Union support.

A grand plan to streamline the EU markets’ supervision is “likely” to be diluted after EU lawmakers pushed for sweeping changes, Maria Luis Albuquerque, the bloc’s financial services commissioner, told us. That’s probably the effect the volume of proposed amendments at the European Parliament will have on efforts to centralize supervision and integrate the region’s financial markets.

Albuquerque also threw her weight behind cross-border banking mergers, arguing that many of the challenges facing the industry are down to a lack of scale. Her comments follow months of wrangling between politicians and bank executives in Germany and Italy over UniCredit SpA’s plan to take over Commerzbank AG, which is seen as a key test of EU banking consolidation,

Nationalist leaders in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland agreed to work together on efforts to rejoin the EU and leave the UK, just days after Donald Trump said he supported Irish unification. They said Brexit has damaged their respective economies, adding that they would work together to eventually rejoin the EU as separate nations.
Nationalists for the first time lead all three regions since May, when Scotland and Wales returned pro-independence first ministers, joining Sinn Fein’s Michelle O’Neill in Northern Ireland.

items.title: Waymo Expands Paid Robotaxi Service to Las Vegas, Its 15th City
body: Alphabet Inc.’s Waymo is now serving paying customers in Las Vegas, marking the 15th US city where it offers hailable robotaxis.
Service will begin Monday, with riders invited “on a rolling basis to ensure a seamless experience,” the company said in a statement. Passengers will be picked up in Waymo’s Ojai minivan.

Waymo has used this phased-in approach before to enter new markets, including Denver, San Diego and Tampa earlier this month. Competitors like Amazon.com Inc.’s Zoox and Hyundai Motor Group-backed Motional already offer robotaxi rides in the Nevada gambling hub.

Waymo has said it wants to reach 1 million paid weekly rides this year in 20 cities globally. It’s already the leading robotaxi operator in the US, where it provides more than 500,000 paid trips a week. The company is also laying the groundwork to test its service in more than a dozen markets, including London and Tokyo.
Read More: Waymo Co-CEO Outlines Path to 1 Million Weekly Trips in 2026

Waymo said it will initially have dozens of vehicles available in Las Vegas with plans to increase that number to “hundreds over time.” The fleet will be managed by Moove, an Uber Technologies Inc.-backed company that also looks after Waymo vehicles in Phoenix and Miami. Waymo currently has more than 4,000 robotaxis in the US.
Read More: Moove Hits $2.1 Billion Valuation in Mubadala-Led Fundraising

The robotaxis will not yet have access to freeways in Las Vegas at this stage. “As we begin service in a new city, it’s typical to add airport and freeway access in future phases,” a Waymo spokesperson said.
The company has been gearing up for a launch in the Nevada city by working with major venues near the Las Vegas Strip to create dedicated ride-hailing zones, applying a similar strategy to Zoox.

Last month, Waymo announced an agreement with the Las Vegas Raiders football team and their home Allegiant Stadium to create a specific pickup and drop-off area at the venue. The company will work to establish a similar setup at select “iconic locations” in the future, the spokesperson said.

items.title: Anthropic Pitches New Claude Tool for Financial Advisors
body: Anthropic PBC is pitching financial advisers on a version of Claude that blends the chatbot with financial analytics and risk management technology run by BlackRock Inc., Vanguard Group Inc. and other firms.
Called Claude for Financial Advisors, the system promises to speed up research, administrative and portfolio-oversight tasks, according to senior executives at Anthropic and BlackRock.

It’s one of the most significant steps so far by the AI firm to expand into the financial industry. The feature — which also connects with tools from Charles Schwab Corp. and iCapital, among others — builds on Anthropic’s earlier introduction of AI agents designed to handle financial services tasks, including drafting pitch decks and reviewing statements.

The firm is making its pitch to the finance industry at a time of growth and tumult for all AI firms. Anthropic and OpenAI, which last week introduced its own financial services feature tailored to investment bankers and equity researchers, are both planning initial public offerings that will net billions for early investors.

At the same time, the rapid growth of artificial intelligence technologies is raising alarm bells for lawmakers and industry leaders worldwide. On Saturday, Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei said development of the most advanced systems must be slowed in order to prevent catastrophe; OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk endorsed his statement.
Anthropic, like OpenAI, has been vying for business customers with specialized services beyond software engineering and coding.
Claude for Financial Advisors is part of that initiative, pitching a more efficient process for advisers that allows them to handle more clients.

“The actual financial adviser community — it’s not that big and it’s actually shrinking,” Jonathan Pelosi, Anthropic’s head of financial services, said in an interview. “These people are retiring, there’s not a ton of them. So great financial guidance is actually not in high supply. If we can do something to help enable these advisers to service more customers, we think of that as an absolute win.”

Anthropic’s tool can connect more advisers to portfolio analytics and investment research tools from firms including BlackRock and Vanguard and could lead to more business for these companies. Financial advisers increasingly rely on “model portfolios” of exchange-traded funds and other investments; BlackRock, for example, said it currently manages about $300 billion in these portfolios.

“One of the biggest trends we’re seeing is advisers wanting to outsource,” Jaime Magyera, head of BlackRock’s US wealth advisory and retirement businesses. “The opportunity around helping advisers build portfolios is not just about better information, it’s about helping them with greater capacity.”
Investment recommendations and decisions would remain up to advisers and their clients.
“You won’t explicitly get investment advice from Claude. We reserve that judgment for the experts,” Pelosi said.

items.title: Comcast and Paramount Consider Shutdown of SkyShowtime in Europe
body: Comcast Corp.’s NBC and Paramount Skydance Corp. are considering winding down their SkyShowtime joint venture, which streams shows and movies in European markets.

The SkyShowtime board wrote to Chief Executive Officer Monty Sarhan on Monday stating that it is considering strategic options for the business — including shutting down the platform — amid a competitive and challenging market, according to a letter reviewed by Bloomberg.

“At this time, we ask that the team remain focused on bringing our audiences the quality of service and programming you have all expertly delivered over the years, and maintaining momentum of the operating business into 2027,” the board wrote.

Sarhan shared the board letter with employees along with his own memo. “I know this news creates uncertainty and, as we work through what comes next, my priority and that of the leadership team, is to be there and support all of you,” he wrote.
The Hollywood Reporter reported about the deliberations earlier.

SkyShowtime launched almost four years ago and is available in 22 markets in smaller European countries, including Spain, Portugal, Denmark and Sweden. It has “several million subscribers,” according to Sarhan’s note, and streams shows and movies from properties like Comcast’s Universal Pictures and Dreamworks film studios and Paramount’s Showtime and Nickelodeon networks. It also shares content with streaming platforms Peacock and Paramount+. American TV series, such as Paramount’s western drama Yellowstone, have gained major traction abroad through the SkyShowtime platform.

Paramount and Comcast are going through their own significant changes. Comcast is planning to spin off NBC and its European media business Sky into a separate, publicly traded company, while Paramount is attempting to finalize a merger with Warner Bros. Discovery Inc.,  which owns HBO Max, despite an antitrust lawsuit brought by 12 state attorneys general.

items.title: Getty Museums Seek to Raise $270 Million, Leave Rate Swaps on Ice
body: One of California’s most prominent art institutions, the Getty, plans to issue $270 million in tax-exempt bonds this week to refinance its debt and extend the suspension of interest-rate swap payments.

The J. Paul Getty Trust, which operates two museum locations in the Los Angeles area, is returning to the municipal bond market after issuing $500 million in debt last year to finance a major renovation of its main campus. The latest bonds, issued through the California Infrastructure and Economic Development Bank, are expected to price Tuesday and will be used to refinance older debt, according to offering documents.

In connection with the new bonds, the trust also plans to extend the suspension of payments on two swap agreements totaling about $270 million until 2031. The swaps are tied to debt with a mandatory tender date of Oct. 1. Such instruments, where an issuer offers to pay a bank a fixed rate in exchange for a floating one, were more popular before the global financial crisis left many municipalities with steep costs tied to the contracts.
After the sale, the trust will have about $1.1 billion in debt outstanding, and it has no plans to raise any additional debt for roughly three more years, according to bond disclosures.

Created by J. Paul Getty in 1953, the trust oversees the oil magnate’s sprawling art collection — including works by Rembrandt, Vincent van Gogh and Édouard Manet — that he accumulated after striking it rich in Southern California’s oil fields.

Getty left the trust $700 million of stock in his company when he died in 1976. The trust has gone on to run Getty’s Malibu villa and opened a museum in the hills above Los Angeles in 1997. The locations, which both offer free admission, house a collection that includes more than 125,000 objects and attracts more than 1.4 million visitors annually.

The trust generates most of its revenue from an investment portfolio that was worth $10.1 billion at the end of March, according to bond disclosures, and is shepherded by a board that includes financial industry veterans John Studzinski, vice-chair of Pacific Investment Management Co., and Clearlake Capital co-founder José E. Feliciano.

“Net annualized returns of 7.8% over the prior five years and prudent spending have led to solid wealth growth,” Moody’s Ratings analysts wrote of the trust on Sept. 3, assigning the bonds the firm’s top rating, Aaa. One caveat the credit grader noted was the trust’s relatively complex debt structure.

The two museums are also grappling with the mounting risk of wildfires, including last week, when a nearby blaze prompted evacuation warnings for the area around the Getty Center. The facility remained closed the following day and the trust continues to face lawsuits over the management of its lands in the lead-up to the 2025 Palisades Fire, which burned around the Getty Center. The organization has denied wrongdoing and weathered the fire without major damage.
Read More: Los Angeles Brush Fire Closes Getty Center Amid Extreme Heat

The Getty Center is slated for a major renovation, in part to improve its fire defenses. The overhaul will shut the facility for nearly one year starting in 2027 and also includes plans to update the center’s entrance with designs by architectural firm Gehry Partners.
The bonds are being underwritten by Jefferies, Morgan Stanley, BofA Securities and TD Financial Products.

items.title: Canada Inflation Data Delayed as Website Issues Plague Statistics Agency
body: Statistics Canada delayed the release of key inflation data Monday after higher-than-usual traffic caused technical problems on its website, the second major economic release affected by access issues in less than a month.

The monthly consumer price index report was published about 30 seconds later than its scheduled release at 8:30 a.m. in Ottawa. Journalists in a media lockup were unable to send their stories until the main release document, known as The Daily, was posted to the website.

“Due to abnormally high traffic volumes encountered on our website this morning, the decision was made to invoke our Business Continuity Plan to ensure prompt release of The Daily,” Statistics Canada said in a statement.

Under the plan, certain data tables are prioritized for release and, depending on the circumstances, publication of the complete suite of tables may be delayed. The agency did not rule out invoking the protocol again if similar circumstances arise.
As of 11:30 a.m. Ottawa time, parts of the website remained unavailable.

The disruption follows similar problems during the Aug. 28 release of second-quarter gross domestic product data, when detailed tables remained unavailable for hours after the headline figures were published.

The two incidents raise questions about reliable and timely access to market-moving government statistics, particularly as economists depend on the underlying tables to assess what is driving headline readings.

Monday’s issue comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney hosts global investors and business leaders in Toronto for the first Canada Investment Summit, part of the government’s effort to catalyze C$1 trillion ($719 billion) in investment over five years. The government is using the two-day gathering to promote Canada as a stable destination for global capital.

items.title: Carney Says Canada Ready for US Trade Talks After Collapse Clarifies Red Lines
body: The dramatic collapse of trade talks with the US in August helped clarify Canada’s negotiating “red lines,” said Prime Minister Mark Carney, who added he’s ready to get back to the table for the right deal.
In an interview with Bloomberg News, he was asked whether it’s a question of who moves first to get negotiations restarted.

“There’s not a pride thing from our perspective,” he said. “We’re practical people that know what our bottom lines are, what our red lines are for sovereignty, for culture, not being restricted on our ability to sign other trade deals.”
The prime minister added: “I think our American colleagues maybe, perhaps, understand those red lines a little more clearly now, given what’s happened. We’re ready to sit down.”

But Canada is “not going to slow down” on its efforts to expand trade with other countries, said Carney, who has invited the world’s leading money managers to Toronto this week for the inaugural Canada Investment Summit — a bid to pull in more foreign direct investment. As soon as it ends, he’ll fly to France for talks on deepening Canada’s relationship with the European Union.

Top-level discussions between the US and Canada fell apart on Aug. 21 over a deal that would have reduced US tariffs on core Canadian sectors like steel and automotive, while eliminating a number of Canadian trade restrictions.

The next day, President Donald Trump’s administration implemented 50% tariffs against about $20 billion of Canadian exports. Canada has retaliated with counter-tariffs hitting the same total dollar value of US exports.

Both sides blamed each other for the blow-up and claimed each had made last-minute demands. Carney said the US wanted to infringe on Canadian cultural protections around the French language and restrict Canada’s ability to sign other trade deals.
Despite this, on Saturday, Trump said a deal with Canada could come “fairly soon,” without elaborating.
Carney said he welcomed those comments and added Canada’s ready to sit down for a deal that respects each side’s sovereignty and Canada’s cultural institutions.

“We’ll sit down when it makes sense. Canada and the US have a very long relationship. We sometimes go through periods where there are tensions in that relationship. Provided we continue this approach, we’ll come to some some agreement at some point.”

items.title: Citadel Securities Sees Europe Bond Yields Capped by Weak Growth
body: The energy shock and central bank tightening that have driven European bond yields higher could ultimately put a lid on them by weakening the region’s economy, according to Citadel Securities.

European and UK bonds bore the brunt of a global selloff last week after the European Central Bank raised rates, citing higher inflation risks. Europe’s reliance on imported energy has left traders bracing for further hikes, but Nohshad Shah, Citadel’s head of EMEA fixed-income sales, said the potential hit to growth may limit how much further rates can go.

Energy costs and inflation worries have also been driving Treasury yields higher, but Citadel sees more scope for rates to rise in the US. Its large oil and gas industry makes the US less vulnerable to higher energy costs. An AI investment boom also gives the economy enough cushion to weather higher rates for longer, said Shah.
That divergence could ultimately be reflected in lower European intermediate forward rates relative to the US, he added.

“I am increasingly skeptical that European belly forward rates can continue to rise once the growth consequences of tighter policy and the energy shock become more predominant in investors’ minds,” Shah wrote. The US “is much better equipped to absorb higher rates than Europe, where stagflation risks are more dominant,” he said.

Shah also warned that risks from the oil shock remain elevated in the US as the war in Iran drags on. Tehran has a greater incentive to widen the conflict by targeting commercial shipping and regional energy infrastructure ahead of the US mid-term elections, he said.
items.title_zh: 城堡证券认为欧洲债券收益率因增长疲软而受限
items.summary_zh: Citadel Securities称，能源冲击和央行紧缩虽推高欧洲债券收益率，但经济走弱将限制其上行空间，美欧利率分化或扩大。

items.title: Trump ataca a CEO de Anthropic por llamado a ralentizar la IA
body: El presidente Donald Trump arremetió contra el director ejecutivo de Anthropic PBC, Dario Amodei, por pedir que se desacelere el desarrollo de la inteligencia artificial, intensificando su oposición a la implantación de nuevas medidas de control para esta tecnología.

En una publicación en redes sociales el lunes, Trump culpó a una “conspiración ENFERMA” por el rechazo de los votantes a los centros de datos de IA y por la creciente preocupación sobre los modelos de vanguardia, y agregó que “el único que está contento con esto es China”.
Suscríbase aquí al boletín Morning Briefing Español y conozca nuestro canal de WhatsApp

“El único control o ‘salvaguardias’ que necesita la IA es un PRESIDENTE FUERTE E INTELIGENTE (¡con un alto coeficiente intelectual!), y EE.UU. lo tiene, ¡y de sobra!”, publicó Trump. “Estamos por delante de China y de todos los demás, y seguiremos así. Teóricos de la conspiración, sediciosos, traidores y filtradores, ¡CUIDADO!”.

Los comentarios de Trump fueron un paso más allá de las declaraciones que hizo durante el fin de semana, cuando reconoció la necesidad de cierta regulación. El presidente, sin embargo, ha rechazado sistemáticamente las advertencias sobre los riesgos de seguridad de la IA y ha hecho hincapié en la importancia de desarrollar la tecnología para mantenerse por delante de China.

El presidente se pronunció días después de que Amodei afirmara que la industria debería pisar el freno en el desarrollo de los modelos más avanzados para que las empresas comprendieran mejor los posibles peligros. Otros líderes del sector de la IA, entre ellos Sam Altman, de OpenAI, y Elon Musk, de SpaceXAI, coincidieron con el llamado de Amodei a reducir la velocidad.

Esto enfrenta directamente a Trump con una industria en la que se ha apoyado como motor del crecimiento económico. El presidente ha convertido la aceleración de la adopción de la IA en todo el país en una pieza central de su agenda. Su administración ha adoptado un enfoque en gran medida poco intervencionista respecto de la regulación de la IA, en línea con su énfasis en acelerar la innovación y la infraestructura del sector.

Trump y su equipo han mantenido reiterados enfrentamientos con Anthropic y Amodei en los últimos meses, y el Departamento de Defensa calificó a la compañía como un riesgo para la cadena de suministro después de que exigiera restricciones al uso militar de sus herramientas.
Pese a las críticas de Trump, las advertencias de figuras del sector sobre las amenazas existenciales que plantea la IA han continuado sin pausa.

Investigadores de IA de Microsoft Inc. publicaron un nuevo conjunto de principios rectores que establecen límites al desarrollo de modelos de vanguardia. En un manifiesto de 15.000 palabras, el equipo señaló que los modelos no deberían tener derechos legales ni personalidad jurídica, y que tampoco deberían estar diseñados para escapar del control humano o engañar a los usuarios. El sistema no debería completar una tarea si para ello necesita infringir los principios rectores de la IA, según el manifiesto.

El debate sobre la seguridad de la IA también se cierne sobre la próxima cumbre de Trump con el presidente chino Xi Jinping, prevista para el 24 de septiembre. El gobierno chino criticó los llamados de ejecutivos tecnológicos estadounidenses a limitar el desarrollo e imponer restricciones más estrictas a los desarrolladores chinos de modelos.

“El alarmismo, la confrontación y la competencia despiadada solo perturbarán el proceso de gobernanza mundial de la IA y no beneficiarán a nadie”, afirmó el portavoz del Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores Guo Jiakun durante una rueda de prensa habitual en Pekín el lunes.

items.title: US Private Credit Default Rate Hits a Record of 6.3%, Fitch Says
body: The default rate for a group of US private debt borrowers rose to a record in August, according to Fitch Ratings.

The trailing 12-month private credit default rate across 1,300 borrowers rose to 6.3% at the end of last month, surpassing the previous high of 6.1% in the prior month, said a report released Monday. Fitch also recorded the highest monthly total of private credit default events in the past year.

“Private credit defaults continued to rise in August, driven by maturity extension transactions that Fitch deems defaults, as uncertainty around rates and inflation has stifled deal flow making it difficult for sponsors to sell struggling portfolio companies ahead of loan maturities,” said Lyle Margolis, Fitch’s head of private credit for North America.

There were 14 recorded instances, out of which 11 involved unique defaulters, while three involved serial defaulters, according to the report. Interest payment deferrals and the introduction of payment-in-kind in lieu of cash interest accounted for 47% of the 89 defaults that occurred over the past year.

For the third consecutive month, stress-induced maturity extensions represented the largest share of default events, Fitch said. Maturity extensions under stress accounted for 45% of defaults in August.
Looking at industries, the highest default activity was registered by healthcare, industrial and manufacturing. The sectors each recorded a 9.9% default rate last month, up from 9.5% in July.

Despite a software sector slowdown stymied by investor fears tied to artificial intelligence disruption this year, the industry “continued to have the lowest default rate” among those rated by Fitch. The technology software sector posted a default rate of 0.6%, down from 1.2% the prior month.
