items.title: Next Africa: IPO Catapults Nigeria's Dangote Up the Ranks of Ultra-Wealthy
body: Welcome to Next Africa, a daily newsletter on where the continent stands now — and where it’s headed. Sign up here. In today’s edition, we look at:
Africa’s wealthiest man is about to get a whole lot richer — at least on paper.
With the continent’s biggest IPO opening on Monday, investors will put a market price on Aliko Dangote’s boldest bet: a $19 billion Nigerian refinery he’s been building for a decade.

Dangote is currently worth $35.3 billion, the Bloomberg Billionaires Index shows. Our calculations show the Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals offering is poised to boost his personal wealth by as much as 65% to $58.2 billion, surpassing that of hedge-fund tycoon Ken Griffin, industrialist Lakshmi Mittal and Alibaba co-founder Jack Ma.
With the Dangote Group mapping out plans for a continent-wide industrial empire, what comes next may be even more significant.

“We, as Nigerians and Africans, must be bold and lead the change to develop our economies,” Dangote said at an IPO signing ceremony. “Only then will the others take us very seriously, only then we’ll be in a position to negotiate and walk away with terms we deserve, not those terms that are given to us.”

He wants to double the capacity of his 700,000-barrel-a-day Nigerian plant by 2029 and set up an another giant processing facility in Kenya. The projects would cement his status as Africa’s biggest crude refiner and extend his reach from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean.
Those plans feed in to his ambition to bolster his conglomerate’s revenue fivefold to $100 billion by the end of the decade. Its interests include sugar, cement processing and shipping.
The billionaire’s companies have long faced criticism over market dominance.

But his landmark IPO is the surest sign yet that African entrepreneurs backed largely by local capital can build world-class businesses, making it a potential game changer for regional capital markets and industrialization efforts.

Solar Industries India agreed to buy South African industrial-explosives and fertilizer firm Omnia for $1.4 billion. The purchase would give billionaire Satyanarayan Nuwal’s firm access to Omnia’s facilities in Africa, Canada, Brazil, Australia and Indonesia. Solar already has operations in Ghana, Nigeria, Tanzania and Zambia.

Warsaw-listed discount retailer Pepco plans to expand manufacturing into Africa to better navigate global supply chain disruptions amid geopolitical turmoil. Soaring freight costs have squeezed European retailers reliant on Asian sourcing.  “Unpredictability is a new normal for the supply chains,” Javier Rubio Fueyo, Pepco’s global sourcing and supply chain director, says in an interview.

South Africa’s fuel-import bill could have been markedly lower if it hadn’t lost  much of its refining capacity, according to the country’s central bank. The cost of shipments could have been $4.7 billion less in the four years through 2024 if they were capped at 25% of demand, the Reserve Bank said. The country’s refining capacity has halved over the past decade.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi pulled off an apparent diplomatic coup over the weekend after he steered rival BRICS nations toward a strongly-worded joint statement despite opposing positions over the war in the Middle East. The bloc stopped short of naming countries, but called for restraint and the avoidance of actions that could further aggravate the situation. South Africa, Egypt and Ethiopia are the African members of BRICS.

Thank you for your responses to our weekly Next Africa Quiz and congratulations to Taofik Adeosun, who was first to correctly identify Sierra Leone as the nation whose former president returned home from Nigeria last week after the government dropped treason charges against him.

South Africa’s potential growth looks set to recover from a prolonged slump, but the rebound has a low ceiling, Bloomberg’s Africa Economist Yvonne Mhango writes. In spite of a Iran-war-related contraction in the second quarter, the forecast shows growth climbing from around 1% in the late 2020s to roughly 2.3% by the mid-2030s, with the message being one of recovery rather than renaissance.

Russia and its fellow BRICS members plan to set up a council to coordinate in space, according to Roscosmos chief Dmitry Bakanov. The new body would aim to facilitate the sharing of satellite data, joint missions and use of members’ respective orbital networks, he said  in an interview in New Delhi. Russia wants to deepen technological links with India and China, while building BRICS into a platform for cooperation outside Western-led institutions.
We’ll be back in your inbox with another edition tomorrow. Send any feedback to nextafrica@bloomberg.net.

items.title: EU's Albuquerque Blames Scale for Banking Woes, Rebuffs Call to Split Package
body: Welcome to the Brussels Edition. I’m Suzanne Lynch, Bloomberg’s Brussels bureau chief, bringing you the latest from the EU each weekday. Make sure you’re signed up.European Union Finance Chief Maria Luis Albuquerque has rebuffed demands by Europe’s biggest banks for Brussels to split its landmark banking competitiveness proposal in two.

The background: the European Commission unveiled a long-awaited proposal to overhaul its banking sector in July. But in a letter last week the heads of eleven lenders including Santander, BNP Paribas and UBS, urged swifter action on reforming capital rules, rather than waiting for agreement on a long stalled deposit scheme. The banks are also calling for an immediate moratorium on any capital increases while the bloc advances its proposals.

Albuquerque rejected the idea that there was any “low-hanging fruit” to cut, instead telling Bloomberg Television that Europe was best served by using a single package to deliver reforms. “If we really want to do something meaningful we need to look at this as a package because everything is connected,” she told Stephen Carroll.
The Portuguese commissioner was also clear that Europe’s banking problems were about scale – not overly-onerous capital requirements that banks argue put them at a disadvantage to the US.

Big deals between lenders in different member states “should have happened a long time ago,” she said. “We do believe that being bigger, operating cross border, ultimately will benefit the clients,” she said.

While “it’s not for the commission to say whether banks should be big or small,” she said it’s important that “we have a regulatory framework which is not standing in the way of good business cases to gain scale.”

Her comments follow months of wrangling between politicians and bank executives in Germany and Italy over UniCredit’s plan to take over Commerzbank. The takeover is seen as a key test of EU banking consolidation, although lenders such as Austria’s Erste and Spain’s Santander, which struck a deal in Poland, have shown what can be done.
The Portuguese commissioner also said that a plan to streamline Europe’s market supervision is “likely” to be diluted after EU lawmakers pushed for sweeping changes.

Maria Municchi, multi asset fund manager at M&G Investments, discussed the outlook for the artificial intelligence trade after leaders of the biggest firms proposed slowing the technology’s development over the weekend. She told Bloomberg Television that while “price will continue to behave pretty well,” markets are becoming “a little bit more wary” about whether the capex boom will translate into delivered earnings.

Covered bonds issued by French banks and backed largely by mortgages now yield almost 30 basis points less than 10-year French government debt, the most extreme inversion ever, based on data compiled by Bloomberg. As recently as four months ago, the two traded at roughly the same yield. The divergence upends one of the basic assumptions of fixed income — that sovereign debt should be the safest borrowing benchmark in its home market. Instead, mounting concern over France’s budget deficit, rising debt-servicing costs and political uncertainty ahead of April’s presidential election is forcing investors to demand more to lend to the state than against pools of household mortgages.

Europe’s protracted efforts to become an attractive proposition for investors reached a momentous juncture today: the arrival of a consolidated tape. The fragmentation of trading across venues is often blamed for the view that markets in Europe have lower liquidity versus the US, which introduced a country-wide tape five decades ago. Besides issues like diverging legal systems and patchy settlement infrastructure, the European Union has identified piecemeal trading data as one reason investors see the bloc as multiple different markets rather than a single unified one. The tape aims to counter that view by displaying supply and demand data for company shares and exchange-traded funds across the region.
items.title_zh: 欧盟的阿尔布开克将银行业困境归咎于规模问题，拒绝拆分方案的呼吁
items.summary_zh: 欧盟金融主管阿尔布开克拒绝11家大银行分拆银行业改革提案的要求，坚持单一方案推进改革，并称欧洲银行问题在于规模而非资本要求。

items.title: Super El Niño Spurs Traders to Place Early Bets on Mild Winter
body: Global weather traders have been rushing to bet that an unusually powerful El Niño will mean a mild winter in the Northern Hemisphere.

The weather phenomenon is projected to push global temperatures higher, with a 75% chance of surpassing all records dating back to 1950, according to the US Climate Prediction Center. That’s showing up in the obscure but growing market for weather derivatives, where energy companies, hedge funds and proprietary traders can bet on, or protect themselves against, temperatures months ahead.

The clearest market moves are in the US, where the potential for a historic El Niño signal is stronger and traders started positioning unusually early, weather derivative brokers and originators say. Even before El Niño officially emerged in June, traders were putting on positions in May tied to the coming heating season.

Those winter trades on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange arrived roughly three months earlier than normal, said Tim Boyce, head of EMEA weather derivatives at TP ICAP Group Plc in London. Boyce ties those bets — the earliest he’s ever seen — to unusually high confidence that a strong El Niño will bring milder weather to the US during the peak of heating season.
“You’ve had that self-fulfilling prophecy where you’ve had a raft of hedging come on, coupled with a little bit of speculative plays,” he said.

Europe is proving harder to trade. El Niño typically has less pronounced effects across the region, while volatile gas prices mean even a short cold snap could prove costly. That tension is driving utilities and traders toward more flexible protection: demand for bespoke weather hedges that can be adjusted as conditions change has more than tripled this year, according to Theresa Kammel and Pierre Buisson of Munich Re.

Pricing for weather derivatives, which pay out based on a pre-agreed meteorological outcome like temperature, has in recent months increasingly reflected expectations of a warm winter, says Nicholas Ernst, managing director of climate derivatives at BGC Financial.

There has been relatively limited weather trading in Japan this year, broadly consistent with levels seen in recent years, though some traders expect a clearer picture of winter temperature hedging to emerge by November.

Munich Re said its pricing for over-the-counter derivatives is still largely following historical distributions, but the potential for a record-breaking El Niño is significant enough that even Europe is watching it closely.

While no two El Niños are the same, a strong event raises the chances of more severe climate impacts. First-half losses triggered by natural disasters hit $112 billion, according to Munich Re, but doesn’t capture the impact of El Niño, which the reinsurer said brings a “dangerous mix” when combined with the forces of climate change.
The phenomenon is spurring top traders in volatile markets like Brazil to beef up weather expertise to help firms profit from market volatility.
Ernst says the biggest open question among weather traders is how to hedge against an El Niño that’s forecast to be so strong they have no historic guidance for pricing the risks.
“Because we haven’t seen this strong of an El Niño in modern, observable times, will it behave as we assume?”

items.title: Dubai, Abu Dhabi's $3 Trillion Hedge Fund Moat; Saudi Arabia Mulls Gaming Giant
body: Welcome to the Mideast Money newsletter, I’m Adveith Nair. Join us each week as my team and I chronicle the intersection of money and power in a region that’s become one of the most influential in global finance. You can sign up here.
This week: UAE residents return to a new normal, Saudi Arabia weighs creating a global gaming giant, and a little-known investor adds to a more than $40 billion bet on Elon Musk.
But let’s start with the heated race to lure hedge funds.

Greece is suddenly everywhere. Chris Rokos, founder of the eponymous hedge fund, changed his tax residency to Greece from the UK, Millennium Management is preparing to open its first office there and Verition is exploring a presence.

A concerted effort by top officials has led some to considering swapping Mayfair for Aegean views. That came amid a broader rethink among wealthy investors and fund managers about where to base themselves after the UK’s overhaul of its non-domiciled tax regime.

For the UAE, a significant beneficiary of Britain’s non-dom exodus, the attention on Greece comes at an awkward moment. The Gulf country has spent years building itself into a hedge fund hub, drawing on a hard-to-replicate combination of low taxes and money: Abu Dhabi’s $1.8 trillion in sovereign wealth and Dubai’s more than $1 trillion in private capital.

The war has put that model through its toughest test yet, with some traders considering alternatives. Adding to the challenge, Hong Kong, Singapore and even Turkey have stepped up efforts to attract financial firms and wealthy investors.

Greece, too, has a compelling pitch: tax advantages, a European lifestyle and a location outside the conflict zone. But the firms now looking to plant flags in Athens also have substantial ties to the Gulf.

Millennium, for instance, has over 100 employees in Dubai. The firm explored ways to move those who no longer want to be based in the emirate to another location, my colleague Nishant Kumar reported in March, but said it expect to maintain an office. Verition plans to extend its Dubai lease for five years and expand its Middle East presence, while Rokos is preparing to open an Abu Dhabi outpost that it announced amid the war.

When announcing Verition’s decision in March, a representative pointed to two important reasons for the UAE’s allure: Its status as an increasingly important global financial center, and a hub for institutional capital across the Gulf.
Also Read: Hedge Funds Shed Usual Reticence to Vouch for Dubai, Abu Dhabi

Citadel’s decision to open in Dubai is one sign of how far that ecosystem has developed. The firm received approval to operate there during the war, adding one of the world’s biggest hedge funds to a market that has spent years building the infrastructure and talent needed to support it. CEO Ken Griffin had singled out those factors as key to any expansion decision.

Indeed, Dubai now has more than 100 hedge funds registered in its financial center, with over 80 managing above $1 billion. Abu Dhabi has been building its own cluster, led by Brevan Howard, which employs about 150 people in the city and counts the emirate as its biggest risk-taking center.

And then there’s the capital. The $1 trillion Abu Dhabi Investment Authority has been ramping up its work with hedge funds for years, while firms such as ADIC are joining the fray. Meanwhile, Lunate has taken a stake in Brevan Howard and committed $2 billion to one of its investment platforms.
Related Coverage

The competition extends to some of the industry’s biggest names. Billionaire hedge fund titan Ray Dalio established a family office in Abu Dhabi years ago, while oil trader Pierre Andurand moved to Dubai at the start of 2026.

And even amid the war, the UAE’s infrastructure has continued to operate, with regulators offering flexibility to the industry to help navigate disruptions. That resilience is part of the challenge for would-be rivals such as Greece.

Athens will likely continue to attract high-profile hedge fund principals, but the harder task is building institutional density around them. Alongside that moat the UAE has spent years creating, Greece will also have to contend with the Gulf nation’s $3 trillion wall of capital.
How are Middle East hubs dealing with the fallout from the Iran war, and what are investors saying? Tune in to our Live Q&A to find out.
The UAE is seeking to preserve its appeal not just to hedge funds but also to the global rich, even as the Iran war, now in its seventh month, shows few signs of resolution.

A meeting between Iran and several Gulf Arab nations over a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz, set to take place in Oman on Monday, was postponed. The delay was partly down to Saudi Arabia’s frustration over continued attacks on its territory by Iran-supported groups such as the Houthis, Bloomberg News reported. Those attacks, coupled with fears that a prolonged war will further constrain supplies of fuel such as diesel, sent Brent crude prices above $108 a barrel.
The stop-start conflict, which a senior adviser to the UAE’s president recently decried as “the state of neither war nor peace,” is testing the resilience of the Gulf nation’s post-pandemic boom.

For now, it’s business as usual in parts of the economy as residents return after the summer break, schools begin a new academic year and the UAE enters what is typically its busiest season for tourism.

Top private school operators including Brookfield-backed GEMS Education expect enrollment to rise this year, and branches of international institutions where fees can run as high as about $42,000 a year are still opening. Dubai-listed Taaleem’s CEO Alan Williamson said its schools were “still seeing demand outstripping supply even in what we would all agree has been a very challenging period.”

There are signs of momentum elsewhere, too. The UAE’s financial hubs, Dubai International Financial Centre and Abu Dhabi’s ADGM, have continued to expand. While the central bank expects GDP growth to slow to 1.7% this year, economists surveyed by Bloomberg now anticipate a rebound of about 7% in 2027.
Also Read: Abu Dhabi Finance Hub Draws 4,700 New Professionals Despite War

Dubai’s population has also continued to grow, and that’s showing up in traffic. Activity near DIFC recovered to about 90% of pre-war levels before slipping in August during the school break, according to mobility analytics firm xMap. The rebound was slightly more muted around Palm Jumeirah and Dubai Marina, likely because those areas are more dependent on tourism.

But the strains are also evident. Continuing disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has raised import costs and fuel prices while straining supply chains. Airport traffic, hotel occupancy and property sales have dropped, and recruiters say they are having to adjust packages to keep attracting the best talent.
Related Coverage

Saudi Arabia’s wealth fund is considering combining Electronic Arts with Savvy Games, a deal that would bring blockbuster titles including Madden NFL and Pokemon Go under one roof and create one of the world’s biggest gaming firms.

Dow is considering plans to exit its $20 billion chemicals partnership with Saudi Aramco. The US firm held a 35% stake in the venture as of last year, with Aramco owning the remainder. The Saudi oil giant could use the opportunity to buy Dow’s stake and take full ownership.
Aramco is also considering a potential sale of its specialty chemicals business Arlanxeo as the state-owned firm ramps up a multibillion-dollar divestment plan.
Saudi Arabia is planning a Fannie Mae-style sale of residential mortgage-backed securities as it aims to diversify funding for the kingdom’s banks.

The UAE pledged to invest €40 billion in Germany in sectors ranging from artificial intelligence to energy and defense, deepening its ties with Europe and further diversifying its global trade relationships.
Abu Dhabi wealth fund Mubadala has become a backer of Luckin, China’s biggest coffee chain, in a transaction valued at about $1 billion.
Fintech Tabby said it was valued at $6.5 billion in an investment round, putting it ahead of New York-listed peer Klarna.
The Dubai-based owner of a hookah brand promoted by Snoop Dogg has met investors ahead of a possible bond sale.
A consortium led by a unit of Abu Dhabi’s IHC and US-French space startup Loft Orbital plans to invest $1 billion to add 40 satellites to an AI-infused constellation.

Qatar posted a $5.8 billion budget shortfall in the April-to-June period, its widest quarterly deficit in almost a decade, as natural gas revenue plunged after the war effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz. State-owned QatarEnergy, meanwhile, is in discussions to buy liquefied natural gas from US suppliers under long-term agreements, a potential deal that highlights how the conflict is pushing Doha to seek alternative supplies for its customers.
Saudi Arabia’s audacious bid to use golf as a soft-power tool ended with a whimper after LIV Golf, the most expensive sports league launch ever, filed for bankruptcy protection.
Bankers who once chased Gulf IPOs are now looking elsewhere for fees.

Listing volumes in the region have fallen below $1.1 billion so far this year, due in part to the monthslong regional conflict. That’s prompting firms including HSBC and EFG Hermes to pursue business in markets like Egypt, Turkey and India, reports my colleague Laura Gardner Cuesta.
The drop in volumes means Gulf firms have raised less than typically quieter markets like sub-Saharan Africa, where listings have drawn $1.37 billion.
It’s a sharp reversal for Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, where a post-pandemic listing boom offered a buffer against slowdowns in traditional hotspots like London, Hong Kong and New York.
OpenAI and Anthropic’s push to slow AI development will face resistance from Wall Street, the tech industry and Donald Trump.
Also Read: Bridgewater’s Jensen Says AI Will Kill People Before It’s Curbed
Once a coder, Jason Carroll now sits atop Hudson River Trading, one of Wall Street’s most lucrative high-speed trading firms, with a personal fortune of more than $27 billion.
HSBC is looking for a new chief financial officer after Pam Kaur unexpectedly stepped down from the role just two years after her appointment.
As Hong Kong and Singapore compete to attract global talent, here’s how salaries and living costs stack up for expats in the rival hubs.

Aliko Dangote’s net worth is poised to jump by $23 billion with the IPO of his refinery, potentially catapulting Africa’s richest man past US hedge fund tycoon Ken Griffin and technology billionaire Eric Schmidt.
An investor with a spartan website and a name borrowed from an aviation concept has quietly become one of Elon Musk’s biggest backers.
Vy Capital joined investors including Shamal Holding, which invests on behalf of Dubai Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed Al Maktoum, in Boring Co.’s $3 billion funding round.

The Dubai-based firm has backed several of Musk’s ventures over the past decade, amassing a $40 billion stake in SpaceX that makes it the company’s fifth-largest shareholder. It has also invested in brain-interface company Neuralink across multiple rounds.

Founded by Goldman Sachs alums Alexander Tamas and Mateusz Szeszkowski in 2013 to “invest in some of the world’s leading companies and own them for decades,” relatively little is known about Vy itself or its backers.
Beyond Musk’s companies, Vy has forged ties with entities linked to prominent UAE royals.

items.title: Sweden's Small Pro-Business Party Emerges as Election Kingmaker
body: A small Swedish party led by a former McKinsey & Co. consultant has emerged as a kingmaker after Sunday’s inconclusive election.

Center Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, 54, is in pole position to break the deadlock by remaining part of Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson’s center-left bloc, rebuffing overtures by the center-right alliance.

The Center Party’s free-market oriented economic policies have more in common with Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s Moderate Party than they do with those of the Social Democrats and their other potential allies the Left Party, who favor higher taxes to fund investment in welfare. The party has also set a red line to never work with the far-right Sweden Democrats who have been promised cabinet seats for the first time by Kristersson.

With a mere 28,000 votes separating the two blocs, the smaller parties will prove decisive in deciding which side will get a shot at forming a government. The Center Party, with 7.1% of the vote, will have leverage to extract concessions.

“If this turns out to be the election result, the Social Democrats need to look at the big picture,” Center Party Secretary Hannes Hervieu told Expressen. “It clearly demonstrates that voters want neither a shift to the left on economic policy nor significant influence for the Sweden Democrats.”

The center-left bloc is three seats ahead in the tight race that won’t be resolved until Wednesday at the earliest. If the current projection for a narrow Social Democrats win holds, and the party begins talks to form a government, those negotiations could drag on for weeks.
Still, there are internal squabbles within the opposition bloc that need to be ironed out, mainly with the Center Party and the Left Party refusing to be in the same coalition.

Under Sweden’s parliamentary conventions, the party leader out front will be asked to try and form a government. If the parliament fails to back a new prime minister after four rounds of voting, a new election must be held.
“It is clear this could be a complicated process,” the current speaker of the parliament, Andreas Norlen, said in an interview with national broadcaster SR.

On Sunday night, Kristersson said voters had elected a majority that “wants a different economic policy to what the Social Democrats campaigned for” and that he planned to explore whether there was any possibility to find a potential governing coalition from “within that majority.”
The move was widely interpreted as a thinly veiled appeal to the Center Party to swap sides.
Read More: Swedish Left Edges Ahead With Vote Result Too Close to Call

items.title: Daimler Truck Says Customers Pass on High Diesel Prices for Now
body: Record diesel prices are squeezing trucking companies in the US and Europe, though many of Daimler Truck Holding AG’s customers can still pass the additional fuel costs on to their own clients, Chief Executive Officer Karin Rådström said.

The majority of customers “have floaters in their contracts with their customers, which means that they are able to offset the higher diesel price,” Rådström told journalists at the IAA Transportation in Hanover. The bigger problem can be timing, because operators often have to pay for the fuel before being reimbursed, according to the executive.

US diesel prices pushed to another record high on Monday after surpassing $6 a gallon last week for the first time as disruptions to global oil and fuel supplies tighten the market. Since the start of the hostilities in the Middle East, prices have risen more than 60%. The impact can ripple through the wider economy, with trucks carrying more than 70% of US domestic freight by weight, transporting everything from food to construction materials.
North America is Daimler Truck’s biggest market, selling almost half the group’s vehicles in the region across its Freightliner and Western Star brands.
Read More: California Gas Station With $9.99 Diesel Exemplifies Fuel Crisis

Rådström said fuel prices haven’t yet had a noticeable impact in orders, though the wider uncertainty “obviously isn’t good for business,” she said. While high fuel prices could weigh on truck demand, they may also strengthen the case for switching to battery-electric vehicles, according to Achim Puchert, who heads the Mercedes-Benz Trucks business.
The reaction to higher fuel prices is more immediate among passenger-car buyers, according to Stellantis NV’s Europe head Emanuele Cappellano.

“For sure there is a reaction, I mean once you see the oil price growing it immediately reflected some kind of reaction in the market,” Cappellano told journalists. Fleet operators tend to respond more slowly, however, and may delay replacing vehicles rather than immediately switching technologies.
“What we see is that sometimes they prefer slowing down the renewal of the fleet instead of having risk of buying full-electric commercial vehicle.”

Both companies said the biggest obstacle to wider adoption of electric trucks remains a lack of charging infrastructure. They also called for changes to European Union rules that impose penalties on manufacturers that miss emissions targets, saying the industry is unlikely to reach a goal of 35% of newly registered trucks being electric by 2030. Electric trucks currently make up 2% of newly registered vehicles.
Read More: Daimler Truck CEO Sees €1 Billion Fine on EU Emissions Rules

items.title: Canada to Prioritize Tax Rulings for Large Investment Proposals
body: Canada will prioritize requests for income tax clarity related to investments of at least C$1 billion ($720 million), a move meant to help international firms seeking to deploy capital in the nation.

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne will announce the change Monday in Toronto, ahead of the inaugural Canada Investment Summit. The faster processing is intended to “provide additional support to some of the world’s largest investors,” Canada’s tax agency said in a statement seen by Bloomberg News.

So-called advance income tax rulings can provide clarity about how tax authorities will view a proposed transaction. The Canada Revenue Agency typically offers a legally binding, written statement outlining how Canadian tax law will be applied and specifying the taxes for which an entity will be responsible.
Fast-tracked rulings for projects with substantial outlays may allow firms to make decisions more quickly, removing a potential barrier to investment flows.
“When investors are considering major projects, certainty matters,” Champagne said in the statement.

In April, Champagne said the CRA would prioritize rulings for major “nation-building projects,” including large housing and infrastructure plans and those aimed at enhancing productivity and strengthening critical economic sectors.
Without priority access, the CRA said its standard is to issue rulings within 90 days of a request. The statement did not specify how quickly a fast-tracked ruling would be issued.

items.title: Crispin Odey Loses Bid to Overturn UK Financial Services Ban
body: Crispin Odey lost his bid to overturn a lifetime ban on managing money, capping a remarkable fall from grace for the once-feted fund manager.

Odey had taken the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority to a London tribunal to appeal against a lifetime ban from working in the City following a series of accusations of sexual misconduct at his eponymous hedge fund. His bid was dismissed, according to a decision published by The Upper Tribunal.

The FCA banned the money manager last year and fined him over a “lack of integrity.” Odey demonstrated that he was not a “fit and proper person” to work in the financial services industry after he moved to frustrate a disciplinary hearing into his own conduct in late 2021, the regulator said. The tribunal cut Odey’s overall fine to £1.5 million ($2 million) on Monday.
A lawyer for Odey didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Odey Plays The Victim Card in Appeal to Overturn Finance Ban

The hedge fund boss faced at least 46 allegations of inappropriate conduct over a 17-year period at Odey Asset Management according to an internal report conducted by an outside law firm. The accusations ranged in seriousness from an allegation of sexual assault in 2005 to an incident in which Odey forced a receptionist to try on a skirt and show it to him “ostensibly to see if it would fit his daughter.” The regulator’s actions followed a series of pieces about the alleged misconduct in the Financial Times.

“He felt the rules shouldn’t apply to him and acted to save his own skin,” Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said. “During the hearing he reinvented history, painted himself as a victim and displayed no contrition. That arrogant entitlement and the resulting complete disregard for proper governance means Mr. Odey is unfit to work in financial services.”

The March tribunal shed a light on the extent of the crisis that engulfed Odey’s firm around 2021 and 2022. Already under FCA investigation at the time, he dismissed two consecutive executive committees from OAM within a period of four months, leading to accusations of “reckless disregard” for governance.

For Odey the loss ensures he has suffered a comprehensive defeat in a series of legal battles that took place this year. A £79 million libel suit the money manager had taken against the FT was settled before the trial began, with Odey admitting in a letter to the paper that his claim was unlikely to succeed. In May he settled a personal injury suit brought by a number of women who claimed they had been sexually assaulted by him.

“He demonstrated a disregard for standards and requirements that he was reasonably expected to meet based upon the circumstances in question,” the tribunal judges said in the decision. “He sees nothing wrong with his approach, and indeed he wrongly sees himself as the victim of both OAM’s actions and the FCA’s. As he put it in his evidence, he considers that he “was the victim in all this.””

items.title: Canada Inflation Holds at 3% Amid Slower Gasoline Price Growth
body: Canada’s inflation rate was unchanged at 3% last month, matching expectations as gasoline prices rose at a slower annual pace.

While the conflict in the Middle East continues to put upward pressure on energy costs, prices at the pump were 22.8% higher in August than a year earlier, Statistics Canada reported on Monday. That followed a 25.7% increase in July.
The year-over-year slowdown in gasoline prices was offset by higher prices for travel tours and rent.

On a monthly basis, the consumer price index fell by 0.1%, also matching the median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of economists. The Bank of Canada’s preferred median and trim core measures of inflation were unchanged as well at 2% and 1.9%, respectively.
The data suggest underlying price pressures remained under control in August, even as the Bank of Canada grows increasingly concerned about inflationary risks from the Iran war.

The two-year benchmark Canada yield traded about 3 basis points higher at 3.384% as of 8:51 a.m. in Toronto. The Canadian dollar was 0.3% weaker against the US dollar, trading at its lowest intraday level since Sept. 2.

“Underlying inflation remains contained, but Bank of Canada officials will increasingly be looking at the coming passthrough from high oil prices in determining the future path of monetary policy,” Desjardins Group’s Royce Mendes wrote in a note to clients.
Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem warned earlier this month that the longer the conflict in the Middle East goes, the more likely higher energy prices feed through to other prices in the economy.
Macklem said that while renewed trade tensions with the US add to inflation risks, elevated energy prices are a bigger concern.
Hotter-than-expected US inflation data has also solidified expectations of a rate hike by the Federal Reserve this week.
Traders in overnight swaps put the odds of a rate hike by the Bank of Canada next month at about 75%, remaining unchanged after the CPI release.

But many economists say the rate hike expectations may be premature, as the economy shows signs of slower growth in the third quarter, and core measures of inflation remain subdued around the 2% target.

“Yes, core inflation is likely to move up in the coming months, but off a very low level, and is expected to remain with the BOC’s comfort zone. That is driven by our expectations for modest growth in Canada, as the economy continues to be weighed down by the uncertainty and tariffs on our exports to the US,” Leslie Preston, managing director and senior economist with Toronto-Dominion Bank, wrote in a note to investors.

At the same time, there is some evidence that elevated energy costs may be spreading through to the broader economy. The share of CPI components rising at or above 3% rose in August to 37.3% from 34.8% in July.

A three-month moving annualized average of the central bank’s core measures also accelerated to 2.19%, from 2.01% the previous month. Yearly inflation excluding food and energy rose to 2.1% from 1.9%.

Meanwhile, travel tour prices rose at a faster annual pace of 26.1% in August following a 15.2% increase in July, in part due to a base-year effect. A pullback in travel to the US last year weighed on prices in August 2025.
Rents also rose faster at 2.8% annually, up from 2.5% in July.
Meanwhile, grocery price inflation fell below the headline inflation rate for the first time in about two years, rising 2.8% year-over-year, after increasing 3.1% in July.

items.title: Aon Raises $13.5 Billion From Bond Sale to Fund USI Takeover
body: Aon Plc raised $13.5 billion from a high-grade bond offering to help fund its planned acquisition of USI Insurance Services, marking one of the biggest M&A financing deals to come to market in 2026.
Investors placed as much as $65 billion of orders on the sale, with the longest maturity drawing the most demand, according to people familiar with the matter.

Aon sold notes in seven parts, with maturities ranging from three to 30 years. Price talk on the longest tenor tightened by 0.35 percentage point from initial discussions to a yield of 1.15 percentage points above Treasuries, a separate person said, asking not to be identified because they are not authorized to speak publicly.

The transaction came to market even as borrowing costs rose on Monday, with both credit and equity markets reacting to a call by the leaders of the biggest artificial-intelligence firms to slow the technology’s development. Meanwhile, a surge in oil prices has further fueled inflation concerns ahead of Wednesday’s Federal Reserve rate decision, worsening the backdrop for markets.

Last month, Aon agreed to buy USI from KKR and other shareholders in an all-cash $17 billion transaction funded with debt. The purchase, expected to close by year-end, is intended to expand the firm’s footprint with midsized corporate clients. Aon is one of the world’s largest insurance brokers, while USI provides insurance brokerage and consulting services to businesses and individuals.
The company is also expected to sell a $4 billion term loan as part of the deal financing, according to a S&P Global Ratings note.

All of the notes except the 30-year tenor would have to be redeemed at 101 cents on the dollar, plus accrued and unpaid interest, if the USI acquisition falls through or isn’t completed by Dec. 1, 2027.

Fitch Ratings on Monday placed Aon’s debt on Rating Watch Negative, saying the acquisition will “materially increase credit risk for at least the next two years”. Debt is expected to be roughly four times a measure of earnings through the end of 2027, Fitch Ratings said in a note to clients.
The $13.5 billion note offering marked the year’s second-largest high-grade bond deal tied to mergers and acquisitions, trailing only Abbott Laboratories’ $20 billion transaction in February.

The transaction comes during one of the busiest periods of the year for the US investment-grade market. Firms are expected to issue about $55 billion of high-grade debt this week, according to an informal poll of dealers. Last week’s $67.6 billion of supply ranked as the fourth-most this year.

items.title: Steve Ballmer Accepts NBA Penalties Over Clippers Salary Cap Violations
body: Los Angeles Clippers owner Steve Ballmer backed down.

The team initially said it would “vigorously” challenge one of the harshest punishments in NBA history for violating salary cap rules, but Ballmer opted not to fight the penalties that will hamstring the team for years.

“We are committing to put this chapter behind us,” Ballmer said in a statement posted online Sunday night. “We have communicated to the NBA that we are complying with the penalties assessed by the league, have paid the fine, and are moving forward. While there are still disagreements concerning the findings in the report, this is not where I want to focus. Team owners should support, not distract.”

The NBA stripped the Clippers of five first-round draft picks and suspended Ballmer for one year after finding the team had circumvented salary cap rules by facilitating sponsorship agreements between outside companies and star player Kawhi Leonard, who is in the process of being traded.

The Clippers were also fined $30 million, the largest financial penalty in the history of the league. Leonard was penalized $700,000. The star player didn’t face a potential suspension because that’s not one of the punishments for salary cap infractions allowed under the current collective bargaining agreement.

Ballmer had limited options on fighting the penalties. The players union agreed to Leonard’s punishment, which removed arbitration as an avenue. A lawsuit would have been hard to win, according legal experts. There also could be more allegations, after the law firm that investigated the Clippers said it’s still receiving relevant information and would add to the findings if needed.

Ballmer, a billionaire and the former chief executive officer of Microsoft Corp., might also have been swayed by a similar situation more than two decades ago. The NBA stripped the Minnesota Timberwolves of five first-round draft picks and fined the team $3.5 million for breaking salary cap rules with secret payments to a player. But the NBA later returned two picks after the team accepted the punishment.

“This has been a very difficult time for everybody associated with the Clippers, and for that, I have sincere regrets,” Ballmer said in the statement. “I want to apologize to our fans, employees, and my fellow NBA team owners for the distraction and distress this matter has caused, for which I accept responsibility as principal owner.”

items.title: Junk Firms Plot $13 Billion Debt Refinancings as Rate Hikes Loom
body: Junk-rated borrowers across the globe are lining up at least $13 billion in refinancing deals, in a bid to lock in tighter credit spreads ahead of potential central bank interest-rate hikes.

Authentic Brands Group, which owns brands spanning Guess and Dockers, launched Monday a $4.2 billion effort to refinance debt, car wash company Mister Car Wash Inc. is moving ahead with a $2 billion deal to refinance existing debt and fund a shareholder distribution, and aerospace company TransDigm Group Inc. kicked off a $2.5 billion refinancing.

Meanwhile, Europe’s high yield market is set for its busiest week since June, with at least seven deals announced on Monday, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The borrowers, which include auto parts maker ZF Friedrichshafen AG and gambling software firm Playtech Plc, are refinancing maturities several years out, with German pharmaceutical company Gruenenthal GmbH even looking at debt due in 2030.

Borrowers are rushing to market as expectations build for central banks to embark on a round of monetary tightening to combat elevated inflation. Many analysts now predict the Federal Reserve will raise rates at its meeting this week, while traders are fully pricing in four hikes from the European Central Bank and Bank of England by the end of 2027.

“CFOs are doing the maths to work out if it is better to refinance now — possibly with a slightly higher coupon — or to wait and risk an increased market rate,” said Jeremy Duffy, a partner and chair of European leveraged finance at Cahill Gordon & Reindel LLP. “Borrowers are getting in front of things to avoid a rate environment that could get worse.”
Read More: Buyout Debt Worth $138 Billion Set to Land in Credit Markets

Typically, companies start the refinancing process a year to 18 months before their debt comes due. Those that issue floating-rate loans can potentially lock in tighter credit spreads than before, which could offset higher borrowing costs tied to short-term rates linked to central bank policy rates. Firms with fixed-rate debt run the risk of higher coupon payments as benchmark government bond yields have climbed across the globe. On Monday, the US 10-year Treasury yield, a gauge for borrowing costs across the globe, breached 5% for the first time since 2023.

Brightstar Lottery Plc set the tone for high-yield refinancings last week. The gaming and lottery machines company refinanced notes due in April 2028 that had been paying 2.375%, for new debt due in 2032 with a 5% yield.

That was followed by Monday’s deluge of deals, which includes a big step-up in costs for Germany’s ZF Friedrichshafen. The company is selling a €750 million four and a half year bond at a yield of 5.875%, according to a person familiar with the matter. The proceeds will be used to refinance a selection of outstanding notes which have coupons as low as 2% and maturities from mid-2027 to 2028, they said.

Other companies deciding that it is prudent to lock in rates now include Avolta AG, an operator of duty-free shops in airports, which is holding investor calls for a €350 million senior bond sale. It’s looking to partially refinance existing 2027 notes that carry a coupon of 2%. The company is yet to announce a spread level for the new offering, but the Bloomberg high yield index is trading at a yield of 6.3%.

Among other refinancing deals, Playtech is seeking €350 million to redeem existing 2028 notes while Gruenenthal is planning an €850 million sale across fixed and floating rate tranches to repay 2028 and 2030 notes.

items.title: Italian Watchdog Queries Ferretti on Asset Math After Order Drop
body: Italy’s securities regulator has asked Ferretti SpA for information on its assessment of asset values after the yachtmaker cut its annual outlook, according to a document seen by Bloomberg.

In a Sept. 10 letter, Consob requested the analysis supporting Ferretti’s conclusion that there were no indicators of impairment at midyear and that no impairment test was required. The regulator cited weaker orders and reduced guidance among the factors to consider.
Consob also sought updated order figures, including any cancellations, suspensions or delays.
Representatives for Ferretti and Consob declined to comment.

The maker of Riva and Pershing yachts reported in late July that first-half orders fell 27% from a year earlier, citing intensifying competition and customers taking longer to make decisions. Chief Executive Officer Stassi Anastassov described the challenge as primarily commercial rather than financial, with net cash at €95 million ($106 million) as of June.

Consob separately requested details of any distribution agreements in the United Arab Emirates, according to the letter. Ferretti attributed delays in signing Middle Eastern contracts to geopolitical tensions in its July earnings release.

Ferretti is one of Italy’s leading yachtmakers, building vessels for wealthy buyers under brands including Riva, Pershing and Wally. It underwent a management shakeup in May after its top shareholder, China’s Weichai Group, won a vote over board control.
Shares of the company, based in Forlì near the Adriatic coast, have declined around 5% this year, lowering the company’s market value to just below €1 billion.
The group operates seven shipyards in Italy and has customers in more than 70 countries. Its range spans smaller motor yachts to custom-built superyachts.
Bloomberg reported in June that Ferretti was considering making an offer for struggling competitor The Italian Sea Group.
Ferretti is required to provide the requested information within 10 working days of receiving the letter.

items.title: Poor Towns Reject Data Centers That Could Help Their Finances
body: Clinton, Iowa, needs an economic boost. The city has struggled with deficits, its population has been shrinking for decades, and after a sewer upgrade, its debt load has doubled.

Blackstone Inc.-owned QTS has a solution: a massive data center that would bring thousands of construction jobs and provide nearly $200 million in property taxes in its first 10 years, a transformative sum for a place with a $25 million operating budget. Andy Sokolovich, the local economic development cheerleader, calls the project a financial game changer.

“We’ve bonded ourselves to the hilt,” said Sokolovich, the president of Grow Clinton, a nonprofit. “There is very little we can do to rectify our financial situation outside of a development of this caliber.”

But money isn’t everything. Many residents want nothing to do with the data center and view it as a potential source of noise pollution, environmental degradation and rising utility costs, even though QTS has vowed to pay its own way.
"We pay for 100% of the energy and infrastructure improvements needed, so our project costs are not pushed onto ratepayers," the company said in a statement.
Still, local hostility threatens to end QTS’ hopes of breaking ground in the 24,000-person community off the Mississippi River.

Like Clinton, more and more of small town America is confronted with the choice of joining the artificial intelligence boom and reaping the promised benefits — assuming they actually do materialize — or rejecting what some fear will do more harm than good, even if that means sacrificing economic growth.

In the first quarter of this year, local pushback halted or delayed roughly 75 projects in the US worth $130 billion, according to Data Center Watch. More recently, QTS and Brookfield Asset Management-backed Compass Datacenters both gave up on plans to build a 2,100-acre campus in Northern Virginia. And in Independence, Missouri — where the median household income is just over $60,000 — voters this month recalled a city council member who supported tax breaks for a proposed data center.

More than two thirds of new data center proposals are landing in rural America, according to Pew Research Center, and it’s not always easy to say no. Small towns and counties with few other sources of significant revenue often rely on volunteer or part-time leadership to make consequential decisions about complex, multi-billion dollar proposals, just as federal aid that filled local government coffers following the Covid-19 pandemic has dried up.

Some communities have accepted the projects, which credit rating firms say are boosting tax revenue for municipalities across the country. In Cedar Rapids, 85 miles west of Clinton, a QTS facility is expected to generate almost $500 million in net property tax revenue over two decades. Facebook parent Meta Platforms Inc. just opened a $1.2 billion data center in 32,000-person Kuna, Idaho. Alphabet Inc.’s Google is building a data center campus in West Memphis, Arkansas, where fewer than 25,000 people live.

“The fiscal pressure means that communities are weighing the potential economic benefits more heavily,” said Amy Colbert, a professor at the University of Iowa’s Tippie College of Business, who has built an online tool that helps local governments evaluate data center proposals.

The debate over AI infrastructure is also taking on fresh urgency for state and federal politicians, with US midterm elections just a few months away. Republicans are balancing President Donald Trump’s full-throated embrace of data centers — and lambasting of those who oppose them — with pushback from rural residents, while Democrats are weighing environmental concerns against union support for the construction jobs that the projects create.

Some states are now pursuing moratoriums to halt development, and governors who were once data center proponents have significantly cooled on them, including Democrats Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania and JB Pritzker of Illinois, as well as Greg Abbott, a Texas Republican who is usually a staunch backer of Trump.

But grassroots resistance is rising at the same time that challenges for small municipalities are mounting. States are tightening the amount of funding they send to local governments as they expect to receive less funding from national programs such as Medicaid starting next year as the full force of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act begins to take effect.

This presents a conundrum for rural communities: some residents may not like data centers, but small towns have fewer options for growth than big cities and their surrounding suburbs. In some places, internet access is sparse and hospitals are shutting down.
“While on the one hand it might seem to make economic sense, it doesn’t make cultural or social sense,” said Anthony Pipa, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

Take Miles Crosby, whose family has lived on land in Colleton County, South Carolina since the 1940s. His home is on a road named after his mother. He hunts deer, turkey and other game on the property.

Earlier this year, he and another resident sued to block a proposed 859-acre data center campus that would have surrounded Crosby’s home on three sides. The complaint, along with community opposition, helped to prevent the project.

But the community could’ve used the money. In July, S&P Global Ratings dropped the county’s credit grade to A+ from AA-, citing deteriorating finances and declining reserves. Colleton, which has a $40 million budget, would have net more than $100 million annually by the project’s fourth year, according to Brantley Strickland, executive director of the Colleton County Economic Alliance. It also would have created 500 permanent jobs with an average annual salary of $125,000, more than double the county’s median household income, he said.

On Monday, the county's council is set to vote on legislation that would end a six-month data center moratorium passed in July, and replace it with guardrails that would give the developer an opening to build on a less environmentally sensitive site.

About 1,700 miles due west, opposition from locals in Socorro County, New Mexico led to the cancellation of a proposed project that would have spanned 10,000 acres, even as the developer touted its high environmental standards and benefits for the community, where farmers and ranchers anchor the economy.
“It’s out of the question, it’s monstrously harmful,” one dissenter said at a public meeting in May. “It will damage our environment, it will damage our way of life.”
Back in Clinton, Mayor Scott Maddasion and city council members are considering an ordinance intended to set more guardrails on data center development.

Maddasion said he broadly supports the legislation, but acknowledged that it’s difficult for the city to dictate the use of private land. The site QTS is considering has been zoned for heavy industrial use for decades.
However, “the actual development pattern in this area has also been agricultural and residential — not industrial,” said Amy Wisor, a local who opposes the project.

Some residents worry that a data center risks straining the city’s water and sewer infrastructure after it was upgraded in 2023. Clinton’s borrowings for those improvements is guaranteed by revenue from Archer-Daniels-Midland Co., which has a corn processing plant nearby.

Wisor, who relies on wells, fears that a potential 1,000-plus acre QTS facility will suck them dry. QTS said its data centers use a closed-loop system, which "do not consume water for cooling once they are operational."
Sokolovich of Grow Clinton sees data centers as the answer to improving the city’s finances and reaching its goals, like building a sports complex and improving its roads.

“The financial demands of providing even basic services continue to increase,” he wrote in a letter about the QTS proposal. “What if the attraction of a data center could offset the costs and expedite the chance of turning these dreams into reality?”
Maddasion was more circumspect.
“Obviously there’s economic benefits of it. That tax revenue from a data center would be massive compared to what our current general fund is,” he said. “Is it the right fit for Clinton though?”

items.title: US AI Boom Needs $110 Billion of New Power Plants, Moody's Says
body: America’s data center boom will need $110 billion to build 45 gigawatts of new power generation through 2030, according to an analysis by Moody’s Ratings.

The vast majority of that new supply, more than 30 gigawatts, will come from natural gas-fired units and represents about 4 billion cubic feet of incremental gas supply, according to a report Monday. The bulk of the remaining supply will come from solar and energy storage, with nuclear restarts accounting for less than 5%. One gigawatt is roughly equivalent to the output of a traditional nuclear reactor.
The projection is based on the International Energy Agency’s forecast that data centers will consume 426 terawatt-hours in 2030, doubling its share of US electricity usage to 10% from 2025 levels.

Moody’s forecast quantifies what it would take to produce enough megawatts to feed the data centers needed for artificial intelligence and cloud computing that are driving the biggest expansion in US electricity demand in decades, fueling a massive buildout of infrastructure to support it. The White House has called the AI race a national imperative, backing some of the world’s biggest companies as they compete for potentially enormous profits. But the buildout comes at a cost, drawing opposition from Americans worried that the average household and business is subsidizing AI through rising power bills, pollution, water shortages and threats to public lands and private property.

The $110 billion buildout of new power plants alone could add $25 billion to $30 billion a year to electricity costs in the US; how that is passed on to consumers will depend on the rate-making process and other rules for allocating costs in each area, Ryan Wobbrock, senior vice president of ratings at Moody’s Ratings’ global infrastructure finance group, said in an email.

Data centers will pay for as much as $15 billion of those costs directly, because they are paying for power plants to be built on their AI campuses, he said. These behind-the-meter projects at data centers represent about 30% of the total buildout through 2030.

After two decades of lackluster demand growth, the US has been struggling to jumpstart the construction of gas generators in an industry that typically moves with years of lead time. These gas generators are coveted because they can be ordered to ramp up, unlike renewables that are beholden to sunshine and wind speeds.

Amid affordability concerns, “federal and state politicians and regulators are requiring more time to review and structure rates, creating a new source of potential delays for new data center developments,” according to the report led by Wobbrock.“The pace of data center development is increasingly exceeding the speed at which the electric grid can add generation, transmission and interconnection capacity.”

items.title: The Oil Market Needs a Quick Saudi Pipeline Restart
body: Welcome to our guide to the commodities driving the global economy. Today, reporter Alex Longley looks at the oil market repercussions from Saudi Arabia’s closure of a key pipeline.
Last week’s hit to Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline offers the clearest reminder yet, if it was needed, that the oil market is far from out of the woods when it comes to conflict in the Middle East.

The pipeline, which stretches from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea and allows Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, has helped keep the kingdom’s oil flowing during the Iran war. It was struck by militants who launched drones from Iraq last Thursday.
On that day, oil prices jumped more than $8 at one point as satellite images and word of mouth among traders spread news that the kingdom announced publicly the following day.

Even in the days before the attack, oil prices rallied above $100 a barrel. Chinese buying picked up after a hiatus, tightening physical markets after global inventories have run down since the war began.

Fuel markets also remain exceptionally tight, thanks to both the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars, with diesel futures trading around $200 a barrel. That’s set to keep demand for crude elevated in the weeks ahead.

Adding to the pressure, threats from Yemen’s Houthi militants to Saudi flows through the Red Sea have complicated the kingdom’s efforts to keep oil moving, delaying some shipments as cargoes are forced to sail around Africa.
It’s against that backdrop that any restart to the pipeline will be assessed.

If repairs are needed, Aramco has an exceptional track record. In 2019, when attacks claimed by Yemen’s Houthi militants knocked out 5% of global production, Saudi Arabia restored output to where it was before the strikes within a month.

It also managed to bounce back quickly from an earlier attack on the pipeline this year, though that one only produced only limited damage and didn’t require the link to be shut down, people familiar with the matter said at the time.
In the short term, traders will be looking to see how much of its exports the kingdom will divert through the Strait of Hormuz.

So far it has been relatively cautious in its approach to sailing through the waterway since the war began, but even before the latest attack there were signs of a ramp-up in Saudi Persian Gulf loadings.
Whatever happens, the oil market will need a quick fix. It’s currently screaming for barrels.
—Alex Longley, Bloomberg News

The loss of a fifth of liquefied natural gas supply due to the US-Iran war is blowing out costs for Asia’s developing markets, forcing a rethink of the fuel’s long-term future in the region. India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Thailand and Vietnam have spent a collective $7.4 billion since the start of the war on spot LNG. A similar amount of the fuel cost about $3.1 billion under long-term contracts over the same period last year.
Oil pushed higher as Saudi Arabia’s pipeline closure continued to jolt the market.
Asian refiners are waiting for clarity on cargoes due to be picked up at the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Yanbu, which is served by the affected oil link.
Chinese refineries are paying eye-watering premiums to replace lost Middle East crude, snapping up cargoes from Russia, Africa and the Americas in a weeks-long splurge.

US President Donald Trump said he’d warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting oil refineries in Russia amid strikes that have shut down diesel refining and helped drive prices for the fuel to record levels.

The diesel crunch has few quick fixes, with refineries already running near their limits and high prices increasingly left to do the work of curbing demand, writes Bloomberg Opinion columnist Javier Blas.

Monday: Gastech exhibition and conference in Bangkok (through Sept. 17); International Atomic Energy Agency’s General Conference in Vienna (through Sept. 18); Canada Investment Summit in Toronto (through Sept. 15); G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial meeting in Houston (through Sept. 16)

Tuesday: Africa Green Hydrogen Summit in Cape Town (through Sept. 16); Argus North American Biofuels, LCFs & Carbon Markets Summit in Monterey, California (through Sept. 17); American Petroleum Institute weekly oil inventories report
Wednesday: Genscape weekly crude inventory report for ARA; Energy Information Administration weekly report on US oil inventories; Federal Reserve interest rate decisions
Thursday: China’s August output data for base metals and oil products; BNP Paribas Global Markets APAC Conference in Hong Kong; EIA weekly report on US natural gas inventories
Friday: China’s second batch of August trade data, including oil products imports and exports breakdown; Shanghai exchange weekly commodities inventory; Baker Hughes weekly rig count

An emerging super El Niño could weaken China’s liquefied natural gas demand through two channels, according to BloombergNEF. Milder winter temperatures would trim heating needs, while stronger hydropower output next summer could displace gas-fired power generation. Lower consumption by the world’s largest LNG importer could help ease pressure on an increasingly tight global market.

Bloomberg Green returns to New York on Sept. 23 during Climate Week, convening industry leaders, policymakers and climate innovators to explore what’s next in the transition to a more resilient and future-ready world.

items.title: Vance's Childcare Plan Pits Parents Against Each Other
body: Should the federal government give subsidies to parents who stay home to care for their young kids? Absolutely. Should it also subsidize childcare for working parents? For sure. This shouldn’t be an either-or question, but the Trump administration’s new childcare subsidy plan makes it one.

Under the draft proposal, as previewed in a leaked report to the New York Times, stay-at-home parents in low-income households could get up to $9,000 a year to help supplant lost earnings. The money would come from the existing $12 billion fund in the Child Care and Development Block Grant Act. That law provides childcare subsidies to eligible working parents in households making below 85% of the state’s median income.

The policy is a top priority for Vice President JD Vance and is patterned after a proposal drafted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio when he was in the Senate. The concept was promoted by the Heritage Foundation in its Project 2025 blueprint. And Heritage president Kevin Roberts is touting the idea as needed to “reward family foundation, not subsidize its decline.”

It’s an ideological trap. My guess is that the idea has surfaced two months before the midterm elections to revive the “Mommy Wars” debates of the 1980s and 1990s, which wrongly pitted mothers who stay home against those who earn a paycheck. It’s a culture-war issue that agitates leftists and excites right-wing pronatalists in an effort to distract voters from Trump’s policy failures.
Except the proposal won’t work.

If the idea is implemented as described, it’s both impractical and irresponsible. It would force working parents already in the program to compete with married, at-home parents for the same pool of funds.

Under the current program, the federal subsidy is given to working parents and covers only about 1 in 7 of eligible families, or about 870,000 parents. The Trump plan would divide the pie into smaller pieces, promising subsidies to some married couples who want to keep a parent home. That would make it harder for the parents already in the program to keep both their jobs and their childcare.

Americans know the country needs to do better for its kids. More than half of Americans say that it’s better for children and society for kids to be raised in two-parent households. And millions of families may genuinely prefer to have a parent stay home when their children are young. That shouldn’t be a choice that carries the risk of long-term financial vulnerability.

But the  cost of raising kids is growing. According to a 2025 Lending Tree survey of parents with young children, 46% said they have fewer kids than they’d like due to financial constraints. Meanwhile, childcare costs in the US have risen  by a third over the last 15 years. Half of all families live in childcare deserts, driving young families out of rural towns. And according to the US Census, there are 10.9 million one-parent households in the country, of which 80% are led by women.

While the US has the highest rate of children living in single-parent households, we also have none of the social infrastructure offered by many other wealthy countries: universal paid family leave, childcare starting at birth and universal investments in early childhood education.
This is an indictment of existing US policies, not a rationale for cutting off funds to already-struggling single parents.

Politicians of both parties have been watching the crisis mount for years, but have been unable to assemble the political will to address it. Former President Joe Biden proposed $400 billion in far-reaching childcare subsidies and universal pre-K under the first draft of his Build Back Better Act. Republicans accused Biden of socialism, blasted the subsidies as “welfare” and rejected the idea.

Now, a group of policy makers from both the Biden and Obama administrations have proposed Project 2029, a blueprint for a Democratic future that includes universal free childcare and a $1,000 monthly stipend for stay-at-home parents. US Representative Ro Khanna of California has a 10-year plan to spend $780 billion on subsidizing traditional child-care centers, giving grants to stay-at-home parents, and compensating programs for “kin caregivers.”

Any of these plans would represent a vast increase in spending on childcare, but for the last 30 years, researchers who study childcare have learned that public investment in childcare pays for itself through increased workforce participation and tax revenue, higher business productivity and greater economic activity.

And an honest debate would acknowledge that for decades the US has been trying to do childcare assistance on the cheap. If we really want to strengthen “family formation” and meet parents’ affordability needs, we’d recognize that families have diverse childcare needs. We’d supercharge our investment in workable childcare options and reject the Trump administration’s zero-sum illusion of choice.
