items.title: UAE/Saudi Arabia: Bankers Who Chased Gulf IPO Deals Look Elsewhere Amid Slump
body: Just three years ago, global bankers would fly into the Gulf to corner a slice of the world’s hottest market for new share sales. Now, even local advisers are being forced to hunt for business outside the region as deals dwindle.

Listing volumes in the Gulf began tapering off last year and have fallen to under $1.1 billion so far in 2026, due in part to the monthslong regional conflict. That’s prompting a race for fees overseas, with firms including HSBC Holdings Plc and EFG Hermes looking to markets like Egypt, Turkey and India.

The drop in volumes means Gulf firms have raised less than typically quieter markets like sub-Saharan Africa, where listings have drawn $1.37 billion. The gap will widen further after Dangote Petroleum Refinery raises at least $1.6 billion in the continent’s largest-ever IPO.

This marks a sharp turnaround for hubs like Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, where a post-pandemic boom in listings provided a buffer against slowdowns in traditional hotspots like London, Hong Kong and New York. It also presents a stark contrast to the boom in dealmaking by Gulf state-backed investors that’s prompting global firms to add M&A bankers.

The value of such deals involving Gulf entities rose almost 200% in the first half of the year to about $300 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Meanwhile, despite a substantial pipeline for IPOs, the war has injected uncertainty over the timeline and forced bankers to look further afield.
Read More: Wall Street Firms Bolster Gulf Teams to Tackle Wartime M&A Surge

Case in point: HSBC, which consistently ranks as one of the top banks for Gulf equity capital market deals. As business slowed, it turned to secondary share sales in Turkey that have fetched $1.6 billion this year — almost twice as much as the year before, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

HSBC currently tops league tables there with seven such transactions raising a combined $552 million, up from two deals worth $260 million last year. It has more than 50 active mandates for M&A and listings across the Middle East, North Africa and Turkey, according to Mohammed Fannouch, HSBC’s co-head of capital markets and advisory for the region, though like many of its peers, it has yet to complete an IPO in the Gulf this year.

Meanwhile, EFG Hermes, another fixture near the top of Gulf ECM rankings, is working on several IPOs in Egypt, where it has deep roots. That includes a potential Cairo listing of fintech unicorn MNT-Halan’s Egyptian business alongside Citigroup Inc. It’s also helping arrange planned offerings by state-affiliated companies including Banque du Caire SAE and Misr Life Insurance, and advised on the IPO of a small food retailer that’s up almost 150% since its January debut.

Christopher Laing, EFG Hermes’ Dubai-based head of ECM, said the bank considers Egypt a home market, and one that has “performed incredibly well” in the last two years. “The currency has become more stable since the devaluation last year, inflation’s coming down, tourism is improving, the economy is growing,” he said. “So that has helped investor interest enormously.”
Dubai’s own Emirates NBD Bank PJSC, among firms that added staff in recent years to cope with the Gulf IPO boom, is also turning to deals overseas.

The bank has expanded its investment-banking presence in India in recent months and snapped up a majority stake in RBL Bank, as it seeks a share of the country’s substantial deal flow. It has established itself as a regular arranger of international bond deals in Turkey and is looking to gain a foothold in equity capital markets there.
Read More: Emirates NBD Said to Be in Talks to Buy HSBC’s Turkey Unit

And alongside First Abu Dhabi Bank PJSC, Emirates NBD is among arrangers of Airtel Money’s London listing. Hitesh Asarpota, chief executive officer at ENBD Capital, said the cross-border activity comes as more issuers outside of the Gulf look to access the Middle East’s deep pools of liquidity, while regional investors seek exposure to global markets.

Some state-backed lenders are also eking business out of deepening ties with overseas governments. Abu Dhabi and Uzbekistan, for example, have strengthened their relationship through a series of investment partnerships, and Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank PJSC recently came in as a book-runner on the London-Tashkent dual-listing of Uzbekistan’s National Investment Fund.

To be sure, these firms and international peers like Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and JPMorgan Chase & Co. who began flying in top IPO bankers in more frequently during the boom years, have still been winning business in the Gulf — but deals are yet to materialize. EFG Hermes’ Laing expects “lots of new business in the Gulf,” with his bank recently inking several new mandates in Saudi Arabia, although many deals are more likely to launch next year.
Against that drop off in activity, two recent deals indicated another shift in how banks generate fees.

A few years ago, a large chunk of business came from Gulf governments selling shares in key assets in their attempts to deepen capital markets. Over the past two months, some banks have worked on two take-privates instead.
Read More: Inside Abu Dhabi’s Buyout of an $81 Billion Firm

items.title: India August Inflation Accelerates, Narrowing RBI Pause Room
body: India’s inflation accelerated in August, moving closer to the top of the central bank’s 2%-6% target range and potentially narrowing the scope for policymakers to remain on hold for long.

The consumer price index rose 4.82% last month from a year earlier, up from 4.45% in July, data released Monday by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation showed. That was inline with the 4.86% median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of economists. The reading was the highest since December 2024 and marked the third straight month that headline inflation exceeded the Reserve Bank of India’s 4% medium term target.
The acceleration was driven by firmer food prices, while restaurant and transport costs also kept broader price pressures firm.

The data showed that “price pressures have become more persistent rather than a one-month aberration, making the RBI’s policy trade-off difficult,” said Manoranjan Sharma, economist with Infomerics Ratings.

Still, the RBI has signaled it won’t react mechanically to a higher number. Governor Sanjay Malhotra said in an interview Friday that underlying price pressures remain low and policymakers will focus on whether the increase persists and spreads more broadly through the economy.

The RBI has kept its benchmark rate unchanged at 5.25% since the start of the year, one of the few major central banks to remain in wait-and-watch mode despite the economic shocks from the Middle East war. Of late, however, some policymakers have become more alert to inflation risks as oil surges past $108 a barrel and food prices remain elevated.
Read more: Asia Confronts New Inflation, Fiscal Threat as Oil Tops $100

The monetary policy committee next meets in October, with some economists seeing a real risk of the first rate hike since the Middle East war began. Today’s figures could help further shape those expectations.

The RBI’s prolonged pause situation “has changed drastically,” Soumya Kanti Ghosh, an economist at the State Bank of India, wrote in a note Friday, predicting inflation may head toward 6.5% or higher if oil prices remain high.
“Now, we strongly advocate a 25-basis-point rate hike in the upcoming October policy, followed by another in December in quick succession.”

After the numbers, the odds of “an action in October” have increased significantly, said Upasna Bhardwaj, economist at Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd, adding there’s scope for 50 to 75 basis points of cumulative rate hikes by the central bank.

The RBI’s challenge is to keep inflation in check without unnecessarily weakening an economy that has so far weathered the Middle East conflict relatively well. Stronger-than-expected growth of 7.8% in the April-June quarter gives policymakers some room to raise rates if price pressures continue to build.

Food inflation, which accounts for more than a third of the CPI basket, climbed 5.95% from 5.52% a month earlier. Core inflation, which strips volatile food and fuel prices, climbed to 4.2% in August, up from 3.9% in July, as per calculations by Bloomberg Economics.
The data also showed:

A looming threat is that deficient monsoon rains across parts of India could hurt crop yields and supplies, further fanning inflation. Festive-season spending through November could also add to price pressures, economists say.

A sustained rise in global crude prices poses another inflation risk for India, which imports nearly 90% of its oil. A prolonged spell above $100 a barrel could increase pressure to raise retail petrol and diesel prices, feeding directly into inflation and lifting transport and other input costs.

Inflation may climb further as high crude prices combine with strengthening domestic demand. “Demand conditions may add to the momentum going forward, given low real rates, strong credit growth and an unprecedented build-up of surplus liquidity,” said Gaurav Kapur, economist at IndusInd Bank Ltd.

Higher oil prices could also weigh on the rupee by increasing India’s import bill, making overseas goods more expensive. The currency could face another test from the US Federal Reserve’s Sept. 15-16 meeting if policymakers there raise rates or signal further tightening. Malhotra, however, played down the influence of Fed decisions on Indian monetary policy in Friday’s interview.

items.title: Senegal's President to Meet IMF Chief in Washington This Week
body: Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye will hold talks with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva this week, as the country seeks to secure a new program while grappling with a debt burden inflated by billions of dollars of previously undisclosed loans.

Faye and Georgieva will meet in Washington on Tuesday, an IMF spokesperson said by email on Monday. They will discuss “recent economic developments and Senegal’s economic reform program,” the spokesperson said.
Senegalese state broadcaster RTS reported late Sunday that Faye will also meet with World Bank officials in the US capital.

Faye is in Washington for a working visit focused on strengthening Senegal’s economic and financial partnerships, according to Senegal’s presidency. He is scheduled to travel to Abu Dhabi on Sept. 16 for a visit focused on strengthening bilateral relations and economic cooperation with the United Arab Emirates, it said.

Senegal secured a staff-level agreement with the IMF earlier this month for a $2.2 billion program, subject to approval by the fund’s executive board. The West African nation also plans to carry out a debt rework under the Group of 20 Common Framework.
IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack said last week that the fund may approve a new program for Senegal without waiting for the debt reprofiling process to be concluded.

items.title: University of Virginia Darden's New Dean on Business Schools in the AI Era
body: Yael Grushka-Cockayne became dean at the University of Virginia’s Darden School of Business on Aug. 1. The school’s 10th dean and the first woman in its 71-year history, she didn’t need to spend time getting to know staff or the campus, as she’s been a professor and academic leader at Darden for 17 years. It’s Grushka-Cockayne’s knowledge about artificial intelligence, though, that may prove her biggest advantage. Business schools around the world are scrambling to devise strategies to teach and use the transformative technology. Grushka-Cockayne has been working on AI at Darden for several years now, including as co-academic director of the LaCross Institute for Ethical Artificial Intelligence in Business.

She argues that business leaders must understand AI’s capabilities and risks and recognize that AI makes fostering distinctly human capabilities even more important. “I embrace and like AI, yet I understand its shortcomings,” she said in late August.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

I was a very math-oriented child, and later I was drawn to industrial engineering and operations research because I loved quants. In the late 1990s, information systems were both new and exciting, and there was a lot on the hook. The year 2000 was looming, the internet was starting to bloom, and companies realized they could think about the flow of information more efficiently. I focused on what I identified as a need, which was making sure senior leaders recognized the importance of efficiency, of things like the use of resources, project planning and management, and decision-making. Today AI is at the heart of these issues.

AI presents a lot of opportunities, whether it’s freeing up people to think differently or aggregating information in a different manner. There’s value in some of this coming from the bottom up. But if senior leadership doesn’t get involved and generate a cohesive vision, you may have different parts of the business pulling in different directions. Someone needs to say, “We want to leverage AI to accomplish X, Y and Z,” and that comes from the top. This isn’t something you can delegate to your young interns.

AI should enhance learning, not replace it. We’re very committed to our case-method approach, with students studying cases and coming to class prepared to engage in deep and messy conversations, to make sense of things, make decisions and also to listen to others and sometimes change their minds. AI can help our students dig much deeper into cases and experiment with their inquisitiveness, by considering, for instance, how they’d approach a problem if they were a consultant versus an internal manager. The answers they collect are more varied, and when they come to class and share them, that really enriches the discussion.

A lot of my work focuses on forecasting and decision-making amid uncertainty. And I think it’s fair to say that we all feel like the world is getting more uncertain than certain, even with the abundance of technology and data. I hope students come to Darden not only to acquire skills but to gain confidence and become comfortable making decisions amid many more pieces of information. You can’t just rely on analytics — you have to be able to think, “Given this analysis, what do I recommend and why?” AI can give you a specific answer, but you need to understand the context in which you operate and how various contexts might call for very different behaviors, even if the numbers are the same.

That’s a challenge, because people like to think about return on investment in the very short term. I believe there’s short-term value in a Darden MBA, but the real big no-brainer value comes from the longer trajectory of one’s entire career.

My dream job was being a business school professor, and I was living that dream every day. So that does beg the question: Why become an administrator? I’ve been in leadership roles previously at Darden, and I’ve enjoyed making decisions and having them carry weight. For six years, I was a senior associate dean, first for our executive MBA program and then for the residential full-time MBA program, and I’ve been a trustee on our foundation board. Still, I had to ask myself, “Will I be able to bring something new and important to the school, and can I help steward it forward?” The answer to those questions is yes. I have a strong ability to connect with many people — students, faculty, staff, as well as alumni who are located around the world, business leaders and others — and allow them to benefit from each other’s acquaintance. I believe that Darden’s impact can and should be broader and more visible, and I want to help make that happen.

items.title: Trump Doesn't Campaign Well as President in Midterms
body: Donald Trump has proven himself a generational political talent — when he’s not in the Oval Office. But as if he’s Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, he transforms into an incompetent campaign doppelganger as president. Republicans are about to pay the price again.

Trump, during two winning presidential campaigns (out of three), was uniquely adept at validating voters’ concerns, speaking directly to their priorities and proposing unvarnished solutions. Voters felt seen by him; they felt heard. This is why an Electoral College majority in 2016 and a popular vote majority in 2024 pulled the lever for Trump. The first time, concerns about his provocative rhetoric and unconventional behavior were set aside. The second time, voters overlooked his attempt to steal the 2020 election, which included fomenting a riot at the US Capitol.
His record as an incumbent party leader is the exact opposite.

The scoreboard doesn’t lie. Republicans lost control of the House of Representatives in 2018, the first midterm election Trump presided over. Democrats flipped the White House and the US Senate two years later amid Trump’s only reelection campaign as an incumbent president. And this time around, less than eight weeks before Trump’s second midterm election, his party is in danger of losing both chambers of Congress.

“As an outsider, you’d be hard-pressed to find a better challenger than Donald Trump,” said Matt K. Lewis, conservative columnist for the Washington Sun and author of Too Dumb to Fail: How the GOP Went from the Party of Reagan to the Party of Trump. “As a president, you’d be hard pressed to find a worse spokesperson than Donald Trump.”

The president’s keynote address (Wednesday) and closing address (Thursday) during last week’s two-day Trump rally in Dallas — dubbed the first-ever midterm convention by the Republican National Committee — are prime examples.

The GOP’s congressional majorities are threatened because voters are frustrated by Trump’s leadership on the issue that matters most to them. In this midterm campaign, but dating back to the president’s second inauguration, that’s the economy, especially related to the high cost of living: groceries, gasoline, housing, healthcare, interest rates and the like. Compounding the political headwinds for Republicans, voters are convinced he’s insufficiently focused on reducing costs. And Trump’s pitch to voters in Dallas?

He mocked their anxiety about affordability as unfounded and fueled by Democratic disinformation and the media. “They used the word affordability, right? It’s fake,” Trump said during Wednesday’s prime time speech. “I’m bringing prices way down.” Instead, the president fixated on his priorities. Lately, those include building the rip-off, “victory” arch ubiquitous in European capitals; constructing a White House ballroom; and spearheading various remodeling projects in and around Washington, DC. To the extent Trump discussed the economy, he doubled down on an inflationary agenda that has failed to subdue prices: tariffs and trade wars.

Trump and his political team hold a different view of the Republican Party’s midterm election struggles under the 45th and 47th president. They blame both heavy losses in 2018 and current polling that shows Democrats favored to flip the House and competitive in the battle for the Senate on Trump’s absence from the ballot.

They’re not completely wrong. As a candidate, Trump has broadened the GOP coalition, while motivating infrequent voters and grassroots conservatives who oppose establishment politicians to participate in elections and support both him and down-ticket Republicans. Accordingly, there’s a drop-off in midterm elections, when the only GOP candidates on offer are cookie-cutter politicians, giving Democrats a significant voter turnout edge. Indeed, recent surveys show Democrats with a demonstrable advantage in voter enthusiasm.
Team Trump’s counter strategy? Plead with Republican voters to pretend the president is on the ballot, as the commander-in-chief did in Dallas.

That would be a sensible response and not entirely meritless — except for what happened in 2020. In that election, Trump was on the ballot. And although he lost only narrowly to now-former President Joe Biden, it’s why the president lost that’s important.

In that campaign, voters (all of us) were living through a once-in-a-century coronavirus pandemic. People were scared, and surviving Covid-19 was paramount. But other than the first few weeks of the crisis, Trump downplayed the dangers the pandemic posed to health and safety instead. “It affects virtually nobody,” he said of the coronavirus, during a campaign rally in late September of 2020. (Per US government estimates, the number of deaths attributable to the virus was massive.)

Nine weeks after Election Day, Democrats flipped two Senate seats in Georgia in a pair of runoff contests. Trump, who depressed Republican turnout by insisting the 2020 election had been stolen, only helped them.

But Republicans’ Achilles heel this November is not necessarily a lack of interest from the president’s loyal base, voters who think of themselves as MAGA first and GOP second. They continue to adore the president. What’s really endangering Republicans is evaporating support among GOP regulars who have never been Trump’s biggest fans but backed the party’s ticket to block Democrats from power. Maybe the right question to ask is whether the president’s promised $5,000 payoff, in exchange for Republican turnout, is enough to motivate them.
That Trump was compelled to resort to this sort of dubious measure is revealing.

items.title: AI Use for Schoolwork Leaves Students 1.5 Years Behind, OECD Finds
body: Welcome to Bloomberg’s AI Today newsletter. Every weekday we’ll break down artificial intelligence’s threats and opportunities for businesses, workers, finance and economies. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.
As the CEOs of AI companies argue for a slowdown, sending related stocks tumbling, a report from the OECD suggests the technology isn’t making students more impressive.

In a massive global study encompassing 760,000 teens across 91 countries, the policy group found that students who use AI every day perform significantly worse than classmates who don’t use chatbots. The effect is staggering: when adjusted for socio-economic status, kids who rarely use the technology are about a year-and-a-half ahead of the ones who do.
That is bound to intensify global debate about what place AI has in our schools.

In Asian countries, where people are relatively optimistic about AI, some governments have embraced the technology. Beijing has gone all in, mandating AI education starting in primary school. Singapore is close behind. There, the OECD study found, two-thirds of students turn to AI for help with schoolwork. Nearly half said they use AI to draft assignments.

In Seoul, it’s even more pervasive. A separate 2025 survey there found a staggering 95% of the 26,500 middle- and high-school students polled regularly used tools like ChatGPT and Gemini. Last year, South Korea rolled out AI-powered personalized, digital textbooks.

But not everyone approves. Parents and teachers in Seoul fought so back hard that the country’s national assembly ultimately stripped the AI textbooks of their official status. Undeterred, South Korea has announced an “AI for All” initiative that doles out free AI chatbot access to everyone, including children.

In Japan, by contrast, the government has taken a more measured approach to allowing AI in schools. New York is also cautious: the city recently announced a yearlong moratorium on use of chatbots in schools for its youngest students. Los Angeles soon followed suit. Norway has gone even further, banning generative AI in primary schools. In grades 8 to 10, kids still need have teacher supervision to use AI.
The OECD study only fueled that sentiment – a fear that artificial intelligence is prospering at the expense of humanity.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

SoftBank Group shares fell more than 13% in Tokyo trading — their steepest intraday decline since late June — after Anthropic and OpenAI chiefs called for a slowdown in AI development citing safety concerns, and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman confirmed the company will not go public in 2026. The selloff also pushed SoftBank’s credit default swaps to their highest level since March 30, nearing three-year highs.

Anthropic has selected Nasdaq as its listing venue for a highly anticipated IPO that could take place as soon as October and potentially surpass SpaceX’s record-setting $86.3 billion offering. The AI company is on track to generate annualized revenue of over $65 billion. The IPO comes even as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, alongside OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk, called for slowing the pace of AI development due to escalating risks.

The rise of mega AI data centers is driving explosive growth in captive insurance, a self-insurance model traditionally used by mining and oil sectors, as companies building AI infrastructure increasingly bypass traditional insurers to manage their own risks. The AI data centers are often larger than anything conventional insurers have handled.

Wall Street’s biggest banks, including Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, BNY Mellon, JPMorgan Chase, and Wells Fargo, are competing to manage the anticipated IPO windfalls of employees at AI firm Anthropic, which has asked banks to pitch their wealth-management services ahead of a blockbuster listing expected to mint a new wave of millionaires among its staff.

Moonshot AI is targeting $2 billion in annualized revenue by year-end after its annual recurring revenue surpassed $1 billion in August, up from $300 million in June. The surge was driven by the July release of its Kimi K3 model, which topped performance benchmarks at significantly lower costs than leading US competitors. The Beijing-based startup is also raising funds at a $50 billion valuation ahead of a potential Hong Kong IPO later this year.

President Trump is maintaining a hands-off regulatory approach to artificial intelligence as he prepares for a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington this month, where AI safety is expected to be a key issue. The administration is struggling to balance promoting AI adoption and preserving the US lead over China against growing cybersecurity risks, including threats from rogue AI models.

Meanwhile, China’s Foreign Ministry rejected the call from US tech executives to slow AI development, warning that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition” would harm global AI governance. Beijing’s pushback reflects concerns that AI safety arguments could be used as justification for further US restrictions on China’s technology sector.

But China’s State Security Minister Chen Yixin published a detailed warning about AI risks, stating that adversarial use of the technology could threaten China’s political stability, critical infrastructure, and ideological security. The article represents one of Beijing’s most explicit assessments of AI dangers, citing concerns about foreign “hostile forces” and AI’s growing ability to identify system vulnerabilities and create malware.

Oracle is expanding its restructuring plan by an additional $700 million, bringing total estimated job-cut costs to approximately $2.8 billion, as the company faces a cash crunch tied to its expensive build-out of AI data centers for customers including OpenAI. The company has already accrued about $2.1 billion in costs under its “2026 Restructuring Plan,” which consists largely of severance payments.

Critics of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s lengthy warning about AI’s potential threat to humanity say it is vague on concrete solutions, with its most specific recommendation involving external auditors. Columnist Parmy Olson highlights a contradiction in Amodei’s position, as Anthropic continues building increasingly powerful AI systems despite acknowledging the technology could pose existential risks.

Members of both parties in Congress are pushing for new AI regulations, including proposals to ban artificial superintelligence, create a federal regulatory agency, and hold a special legislative session. California state Senator Scott Wiener, previously dismissed as an alarmist, has been vindicated as a pioneer of AI safety legislation. Columnist Erika D. Smith argues that Congress should look to California’s regulatory framework as a model, noting that Congress has a poor track record on AI regulation.

items.title: Indonesia's New Finance Chief Is Seen as Market-Friendly Veteran
body: Suahasil Nazara, Indonesia’s new finance minister, is an experienced insider and familiar face for investors, having served as a deputy over the past seven years.

President Prabowo Subianto’s move Monday to replace maverick Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa is the second surprise shake-up in the finance ministry in about a year, and appears to be calibrated to ease market concerns over the direction of Southeast Asia’s largest economy.

Nazara, 55, was appointed as deputy finance minister by former President Joko Widodo in 2019. He served under former Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati — the widely respected economist who was fired to make room for Purbaya after clashing with Prabowo.

The choice of Nazara, an experienced domestic fiscal policy official, could “help restore market confidence and stabilize macro-fiscal management,” said Harry Su, managing director of research at PT Samuel Sekuritas Indonesia.
The appointment appeared to be welcomed by markets, with the benchmark stock index reversing most of the day’s losses.
Read More: Indonesia New Finance Minister a Sign of Prudence, Analysts Say

The move comes amid growing friction over revenue targets, budget implementation and policy coordination, including government fund transfers to the regions and contributions from the wealth fund Danantara, Su said.

The appointment is likely to ensure stability in fiscal policy and limit transition risks given Nazara’s long-standing role at the ministry, according to Irman Faiz, chief economist at PT Bank Danamon in Jakarta. His technocratic background also provides institutional continuity in managing the state budget, he said.

Nazara’s bigger challenge, however, will be the same as his predecessors’: balancing Prabowo’s ambitious growth agenda with increasingly constrained fiscal space. That will require preserving credibility, while shifting spending away from programs that have limited payoff for the economy, Faiz said.

The government is targeting 6% economic growth and a fiscal deficit of 2.4% of GDP in 2027, while Bank Danamon forecasts 5.1% growth and a deficit of about 2.75% — still within the statutory 3% limit.

Nazara was reappointed as deputy finance minister under Prabowo in October 2024. He earlier served as head of the Finance Ministry’s Fiscal Policy Agency from 2016 to 2019, after becoming acting head in 2015.

Nazara began his career as an economics lecturer at the University of Indonesia in 1999 and became a professor in 2009. He held several academic and policy positions, including head of the university’s economics department, and worked on fiscal decentralization, regional autonomy and poverty reduction. He also served on the National Economic Committee from 2013 to 2014.
He holds a bachelor’s degree in economics from the University of Indonesia, a master’s degree from Cornell University and a doctorate in economics from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

items.title: China, US Wary Over Calls to Slow AI Development in Race for Supremacy
body: Those with the clearest inside knowledge of AI frontier models are suddenly agreeing that slowing down the pace of development is advisable. But with the US and China competing in a race for tech supremacy, any deceleration risks allowing the rival to get ahead. Caution, in other words, could equal surrender.

Countries should promote “open, inclusive, universally beneficial and ethical” AI development, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing in Beijing. “Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve the interests of no one,” he said.

Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for companies to moderate the pace at which they improve AI capabilities, warning that safeguards are failing to keep up. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backed Amodei’s proposal to give independent evaluators employee-like access, while Elon Musk agreed with the Anthropic chief.

Yet Amodei also argued that any effort by US companies to moderate development would be constrained by the lead they maintain over China. If American labs slowed too much, Beijing could pull ahead and create what he described as a grave danger to the US and the world. State-run Global Times attacked Amodei’s proposals, accusing him of waging a “silent AI Cold War” to suppress China’s technological development.
The dispute is intensifying days before anticipated AI discussions ahead of US President Donald Trump’s summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Sept. 24.

“The boundary between ‘AI safety’ and ‘AI competition’ is becoming increasingly blurred,” said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Center for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.

All this talk of slowing AI development weighed on tech stocks. Nasdaq 100 futures sank 1.8%. An ETF tracking key chip shares dropped 4.7% in early trading as traders fretted that efforts to rein in AI could weigh on the boom driving hundreds of billions of dollars in capital spending. OpenAI backer SoftBank slid the most in nearly three months, while South Korea’s Kospi index dropped 3.3%. S&P 500 contracts were down 0.8%.

The selloff in tech stocks comes at the start of a week in which both the Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan face pressure to raise rates as policymakers meet Wednesday and Friday, respectively. While a Bank of England hike on Thursday isn’t anticipated, the prospect of a shift toward an increase in November remains on the cards.

Pricier energy: Oil pushed higher as Saudi Arabia’s closure of a major crude pipeline following attacks jolted the market, with the move disrupting a route that’s been key to bypassing the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Iran war.

Brent rose as much as 3.9% to above $108 a barrel, before paring gains, while West Texas Intermediate was near $103. Saudi Arabia said late on Friday that it had halted the East-West pipeline as a precaution after attacks the previous day. There’s been no indication of when operations will resume.
No drones: Beijing has banned the possession and use of recreational drones as part of moves to bolster security in the capital after a light plane crashed into the city’s tallest skyscraper in June.

The restrictions — some of the tightest in the world on drones — come after a two-seat light plane flew into the 109-story Citic Tower in June, killing the pilot and injuring 13 others. The incident took place just several kilometers away from the headquarters of the ruling Communist Party and residence of top leaders.

LNG rethink: The loss of a fifth of liquefied natural gas supply due to the US-Iran war is blowing out costs for Asia’s developing markets, and forcing them to reconsider the fuel’s long-term future in the region.

Qatari shipments of LNG through the Strait of Hormuz have all but dried up since the conflict started at the end of February. That’s deprived Asian buyers of contracted supply of the power-station and industrial fuel, pushing them into the spot market where prices are surging.
No talks: A meeting between Iran and several Gulf Arab nations over a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz was postponed, highlighting tensions with the Islamic Republic.

Talks were set to take place in Oman on Monday but was delayed “for now” after a request from Saudi Arabia, according to Iran’s foreign ministry. That was partly down to the kingdom’s frustration over continued attacks on its territory by Iran-supported groups such as the Houthis, said one person familiar with the matter.

items.title: Risk of AI Slowdown Prompts Angst Among Tech Investors
body: Given the amount of investor cash that has flooded into stock market bets on AI, bulls have little room for error: Those wagers have to pay off, and relatively quickly, or prices will head lower.

That’s why the talk about a slowdown in AI development is such a threat to the market. It’s adding to existing concerns over valuation and momentum, which is a polite way of saying plenty of investors think this is a bubble.
The usual AI bellwethers are taking a hit:
These fears about the safety of AI are landing in a market that’s already skittish. Oil prices are jumping anew and investors are ramping up their bets on a Fed interest rate hike.
For now, the declines are relatively contained. But they just show how jumpy traders are.

“Investors will undoubtedly be questioning the AI boom’s trajectory this week,” said Josh Gilbert at eToro. “Investors are selling first and working out the details later.” —Phil Serafino, with Youkyung Lee
Central banks face a pivotal week as mounting inflation risks heap pressure on them to raise interest rates.
Three decisions, starting Wednesday with the Fed and followed on successive days by peers in the UK and Japan, may recast the global monetary policy landscape for the rest of 2026 and beyond.

The US will be most closely watched in the wake of a higher-than-expected core inflation reading on Friday. That stoked investor bets that Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and his colleagues will raise their benchmark rate, probably in defiance of Donald Trump’s wishes.
Click here for the full rundown of the week ahead. —Craig Stirling
With the yield on the 10-year US Treasury note still hovering just below 5%, the question is: So what?

There’s nothing inherently significant about that level, which the benchmark yield hasn’t closed above since 2007. But round numbers are often key pivot points that can catalyze decisions by investors and policymakers.

More broadly, Treasury yields are important because they serve as a baseline for other loans. In the stock market, they’re used to gauge the present value of profits expected in the years ahead. The more yields rise, the smaller those earnings look.
So elevated bond yields could start exerting a drag on stocks, which have been hovering near records because of the profits thrown off by the AI boom and the resilience in the economy.

“If you saw bond yields move to the 5% or 5.25% level I think that’s where you will see some indigestion from the equity market,” said Grace Peters at JPMorgan Chase Private Bank. “5% psychologically has an impact.” —Greg Ritchie and Michael MacKenzie

items.title: AI Data Center Boom Is Changing CMBS Risks
body: The commercial mortgage backed securities market, long a mainstay of financing for America’s offices, apartments and malls, is being reshaped by a surge in data-center deals, forcing investors to grapple with an entirely new set of risks.

From power availability and grid constraints to rapidly evolving requirements for cooling and computing density, CMBS buyers have been pushed into areas of underwriting that have historically had little to do with commercial real estate. Even familiar questions about tenant demand and stability are changing as facilities depend on a handful of often secretive hyperscalers whose future needs can be difficult to gauge. If those tenants leave when their leases expire in the coming years, highly specialized buildings could be costly to repurpose.

About $17 billion of data-center CMBS has been issued since the start of 2025 — more than triple the amount sold over the previous two years. During that span, data centers have grown to account for roughly 8% of new commercial property bond deals. With billions more in the pipeline, industry veterans are rapidly revamping their risk-assessment playbooks to try to steer clear of any potential blowups that could leave a hole in their portfolios.

“True data centers that are measured in units of compute and megawatts — it’s a totally different universe for real estate investors,” said Alex Killick, a senior managing director at CWCapital Asset Management. “These are metrics that aren’t easily translated to what we’re used to. It’s difficult to re-underwrite years later. We do that every day with an office deal or a hotel CMBS. How do I do that with a data center two years from now?”
Killick said CWCapital is developing a new set of stress tests for the sector to try to answer that question.

That same dilemma is evident at Axonic Capital, where portfolio manager Steven Jury has taken a cautious approach, keeping data centers a small part of the firm’s portfolio and emphasizing diversification across tenants, use cases and geographies. Most data center CMBS are structured as single-asset, single-borrower transactions, or SASBs, in which one large mortgage – often tied to a single facility or complex – backs the bonds.

“What these assets will be worth — and who will need them — five, 10 or 20 years from now” is the hard question, Jury said. “Technology, tenant demand and the supply landscape can all change significantly over that time.”
Many of the risks CMBS buyers have long had to weigh still apply, but the factors shaping them look very different when it comes to data centers.

Take the lease agreements themselves. Provisions covering power costs, minimum capacity commitments and downtime determine who absorbs unexpected expenses, which can reduce the cash available for servicing debt. Scrutinizing those terms can also be more difficult, with tenants often insisting that their identities and other lease details be kept confidential.

“Traditional CRE investors know how to underwrite offices, apartments, warehouses and retail because leases tend to be relatively standardized and tenant information is reasonably transparent,” said Ben Hunsaker, a portfolio manager at Beach Point Capital Management. “Data centers are much more opaque.”
For more CMBS coverage, subscribe to the Structured Finance Weekly

Location is another example. Instead of judging properties based on how close they are to transportation, amenities or a city’s core, prime sites are now the ones with access to cheap electricity and available transmission capacity. Those advantages can determine how competitive facilities remain and what they’re worth when loans mature.

Tenant concentration and lease rollover risk have also changed. In an office or apartment, releasing risk is often a simple matter of finding another client. When it comes to data centers, however, just as critical is whether bespoke electrical and cooling setups can even accommodate other firms, and what the ultimate price tag would be to overhaul a facility if they can’t.
For CMBS investors, that raises the prospect of higher capital spending, longer periods without rental income and weaker recoveries if a borrower runs into trouble.

“It’s really, really difficult for me to wrap my head around all of the nuanced risks,” said Stephen Buschbom, head of applied research and analytics at data firm Trepp. “These properties look and act more like infrastructure and nuanced tech plays than they do traditional real estate,” he said.
Then there are considerations that are almost entirely new for CMBS buyers.

The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence chips can drive sharply higher power and cooling requirements. A facility designed around one generation of hardware could therefore become outdated in just a few years, reducing its value and making its debt harder to refinance.

“With traditional real estate, you can model an obsolescence cycle in decades. Data centers are a completely different story,” Killick said. “The chips you put in six months ago could be supplanted by who knows what. That alone makes underwriting very difficult.”

The industry is also confronting a level of opposition that’s rarely seen elsewhere in commercial real estate, turning data-centers into a major political issue both at the local and national level. Concerns over utility costs and the strain on local infrastructure have fueled calls to restrict new developments in some communities, making the future regulatory environment particularly hard to predict, market watchers say.
Read More: Poor Towns Reject Data Centers That Could Help Their Finances

Some familiar worries remain, too, chief among them oversupply. Big tech has already issued more than $429 billion of debt globally this year to fund the AI buildout. While that borrowing spans fixed-income markets well beyond CMBS, investor fatigue around the financing boom is crossing over into property bonds.

Just last week, the top-rated tranche of a $356 million bond backed by a 30-megawatt facility near Elk Grove Village, Illinois, priced notably wider than initial guidance, marking the third such instance in recent months. In fact, AAA data center deals now pay an average of 1.65 percentage points above their floating-rate benchmark after their risk premiums widened since the start of the year, versus 0.93 for office, 1.05 for retail and 1.25 for industrial, Barclays Plc data show.
With a large pipeline of projects soon needing financing, Citigroup Inc. expects issuance to jump roughly 50% next year to between $18 billion and $20 billion.

“Rising supply that we expect next year poses a longer-term mark-to-market risk, particularly if demand becomes more tenuous,” Jeffrey Berenbaum, director of research at Citigroup Global Markets, wrote in a report earlier this month.
Still, demand for computing capacity continues to far outstrip available supply, helping underpin investor confidence in the sector.
Those dynamics could shift quickly, however, said Bob Neighoff, a portfolio manager at Mariner Investment Group.
“Right now it may look like you may have AA rated tenant demand leased out for approximately 15-30 years,” he said. “But if those go away, you’re left with the world’s biggest pickleball court.”

items.title: Dangote Refinery IPO Rush Crashes Some Nigerian Trading Apps
body: Demand for shares in Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE overwhelmed some of the many Nigerian investing apps soon after an initial public offering opened Monday.

The share sale on the Nigerian Stock Exchange in Lagos, the commercial capital, is the biggest ever in Africa. Minutes after it was officially announced, Bamboo posted on X that it was working to get its app “up and running” again. There were 40% more account openings in the past week than in all of May, which was previously the company’s best month on record, a Bamboo spokesperson told Bloomberg.

Cowrywise, which had been promoting the offer on social media, spent all morning working to restore its service after “seeing more traffic than usual”. The fintech announced on X it was back up at 1.21 p.m. in Lagos.

Pent-up demand for a stake in the refinery of Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, is testing Nigeria’s fintech infrastructure. The billionaire is opening up ownership of the company, offering shares at 40 US cents apiece, with a minimum investment of just $4. He’s courting ordinary Africans and by enlisting a wide range of platforms including fintechs, mobile-phone operators, and banks.
Read More: Dangote Courts Retail Investors With $4 Entry to Record IPO

More than 50 investment intermediaries were listed on the IPO prospectus. The company expects to raise at least $1.6 billion from the offering, which closes on Oct. 13 and values the business at nearly $50 billion. The refinery, which started commercial operations in February 2024, was built for $20 billion and processes 700,000 barrels of crude a day.

items.title: YPF Close to Signing More Argentina LNG Sales Contracts
body: Argentina’s state-run YPF SA is close to signing several liquefied natural gas sales contracts for a proposed $24 billion export plant, Chief Executive Officer Horacio Marin said Monday, a key step toward a green light for the facility.

The company will soon sign two to three 0.5 million to 1.5 million ton-per-year LNG deals, Marin said on the sidelines of the Gastech conference in Bangkok on Monday. The company aims to secure those deals before making a final investment decision on the project in November, he said.

Argentina LNG is a venture that includes Italy’s Eni SpA and Abu Dhabi’s XRG along with YPF. The three energy firms hold roughly equal equity stakes. An offshore LNG terminal on Argentina’s Atlantic coast, it would produce 12 million tons a year, making it one of the biggest floating facilities in the world.

Even as the partners schedule the investment decision for November, a financing deal to fund a big chunk of the $24 billion — an unprecedented sum for a single project in Argentina — might not be sealed in time. When asked if it’d be likely for a consortium of lenders to have fully committed to putting down the money before the November announcement, Marin said: “No. But there will be letters of intent that they will finish the process.”

The potential sales contracts come as the global LNG market is in upheaval after months of disruption in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, effectively choking off about a fifth of global supply of the super-chilled fuel. LNG buyers in Asia and elsewhere are looking to diversify away from the Middle East as a result, seeking to reduce future risk.

items.title: ECB's Schnabel Says Energy-Price Trends 'Quite Concerning'
body: European Central Bank Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel said recent energy-price developments have been “quite concerning” as officials weigh further interest-rate hikes following last week’s increase.
“Its not just oil, but also diesel,” the German official said Monday in Berlin. “Refining capacities have reduced drastically and can’t be rebuilt quickly.”

Speaking at a conference with German Economy minister Katherina Reiche, Schnabel also highlighted gas prices as a reason to worry. “There is an issue of low storages in Europe and of competition with Asia for LNG supplies,” she said.

The ECB last week raised borrowing costs for a second time since the Iran war sent energy prices soaring and warned that risks to inflation are tilted to the upside, with the potential for the energy shock to intensify further and affect prices and wages more than currently expected.

Natural gas prices, in particular, could increase if there are further supply disruptions or an unusually cold winter coinciding with low storage levels, it warned. In Europe, costs have already nearly tripled so far this year and the bloc is running out of time to rebuild its abnormally low inventories before winter.

While the ECB remains data-dependent and isn’t pre-committing, ECB officials expect rates to rise further, people familiar with their thinking told Bloomberg last week. The December meeting is seen as the most likely date for a third quarter-point increase, though October isn’t excluded.
Schnabel called last week’s step a “kind of a logical response to the expected deviation of inflation from our target over the medium term in the absence of appropriate monetary-policy action.”

“Whether that is enough, we need to see,” she said, pointing to the ECB’s meeting-by-meeting approach and a focus on core inflation as well as non-energy goods and services. “The next decisions are going to be taken on the basis on incoming data.”

items.title: Warsh and the Fed Need Clarity More Than Certainty
body: Kevin Warsh has rightly called into question the effectiveness of the Federal Reserve’s communications — but his arrival as chairman only seems to have made the problem worse. To put this right after the next Fed meeting this week, he’ll need to rethink his approach to explaining where things stand.

Friday’s release of inflation data for August hasn’t helped. Consumer prices rose 3.4% year over year; excluding food and energy, 2.4%. This was worse than forecasters had expected, and it gave little reason to think inflation is still on track toward the central bank’s 2% target. Investors promptly priced in a 90% chance that the Fed will raise its policy rate on Wednesday.

This shift in sentiment, together with the disappointing inflation numbers, might be enough to force the Fed’s hand. On balance, a quarter-point rise in the federal funds rate would be wise. The fact remains, the right decision is by no means clear-cut.
For a start, policy changes should never turn on one month’s noisy data. More important, the outlook is still extremely uncertain.

Recent events have delivered an extraordinary series of shocks to the US economy. Energy prices have surged because of the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, and Washington’s unprecedented use of threatened and actual tariffs has helped raise prices across the board. At the same time, a remarkable surge of investment in AI data centers has generated additional aggregate demand. With all this in play, it’s hardly surprising that above-target inflation has proved so persistent.

Yet what this implies for monetary policy is debatable. The supply shocks could prove to be short-lived; if so, tighter policy (which takes time to reduce demand) would be a mistake. And in due course the AI revolution should boost productivity, in which case inflation will subside without higher rates. At the moment, wages aren’t rising immoderately, and longer-term inflation expectations remain well-anchored, which is reassuring. But inflation has been well above target for five years, which isn’t.
What’s the Fed to do? Hike because the balance of risks is shifting toward entrenched excess inflation, or wait a while longer for more data? Reasonable people can — and should — disagree.

At the July policy meeting, officials voted 9-3 to hold the federal funds rate at 3.5% to 3.75% — an eminently defensible decision. To some observers, though, this division was a bad sign: If the Fed’s policymakers disagree, something is wrong. In truth, when the outlook is highly uncertain, honest disagreement is desirable.

Clarity about how officials are reading the data is essential. Failing to explain his own thinking was where Warsh went wrong in July — a mistake he mustn’t repeat. But clarity can’t dispel the uncertainty. Many investors, analysts and commentators seek certainty in monetary policy when none is possible. Failing to acknowledge what’s unknown delivers less clarity and more confusion. When policymakers blur their true positions to project greater unity, they exaggerate the Fed’s collective confidence that it’s getting the policy right. Better to agree to differ, vote according to their best judgment and let the majority decide.

This week’s interest rate decision is another close call, and it helps nobody to pretend otherwise. As more data arrives, views will continue to shift. In the meantime, what counts is that the Fed’s officials keep an open mind and are honest with themselves and the public about their reasoning.

items.title: US expected to rescind greenhouse gas rules for fossil fuel power plants
body: The EPA is expected to deliver another crucial revision to US climate standards, removing rules covering pollution from fossil fuel-fired power plants. Today’s edition looks at the anticipated changes, which follow an earlier loosening of rules for vehicle emissions.

In the UK, retailers say sales struggled in blistering summer temperatures and are warning that heat waves are changing shoppers’ behavior — putting even the nation’s cherished hot cup of tea at risk.
And we take you to the Dutch village that’s under threat from Europe’s energy transition.Subscribe to Bloomberg.com for unlimited access to all our coverage.
By Zahra Hirji, Ari Natter, and Jennifer A Dlouhy
The US Environmental Protection Agency is expected to formally rescind carbon pollution standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants as soon as Monday, according to people familiar with the matter.

The Trump administration’s latest major climate rollback is expected to come on the sidelines of a Group of 20 energy ministers’ meeting in Houston, said the people, who asked not to be named because the details aren’t yet public. Earlier this year, the EPA rescinded similar climate standards for vehicles and the 2009 endangerment finding, a landmark ruling which held that greenhouse gases threaten human health.

Under Trump, the EPA first proposed rolling back the power-plant climate rules last summer. This week, the agency is finalizing a piece of the initial proposal — scrapping Biden-era mandates requiring existing and future US fossil fuel-fired power plants to deploy specific emissions-reduction technologies, including carbon capture and storage, to sharply cut their greenhouse gas emissions in the coming decades, according to the people.

Agency officials also plan to propose a separate rule repealing the federal finding that greenhouse gases from power plants specifically pose a threat, effectively a separate endangerment finding for power plants under the Clean Air Act.

Power plants are the US’s largest industrial source of greenhouse gas emissions. If the US power sector were a country by itself, it would rank as the world’s sixth-largest emitter of greenhouse gases, according to a New York University School of Law’s Institute for Policy Integrity analysis of 2022 emissions data.
The EPA didn’t respond to requests for comment outside business hours Sunday.
By Olivia Rudgard and Maddie Parker
Britain’s obsession with a nice cup of tea is famous around the world. But as the climate changes, that love affair is wilting in the heat.

A scorching summer dampened demand for tea, according to Associated British Foods Plc, the owner of tea brand Twinings and malt-drink brand Ovaltine. Hot beverages fell out of favor with customers as temperatures rose as high as 38C (100.4F).

This summer has been a record-breaker. It was western Europe’s hottest summer on record, with heat waves in many countries that began early and persisted from May to August. Spain endured 61 days of heat-wave conditions, Germany’s temperature hit a new all-time high and the UK had an unprecedented 40 days of temperatures over 30C.British retail sales struggled in blistering temperatures. Even England’s consumer-confidence-boosting progression to the World Cup semi-final couldn’t balance out shoppers’ unwillingness to brave the high street.

Heat is becoming a bigger consideration for British retailers, says Steve Fergus, national head of retail and wholesale at Barclays UK’s corporate bank, with growing evidence that shoppers’ behavior changes as the temperature rises into increasingly uncomfortable territory. “Adapting to hotter conditions is becoming a commercial as well as an operational priority,” he says.

Climber Alex Honnold is best known as the star of Free Solo, an Oscar-winning documentary that followed his rope-free ascent of the 3,000-foot (1,000-meter) face of Yosemite’s El Capitan. But he has also established the Honnold Foundation to bring solar power to those who most need it. This week on Zero, Bloomberg’s Akshat Rathi asks Honnold how he gets big things done and why helping communities get clean energy has become his other passion in life.

items.title: Home Insurance: We're Making a $3 Trillion Financial Hole Even Deeper
body: The first law of holes states that if you find yourself in one, stop digging. The US is in a $3 trillion home-insurance hole, but instead of putting down its shovels, it’s handing out shiny new ones that will help us dig even deeper.

Never in recorded human history has the planet been hotter, and that extra atmospheric energy is turbo-boosting natural disasters, which are inflating home-insurance premiums and pushing an increasing number of people out of standard policies altogether. State-managed insurers of last resort are expensive and limit their coverage.

The result is a large and widening gap between the amount of insurance coverage the US housing market enjoys and the amount of climate damage it could theoretically suffer. That gap has been estimated at $2.7 trillion, which is almost certainly too conservative because it’s based only on potential flood and wildfire losses.

Meanwhile, the last refuge for people seeking insurance is increasingly the market for “non-admitted” insurance lines, also known as “surplus” lines. This once-obscure product has long served niche needs, such as covering commercial real estate or risky-but-hard-to-price assets like Patrick Mahomes’ knees. Increasingly, it’s covering Grandma’s condo. This may not be such a great deal for Grandma.

That “non-admitted” moniker is the big clue. It refers to the fact that these lines don’t have the same regulatory constraints or backstops as standard policies. Typically, no government arbiter approves their premiums, which tend to be higher than standard ones. They tend to rely heavily on reinsurance, giving your insurance company’s insurance company a bigger role in setting the premiums, for better or worse. Their customer protections aren’t as protective. They often run light on capital, meaning a significant disaster could leave them without the cash to pay you. And if they do go under financially, they’re part of no rescue fund that would step in to pay your claims.
For certain uses, all of that may be fine. But for the purpose of insuring your house, it’s problematic.

And as soaring premiums and insurer abandonment push more and more homeowners out of the normal insurance market, these surplus lines are being used for just that purpose. The market is reaching far beyond its traditionally well-off customers and even starting to affect affordable-housing developers, according to a new report by the Climate Cabinet, a nonprofit advocacy group.

“This is exacerbating the already bad affordable-housing shortage in this country,” Jordan Haedtler, a former House Financial Services Committee staff member and climate finance strategist who co-wrote the report, told me. “Any policymakers looking to resolve their affordable housing shortage should strengthen oversight over surplus lines at the same time.”

The number of these policies written for homeowners more than doubled between 2020 and 2024, according to data from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners. Premiums for surplus lines to homeowners jumped 29.5% in 2025 to $4.14 billion, according to S&P Global, even as commercial premiums dipped.

That is still a relative pittance compared with the roughly $190 billion home-insurance market, just as a $2.7 trillion coverage hole pales compared with a $55 trillion housing market. But the rapid growth rates of both surplus lines and the coverage shortage are accelerating.

Insurance companies are no longer just shrinking traditional coverage in famously climate-unfriendly states such as California and Florida. The increasing destructiveness of plain old thunderstorms and the spread of wildfires mean the new faces of the home-insurance crisis are in places like Utah, which recently became the top US state for home policy nonrenewals.

In the Beehive State, along with Arizona and Nevada, there’s also no state-backed insurer of last resort. That means homeowners who lose coverage there have no alternative but to buy riskier surplus insurance. Meanwhile, states like Florida are trying to shrink their last-resort insurers, with surplus lines picking up much of the slack. And the Trump administration’s goal of kicking people off of the National Flood Insurance Program will send even more homeowners to surplus carriers.

What this adds up to is a growing population of homeowners at risk of finding out the hard way that their expensive policies won’t pay for their new roof, wildfire damage or flooded basement. The $2.7 trillion hole gets even deeper.

The answer is to make these niche insurance products more like their better-regulated cousins, and the Climate Cabinet report offers several suggestions. The first step would be to shine a light on this opaque market, giving regulators and homeowners publicly available data about its size and risks, information that is now hard to find. California and Florida, where surplus lines have been insuring houses for a long time, collect and publish these numbers. That should be the norm, not the exception.

Surplus insurers should also meet some basic capital requirements and submit to regular financial exams. They shouldn’t be able to hide their finances inside a nest of related companies. Their customers should get basic protections, including a requirement that they exhaust every possible avenue looking for regular insurance before turning to less-regulated products. States like Louisiana, Virginia, Mississippi and Wisconsin, which have recently done away with such due-diligence requirements altogether, need to think again.

Finally, they should pay into emergency pools that cover homeowners when individual carriers go bust. And they should contribute to mitigation funds that can help make disasters less expensive in the first place. It’s time these insurers helped fill the home-insurance hole instead of making it bigger.

items.title: US Miner Signs Rwanda Tungsten Deal to Grow Western Supply
body: An American miner is partnering with Rwanda’s government to source and process tungsten from the African nation, extending a push to build a Western-aligned supply chain for the strategic metal that reduces reliance on China.

Rwanda will take a 25% stake in a local unit of Almonty Industries Inc. by contributing an exploration concession and a processing license, according to a binding agreement disclosed Monday. The Dillon, Montana-based company will maintain the balance of the ownership.

The deal underscores growing efforts by the US and its allies to secure supplies of critical minerals outside China, which dominates global tungsten production and processing. Chinese export curbs and rising military demand in recent years have squeezed the market for a metal that’s used in armor-piercing weaponry and semiconductors.

The US government helped structure the Rwanda partnership and provided political support, but isn’t putting up funding, Almonty Chief Executive Officer Lewis Black said in an interview. Tungsten will be shipped to customers in the US, Europe, Japan and South Korea, he said.

Rather than waiting years for a new mine to be developed, the partnership plans to begin acquiring ore, pre-concentrate and panning tailings from existing licensed Rwandan producers, including small-scale miners. That material can initially be sold, upgraded or exported while the partners work toward building a permanent collection and processing facility in Rwanda.

The venture also plans to deploy a mobile processing unit near existing tailings dams and explore the roughly 32-square-kilometer (12-square-mile) Shyorongi concession. The structure is intended to give Almonty access to near-term tungsten supply while simultaneously developing a larger domestic processing and production base. It’s seen as a blueprint for other countries where small-scale tungsten mining is practiced, Black said.

Still, tapping Rwanda’s existing mining industry presents challenges, including ensuring material from a fragmented small-scale sector meets Western standards on labor, environmental practices and traceability. Rwanda has faced longstanding allegations that tungsten smuggled from neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo and Burundi is laundered through its supply chain and exported as Rwandan.
Read More: Munitions Metal Tungsten Eclipses Gold, Copper in 557% Rally

Black said the venture is both a short-term solution for the West, given how long it takes to build new mines, and a way to help formalize Rwanda’s mining industry and improve traceability. “Traders can play with the pirates,” he said. “We’re only interested in licensed domestic output.”

Rwanda is the only African nation among the world’s 10 largest tungsten producers, giving it an outsized role in Western efforts to diversify supply. Trinity Metals Ltd., which operates the large-scale Nyakabingo mine in Rwanda, said in June that more than 320 tons of high-grade concentrate had been shipped to a processing facility in Pennsylvania since an offtake agreement was struck last year, supplying as much as 20% of US primary tungsten concentrate consumption.

China accounts for the vast majority of global mine production and has a dominant position further down the tungsten supply chain, making the metal one of several commodities that Washington has identified as vulnerable to supply disruptions.

At almost $3,000 a metric ton unit, tungsten prices are up more than eightfold since Beijing added certain products to its export control list in February 2025. Gains accelerated earlier this year as buyers exhausted stockpiles and Middle East conflict sharpened focus on military demand, before stabilizing in recent months.

High prices alone won’t be enough to resolve the squeeze, with projects facing constraints in financing, permitting and construction, according to investment researchers The Oregon Group. That increases the importance of government support and long-term offtake agreements. In a separate announcement Monday, the Pentagon committed $450 million to Elmet Group to expand US manufacturing and support investments in tungsten mining and processing.
Read More: US Moves to Keep Tungsten Scrap, Battery Black Mass at Home

Almonty describes itself as a turnaround investor-operator specializing in conflict-free tungsten and cooperating with several governments. It is ramping up a major mine in South Korea, has established operations in Portugal and has additional projects in Spain and the US.
The Rwanda partnership aims to modernize and expand the local industry while strengthening trade and long-term mineral supply links between Rwanda and the US, according to the company.
Almonty shares slipped 1.9% at 10:30 a.m. in New York Monday, reducing a year-to-date gain to 72%.

items.title: UK's Regional Leaders to Unite on Efforts to Rejoin EU
body: Nationalist leaders in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland agreed to work together on efforts to rejoin the European Union and leave the UK, just days after Donald Trump said he supported Irish unification.

“Each of our nations has the right to determine its own future, through democratic means,” the leaders of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales said in a statement. “We call for the British Government to prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change in each jurisdiction.”
They also said Brexit has damaged their respective economies, adding that they would work together to eventually rejoin the European Union as separate nations.

“Scotland was taken out of the EU against our will and nothing that’s happened since then has done anything other than fuel the sentiment in Scotland that the sooner we can become a member of the European Union again the better,” Scottish First Minister John Swinney said at a press conference in Cardiff on Monday.
Nationalists have for the first time lead all three regions since May, when Scotland and Wales returned pro-independence first ministers, joining Sinn Fein’s Michelle O’Neill in Northern Ireland.
Read more: Nationalist Wins in UK Lift Case for Irish Unity, Sinn Fein Says

“The prime minister is committed to delivering change across all four nations of the United Kingdom,” a spokesperson for UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told reporters Monday. “He believes strongly in the union. The United Kingdom is at its best when people come together around shared values and problem solving, rather than division.”

The meeting also takes place days after US President Donald Trump made an unprecedented wade into the debate on the union, saying he would “love” to see unity between the Republic of Ireland and the UK region, Northern Ireland.
It’s a remark that puts him at odds with Burnham who recently said the issue is off the table, something he reiterated in the wake of Trump’s comments.

A referendum on Irish reunification can only be called by the UK Secretary of State when they believe a majority of people in Northern Ireland would favor it, as set out in the Good Friday Agreement that ended decades of conflict in the region.

Trump’s comment “reflects the fact that unity debate is alive,” O’Neill said in Cardiff. “The message that we want Number 10, Downing Street to hear is that now is the time to do the preparation and to plan, and facilitate the arrangement for all of us in our respective ways.”
Read more: Scotland Leader Pushes Independence Vote After Burnham Remarks
While support for Irish unification is growing in Northern Ireland, recent polling suggests there is still no clear majority in favor.

In Scotland, Swinney is seeking to revive the Scottish National Party’s push for independence. Last week, he wrote to Burnham seeking talks on Scotland’s constitutional future and a potential legal mechanism for another vote.
The leaders jointly agreed to share ideas on how to grow their economies and expand their own energy resources.

items.title: Dangote to Start New Refinery in Kenya This Month as IPO Opens
body: Africa’s biggest oil-refining business will start work on a second facility on Kenya’s coast at the end of the month, with the complex set to be ready in three years.

Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, made the announcement about the planned processing plant at Lamu during the opening of the initial public offering — the continent’s largest — for his energy business in Lagos, Nigeria’s commercial capital.
Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals Fze also plans a 2,650-kilometer (1,646-mile) pipeline that will run from Namibia through Botswana and to South Africa, he said.
“We are also taking up another line, which will now go to Zimbabwe,” Dangote said, adding that work on this will start next month.

Dangote is expected to raise about $1.6 billion from the IPO that will value the business at almost $50 billion. It’s part of plans for an Africa-wide empire that will double capacity of his Nigerian refinery to create one of the world’s biggest and build the processing plant in Kenya to extend his reach from the Atlantic to Indian Oceans.
