items.title: Expats Set to Tip Tightest Swedish Electoral Race in Century
body: Welcome to Balance of Power, bringing you the latest in global politics. If you haven’t yet, sign up here.
If Europe was looking to Swedish exceptionalism to provide answers on the direction of travel of the far right, it will walk away sorely disappointed.
It’s a mess, just like everywhere else.
At a time when global politics, economies and — if the titans of AI are to be believed — even the future of humanity are under assault, Sweden may seem a haven of sorts, wealthy and predictable.

But yesterday’s election was meant to settle the big question of whether the center-left, here in the form of the once-ubiquitous Social Democrats, could offer like-minded parties in Europe and perhaps even Democrats in the US a new model to vanquish the populist threat.
That, or whether liberal democracies need to hold their collective nose and accept that a party with neo-Nazi roots has a right to govern if voters wish it.
The answer is an unsatisfying “who knows?” in a race too close to call, and one that will be settled by a fistful of votes.
Bizarrely, Peru, where vote counting dragged on for weeks, offers one clue.
There the outcome was settled by the diaspora. And it might be Swedish expats, and their yet-uncounted votes cast in ballot boxes in Ikea, that tip the scales.

Politics in the home country of the Nobel Prize, Volvo and H&M went from being dominated by one party that created an enviable model for progressive taxation and generous welfare to being turned inside out by an insurgent force, the Sweden Democrats. It rode anti-immigration sentiment to become the second-biggest party.
Both were humbled in the most tightly contested election in more than a century.
The Social Democrats had their poorest showing in more than 100 years. The Sweden Democrats dropped to third place as they, too, hit a wall.
Voter frustration, political fragmentation and complicated coalition talks are getting worse. None of which bodes well for elections in France, Spain and Italy looming in 2027.

Anthropic and OpenAI will have to weigh their calls to tap the brakes on artificial-intelligence development against forces in the tech industry, financial markets and the Trump administration that are likely to resist a deceleration. A 3,800-word missive Saturday by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei — endorsed by Sam Altman of OpenAI and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk — said development of the most advanced systems must be slowed to prevent AI slipping beyond human control and inflicting catastrophic harm.

French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said the government will aim to find savings of about €30 billion ($35 billion) in next year’s budget in a bid to rein in the deficit. The curbs will come mostly on government spending so as not to hurt consumer purchasing power or raise taxes, he said in an interview published in Le Parisien’s Sunday edition.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s first sit-down on Indian soil in seven years signaled a will to further repair ties and manage an unpredictable Donald Trump, but fundamental differences remain despite the good vibes flowing from the 10-nation BRICS summit in New Delhi. The bilateral meeting was a symbolic moment for the world’s two most populous nations, which are emerging from a multi-decade low point in relations fueled by bloody border clashes and deep strategic distrust.

The locomotive of a passenger train traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw was hit by a Russian drone near the Polish border, Ukraine said, minutes after another train carrying former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt and UK ex-Prime Minister Boris Johnson left the station. Trump meanwhile said he’d warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries amid strikes that have shut down diesel refining and helped drive prices to a record.

A planned meeting between Iran and several Gulf nations today on creating a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz has been postponed “in the interests of consensus,” Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, said in an X post, without offering details on next steps. Iran said the meeting of foreign ministers was postponed at the request of regional countries, according to the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency.

A candidate backed by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s ruling party ousted the incumbent governor of Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture in an election yesterday, delivering a boost to the premier’s push for a stronger military to stave off threats from China.

Malaysian authorities charged former minister Jamil Khir Baharom for allegedly misappropriating 860 million ringgit ($210 million) from the Muslim pilgrimage fund Tabung Haji, making him the second United Malays National Organisation leader to be charged over the fund in as many weeks.

Australia’s far-right One Nation party is proposing to cut the number of temporary migrants by about 750,000 over three years, aiming to capitalize on discontent over cost-of-living pressures and a housing squeeze.

UK Housing Secretary Angela Rayner suggested that planned legislation might affect record donations totalling £72 million ($97 million) to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, sums that far outstrip funding raised by the ruling Labour and main opposition Conservative parties so far this year.
Sign up for the Washington Edition newsletter for news from the US capital and watch Balance of Power at 1 and 5 p.m. ET weekdays on Bloomberg Television.

The number of Britons aged 65 and over in work topped 1.7 million earlier this year as longer life expectancy and better health delay retirement, while cost-of-living pressures have also convinced people from the baby-boomer generation to stay on the payroll a little longer. Employment rates for the group — many of whom are beyond state pension age — are at a record high. But that has ramifications for those at the other end of the scale: In the early 2000s, Britain had as many as 10 young workers for every person over-65 with a job; today there are just two.

Swiss billionaire Christoph Blocher, who founded an anti-immigrant, nationalist political party, is campaigning for a constitutional change to eliminate flexibility in how Switzerland applies its neutrality, with a vote set to take place on Sept. 27. The government opposes the move, saying it supports staying neutral but wants some flexibility, with the action seen as a head-to-head between two competing visions for Switzerland’s role in international relations.

items.title: Catania Airport Suspends Flights Due to Volcanic Activity
body: Italy’s Catania Airport has extended a flight suspension caused by volcanic activity from nearby Mount Etna, after an eruption last month led to major disruptions at Sicily’s busiest airline hub.
In an updated statement, the airport said it suspended arrivals and departures until 10 p.m. local time on Monday. An earlier halt to arrivals was due to expire at 4 p.m.
Ashes from Etna released at high altitude caused the airspace closure, operator Società Aeroporto Catania said in a statement on its website.
Hundreds of flights were cancelled or rerouted last month during Italy’s peak travel season as Europe’s most active volcano began its latest flare-up.
Catania is Sicily’s busiest airport by number of passengers, and the fifth busiest in Italy.

items.title: Thailand Election Commission Refers Senate-Rigging Cases to Court
body: Thailand’s Election Commission will send dozens of alleged Senate vote-rigging cases to the Supreme Court, while clearing cabinet ministers and members of Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul’s ruling Bhumjaithai Party.

The seven-member commission voted to pursue legal action against 77 people for alleged wrongdoing during the 2024 election of Thailand’s 200-member Senate, Chairman Narong Klunwarin said Monday. They include 26 sitting senators, and 36 candidates who voted in the Senate election.
None of those accused in the case includes ministers, political party executives or other administration officials.
At the center of the controversy is Thailand’s complex Senate selection system, in which the approved candidates vote among themselves.

Critics and some unidentified witnesses had alleged that votes in 2024 were coordinated and guided to elect a predetermined slate of candidates aligned with Anutin’s conservative Bhumjaithai Party. Investigators focused on allegations that candidates were recruited, instructed to vote in a coordinated manner, or received monetary compensation.

So many of the successful candidates had links to Anutin, the party or Newin Chidchob, the party’s power broker, that the upper chamber was given the nickname “Blue Senate” in a nod to the party’s color.

More than 400 people were involved in an initial joint probe conducted by election officials and the Department of Special Investigation of the Thai police, Narong said Friday. Anutin, 12 of his ministers and 138 senators were among those investigated, according to legal watchdog iLaw. A separate review panel set up by the commission, however, later voted to recommend dropping the cases, citing insufficient evidence.

Some witnesses implicated Newin, his son Chaichanok Chidchob, the Bhumjaithai Party’s secretary-general, and two ministers in the Prime Minister’s Office in organizing meetings among candidates, coordinating their votes and making payments, Narong said. All denied the allegations, and the commission decided not to pursue action against them because there was insufficient evidence to corroborate the witnesses’ claims, he said.
A presentation at the briefing showed that witnesses had implicated 21 Bhumjaithai-linked politicians, including the party leader, though it did not name Anutin directly.
Anutin has also denied any involvement.

“From a political viewpoint, the few at the bottom are being sacrificed to save those at the top,” said Purawich Watanasukh, a political science lecturer at Thammasat University. “The issue has now been framed as a matter of individual wrongdoing rather than mass coordination.”

The Senate is a key political force in Thailand, with control over appointments to independent institutions that often determine the fate of politicians and parties, including approving judges for the Constitutional Court.
As well, four of the Election Commission’s current seven members were appointed by the Senate it’s investigating.
For Anutin, the episode risks adding further political pressure after a period of relative stability following his election in February.

Veteran protest leader Sondhi Limthongkul, whose mass demonstrations helped oust the government two decades ago, is now mobilizing supporters against Anutin’s administration over alleged corruption, political interference and its handling of foreign criminal networks.

Anutin also faces another legal test Sept. 28, when the Constitutional Court will rule on whether the use of barcodes and QR codes on ballots in February’s general election had violated the constitution, which could jeopardize the validity of his victory.
The Election Commission will submit the cases to the Supreme Court within 60 days. If the court accepts them for consideration, sitting senators could be suspended from their duties pending a ruling.

items.title: Lula and Bolsonaro in Dead Heat Ahead of Brazil Vote, Polls Show
body: Leia em português
Lea en español

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and conservative challenger Flávio Bolsonaro appeared statistically tied in a pair of new polls ahead of Brazil’s election, as a crisis inside the country’s Supreme Court clouds the October vote.

Lula would lead a runoff 47%-46%, according to a BTG/Nexus survey published Monday, after gaining 2 points from the previous poll. The movement was within the survey’s 2-point margin of error, leaving the race in a statistical dead heat.

A Quaest poll published later Monday found Bolsonaro ahead of Lula 42% to 40%, a slight change from last week, when they were even at 41% in a runoff scenario. His lead is within the poll’s 2 percentage point margin of error, keeping the race virtually tied.

A fresh series of revelations suggesting ties between Daniel Vorcaro, the jailed owner of Banco Master SA, and Supreme Court justices has jolted the race just weeks before the Oct. 4 first-round vote.

In response, the court’s president has unsealed investigations into Vorcaro. They indicate that federal police are probing Bolsonaro over allegations of money laundering, corruption and tax crimes after he approached the banker for funding for a film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flávio Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing.

The crisis also carries risk for Lula. The leftist leader is perceived as a close ally of Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who is also facing scrutiny over alleged ties to Vorcaro. A slowing economy and corruption allegations against one of his son’s have also weighed on Lula’s reelection bid in recent weeks. Lula’s son has denied wrongdoing.
Read More: Bolsonaro Urges Transparency as Court Probes Ties to Banker
A separate Datafolha survey released Friday showed the contest neck and neck, with Lula holding a slight numerical advantage.
BTG/Nexus interviewed 2,003 people on Sept. 11-13. Quaest surveyed 2,004 people on Sept. 10-13.

items.title: Dollarization: What Adopting the US Dollar Would Mean for Venezuela
body: Lea en español
As Venezuela seeks stability after years of inflation and turmoil, proposals to formally dollarize the economy have moved into the political mainstream.
Opposition lawmaker Antonio Ecarri is working with US economist Steve Hanke on legislation to formally adopt the dollar as Venezuela’s currency.

Dollars are already widely used informally, but making them the official currency would be a far more consequential step. More than half of Venezuelans support the idea, according to an AtlasIntel survey for Bloomberg News conducted in May.
Here’s what it would mean, how it could work, and what lessons Venezuela can draw from countries that have tried it before.

Official dollarization would mean adopting the US dollar as Venezuela’s official currency, replacing the bolivar not just in everyday transactions but across the financial system. Bolivar-denominated cash, deposits, debts, contracts and wages would have to be converted into dollars at an official exchange rate.

Venezuela has been a partially dollarized economy since hyperinflation drove businesses and households toward the US currency around 2019. Greenbacks are widely used for pricing and savings, but public finances are denominated in bolivars and the central bank continues to issue the currency.

Ecarri plans to bring his legislative proposal before the National Assembly. But the assembly’s President Jorge Rodríguez already rejected the idea, citing a constitutional provision that establishes the bolivar as Venezuela’s monetary unit and gives the central bank authority over monetary policy. Other Venezuelan authorities have also publicly defended the bolivar in recent weeks.

Prospects for dollarization may ultimately depend on the US position. The US government has taken an aggressive role in steering acting President Delcy Rodríguez’s government since seizing longtime President Nicolás Maduro in January, including by asserting oversight over some of its oil revenue and spending. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has advocated a greater role for the dollar in Venezuela, saying in a June interview that “Venezuela is going to be invoicing in dollars” and that the US currency would be “the centerpiece of their trade.” The administration, however, has not publicly announced plans to fully dollarize Venezuela or replace the bolivar as legal tender.

Decades of high inflation — including hyperinflation between late 2017 and early 2021 — eroded confidence in the bolivar, as did restrictions on freely buying and selling foreign currencies. Supporters argue that official dollarization would boost confidence in Venezuela’s monetary system by reducing exposure to inflation and the risk of a decline in the bolivar’s value against the dollar.

In addition, dollarization would increase confidence by preventing governments from financing deficits through money creation, Pedro Palma, an emeritus economics professor at the Institute of Advanced Administrative Studies, said during a webcast.
Supporters of formal dollarization argue that adopting the dollar officially would also eliminate frictions created by the coexistence of two currencies.

The recent oil agreement between Venezuela’s interim authorities and the US is set to restore the US as a major buyer of Venezuelan crude. Greater trade with the US would strengthen the rationale for Venezuela to adopt the currency of its main trading partner, said Francisco Rodríguez, a Venezuelan economist and professor of international affairs at the University of Denver, who nevertheless remains critical of the oil deal.

Venezuela would surrender control over monetary policy and its exchange rate, limiting its ability to respond to recessions, banking crises or external shocks. The economy would instead have to absorb those shocks through lower wages, higher unemployment or fiscal tightening. The availability of dollars in the economy would depend more heavily on dollars from exports, investment, remittances or external borrowing — a potential constraint if access to international financing remains limited.

Dollarization would also neither guarantee fiscal discipline nor solve Venezuela’s broader structural problems. Governments can still run large deficits, accumulate unsustainable debt and default without control of their currency, economist Omar Zambrano has argued. And while the dollar could help stabilize prices, it would not by itself boost oil production, restore credit markets or attract investment.
Critics say Venezuela has already captured many of the benefits of dollarization without fully giving up control over monetary policy.

Implementation would require converting bolivars into dollars at a uniform exchange rate and determining how deposits, loans, wages and government obligations are treated. The conversion rate would be crucial: setting it too strong could leave the economy overvalued or short of dollars, while setting it too weak could erode the value of wages, savings and other bolivar-denominated assets.

Another key question is how many dollars Venezuela would need, which depends on what authorities commit to convert. Rodríguez argues that the monetary base, estimated at about $2.5 billion, is small enough to be covered with existing reserves. But Gustavo García, a former Inter-American Development Bank economist, said that full dollarization would require enough dollars to cover broader financial liabilities, including bank deposits, making implementation much more demanding.

The Venezuelan Academy of Economic Sciences also lists among the economic and institutional conditions for successful dollarization the need to amend or repeal the legal and constitutional framework governing legal tender.
The central bank would be deeply constrained. It would no longer issue bolivars, set independent monetary policy or manage the exchange rate in the traditional sense.

Still, the institution could continue to manage reserves, supervise banks, monitor financial risks and provide limited liquidity support. But without the ability to print money, its lender-of-last-resort role would be much weaker, making access to emergency dollars — through arrangements with the US Federal Reserve or a reserve pool shared with other countries or international banking institutions — especially important.
Countries that have dollarized, including Ecuador and El Salvador, have retained central banks, though with far narrower responsibilities than those of countries that issue their own currencies.

Ecuador, which dollarized in 2000 after a banking and currency crisis, shows that dollarization can stabilize an economy and prove politically durable. But it didn’t guarantee fiscal discipline. Zambrano has pointed to later fiscal problems in Ecuador as evidence that stronger fiscal rules and institutions are still needed.

El Salvador also shows that adopting the dollar does not automatically strengthen domestic industry. While dollarization helped lower interest rates and consolidate already-low inflation, it was followed by years of sluggish growth and weak export performance amid low investment and competitiveness pressures.

Peru and Brazil show that countries can defeat hyperinflation and restore stability without abandoning their currencies. Both initially relied on broader stabilization programs, then adopted inflation targeting and strengthened monetary and fiscal institutions to help preserve price stability.
Chile and Colombia followed similar paths toward independent central banks, inflation targeting and more flexible exchange rates, emerging from bouts of instability without ditching their currencies.

The transition can also carry steep political costs: Ecuador’s president was ousted amid broader economic unrest less than two weeks after announcing dollarization in 2000, while its introduction in El Salvador the following year triggered protests and complaints that converting prices into dollars was raising everyday costs.

items.title: Iran-Gulf Talks Delayed as Saudi Counters Houthi Attacks
body: A meeting between Iran and several Gulf Arab nations over a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz was postponed, highlighting tensions with the Islamic Republic.

Talks were set to take place in Oman on Monday but was delayed “for now” after a request from Saudi Arabia, according to Iran’s foreign ministry. That was partly down to the kingdom’s frustration over continued attacks on its territory by Iran-supported groups such as the Houthis, said one person familiar with the matter, asking not to be identified by name discussing sensitive matters.
“Saudi Arabia’s request to postpone the regional summit and attribute it to developments in Yemen is a diversion from the root causes of this crisis,” Iran’s foreign ministry said Monday.
The Saudi government didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Brent crude prices have topped $108 a barrel in recent days due to fears that a prolonged war in the Middle East will further constrain supplies of fuel such as diesel.

On Monday, President Donald Trump appeared to suggest the US was open to new talks aimed at ending the broader war, saying in a social media post that “Iran wants to make a deal, quickly and badly,” a claim he has made repeatedly since the war began without offering evidence. Trump added that he “will determine whether or not the U.S.A. will choose to engage” and suggested the US was “open” to the idea.

Badr Albusaidi, the foreign minister of Oman, which has been negotiating with Iran for weeks over the management of maritime traffic through the strait, said late Sunday the decision to postpone the regional Gulf talks was taken “in the interests of consensus.”
The meeting would have been the first between Iran, members of the Gulf Cooperation Council and Iraq since the US and Israel started the war with the Islamic Republic in February.
Yet, the escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia-backed forces and the Houthis, a group based in neighboring Yemen, complicated the plans.

The kingdom’s energy infrastructure towns in the south west have come under heavy attack from the Houthis this month. In addition, Saudi Arabia’s key East-West oil pipeline was shut last week after multiple drone attacks from Iraq, according to the government. Several Iran-backed militias operate in Iraq.

Yemen’s Houthis said they targeted a Saudi airbase in Khamis Mushait on Monday, according to statement. Riyadh, which earlier issued an alert for potential danger in the south-western city, has not confirmed any targets.
In the days ahead of the planned meeting, it wasn’t clear which nations would attend. Bahrain had ruled out participating, citing recent Iranian-backed attacks on Gulf sites.

Gulf states were targeted by thousands of missile and drone attacks in Iran’s retaliation against US interests in the region. Despite their anger, they have kept diplomatic channels with Tehran open and one of their main aims is to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, through which they normally ship the bulk of their oil and natural gas exports.

The meeting in Salalah would have seen participants discuss a proposal from Oman and Iran. Broadly, that deal would give Iran the right to determine which ships can enter the Persian Gulf and possibly charge them fees of some kind.

While the GCC bloc — a group of six including the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, as well as Saudi Arabia and Oman — have said they want free passage for vessels, they may accept a temporary deal that would fall short of that but still see shipping traffic pick up.

Tehran had indicated any deal wouldn’t amount to a full reopening and it would still decide on which ships could cross the strait. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had described the proposed meeting as an “important event” and a step toward building trust.

Soaring prices at the pumps pose a problem for Trump’s Republican Party with just over 50 days to go before midterm elections. On Monday, Trump said in a post that Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking Russian energy facilities, and that Moscow had agreed to do the same, causing elevated diesel futures to pare gains — though there was no public confirmation from either country.
Read more: Trump Says Ukraine, Russia Agree Not to Hit Energy Targets
Asked earlier Sunday about a possible meeting of Gulf nations with Iran, Trump told reporters, “I don’t care. That’s up to them. That’s fine.”

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright had also downplayed the chances of a Hormuz deal during an interview Sunday. He said markets will need to continue relying on transit that he estimates is supplying 10 million barrels a day of crude and oil products through the Strait of Hormuz.

Together with bypass pipelines, that means “we’re back to two-thirds or north of two-thirds of the previous flows,” Wright said. “So the world oil markets are tighter than we’d like today, but they’re not overly tight.”
Read More: US Energy Chief Downplays Chance of Hormuz Advance With Iran

The US and Iran exchanged strikes on oil tankers in the Persian Gulf earlier this month. Tensions flared again in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, with UK Maritime Trade Operations saying Sunday a fire broke out on a ship hit by a projectile the day before.
Iran’s state-run IRIB reported an “enemy strike” on a commercial vessel off Iran’s Qeshm and Hengam islands that killed one person.

items.title: OpenAI's Brockman Says an AI Pause Should Focus on Frontier
body: Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president and co-founder, argued that any slowdown in artificial intelligence development should be limited to companies like his that are building the most powerful models.

“A lot of people have this reaction of saying, ‘Well, am I going to be able to keep making my open source model? Am I going to be able to keep doing my hobby aside project?’ And the answer should be absolutely yes,” Brockman said on Bloomberg’s Odd Lots podcast. “When we’re talking about pacing, we’re really talking about this frontier. We’re talking about these massive supercomputers that are hundreds of billions of dollars worth of capital expenditure.”

Brockman spoke in an interview before Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei’s Saturday blog post on the escalating risks of AI, where he pledged to slow the pace of advanced models. OpenAI chief Sam Altman swiftly endorsed Amodei’s call for independent evaluators. Altman also said in an interview over the weekend that his company wouldn’t go public this year as it addresses safety-related concerns.
Read More: Amodei, Altman, Musk Call for Slowing AI Model Development

Amodei’s post comes as the industry increasingly warns that the rapid pace of AI development could pose risks to society. The proposed curbs from the frontier AI labs sent stocks down on Monday, as investors worry that such decisions would limit corporate spending on a sector that has powered much of the market’s rally.

In the interview, Brockman noted how OpenAI had slowed down its frequency of training AI models after the recent Hugging Face hack, where OpenAI’s autonomous agents broke into another company’s servers during testing.

That case was “not a surprise” to OpenAI, according to Brockman, since those agents had not gone through the company’s “alignment training” — an industry term for protocols to ensure safety. But Brockman said the episode pushed OpenAI to improve its internal security measures. “We did a very painful retooling of a lot of our processes” in the aftermath, he said.

OpenAI and Anthropic have been criticized for calling for broader regulation and pauses in AI activity as a way to undercut competitors developing open-source alternatives. Many of these models are coming out of China, whose rapid advances in AI are an intense focus for the US administration. When asked about China, Brockman proposed the concept of global “coordination” and international treaties on the long-term development of AI.
Read More: China Rejects AI ‘Fearmongering’ After Amodei Urges Slowdown
As AI technology advances, the industry would move beyond “a commercial phase that’s really about competition,” Brockman said.
There will be a phase where the technology itself will be “so much bigger than any person, any company, even any country,” he added. “It’s really about humanity as a whole.”

items.title: China's Credit Expansion Misses Forecast as Loan Demand Sags
body: China’s credit expansion fell well short of expectations in August from a year ago, as subdued borrowing by households and businesses outweighed the support from government bond sales.

Aggregate financing, a broad measure of credit, increased 1.66 trillion yuan ($247 billion) last month, according to Bloomberg calculations based on data released by the People’s Bank of China on Monday. That compares with the median forecast of 2.1 trillion yuan by economists.

Weak bank lending was the main culprit of the slowdown. Financial institutions extended just 60 billion yuan of new yuan loans in the month, less than a sixth of the median forecast of 404 billion yuan.

Credit activity typically rebounds in August after a lull in July, as banks ramp up lending to meet their quarterly targets. That makes the latest reading particularly weak following a rare contraction in loans in the previous month.

Loan growth has slowed sharply since 2023 as households and companies have become less willing to borrow. The stock of loans to the real economy grew only 5% in August from a year ago, the slowest pace on record and down from nearly 12% three years ago.

The central bank has called on markets to stop fixating on loans to gauge its support for the economy, citing a structural transition from property to high-tech industries that has naturally reduced demand for bank lending.

Even so, the reluctance of consumers and businesses to take on debt points to weak confidence in the economic outlook. Earlier this year, borrowings held by Chinese households contracted for the first time since 1995.

“The PBOC does not appear overly concerned about the continued weakness in credit growth,” Nguyen Hoang Nam, China economist at Capital Economics, said in a note. “But growing financial pressures in China’s highly indebted corporate sector mean that the PBOC will eventually come under pressure to resume monetary easing.”

Household mid and long-term loans, which largely reflect mortgages, shrank for the fifth time this year. That suggests households repaid more debt than they took on. Comparable loans to companies, an indication of their willingness to invest, were less than half the amount recorded three years ago.

Government borrowing, meanwhile, has played an increasingly important role in supporting overall credit growth. Government bond sales added about 1 trillion yuan to the August total, although their contribution was slightly smaller than in July.

Central and local governments had used about 68% of their annual bond issuance quota through August, trailing the 76% pace recorded a year earlier. With authorities pledging to act faster in implementing budget plans, stronger expenditure and bond sales could potentially support credit growth in the rest of this year.

items.title: Finland Will Join France's Nuclear Deterrence Initiative
body: Finland said it will join France’s nuclear deterrence initiative intended to strengthen European defenses against an increasingly hostile Russia.

The move opens up the possibility of temporarily deploying France’s strategic air forces in the Nordic country, according to a statement from the Finnish Defense Ministry on Monday. Other possible forms of cooperation include dialog on the French nuclear doctrine and joint exercises where Finland observes or contributes conventional capabilities, the ministry said.
The move comes just months after a nuclear weapons ban was lifted in a major policy shift, with the government insisting Finland has no plans to host nuclear weapons.
Read More: Finland Lifts Nuclear Weapons Ban as Security Risks Grow
“This is a natural step as our close allies Norway, Sweden and Denmark have already joined the initiative,” Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen said.
Earlier this year, President Emmanuel Macron opened up France’s nuclear deterrence to European peers, with eight countries initially joining the initiative and Norway following at a later stage.
Explainer: Can French Nuclear Weapons Protect European Allies?

“No nuclear weapons will be stationed in Finland in peacetime,” President Alexander Stubb told media gathered at his residence in Helsinki. An important aspect of the cooperation is that Finland will gain a better understanding of how France intends to operate its nuclear deterrent, Stubb said.

European governments have been reassessing deterrence policies amid uncertainty over Russia’s intentions and questions about the long-term reliability of the US security guarantee. While President Donald Trump has not suggested the US would withdraw its nuclear protection, doubts about future US commitments have prompted some governments to bolster their own defenses.

“Europe must assume a greater role both in conventional defense and in nuclear burden sharing. Discussions on reinforcing nuclear deterrence and strengthening the security of Europe are essential for Finland’s defense,” Häkkänen said.

Asked whether the move will increase the potential for Russian hybrid attacks, Stubb said that “Russia has reacted negatively to the initiative, and we assume that will also be the case following this announcement.”

items.title: This Energy Shock Is Shredding Central Banks' Rates Playbook
body: How should central banks respond to supply shocks such as oil prices jumping in the face of the US-Israel war with Iran? Policymakers have long believed these to be inherently fleeting. Hiking interest rates to counteract them, by that logic, does more harm than good; it hurts economic growth and the labor market, when simply waiting out the shock would have sufficed.

Yet the world’s most important monetary policy authorities are abandoning this decades-old doctrine — a risky but necessary move in the face of a conflict that’s dragged on for six months. The Iran war has kept energy prices elevated for long enough that they’re now seeping into household and business psychology and may make too-high inflation chronic. Policymakers can thank President Donald Trump for putting them in this bind.

The look-through doctrine was always premised on the idea that inflation expectations were well-anchored — that consumers and businesses believed these disruptions would indeed be ephemeral, and that their central bankers could be counted on to bring inflation back to normal if needed. That faith has been shaken by a series of shocks that have blurred together as one extended inflation episode. The greater risk now is inaction, even if tighter policy spreads economic pain via higher borrowing costs and weaker growth.

Following last week’s European Central Bank rate increase, swaps and futures markets now imply high odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike on Wednesday; a Bank of Japan increase on Friday; and potential moves over the subsequent eight weeks from the Reserve Bank of Australia, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England.

The macroeconomic backdrops in these countries are nuanced and varied: The euro area and UK are most immediately susceptible to rising energy prices (they import most of their fuel, including the natural gas that powers households and industry). JapanJapan also imports an overwhelming share of energy but blunts immediate passthrough with regulated utility prices and subsidies., another big energy importer, is “normalizing” rates from an extremely low level. And the US, a large energy producer, has the strongest economy, rendering the tradeoffs of hiking a bit less painful.

A few of these banks might have increased rates anyway, but the energy shock has provided the impetus for acting now in a globally synchronized manner. Rate hikes have become increasingly inevitable as WTI crude futures returned to around $100 a barrel, US gasoline prices jumped to the highest since May and diesel — the workhorse that fuels everything from power generation and home heating to trucks, tractors and locomotives — rose above $6 a gallon for the first time ever.
So what happened to the doctrine of looking through shocks?

The argument used to be that supply disruptions tend to produce one-time price jumps that subsequently give way to reversions to the mean. A military conflict that drives oil higher, an avian flu outbreak that sends egg prices skyrocketing, a frost that kills off part of the coffee harvest — the commodity-price surges they produce on the way up are often matched by equally sizable collapses. They are one-time taxes on households, and they prompt less spending on other products, ultimately reducing inflation in other parts of the consumer basket. Price shocks can be painful to businesses and households, but their distress often manifests as slower growth, rather than persistent inflation.

The Fed, under Alan Greenspan, cut rates in the early 1990s as the Gulf War sent oil prices soaring and headline inflation higher. He was vindicated for doing so when inflation proved short-lived and the economy weakened. The same proved true when former Chair Ben Bernanke held rates steady in 2011 as oil spiked amid the Arab Spring.

I argued just last year that the look-through consensus was as strong and applicable as ever toward the end of a prior 12-day US-Israel military campaign against Iran. The Strait of Hormuz, the key shipping lane for global petroleum products, stayed open, WTI peaked around $75 a barrel and inflation was only modestly elevated. But I’ve changed my mind since. I am no longer confident that the public’s faith in inflation remaining contained can be counted on, even though the highly imperfect surveys of household inflation expectations aren’t any worse today than they were then.

First, this isn’t an isolated shock. During the Gulf War, oil spiked once around the August 1990 start of the conflict, and inflation cooled a few months later, as Saudi Arabia and others boosted output to replace the lost Iraqi and Kuwaiti supply. The Arab Spring-era Libya crisis was similarly short-lived in 2011. Today’s households, by contrast, have experienced the Covid-19 supply chain snarls; the Russian invasion of Ukraine; an artificial intelligence-induced jump in many computer-related prices; a year and a half of continuous ups-and-downs in tariff rates in the US; the 2025 Iran military campaign — and now the 2026 version that’s shuttered the Strait and lasted half a year. The latter three events were explicitly White House policy choices, and there’s little reason to believe that Trump will stop playing with matches anytime soon. That’s a lot harder to look through.

Second, the periods between the shocks have produced warm inflation as well. In the US and globally, inflation has been consistently above normal for five and a half years. That’s more than long enough for the public to lose faith in central bank commitments to their targets.

In 2023 and 2024, we could at least take heart in knowing that the trajectory of global inflation was mostly toward cooling. When that progress started to stall, there was a reasonable case to be made for patience. But in 2026, there’s no longer any excuse for taking a passive approach to a phenomenon that’s been with us for far too long. What we’ve been doing isn’t working, and people are starting to forget what it was like to live in an economy with stable prices.

When Trump returned to the presidency last year, the global disinflation story was still broadly encouraging, but also demonstrably fragile. If we had avoided policy missteps, there was a real chance that inflation might have returned to a semblance of the old normal. Unfortunately, the White House exhibited disregard for our uniquely brittle inflation psychology. The biggest risk today isn’t accidentally triggering an economic slowdown with over-eager monetary tightening; it’s in delaying action on the basis of an old doctrine that never contemplated the era of Donald Trump.

items.title: Mark Carney Seeks C$1 Trillion of Investment Amid US Trade Strains
body: For Mark Carney, walking away from trade talks with US President Donald Trump was politically popular. Now Canada’s leader has to contend with a more difficult economic reality.

The new 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods will hammer many small- and medium-sized businesses, including family firms, that up to this point have been largely sheltered from the trade war. Jobs data in the world’s 10th-biggest economy suggest important sectors like auto parts and forestry are already hurting.

That means Carney has an urgent task: Reshape the economy to account for a hostile US, harnessing the political goodwill at his back to push through measures that might otherwise lack broad support. The list includes pro-business tax and regulatory reforms, privatizing public assets like airports and spending billions in government money to get Canada’s natural resources to foreign markets faster.
To fund the transition, his plan hinges on convincing deep-pocketed investors that Canada is a place where they can find attractive returns.

A key step comes Monday and Tuesday in Toronto, when Carney’s brainchild, the first-ever Canada Investment Summit, will draw money managers collectively overseeing more than $70 trillion in assets. The prime minister, along with other top officials and business titans, will pitch the likes of Blackstone Inc., Singapore’s Temasek Holdings Pte and Apollo Global Management on putting their money into Canada.

“Canada is one of the most connected economies in the world. We have trade deals covering 1.5 billion consumers,” Carney said in an interview with Bloomberg News. “We also have been making some big changes over the course of the last year-and-a-half. Now’s the time to look at Canada afresh.”

Executives at global funds, as well as Canadian investors and pension plans, will peruse a prospectus featuring more than 160 projects in need of hundreds of billions of dollars of funding, spanning data centers, advanced manufacturing facilities, liquefied natural gas terminals, ports and dozens of mines.

“We have a super-cycle of investment opportunity that I just have not seen in my career,” Toronto-Dominion Bank Chief Executive Officer Raymond Chun said in an interview, adding he couldn’t recall another time a similar group of the world’s leading asset managers met to discuss investing in Canada.
Carney’s ambition is to use government money and private dollars to generate C$1 trillion ($720 billion) of investment over the next five years.
Read More: Carney Says US Deal Possible, Blow-Up Helped Clarify ‘Red Lines’
The prime minister acknowledges the challenge. “There are very few people who get up in the morning and think about Canada,” he has said.

To change that — at least for a few days this week — he’s tapping what may be one of the world’s most enviable Rolodexes, built after a career at Goldman Sachs Group Inc., then steering the central banks of Canada and the UK and chairing Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. (He was also chair of Bloomberg Inc.)
He entered politics just last year, harnessing anti-Trump sentiment to lead the Liberal Party to a surprise fourth straight election victory.

Carney inherited an economy with problems that went far beyond the country’s trade fight. Growth in per capita gross domestic product has lagged behind other major economies in recent years, with weak business investment and stubbornly low productivity gains. Some investors had also come to see Canada as an increasingly difficult and unpredictable place to put money, particularly after high-profile resource projects were delayed, rejected or abandoned.

Heather Exner-Pirot, director of natural resources at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, a think tank, said the country’s “investability reputation was severely harmed” during Justin Trudeau’s decade as prime minister from 2015 to 2025. She recalled New York investors derisively calling the Impact Assessment Act — a 2019 federal law governing reviews of major resource projects — the “Don’t Invest in Canada Act.”

Carney acknowledged the country has some structural economic problems. “We’ve been slow on moving on a series of areas with respect to regulatory approvals and other factors,” he said in the interview.

The government put in measures last year to speed up project approvals. There’s more to come, Carney said. “We’re going to double down on that strategy, you’ll see in the coming weeks, with additional measures that spread that across the economy.”
Carney now has the opportunity “to change some minds,” Exner-Pirot said. And recent foreign-investment data does show some green shoots.

The trade war and Trump’s threats to make Canada the 51st state have given Carney the political capital to address some of these longstanding investor bugbears by casting moves such as tax changes and faster project approvals as matters of national sovereignty. His government is pursuing a massive expansion in defense spending, and has created a separate office to streamline major projects.

Ahead of the summit, Carney’s office compiled investment opportunities. The resulting list includes a proposed crude-oil pipeline to Canada’s west coast, the Ksi Lisims LNG export facility in British Columbia and a C$14.5 billion data-center campus in Alberta.

Carney has invoked history to frame his push for new infrastructure as a spiritual sequel to the legacy of Canada’s first prime minister, John A. Macdonald, who held office for about 19 years until his death in 1891. In a public address earlier this week, Carney pointed to how the US put 50% tariffs on Canadian exports in 1890 as a prelude to possible annexation.
“Sound familiar?” the current prime minister quipped.
Macdonald “recognized the threat of an expansionist United States for what it was and raced to unite this land” economically with projects including an east-to-west railroad, Carney said.
“Now we’re developing around that line, north and south,” and “connecting with new partners in Asia and Europe,” he said.
The investment summit could be part of that.

“The event serves as a practical mechanism to reverse a decade of flat business investment,” John Aiken, the director of Canada research at Jefferies Financial Group Inc., said in a report. But it isn’t clear Canada can convert “ambition, capital availability, and policy support into executable projects that generate durable private-sector returns.”

Carney’s popularity is at near-record highs after suspending trade talks with the US in late August, with 60% approval, almost double his opposition rival. That may help rally public support behind some difficult and controversial projects, such as a new crude oil pipeline to the BC coast.

More than a third of the summit prospectus features minerals and mining projects. Troilus Mining Corp. has capital needs of $1.1 billion to develop a gold and copper project in Quebec. A nuclear-fuel services project described as “Canada’s first uranium refining and conversion facility in more than 40 years” is also seeking investors.
“We’ve got so much coordination and enthusiasm across the country,” said Greg McNab, co-chair for the mining practice at law firm Dentons. “It’s hard not to get swept up in it.”

The prime minister is also pursuing new and deeper relationships abroad. As soon as the investment summit wraps, he’s set to fly to France for an expected announcement about a closer trade and security alliance between Canada and the European Union.

Canada’s government now has a distinctively pro-business makeup. Carney installed allies from Goldman and Royal Bank of Canada in top posts and put former bankers and chief executives in charge of parts of Canada’s civil service.
He also appointed Dominic Barton, chair of global mining company Rio Tinto Plc and a former ambassador to China, as the chair of Invest in Canada, a body created to attract foreign direct investment.

The government is exploring allowing private investment in the country’s biggest airports and has discussed the idea with some of its large public pension funds, which manage trillions of dollars collectively. The prospect is already attracting opposition from labor groups, but Carney may have room to maneuver.

Relying on bureaucrats and officials to chart the country’s economic course brings its own challenges. Privately, some executives and investors say Canada’s bureaucracy is risk-averse and has little experience connecting Canadian companies with global investors.

Although Carney has moved to streamline project approvals, rolled back some Trudeau-era climate policies and even pushed for a new oil pipeline, energy executives remain wary, recalling rejected projects such as Enbridge Inc.’s northwest oil pipeline and TC Energy Corp. scrapping a C$15.7 billion pipeline to the Atlantic Coast. Canada could help bring investors off the sidelines by backing projects itself, according to TD’s deputy chief economist, Derek Burleton.

Carney and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne have repeatedly touted Canada’s room for fiscal flexibility, even as other developed nations have seen their bond markets hit in recent months amid worries about deficits.

That’s allowed the government to roll out C$7.5 billion in support for tariff-hit workers and businesses this month on top of billions in aid last year. Some hope it could also portend a more favorable tax code, with faster write-offs for capital spending and other investor-friendly measures.
But Carney’s government is already projecting C$242 billion in federal deficits over four years. Market jitters may keep any further expansion of borrowing in check, Burleton warned.
“The bond market vigilantes are starting to punish governments for running high deficits,” he said. “Canada has an advantage on this front, but we need to maintain it and if anything improve it.”

One challenge in getting big projects off the ground is a possible labor shortage. Immigration restrictions have resulted in Canada’s population growth falling to zero in the past year. Getting enough skilled workers to build ports, roads and complex energy facilities in remote and frigid parts of the world’s second-largest country won’t be an easy task.

Canada has plenty of factors working in its favor, but ultimately many of the projects being discussed will take a decade or more to come to fruition, even if all goes to plan. And one of the country’s economic realities will always remain its proximity to the US market. Severing those ties completely is unrealistic.
“There isn’t any easy button one can push, there’s no real switch,” Burleton said. “We would have done it by now.”

items.title: Developer Concord Pacific Buys Wind Farm, Plots Data Centers
body: Concord Pacific Developments Inc. acquired a field of fifty wind turbines from Potentia Renewables Inc. for several hundred million Canadian dollars, deepening the Canadian developer’s long-term bet on renewables, its CEO said, adding that he’s working on a move into data centers too.

The Golden South Wind Project is the largest active wind farm in western Canada’s prairie province of Saskatchewan. It has capacity of 210 megawatts, with 200 megawatts of that contracted — which it says is enough to supply 100,000 homes. It has a power-purchase agreement with the provincial utility Saskatchewan Power Corp.

“It’s an expanding sector, and it’s a good, reliable, steady investment,” Concord Pacific Chief Executive Officer Terry Hui said in an interview. He added that Canada’s federal government wants to grow the sector.
Vancouver-based Concord Pacific was founded in 1987. It’s one of Canada’s largest real estate developers and is behind some of the key projects that make up Vancouver’s skyline.

It branched into renewable energy about 15 years ago. The Saskatchewan deal almost doubles that arm of the company’s total installed capacity, to about 543 megawatts. It has plans for other projects in early stages of development which could generate several hundred megawatts more.
“There are a lot bigger plans than this,” Hui said, pointing to the Amisk Hydroelectric Project in northwest Alberta, currently in the planning stages.
Artificial intelligence is one factor, along with others like electric vehicles, that are likely to create “big increased demand” for power, and that “can be supported by renewables,” Hui said.
Concord Pacific is also working on building “a few” so-called powered shells — purpose-built facilities to house AI data centers — across Canada, Hui added.
These server farms would be “urban, low latency, smaller-scale” and under 50 megawatts. “It’s not hyper-scale,” he said.

items.title: Amundi Buys Two-Year Treasuries To Insure Against Growth Slowdown
body: Amundi SA, Europe’s largest asset manager, is looking for opportunities in global bond markets after the recent selloff, and is buying two-year US Treasuries to protect against the risk of economic growth slowing due to elevated oil prices.

The US two-year yield climbed above 4.50% last week for the first time since 2024 as traders ramped up bets on Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes. But rising bond yields and energy prices pose a risk to the so-far-resilient US economy, said Nicolas Dahan, a senior portfolio manager for global bonds and currencies at the $2.8 trillion Paris-based asset manager.
Should the Fed be forced to rethink its tightening path in the face of a slowing economy, two-year yields - the most sensitive to interest-rate changes - would likely fall.

“A growth slowdown due to higher oil prices is becoming a non-electable risk,” Dahan said in an interview Friday. “Above 4.50%, we think that the US two-year can become a hedge to that risk, and that’s why we are starting to buy it to reduce our short-front end on the US curve.”

Global bond markets have been hit as hostilities in the Middle East pushed Brent crude above $100 a barrel and high debt levels remained a concern. Germany’s 10-year yield touched its highest since 2009 after the European Central Bank raised interest rates for the second time since the war broke out in late February.

The 10-year Treasury yield, a benchmark for borrowing costs in the US and throughout the world, remains within a shouting distance below the psychologically important 5% level, which it has reached only once — and briefly — since 2007. The yield rose two basis points on Monday to 4.99% after climbing 19 basis points last week.
Read more: A 5% Treasury Yield Is Raising New Risks for Markets, Economy

Amundi had previously been short US, European and UK fixed income, looking instead to emerging markets with strong real interest rates and economic growth, Dahan said. But with developed-market yields at current levels, there may be opportunities buy, he said.
“We are slowly coming back to being long duration,” Dahan said. “We are coming back to developed markets slowly and steadily.”

The spike in yields affects borrowing costs for corporates and sovereigns, including US mortgage rates, a politically salient metric for US voters ahead of the midterm elections, which are already at their highest level in over a year.

That’s raised the stakes for Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh going into Wednesday’s policy meeting, with some investors believing the central bank is already behind the curve as inflation persists well above its target. But with the oil-supply shock, repricing of central bank policies and “capitulation on bond markets,” things could change quickly, Dahan said.

“As much as we stayed away from the core markets we now have an opportunity — the same type of opportunity we had a few years back where, within the hiking cycle, we saw many central banks pivot,” he said.

items.title: Indonesia's Prabowo Ousts Finance Chief Purbaya After Rocky Year
body: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto removed Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa just a year after his appointment, replacing a policymaker whose unorthodox approach and push for more spending had unsettled investors.

Prabowo appointed Deputy Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara as the new finance chief on Monday at the presidential palace in Jakarta. Nazara has served as deputy finance minister since 2019 and has been closely involved in fiscal policymaking and state budget management.

Indonesian stocks erased nearly all of a 2.6% decline, while the 10-year government bond yield was unchanged at 7.17%. The dollar-rupiah one-month non-deliverable forwards pared gains to 0.4% from as much as 0.6% earlier.
Nazara is taking charge of the finance ministry as it finalizes preparations for the 2027 state budget, which aims to support Prabowo’s priority programs without breaching the legal deficit limit.
The new finance chief assured investors of stability and prudence, saying he would keep the budget shortfall below 3% of gross domestic product, the legal ceiling.
“This is just a continuation, not a change,” Nazara said. “I have been serving in the Ministry of Finance, and we will continue to safeguard the state’s finances in an even better manner.”

Purbaya’s removal comes just days after he marked one year as finance minister, having been appointed last September to replace the long-serving Sri Mulyani Indrawati in the wake of deadly street protests. During his brief tenure, he rattled investors with plans to aggressively ramp up state spending and boost liquidity in the financial system in a bid to lift economic growth to a pace not seen since the 1990s.
Among Purbaya’s initiatives was the injection of 200 trillion rupiah of government cash reserves held at Bank Indonesia into state-owned banks to boost lending and economic activity.

That put his ministry at odds with monetary authorities. Former Bank Indonesia Governor Perry Warjiyo unexpectedly resigned in July as Purbaya pushed for more liquidity in the financial system while the central bank sought higher interest rates to support the rupiah.

The government has faced pressure to balance its push for faster economic growth with fiscal credibility, with investors especially focused on Indonesia’s budget deficit. It’s expected to hit 2.85% of GDP this year, just below the 3% legal limit.

“Former Finance Minister Purbaya’s measures delivered mixed results at best,” said Lavanya Venkateswaran, senior economist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. She said Nazara is seen as a credible and experienced technocrat who would be well aware of Indonesia’s fiscal challenges. “The shift signals a steady hand for overall policymaking.”
Henry Wibowo, a former JPMorgan Chase & Co. strategist who co-founded Alphagate Capital in Jakarta, said Nazara’s appointment would build greater confidence in prudent fiscal management.

“We expect the government to remain committed to maintaining fiscal discipline, including keeping the budget deficit below 3% of GDP,” Wibowo said. “This should help reassure investors about Indonesia’s fiscal credibility and provide greater policy certainty at a time when markets remain particularly sensitive to fiscal risks.”

items.title: S.Africa Refinery Closures Added $4.7 Billion to Oil-Import Bill
body: South Africa’s oil-import bill could have been 76 billion rand ($4.7 billion) lower if it had not closed a large part of its refinery capacity, according to the country’s central bank.

The spending could on average have been 6.1% less in the four years through 2024 if the cap to the import of refined petroleum products was at 25%, the Reserve Bank said in an economic note published last week. Refinery closures have cut petroleum-related manufacturing output by roughly 20% since 2019, displacing an estimated 5,400 direct and indirect jobs, it said.

South Africa’s refining capacity has halved over the past decade and imported refined products now supply more than half of domestic fuel demand, raising exposure to global price shocks and shipping disruptions, the Reserve Bank said. This dependence also increases South Africa’s vulnerability to rand volatility, it said.

The continent’s biggest economy only has two operational crude-refining facilities, Sasol Ltd.’s Natref facility and Astron Energy’s plant in Cape Town, with a combined total capacity to process about 208,000 barrels a day. The Central Energy fund said last week it intends to rebuild the Sapref refinery south of the port city of Durban, which was idled after 2022 floods in the KwaZulu-Natal province damaged the facility, targeting throughput of 400,000 barrels daily.
South Africa’s gasoline and diesel prices reached record levels earlier this year as the cost of oil surged due to the the war in Iran.
Business Day newspaper reporter on the Reserve Bank note earlier.

items.title: Alcon CEO Says US Drug Pricing Deal May Limit European Products
body: Alcon Inc. Chief Executive Officer David Endicott warned that the Trump administration’s push to link US drug prices to those in other countries abroad could result in some medicines not being launched in Europe.

Many innovative products are cheaper in other countries and the White House wants US prices to align with those. Some companies may choose not to sell in Europe rather than cut their prices in the huge American market.

The idea is that “different prices outside the US are going to be negotiated by the US,” Endicott said in an interview with Bloomberg Television Monday. “We’re trying to make sure we maintain access as broadly as we can, but obviously being responsible to shareholders.”

Alcon, a Swiss eye-care company that makes surgical equipment, contact lenses and medicines, was among nine additional pharmaceutical and biotech companies that reached drug-pricing agreements with the US at the end of August.
The agreement is aimed at ensuring Alcon’s medicines remain available to US patients as the administration seeks to tie US prices to those charged in other developed countries.

“Every market is going to develop its own reimbursement system, its own negotiation, and we do that around the world,” Endicott said. “We’ll continue to push around the world to figure out what that implication means as we negotiate prices as we always have.”

items.title: Ports Giant DP World Redraws Hormuz Logistics With Truck Bet
body: Supply Lines is a daily newsletter that tracks global trade. Sign up here.

Ports giant DP World is expanding its overland logistics network in a bet that shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — vital for its flagship container and industrial hub in the United Arab Emirates — won’t return to the status quo from before the US-Iran war.

The Dubai-based firm plans to grow its truck fleet by about 40% and add new land routes to diversify supply chains linking Europe, the US and Asia to the Persian Gulf, Chief Operating Officer for Freight Forwarding Europe Stephen Whittingham told Bloomberg in an interview.

“I think we’ll never get back to the original normal,” Whittingham said. “There’s always going to be a level of uncertainty that exists now around this this geography, and so I think having options is really where DP World has said we’re going to be able to mitigate risk.”

The comments underline how the Iran war’s shock to global supply chains is likely to outlast the conflict itself, as countries and companies alike seek to reduce their dependence on the highly contested waterway. The diversification drive also aligns with the UAE’s aim to cut its reliance on the strait to zero.
Read More: Hormuz Halt Rewires Trade to Turn Desert Roads Into Vital Links

Within days of Iran closing the strait, DP World launched a road service from western Europe to the Gulf through Turkey that currently handles as many as 50 trucks per week, Whittingham said. Most of the cargo demand is for automotive parts and everyday consumer products, he added.
As an example, a one-way trip from Amsterdam to Dubai via Turkey would be a 6,700 kilometer (4,160 mile) journey.
DP World also set up hybrid sea-and-road services for shipments from Asia and the US, also via Turkey.

The company now wants to grow its fleet of trucks to 1,000 from 700 currently that provide a “land bridge” within the region to ports outside the Persian Gulf like Fujairah in the UAE, Salalah in Oman and Jeddah in Saudi Arabia, he said.

DP World operates ports and terminals in 84 countries from China to South America, but had to briefly suspend operations at its Jebel Ali facility in the UAE due to debris from an intercepted Iranian attack.

Before the conflict, Jebel Ali was the busiest container port outside of Asia, ranking in the top 10 globally and serving mostly as a transshipment hub integrated with one of the world’s largest industrial free zones.
But Jebel Ali reportedly saw a nearly 60% drop in volumes during the first half of the year from a year earlier, according to Alphaliner data, pushing it down to 32nd biggest by volumes in the world.

On new routes, the next target is to bring cargo over land from Europe to Iraq then load it onto ships to cross the Gulf to the UAE. Talks with authorities in Baghdad for a “permanent service” are ongoing, Whittingham said.
All that diversification comes at a cost. Shipping goods from Europe to the Gulf via land is typically three to four times more expensive than sea, he said.
But he expects some customers to continue to use the service even once Hormuz re-opens.

“I don’t think it’s going to go away completely,” he said, adding that even now, customers often find pure truck services more reliable than multimodal ones amid disruptions to shipping from the Black Sea to the Middle East.
“If you needed a truck tomorrow, you could get a truck tomorrow.”
DP World is also investing in its ports network, most notably with plans announced in July to develop two new deepwater terminals on the UAE’s eastern coast – outside the strait.
Read More: DP World to Build UAE Container Gateway Outside of Hormuz
It’s also committed around $800 million to terminal upgrades at Jeddah in Saudi Arabia and Tartus on Syria’s Mediterranean coast, both of which would link to the trucking networks.
Funding for such projects received a boost last week when the company sold $1.6 billion in bonds.

“DP World’s strong liquidity provides a substantial buffer against prolonged Middle East disruption,” Bloomberg Intelligence Credit Analyst Sharon Chen wrote in a note on Thursday. The bond deal “demonstrates continued funding access, albeit at a sizable spread premium.”

items.summary_zh: 迪拜环球港务拟将卡车车队扩大约40%并新增陆路路线，以降低对霍尔木兹海峡的依赖，已开通经土耳其的欧亚陆运，每周最多50辆卡车。

items.title: China Passes Halfway Mark of US Soybean Pledge Ahead of Xi Visit
body: China has fulfilled more than half of its annual US soybean purchase pledge, offering a bright spot for trade between the world’s two largest economies ahead of President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington.

State-owned traders booked at least 1 million tons of US soybeans last week, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named as they’re not authorized to talk to the media. That has brought total purchases for the current season close to 13 million tons, the people said, more than half of the 25 million-ton annual target Washington says Beijing has committed to through 2028.

The target is part of a wider trade truce struck between the two sides last year. The deal helped drive a rebound in crop flows, which largely stalled at the start of US President Donald Trump’s latest term due to a blitz of tariffs between the countries.

Xi and Trump are preparing to meet in late September in the US for a closely watched trade summit, their second this year. China has also pledged to buy at least $17 billion of US agricultural products on top of the soybean purchases, with the figure prorated for 2026, the White House said in May.
The US Department of Agriculture last week reported more than 600,000 tons of soybean sales for delivery to China in the 2026-27 marketing year. No sales were reported Monday.
Soybean futures in Chicago rose as much as 1% on Monday, rebounding after steep losses last week.

The recent ramp-up in exports has helped bring soybean prices to the highest since 2023, giving American farmers a boost just ahead of harvest. Meanwhile, increased biofuel blending requirements in the US and elsewhere have also raised demand for domestic processing.

Continued purchases will be needed to sustain the rally, said Joe Davis, a director of commodity sales at Futures International LLC. Longer-term trade prospects also remain clouded as tensions between the countries flare over other issues, from competition over artificial intelligence to arm sales to Taiwan.
USDA data showed shipments of American soybeans accelerating to the most since April in the latest week, with China the top destination.
The exports are an “encouraging sign as we shift towards fulfilling the growing sales book for the fall period,” StoneX analyst Mike Castle said in a note.
Separately, in its September report on Friday, the USDA raised its soybean production and yield estimates, defying analysts’ expectations for cuts.

CHS Inc., the biggest farm cooperative, earlier on Monday announced plans to built a $700 million soy crushing plant near Evansville, Wisconsin, with construction expected to start this year and completion targeted for autumn 2028. The company said strong demand and a friendly policy environment “reinforce the need for additional soybean processing capacity in the US.”

items.summary_zh: 中国已采购近1300万吨美国大豆，超过年度目标2500万吨的一半，提振中美贸易与大豆价格。

items.title: Thai Billionaire Revives Vietnam Gas Projects in Overseas Push
body: Thailand’s largest private power producer Gulf Development Pcl is reviving plans for major gas-fired projects in Vietnam as billionaire Sarath Ratanavadi looks overseas for new sources of growth.

“We’re renewing plans for the large gas-fired power project in Vietnam after putting it on hold for some time,” founder and chief executive officer Sarath said in an interview on Monday. “Vietnam has strong potential, with rapid economic growth driving rising electricity demand.”
Gulf may pursue further investments in the country, he said at Gastech 2026, a major liquefied natural gas industry gathering, in Bangkok. He did not specify their size.

Vietnam’s push for at least 10% economic growth is intensifying pressure on its power grid as new factories, infrastructure projects and technology development lift electricity demand faster than new generation and transmission capacity can be added. Power blackouts in 2023 exposed the risks, when drought-hit hydropower and surging demand forced outages at factories in the north.

Gulf and the Vietnamese government in 2019 signed an agreement to study a 6,000-megawatt gas-fired plant and LNG terminal in Ninh Thuan province. The company already operates three renewable-energy projects there with combined capacity of 247 megawatts, according to the company’s website.
Sarath, Thailand’s richest person, was among a group of business leaders who met Vietnamese President To Lam during his visit to Bangkok in May.
Read More: Vietnam, Thailand Agree to Deepen Ties in To Lam’s First Visit

Gulf is looking at other areas for expansion as well. In Europe, it is exploring further investment in renewable energy projects, Sarath said, without giving details. The company is considering more spending on data centers as artificial intelligence and cloud computing increase electricity demand.

The Thai company has said it will invest up to 140 billion baht ($4.2 billion) through 2030, mostly in renewable energy. About a tenth is earmarked for its digital businesses, including cloud services and AI infrastructure.

Its first 25-megawatt data center has been fully operational since June, while two more facilities totaling as much as 138 megawatts of power demand are under development. Gulf aims to add as much as 2,000 megawatts of data-center capacity over five years and has partnerships with Microsoft Corp. and Singapore Telecommunications Ltd., as well as an agreement with Alphabet Inc.’s Google to explore business opportunities.
Read More: Thai Billionaire Sarath Deepens Bet on AI in Google Tie-Up
The company was formed in 2025 by combining Sarath’s interests across energy, telecommunications, ports and toll roads. It owns or operates power assets in the US, UK, Germany, Laos and Vietnam.
Sarath’s fortune has climbed $4.6 billion this year to $16.4 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

items.summary_zh: 泰国最大私营电力生产商Gulf计划重启越南大型燃气发电项目，以寻求海外增长。

items.title: OpenAI President Greg Brockman on Doing Business in the Wake of Hugging Face
body: Listen to Odd Lots on Apple PodcastsListen to Odd Lots on SpotifyWatch Odd Lots on YouTubeSubscribe to the newsletter

According to OpenAI President Greg Brockman, the models that escaped their sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face's servers had yet to go through alignment training. That they were able to break free of the testing environment was not a surprise to OpenAI, but what has happened since has forced them to rethink some things. Today, we talk to Brockman about what OpenAI has learned since the hacking incident and we discuss why he thinks the conversation around model development has to change. We also talk about how OpenAI collaborates and communicates with competitors like Anthropic, how he thinks models should be evaluating what counts as “good writing,” and, of course, we get his thoughts on how seriously we should be worried about the AI doomsday scenarios.

items.summary_zh: OpenAI总裁Brockman称，逃脱沙箱并入侵Hugging Face服务器的模型未经过对齐训练，此事迫使OpenAI重新思考。

items.title: ECB Won't Hesitate to Hike Further If Needed, Kazimir Says
body: The European Central Bank won’t hesitate to raise interest rates further if necessary, though it will take time to determine its next steps, according to Governing Council member Peter Kazimir.
“We will take each decision when it is needed, and we will not waver when the evidence calls for action,” Kazimir said Monday in an op-ed on the website of Slovakia’s central bank, which he heads.

Officials, however, will first need to assess whether indirect effects from the war-induced surge in energy costs are developing as expected and “whether demand and labor-market conditions have become strong enough to generate second-round effects,” he said.

The ECB raised its borrowing costs by a quarter-point to 2.5% last week, its second hike since the Iran war began, as another jump in oil prices fuels inflation. While the bank repeated that it isn’t pre-committing to future moves, upgraded inflation forecasts and signs of resilient euro-zone growth led markets to price further tightening. Traders are now betting on three more rate increases by October 2027.
Kazimir said Monday that markets understand “very well” how the ECB responds to incoming information, creating “valuable space for careful observation and judgment.”
“It allows us to act when necessary,” he said, stressing the ECB’s flexibility after last week’s move. “We should not confuse an open mind about the next decision with hesitation.”

Kazimir argued that inflation risks are “clearly tilted to the upside,” and while stronger-than-expected growth is contributing to that, the main source of dangers to prices continues to be energy. He added that he’s increasingly focused on natural gas and electricity.
“The longer elevated energy costs persist, the greater the risk that they become embedded in longer-term expectations, wages and prices,” he said.

Speaking in Vilnius, Kazimir’s Lithuanian counterpart Gediminas Simkus said that while December is maybe the natural time for a re-assessment of the euro-zone economy, energy prices must be looked at closely before next month’s meeting.

“As early as October, we’ll be able to evaluate the inflation outlook, whether it’s deteriorating or the situation is improving,” he told reporters. “I can’t rule out any specific meeting. We’ll make our decisions based on incoming data.”
Latvia’s Martins Kazaks, meanwhile, said the case for more tightening is building.​
“Interest rates may need to wade into restrictive territory,” he told Reuters, while stressing that the ECB can afford to move “stepwise” and “without rush.”
In an interview with Econostream, Greek central-bank Governor Yannis Stournaras said the ECB is acting now to avoid major tightening down the line.

“Timely and prudent monetary-policy intervention is intended to limit the risk of inflationary pressures becoming more widespread and permanent, while limiting the risk of more abrupt and painful interest-rate hikes being required later on,” he said.
