items.title: BioNTech Lung Cancer Drug Lifts Survival Versus Chemotherapy
body: BioNTech SE said its experimental drug gotistobart nearly doubled the median survival of patients with an aggressive form of lung cancer compared to chemotherapy.

Patients treated with gotistobart lived for a median 18.5 months, compared with 10 months for those given the standard-of-care chemotherapy, BioNTech said in a release on Monday. The updated results are from a late-stage study evaluating patients with metastatic squamous non-small cell lung cancer whose disease progressed on prior immunotherapy and chemotherapy.
Earlier data showed that gotistobart reduced the risk of death by 54% compared to chemotherapy, though median overall survival wasn’t reached at the time.
BioNTech American Depositary Receipts rose as much as 7.9% in pre-market trading on Monday.

“Current survival expectations with established therapies remain less than a year, and despite numerous development efforts, chemotherapy has remained the standard of care in this setting for more than a decade,” said Rama Balaraman, a principal investigator in the trial and medical oncologist.

If the survival benefit is confirmed in the next leg of the late-stage study, the drug could provide a chemotherapy-free option and “transform the standard of care” for this patient population, Balaraman added.

The results bolster BioNTech’s efforts to bring multiple cancer medicines to market by 2030 as sales of its Covid-19 vaccine decline. The German company is also undergoing a leadership transition, with co-founders Ugur Sahin and Özlem Türeci preparing to leave the company by the end of the year for a new venture. Guido Oelkers is set to succeed Sahin as the company’s chief executive officer by February at the latest.

The company suffered a setback last month when it abandoned a study for a personalized vaccine for colorectal cancer patients. Hopes for the mRNA treatment had been raised by the success of rival drugmakers Moderna Inc. and Merck & Co. for a treatment of the same class for melanoma.
Read: BioNTech, Roche Scrap Cancer Vaccine Trial in Blow to Field

For gotistobart, BioNTech is collaborating with US company OncoC4. The drug is designed to help the immune system attack cancer by removing cells that help tumors evade the body’s defences. BioNTech said the safety profile of the drug was “consistent with previously reported data and remained manageable.”

items.title: Chevron Seeks EU Clarity on Methane Before LNG Import Investment
body: Chevron Corp. is considering investing in European liquefied natural gas import capacity, but needs greater clarity on the bloc’s methane rules before making a long-term commitment, according to the head of its gas business.

The US oil major is interested in building out regasification capacity as part of an expansion of its pipeline-gas business in Europe, Freeman Shaheen, Chevron’s president for global gas, said in an interview last week. Such capacity would allow Chevron to deliver imported gas directly into the continent’s grid and reach downstream customers.
“We’re very interested in Europe,” Shaheen said. With regasification capacity — which turns LNG back into a gaseous state — “you can supply directly into the grid and help support that market.”
Europe’s reliance on LNG imports from the US and elsewhere has grown sharply ever since it lost most Russian pipeline deliveries during the 2022 energy crisis.

But according to Chevron, investing further in the infrastructure that supports such imports requires having greater clarity on Europe’s methane rules, Shaheen said. Under the European Union’s latest proposal, fossil-fuel imports will have to comply with monitoring, reporting and verification requirements aimed at reducing methane emissions, and by 2030, imports exceeding a certain methane-intensity threshold will face penalties.

Natural gas is primarily methane, and sometimes there are leaks or emissions during its production and transport. The potent greenhouse gas traps around 80 times more heat than CO2 in the atmosphere over a two-decade time span, and tackling methane is seen as key to curbing temperatures rises in the short-term.

The US government has warned that its output will head elsewhere if the bloc refuses to ease its rules, and industry associations have also called for a re-opening of the regulation. The debate is likely to grow louder before the end of the year.

“If you’re going to make long-term commitments on regas, you need to have better clarity around those regulatory issues as well,” Shaheen said. “For the right terms and the right regulatory environment, we’d be very interested in partnering with the right people.”

Chevron is more generally exploring how to expand its LNG business. Some opportunities the company is considering include monetizing its gas resources in the Eastern Mediterranean and Argentina, potentially with a floating LNG export plant, as well as looking at potentially more supply from the US, Shaheen said.

items.title: China Rejects AI 'Fearmongering' After Amodei Urges Slowdown
body: China criticized calls from leading US technology executives to put the brakes on artificial intelligence development and impose tighter curbs on Chinese model makers.

“Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve the interests of no one,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing in Beijing on Monday.

“The development of artificial intelligence bears on the common well-being of all humanity,” he added, in response to a question on calls to slow frontier models and claims a Chinese advantage in AI could “pose grave danger” to the world.

Over the weekend, Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei made a public call for companies to slow the pace at which they improve AI capabilities, which was backed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk. His 3,800-word essay pushed for democracies to maintain “as large as possible” lead in AI, tighter controls on advanced chip sales to China and a crackdown on using American models’ output to train competing systems, a practice known as distillation.
Read More: Are We Losing Control of AI? What’s Driving Fears

The dispute over frontier technology is intensifying days before officials from the US and China are set to hold AI discussions ahead of Donald Trump’s summit with Xi Jinping on Sept. 24. The spat suggests even shared concerns over cyberattacks, misinformation and the potential loss of control over advanced systems may not be enough to produce an agreement between the world’s biggest economies.

China worries the US could invoke safety or national security to justify broader restrictions, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Center for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.

“The boundary between AI safety and AI competition is becoming increasingly blurred,” added Sun, who has discussed AI with US counterparts. “If every safety question becomes interpreted through the lens of strategic competition, meaningful dialogue will be difficult.”

In the summit lead up, Communist Party officials have also aired their own concerns over the rapid development of AI. Over the weekend, China’s top spy Chen Yixin published one of his nation’s most detailed accounts of Beijing’s fears, with a focus on regime security. In the article, he stated misuse by adversaries could threaten China’s political and ideological security as well as critical infrastructure.
Read More: AI Bosses Risk Clash With Wall Street and Trump Over Safety

China’s cyberspace regulator on Monday released an updated AI safety governance framework to address emerging risks as the technology evolves. The framework warns AI is making cyberattacks more scalable and sophisticated, and calls for vigilance over whether the speed of technological development could exceed human expectations and control.

The Foreign Ministry’s response suggests Beijing, and the country’s AI industry, will continue to chart its own course. Unlike some of their American counterparts, China’s top AI executives have largely refrained from calling for brakes on AI development as a safeguard, while the government has promoted the technology as a driver of economic growth and national power.

Xi and his lieutenants have proclaimed Chinese AI at the forefront of the country’s economy, celebrating entrepreneurs including DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng and advances by companies such as Huawei Technologies Co. and Moonshot AI.

“When we try to accelerate u tell me to slow down? omg...,” Justin Lin, one of the key former architects of Alibaba’s Qwen model, posted on X. “U can do whatev u want. stop pretending u need any permissions.”

The breakneck pace of Chinese AI development shows up in near-weekly model releases and upgrades to — perhaps most visibly — the velocity of capital-raising. In private, AI entrepreneurs and engineers grouse more about the need to keep up and ideally overtake their rivals in model iteration, as well reaching the ultimate goal of artificial general intelligence or AGI, rather than dwell on the risks of AI going rogue. That over-arching drive stems from the fact that Chinese AI still lags the best from the West, despite a narrowing gap.

“Beijing views AI as a once‑in‑a‑lifetime opportunity to reshape the technological balance with Washington, and it is unlikely to slow down voluntarily,” said George Chen, a partner at The Asia Group. “If you are No. 2, you do not stop at No. 2.”
Read More: China Spy Chief Warns of AI Risks as Anthropic CEO Urges Brakes

In Amodei’s account, the risk goes beyond economic competition. He echoed Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s earlier statement that a Chinese lead in AI would pose a threat to the US and the world. China could use superior AI to gain a military advantage over democracies, including through autonomous or AI-enabled drones, he wrote.
Amodei also advocated for eventual cooperation with China on global pacing, but said any agreement would require “ironclad verifiability.”

The warnings reveal both common ground and a widening divide. US technology leaders and Chinese officials agree that increasingly powerful models require oversight. But they differ sharply over how those dangers should be defined and who should set the rules.

In his article, Chen called for greater research on advanced chips and a faster buildout of AI infrastructure, even as he urged tighter supervision. Neither his article, which was likely prepared before the latest safety calls, nor the Global Times commentary suggested China intends to moderate the pace of its own development.

US export controls remain a major constraint. Huawei and other Chinese companies are developing more powerful hardware, but restrictions on advanced chips complicate efforts by DeepSeek, Tencent Holdings Ltd. and other developers to assemble the large computing clusters needed to train and operate frontier models efficiently.

That makes questions of restraint especially contentious. Chinese officials may see calls to slow development as locking in an existing US advantage, while Washington is unlikely to accept limits without credible ways to verify China’s compliance.

“If the US is taking the initiative to seek cooperation with China on this matter, shouldn’t the US also show some willingness to accommodate China’s long-standing concerns regarding AI?” said Jiang Tianjiao, a research fellow at the Center for Global AI Innovative Governance and an associate professor at Fudan University.
— Lucille Liu, Colum Murphy, Luz Ding, Nectar Gan, Qianwei Zhang, Foster Wong

items.summary_zh: 中方批评美国科技高管呼吁放缓AI发展并限制中国模型，外交部称恐惧与对抗无益于全球AI治理。

items.title: Hugo Boss Chairman Sturm to Step Down Amid Frasers Pressure
body: Hugo Boss AG said Chairman Stephan Sturm will step down, as largest shareholder Frasers Group Plc seeks to beef up its board representation alongside its takeover bid for the German fashion house.
Sturm, who joined the supervisory board in 2025, will leave Oct. 15 following what Hugo Boss called “constructive discussions against the backdrop of the recent changes” in its shareholder structure.

After its takeover effort fell short of a majority stake, Frasers is pushing for greater influence over Boss. The UK company behind Sports Direct, Flannels and House of Fraser said this month it still intends to boost its holding beyond 50%.

Controlled by British billionaire Mike Ashley, Frasers said Monday Sturm’s departure follows talks on boosting its presence on the supervisory board, which Frasers Chief Executive Officer Michael Murray already joined last year. It said it will seek the appointment of Robert Palmer as an additional member of the body.
Shares in Frasers and Hugo Boss were little changed Monday in early trading in London and Frankfurt respectively.
Read More: Frasers Still Seeks Hugo Boss Majority After Bid Fell Short

Sturm’s exit may stoke investor fears over the board’s independence. Ingo Speich, head of sustainability and corporate governance at Deka Investment, said this month an independent chairman is “indispensable for maintaining credibility in the capital markets and safeguarding the rights of all shareholders.”

Frasers wants Murray to take over as CEO of the German firm, The Times newspaper has reported, citing people it didn’t identify. Current CEO Daniel Grieder is in the midst of a second turnaround plan since taking the helm in 2021.

While Hugo Boss has continued to describe the relationship with Frasers as “constructive,” the company ended its share buyback program early after Frasers said it wanted a majority stake — a move that removed a route by which Frasers could have increased its holding without buying additional shares.

items.title: ICBC, HSBC Among Major Lenders on $30 Billion ByteDance Loan
body: ByteDance Ltd., the developer of TikTok, has signed a $29.6 billion loan with more than two dozens lenders, including Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Ltd. and HSBC Holdings Plc, in one of Asia’s biggest dollar-denominated deals this year.

The three-year borrowing, which could be extended to as long as five years, attracted 28 banks, some of which committed via various branches or subsidiaries, according to a person familiar with the matter. The signing took place last week, according to the person, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.

The deal signals that support for the Chinese tech giant, which is on the forefront of developing artificial intelligence technology, is still strong, despite a tight interest margin. The loan size was a jump from the $20 billion ByteDance was originally seeking.

Chinese banks emerged as the biggest lender group, with 15 of them committing a combined $18.9 billion, or 64% of the upsized loan. ICBC agreed to fund $3 billion, followed by Bank of China Ltd.’s $2.5 billion and China Construction Bank’s $1.5 billion.
HSBC and two other foreign banks have committed $1.5 billion each.
ByteDance, HSBC, ICBC, BOC and CCB didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The financing came together just days before leaders of the world’s biggest artificial intelligence platforms, including OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman, Anthropic PBC CEO Dario Amodei and xAI Corp. co-founder Elon Musk, said it’s time to slow the development pace of their most advanced — and most lucrative — models, citing escalating risks of the technology.

Proceeds from ByteDance’s loan will be used for general corporate purposes, as it builds up its AI ambitions. ByteDance’s last loan deal was in 2024, when it raised $10.8 billion via about 20 lenders.

Its latest loan is Asia’s second-largest dollar-denominated borrowing this year, behind SoftBank Group Corp.’s $40 billion bridge loan signed in March. It offers an opening margin of 68 basis points over the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, which will adjust if it extends the tenor. As a comparison, SoftBank’s bridge loan would pay an initial margin of about 250 basis point over the same benchmark.

items.title: Burnham Urges 'Culture Shift' to Reward Risk Takers
body: Morning, I’m Louise Moon from Bloomberg UK’s breaking news team, bringing you up to speed on today’s top business stories.
Is the prime minister of vibes striking again?

In the latest exposition of his vision for Britain, Andy Burnham has said the country needs a “culture shift” to make it easier to start companies and reward risk-taking. He’s pledging to bring the model that helped boost growth rates in Manchester — where Burnham was mayor — to the rest of the country.

“It means ensuring ambition is rewarded, making it easier to start and grow a business, and giving people the confidence that if they have a great idea, they’ll get all the support they need to bring it to life,” said Burnham.
Great vibes, no doubt, but what action? The PM is hosting a roundtable with big business bosses today, including from HSBC, Rolls Royce, BT and Sainsbury’s, so stay tuned.

Of course, the context is next month’s budget. Executives from retailers to banks have warned Burnham and Chancellor John Healey against further tax rises to shore up public finances, so the PM will be wanting to quell those concerns.
What’s your take? Ping me on X, LinkedIn or drop me an email at lmoon13@bloomberg.net. Oh, and do subscribe to Bloomberg.com for unlimited access to trusted business journalism on the UK, and beyond.

Employment rates for Britain’s boomers are at a record high, as young workers struggle to get a job. The latest ONS figures show the numbers of Brits aged 65 and over in work topped 1.7 million, thanks partly to longer life expectancy and as rising costs of living convince people to stay in jobs.

The failure of AstraZeneca’s trial of its breast-cancer pill could cut several billion dollars from the drug’s potential sales, according to analysts. Bloomberg Intelligence estimates the treatment’s failure in a late-stage study could cut peak sales by up to $3.8 billion.

Plus, the Bank of England’s dovish majority will be tested this week thanks to upside price pressures from the Iran war. While the expectation is still for interest rates being held at 3.75%, traders have ramped up bets on a hike by the end of the year.
Here’s your daily snap analysis from Bloomberg UK’s Markets Today blog:
The week is kicking off with the two mega-sized, overarching market topics firmly ensconced at the fore: oil and AI.

Oil prices dominated the market action last week as Brent vaulted over $100 again, sending bond yields tumbling and stocks going in the same direction in the UK and Europe. This morning, crude is rising on a Saudi pipeline shutdown.

For the UK, this keeps inflationary concerns top of mind. The Bank of England’s latest decision is coming Thursday and this jump for both oil and gas, plus the forecast for food prices to keep rising, is likely to pepper the outlook.

AI, meanwhile, is grappling with an existential crisis. Anthropic and OpenAI have both said that development of the most advanced systems needs to be slowed to prevent AI from slipping beyond our control and inflicting catastrophe. Basically, you know, trying to avoid Terminator 2.

The cash being splashed on building out AI is currently the most prominent driving force in industrial spending and is contributing to the global economy. That’ll mean some pushback from various areas of financial markets and the political sphere. One would imagine then that this existential crisis will only grow.
— Sam Unsted
Check Bloomberg UK’s Markets Today blog for updates all day.
The latest labour market data is due tomorrow. Bloomberg Intelligence expects it to show further signs of softness, continuing the trends of payrolls and vacancies having fallen since the Iran war.

Behind Chris Rokos’s move to Athens is a wider Greek campaign to lure hedge funds, with the pitch of a safe, stable and predictable tax environment alongside balmy weather and good quality of life. What is the flat tax for foreign earners that Greece debuted in late 2019?
[Friday’s answer: According to the Bloomberg Billionaire Index, tech entrepreneurs Elon Musk, Larry Page, Jeff Bezos, Sergey Brin and Michael Dell are all in the top 10 world’s richest.]

items.title: Latvian Carrier Air Baltic Seeks Chapter 11 Restructuring
body: Air Baltic Corp AS filed for bankruptcy protection as the Latvian carrier battles to restructure its hefty debt burden and buckles under the weight of high fuel prices and travel disruptions.

The company initiated the process in New York and has received a €350 million ($404 million) debtor-in-possession financing commitment from a group of funds to support operations during Chapter 11 proceedings, according to a statement on Monday.

The filing ensures that “the company will have a strong balance sheet and also it can get rid of some of the less favorable contractual commitments that it currently has,” Air Baltic Chief Executive Officer Erno Hilden said in an interview Monday. “Ultimately, we will also see what the ownership structure is going to be.” The new financing pays a floating rate of interest which currently stands at around 12%.

The surprise move is a stark reversal for the nation’s flag carrier, which as recently as last year considered an initial public offering, touting its modern fleet and strong regional focus. But the company has struggled with its debt load in the wake of severe obstacles, including soaring fuel costs, engine issues, disruption from the war in Ukraine and a slow recovery from the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic.
A court hearing that could determine how the company distributes funds is expected in “coming days,” he added.

The conflict between the US and Iran that began at the end of February and the subsequent surge in fuel prices ultimately tipped Air Baltic’s finances into deep distress. Fuel costs typically make up more than a fifth of the airline’s operating expenses and prices rose around 109% at their peak from their January 2026 levels, according to court filings.

While many airlines hedge their fuel costs, in March Air Baltic sold all of its remaining hedges to generate around €5.7 million of emergency liquidity. That meant the airline was then entirely exposed to fluctuations in market prices and was unable to pass this cost increase onto consumers, the filing shows.

Last month, Air Baltic said it would downsize its all-Airbus SE fleet to 40 aircraft by 2031, compared with 100 under a previous plan. The company’s business strategy hasn’t changed, and the airline will continue rolling out SpaceX’s Starlink Wi-Fi, Hilden said.
“What comes to future commitments for new deliveries, that is something that will really be dealt with during the process,” he said.
The airline plays a critical role for transit in the region, handling more than half of all passengers in the Baltic country’s capital, about one-third in Estonia and 14% in Lithuania.
The financing was arranged by Strategic Value Partners and funded by Barclays, Hayfin Capital Management, Morgan Stanley, Oaktree Capital Management alongside SVP.

Last year, the Air Baltic board ousted former CEO Martin Gauss, who worked at the carrier for more than 13 years, eventually replacing him with Hilden, who previously handled Nordic airline SAS AB’s restructuring in 2022. SAS filed for Chapter 11 in 2022 and exited two years later.
Even before this year’s spike in fuel prices, Air Baltic said it would require a cash injection of €100 million to €150 million to finance operations through 2026 and during the 2027 winter season.

Air Baltic had been touting the possibility of an IPO to help address its cash needs since 2018, but those plans were repeatedly delayed by external and operational hurdles. Deutsche Lufthansa AG holds a 10% stake in Air Baltic after investing €14 million last year.
During the Chapter 11 process, “flights will operate as scheduled, tickets and reservations will remain valid, and customer service will continue as usual,” the airline said.

The announcement comes a day before holders of Air Baltic’s €380 million bond were due to meet to decide whether to allow a deal that would have helped stave off a process such as a Chapter 11. Two funds — Polus Capital Management and Klirmark Capital — had been offering to provide as much as €257 million of “interim financing” that would have allowed Air Baltic more time to agree a debt restructuring.
Read more: Air Baltic Puts Polus-Backed Financing Plan to Bondholder Vote

“Negotiations with bondholders were not progressing,” Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs wrote in a post on social media site X on Monday. “Several investors who had purchased the bonds on the exchange at approximately 70 percent of their face value were banking on the liquidation of airBaltic and the recovery of pledged assets rather than on the company’s restructuring.”

The decision to pick a Chapter 11 process and DIP financing over the offer being considered by bondholders reflected the company’s view it provided a better prospect of meeting its “urgent” liquidity needs, according to the filing.

items.title: Uniper to Sell Stake in Opal Gas Pipe to Meet EU Bailout Demands
body: Uniper SE agreed to sell its stake in Germany’s Opal gas pipeline to Ardian SAS-backed investor Hy24, fulfilling another of the European Union’s conditions attached to its state bailout.

Uniper will divest all of holding company Lubmin-Brandov Assets GmbH & Co., which owns 20% of the pipeline, the utility said Monday in a statement. The remaining 80% is held by state-owned Gascade Gastransport GmbH.

The disposal was a condition stipulated by the European Commission when it approved Berlin’s multibillion-euro rescue of the utility in 2022, at the height of Europe’s energy crisis. Uniper remains a cornerstone of Germany’s energy system as one of its largest gas importers and power-plant operators.

Under commitments made to the EU, Germany must reduce its stake in Uniper to about 25% by the end of 2028. The government this year launched a sale process and asked for non-binding offers by Sept. 21. An initial public offering remains an alternative route for Berlin to reduce its holding.
Read More: Germany Is Said to Seek Bids for Nationalized Energy Firm Uniper

Other disposals remain outstanding. Uniper’s sale of a majority interest in former Russian subsidiary Unipro is stalled pending Moscow’s approval, prompting the company to write down the stake by €2.6 billion ($3 billion). The sale of its helium business, another condition of the bailout, is expected to be completed this year.
Hy24 is a hydrogen investment joint venture owned by private equity firm Ardian and asset manager FiveT Hydrogen.

items.title: Novo Will Use Shorter Name to Boost Recognition in Obesity
body: Novo Nordisk A/S will shorten its name for day-to-day use to just Novo in a bid to become more recognizable in its obesity market war with Eli Lilly & Co.

The drugmaker is also tweaking its logo, shifting its trademark bull to look to the right, it said Monday. The change comes as Lilly also increasingly leans on a single-name identity, dropping the word “Eli” from its marketing materials. Like Lilly, Novo will retain its full name as a legal global company name.

Chief Executive Officer Mike Doustdar is pushing Novo to become leaner and more competitive as the Danish company tries to wrest back a larger share of the obesity market it pioneered from Lilly. The brand is “strategically important,” Doustdar said.

For Novo, stripping “Nordisk” from the everyday name removes a link to the company’s history. The drugmaker was founded as Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium in 1923, bringing the newly-discovered technology for producing insulin to Denmark. Former employees founded the rival Novo branch two years later, and the two merged in 1989.
Doustdar will present the new brand identity to employees tomorrow. Next week, he will face investors at the company’s annual capital markets day.

“A new name, logo, and slogan must be accompanied by a true strategic change,” Evan David Seigerman, an analyst at BMO Capital Markets, wrote in a note. Next week’s meeting “must bring substance and strategic direction to support a sustainable organization into the 2030s and beyond.”

items.title: Skills and Goals Bosses Are Aiming for by the End of 2026
body: Welcome to the CEO Diet, a monthly series in Bloomberg Businessweek in which executives from around the world tell us how they manage their time in and out of the office. Among the topics they’ve discussed: what they learned from their first job and advice they’ve ignored for better or worse; how they psych themselves up for big moments;  use AI to save time; and optimize their sleep routine.

Company leaders should have several obvious skills under their belt: decision-making, delegation, resilience and the ability to manage a successful feedback loop among them. But some CEOs and founders are choosing to master subjects and fields with less of an apparent tie to business. Think podcasting, cooking, learning to say no and teaching yourself to play a couple dozen Stevie Wonder songs on the guitar. Because a deadline always helps, we got 12 leaders in Europe and the US to tell us the talents they’re working to excel at in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Mia Drennan founded the UK-based GLAS (Global Loan Agency Services) with £6,000 ($8,120) in 2011. Now her company, which specializes in financial services such as the namesake loans and debt administration, has an annual revenue of £100 million. And she she has a new obsession. “I’m working on mastering the art of podcasting. I’m comfortable being interviewed, but I’ve always been fascinated by what happens on the other side of the microphone. In Q4 I’m learning what it takes to orchestrate a compelling conversation.” Drennan is getting ready to launch The Lonely Female Founder podcast; to support it, she’s been testing equipment and refining her vocal technique. She’s also been “studying how great hosts listen, respond and draw out a story.” It is, she says, “an entirely different world from my usual day-to-day in bonds and loans.”

In 2017, Eric Liu  launched the popular Asian food delivery service HungryPanda. At the time he was a computer science student at the University of Nottingham in England and dissatisfied with the quality of the Chinese food options on mainstream delivery apps. HungryPanda now operates in 80 cities in 10 countries with more than 10 million users. The skill Liu wants to master: candor. “Saying what I genuinely think, clearly and directly. As a CEO, you naturally become more careful with words.” He reasons, “people — whether they’re our colleagues, partners or users — increasingly value hearing directly from the person behind the title: what I believe, what I care about, and sometimes what I disagree with. I’d rather be clear and genuine than perfectly scripted.”

Job van der Voort’s perspective is multifaceted and global. As CEO of Remote, he oversees an international employment and payroll infrastructure company. This season he’s zeroed in on a specific skill, learning to snowboard. “I already booked a trip to Austria for this winter, so I have no choice but to master it,” he says. “I haven’t prepped at all — just booked the lift tickets, flights and hotel, and figured I’d deal with it in Austria. If I waited until I ‘felt ready,’ I’d still be waiting.” Van der Voort’s philosophy is straightforward. “You learn and get good at doing things by actually doing them, not by reading about them. I apply the same logic to AI. You get better at it by using it, not by waiting until you understand it perfectly first.”

“The skill I’m working on this quarter is cooking Ayurvedically, which for me means learning to eat for my constitution,” explains Raj Mehra, the CEO of Sage, a healthcare platform for seniors based in New York. Earlier this year, his company raised $65 million in Series C funding from  Goldman Sachs Group Inc.  Mahera elaborates, “I’m a Pitta, which is a polite way of saying I run hot and I like spicy food, both of which I’m supposed to do less of. My daughter just turned 1, so we’re starting to eat together now, and it feels like the right moment to dive deeper into a practice I love. There’s nothing to optimize here, either. You notice how you feel a few hours later and adjust.”

“I’m a longtime musician, and I play guitar in a soul and R&B jam every Monday in LA with some of the best musicians in the world, says Ari Bloom. As co-founder and CEO of A-Frame Brands, his day job is to work on private labels, often with high-profile collaborators like tennis star Naomi Osaka’s skincare line, Kinlo, and Dwayne Wade and Gabrielle Union’s baby care line, Proudly. “Every year,” Bloom continues, “I try to learn and perform the equivalent amount of new songs from that calendar year number.” This year, “I’m on the hook for 26 new songs. I’m about half way there, and focusing on Stevie Wonder’s catalogue right now.”

Before she became CEO of the home furnishings company Ruggable in early 2025, Nicole Otto spent 16 years working at Nike Inc.; she’s a veteran of pressure-filled scenarios. “I’m in the active pursuit of practicing gratitude in all situations, even the most difficult and trying.” She admits, “I’m not sure I’ll ever master the skill. But the pursuit keeps me grounded and focused on the positive and appreciative of the kindness, talent, creativity and friendships around me.” A follow-up skill set: mastering AI prompts.

Felix Van de Maele  co-founded Collibra in Belgium in 2008 as an academic research project focused on the business of data. It’s evolved into an AI control platform for major organizations; at its latest funding round in late 2021, it was valued at $5.25 billion. “I’m trying to master using Claude by voice during my commute.” He enumerates his priorities: “Can it brief me on customer updates, summarize the latest news, flag what my leadership team should be paying attention to or help me prepare for the day’s toughest meetings?” As someone who spends a lot of time thinking through strategy and difficult decisions, he says he’s “experimenting with using that time to have real conversations with AI instead of waiting until I’m at my desk. If I can turn drive time into productive thinking time, that’s a win.”

Konstantin Sidorov, founder and CEO of venture capital fund London Technology Club in the UK, has complementary goals for the next few months. “Maintaining my health and fitness is fundamental to performing at my best as a CEO, but I also want to use technology to help me achieve specific personal goals,” he says. The executive recently started using the wearable Whoop and has been happy with the training insights it’s provided. “In Q4 I would like to explore how AI could use this data to help me prepare for a future mountaineering expedition, from optimizing my training and recovery to personalizing my nutrition and supplementation. I am particularly interested in ketone esters and whether they could support endurance and performance at altitude.”

“In Q4, I’m working on saying no more,” says Kevin Gould.  He’s the founder and CEO of consumer brands holding company, Kombo Ventures; among its holdings is the beauty-focused Glamnetic which has generated $100 million in revenue. “Protecting my time and energy for the few things that actually move the needle. As the business scales, focus matters more than ever.” He’s prioritizing “high-leverage, high-reward activities over chasing every opportunity that looks good on paper. Shiny object syndrome is real, and trying to do too much at once can hurt a business more than it helps.”

Kolin Jones, founder and CEO of Amalfi Jets, an LA-based private jet charter company, is another executive focused on messaging. “One of the biggest skills I’d like to master in Q4 is authentic communication. I think it’s common for CEOs of growing businesses to get caught up in the numbers, growth trajectory and various KPIs”  or key performance indicators. “However,” he continues, it gets “hard to step away from the numbers. As projects get more complex and technical, communication to the team helps motivate and build them up. I’m working on that.”

June Haynes is CEO and co-founder of Jjuin, the home decor brand whose inaugural bricks and mortar branch opened in East Hampton, New York, in June. That launch has inspired her to become proficient in a couple new fields. “Two technical skillsets I’ve set my sights on are learning a robust inventory management system to manage my now omnichannel operation, and tapping into AI forecasting.” Haynes is tracking the difference between the top sellers online — vases and objects d’art — and in the store, which veer more toward fragrances and serving trays. “Mastering both these skills gives me the ability to not only track and identify customer shopping preferences and sell-through patterns but also predict demand that will guide both our product design and inventory selection for next year’s collections.”

items.title: Japan's Chubu Electric Halts Plans for Nuclear Restart
body: Chubu Electric Power Co. halted plans to restart an atomic power plant in central Japan after an independent committee ruled the company acted inappropriately when submitting earthquake-safety data.

Chubu manipulated parts of its seismic assessment in a way that played down some of the risks, the committee said in its report. The utility’s two most senior executives also stepped down on Monday after the committee made public the findings of a months-long investigation into proposals related to the Hamaoka plant.
President Kingo Hayashi and Chairman Satoru Katsuno announced their resignations at a news conference in the city of Nagoya.

The withdrawal of Chubu’s application to restart the No. 3 and No. 4 reactors at Hamaoka deals a fresh blow to Japan’s attempts to revitalize its atomic power sector, which is still recovering after the country shut all of its reactors in the wake of the 2011 Fukushima disaster.

“We will likely not see Hamaoka operational until the mid 2030s, not unless there is a radical restructuring of the asset itself or the operating company,” said Yuriy Humber, the founder of  Tokyo-based consulting firm Yuri Group. “For the country, it’s an additional blow in terms of securing the capacity needed to meet the 20% target.”
Japan aims to have nuclear power make up 20% of its electricity generation by 2040.

About half of Japan’s commercially available reactors have restarted since the disaster, with data centers driving increased electricity demand, but confidence in the sector remains fragile and some projects have run into trouble. Earlier this month, the country’s nuclear regulator rejected safety measures proposed by the owner of Hokkaido’s only facility.
Read More: Japan Aims to Replace Up to 14 Atomic Power Reactors by 2050s

Chubu Electric, which supplies power to several prefectures across central Japan, first disclosed possible misconduct to the regulator in January, saying it had established an independent panel of experts to probe the selection of seismic data – a key consideration in one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries.
That panel’s verdict, delivered publicly during a separate media briefing on Monday, confirmed that the company had acted inappropriately. Japanese broadcaster NHK first reported the news last week.

The issue “puts the Hamaoka nuclear plant to the back of the queue in terms of potential restarts,” said Llewelyn Hughes, director of the Institute for Climate, Energy and Disaster Solutions at the Australian National University. The plant already faced challenges, both technical and in terms of local consent, he added.
Chubu Electric has no other nuclear reactors in operation. Minoru Yasui will replace Hayashi as the company’s president, Chubu said in a statement.

items.title: Astra Breast Cancer Pill Miss May Trim Billions From Sales
body: AstraZeneca Plc’s breast-cancer pill trial failure could cut several billion dollars from the drug’s potential sales, according to analysts.

The drug called Etcamah failed to delay disease progression more than the standard treatment in a late-stage study of patients whose breast cancer has come back or spread but hadn’t yet received any treatment for their disease, the drugmaker said late Friday.
The shares rose as much as 1.6% in early London trading. They have fallen by about 14% since the start of the year.

The medicine, which is already approved in a narrower patient population with a specific cancer mutation, works as a hormone therapy to stop estrogen from attaching to cancer cells and helping them to grow.

The failure could reduce 2035 sales by between $2.6 billion and $3.8 billion, according to Bloomberg Intelligence’s John Murphy. Estimates from Trung Huynh at RBC Capital Markets put potential revenue from this indication at around $1 billion.

Still, expectations around success in this setting were lower after Roche Holding AG failed to show a benefit with its rival experimental drug giredestrant in a similar setting. The bigger test for Etcamah will be results from ongoing studies in a much larger patient population. Some analysts hadn’t included sales from this indication in their forecasts.

Long known for its expertise in developing blockbuster cancer medicines, Chief Executive Officer Pascal Soriot is now under pressure to prove the internal pipeline of new drugs can succeed. Astra also reported positive data over the weekend from two other medicines for lung cancer.

Rival GSK’s shares rose as much as 2.7% after it reported positive data in a mid-stage trial for Jideytro in non-small cell lung cancer. Its partner Hansoh Pharmaceutical Group Co. Ltd. also said a late stage trial of another medicine helped reduce the risk of death by 54% in Chinese patients with a type of small cell lung cancer.

items.title: Solar Industries Bids $1.4 Billion for South Africa's Omnia
body: Solar Industries India Ltd. agreed to acquire South African industrial-explosives and fertilizer firm Omnia Holdings Ltd. for 21.8 billion rand ($1.4 billion), seeking to expand in the continent’s mining and agriculture industries.

The Nagpur, India-based company offered 134.5 rand per share, a 14.3% premium to Friday’s closing price. Omnia surged as much as 7.5% on Monday and traded 4.2% higher at 9:20 a.m. in Johannesburg, giving it a market value of 19.8 billion rand.

For Solar Industries, led by billionaire Satyanarayan Nuwal, the acquisition will be its latest in South Africa, where it controls Problast BS Ltd. The purchase will help the Indian firm expand across southern Africa and get access to Omnia’s facilities in Canada, Brazil, Australia and Indonesia, Omnia Chief Executive Officer Seelan Gobalsamy said.
“The deal is about growth,” Gobalsamy said in an interview on Monday. “It’s about accelerating growth to put balance sheets together.”
Shares of Solar have surged more than 80% this year, valuing the firm at 2.02 trillion rupees ($21.1 billion).

Solar already has operations in Ghana, Nigeria, Tanzania and Zambia. Buying Johannesburg-based Omnia gives it access to South Africa, which is home to the world’s biggest platinum mines, is the continent’s biggest corn grower and the largest global exporter of citrus.
The Indian firm has “immense technology” such as drones and autonomous robotics that can assist Omnia in its agriculture and mining businesses, said Gobalsamy.

“We are accelerating our agri business in Australia to all parts of the world — that is a biologicals business focused on crop health,” said Gobalsamy. “We see this opportunity to grow that even faster. Solar has a very strong position in India that could help us,” he said.
Omnia’s earnings climbed 21% in the year through March, with operating profit roughly split between its mining and agricultural units.

items.title: Monte Paschi Vows to Keep Up Bids Even If Intesa Takes It Over
body: Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena SpA pledged to keep pursuing its twin offers for Banco BPM SpA and Banca Generali SpA even if it gets bought by Intesa Sanpaolo SpA.
The bids are “irrevocable” and not subject to Intesa’s takeover, Monte Paschi said in a statement Monday.
The lender also said its offer for Banco BPM showed an implied 3.4% premium at Sept. 11 prices and the one for Banca Generali had a 12.8% premium based on the same date.

Monte Paschi CEO Luigi Lovaglio in August announced separate bids for Banco BPM and Banca Generali. The move was widely seen as an effort to thwart a takeover offer from Intesa for the Siena-based lender.
To achieve the goals, Lovaglio would have to convince his shareholders that his strategy is better than Intesa’s proposal and then win over investors in the two targets as well.
The meeting to get approval from Monte Paschi’s investors is set for Oct. 29.
Read More: Paschi Offers to Buy BPM, Banca Generali for €34 Billion

Intesa offered in June to buy Monte Paschi in a deal that would strengthen its dominant position in the country, expand its wealth and investment banking operations through the addition of Mediobanca SpA and leave it with a large minority stake in Italy’s biggest insurer, Assicurazioni Generali SpA.

Intesa plans to start its offer in the fourth quarter, as soon as it obtains regulatory permissions. While Monte Paschi’s board hasn’t formally rejected the bid, it has questioned both the price and the plan to divest a substantial portion of its assets.

Monte Paschi estimates around €1.4 billion ($1.6 billion) pre-tax run-rate synergies per year from the Banco BPM deal, while targeting about €400 million pre-tax run-rate synergies per year for Banca Generali, it said in the document on Monday.

items.title: Data Center Firm Firmus Said to Seek $5 Billion in Australia IPO
body: Firmus Technologies Pty is looking to raise as much as $5 billion in an initial public offering in Australia, according to people familiar with the matter.

The data center provider is targeting a listing at the end of October, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is private. Deliberations are ongoing and details of the offering, including its size and timing, could change, the people said.
A representative for Firmus declined to comment.

The deal is shaping up to be as one of the largest-ever IPOs in Australia, on par with Medibank Pvt’s offering in 2014, which raised just a hair under $5 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That would be a welcome boost to the country’s primary market, where proceeds this year are just over $1 billion, after surpassing $2 billion each of the previous two years.

Firmus would be joining in a wave massive fundraising by firms along the artificial intelligence supply chain, which has boosted IPO markets from the US to Hong Kong and China. Other deals vying for investors the rest of the year include the mega listing of Claude chatbot maker Anthropic PBC and China’s Moonshot AI, which is looking to raise $5 billion in a Hong Kong IPO, people familiar with the matter have said.

The Australian firm has inked a number of contracts with major US technology firms in the lead-up to its listing, including an agreement to provide OpenAI with computing power out of two data center sites in Malaysia. It also got $2 billion in commitments from a group including Jane Street and Nvidia Corp. in August.
The AFR reported on the potential size of the offering earlier.

items.title: Asian Refiners Seek Saudi Updates After Oil Pipeline Closure
body: Asian oil refiners are waiting for clarity on cargoes due to be picked up at Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea port of Yanbu, after the kingdom was forced to close a vital pipeline that serves the terminal following drone attacks.

At least four processors hadn’t yet received any official communications after asking for details of the operation’s status, traders involved in the discussions said. Saudi marketing executives had also not responded to inquires about the extent of damage to the East-West pipeline, they said, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter.
Absent information on delays, two of the refiners expect to collect their cargoes on schedule, the traders said.
State-owned Saudi Aramco declined to comment.

Aramco announced on Friday that it had shut the pipeline — which runs from inland oil fields to the Red Sea — as a precautionary measure after the strikes from drones launched from Iraq. The infrastructure attacks mark an intensification of the Middle East war, at a time when Iran-backed Houthi militants have also targeted Saudi energy facilities and seized territory in Yemen.
Read More: Houthi-Saudi Clash Escalates as Rebels Push Into Key Strait

At least four empty oil tankers appear to be idling off Yanbu, according to ship-tracking data, all of which had been scheduled to load from the terminal last week or over the weekend. Other vessels may also be in the area, as many ships turn off their transponders when approaching the port, due to security concerns. Jamming and other scrambling practices can also make ship tracking less reliable.

The US-Iran war has curbed oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, making Yanbu and the East-West pipeline far more important to Riyadh. The kingdom shipped around 5 million barrels a day of oil from the port through much of the war, although flows dropped to around half that level from late July after the Houthis declared an embargo of Saudi ports and started attacking ships in the Red Sea.
The attack on the pipeline and the delays at Yanbu helped push up Brent crude by as much as 3.7% on Monday. The global benchmark is near the highest since May.

“The closure of the Saudi East–West Pipeline further reduces routing flexibility for Asian refiners at a time when several key oil transit routes are already under pressure,” said Sumit Ritolia, senior manager of modeling at analytics firm Kpler. “Diversification can reduce supply disruption risk, but it cannot fully offset the cost impact when several major oil routes are stressed at the same time.”

items.title: Stocks Decline After Call to Slow AI Development
body: Good morning. Stocks tumble on AI slowdown concerns, while oil jumps as woes deepen in the Middle East. And Sweden’s election is too close to call. Listen to the day’s top stories.

Asian stocks and US equity futures retreated after major AI companies called for a slowdown in the technology’s development. Shares of SoftBank, one of OpenAI’s biggest backers, slid more than 10% in Tokyo. Over the weekend, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei said the company would introduce additional safeguards and urged the broader industry to slow the development of its most advanced models. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backed the proposal, while also telling Fortune that his company won’t go public this year as it prioritizes safety. Read more about how the call for restraint from AI bosses puts them at odds with Wall Street and Donald Trump.

Oil advanced after Saudi Arabia shut a major crude pipeline following attacks, disrupting a route that’s been used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Iran war and deepening a global energy crunch. A planned meeting between Iran and several Gulf nations on creating a temporary shipping lane through Hormuz was also postponed, adding to uncertainty. Check out our Markets Today live blog for all the latest news and analysis relevant to UK assets.

Sweden’s election is shaping up to be the tightest in its history, with the outcome set to hinge on the complete counting in coming days. At the beginning of the night, exit polls indicated the center-left bloc was on course to reclaim power, but that lead evaporated within hours, leaving open the possibility that the center-right coalition could nudge ahead, as it did in 2022. This time, though, the long-shut-out far right would join a government for the first time.

Donald Trump defended his remarks calling for the unification of Ireland as “fairly routine,” standing by comments that have sparked controversy in Northern Ireland. “I’ve always loved the people of Ireland, and it just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland, and you have Ireland, and it would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is put them together,” Trump told reporters Sunday. Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin said some of the responses to Trump’s comments were “an overreaction” and that while he believes in Irish unity, he didn’t offer any timeline.

items.title: UK's Boomers Cling to Jobs as Young People Get Locked Out
body: In the early 2000s, Britain had as many as 10 young workers for every person over-65 with a job. Today there are just two, as older employees hang on for longer and first jobs are harder to come by.

The number of Britons aged 65 and over in work topped 1.7 million earlier this year, according to the latest Office for National Statistics figures. Longer life expectancy and better health are delaying retirement, while cost-of-living pressures have also convinced people from the baby-boomer generation to stay on the payroll a little longer.
Employment rates for the group — many of whom are beyond state pension age — are at a record high.

In an ideal world, this would create a workforce in which multiple generations freely exchange skills and experience. However, the UK is suffering from what the Bank of England calls a “low hire, low fire” labor market, keeping young people stuck on the outside.

Youth unemployment is close to its highest rate in more than a decade, officials figures show, while entry-level jobs have plunged. Young people are signing up for emergency degrees to delay their entry into an increasingly unwelcoming labor market.

Almost a million 16-24 year-olds are out of work or education entirely, a NEET crisis as it’s known in the UK. The country’s Labour government is trying to understand the problem but has been accused of driving up the cost of hiring young workers.
Read More: UK Youth Unemployment Czar Hints at Change in Minimum Wage

Weak growth and a volatile global backdrop are making employers wary of hiring. And with fewer jobs opening up, workers postponing retirement can have “a knock-on effect” on how many jobs are created for young people, according to Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation at Lancaster University.

The youth unemployment crisis is a priority for Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has expanded a program to subsidize minimum-wage jobs for young people, and announced plans to overhaul vocational paths into work.

Some of the left of the party want the government to go further to address what they see as generation unfairness. A recent report from the Institute for Public Policy Research, a Labour-leaning think tank, called on the government to direct taxes away from young workers and toward pensioners, by targeting property and other wealth.

While Britain’s overall employment rate has held relatively steady, only half of 16-24 year-olds are in work, down more than four points since 2022 — a drop similar in scale to the pandemic and the 2008 financial crisis, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies.

During the pandemic, the UK seemed to be facing a very different problem as a wave of the baby-boomer generation decided to retire early. Cost-of-living pressures have drawn some back in, however. Roughly one in six retirees have either returned to work or were considering it, according to a 2026 Standard Life survey.

“There might also be an element of older people topping up their income and working part-time in lower-skilled or lower-paid sectors, in jobs that might’ve gone to young people in the past,” said Bruna Skarica, chief UK economist at Morgan Stanley.

The bigger shift, however, is that people are staying in work for longer, helped by better health and the rise in flexible working since the pandemic, according to Alessandro De Arcangelis, senior research and policy analyst at Lewis Silkin.

UK firms are actively targeting older candidates and changing their benefits packages to retain workers approaching retirement, according to Natalie Hall, managing director at 55/Redefined, a firm helping companies attract older talent.

Veolia, an environmental-services company, has a dedicated UK careers page for over 50s, advertising flexible working arrangements and wellbeing support such as free physiotherapy. Insurer AXA offers training and re-skilling opportunities for over 50s, while advertiser Dentsu has launched an apprenticeship program aimed at the age group.

AI is also creating winners and losers along generational lines. The technology can help older employees work longer while rewarding experience, as bots take on tasks traditionally given to junior hires. Graduate roles as a share of vacancies have halved since 2022, according to Indeed.
“AI may very well enable you to extend your working life,” said Harrison from Lancaster University. “If you’re a young person, the threat may very well be more direct.”

“We have a number of clients who’ve actually approached us saying, ‘we just want to get rid of some junior staff and replace them with AIs’,” De Arcangelis added. “There is more pressure to rely on more senior workers.”

Remote work may be a factor, too. A Federal Reserve Bank of New York study attributed most of the rise in unemployment among young graduates to the work-from-home trend, suggesting firms are reluctant to hire juniors remotely because it makes training and development harder.

“As a millennial, I remember the old stereotype of saying ‘we are hiring for an entry-level position, but require five years’ experience’,” De Arcangelis added. “That sort of paradox has become even bigger.”

items.title: EU Chief Rejects Banks' Bid to Split Reform Package in Two
body: Maria Luis Albuquerque, the European Union’s financial services commissioner, has rejected demands by banks to split up a grand plan to boost the bloc’s financial system.

In an interview with Bloomberg TV, she said Europe was best served by using a single package to deliver reforms that cut red tape, reduce barriers on activities across national borders and ease some regulations.

“This is not for the sake of banks, this is for the sake of the EU economy,” she said. “If we really want to do something meaningful we need to look at this as a package because everything is connected.”

Leaders of 11 top banks in the EU, Switzerland and the UK last week called on the EU to prioritize “simplification” reforms in the short term and allow more time to discuss thorny issues like Europe’s 11-year-old proposal for mutualizing deposit insurance across the bloc.

Banks fear that wrangling over the deposit plan will jeopardize the entire package the EU promised to announce by the first quarter of next year. But Albuquerque countered that the landscape had changed “dramatically” since Europe’s last failed attempt to progress the idea back in 2022.
“I have never seen such a unanimous call for us to get closer together, work closer together, let’s face this as Europe rather than individual member states,” she said.

“Because this is not about the technical debate, this is about politics, pure politics. And politics is about what is happening around and inside Europe and that is where I see a bigger impetus than ever before.”

Solving the deposit insurance logjam will allow Europe to breakdown the national barriers that trap capital and liquidity in different states, easing the fragmentation that the European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, believes is holding back the bloc’s financial system.

The US, meanwhile, has been rapidly weakening regulation and supervision under President Donald Trump’s administration, while the UK has also enacted a series of reforms including reducing the normal level of capital banks must hold.

One of the most contentious aspects floated by the EU in July is revisiting a new global capital rule known as the output floor, which constrains banks from using models to reduce their capital requirements.
The ECB opposes the change. Albuquerque told Bloomberg there was an “ongoing dialogue” between supervisors and the commission on the measure, but she could not “prejudge” the outcome.

The EU has asked for submission to its banking proposals by September 17. Albuquerque said that she was “more than happy to take all the feedback”, but that their last round of outreach generated more than 10,000 pages of feedback so “I wonder what was left unsaid.”

items.title: Philippine Marcos' Cousin to be Transferred from Hospital to Regular Jail
body: The Philippines’ anti-graft court ordered on Monday the transfer of Martin Romualdez, the lawmaker-cousin of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. accused of plunder, from a hospital to a regular jail.

The Sandiganbayan court’s order came after the medical director of the University of the Philippines - Philippine General Hospital testified that Romualdez’s heart-attack risk is low and he doesn’t need continued hospital confinement.

Last week, the former house speaker was admitted at an upscale private hospital after the anti-graft court ordered his arrest for a plunder case connected to a multi-billion peso corruption scandal involving flood infrastructure projects. He has denied any wrongdoing.
Romualdez, who is scheduled for arraignment on Wednesday, has been seeking continued hospital stay citing health risks.
Read More: What’s Behind the Flood Graft Scandal in Philippines?: QuickTake

Marcos is under pressure to show that his move to expose the corruption scandal has led to better government spending and cases against those allegedly involved, including his cousin. The scandal has caused the economy to stumble into a deeper slowdown, as it paralyzed government spending and dampened consumer and business confidence.

items.title: OpenAI's Altman Voices Support for 'Pacing' AI Development
body: OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman on Sunday added his support to the idea of “pacing” AI development, so that cutting-edge models don’t outrun the ability of humans to maintain control.

Altman, echoing the language of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, said there’ll be a cost to this shift of focus to safety, but it’ll be worth it in order to maintain confidence that US companies are developing increasingly capable artificial intelligence responsibly.

“No amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring,” the OpenAI chief said in a post on X, emphasizing also that the idea of ensuring safety doesn’t mean halting progress. “When we talk about ‘pacing’, we do not mean ‘stopping’.”

The comments come shortly after Amodei and SpaceXAI boss Elon Musk, in a rare moment of unity, called for tapping the breaks on AI development. Altman earlier this month told OpenAI staff that the startup is open to slowing advances in frontier technology to better understand the risks, and he has also confirmed that the company won’t go public in 2026 while prioritizing safety-related concerns.
Read More: AI Bosses Risk Clash With Wall Street and Trump Over Safety

AI-related stocks in Asia fell on Monday. Major OpenAI investor SoftBank Group Corp.’s shares dropped 13% in Tokyo, while South Korea’s Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc. both shed more than 4% in Seoul.

In his Sunday post on X, Altman reiterated OpenAI’s support for a federal AI framework, and said that AI firms need Washington’s help with international coordination, amid widespread concerns that even if US AI firms slow down their development, Chinese rivals will not do so.

items.title: Australian Miner Seeks Cheaper Bond to Refinance Private Loan
body: Australian miner GM3 is gauging investor sentiment for a possible bond issue to refinance a $600 million private credit loan, adding to a list of borrowers turning to public debt markets to try to lower funding costs.

The company has met investors this month to pitch a potential bond deal, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. GM3 is seeking to sell the note at a mid-to-high single-digit yield, lower than the mid-teens rate on its private credit loan, the people said.
The size of the bond hasn’t been decided but could be as much as $600 million, they people said. Negotiations are still ongoing and a deal may not be reached, they added.
GM3 did not respond to a Bloomberg request to comment.

The potential refinancing reflects an option for borrowers to replace private credit with cheaper, longer-dated funding in public markets. Private loans typically cost more than comparable public debt, a premium borrowers often accept for faster execution and more flexible terms.

The move comes just over four months after Australian coal producer Whitehaven Coal Ltd. sold $900 million of global bonds to refinance a more expensive $1.1 billion private credit facility that helped fund its acquisition of the Daunia mine and Blackwater coal mines in Queensland.

GM3, formerly Illawarra Metallurgical Coal, was acquired from South32 in 2024 for $1.65 billion by a consortium of Indonesia’s Widjaja family-controlled Golden Energy and Resources Ltd. and Australian miner M Resources Ltd. The acquisition was backed by the $600 million loan provided by Deutsche Bank and private credit funds including Davidson Kempner Capital Management and Farallon Capital Management.
Some of the original lenders have since sold portions of their holdings in the secondary market, according to the people.
Golden Energy and Resources declined to comment, while M Resources did not respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Oman Calls for Alternative LNG Routes That Can Bypass Hormuz
body: Alternative routes are needed to allow flows of liquefied natural gas to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, Oman’s energy minister told a major gathering of gas producers and traders, as months of conflict in the Persian Gulf continue to disrupt shipments.

“Let’s identify alternative export options,” Salim Al-Aufi, Oman’s minister of energy and minerals, said at the Gastech conference in Bangkok on Monday. “Be it north or through Oman or through Yemen. Diversify your options to get the resources out of the area.”

The comments come as Adnoc Gas Plc considers a new LNG export facility outside Hormuz, a key conduit for a fifth of global supply of the super-chilled fuel in normal times. Oman currently operates one LNG export plant on the eastern side of the country that doesn’t depend on Hormuz.
The war in the region has exposed Gulf nations’ reliance on a single waterway for the bulk of exports, forcing them to come up with workarounds to keep their exports flowing and economies running.

items.title: Pepco Bets on Africa Supply Hubs as Global Shipping Lanes Fray
body: Warsaw-listed discount retailer Pepco Group NV plans to expand its manufacturing footprint into Africa to better navigate global supply chains that have been upended by geopolitical turmoil.

The escalation of war with Iran this year has further complicated global trade paths already shaken by Houthi threats in the southern Red Sea, which forced shipping lines to reroute vessels bound for Europe from Asia around the Cape of Good Hope. The diversion adds to transit times and has sent freight rates soaring, squeezing European retailers reliant on Asian sourcing.

While the disruptions have affected fast-fashion competitors dependent on rapid seasonal inventory turnover, Pepco argues that its strategy of sourcing goods with extended wait times has largely insulated it from the initial shock.

“Unpredictability is a new normal for the supply chains,” Javier Rubio Fueyo, Pepco’s global sourcing and supply chain director, said in an interview. “It is also a new normal for all the retail area.”

Currently, most of the toys, home accessories and clothing sold across the company’s 4,000 stores in around 18 European countries arrive via ocean freight from Asia, primarily routed around southern Africa. This reliance creates a long and complex supply chain, prompting the “value for money” retailer to explore new sourcing hubs, including in Africa, Fueyo said.

In the near term, Pepco is actively building resilience against prevailing volatility. To hedge against the turbulence, Pepco supplements its standard sea freight with a premium, fast shipment service from Far East to Europe. While more expensive, this option cuts delivery times by two to three weeks.

The retailer leaned heavily on this premium tier in August to bypass disruptions caused by typhoons in China, but expects to reduce its usage in September. Typically, standard freight accounts for 85% of regular shipments, while the premium tier makes up 10% to 15%, depending on market volatility. Air freight constitutes less than 1% of its total shipments.

To control costs, Pepco negotiates full-year rates for both shipment types once a year to avoid “crazy spot rates that we see on the market today,” according to Fueyo. The group is also testing artificial intelligence to better predict transit times.
It will take three to five years for the firm to fully diversify its supply chains, according to the director.

As part of its logistics overhaul, Pepco is preparing to open a distribution center near the Baltic Sea port city of Gdansk in Poland, capitalizing on the country’s balance of operational efficiency, proximity to its key stores and access to experienced talent.

The group is also accelerating its push into western Europe, planning to open at least 600 new stores across existing markets between its fiscal years 2027 and 2030. To support this growth, Pepco aims to have a new distribution center in Italy next year as the local market is “booming.”
Further east, Pepco plans to open its first store in Ukraine this October. Initial sales will be serviced by existing distribution centers in neighboring Poland, Romania and Hungary.
“When we reach a certain business volume and the country’s situation improves, we will think about having our own distribution resource there,” Fueyo said.

Pepco shares have surged 34% so far this year, giving it a market value of 23.2 billion zloty ($6.2 billion). The stock has slightly outperformed Warsaw’s WIG20 Index, which climbed 30% in the same period.

items.title: Skiing Aussies Drive New Zealand Tourist Arrivals to July Record
body: New Zealand tourist arrivals hit a record high for July, with overseas visitor numbers for the month finally exceeding pre-pandemic levels, aided by a surge in Australians cashing in on a favorable exchange rate.

Visitors from Australia totaled 134,900 in July, making up more than half of the 256,600 arrivals, according to Statistics New Zealand data released Monday in Wellington. July was the first month that overseas visitor arrivals have exceeded their pre-Covid level, compared with the same month in 2019.

Queenstown Airport, the air-travel hub for South Island ski destinations, reported international passenger numbers in July increased by 22% from a year earlier, according to data from Auckland Airport, which has a strategic alliance with its Queenstown counterpart. The southern airport can be used as a proxy for trans-Tasman travel as its only scheduled international commercial flights originate from Australia.

The influx of tourists came as Australia’s dollar surged in May to its strongest level against the kiwi in more than 13 years. The Aussie’s strength has extended into the third quarter, with A$1 buying about NZ$1.24 on Monday to give Australian tourists greater purchasing power.

New Zealand’s tourism industry, the nation’s largest export earner after dairy, has struggled to recover from strict Covid measures that shut the nation’s borders and hammered operators. The sector has become an important component of the government’s economic growth strategy and a rare bright spot ahead of November’s election.

By contrast, local consumer spending and investment have been subdued due to high fuel costs and uncertainty. Second quarter gross domestic product data on Thursday are forecast to show the economy all-but stagnated in the period.
Read more: Aussie Newlyweds, Rugby Fans Cash In on New Zealand Bargains
Tourism and Hospitality Minister Louise Upston said Monday’s data show that international tourism is continuing to build momentum.

“We’ve welcomed 3.69 million arrivals in the year to July – up 9% on the year prior,” she said in a statement. “These results are another positive step towards our goal of doubling the value of tourism exports by 2034, supporting businesses, jobs, and our local communities.”

Still, Infometrics economist Nick Brunsdon warned a sharp rebound in oil prices since July threatened the tourism recovery, with the effect most profound for long-haul flights from North America and Europe.
“The weak New Zealand dollar seems to keep attracting Australian tourists, which provides a helpful buffer,” he said.

items.title: Emerging Markets Slide as Oil, AI Concerns Sap Risk Appetite
body: Emerging-market assets fell at the start of a key week for global markets, as elevated oil prices and concerns over the pace of artificial-intelligence development weighed on currencies and stocks ahead of an expected Federal Reserve interest-rate hike — its first since 2023.

An MSCI Inc. index of developing-nation currencies ended the day 0.2% lower Monday, posting the longest run of declines in almost three months. The Chilean peso lagged in a basket of 22 exchange rates tracked by Bloomberg, slumping more than 1% against the dollar. In credit markets, the extra yield investors demand to own emerging-market sovereign bonds rather than Treasuries widened two basis points, JPMorgan Chase & Co. data show.

After core inflation came in hotter than expected in the US last week, markets are almost fully pricing in a 25-basis-point increase in borrowing costs by policymakers led by Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh on Wednesday. Still, Monday’s selloff eased as Brent crude pared some of its gains and 10-year US Treasury yields retreated after touching 5% for the first time since 2023.

“EMFX’s sensitivity to global risk sentiment and higher oil prices will most likely result in mild weakness over the coming days,” said Phoenix Kalen, global head of emerging-markets research at Societe Generale in London.
At the same time, she said, investors have become more selective in recent years, drawing clearer distinctions between currencies that are more or less vulnerable to global shocks.
Read More: Emerging Markets Can Weather Fed Risk After Oil Jump and War

Developing-nation equities also dropped for a third session. South Korea’s Kospi slid more than 3% after major AI firms called for a slowdown in the technology’s development, raising concerns about a sector that has been a key driver of this year’s rally.

“For markets, the key question is whether this is the first sign that the extraordinary AI investment cycle might eventually moderate,” Deutsche Bank strategists said in a note. “For now, that seems unlikely. The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.”

Brent crude rose toward $110 per barrel earlier in the day after Saudi Arabia closed its East-West pipeline, a key alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz for its oil exports, following multiple attacks. The pipeline will mostly be out of service for several weeks, the AP reported, citing regional officials.
Later, oil pared its gains after President Donald Trump said Ukraine and Russia have agreed not to hit each other’s energy targets.
Read More: Oil Surges as Saudi Pipeline Shutdown Brings Fresh Supply Risk

Traders are awaiting a string of central-bank decisions this week, starting with the Fed on Wednesday, followed by the Bank of England and Bank of Japan, for clues on the path for global interest rates as policymakers grapple with renewed inflation risks from higher oil prices.

items.title: Ligent Technologies Seeks $727 Million in Hong Kong IPO
body: AI computing networks maker Ligent Technologies Inc. is seeking to raise as much as HK$5.7 billion ($727 million) in a Hong Kong initial public offering, adding to a surge of listings this year tied to the global artificial intelligence buildout.

The Chinese company headquartered in San Jose, California is offering 172 million shares at HK$32.96 apiece, according to a filing to the Hong Kong stock exchange. Trading is expected to begin Sept. 22.
Citigroup Inc. and Citic Securities Co. are joint sponsors on the deal.

Hong Kong IPOs have raised $44 billion this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, driven by technology firms tapping equity markets to fund their AI ambitions. With brisk follow‑on offerings, the city is on track for its strongest fundraising since 2021. At the same time, investors have turned more cautious around AI stocks amid concerns over lofty valuations and excessive spending.
Read More: Z.AI’s Cash Burn Drives Alibaba-Like HK Fundraising Spree
Ligent Technologies offers optical‑communication and interconnect solutions, combining optical‑module and chip research and development with large‑scale production.

Cornerstone investors — which get guaranteed allocation in the deal in exchange for holding the stock for at least six months — signed up for about 47% of the base offering. They include Primavera Investment Fund, Greater Bay Area Homeland Investment Ltd. and CFTC Paragon SP, as well as chipmakers GigaDevice Semiconductor Inc. and a unit of Amlogic Shanghai Co.
Proceeds will be used for the research and development of new products and technologies, and expanding production capacity for optical transceivers and optical chips.

Ligent’s local rival Zhongji Innolight Co., which makes optical transceivers essential to the data center buildout, began trading in Hong Kong in July after raising $6.8 billion in the city’s largest listing in seven years. Innolight’s shares have gained 14% since Hong Kong debut.
